briefing.focus: UPDATED Jul 30. LINK.2.1 + L.A.B. Pistol 0 grip: zero built-in press, and film confirms the shaft sits DEAD VERTICAL at address, repeating to a third of a degree. That is the configuration this putter was designed to be presented in — so the setup below is built around it rather than around the old 2° grip rule. GET LOW, TRAIL FOOT back, hands even.

sections.t: THE HEADLINE — get low
sections.b: Your words, and they go at the top of the plan rather than the bottom of a setup list: bending over is the most massive thing, and getting low is where you feel most comfortable. That is the feel to remember when everything else has drifted. If you only carry one thought to the practice green, carry this one — not the press, not the rehearsals, not the pace word. Deep bend, stand close, eyes down.

sections.t: Why the bend is more than comfort
sections.b: Two real mechanisms sit under that feel. FIRST — the LINK.2.1 is Lie Angle Balanced, exactly like the DF3i was, and that balance is only true when the shaft is presented at the lie angle it was built for. Stand too tall or too far away and the toe drops, the shaft leaves its designed lie, and the zero-torque property you switched putters for quietly degrades. Posture is what delivers the technology — and that is just as true of the blade as it was of the mallet. It also makes the build spec non-negotiable: your DF3i was 34", set flat. Confirm the LINK is the same before you read anything into how it rolls. SECOND — more bend lets the arms hang freer and tilts the shoulders onto a STEEPER plane, and a steeper shoulder plane is what produces a straight-back-straight-through stroke. Standing tall flattens that plane and builds an arc into the stroke whether you want one or not. Your stroke is SBST on film. The deep bend is the posture that matches it.

sections.t: The setup
sections.b:
BEND OVER, stand close, eyes down through the strike. Ball off the LEFT BREAST. Weight stacked ON the ball — pressure over it, not on the trail foot. TRAIL FOOT a touch BACK — it creeps forward on its own and opens you. Rock the shoulders, no hands. Loose grip.

THE HANDS RULE HAS CHANGED. It used to read 'hands EVEN with the ball; the grip's built-in 2° supplies the lean.' That was a Press Pistol 2° rule and that grip went back with the DF3i. On the LINK.2.1, hands even with the ball produces a shaft that is dead VERTICAL — confirmed on face-on film Jul 30, repeating to a third of a degree across 59 frames. Vertical shaft means ZERO forward lean, which means you are now delivering the putter's FULL static loft instead of static-minus-two. Same address picture, completely different delivery.

sections.t: THE PRESS — settled from first principles
sections.b:
Start from what you are actually holding. The Pistol 0 is L.A.B.'s NEUTRAL grip — the zero in the name is zero built-in press. That is a deliberate design choice on a lie-angle-balanced putter: the whole premise is a head that squares itself when the shaft is presented at its designed lie and the hands stop interfering. A neutral grip is what lets that happen. Your film says the presentation is already right — lie at about 68° as built, shaft vertical, repeating to a third of a degree across 59 frames.

So the recommendation is: DO NOT add lean with your hands. Not because a press is dangerous — with a neutral grip it cannot push loft below zero the way it could on the old setup — but because this configuration is already delivering what it was engineered to deliver, and your address repeatability is the best number on your card. Adding a hand-made lean would replace a position that repeats to 0.3° with one that depends on feel, on the day, under pressure. That is a bad trade on any putter and a particularly bad one on a putter whose entire selling point is that it does not need your hands.

Keep a trigger if it helps you start the motion — a soft press moved with the body is fine. Its job is RHYTHM only. The single rule that matters is that it is IDENTICAL every putt, because a press that varies is a loft that varies is a pace that varies, and pace is the open fault.

sections.t: What this putter needs from the setup
sections.b:
A lie-angle-balanced putter makes one demand of you and it is not a stroke demand: present the shaft at the lie it was built for. Get that wrong — stand tall, reach for it — and the toe drops, the shaft leaves its designed lie, and the self-squaring property you bought degrades. That is why the deep bend matters mechanically here and not just for comfort, and the Jul 30 film says you are doing it: presentation measured around 68°, which is the window these are built in.

Everything else in this routine came from film of YOUR stroke — path, shoulder plane, stance line, trigger — so none of it is putter-specific and none of it changes. The two things that ARE this putter's business are the lie presentation above and your AIM PICTURE, because a narrow blade topline frames the target differently from a mallet and start line is the open fault. Re-check aim with a stick; leave the stroke alone.

sections.t: THE TRAIL FOOT — the alignment leak
sections.b: Self-reported Jul 29 and worth taking seriously: your right foot creeps UP — forward, toward the target line — and it drags the stance line open with it. Open the feet and the shoulders follow, so you end up aimed LEFT of where you think you are. The fix is exactly what you said: set that trail foot a touch further back than feels natural. Expect it to feel CLOSED, like you're aimed right. That feeling is the correction, not an error — you're recalibrating off an open baseline, so square will read as closed until it beds in. Trust the line you set, not the feel, for the first few sessions.

sections.t: Why it wrecks the takeaway specifically
sections.b: Because in an SBST stroke the shoulder line IS the track. There's no arc to absorb a misaligned setup — 'straight back' is straight back along whatever line your shoulders are on, so an open stance doesn't just aim you left, it points the whole stroke left. Then one of two things happens, and both are bad: you feel it immediately and manipulate the takeaway to save it, which puts the HANDS back in charge of a stroke built to have no hands in it — or you don't, and the ball starts left. That's why a stance error shows up as a takeaway problem. The takeaway is fine; it's obeying a line that's wrong.

sections.t: This is the miss the putter can't fix
sections.b: Your signature miss is LEFT on short putts — the through-line of the entire putter saga, and it showed up AGAIN on the course Jul 29 with a zero-torque putter in your hands. That is the most useful data point you've generated in weeks, because it rules the head out. A perfectly square face aimed at a target that's left of the hole produces precisely that miss, and no putter ever built will save you from it. Zero-torque guarantees the FACE stays square; it cannot guarantee the face is square TO THE RIGHT THING. Note the split that makes the case: your last two 10-ball blocks started 10/10 on line on the mat, and then you pulled it on grass. Stance creep is a course-and-pressure fault — mat reps are exactly where it wouldn't show. And one thing to redo with the new putter: you changed sight lines. A narrow blade topline frames the target differently from a wide mallet, so re-run the alignment-stick check in your first LINK session and don't assume your aim carried over.

sections.t: The check that costs nothing
sections.b: Lay a club or an alignment stick down the target line just outside the ball on the practice green and set up to it — your toes should run PARALLEL to it, not converging toward it. Ten seconds, and it recalibrates the feel. The structural safeguard is already in your routine: aim the FACE to the spot FIRST, then build the stance around it. Keep that order religiously. If you build the stance first, the face gets aimed to a crooked body; if you aim the face first and the stance then creeps, the mismatch shows up as discomfort — and discomfort you can feel is information you can act on.

sections.t: THE TRIGGER — settled: soft press, moved with the body
sections.b: Keep the soft press — a genuinely small one, made as the body starts to move. But understand that its JOB has changed. With the Press Pistol it was pure rhythm, because the grip was already supplying the lean and any extra was double-counting; that is why 'keep it tiny' was such a hard rule and why a held press was such a problem on Jul 29. With a neutral grip there is no lean coming from anywhere else, so a soft press is now the ONLY forward lean in the stroke rather than a surplus on top of it. The old warning relaxes accordingly: a small press can no longer stack loft off the bottom of the scale. It still wants to be soft and it still wants to move with the body — that is what makes it release instead of being held — but it is no longer a thing to be afraid of.

sections.t: The one rule — softness IS the safeguard
sections.b:
REWRITTEN Jul 30. The old rule existed because the press was adding lean on top of a grip that already had 2° built in, so a firm press pushed the effective loft below zero and the ball got driven into the turf. That arithmetic is gone. Starting from vertical, a soft press moves you toward the loft you used to deliver, not past it.

So the rule now is CONSISTENCY rather than smallness: same press, same size, every putt. A press that varies is a loft that varies, which is a PACE that varies — and pace is the fault with the least evidence against it. The two drift signals still apply: if it starts to feel FIRM, or like a POSITION you sit in rather than a motion you pass through, it has crept back toward a hold.

sections.t: If it creeps back into a hold
sections.b: The alternatives stay on the shelf rather than getting deleted, because you may want one later: THE FLOAT — lift the head a hair off the turf before takeaway; no hand action at all and it removes ground friction. THE WHOLE-PUTTER WAGGLE — small forward-and-back from the shoulders, wrists silent. THE LEAD-SHOULDER SETTLE — a soft downward press of the shoulder that already runs the stroke. THE TRAIL-KNEE KICK — furthest from the hands, and the same trigger your full-swing routine uses. Any of them will break inertia without the hands touching shaft lean. You don't need one right now.

sections.t: How to tell it's releasing
sections.b: One face-on clip settles it: compare shaft lean at ADDRESS with shaft lean at IMPACT. Close to equal means the soft press is passing through the way it should. Meaningfully more at impact means it's being carried in, whatever it felt like — and feel is exactly what got this wrong the first time. The free check needs no camera: a purely rolling ball makes one clean click, a ball driven down into the green adds a faint scuff a beat later. Listen for the scuff.

sections.t: Stop shopping
sections.b: Straight talk, because you called it yourself. That's three putters in a month, and the DF3i got 12 days and not one calibrated lag session before you convicted it. Twelve days isn't enough to convict a putter — it's enough to convict a power curve you never built. The swap itself is defensible: you kept zero-torque and you changed shape, which is a real preference and not a mistake. What isn't survivable is doing it again in two weeks. So the LINK gets a gate: two weeks, a 20-ball 5-footer test and a 30-foot lag ladder each week, and the verdict comes off those numbers rather than off an afternoon's feel. Keep the DF3i in the bullpen until then — don't sell it. And keep the stroke frozen while the head is the variable: the deep bend and the soft press were both decided from clear feel and both are mechanically sound. One variable at a time.

sections.t: Why beside the ball and not behind it
sections.b: Rehearsing in your true putting posture — same deep bend, same arm hang, same shoulder plane — means the stroke that FEELS like 30 feet is the stroke you actually make. Magnitude transfers one-to-one. Rehearsing from behind the ball reads the break better, but you're standing upright there, so the size you feel is only an approximation. Your open fault is pace magnitude, not reading: path ✓, face ✓, start lines 10/10 twice over. Optimise the thing that's broken.

sections.t: Keep the order of the two rehearsals
sections.b: Ball-look first (path and contact), hole-look second (pace). The last thing you feel is the thing you carry in — so the pace stroke must be the last one. If the hole stroke ever drifts to first, the pace feel gets overwritten by the contact feel and you're back to guessing distance. Finish rehearsal 2 WITH the soft press, at its real size: it's the one part of the stroke that never used to get a practice rep, which is how it drifted last time without you noticing.

sections.t: Two rules underneath it
sections.b: SAME BEAT COUNT, EVERY PUTT — a routine that varies in length is itself a pace variable, and the putts where you take an extra look are the ones that come up short. And a VERBAL BACKSTOP is worth testing: say the pace intention right before the press ('die it a foot past', 'back of the cup'). Feel decays, a word doesn't.

sections.t: Still to test — lags
sections.b: This is no longer a someday item — it's the top of the card. Yesterday's round was lags coming up SHORT and short putts running HOT, which is not two faults but one: a power curve you haven't learned, so you under-hit the long ones and over-hit the short ones. A new head resets that curve to zero, so the reps have to be deliberate. The block test, twice a week: 10 balls from 30 feet, and measure the SPREAD of stopping points plus how many finish short. Then the experiment worth running while you're there — past ~25 feet, keep your eyes ON THE HOLE through the actual stroke, not just the rehearsal. Feels absurd, works well; the ball isn't moving, you don't need to watch it. 10 eyes-on-ball vs 10 eyes-on-hole, same session, compare the spreads.

steps: Read it from BEHIND the ball — pick the line and a spot a few inches ahead of it
Step BESIDE the ball — BEND OVER, stand close, full putting posture
Rehearsal 1 — eyes on the BALL. Path and contact.
Rehearsal 2 — eyes on the HOLE. Pace. Finish it with the soft press.
Step in — set the FACE to the spot first, then build the stance around it (trail foot a touch BACK)
Spot → ball → soft press with the body → putt
rules: GET LOW — the deep bend is what presents the lie this putter needs
TRAIL FOOT back — square will feel closed
Hands EVEN — with a Pistol 0 that means zero lean and full loft, by design
No hand-made lean — the trigger is rhythm only, identical every putt

Wide open — this putter has no distance baseline at all. What the vertical address turns into at impact is still unmeasured. With the stock Pistol 0 and a 0° shaft-lean design there is no built-in lean to protect, so the question is simply repeatability. One slo-mo face-on set — white tape on the shaft, 240 fps, lights on — settles it.

briefing.course: The LINK.2.1 Sweet Spot — why the shaft lies to you
briefing.focus: Jul 30, researched. Your hunch — that the real centre of this head sits closer to the heel than the shaft position suggests — has a genuine mechanism behind it, and it lands squarely on the one fault still open. Here is what L.A.B. actually publish, where the evidence stops, and the two five-minute tests that settle it for YOUR head.

sections.t: Your instinct is sound — here is the mechanism
sections.b:
Lie Angle Balance has one requirement: the axis of the shaft has to point into the head's centre of gravity. That is geometrically awkward on a heel-shafted putter, because the shaft enters at the end of the head rather than the middle — which is exactly why the LINK uses an aluminium RISER HOSEL. L.A.B. build a different riser for every lie angle: flatter lies get a shorter riser, more upright lies a taller one, so the shaft axis keeps pointing at the same place inside the head no matter what lie you are fitted for. It also means they never have to bend the hosel or change its onset to hit a lie number.

And here is the part that answers your question directly. L.A.B.'s own explanation of the riser system says they needed the base of the shaft to point at a position on the head that is — their words — NOT NECESSARILY AT THE CENTRE OF GRAVITY the way it is with other companies' putters. So on this putter the shaft's position genuinely is a poor guide to where the mass sits. Reading the centre off the hosel, the way you would with a Newport, does not transfer here. That instinct was right.

sections.t: The trap they designed around — the 'graduated sweet spot'
sections.b:
There is a counterweight to the hunch, and it is worth knowing because it cuts the other way. If you chase lie-angle balance purely by shuffling MASS around inside the head — adding weight until the thing passes the balance test — what you end up with is something L.A.B. call a GRADUATED SWEET SPOT: a sweet spot that is neither centred nor symmetrically shaped. That is the failure mode of the weight-placement approach, and the Riser Hosel System exists precisely to avoid it, by solving the balance problem with hosel geometry instead of with lead.

So L.A.B.'s position is that the LINK's sweet spot is NOT skewed — that is the whole point of building it their way. Take that as a design claim rather than a measurement of your particular head, but take it seriously: it is a specific, falsifiable answer to exactly the thing you were suspicious of.

sections.t: Where the evidence stops
sections.b:
What I could not find anywhere is a published figure for where the LINK.2.1's sweet spot actually sits relative to the sight line — no manufacturer diagram, no independent measurement, and several of the deeper technical write-ups were unreachable. So the honest position is: the mechanism you suspected is real and acknowledged, the manufacturer claims their design neutralises it, and nobody has published the number.

Which is fine, because this is one of the rare equipment questions you can settle yourself in five minutes, on your own head, to a precision that matters. Do not take a direction on faith in either direction — measure it.

sections.t: TEST 1 — find the true sweet spot (2 minutes)
sections.b:
Hold the putter loosely by the very top of the grip, pinched between finger and thumb so the head hangs completely free. Take a pencil eraser, or the edge of a ball, and tap gently along the face, working from heel to toe in small steps.

Almost everywhere you tap, the head will twist in your fingers. At one spot it will not — it rebounds straight back with no rotation at all, and the sound goes noticeably more solid. That point is the centre of percussion, and it is the true sweet spot: the one place where an impact produces no twist. Mark it with a dot of tape or a marker, then look at where it sits relative to the sight line and relative to where you have been setting the ball. Run it three times before you believe it.

sections.t: TEST 2 — find where you ACTUALLY strike it (5 minutes)
sections.b:
This is the one that matters more. Impact tape, a dry-erase marker scribbled across the face, or a light dusting of foot spray — any of them will show the strike. Hit ten putts at your normal length and photograph the pattern.

The sweet spot's location only costs you anything if your STRIKE does not match it. A head with a heel-biased centre is harmless if you happen to strike it there; a perfectly centred one is expensive if you are consistently missing it. Test 1 without Test 2 tells you nothing actionable. Do both in the same session and compare the two marks.

sections.t: WHY THIS LANDS ON THE OPEN FAULT
sections.b:
This is not a curiosity — it is a live candidate for the exact miss you have measured. On a right-handed putter, a strike toward the HEEL rotates the face CLOSED through impact and starts the ball LEFT. A strike toward the toe opens it and starts the ball right. Your measured miss is 1.5° and 1.7° LEFT on two of three overhead putts.

Now add the head you chose. A narrow-body blade carries less MOI than a mallet, so for the same distance off centre it rotates MORE. The direction penalty for a miss-hit is amplified on this putter specifically — the same strike that a DF3i would have half-eaten shows up in your start line here.

And strike location has never been measured. Not once. Your path is straight, your stance is square, your early lift is gone and your address is vertical and repeatable — every other candidate has been filmed. This one costs a strip of tape and it is the cheapest untested explanation left, sitting alongside aim and face-at-impact.

sections.t: What each answer changes
sections.b:
IF THE STRIKE IS HEEL-BIASED: that is very likely a large part of the left start line, and the fix is setup, not stroke — shift the ball a fraction toward the toe, or change where you set the head behind the ball at address, then re-run the overhead start-line test and watch the number move. Do not touch the stroke.

IF THE STRIKE IS CENTRED: strike is cleared and eliminated, and the left start is aim or face-at-impact — which is where the overhead and slo-mo work goes next. Either way you have removed a variable from a list that is already short, which is the whole game now.

sections.t: Confirmed build specs, while we are here
sections.b:
The research turned up the stock LINK.2.1 numbers and they corroborate the film neatly. Stock spec is 69° LIE, 2° EFFECTIVE LOFT, 0° SHAFT LEAN, and — this is the one — a L.A.B. PISTOL 0 as the stock grip.

Two independent confirmations fall out of that. The face-on film measured your lie presentation at about 68° against a 69° spec, and measured the shaft dead vertical against a 0° shaft-lean spec. Both match. But the important one is the grip: the Pistol 0 is what this putter SHIPS with. The neutral, no-lean setup is not something that happened to you by accident when the Press Pistol went back with the DF3i — it is the configuration L.A.B. designed this head to be presented in. That is the strongest argument yet for leaving it alone and not manufacturing lean with your hands.

sections.b: Because in an SBST stroke the shoulder line IS the track. There's no arc to absorb a misaligned setup — 'straight back' is straight back along whatever line your shoulders are on, so an open stance doesn't just aim you left, it points the whole stroke left. Then one of two things happens, and both are bad: you feel it immediately and manipulate the takeaway to save it, which puts the HANDS back in charge of a stroke built to have no hands in it — or you don't, and the ball starts left. That's why a stance error shows up as a takeaway problem. The takeaway is fine; it's obeying a line that's wrong.
sections.k: In a straight stroke the shoulder line IS the track, so an open stance points the whole stroke left.

sections.t: This is the miss the putter can't fix
sections.b: Your signature miss is LEFT on short putts — the through-line of the entire putter saga, and it showed up AGAIN on the course Jul 29 with a zero-torque putter in your hands. That is the most useful data point you've generated in weeks, because it rules the head out. A perfectly square face aimed at a target that's left of the hole produces precisely that miss, and no putter ever built will save you from it. Zero-torque guarantees the FACE stays square; it cannot guarantee the face is square TO THE RIGHT THING. Note the split that makes the case: your last two 10-ball blocks started 10/10 on line on the mat, and then you pulled it on grass. Stance creep is a course-and-pressure fault — mat reps are exactly where it wouldn't show. And one thing to redo with the new putter: you changed sight lines. A narrow blade topline frames the target differently from a wide mallet, so re-run the alignment-stick check in your first LINK session and don't assume your aim carried over.
sections.k: A square face aimed at the wrong target still misses left, and no putter can fix that.

sections.t: The check that costs nothing
sections.b: Lay a club or an alignment stick down the target line just outside the ball on the practice green and set up to it — your toes should run PARALLEL to it, not converging toward it. Ten seconds, and it recalibrates the feel. The structural safeguard is already in your routine: aim the FACE to the spot FIRST, then build the stance around it. Keep that order religiously. If you build the stance first, the face gets aimed to a crooked body; if you aim the face first and the stance then creeps, the mismatch shows up as discomfort — and discomfort you can feel is information you can act on.
sections.k: Alignment stick on the practice green: toes parallel, not converging. Ten seconds, recalibrates the feel.

sections.t: THE TRIGGER — settled: soft press, moved with the body
sections.b: Keep the soft press — a genuinely small one, made as the body starts to move. But understand that its JOB has changed. With the Press Pistol it was pure rhythm, because the grip was already supplying the lean and any extra was double-counting; that is why 'keep it tiny' was such a hard rule and why a held press was such a problem on Jul 29. With a neutral grip there is no lean coming from anywhere else, so a soft press is now the ONLY forward lean in the stroke rather than a surplus on top of it. The old warning relaxes accordingly: a small press can no longer stack loft off the bottom of the scale. It still wants to be soft and it still wants to move with the body — that is what makes it release instead of being held — but it is no longer a thing to be afraid of.
sections.k: Keep the soft press, but its only job now is rhythm — it isn't supplying lean any more.

sections.t: The one rule — softness IS the safeguard
sections.b:
REWRITTEN Jul 30. The old rule existed because the press was adding lean on top of a grip that already had 2° built in, so a firm press pushed the effective loft below zero and the ball got driven into the turf. That arithmetic is gone. Starting from vertical, a soft press moves you toward the loft you used to deliver, not past it.

So the rule now is CONSISTENCY rather than smallness: same press, same size, every putt. A press that varies is a loft that varies, which is a PACE that varies — and pace is the fault with the least evidence against it. The two drift signals still apply: if it starts to feel FIRM, or like a POSITION you sit in rather than a motion you pass through, it has crept back toward a hold.
sections.k: The rule is consistency, not smallness: same press, same size, every putt.

sections.t: If it creeps back into a hold
sections.b: The alternatives stay on the shelf rather than getting deleted, because you may want one later: THE FLOAT — lift the head a hair off the turf before takeaway; no hand action at all and it removes ground friction. THE WHOLE-PUTTER WAGGLE — small forward-and-back from the shoulders, wrists silent. THE LEAD-SHOULDER SETTLE — a soft downward press of the shoulder that already runs the stroke. THE TRAIL-KNEE KICK — furthest from the hands, and the same trigger your full-swing routine uses. Any of them will break inertia without the hands touching shaft lean. You don't need one right now.
sections.k: Alternatives on the shelf if the press ever creeps back into a hold — float, waggle, shoulder settle, knee kick.

sections.t: How to tell it's releasing
sections.b: One face-on clip settles it: compare shaft lean at ADDRESS with shaft lean at IMPACT. Close to equal means the soft press is passing through the way it should. Meaningfully more at impact means it's being carried in, whatever it felt like — and feel is exactly what got this wrong the first time. The free check needs no camera: a purely rolling ball makes one clean click, a ball driven down into the green adds a faint scuff a beat later. Listen for the scuff.
sections.k: One face-on clip settles it: shaft lean at address versus at impact. No camera? Listen for the scuff.

sections.t: Stop shopping
sections.b: Straight talk, because you called it yourself. That's three putters in a month, and the DF3i got 12 days and not one calibrated lag session before you convicted it. Twelve days isn't enough to convict a putter — it's enough to convict a power curve you never built. The swap itself is defensible: you kept zero-torque and you changed shape, which is a real preference and not a mistake. What isn't survivable is doing it again in two weeks. So the LINK gets a gate: two weeks, a 20-ball 5-footer test and a 30-foot lag ladder each week, and the verdict comes off those numbers rather than off an afternoon's feel. Keep the DF3i in the bullpen until then — don't sell it. And keep the stroke frozen while the head is the variable: the deep bend and the soft press were both decided from clear feel and both are mechanically sound. One variable at a time.
sections.k: Three putters in a month. Change things on film evidence, not on an afternoon's feeling.

sections.t: Why beside the ball and not behind it
sections.b: Rehearsing in your true putting posture — same deep bend, same arm hang, same shoulder plane — means the stroke that FEELS like 30 feet is the stroke you actually make. Magnitude transfers one-to-one. Rehearsing from behind the ball reads the break better, but you're standing upright there, so the size you feel is only an approximation. Your open fault is pace magnitude, not reading: path ✓, face ✓, start lines 10/10 twice over. Optimise the thing that's broken.
sections.k: Rehearse in your real posture beside the ball, because magnitude transfers one-to-one that way.

sections.t: Keep the order of the two rehearsals
sections.b: Ball-look first (path and contact), hole-look second (pace). The last thing you feel is the thing you carry in — so the pace stroke must be the last one. If the hole stroke ever drifts to first, the pace feel gets overwritten by the contact feel and you're back to guessing distance. Finish rehearsal 2 WITH the soft press, at its real size: it's the one part of the stroke that never used to get a practice rep, which is how it drifted last time without you noticing.
sections.k: Ball-look first, hole-look second — the last thing you feel is what you carry in.

sections.t: Two rules underneath it
sections.b: SAME BEAT COUNT, EVERY PUTT — a routine that varies in length is itself a pace variable, and the putts where you take an extra look are the ones that come up short. And a VERBAL BACKSTOP is worth testing: say the pace intention right before the press ('die it a foot past', 'back of the cup'). Feel decays, a word doesn't.
sections.k: Same beat count every putt, and try saying the pace intention out loud before the press.

sections.t: Still to test — lags
sections.b: This is no longer a someday item — it's the top of the card. Yesterday's round was lags coming up SHORT and short putts running HOT, which is not two faults but one: a power curve you haven't learned, so you under-hit the long ones and over-hit the short ones. A new head resets that curve to zero, so the reps have to be deliberate. The block test, twice a week: 10 balls from 30 feet, and measure the SPREAD of stopping points plus how many finish short. Then the experiment worth running while you're there — past ~25 feet, keep your eyes ON THE HOLE through the actual stroke, not just the rehearsal. Feels absurd, works well; the ball isn't moving, you don't need to watch it. 10 eyes-on-ball vs 10 eyes-on-hole, same session, compare the spreads.
sections.k: Past 25 feet, test keeping your eyes ON THE HOLE through the stroke. Block test, not mid-round.

steps: Read it from BEHIND the ball — pick the line and a spot a few inches ahead of it
Step BESIDE the ball — BEND OVER, stand close, full putting posture
Rehearsal 1 — eyes on the BALL. Path and contact.
Rehearsal 2 — eyes on the HOLE. Pace. Finish it with the soft press.
Step in — set the FACE to the spot first, then build the stance around it (trail foot a touch BACK)
Spot → ball → soft press with the body → putt
rules: GET LOW — the deep bend is what presents the lie this putter needs
TRAIL FOOT back — square will feel closed
Hands EVEN — with a Pistol 0 that means zero lean and full loft, by design
No hand-made lean — the trigger is rhythm only, identical every putt
Aim the FACE first, then build the stance to it

briefing.course: The LINK.2.1 — Setup, Gate and Levers
briefing.focus: Jul 30. LINK.2.1 with a L.A.B. Pistol 0 grip — zero built-in press, confirmed by film showing a dead-vertical shaft at address. This plan is written from what THIS putter is and what it has actually measured, not from what the DF3i used to do. The DF3i appears only as history.

sections.t: First — this is a legal move
sections.b: You didn't undo the fix. The LINK.2.1 is Lie Angle Balanced — the same zero-torque technology as the DF3i, in L.A.B.'s narrow-body heel-shafted blade. The thing that made the Phantom 7.5 wrong for you (toe flow fighting a straight-back-straight-through stroke) is still absent from your bag. So this is a SHAPE change, not a technology change, and it doesn't reopen the mismatch that started this whole saga. Worth saying clearly because it looks like a step back toward a blade: it isn't. You've got the blade LOOK you've always been drawn to sitting on top of the mechanics your stroke actually needs. That's about the best outcome available here.
sections.k: You kept zero-torque and changed shape only — the SBST fix is intact, this isn't a step back.

sections.t: "It felt like a lot" is real information
sections.b: The DF3i is a wide, deep, high-MOI mallet. The LINK.2.1 is a narrow blade. That's a large change in what sits behind the ball, and it changes the sight line, the perceived weight, and how much the head seems to be asking for. Don't apologise for it or file it under 'being crazy' — putter feel drives COMMITMENT, and commitment is worth measurable strokes on short putts. A putter you trust at address is not a soft consideration. The mistake would be acting on feel and then never measuring; the feel itself is fine.
sections.k: Putter feel drives commitment, which is worth real strokes. Don't file it under being crazy.

sections.t: What a narrow blade asks of you
sections.b:
The LINK.2.1 is a narrow-body heel-shafted blade. Narrow blades carry less MOI than mallets do, which means an off-centre strike loses more ball speed than a centred one — the head twists a fraction more and hands back less energy. That is a property of the shape you chose, not a defect and not a comparison with anything: it means STRIKE QUALITY is a live variable for you in a way it is not for everyone.

The upside is the same property read the other way. A blade REPORTS the strike — you feel and hear centre versus heel, where a big forgiving head muffles the difference. That feedback is exactly what you need while you are building this putter's distance calibration from nothing, because it tells you whether a short lag was a small stroke or a bad hit. Use it: on every lag rep, note whether the miss was a pace error or a strike error. Those need different fixes and only you can tell them apart in the moment.
sections.k: A narrow blade punishes off-centre strikes harder — but it also reports them, which you need while calibrating.

sections.t: Yesterday's round, read properly
sections.b: Lags finishing SHORT and short putts BLOWN BY look like two contradictory faults. They're one. It's the signature of an uncalibrated power curve: with no reliable mapping from stroke size to distance, you default to too-small when the number is big and too-big when the number is small — and both errors show up in the same round. That is not a defect in the DF3i. It's what 12 days with any new head looks like when none of those days included a lag session. The lesson transfers directly: the LINK will have its own curve, and you'll get the same round again unless you build it deliberately.
sections.k: Short lags and hot short putts aren't two faults; they're one uncalibrated power curve.

sections.t: The pull left travels with you
sections.b: The left miss appeared again on the course while you were holding a zero-torque putter. That's the cleanest evidence yet that the head was never the cause. It points at the alignment leak already on your card: the trail foot creeping forward, opening the stance line, aiming you left — and in an SBST stroke the shoulder line IS the track, so an open stance doesn't just aim you left, it points the whole stroke left. Zero-torque protects the face; it can't protect where the face is pointing. Trail foot a touch back, aim the FACE to the spot before you build the stance, and expect square to feel closed for a few sessions.
sections.k: The left miss appeared with a zero-torque putter in hand, so the head was never the cause.

sections.t: The spec — one answered, one still open
sections.b:
Lie Angle Balanced is only TRUE at the length and lie the putter was built for — that is not marketing, it is the whole mechanism. Your DF3i was 34" and set flat. STILL CONFIRM the LINK's numbers match, because a putter a degree or two off your fitted lie has its headline technology partly switched off. Encouraging sign: face-on film Jul 30 measured the shaft presented at about 68° of lie, which is the window L.A.B. builds these in.

THE GRIP QUESTION IS ANSWERED, AND THE ANSWER MATTERS. The Press Pistol 2° went back with the DF3i. Your old setup rule — 'hands even with the ball, the grip's 2° supplies the lean' — no longer supplies anything, and film confirms it: the shaft now sits DEAD VERTICAL at address, repeating to a third of a degree. Vertical means zero forward lean, which means you are delivering the putter's FULL static loft where you used to deliver roughly static-minus-two. Same address picture, different launch. So the LINK's power curve is moving for TWO reasons at once — a lighter, lower-MOI head AND about two degrees more loft at impact — which is exactly why the lag ladder is the thing to run before drawing any conclusion about this putter.
sections.k: Grip question answered: no built-in lean. Lie still needs confirming at 34", set flat.

sections.t: Head weight is the adjustable variable — later
sections.b:
L.A.B. build static head weight to the putter's LENGTH, so your 34" LINK.2.1 left the shop at a specific spec. That number is the one real hardware lever left on this putter, and it is the right lever for distance control: more head weight makes a given distance need a shorter, more repeatable stroke, less makes it need a longer one with more feel on the short putts.

Do not touch it yet, and the reason is specific to where you are: you have no baseline on this putter at all. Changing weight now would mean tuning against a number you have never measured. Run the two weeks below first. If pace is still scattered with the address position and stroke held fixed, THEN ask L.A.B. what weight your build carries and what the alternatives are for the 2.1 at 34". Cheaper than a putter, and it is the change that actually addresses the symptom.
sections.k: Head weight is the one real hardware lever left — but not until you have a baseline to tune against.

sections.t: THE GATE — how the LINK gets judged
sections.b:
Two weeks, judged on the three things that have actually been MEASURED on this putter — not on a borrowed pass mark.

1. START LINE, the confirmed fault. Overhead film already measured it: 1.5° and 1.7° left on two of three putts, 0.2° on the third. So test it the way it was measured rather than by counting makes — phone overhead, five putts, compare the ball's roll to the mat's centre line. TARGET: median inside 0.5°, which is under half an inch at four feet. Counting made putts cannot see this; a 1.5° miss still drops from four feet and still misses from eight.

2. PACE, the fault with no evidence either way. 30-foot lag ladder, twice a week, ten balls. Log the SPREAD of stopping points and how many finish SHORT, and mark whether each miss was pace or strike. TARGET: no more than one in ten finishing short of the hole. Short is the one that is never in.

3. DELIVERY, now that the grip is neutral. One slo-mo face-on set with tape on the shaft to confirm what the vertical address turns into at impact. Early lift is already answered ✓.
sections.k: Two weeks, judged on start line measured overhead, lag-ladder spread, and one slo-mo set.

sections.t: The bar for changing anything again
sections.b:
The LINK.2.1 has now been measured more thoroughly in one day than anything else in the bag: path straight, tempo 2.0:1, stance square, early lift absent, lie presented as built, address shaft vertical and repeatable to a third of a degree. That is a lot of green. The one red is start line, and start line is a face-and-aim problem, which is the one thing no head change has ever fixed for you.

So the bar is simple and it is about this putter on its own terms: nothing else changes — not the head, not the grip, not the weight, not the stroke — until the two-week numbers exist. Keep the DF3i in the bullpen as an asset, not as a benchmark; it never got a calibrated baseline, so there is no number of its to beat. The LINK is being judged against the targets above, not against a memory.
sections.k: Nothing else changes until those numbers exist. The DF3i is an asset in the bullpen, not a benchmark.

rules: Confirm the build: 34", lie flat (presentation measured ~68° ✓)
Grip is a Pistol 0 — no built-in press, so hands even = zero lean, full loft
Start line is the fault: measure it OVERHEAD, target inside 0.5°
30-ft lag ladder twice a week — log spread, shorts, and pace-vs-strike
Nothing else changes for two weeks

briefing.course: The LINK.2.1 Sweet Spot — why the shaft lies to you
briefing.focus: Jul 30, researched. Your hunch — that the real centre of this head sits closer to the heel than the shaft position suggests — has a genuine mechanism behind it, and it lands squarely on the one fault still open. Here is what L.A.B. actually publish, where the evidence stops, and the two five-minute tests that settle it for YOUR head.

sections.t: Your instinct is sound — here is the mechanism
sections.b:
Lie Angle Balance has one requirement: the axis of the shaft has to point into the head's centre of gravity. That is geometrically awkward on a heel-shafted putter, because the shaft enters at the end of the head rather than the middle — which is exactly why the LINK uses an aluminium RISER HOSEL. L.A.B. build a different riser for every lie angle: flatter lies get a shorter riser, more upright lies a taller one, so the shaft axis keeps pointing at the same place inside the head no matter what lie you are fitted for. It also means they never have to bend the hosel or change its onset to hit a lie number.

And here is the part that answers your question directly. L.A.B.'s own explanation of the riser system says they needed the base of the shaft to point at a position on the head that is — their words — NOT NECESSARILY AT THE CENTRE OF GRAVITY the way it is with other companies' putters. So on this putter the shaft's position genuinely is a poor guide to where the mass sits. Reading the centre off the hosel, the way you would with a Newport, does not transfer here. That instinct was right.
sections.k: Right instinct: the riser hosel means the shaft genuinely isn't a pointer to the head's centre.

sections.t: The trap they designed around — the 'graduated sweet spot'
sections.b:
There is a counterweight to the hunch, and it is worth knowing because it cuts the other way. If you chase lie-angle balance purely by shuffling MASS around inside the head — adding weight until the thing passes the balance test — what you end up with is something L.A.B. call a GRADUATED SWEET SPOT: a sweet spot that is neither centred nor symmetrically shaped. That is the failure mode of the weight-placement approach, and the Riser Hosel System exists precisely to avoid it, by solving the balance problem with hosel geometry instead of with lead.

So L.A.B.'s position is that the LINK's sweet spot is NOT skewed — that is the whole point of building it their way. Take that as a design claim rather than a measurement of your particular head, but take it seriously: it is a specific, falsifiable answer to exactly the thing you were suspicious of.
sections.k: But chasing balance with weight is what skews a sweet spot, and the riser exists to avoid exactly that.

sections.t: Where the evidence stops
sections.b:
What I could not find anywhere is a published figure for where the LINK.2.1's sweet spot actually sits relative to the sight line — no manufacturer diagram, no independent measurement, and several of the deeper technical write-ups were unreachable. So the honest position is: the mechanism you suspected is real and acknowledged, the manufacturer claims their design neutralises it, and nobody has published the number.

Which is fine, because this is one of the rare equipment questions you can settle yourself in five minutes, on your own head, to a precision that matters. Do not take a direction on faith in either direction — measure it.
sections.k: Nobody publishes where the LINK's sweet spot actually sits — so measure it rather than assume it.

sections.t: TEST 1 — find the true sweet spot (2 minutes)
sections.b:
Hold the putter loosely by the very top of the grip, pinched between finger and thumb so the head hangs completely free. Take a pencil eraser, or the edge of a ball, and tap gently along the face, working from heel to toe in small steps.

Almost everywhere you tap, the head will twist in your fingers. At one spot it will not — it rebounds straight back with no rotation at all, and the sound goes noticeably more solid. That point is the centre of percussion, and it is the true sweet spot: the one place where an impact produces no twist. Mark it with a dot of tape or a marker, then look at where it sits relative to the sight line and relative to where you have been setting the ball. Run it three times before you believe it.
sections.k: Hang the putter, tap along the face, find the one spot that doesn't twist. Mark it.

sections.t: TEST 2 — find where you ACTUALLY strike it (5 minutes)
sections.b:
This is the one that matters more. Impact tape, a dry-erase marker scribbled across the face, or a light dusting of foot spray — any of them will show the strike. Hit ten putts at your normal length and photograph the pattern.

The sweet spot's location only costs you anything if your STRIKE does not match it. A head with a heel-biased centre is harmless if you happen to strike it there; a perfectly centred one is expensive if you are consistently missing it. Test 1 without Test 2 tells you nothing actionable. Do both in the same session and compare the two marks.
sections.k: Tape or spray the face and hit ten. Where you strike matters more than where the sweet spot is.

sections.t: WHY THIS LANDS ON THE OPEN FAULT
sections.b:
This is not a curiosity — it is a live candidate for the exact miss you have measured. On a right-handed putter, a strike toward the HEEL rotates the face CLOSED through impact and starts the ball LEFT. A strike toward the toe opens it and starts the ball right. Your measured miss is 1.5° and 1.7° LEFT on two of three overhead putts.

Now add the head you chose. A narrow-body blade carries less MOI than a mallet, so for the same distance off centre it rotates MORE. The direction penalty for a miss-hit is amplified on this putter specifically — the same strike that a DF3i would have half-eaten shows up in your start line here.

And strike location has never been measured. Not once. Your path is straight, your stance is square, your early lift is gone and your address is vertical and repeatable — every other candidate has been filmed. This one costs a strip of tape and it is the cheapest untested explanation left, sitting alongside aim and face-at-impact.
sections.k: A heel strike closes the face and starts the ball LEFT — your exact measured miss, never once checked.

sections.t: What each answer changes
sections.b:
IF THE STRIKE IS HEEL-BIASED: that is very likely a large part of the left start line, and the fix is setup, not stroke — shift the ball a fraction toward the toe, or change where you set the head behind the ball at address, then re-run the overhead start-line test and watch the number move. Do not touch the stroke.

IF THE STRIKE IS CENTRED: strike is cleared and eliminated, and the left start is aim or face-at-impact — which is where the overhead and slo-mo work goes next. Either way you have removed a variable from a list that is already short, which is the whole game now.
sections.k: Heel-biased strike is a setup fix; centred strike clears it and points at aim or face.

sections.t: Confirmed build specs, while we are here
sections.b:
The research turned up the stock LINK.2.1 numbers and they corroborate the film neatly. Stock spec is 69° LIE, 2° EFFECTIVE LOFT, 0° SHAFT LEAN, and — this is the one — a L.A.B. PISTOL 0 as the stock grip.

Two independent confirmations fall out of that. The face-on film measured your lie presentation at about 68° against a 69° spec, and measured the shaft dead vertical against a 0° shaft-lean spec. Both match. But the important one is the grip: the Pistol 0 is what this putter SHIPS with. The neutral, no-lean setup is not something that happened to you by accident when the Press Pistol went back with the DF3i — it is the configuration L.A.B. designed this head to be presented in. That is the strongest argument yet for leaving it alone and not manufacturing lean with your hands.
sections.k: Stock spec is 69° lie, 2° loft, 0° shaft lean, Pistol 0 grip — the film matches all of it.

steps: Hang the putter from the top of the grip, pinched loosely
Tap heel-to-toe with an eraser — find the spot with NO twist
Mark it, and note where it sits vs the sight line
Tape or spray the face, hit 10 putts, photograph the pattern
Compare the two marks — that gap is the thing that costs you
rules: The shaft is not a pointer to the centre — the riser breaks that link
Tap test finds the sweet spot; tape test finds where you hit it
HEEL strike closes the face and starts it LEFT — your exact miss
Narrow blade = less MOI = bigger penalty for the same miss-hit
Measure both before moving ball position

briefing.focus: You feel better with the weight BACK while the ball sits off the front foot — and you've heard the weight is supposed to be forward. Here's what that combination actually costs you, why it lands squarely on the one putting fault still open on your card, and how to settle it with evidence instead of dogma. UPDATED Jul 30 for the LINK.2.1: the blade has far less MOI than the DF3i mallet, so a wandering low point now costs real distance — everything below matters more, not less.

sections.t: What 'weight forward' is actually for
sections.b: It isn't a rule for its own sake. Lead-side pressure does one job: it PINS THE LOW POINT of the stroke. Where your weight sits decides where the arc bottoms out, and where the arc bottoms out decides how the LINK.2.1 meets the ball. That's the whole mechanism — everything below follows from it.
sections.k: Lead-side pressure does one job: it pins where the stroke bottoms out.

sections.t: The cost — loft, hop, skid, short
sections.b: Ball off the FRONT foot is correct. But weight back moves the bottom of the arc BEHIND the ball, so by the time the putter arrives the head is climbing hard and the shaft is leaning AWAY from the target. That adds loft you never asked for. The ball launches slightly, HOPS, SKIDS, and only then starts rolling. Every bit of that hop is energy that was supposed to become roll — so the putt arrives soft. Worse, the skid distance changes with green speed and grain, so your PACE stops being repeatable from green to green.
sections.k: Hanging back adds loft, and added loft makes the ball hop, skid and arrive short.

sections.t: Why this is your fault, specifically
sections.b: Read the card. Path: settled. Face: settled. Start line: 10/10 clean, twice over. The ONE thing still open is pace — lags coming up short at Hudson Hills, arrivals dying on the mat, and both genuine misses in the Stage-0 4-footer block DIED at the hole. Hop-and-skid off a back-weighted low point is the textbook cause of exactly that signature. Your stroke is no longer the problem. Your strike quality might be.
sections.k: Pace is your one open fault, which is exactly what a wandering low point damages.

sections.t: The second cost — the pull
sections.b: Sitting back drops the trail shoulder and slides your EYELINE behind the ball. Eyes behind the ball make you see the line right of where it truly is, and you square it up with a whisker of pull. Both real misses in the Stage-0 block settled on the PULL side — logged there as a lean, not proof. This belongs on that candidate-cause list.
sections.k: Weight back also leaves the face open through impact — a second route to a missed line.

sections.t: The third cost — the flip can come back
sections.b: Hanging back leaves the hands behind the ball through impact. Hands behind = the wrists want to save it = a flick. That flick was the engine of the old blow-through left miss. The LINK.2.1's zero-torque head has buried that miss on film — but hands-behind is the one setup that can wake it up.
sections.k: Hands behind the ball invite a wrist flick, the old engine of the blow-through miss.

sections.t: Before changing anything — feel isn't real
sections.b: Your own Golf Mind note states the principle: 'Hands over the ball: it FEELS like a forward press, but it isn't.' The same illusion runs in reverse. Weight that FEELS back is often pressure that's actually close to neutral — and neutral may be perfectly fine. Don't discard a setup you putt well from on the strength of a feel. FILM IT FACE-ON first. That single clip also closes the early-lift fault, the last open item from Session 8.
sections.k: Feel isn't evidence. Film it before you change anything, because comfort lies.

sections.t: What has to be true (the real checklist)
sections.b: Forget 'weight forward' as a slogan. Four things actually matter, and you can keep your comfort as long as they hold. (1) STERNUM at or just ahead of the ball. (2) HANDS level with or a touch ahead of the ball at impact — never behind it. (3) LOW POINT at or just behind the ball, so the LINK.2.1 is a HAIR ascending at contact — that slight upstroke is what produces true roll. (4) PRESSURE around 55/45 lead — enough to anchor the low point, not so much that you start steering. If your weight-back feel still delivers 1 through 3, keep it.
sections.k: Four things must be true: sternum over the ball, hands never behind, low point at or just behind it, 55/45 lead.

sections.t: One thing in your favor
sections.b: This section used to say the head would cover for you. On the LINK.2.1 it won't, and that's the honest update. The DF3i was a wide, heavy mallet — high MOI, self-squaring, happy to be swung rather than steered, and forgiving of a low point that wandered. The LINK.2.1 is a narrow blade: same zero-torque Lie Angle Balanced technology, so the FACE is still protected, but far less MOI, so a strike off the middle bleeds more distance than it used to. That doesn't change a single instruction above — it raises the stakes on all of them. Low point pinned at or just behind the ball, hands never behind it: on a mallet those were worth a little consistency, on a blade they're worth the difference between a lag that finishes and one that dies four feet short. The flip side is genuinely useful: a blade REPORTS a bad strike where a mallet muffles it, so this putter will tell you fast whether your low point is where you think it is. Listen to it.
sections.k: The blade won't cover for you the way the mallet did — but it will tell you the truth faster.

sections.t: Settle it with data
sections.b: A/B LAG LADDER — 30 feet, two blocks of 10. Block A: your current feel. Block B: the change you're testing, everything else identical. Mark where each ball STOPS and measure the spread. Tighter spread wins — that's the answer, not anyone's opinion. SOUND TEST: a purely rolling ball makes one clean click; a hopping ball adds a faint scuff a beat later — listen for the scuff. FACE-ON CLIP: check shaft lean at impact and where the head bottoms out relative to the ball. Note the weight question itself is already settled on the mat (ball off the left breast, weight stacked ON the ball) — this ladder is here as the measuring protocol for any future change, not an open question. One amendment as of Jul 30: the head changed, so the A/B is now the FIRST thing that gets run on the LINK.2.1 rather than a follow-up — you're building this putter's power curve from scratch anyway, and you may as well build it with the low point in the right place instead of calibrating around a fault.
sections.k: A/B it on the mat and let the stopping points decide, not the feel.

briefing.focus: A checkpoint map of WHERE the body goes — feet, knees, hips, spine, hands, head — from address to finish, so you can freeze each spot in a mirror or on video and match it. Built to answer 'where am I supposed to be?' — especially the hips (see the last two sections). RH references: LEAD = left, TRAIL = right.

sections.t: How to use this
sections.b: Don't try to hit all of these at once — that's paralysis. Pick ONE checkpoint per session, rehearse it slowly in a mirror (face-on) and on a down-the-line phone clip, then hit a few balls letting it happen. Positions are a map, not a swing thought for over the ball. Everything below is for a right-handed golfer: LEAD side = left, TRAIL side = right.
sections.k: One checkpoint per session, in a mirror — this is a map, not a swing thought.

sections.t: 1 · Address — the setup everything else depends on
sections.b: FEET: shoulder-width for irons (insides of the heels about under your armpits), a touch wider for driver. Flare the LEAD foot out ~20–30° — this pre-clears room for the hips to turn through later. WEIGHT: 50/50 for irons, balanced on the arches (not toes, not heels); driver slightly on the trail side (~55/45). KNEES: soft athletic flex, like the top of a light squat — not locked, not deep. HIPS: hinge from the hip SOCKETS, not the waist — push your butt back like you're closing a car door with it. Pelvis neutral, hips level, small natural arch in the low back. SPINE/CHEST: tilt forward from that hinge so your chest is over the balls of your feet, plus a slight trail-shoulder-lower tilt (natural, since the trail hand sits lower on the grip). ARMS/HANDS: let the arms hang straight down from the shoulders — hands roughly under your chin, over your shoelaces. Irons: slight shaft lean, hands over the lead thigh. Driver: hands level with the ball. HEAD: steady, eyes down, chin UP off your chest so the lead shoulder can turn under it. BALL: driver off the lead heel; irons center to just right of center (your Golf Mind note).
sections.k: Feet shoulder-width, lead foot flared 20–30°, weight on the arches, chin off the chest.

sections.t: 2 · Takeaway — halfway back (club parallel to the ground)
sections.b: Move it back in ONE PIECE — hands, arms and chest turn together, no early wrist roll. FEET/KNEES: quiet; weight just starting to press into the trail heel. HIPS: barely rotating — the TRAIL hip is turning BEHIND you, not sliding out over the trail foot (that slide is a sway). CHECKPOINT: shaft parallel to the target line, toe pointing up, hands over the trail thigh, lead arm straight and still across the chest.
sections.k: One-piece takeaway: the trail hip turns BEHIND you, it doesn't slide out over the foot.

sections.t: 3 · Top of the backswing
sections.b: FEET: pressure loaded into the trail heel and instep; lead heel can stay down or lift slightly — either is fine. KNEES: the TRAIL knee HOLDS its address flex — if it straightens, you've swayed/stood up. HIPS: turned ~45° so your belt buckle points right of the ball, and you feel LOADED into the trail glute — like you're sitting into that right hip. Trail hip should still be inside the trail foot (outside it = sway). SPINE: same tilt you set at address, unchanged. SHOULDERS: turned ~90°, lead shoulder under the chin, upper back to the target — shoulders turn about twice as much as the hips (that gap is your coil). ARMS/HANDS: lead arm comfortably straight; TRAIL ELBOW points more DOWN at the ground and stays IN FRONT of the trail-hip seam (your working feel); shaft points at / parallel to the target line — not laid off across it. HEAD: still behind the ball, quiet.
sections.k: Trail knee holds its flex and hips turn ~45° — if the knee straightens, you've swayed.

sections.t: 4 · Transition — how the downswing STARTS (your problem spot)
sections.b: The ORDER is the whole game, and it runs ground-up WHILE the club is still finishing the backswing. (1) FEET/PRESSURE FIRST: press down into the LEAD foot — feel pressure move to the lead heel/instep. (2) HIPS SECOND: the LEAD hip then CLEARS — it rotates open (turns left) and back behind you and UP — while (3) the arms and club simply DROP into the slot (this is exactly your one-arm feel). You are NOT shoving the hips toward the target; you're turning them out of the way so the arms have room to fall. TRAIL SIDE: trail heel starts to lift, trail knee kicks in toward the lead knee. CHECKPOINT (down-the-line): when your hands reach hip height, the shaft should point at or just outside the ball and your hips are ALREADY opening. If the hands get to the ball before the hips have turned, you cast.
sections.k: Your problem spot. The order is ground-up: pressure into the lead foot, then hips, then chest, then arms.

sections.t: 5 · Impact — the position all of it is for
sections.b: FEET: ~80–90% of pressure on the LEAD foot; trail foot up on the inside of the toe. LEAD LEG: straightening / 'posting up' — this extension pulls the hips up and around and is a big chunk of the speed you lose when you slide instead. HIPS: OPEN ~35–45° to the target — belt buckle already pointing LEFT of the ball, lead hip HIGH and behind you. SPINE/CHEST: still tilted, chest 'covering' the ball; for irons and wedges you stay DOWN through it. HANDS: ahead of the ball for irons (shaft lean, hands over the lead thigh); level for driver so you catch it slightly on the up. HEAD: still behind the ball, eyes down. This is the money frame — most of the checkpoints above exist only to get you here.
sections.k: Impact is 80–90% on the lead foot with the lead leg posting up and the hips already open 35–45°.

sections.t: 6 · Follow-through & finish
sections.b: Keep rotating — the belt buckle turns from left-of-the-ball all the way to facing the target and past it. FEET: fully onto the lead foot, trail foot balanced on the toe with the laces to the target. HIPS: fully cleared and open, LEAD LEG tall and straight. CHEST: faces the target, then left of it. ARMS: extend down the line just after impact (the 'chase'), then fold up to a tall, balanced finish. Test: if you can HOLD the finish for 3 seconds without falling off balance, your sequence and weight shift were good.
sections.k: Keep rotating to a full, tall finish — the belt buckle ends past the target.

sections.t: 7 · The HIPS in plain terms — SLIDE vs CLEAR (read twice)
sections.b: You're unsure here, so plainly: coming down, the hips can do two different things. A SLIDE is the hips moving SIDEWAYS toward the target — the belt buckle stays pointing at the ball, the hips stay 'closed,' and your upper body hangs back to counterbalance. That is the 'great at the top, lose it through contact' miss: no speed, hands flip to square the face, thin or fat strikes. A CLEAR (what you want) is the hips ROTATING — the lead hip turns back behind you and up as the lead leg straightens, so the belt buckle points LEFT of the ball at impact. THREE IMAGES that make it click: (a) There's a wall just behind your lead butt cheek — clearing = that cheek moves BACK to the wall, not toward the target. (b) You're standing in a barrel — you can TURN inside it but you can't slide out of it. (c) Pull your lead back pocket around behind you and up. Note: a SMALL lateral shift is real and necessary — but it happens in the FEET (pressure to the lead foot), and THEN the hips turn. Feet shift, hips spin — never the whole pelvis sliding as one block.
sections.k: Read twice: a slide keeps the buckle at the ball, a clear turns it left around a post.

sections.t: 8 · How to groove it (feel beats positions)
sections.b: Positions are for the mirror; feels are for hitting. Best hip drills, all in your Swing Focus plan: TRAIL-FOOT-BACK step-through and LEAD-HIP-TO-THE-WALL — both make 'clear, don't slide' automatic because sliding is physically blocked. Then the ONE-HANDED Miracle 201 drop to feel the club fall while the hips open. Rehearse a checkpoint at ~50% speed until the shape is in; full speed returns on its own once the body trusts the position. One checkpoint at a time — stack them over weeks, not in one range session.
sections.k: Positions are for the mirror, feels are for hitting — groove it with the trail-foot-back and wall drills.

rules: ONE checkpoint per session — not all nine
Ground-up order in transition: pressure → hips → chest → arms
CLEAR the hips around a post, never slide them at the target
Mirror for positions, drills for feels

briefing.focus: Your WINNERSPIRIT Miracle 201 is the perfect home tool for the two things the Jul 26 film flagged: sequencing (hips lead) and releasing THROUGH contact instead of losing it. WORKING (Jul 27): one-handed reps are landing the drop into the slot. This is the standing at-home practice plan. Pairs with the Swing Focus plan.

sections.t: ✓ What's working — one-handed reps
sections.b: CONFIRMED (Jul 27): swinging the 201 ONE-HANDED (trail/right hand only) is landing the 'drop into the slot' feel for you — the heavy head with a single hand exaggerates the shallowing and lag you're chasing, and makes an early cast obvious. Lean on it: start every session with a few slow one-handed reps (and use them inside Drill 1) before going two-handed, and reach for it any time the top feels across the line.
sections.k: One-handed trail-arm reps are the confirmed winner — they land the drop into the slot.

sections.t: How the tool talks to you (read first)
sections.b: The Miracle 201 is a weighted (~550g), whippy carbon/glass-fiber trainer with TWO feedback channels. (1) THE CLICK: a slider fires an audible click at the point of maximum speed in your swing — WHERE you hear it tells you WHEN you're releasing. (2) THE SPEED DIAL: adjustable from ~15–50 m/s (≈34–111 mph); it sets how much speed is needed to trigger the click. Turn it DOWN for tempo work, UP to demand more clubhead speed or simulate a longer club. Because the shaft is heavy and flexible, you physically cannot rush it — it forces you to load and wait, which is exactly the medicine for your quick, across-the-line top.
sections.k: Two feedback channels: WHERE the click fires tells you when you release, the bend tells you if you snatched.

sections.t: Setup & safety — every session
sections.b: Space: ~8 ft clear all around and a high ceiling (garage, basement with clearance, or backyard). Never near people, lights, or a TV. Hold it with your normal CONVENTIONAL grip and your real posture — this only transfers if the setup matches your actual swing. WARM UP FIRST: 20–30 slow, smooth swings before anything hard — at 550g it's heavier than your driver and a cold max swing is how you tweak a back or oblique. Do a few swings LEFT-handed too (opposite of normal) each session — it balances the body and builds the anti-rotation muscles that protect you.
sections.k: Eight feet of clearance, normal grip, real posture — it only transfers if the setup matches.

sections.t: Drill 1 · Tempo & sequencing — the load-and-wait (core)
sections.b: Dial LOW. Make smooth 3:1 swings and FEEL the shaft bend and lag behind your hands at the top — if you snatch from the top it flails and clicks early/weak. Count 'one-and-… two': long patient load back, unhurried transition, then let it sling. Warm into it with the ONE-HANDED reps that are working for you, then go two-handed. This directly rewires the 'great at the top but quick coming down' pattern. 2 sets of 10, both directions. This is the most important drill on the list — do it every session.
sections.k: Low dial, smooth 3:1 swings: load patiently and let it sling rather than snatching from the top.

sections.t: Drill 2 · Impact timing — make the CLICK fire PAST the ball
sections.b: This one targets your exact complaint: 'lose it through contact.' GOAL: the click should crack at the BOTTOM of the arc — at or just PAST your lead leg — not up in the downswing. An EARLY click = casting / throwing the release away before impact (all your speed spent above the ball). Keep the wrists hinged and let the head release LATE so the click fires down by where the ball would be. 3 sets of 8. Listen every rep and adjust until the click consistently lives at/after the bottom.
sections.k: This targets 'losing it through contact' — the click must crack at or PAST your lead leg, never early.

sections.t: Drill 3 · Transition & hips-lead (ties to Swing Focus)
sections.b: From the top, start down with the LOWER BODY — feel the lead hip clear BACK and UP while the trainer's head still lags behind. Because the head is heavy and slow to catch up, it exaggerates the hips-lead-hands feeling you need. If you spin the shoulders/arms first, the click comes early and weak — instant feedback that you cast. Do this right after the wall / trail-foot-back drills in your Swing Focus plan so the feel carries over. 2 sets of 8.
sections.k: Start down with the lead hip clearing back and up while the heavy head still lags behind.

sections.t: Drill 4 · Top-of-swing check — kill the laid-off shaft
sections.b: Slow reps to a PAUSE at the top. Feel the trail (right) elbow point down and stay IN FRONT of your trail-hip seam — the whippy shaft makes an across-the-line/laid-off top feel obviously 'stuck' and off-plane, which a normal club hides. Check in a mirror or a phone on a tripod that the shaft points at the target line, not right of it. 10 slow reps, no speed — this is a position drill.
sections.k: Slow reps to a pause: trail elbow down and in front of the hip seam kills the laid-off top.

sections.t: Drill 5 · Speed sets (separate days)
sections.b: Dial UP. After a full warm-up: all-out swings for pure speed — at higher dial settings the click ONLY fires if you genuinely accelerate through the bottom. Protocol: 3 sets of 5 MAX-effort swings with full rest between sets (this is nervous-system/speed work — quality over quantity, never grind it into cardio). Throw in a few non-dominant-side swings. Benchmark: the highest dial setting you can consistently trigger — track it over weeks and watch it climb.
sections.k: Separate speed days only: 3 sets of 5 max-effort swings, full rest, never on a tempo day.

sections.t: Weekly plan & what to log
sections.b: 2–3 short sessions/week, 10–15 min each — and DON'T max out every time: alternate a TEMPO/TIMING day (Drills 1–4, low dial) with a SPEED day (Drill 5, high dial). Pre-round: 15–20 easy swings as a dynamic warm-up and tempo primer. Log in Coach: the dial setting you can reliably trigger, and whether the click is firing at/past the ball yet. Next time you film at the sim we'll check whether the later release and hips-lead carried into the real swing.
sections.k: 2–3 sessions a week, 10–15 minutes, alternating tempo days and speed days. Don't max out every time.

rules: One-handed trail-arm reps are the go-to reset
The CLICK must fire at or past the lead leg
Alternate tempo days and speed days — never both
Normal grip, real posture, 8 ft of clear space

briefing.course: Swing Focus — Hips & the Laid-Off Top
briefing.focus: Good ground-up sequencing (keep) and a slightly across-the-line top (fix); your read — 'great at the top, lose it through contact' — is hip clearance in transition, and it's the SAME root as your lifelong over-the-top slice (Fix 3). WORKING (Jul 27): one-handed Miracle 201 swings are landing the drop into the slot. Standing swing plan until the next filmed check.

sections.t: ✓ What's working — one-handed Miracle 201 drop
sections.b: CONFIRMED (Jul 27): swinging the MIRACLE 201 ONE-HANDED (trail/right hand only) tonight really helped you FEEL the club drop into the slot in transition. Make it your go-to reset — the heavy, whippy head with just the trail hand forces the elbow to lead DOWN (in front of the trail-hip seam) and shallows the shaft, so the hips can clear instead of the club laying off. Use it as a warm-up primer and any time the top gets across the line: a few slow one-handed 201 reps feeling the drop, then blend it into your two-hand swing. A club held trail-arm-only works as a stand-in when the trainer isn't handy.
sections.k: One-handed Miracle 201 swings are the confirmed fix-feel for the transition drop.

sections.t: The one connection: laid-off top, stalled hips AND the over-the-top slice are one story
sections.b: When the club gets across the line / laid off at the top (shaft pointing right of target, trail elbow drifting behind you), the downswing has to re-route the club to save the shot. Two re-routes usually happen together: the hips SLIDE toward the target and the chest hangs back (the 'lose it through contact' feel), AND the trail shoulder throws the club OUT over the plane so it cuts across the ball — that's the over-the-top slice. One cause, three symptoms. So we don't chase three fixes: clean up the top, drop the club into the slot (shallow), and let the hips CLEAR — and all three symptoms go with it.
sections.k: The laid-off top, the sliding hips and the lifelong slice are one fault, not three.

sections.t: What the film showed (both clubs, Jul 26)
sections.b: GOOD, protect it: full coil, head behind the ball (driver), lower-body-led transition on both, and a balanced held finish. WEDGE bonus: spine angle stayed, you covered the ball — a proper descending strike. TO FIX: (1) slightly across-the-line top on BOTH clubs — one feel fixes both; (2) driver hips look to slide level through impact instead of clearing up-and-around. No launch numbers were in frame, so path/attack-angle/spin are still unmeasured — that's the next data to grab.
sections.k: Film says: coil, head behind the ball and lower-body-led transition are all good — protect them.

sections.t: Fix 1 · Clean up the top (trail elbow in front)
sections.b: FEEL: at the top, the trail (right) elbow points more DOWN at the ground and stays in FRONT of your trail-hip seam, keeping the club a hair more in front of your chest. Right now the elbow drifts behind you, which lays the shaft off. DRILL — the one-handed Miracle 201 (or club trail-arm-only): make slow half-swings feeling the trail elbow lead down into the slot; pause at the top and check the shaft points AT the target line, not right of it. Mirror or a phone on a tripod DTL at the top confirms it. 10 slow reps before you hit balls. (This is the drill that's working for you — see 'What's working' above.)
sections.k: Fix 1: trail elbow points down and stays in FRONT of the hip seam at the top.

sections.t: Fix 2 · Clear the hips, don't slide them
sections.b: FEEL: from the top, the lead (left) hip clears BACK and UP — belt buckle turning left and rotating open — while your chest stays over the ball a beat longer. Not a slide toward the target; a turn around a post. This is where your speed and your 'through contact' consistency live. DRILLS: (a) Trail-foot-back / step-through: hit half wedges stepping the trail foot back through impact — forces rotation over slide. (b) Lead-hip-to-the-wall: set up with your lead hip a few inches off a wall/bag; on the downswing the hip should clear so it just brushes back and up, not bump forward into it. (c) Chair/impact-bag: feel the trail glute fire and the hips deepen (not thrust toward the ball) so you don't early-extend. 2–3 sets of 10 each, twice a week.
sections.k: Fix 2: the lead hip clears BACK and UP while the chest stays over the ball a beat longer.

sections.t: Fix 3 · Your over-the-top slice — same root, plus the path & face piece
sections.b: The lifelong slice comes from the SAME move: OVER THE TOP means in transition the upper body (trail shoulder) takes over and throws the club OUT and over the plane, so it swings across the ball OUT-TO-IN; with an open face that start-left, curve-right is your slice (a square face on that same path is a pull). Everything in this plan already fixes the CAUSE — the one-handed drop shallows the club, the trail elbow leading down puts it on line, and the hips CLEARING makes room so the arms deliver from the INSIDE instead of over the top. The extra piece is PATH then FACE. (1) PATH feel: from the top, feel the club fall behind you and swing OUT toward right-center field (in-to-out). DRILL — put a headcover/water bottle a few inches OUTSIDE the ball on the target line; swing so you miss it (coming over the top clips it). (2) FACE: a slice also needs an open face — once your path comes from the inside, if the ball still fades or you start pulling, the face is open to the path; with your conventional grip, let the trail forearm rotate/release through and check the grip isn't too weak. Fix PATH FIRST — chasing the face while still coming over the top just makes a bigger slice or a smother-hook.
sections.k: Fix 3: the slice is the same root — a headcover outside the ball forces the in-to-out path.

sections.t: Driver vs wedge — keep them different on purpose
sections.b: DRIVER: ball forward, hips clearing up-and-around so you hit slightly UP — that's carry and less spin. WEDGE: keep exactly what the film showed — stay down, cover the ball, hit DOWN; don't let 'clear the hips' turn into standing up out of a wedge. Same sequencing engine, opposite low-point. If a swing thought bleeds the wrong way, park it — the wedge is already good.
sections.k: Keep driver and wedge deliberately different: up on the driver, down and covering on the wedge.

sections.t: How to test it at the sim (get the numbers this time)
sections.b: The visual read can only go so far without data. Next session, capture and log these: DRIVER — attack angle (want positive / hitting up), CLUB PATH (over-the-top shows as a negative/left number — you want it near zero to slightly positive/right), FACE-TO-PATH (that's what curves it), spin, and ball speed. WEDGES — carry, spin, launch, and gap-check 60/56/50 against the ladder (80/95/108). Film one DTL clip at hand height + one face-on per club. Bring those back and we can prove whether the path is actually coming from the inside now.
sections.k: Stop guessing from video — get attack angle, club path and face-to-path at the next sim session.

rules: Trail elbow DOWN and in FRONT — the one thought
Clear the lead hip back and up; don't slide
Same root fixes the top, the hips and the slice
Next sim session: get path and face-to-path numbers

briefing.focus: Jack's own swing thoughts & setup keys, in his words — the go-to reference before a round or a range session. Grip settled: conventional. Putting routine locked Jul 28.

sections.t: Driver — the big stick
sections.b: Aim the CENTER of the fairway — the start line tends to pull left, so center-aim leaves room. The straight ball comes from a LONGER, fuller swing — commit to that one. A tighter, shorter swing turns it into a cut, and when that goes wrong the miss is a PUSH-SLICE. So: full swing for straight; if you shorten it, expect the cut and know the push-slice is the bad one.
