sections.k: Aim centre — your start line pulls left, and the straight ball needs a LONGER swing, not a tighter one.

sections.t: Mini driver
sections.b: Club setup: the r7 Quad's adjustable WEIGHTS are set in the BACK position. Tee it LOW for the piercing straight ball — NEVER at normal driver-tee height. From that setup you can work it both ways, draw or fade. This is the fairway-finder off the tee; weights back + low tee is what makes it behave.
sections.k: Weights back, teed LOW for the piercing ball. This is the fairway-finder, not a second driver.

sections.t: Irons
sections.b: Ball position right of center, toward the trail (right) thigh. The new KING TECs fly HIGHER and longer than the old set — trust the extra height. When you need to flight it down or take something off, CHOKE DOWN and hit the control shot rather than just swinging soft.
sections.k: Ball back toward the trail thigh; the KING TECs fly higher than the old set, so trust the height.

sections.t: Wedges
sections.b: (Open — fill in as you dial the Vokeys: your go-to feels for full vs. partial, and any open-face/flop keys. Ladder to stay honest: 60°→80 · 56°→95 · 50°→108 · PW→122.)
sections.k: Open — fill in your Vokey feels as you dial them. Ladder: 60°→80 · 56°→95 · 50°→108 · PW→122.

sections.t: Putting — LINK.2.1
sections.b: Ball off the LEFT BREAST — chest reference, not foot: the arc centers on your sternum, so the cue survives a change in stance width. WEIGHT STACKED ON THE BALL — that's what pins the low point. Rock the SHOULDERS, no hands. LOOSE grip. AT ADDRESS the hands sit EVEN with the ball — on the LINK.2.1's Pistol 0 grip that means a DEAD VERTICAL shaft and zero forward lean, which is what this putter is built for (confirmed on film Jul 30); the PRESS is a separate trigger that starts the stroke — same size every time or the loft changes and pace goes with it. Bend over MORE, stand CLOSE, eyes DOWN through the strike. ROUTINE: read and pick your spot from behind → step BESIDE the ball in full posture and take two rehearsals, eyes-on-ball then eyes-on-hole (the hole one is the PACE stroke — keep it last, and finish it with the press) → step in, face to the spot first, then stance → spot, ball, press, go. Grip settled: conventional / reverse-overlap.
sections.k: Ball off the left breast, weight stacked on it, shoulders rock, hands even — and on the Pistol 0 that means zero lean.

rules: Driver: aim centre, swing LONGER not tighter
Mini driver: tee it LOW, weights back
Irons: trust the extra height, choke down to flight it
Putter: hands even, shoulders rock, no hands

briefing.focus: Five 9-hole matches with your brother at Wianno Club (Osterville, MA), Jul 9–11 2026, Blue tees, par 35. 45 holes, 212 strokes, +37. Transcribed from the GHIN cards — every total reconciles against the hole-by-hole and the bogey/double markings.

sections.t: The five cards
sections.k: Five cards, 45 holes, +37 — every total reconciles against the hole-by-hole.

sections.t: The scoring mix — 45 holes
sections.b: 1 birdie · 16 pars · 18 bogeys · 10 DOUBLES. That's the whole story in one line. Ten doubles is ten strokes handed over, and it's more than a quarter of your +37. Paired as 18s: Jul 10 = 84, Jul 11 = 82 — differentials of roughly 12.2 and 10.4 against an 11.1 index, so you played about to your handicap, not above or below it.
sections.k: 1 birdie, 16 pars, 18 bogeys and 10 DOUBLES. The doubles are more than a quarter of the damage.

sections.t: THE FINDING — doubles are the entire gap
sections.b: Look at Jul 11 front: 41 with ZERO doubles and ZERO birdies — six bogeys and three pars, nothing else. Now Jul 9 front: 46 with FOUR doubles. Same golfer, same tees, two days apart, five shots apart, and the difference is entirely doubles. You do not need to make more putts or hit it further to shoot 38. You need to stop making 6s. The doubles line up almost perfectly with the score every round: 4 doubles → 46 · 3 → 44 · 2 → 40 · 1 → 41 · 0 → 41.
sections.k: Same golfer, two days apart: 41 with no doubles versus 46 with four. The doubles ARE the gap.

sections.t: THE OPENING HOLE — +7 across five nines
sections.b: Your first hole of each nine: 6, 6, 5 on the front and 4, 6 on the back. Par 4 every time. That's 27 strokes on 20 par — SEVEN over, on five holes, before you've settled into anything. You never once made par on the opening hole of the front nine in three tries. This is the single most concentrated leak in the whole event, and it is not a swing problem — it's a not-warmed-up problem.
sections.k: You never parred an opening hole all week — +7 across five of them, before settling into anything.

sections.t: What that validates
sections.b: The Swing Routine plan already carries a 'Warm-up primer — before the first tee' section: a few slow one-handed Miracle 201 reps (or trail-arm-only with a club) feeling the elbow lead down into the slot, then blend into two-hand swings. Consider this the evidence for it. Prime the feel before the first tee rather than hunting for it on the 4th hole — on this card, hunting for it cost you a shot and a half per opening hole.
sections.k: That's what the warm-up primer in the Swing Routine plan is for. Use it.

sections.t: Par 3s are bleeding — and there's no driver involved
sections.b: 13 par-3 plays, +11. That's +0.85 a hole, essentially the same rate as your par 4s (+0.92) — but on par 3s the tee shot is an iron and there's no driving miss to blame. That points at iron control and green-hitting, not the swing faults on your card. Worst offender: HOLE 3 (par 3) went 5, 5, 4 — five over in three plays, never a par. One hole, +5.
sections.k: Par 3s cost +11 with no driver involved, so this is iron control, not a driving miss.

sections.t: Hole 1 and Hole 3 together
sections.b: Those two holes alone account for +10 of your +37, across just 6 of 45 holes played. Roughly a quarter of everything you lost came from two holes you played six times. If you get another crack at Wianno, they are the entire prep list.
sections.k: Holes 1 and 3 alone were +10 of your +37, from six of the forty-five holes played.

sections.t: Par 5s — no offense at all
sections.b: 8 par-5 plays: four bogeys, four pars, ZERO birdies. +4 total. Par 5s are supposed to be where a mid-single-digit makes his money, and you didn't convert one all week. Your wedge ladder off the 44° PW (60°→80 · 56°→95 · 50°→108 · PW→122) exists precisely so the third shot into a par 5 is a number rather than a guess — decide the lay-up yardage from the ladder rather than hitting it as far as it goes.
sections.k: Eight par-5 plays, zero birdies. Take the ladder number on every lay-up.

sections.t: One caveat on the data
sections.b: These were matches, so some of these scores are most-likely-score postings rather than holed-out strokes. That mostly affects the doubles — a picked-up hole posts as a net double. The trend and the opening-hole pattern hold regardless, but don't read the double count as gospel on any single hole.
sections.k: These were matches, so some scores are most-likely-score postings — the trend holds, the doubles are softer.

sections.t: Handicap flag
sections.b: The GHIN cards show a Handicap Index of 11.1. Caddie HQ's profile still says 8.5. Update it in Settings so the app's math (and any future round prep) works off the real number — profile isn't something the coach feed can push.
sections.k: GHIN says your index is 11.1 and the app still says 8.5 — update it in Settings.

rules: Doubles are the whole gap — 10 of them, a quarter of +37
You never parred an opening hole: warm up before the first tee
Par 3s bled +11 with no driver to blame
Zero par-5 birdies — take the ladder number

briefing.focus: A pre-shot routine built around YOUR pattern, not a generic one. Everything here is aimed at the single root cause the Jul 26 film found: an across-the-line top that forces a re-route, which shows up as sliding hips and the over-the-top slice. The routine's job is to stop you re-routing — and re-routing is something you do OVER the ball, so the routine gets the deciding done before you're standing there.

sections.t: The architecture — two zones
sections.b: BEHIND THE BALL is where every decision and every rehearsal happens. AT THE BALL is execution only — no thinking, no adjusting, no second guesses. This is the opposite of what we locked for putting, and deliberately so: in putting you rehearse beside the ball because stroke SIZE has to transfer exactly. In the full swing you're not calibrating magnitude, you're calibrating SHAPE and SEQUENCE — those transfer fine from behind the ball, and the commitment you buy is worth more. Different problem, different answer.
sections.k: Decisions and rehearsals happen BEHIND the ball. At the ball is execution only — deliberately the opposite of putting.

sections.t: 1 · Decide (behind the ball)
sections.b: Lie, wind, number, and where the trouble ISN'T. Then pick a SPECIFIC target — a tree, a bunker lip, a chimney — never 'the fairway'. DRIVER: aim the CENTER of the fairway, because your start line tends to pull left and center-aim leaves you room. Commit to ONE shape and say it out loud in your head. Then stop deciding — anything you reconsider later gets reconsidered over the ball, which is exactly where your swing falls apart.
sections.k: Pick a specific target, never 'the fairway'. Driver aims centre because your start line pulls left.

sections.t: 2 · Rehearse (behind the ball, facing the target)
sections.b: ONE rehearsal swing. Not three. Feel the trail (right) elbow drop DOWN and stay IN FRONT of your trail-hip seam — that is the whole fix, and it's the one that repairs the top, the hips and the slice together. If the last swing felt across the line, make this a TRAIL-ARM-ONLY rehearsal instead: one hand, slow, feeling the drop into the slot. That's the feel that's been landing for you with the one-handed Miracle 201, and a normal club held trail-arm-only is a fine stand-in on the course.
sections.k: ONE rehearsal, facing the target, feeling the trail elbow drop down and in front.

sections.t: 3 · Aim (stepping in)
sections.b: Pick an intermediate spot a foot or two ahead of the ball on your start line. Set the CLUBFACE to that spot FIRST, then build the stance around the face — never the other way round. Feet shoulder-width (a touch wider for driver), lead foot flared 20–30° so the hips have somewhere to go. Ball off the lead heel for driver, center to just right of center for irons. Weight 50/50 irons, ~55/45 trail side for driver. Hinge from the hip SOCKETS, chin UP off the chest so the lead shoulder can turn under it.
sections.k: Set the CLUBFACE to an intermediate spot first, then build the stance around it.

sections.t: 4 · Go (no decisions left)
sections.b: One look at the target. One look back to the ball. Then a TRIGGER — a small waggle or a kick of the trail knee. Never start a swing from a frozen stand; a static start is where the snatch comes from, and the snatch is what lays the club off. Count it: 'one-and-… two.' Long patient load, unhurried transition, 3:1. Then hold the finish for THREE SECONDS. If you can't hold it, the sequence or the weight shift was off — that's free feedback on every single swing.
sections.k: One look at the target, one back to the ball, then a trigger — never start from frozen.

sections.t: The one-thought rule
sections.b: ONE swing thought at a time. If you have two, you have none. Yours is the trail elbow — down and in front of the trail-hip seam. Everything else on your card (hip clearance, the slice, the laid-off top) is downstream of that one feel, which is exactly why you don't need a second thought. Rotate a different thought in only when the film says the root has moved.
sections.k: One swing thought at a time. If you have two, you have none. Yours is the trail elbow.

sections.t: The step-off rule
sections.b: If anything feels wrong once you're over the ball — alignment, the number, a gust, a stray thought — STEP OFF and restart from behind the ball. Do not fix it standing there. Over-the-ball corrections are precisely how a re-route gets built into a swing, and re-routing is your documented fault. Stepping off costs eight seconds; a re-route costs the shot.
sections.k: Anything feels wrong over the ball — step off and restart. Never fix it standing there.

sections.t: Under pressure — longer, not shorter
sections.b: Your own note: the straight ball comes from a LONGER, fuller swing; a tighter, shorter swing turns into a cut, and when that goes wrong the miss is a PUSH-SLICE. Pressure makes everyone shorten and steer, so this is the rule that needs saying out loud before a tee shot that matters — when in doubt, commit to MORE swing, never less. Steering is the re-route wearing a disguise.
sections.k: Pressure makes everyone shorten and steer. Yours is the opposite rule: longer, fuller.

sections.t: Warm-up primer — before the first tee
sections.b: A few slow ONE-HANDED reps with the Miracle 201, or trail-arm-only with a club, feeling the elbow lead down into the slot. Then blend into two-hand swings. This is your documented working feel — prime it before the round rather than hunting for it on the 4th hole. And keep the routine's beat count identical from the range to the 18th; a routine that shortens under pressure isn't a routine.
sections.k: Prime the one-handed drop feel before the first tee, not after the round has started.

sections.t: Wedges — one addition
sections.b: Everything above holds, plus: partial distances come from a CONTROLLED length and flight, not a full send with a soft grip. Choke down and hit the control shot. Your ladder off the 44° PW: 60°→80 · 56°→95 · 50°→108 · PW→122. Decide the NUMBER behind the ball like any other shot — the wedge swing on film is already good (spine held, ball-first, covering it); it's the distance decision that needs the routine.
sections.k: Partial wedges come from a controlled length, not a full send with a soft grip.

steps: Behind the ball — lie, wind, number, and where the trouble ISN'T
Pick a SPECIFIC target (driver: centre of the fairway)
Commit to one shape — then stop deciding
ONE rehearsal — trail elbow DOWN and IN FRONT of the trail-hip seam
Step in — clubface to the spot FIRST, then stance around it
One look at the target, one look back at the ball
Trigger — small waggle or trail-knee kick. Never start frozen.
Count 'one-and-… two' → swing → hold the finish 3 seconds
rules: ONE swing thought: the trail elbow
Feels wrong over the ball? STEP OFF and restart
Under pressure: LONGER, never shorter

briefing.focus: Three seasons of GHIN — 44 posted scores and 38 rounds of hole-by-hole detail. Scoring average went 85.2 → 83.6 → 86.7, and the one metric that has worsened every single year without exception is your par-5 average.

sections.t: The three seasons
sections.b: 2023 · 23 posted scores, avg 85.2, range 75–96 · 20 rounds of detail — 5% birdies, 32% pars, 41% bogeys, 20% doubles, 2% triples, par-or-better 37%. 2024 · 9 posted, avg 83.6, range 79–88 · 8 rounds of detail — 4% birdies, 39% pars, 43% bogeys, 13% doubles, 1% triples, par-or-better 43%. 2025 · 12 posted, avg 86.7, range 83–90 · 10 rounds of detail — 2% birdies, 30% pars, 47% bogeys, 20% doubles, 1% triples, par-or-better 32%. (GHIN's two round counts differ because the scoring donut only counts rounds you entered hole-by-hole.)
sections.k: Three seasons: 85.2 → 83.6 → 86.7, from 44 posted scores and 38 rounds of hole detail.

sections.t: THE FINDING — par 5s have gotten worse every year
sections.b: 5.46 → 5.72 → 5.88. It is the only number across three seasons that moves in one direction with no exceptions, and it has cost you about a stroke and a half a round from where it started. On a par-72 with four par 5s, 2023's average gave you +1.8 on them; 2025 gave you +3.5. Par 5s are the holes a mid-single-digit is SUPPOSED to feed on — you get a wedge in your hand on the third shot by design. Instead they've quietly become your worst holes relative to par.
sections.k: Par-5 average has worsened every year with no exceptions: 5.46 → 5.72 → 5.88.

sections.t: It's the same finding Wianno gave you
sections.b: The member-guest cards said it independently: 8 par-5 plays, four pars and four bogeys, ZERO birdies, +4. Two completely different data sources, same conclusion. That's no longer a small-sample fluke — it's the standing pattern, and it's the single most concrete thing on your whole card to attack. The fix is already written down: decide the lay-up off the ladder (PW 122 · 50° 108 · 56° 95 · 60° 80) so the third shot is a NUMBER you own rather than whatever's left after hitting it as far as it goes.
sections.k: Wianno said the same thing independently — zero par-5 birdies. Two sources, one conclusion.

sections.t: 2025 gave back everything 2024 gained
sections.b: Bogeys went 43% → 47% and pars fell 39% → 30% — nine points of pars converting almost one-for-one into bogeys. Doubles went back up too, 13% → 20%. So 2025 wasn't one blow-up round dragging an average down; it was the ordinary hole getting worse. The posted scoring average confirms it from the other direction: 83.6 → 86.7 is a three-shot round-for-round regression, and it lands you slightly worse than 2023 as well.
sections.k: 2025 gave back 2024 entirely: nine points of pars converted almost one-for-one into bogeys.

sections.t: The range is the part nobody looks at
sections.b: 2023 ran 75 to 96 — a 21-shot spread. 2025 ran 83 to 90 — seven. Read that carefully, because it cuts both ways. The bad days genuinely got better: no 96s, no blow-up rounds at all, which fits the doubles staying survivable. But the good days disappeared completely. You have not broken 83 in two seasons, and your best round in three years is a 75 that's now more than two years old. That is the profile of a player who has stopped making birdies — 5% → 4% → 2% — rather than one who has started making messes.
sections.k: The spread narrowed from 21 shots to seven — the bad days improved, but the good days vanished too.

sections.t: What 2024 proves you can do
sections.b: Don't dismiss 2024 as a fluke just because it's nine scores. 39% pars, 13% doubles and an 83.6 average is genuinely good golf, and the par-4 average — 4.65 — is nearly THREE TENTHS better than either year on either side of it. Ten par 4s a round makes that worth about three strokes on its own. Whatever you were doing in 2024 off the tee and into the green, that's the level, and it's yours; it's two years old, not theoretical.
sections.k: 2024 wasn't a fluke: 39% pars and a 4.65 par-4 average is genuinely good golf you've already played.

sections.t: The one thing that held up
sections.b: Par 3s: 3.88 → 3.70 → 3.74. They improved from 2023 and then stayed improved through the bad year. That's a real gain and worth knowing, because it means 2025 was not a general ball-striking collapse — one-shot holes held while the two- and three-shot holes fell apart. That points at what happens AFTER the tee shot, not at the swing itself.
sections.k: Par 3s improved and stayed improved, so 2025 was not a general ball-striking collapse.

sections.t: Read the sample sizes honestly
sections.b: Nine posted scores in 2024 against twenty-three in 2023 — small samples move a lot, and none of this is adjusted for course difficulty, tees, or conditions, though the differentials on your score history run a wide 8.4 to 20.4 regardless. Only two rounds in three years carry GHIN's shot-level detail, so there's no fairways/greens/putts data behind any of it to explain WHY. Treat the year-over-year direction as real and the exact decimals as noisy. What survives that caveat is the par-5 line, because it moves the same way three years running and Wianno confirms it from a separate source.
sections.k: Nine scores in 2024 against 23 in 2023 — small samples move, and none of this adjusts for course or tees.

sections.t: The one job
sections.b: Don't try to fix all of this. Par 5s are the leak with the most evidence behind it, the clearest mechanism, and a fix that's already on your card and costs nothing to apply. Take the ladder number on every par-5 lay-up for the rest of this season and watch that 5.88. Everything else here is context.
sections.k: Don't fix all of it. Par 5s have the most evidence, the clearest mechanism and a free fix.

rules: Par 5s are the leak — worse every year for three years
Two independent sources agree: zero par-5 birdies
2024 proves you can play to 83.6 — it isn't aspirational
One job only: take the ladder number on par-5 lay-ups

briefing.focus: Scramble, not stroke play. Your job is to be the team's SECOND ball — when someone's already safe, swing free and go at the flag. And on every lay-up, leave the team one of YOUR numbers (122 · 108 · 95 · 80), never a 70-yard guess. First round with the LINK.2.1 — treat every early putt as free calibration.

sections.t: The course in one paragraph
sections.b: Beekman Golf Course, Hopewell Junction NY (11 Country Club Rd) — a 1964 Cortlandt Fish public 27-holer in the Berkshire foothills where they rise out of the Hudson Valley, about an hour's drive for you. Three nines — HIGHLAND (3,142 yds, par 36, ~124 slope), VALLEY (2,952, par 35, ~118), TACONIC (3,125, par 36, ~126) — played in three 18-hole pairings between 6,485 and 6,532 yards. Zoysia fairways, which is the detail worth knowing: zoysia sits the ball UP on a tight, firm cushion, so contact is clean and there's less grab than the bent/poa you're used to. Reviews are consistent — well-kept greens, all three nines hilly, and it doesn't drain well, so wet spots after rain.
sections.k: A hilly 1964 public 27-holer an hour away, three nines that play as genuinely different courses.

sections.t: Find out which two nines you're playing
sections.b: Ask at check-in, because the three nines are genuinely different golf courses. TACONIC is the hardest: narrowest fairways and the water — the par-5 6th has a pond fronting the green, which in a scramble is a decision hole, not a hero hole. HIGHLAND climbs over 500 feet to a panorama of Stormville Mountain: elevation change on nearly every shot, blind or semi-blind looks, and the yardage on the sprinkler head is a starting point, not the answer. VALLEY is the gentlest and flattest of the three — that's your birdie nine, and a scramble team that only pars the Valley holes has already lost the tournament.
sections.k: Ask at check-in which two nines you've got — Taconic is the hardest and has the water.

sections.t: Scramble math — where teams actually win
sections.b: You don't win a scramble by avoiding doubles; the format erases those for you. You win it by converting the 5–7 genuinely gettable holes and by never wasting a hole where all four of you miss. So the whole game is about SEQUENCING: get one ball safe, then let everyone else be aggressive off that safety net. The single biggest error you'll see all day is the team's last hitter playing conservatively when a ball is already in the fairway — that shot is completely free, and a free shot played safe is a shot thrown away.
sections.k: Scrambles are won by converting the gettable holes and never wasting one, so sequencing is everything.

sections.t: Your role off the tee
sections.b: You have the perfect scramble bag for this: mini driver (~220) and the KING TEC 2-iron (~205) for when a ball simply has to be in the short grass, and the Stealth 2 for when one already is. Rule for the day: if nobody is safe yet, hit the club you'd bet $100 finds the fairway — on Taconic's tight holes and Highland's blind ones, that's the mini or the 2-iron, and nobody on your team will ever complain about a ball in play. If someone IS safe, take the driver and take the whole thing on. Your own note from the swing plan applies double here: the straight one comes from a LONGER, fuller swing; steering it is what turns it into the push-slice. In a scramble you have permission to make the fullest swing you own.
sections.k: If nobody's safe yet, mini driver or the 2-iron. If someone is, let the Stealth 2 go.

sections.t: Approaches — the lay-up is the shot that scores
sections.b: This is the biggest edge you personally bring, and almost nobody uses it. In a scramble you CHOOSE the yardage for the next shot. On any par 5 you're laying up on — including Taconic's 6th over the water — pick the ball that leaves a full 95 (56°) or a full 108 (50°), not the one that's 18 yards closer and leaves a nervy three-quarter 70-yarder. Same on a punch-out. Your ladder off the 44° PW: PW 122 · 50° 108 · 56° 95 · 60° 80. Say the number out loud when the team is choosing the ball — it's the most useful sentence you can contribute all day. On approaches themselves: first player in plays to the CENTER of the green, everyone after that fires at the flag. Uphill into these hillside greens, club UP; anything short rolls back down to you.
sections.k: Your biggest edge, and almost nobody uses it: in a scramble you CHOOSE the next yardage. Lay up to 122, 108, 95 or 80.

sections.t: The hill, the lies, and your free club-length
sections.b: All three nines are hilly, so you'll get very few flat lies — except that a scramble hands you a club-length of relief (confirm no-closer-to-the-hole at check-in). USE IT properly: don't just drop it where it's convenient, walk it to the flattest stance and the best ANGLE into the flag, and get out of any divot or wet spot. When you're stuck with a slope: ball above your feet turns it LEFT — with your strong lofts take one less and aim at the right edge; ball below the feet leaks right, so widen the stance and swing smooth. On the Highland especially, trust the elevation over the number.
sections.k: Few flat lies all day — use your club-length of relief to buy a LIE, not just a spot.

sections.t: Putting — the whole team's read is yours to use
sections.b: Best sequencing: whoever's least confident putts first and the best putter goes last, so the last ball has watched three balls take the line. Everyone marks the spot and putts from it. Two things that win scrambles on the green: the early putters should get the ball PAST the hole so the team learns the break and the speed — a putt left short teaches nothing — and the last putter plays the read that the first three just paid for. For you specifically — and note this is your FIRST round with the LINK.2.1, two days after the swap: the putter still handles the face (it's zero-torque, same as the DF3i), so your job is pace, and pace is exactly what you haven't calibrated on this head yet. A scramble is the perfect place to learn it at zero cost — you're often putting after someone's already safe, so roll the early ones firmly PAST and let the misses teach you the new power curve, and the routine still runs on every putt, including the 3-footer after a teammate has already stuffed it close. Your signature miss is left on the short ones, and 'gimme' tap-ins in a scramble are exactly where a stroke gets loose.
sections.k: First round with the LINK.2.1: early putts roll firmly past so the team learns the line and you learn the pace.

sections.t: The opening hole — you have data on this
sections.b: Wianno told you the truth in numbers: across five opening holes you went 6, 6, 5, 4, 6 — SEVEN over par on five holes, and never a par on the first hole of a front nine. That's a not-warmed-up problem, not a swing problem, and you're driving an hour to a 7 AM-ish start. Get there early enough for the warm-up primer off the swing plan: a few slow ONE-HANDED reps (Miracle 201 or trail-arm-only), feeling the trail elbow lead down into the slot, then blend to two-handed swings. Then five minutes on the putting green for pace only — zoysia surrounds and well-kept greens mean you want the speed calibrated before the first putt counts for four people.
sections.k: You've never parred an opening hole at Wianno — warm up before the first tee, don't discover it there.

sections.t: Confirm these at check-in
sections.b: Scramble formats vary and the details change your strategy: (1) is there a MINIMUM DRIVES rule — most events require each player's tee shot be used two or three times? If so, bank yours early on the wide holes rather than discovering on 17 that you owe two. (2) Net or gross, and how team handicap is figured. (3) Whether they're selling mulligans/skins — buy them for the tightest tee shots, not the first hole. (4) Cart path only? On a course this hilly, that changes club selection every hole. (5) Which nines, and shotgun or tee times.
sections.k: Confirm the format details at check-in: minimum drives, relief, and whether it's best ball or true scramble.

sections.t: Mindset for the day
sections.b: Early August, hilly, an hour in the car first — take the cart, drink more than you think, and load the weather tile at the first tee so the ladder's Today column adjusts your carries for the heat. This is the one round all year where your worst shot literally does not exist, so the risk-management instincts that serve you in stroke play are mostly wrong here: be the guy who takes on the flag once a teammate is safe. Log it in Coach afterward — score, the holes you converted, and any hole where all four of you missed — and I'll debrief it against this plan.
sections.k: Hilly, early August, an hour in the car — take the cart, drink more than you think, load the weather tile.

rules: Be the SECOND ball — go at the flag when someone's already safe
Every lay-up leaves one of YOUR numbers: 122 · 108 · 95 · 80
Use the club-length to buy a LIE, not just a spot
Warm up before the first tee — the data says so

briefing.focus: You feel better with the weight BACK while the ball sits off the front foot — and you've heard the weight is supposed to be forward. Here's what that combination actually costs you, why it lands squarely on the one putting fault still open on your card, and how to settle it with evidence instead of dogma. UPDATED Jul 30 for the LINK.2.1: the blade has far less MOI than the DF3i mallet, so a wandering low point now costs real distance — everything below matters more, not less.

sections.t: What 'weight forward' is actually for
sections.b: It isn't a rule for its own sake. Lead-side pressure does one job: it PINS THE LOW POINT of the stroke. Where your weight sits decides where the arc bottoms out, and where the arc bottoms out decides how the LINK.2.1 meets the ball. That's the whole mechanism — everything below follows from it.
sections.k: Lead-side pressure does one job: it pins where the stroke bottoms out.

sections.t: The cost — loft, hop, skid, short
sections.b: Ball off the FRONT foot is correct. But weight back moves the bottom of the arc BEHIND the ball, so by the time the putter arrives the head is climbing hard and the shaft is leaning AWAY from the target. That adds loft you never asked for. The ball launches slightly, HOPS, SKIDS, and only then starts rolling. Every bit of that hop is energy that was supposed to become roll — so the putt arrives soft. Worse, the skid distance changes with green speed and grain, so your PACE stops being repeatable from green to green.
sections.k: Hanging back adds loft, and added loft makes the ball hop, skid and arrive short.

sections.t: Why this is your fault, specifically
sections.b: Read the card. Path: settled. Face: settled. Start line: 10/10 clean, twice over. The ONE thing still open is pace — lags coming up short at Hudson Hills, arrivals dying on the mat, and both genuine misses in the Stage-0 4-footer block DIED at the hole. Hop-and-skid off a back-weighted low point is the textbook cause of exactly that signature. Your stroke is no longer the problem. Your strike quality might be.
sections.k: Pace is your one open fault, which is exactly what a wandering low point damages.

sections.t: The second cost — the pull
sections.b: Sitting back drops the trail shoulder and slides your EYELINE behind the ball. Eyes behind the ball make you see the line right of where it truly is, and you square it up with a whisker of pull. Both real misses in the Stage-0 block settled on the PULL side — logged there as a lean, not proof. This belongs on that candidate-cause list.
sections.k: Weight back also leaves the face open through impact — a second route to a missed line.

sections.t: The third cost — the flip can come back
sections.b: Hanging back leaves the hands behind the ball through impact. Hands behind = the wrists want to save it = a flick. That flick was the engine of the old blow-through left miss. The LINK.2.1's zero-torque head has buried that miss on film — but hands-behind is the one setup that can wake it up.
sections.k: Hands behind the ball invite a wrist flick, the old engine of the blow-through miss.

sections.t: Before changing anything — feel isn't real
sections.b: Your own Golf Mind note states the principle: 'Hands over the ball: it FEELS like a forward press, but it isn't.' The same illusion runs in reverse. Weight that FEELS back is often pressure that's actually close to neutral — and neutral may be perfectly fine. Don't discard a setup you putt well from on the strength of a feel. FILM IT FACE-ON first. That single clip also closes the early-lift fault, the last open item from Session 8.
sections.k: Feel isn't evidence. Film it before you change anything, because comfort lies.

sections.t: What has to be true (the real checklist)
sections.b: Forget 'weight forward' as a slogan. Four things actually matter, and you can keep your comfort as long as they hold. (1) STERNUM at or just ahead of the ball. (2) HANDS level with or a touch ahead of the ball at impact — never behind it. (3) LOW POINT at or just behind the ball, so the LINK.2.1 is a HAIR ascending at contact — that slight upstroke is what produces true roll. (4) PRESSURE around 55/45 lead — enough to anchor the low point, not so much that you start steering. If your weight-back feel still delivers 1 through 3, keep it.
sections.k: Four things must be true: sternum over the ball, hands never behind, low point at or just behind it, 55/45 lead.

sections.t: One thing in your favor
sections.b: This section used to say the head would cover for you. On the LINK.2.1 it won't, and that's the honest update. The DF3i was a wide, heavy mallet — high MOI, self-squaring, happy to be swung rather than steered, and forgiving of a low point that wandered. The LINK.2.1 is a narrow blade: same zero-torque Lie Angle Balanced technology, so the FACE is still protected, but far less MOI, so a strike off the middle bleeds more distance than it used to. That doesn't change a single instruction above — it raises the stakes on all of them. Low point pinned at or just behind the ball, hands never behind it: on a mallet those were worth a little consistency, on a blade they're worth the difference between a lag that finishes and one that dies four feet short. The flip side is genuinely useful: a blade REPORTS a bad strike where a mallet muffles it, so this putter will tell you fast whether your low point is where you think it is. Listen to it.
sections.k: The blade won't cover for you the way the mallet did — but it will tell you the truth faster.

sections.t: Settle it with data
sections.b: A/B LAG LADDER — 30 feet, two blocks of 10. Block A: your current feel. Block B: the change you're testing, everything else identical. Mark where each ball STOPS and measure the spread. Tighter spread wins — that's the answer, not anyone's opinion. SOUND TEST: a purely rolling ball makes one clean click; a hopping ball adds a faint scuff a beat later — listen for the scuff. FACE-ON CLIP: check shaft lean at impact and where the head bottoms out relative to the ball. Note the weight question itself is already settled on the mat (ball off the left breast, weight stacked ON the ball) — this ladder is here as the measuring protocol for any future change, not an open question. One amendment as of Jul 30: the head changed, so the A/B is now the FIRST thing that gets run on the LINK.2.1 rather than a follow-up — you're building this putter's power curve from scratch anyway, and you may as well build it with the low point in the right place instead of calibrating around a fault.
sections.k: A/B it on the mat and let the stopping points decide, not the feel.

rules: Lead-side pressure has ONE job: pinning the low point
Sternum over the ball, hands NEVER behind it at impact
Low point at or just behind the ball = true roll
The blade reports the strike — feel isn't evidence, film it

entries.setup: 21 clips · 3× overhead + 5× ground DTL + 5× target-side + 6× face-on (1 at 120 fps) + 2× elevated overhead · L.A.B. LINK.2.1 · first full day on the new putter
entries.finding: The day in one line: tempo 2.0:1 ✓, path straight ✓, stance square ✓, early lift CLOSED ✓, address shaft dead vertical and matching the 0° design spec ✓ — and one red, the ball starting 1.5–1.7° LEFT on two of three measured putts. Path is neutral and the feet are square, so the face is pointing left at impact; aim versus closing is still unseparated. Lean at impact remains unmeasured (shaft blurs out) and pace remains untested (all mat reps, no lag work).

metrics.n: ¼–½" inside at the top, on line by impact
sole within 0.05–0.08" for 83 ms into impact
sd 0.3° over 59 frames — the 0° design spec
shaft blurs out; needs tape + 240 fps

detail.story:
Twenty-one clips across five camera positions, all in one day. Overhead (3), ground-level down-the-line (5), target-side down-the-line (5), face-on (6, one of them genuine 120 fps slow motion), and an elevated overhead showing the hands (2). This is the single record for the day.

WHAT IS NOW SETTLED. Tempo is 2.0:1 and repeatable — seven of eight down-the-line clips landed between 1.9 and 2.1, measured two independent ways that agreed. Path is straight: the head works a quarter to a half inch inside at the top and is back on the line by impact, which is SBST confirmed on the new head. The stance is square to slightly CLOSED (toe line 0.6°, 2.9°, 3.6°), so the trail-foot creep that headed the fault list for two days is fixed and closed. Early lift — open since Session 1 — is gone: at 120 fps and 37.5 px/inch the sole held within 0.05–0.08" of its address height for the full 83 ms into impact, flat across ten consecutive frames, and never dropped below address height. And the address shaft is dead vertical, repeating to a third of a degree across 59 frames, which is exactly the LINK.2.1's published 0° shaft-lean spec with the Pistol 0 grip. Lie presented at about 68° against a 69° build. The setup is doing what the putter was designed for.

THE ONE RED. Two of three overhead putts started 1.5° and 1.7° LEFT of the mat's centre line — 1.3–1.4 inches left at four feet, about two inches at six — with the third dead straight. The third putt is the control: same fixed camera, same measurement, no drift, so the left reading is real. Path measured neutral and start direction on a putt is dominated by the face, so the face was pointing left at impact. The feet are ruled out. It is aim or it is the face closing, and neither has been separated yet.

WHAT THE ELEVATED OVERHEAD ADDED. The last two clips look down from in front and catch the hands, shaft and ball together. Ball position reads correct — well forward, toward the lead foot, matching the off-the-left-breast cue — and the hands sit over the ball line with the shaft running essentially straight down, consistent with the face-on measurement. Note these two also contain practice strokes before the real one, which is worth knowing when reading them back.
detail.compare: Against Session 5 on the DF3i: that session showed 5 of 5 balls starting on the centre line by eye, and two mat blocks ran 10/10. This is the first time start line has been MEASURED in degrees, and 1.5° is small enough to have looked fine on those earlier clips — 1.3" at four feet still finds the middle of a 4.25" hole. That is exactly why it hid on the mat and showed on the course: a make at four feet, an edge at six, a miss at ten. Tempo also moved, 2.4:1 with the DF3i to 2.0:1 with the LINK — both inside the window, the blade perhaps wanting a slightly quicker transition.
detail.limits:
Lean AT impact is still not measured, and that is a measurement failure rather than a finding: the thin black shaft blurs against a dim floor at impact speed, only one frame in the window fit reliably, and two independent methods disagreed on it by 1.6° — the size of the effect itself. White tape on the shaft, 240 fps and more light fixes it.

The two elevated-overhead clips could not be measured numerically at all. They are dim (mean brightness 78 of 255), not slow motion (22.6 and 25.7 fps), and shot from an angle where a vertical object's projection depends on where it sits relative to the camera — so absolute shaft lean cannot be recovered from them. They are a good qualitative check on ball position and a poor instrument for hands and shaft. Face-on remains the angle for that question.

Also untouched: face ANGLE, which no face-on camera can see and which is what separates aimed-left from closing-through-impact. That needs the overhead. And pace — every clip today was a flat mat rep with no lag work, so the fault with the least evidence against it still has none.

briefing.focus: UPDATED Jul 30. LINK.2.1 + Pistol 0: zero built-in press, and film confirms a DEAD VERTICAL shaft at address — which puts your hands about 1.3" BEHIND the ball, and that is correct geometry rather than a fault. The old 'hands even with the ball' cue is retired. GET LOW, TRAIL FOOT back, hands over the clubhead.

sections.t: THE HEADLINE — get low
sections.b: Your words, and they go at the top of the plan rather than the bottom of a setup list: bending over is the most massive thing, and getting low is where you feel most comfortable. That is the feel to remember when everything else has drifted. If you only carry one thought to the practice green, carry this one — not the press, not the rehearsals, not the pace word. Deep bend, stand close, eyes down.
sections.k: Bend over and get low — that's the anchor feel everything else hangs off.

sections.t: Why the bend is more than comfort
sections.b: Two real mechanisms sit under that feel. FIRST — the LINK.2.1 is Lie Angle Balanced, exactly like the DF3i was, and that balance is only true when the shaft is presented at the lie angle it was built for. Stand too tall or too far away and the toe drops, the shaft leaves its designed lie, and the zero-torque property you switched putters for quietly degrades. Posture is what delivers the technology — and that is just as true of the blade as it was of the mallet. It also makes the build spec non-negotiable: your DF3i was 34", set flat. Confirm the LINK is the same before you read anything into how it rolls. SECOND — more bend lets the arms hang freer and tilts the shoulders onto a STEEPER plane, and a steeper shoulder plane is what produces a straight-back-straight-through stroke. Standing tall flattens that plane and builds an arc into the stroke whether you want one or not. Your stroke is SBST on film. The deep bend is the posture that matches it.
sections.k: The bend isn't comfort: it presents the lie the putter needs, and steepens the shoulder plane that makes the stroke straight.

sections.t: The setup
sections.b:
BEND OVER, stand close, eyes down through the strike. Ball off the LEFT BREAST. Weight stacked ON the ball — pressure over it, not on the trail foot. TRAIL FOOT a touch BACK — it creeps forward on its own and opens you. Rock the shoulders, no hands. Loose grip.

THE HANDS CUE IS RETIRED. It used to read 'hands EVEN with the ball; the grip's built-in 2° supplies the lean.' Both halves of that died with the Press Pistol. Overhead stills measured Jul 30 show what actually happens now: the shaft sits essentially vertical (+1.3° projected, fitted over 970 rows of shaft) and your hands sit about 1.35 INCHES BEHIND the centre of the ball.

That is not a fault and there is nothing to fix. It is pure geometry. With the face resting against the ball, the ball's centre is half a ball ahead of the face — 0.84" — and on a heel-shafted putter the shaft axis sits roughly another half inch behind the face. Add them up and a perfectly vertical shaft puts your hands about 1.3" behind the ball. The old cue was only ever reachable because the Press Pistol's 2° leaned the shaft for you. With a Pistol 0 you cannot have hands-over-ball AND a vertical shaft, and the vertical shaft is the one the putter was built around.

THE CUE NOW: hands over the CLUBHEAD. Let them sit where a hanging shaft puts them. They arrive level with the ball at impact anyway, because by then the head has travelled forward to meet it — which is exactly the 'level, never behind' rule your low-point plan asks for.
sections.k: Hands sit over the CLUBHEAD, about a ball and a half behind the ball — that's what a vertical shaft gives you.

sections.t: THE PRESS — settled from first principles
sections.b:
Start from what you are actually holding. The Pistol 0 is L.A.B.'s NEUTRAL grip — the zero in the name is zero built-in press. That is a deliberate design choice on a lie-angle-balanced putter: the whole premise is a head that squares itself when the shaft is presented at its designed lie and the hands stop interfering. A neutral grip is what lets that happen. Your film says the presentation is already right — lie at about 68° as built, shaft vertical, repeating to a third of a degree across 59 frames.

So the recommendation is: DO NOT add lean with your hands. Not because a press is dangerous — with a neutral grip it cannot push loft below zero the way it could on the old setup — but because this configuration is already delivering what it was engineered to deliver, and your address repeatability is the best number on your card. Adding a hand-made lean would replace a position that repeats to 0.3° with one that depends on feel, on the day, under pressure. That is a bad trade on any putter and a particularly bad one on a putter whose entire selling point is that it does not need your hands.

Keep a trigger if it helps you start the motion — a soft press moved with the body is fine. Its job is RHYTHM only. The single rule that matters is that it is IDENTICAL every putt, because a press that varies is a loft that varies is a pace that varies, and pace is the open fault.
sections.k: Don't manufacture lean with your hands. The Pistol 0 and a vertical shaft are what this putter was built for.

sections.t: What this putter needs from the setup
sections.b:
A lie-angle-balanced putter makes one demand of you and it is not a stroke demand: present the shaft at the lie it was built for. Get that wrong — stand tall, reach for it — and the toe drops, the shaft leaves its designed lie, and the self-squaring property you bought degrades. That is why the deep bend matters mechanically here and not just for comfort, and the Jul 30 film says you are doing it: presentation measured around 68°, which is the window these are built in.

Everything else in this routine came from film of YOUR stroke — path, shoulder plane, stance line, trigger — so none of it is putter-specific and none of it changes. The two things that ARE this putter's business are the lie presentation above and your AIM PICTURE, because a narrow blade topline frames the target differently from a mallet and start line is the open fault. Re-check aim with a stick; leave the stroke alone.
sections.k: Present the shaft at its built lie and re-check your aim picture. Leave the stroke alone.

sections.t: THE TRAIL FOOT — the alignment leak
sections.b: Self-reported Jul 29 and worth taking seriously: your right foot creeps UP — forward, toward the target line — and it drags the stance line open with it. Open the feet and the shoulders follow, so you end up aimed LEFT of where you think you are. The fix is exactly what you said: set that trail foot a touch further back than feels natural. Expect it to feel CLOSED, like you're aimed right. That feeling is the correction, not an error — you're recalibrating off an open baseline, so square will read as closed until it beds in. Trust the line you set, not the feel, for the first few sessions.
sections.k: Your trail foot creeps forward, opens the stance and aims you left. Set it back — square will feel closed.

sections.t: Why it wrecks the takeaway specifically
sections.b: Because in an SBST stroke the shoulder line IS the track. There's no arc to absorb a misaligned setup — 'straight back' is straight back along whatever line your shoulders are on, so an open stance doesn't just aim you left, it points the whole stroke left. Then one of two things happens, and both are bad: you feel it immediately and manipulate the takeaway to save it, which puts the HANDS back in charge of a stroke built to have no hands in it — or you don't, and the ball starts left. That's why a stance error shows up as a takeaway problem. The takeaway is fine; it's obeying a line that's wrong.
sections.k: In a straight stroke the shoulder line IS the track, so an open stance points the whole stroke left.

sections.t: This is the miss the putter can't fix
sections.b: Your signature miss is LEFT on short putts — the through-line of the entire putter saga, and it showed up AGAIN on the course Jul 29 with a zero-torque putter in your hands. That is the most useful data point you've generated in weeks, because it rules the head out. A perfectly square face aimed at a target that's left of the hole produces precisely that miss, and no putter ever built will save you from it. Zero-torque guarantees the FACE stays square; it cannot guarantee the face is square TO THE RIGHT THING. Note the split that makes the case: your last two 10-ball blocks started 10/10 on line on the mat, and then you pulled it on grass. Stance creep is a course-and-pressure fault — mat reps are exactly where it wouldn't show. And one thing to redo with the new putter: you changed sight lines. A narrow blade topline frames the target differently from a wide mallet, so re-run the alignment-stick check in your first LINK session and don't assume your aim carried over.
sections.k: A square face aimed at the wrong target still misses left, and no putter can fix that.

sections.t: The check that costs nothing
sections.b: Lay a club or an alignment stick down the target line just outside the ball on the practice green and set up to it — your toes should run PARALLEL to it, not converging toward it. Ten seconds, and it recalibrates the feel. The structural safeguard is already in your routine: aim the FACE to the spot FIRST, then build the stance around it. Keep that order religiously. If you build the stance first, the face gets aimed to a crooked body; if you aim the face first and the stance then creeps, the mismatch shows up as discomfort — and discomfort you can feel is information you can act on.
sections.k: Alignment stick on the practice green: toes parallel, not converging. Ten seconds, recalibrates the feel.

sections.t: THE TRIGGER — settled: soft press, moved with the body
sections.b: Keep the soft press — a genuinely small one, made as the body starts to move. But understand that its JOB has changed. With the Press Pistol it was pure rhythm, because the grip was already supplying the lean and any extra was double-counting; that is why 'keep it tiny' was such a hard rule and why a held press was such a problem on Jul 29. With a neutral grip there is no lean coming from anywhere else, so a soft press is now the ONLY forward lean in the stroke rather than a surplus on top of it. The old warning relaxes accordingly: a small press can no longer stack loft off the bottom of the scale. It still wants to be soft and it still wants to move with the body — that is what makes it release instead of being held — but it is no longer a thing to be afraid of.
sections.k: Keep the soft press, but its only job now is rhythm — it isn't supplying lean any more.

sections.t: The one rule — softness IS the safeguard
sections.b:
REWRITTEN Jul 30. The old rule existed because the press was adding lean on top of a grip that already had 2° built in, so a firm press pushed the effective loft below zero and the ball got driven into the turf. That arithmetic is gone. Starting from vertical, a soft press moves you toward the loft you used to deliver, not past it.

So the rule now is CONSISTENCY rather than smallness: same press, same size, every putt. A press that varies is a loft that varies, which is a PACE that varies — and pace is the fault with the least evidence against it. The two drift signals still apply: if it starts to feel FIRM, or like a POSITION you sit in rather than a motion you pass through, it has crept back toward a hold.
sections.k: The rule is consistency, not smallness: same press, same size, every putt.

sections.t: If it creeps back into a hold
sections.b: The alternatives stay on the shelf rather than getting deleted, because you may want one later: THE FLOAT — lift the head a hair off the turf before takeaway; no hand action at all and it removes ground friction. THE WHOLE-PUTTER WAGGLE — small forward-and-back from the shoulders, wrists silent. THE LEAD-SHOULDER SETTLE — a soft downward press of the shoulder that already runs the stroke. THE TRAIL-KNEE KICK — furthest from the hands, and the same trigger your full-swing routine uses. Any of them will break inertia without the hands touching shaft lean. You don't need one right now.
sections.k: Alternatives on the shelf if the press ever creeps back into a hold — float, waggle, shoulder settle, knee kick.

sections.t: How to tell it's releasing
sections.b: One face-on clip settles it: compare shaft lean at ADDRESS with shaft lean at IMPACT. Close to equal means the soft press is passing through the way it should. Meaningfully more at impact means it's being carried in, whatever it felt like — and feel is exactly what got this wrong the first time. The free check needs no camera: a purely rolling ball makes one clean click, a ball driven down into the green adds a faint scuff a beat later. Listen for the scuff.
sections.k: One face-on clip settles it: shaft lean at address versus at impact. No camera? Listen for the scuff.

sections.t: Stop shopping
sections.b: Straight talk, because you called it yourself. That's three putters in a month, and the DF3i got 12 days and not one calibrated lag session before you convicted it. Twelve days isn't enough to convict a putter — it's enough to convict a power curve you never built. The swap itself is defensible: you kept zero-torque and you changed shape, which is a real preference and not a mistake. What isn't survivable is doing it again in two weeks. So the LINK gets a gate: two weeks, a 20-ball 5-footer test and a 30-foot lag ladder each week, and the verdict comes off those numbers rather than off an afternoon's feel. Keep the DF3i in the bullpen until then — don't sell it. And keep the stroke frozen while the head is the variable: the deep bend and the soft press were both decided from clear feel and both are mechanically sound. One variable at a time.
sections.k: Three putters in a month. Change things on film evidence, not on an afternoon's feeling.

sections.t: Why beside the ball and not behind it
sections.b: Rehearsing in your true putting posture — same deep bend, same arm hang, same shoulder plane — means the stroke that FEELS like 30 feet is the stroke you actually make. Magnitude transfers one-to-one. Rehearsing from behind the ball reads the break better, but you're standing upright there, so the size you feel is only an approximation. Your open fault is pace magnitude, not reading: path ✓, face ✓, start lines 10/10 twice over. Optimise the thing that's broken.
sections.k: Rehearse in your real posture beside the ball, because magnitude transfers one-to-one that way.

sections.t: Keep the order of the two rehearsals
sections.b: Ball-look first (path and contact), hole-look second (pace). The last thing you feel is the thing you carry in — so the pace stroke must be the last one. If the hole stroke ever drifts to first, the pace feel gets overwritten by the contact feel and you're back to guessing distance. Finish rehearsal 2 WITH the soft press, at its real size: it's the one part of the stroke that never used to get a practice rep, which is how it drifted last time without you noticing.
sections.k: Ball-look first, hole-look second — the last thing you feel is what you carry in.

sections.t: Two rules underneath it
sections.b: SAME BEAT COUNT, EVERY PUTT — a routine that varies in length is itself a pace variable, and the putts where you take an extra look are the ones that come up short. And a VERBAL BACKSTOP is worth testing: say the pace intention right before the press ('die it a foot past', 'back of the cup'). Feel decays, a word doesn't.
sections.k: Same beat count every putt, and try saying the pace intention out loud before the press.

sections.t: Still to test — lags
sections.b: This is no longer a someday item — it's the top of the card. Yesterday's round was lags coming up SHORT and short putts running HOT, which is not two faults but one: a power curve you haven't learned, so you under-hit the long ones and over-hit the short ones. A new head resets that curve to zero, so the reps have to be deliberate. The block test, twice a week: 10 balls from 30 feet, and measure the SPREAD of stopping points plus how many finish short. Then the experiment worth running while you're there — past ~25 feet, keep your eyes ON THE HOLE through the actual stroke, not just the rehearsal. Feels absurd, works well; the ball isn't moving, you don't need to watch it. 10 eyes-on-ball vs 10 eyes-on-hole, same session, compare the spreads.
sections.k: Past 25 feet, test keeping your eyes ON THE HOLE through the stroke. Block test, not mid-round.

steps: Read it from BEHIND the ball — pick the line and a spot a few inches ahead of it
Step BESIDE the ball — BEND OVER, stand close, full putting posture
Rehearsal 1 — eyes on the BALL. Path and contact.
Rehearsal 2 — eyes on the HOLE. Pace. Finish it with the soft press.
Step in — set the FACE to the spot first, then build the stance around it (trail foot a touch BACK)
Spot → ball → soft press with the body → putt
rules: GET LOW — the deep bend is what presents the lie this putter needs
TRAIL FOOT back — square will feel closed
Hands over the CLUBHEAD — that's ~1.3" behind the ball, and it's correct
No hand-made lean — the trigger is rhythm only, identical every putt
Aim the FACE first, then build the stance to it

briefing.focus: Jack's own swing thoughts & setup keys, in his words — the go-to reference before a round or a range session. Grip settled: conventional. Putting routine locked Jul 28.

sections.t: Driver — the big stick
sections.b: Aim the CENTER of the fairway — the start line tends to pull left, so center-aim leaves room. The straight ball comes from a LONGER, fuller swing — commit to that one. A tighter, shorter swing turns it into a cut, and when that goes wrong the miss is a PUSH-SLICE. So: full swing for straight; if you shorten it, expect the cut and know the push-slice is the bad one.
sections.k: Aim centre — your start line pulls left, and the straight ball needs a LONGER swing, not a tighter one.

sections.t: Mini driver
sections.b: Club setup: the r7 Quad's adjustable WEIGHTS are set in the BACK position. Tee it LOW for the piercing straight ball — NEVER at normal driver-tee height. From that setup you can work it both ways, draw or fade. This is the fairway-finder off the tee; weights back + low tee is what makes it behave.
sections.k: Weights back, teed LOW for the piercing ball. This is the fairway-finder, not a second driver.

sections.t: Irons
sections.b: Ball position right of center, toward the trail (right) thigh. The new KING TECs fly HIGHER and longer than the old set — trust the extra height. When you need to flight it down or take something off, CHOKE DOWN and hit the control shot rather than just swinging soft.
sections.k: Ball back toward the trail thigh; the KING TECs fly higher than the old set, so trust the height.

sections.t: Wedges
sections.b: (Open — fill in as you dial the Vokeys: your go-to feels for full vs. partial, and any open-face/flop keys. Ladder to stay honest: 60°→80 · 56°→95 · 50°→108 · PW→122.)
sections.k: Open — fill in your Vokey feels as you dial them. Ladder: 60°→80 · 56°→95 · 50°→108 · PW→122.

sections.t: Putting — LINK.2.1
sections.b: Ball off the LEFT BREAST — chest reference, not foot: the arc centers on your sternum, so the cue survives a change in stance width. WEIGHT STACKED ON THE BALL — that's what pins the low point. Rock the SHOULDERS, no hands. LOOSE grip. AT ADDRESS the hands sit over the CLUBHEAD, which puts them about 1.35" BEHIND the ball — measured Jul 30, and it is correct: a vertical shaft plus a face resting on the ball can't put them anywhere else. Don't chase hands-over-ball; that was a Press Pistol cue and the grip is a Pistol 0 now; the PRESS is a separate trigger that starts the stroke — same size every time or the loft changes and pace goes with it. Bend over MORE, stand CLOSE, eyes DOWN through the strike. ROUTINE: read and pick your spot from behind → step BESIDE the ball in full posture and take two rehearsals, eyes-on-ball then eyes-on-hole (the hole one is the PACE stroke — keep it last, and finish it with the press) → step in, face to the spot first, then stance → spot, ball, press, go. Grip settled: conventional / reverse-overlap.
sections.k: Ball off the left breast, weight stacked on it, shoulders rock — and hands over the CLUBHEAD, not the ball.

rules: Driver: aim centre, swing LONGER not tighter
Mini driver: tee it LOW, weights back
Irons: trust the extra height, choke down to flight it
Putter: hands even, shoulders rock, no hands

entries.setup: 23 clips + 4 stills · 3× overhead + 5× ground DTL + 5× target-side + 6× face-on (1 at 120 fps) + 2× elevated overhead, plus address & contact stills · L.A.B. LINK.2.1
entries.finding: The day in one line: tempo 2.0:1 ✓, path straight ✓, stance square ✓, early lift CLOSED ✓, address shaft dead vertical matching the 0° design spec ✓, and hands measured 1.35" BEHIND the ball at address — which is correct geometry for a vertical shaft on a heel-shafted putter, not a fault (it retires the old 'hands even with the ball' cue). One red: the ball starting 1.5–1.7° LEFT on two of three measured putts, with a neutral path and square feet, so the face is pointing left at impact. Lean AT impact still unmeasured — the two contact stills disagree by more than the effect.

club.spec: 34" ✓ · Zero-torque (Lie Angle Balanced) · wide high-MOI mallet · ACCRA x L.A.B. Black shaft · L.A.B. Press Pistol 2° grip
club.note: THE PUTTER. Bought Jul 18 · PGA Tour Superstore · 34" confirmed, sole set flat. Back in the bag Aug 1 after the Beekman scramble — putted great, and the LINK.2.1's two-week gate closed early in the mallet's favour. Zero-torque, so the SBST fix that started this whole saga is intact, and a wide high-MOI head forgives an off-centre strike far more than the blade did. Two things carry: the pace complaint that benched it on Jul 30 was never tested (not one calibrated lag session), so treat this head as having no proven fault — just a power curve you never built. And the GRIP comes back with it: the Press Pistol 2° supplies the shaft lean, so 'hands EVEN with the ball' is the correct cue again and any forward press stays tiny. The vertical-shaft, hands-1.35"-behind geometry belonged to the LINK's Pistol 0 — don't carry it across.

IN STORAGE from Aug 1 — out of the bag after the DF3i won the scramble outright. Nothing on the card convicts this head: it produced the best measured numbers of the whole project (tempo 2.0:1 across seven of eight clips, address repeating to 0.3° over 59 frames, stance square, early lift closed). It loses on REDUNDANCY, not performance — two L.A.B. zero-torque putters do one job and only one can be gamed. LIKELY RETURNING: find the receipt and confirm the return window before it lapses, then make it a decision rather than a default. If it goes back, the L.A.B. Pistol 0 grip goes with it.

entries.text: L.A.B. LINK.2.1 → L.A.B. DF3i: the mallet is back after the Aug 1 Beekman scramble and the gate is closed early. LINK.2.1 to storage and probably back to the shop — liked it, but two zero-torque L.A.B. putters is one too many.

EQUIPMENT — Settle the LINK.2.1 before the return window lapses: find the receipt, confirm the deadline, write the date down, then decide keep-or-return deliberately. You're leaning return and the reasoning is sound — you like the putter, but you shouldn't own two zero-torque L.A.B. heads. If it goes back the Pistol 0 grip goes with it; the DF3i keeps its Press Pistol 2°. And whichever way it lands, keep the DF3i and the Newport 2 — one spare is enough, and that slot is already filled.

PUTTING — Same two tests, now on the DF3i (~7 minutes). (1) Hang it from the top of the grip and tap heel-to-toe with an eraser; the spot with NO twist is the true sweet spot — mark it and note where it sits against the sight line. (2) Tape or foot-spray the face, hit 10 putts, photograph the strike pattern. A heel strike closes the face and starts the ball LEFT, which is exactly the 1.5–1.7° miss measured overhead. The wide mallet punishes an off-centre hit less than the blade did, so this matters somewhat less than it did on the LINK — but strike location has never been measured on any putter you own, and it's still the cheapest untested explanation for the left start.

PUTTING — The 30-ft LAG LADDER, twice a week, on the DF3i: 10 balls, log the SPREAD of stopping points and how many finish SHORT. Target no more than 1 in 10 short. This is the single thing that never happened in the DF3i's first 12 days — the pace complaint that benched it on Jul 30 was a feeling, not a number, and building this curve is what stops the next afternoon's feel from moving a putter again.

PUTTING — Bed in the settled stroke on the DF3i: deep bend / stand close, and the SOFT press moved with the body. NOTE THE GRIP REVERSION — the Press Pistol 2° is back, so it supplies the lean on its own and the press must stay genuinely TINY; that 'don't double-count the lean' rule went quiet on the Pistol 0 and is live again. Confirm on one face-on clip: shaft lean at address versus at impact. The stroke does NOT change because the head did.

PUTTING — Before the next face-on set: wrap WHITE TAPE around the shaft ~6" above the head, switch Slo-Mo to 240 fps (Settings › Camera › Record Slo-mo › 1080p/240), lights on. The angle is already right — the only thing blocking the shaft-lean verdict is that a thin black shaft blurs out against a dim floor at impact speed. What you're measuring has changed with the head: on the DF3i's Press Pistol 2° expect roughly 2° of lean already there at address, and the question is whether it holds to impact or gets added to.

faults.why: THE fault, and it survives the head change — which is the most useful thing about it. Overhead film Jul 30 measured 1.5° and 1.7° LEFT on two of three putts — 1.3–1.4" left at 4 ft, ~2" at 6 ft — with the third dead straight and a neutral measured path. Not equipment (it has now outlived three putters), not the stance (toe line measured 0.6–3.6° CLOSED). Three candidates remain: aim, face-at-impact, and strike location. Re-test it the way it was measured — overhead, five putts, roll versus the mat centre line — on the DF3i this time, and target a median inside 0.5°.

THE priority now. The DF3i is back and it still has no distance baseline — it got 12 days and not one calibrated lag session before being convicted for short lags and hot short putts, which is one fault (an unlearned power curve), not two. What changed with the head: a wide high-MOI mallet holds ball speed better on an off-centre strike than the blade did, so its curve should be the more repeatable of the two once you actually build it. 30-ft lag ladder twice a week: log spread, how many finish SHORT, and whether each miss was pace or strike. Target no more than 1 in 10 short.

Still never measured, on any putter, not once — but the stakes drop with the mallet back. A strike toward the HEEL rotates the face closed and starts the ball LEFT, precisely the measured miss. The LINK made this urgent because a narrow blade carries less MOI and twists more for the same distance off centre, and because its riser hosel meant the shaft was a poor guide to where the head's mass sat. The DF3i is wide, deep and high-MOI, so the same miss costs less — less, not nothing. Seven minutes settles it: tap test to find the sweet spot, tape test to find the strike, compare.

Reopened by the grip reversion. With the LINK's Pistol 0 there was no built-in lean to protect and the only question was repeatability. The DF3i's Press Pistol 2° supplies real lean at address, which brings back the old failure mode: a press added on top of it stacks loft off the bottom of the scale and drives the ball into the turf. One slo-mo face-on set — white tape on the shaft, 240 fps, lights on — compares lean at address with lean at impact and settles it.

CLOSED Jul 30 ✓. At 120 fps and 37.5 px/inch the sole held within 0.05–0.08" of its address height for the full 83 ms into impact, flat across ten consecutive frames, and never dropped below address height. The rise afterwards is the follow-through arc. Measured on the LINK, but this is a stroke property rather than a head property — it should carry. Wants two more slo-mo strokes on sample size, and the next face-on set gives them for free.
CLOSED Jul 30 ✓ — overhead film measured the toe line 0.6°, 2.9° and 3.6° CLOSED to the target line across three reps. Never open.

metrics.name: Path
metrics.verdict: SETTLED — straight (SBST) across 20+ clips and four putters. Measured again Jul 30: ¼–½" inside at the top, back on the line by impact. Path is yours, not the putter's, which is why the head going back to the DF3i doesn't reopen it.

metrics.name: Tempo / load
metrics.verdict: SETTLED — 2.0:1 measured on the LINK.2.1, seven of eight clips between 1.9 and 2.1, two independent ways. Was 2.4:1 on the DF3i, which is the head now back in play. Both sit inside the window; stop checking this one.

metrics.name: Face at impact
metrics.verdict: REOPENED Jul 30 — zero-torque guarantees the face won't TWIST, and it doesn't. It cannot guarantee where the face POINTS, and on 2 of 3 measured putts it pointed ~1.5° left at impact. Aimed there or closed through: only a face-on clip separates them, and that clip is now owed on the DF3i.

metrics.name: Early lift
metrics.verdict: CLOSED Jul 30 ✓ — the sole held within 0.05–0.08" of address height for the full 83 ms into impact, flat across ten consecutive frames. The oldest open item on the card, finally shut. It's a stroke property, not a head property, so it carries back to the mallet — but take two more slo-mo strokes on sample size.

metrics.name: Start line / aim
metrics.verdict: THE FAULT, and it outlived the putter. 1.5° and 1.7° LEFT on two of three overhead putts — 1.3–1.4" left at 4 ft, ~2" at 6 ft — with one dead straight. Small enough to hide on the mat, big enough to miss from 6 feet. Re-measure on the DF3i, and note that its wider topline frames the target differently again: re-run the alignment-stick check, don't assume aim carried over.

metrics.name: Stance line
metrics.verdict: NEW and CLOSED on arrival. Measured off the overhead frames: the toe line ran 0.6°, 2.9° and 3.6° CLOSED to the target line — never open on any rep. The trail-foot creep is fixed. Look higher for the aim leak.

briefing.focus: Aug 1, Beekman scramble. The DF3i went back in, putted great, and the LINK.2.1's two-week gate closes early in the mallet's favour. The DF3i is the putter going forward; the LINK goes to storage and probably back to the shop. This plan is the record of what got decided, the one setup change that comes back with it, and the two things left to do before the decision is actually finished.
rules: The DF3i is the putter — the head is settled, stop shopping
The LINK didn't fail; it lost on redundancy
Press Pistol 2° is back: hands EVEN with the ball, press stays tiny
Build the power curve you never built — lag ladder, twice a week
Find the LINK's return window before it lapses

sections.t: What actually got decided
sections.k: The right head, on thin evidence — so build the number this time.
sections.b:
The scramble was the DF3i's first round back and it putted great. That settles which head goes in the bag, and it's a good landing: you're back on the putter you've rolled your best with, it's still zero-torque, and the SBST mismatch that started this entire saga stays buried.

Worth being straight about the evidence, though. That's one round — and a scramble, where you're often putting after a teammate has already shown you the line and the pace. It is the friendliest putting environment that exists. That doesn't make the decision wrong; it makes it under-supported, which matters only because under-supported is exactly how the DF3i got benched twelve days ago. A feeling on the course put it out and a feeling on the course put it back. The fix is the same either way: build the pace number, and the decision stops depending on how any single afternoon went.

sections.t: The LINK didn't fail — worth saying plainly
sections.k: It lost on redundancy, not performance. Two zero-torque L.A.B. putters do one job.
sections.b:
Nothing on your card convicts the LINK.2.1. It produced the best measured numbers of the whole project: tempo 2.0:1 across seven of eight clips, an address position repeating to a third of a degree over 59 frames, a stance line measured square, and early lift closed for the first time since Session 1. What it never got was a pace baseline — the same thing the DF3i never got.

So your read is the right one, and it's the honest version: you like the putter, and you shouldn't own two. That's a redundancy call, not a performance call. Keeping both would mean two heads, two power curves, and a live temptation to switch every time a short one lipped out — which is precisely the loop that produced three putters in a month.

sections.t: The grip change comes back with it
sections.k: Press Pistol 2° means hands EVEN with the ball again — the vertical-shaft geometry was the LINK's, not yours.
sections.b:
This is the one thing that quietly changes your setup, and it's easy to miss because it looks like nothing.

The LINK ships with a L.A.B. Pistol 0 — zero built-in press — and the Jul 30 film measured exactly what that produces: a dead vertical shaft at address with your hands about 1.35" BEHIND the ball. Correct geometry for that putter, and the routine plan was rewritten around it.

The DF3i carries the Press Pistol 2°, and that grip leans the shaft for you. So the cue reverts: HANDS EVEN with the ball, and the grip supplies the lean. Do not carry the 'hands over the clubhead' feel across — on this grip it would be lean on top of lean.

And the rule that travelled with it is live again: keep any forward press genuinely TINY. With 2° already built in, a firm press pushes effective loft off the bottom of the scale and drives the ball into the turf. On the Pistol 0 there was no lean to double-count and that warning relaxed. On the DF3i it doesn't.

sections.t: What the mallet gives you back
sections.k: High MOI means an off-centre strike costs less — the strike question drops down the list, it doesn't disappear.
sections.b:
The DF3i is a wide, deep, high-MOI mallet; the LINK.2.1 is a narrow blade. In practice that means an off-centre strike on the mallet bleeds less ball speed and twists the head less than the same miss on the blade. That takes real pressure off the strike-location question that opened on Jul 30.

It does not close it. A heel strike still closes the face and still starts the ball left, which is still your signature miss, and strike location has never once been measured on any putter you own. The tap test and the tape test are seven minutes. Run them on the mallet.

The flip side is the honest cost of the swap: a blade REPORTS a bad strike where a mallet muffles it. The DF3i is more forgiving and less informative. That raises the value of measuring rather than feeling — which, given how this month has gone, is the theme.

sections.t: The one thing that has to happen this time
sections.k: Twelve days and no lag ladder is what benched the DF3i. Build the power curve.
sections.b:
The DF3i was convicted on Jul 30 for lags coming up short and short putts running hot. That is not two faults — it's one power curve you hadn't learned, so you under-hit the long ones and over-hit the short ones. And it got convicted without a single calibrated lag session, which means the complaint was never actually tested against the head.

So the standing item, twice a week: 10 balls from 30 feet, log the SPREAD of the stopping points and how many finish SHORT. Target no more than 1 in 10 short. That one number would have saved you the whole detour, and it is still the cheapest thing on the card.

sections.t: Before the window closes
sections.k: Find the receipt and the deadline, then decide keep-or-return on purpose.
sections.b:
You're leaning return, and the reasoning holds. Make it a decision rather than a lapse: find the receipt, confirm the return window, and put the date somewhere you will actually see it.

If it goes back, the Pistol 0 goes with it. If the window has already closed the answer changes on its own — you keep it, it sits in storage as the control, and you don't game it.

One caution either way: don't clear the shelf to make room. The Newport 2 is the bullpen blade and the DF3i is the gamer; one spare is enough, and that slot is already filled.

sections.t: Stop shopping — the version that applies now
sections.k: The head is settled. From here the next thing that changes should be a number, not a putter.
sections.b:
The line from the routine plan, updated for where you actually are: that was three putters in a month, and the head has now settled on the one you've putted best with. The rule from here is simple — the next thing that changes is a NUMBER on the card, not a head in the bag.

Path: settled. Tempo: settled. Stance line: square. Early lift: closed. What's open is start line and pace, and neither of those has ever been a shopping problem.

briefing.focus: UPDATED Aug 2. The DF3i is back and so is its Press Pistol 2° grip — which means the grip supplies the shaft lean again and the cue reverts to HANDS EVEN WITH THE BALL. The vertical-shaft, hands-1.35"-behind geometry measured on Jul 30 was true of the LINK's Pistol 0 and is retired with it. Everything that came off film of YOUR stroke is unchanged: GET LOW, TRAIL FOOT back, rock the shoulders.

sections.t: THE HEADLINE — get low
sections.b: Your words, and they go at the top of the plan rather than the bottom of a setup list: bending over is the most massive thing, and getting low is where you feel most comfortable. That is the feel to remember when everything else has drifted. If you only carry one thought to the practice green, carry this one — not the press, not the rehearsals, not the pace word. Deep bend, stand close, eyes down.
sections.k: Bend over and get low — that's the anchor feel everything else hangs off.

sections.t: Why the bend is more than comfort
sections.b: Two real mechanisms sit under that feel. FIRST — the DF3i is Lie Angle Balanced, and that balance is only true when the shaft is presented at the lie angle it was built for. Stand too tall or too far away and the toe drops, the shaft leaves its designed lie, and the zero-torque property this whole project was built on quietly degrades.
