club.note: THE PUTTER from Aug 10 — back in the bag by choice, one day after the keep decision that had it down as the indoor practice head. The DF3i goes to the bullpen; do NOT sell either until this one has an actual scoreboard. GRIP CUE FLIPS BACK: this carries the L.A.B. Pistol 0, zero built-in press, so the shaft stands DEAD VERTICAL at address and your hands sit about 1.35" BEHIND the ball — measured on film Jul 30, repeatable to 0.3°. That is the correct geometry for this putter. The 'hands EVEN with the ball' cue belongs to the DF3i's Press Pistol 2° and must not be carried across: on a 0°-lean, 2°-effective-loft build it is lean you are adding by hand, and it delofts a face that has almost nothing to give. Don't manufacture lean — let the putter sit where it was designed to sit. WHAT COMES WITH IT: the only two reds on the evolution grid — face at impact and the 1.5–1.7° LEFT start line — were both measured on THIS head on Jul 30, and the DF3i's first filmed column carried none. So the swap re-opens the start-line question rather than settling it. Narrow blade means less MOI than the mallet, so a heel strike twists the face closed harder for the same miss — which is exactly your signature miss — and strike location has still never been measured on any putter you own. That makes the tape test MORE urgent, not less. In its favour: tempo measured 2.0:1 on this head against 2.4:1 on the DF3i, and 2:1 is the target. Every measurement from here runs on this putter.

OUT OF THE BAG Aug 10 — the LINK.2.1 goes back in and this becomes the bullpen mallet. HOLD IT, don't sell: it has the only real scoreboard either head owns (8/10 from four feet, Jul 20), it was never convicted of anything measured, and it is the high-MOI control if the blade's start line misbehaves again. The Press Pistol 2° stays on it and is NOT to be swapped — Lie Angle Balance is a property of the assembled club, grip included. GUARD, and this is the live one: the two putters ask for different hands. Press Pistol 2° = hands EVEN with the ball, the grip supplies the lean. Pistol 0 on the LINK = shaft vertical, hands ~1.35" behind. Don't roll a set on this head and walk straight to the gamer, or the other way — reset the hands on whichever one you're about to play. If the LINK gets filmed, film a DF3i set alongside it: tempo ran 2.4:1 here against 2.0:1 on the blade, so transfer between the two is still not proven in either direction.

entries.text: L.A.B. LINK.2.1 back in the bag Aug 10 — gamer again, one day after being kept as the indoor practice putter. DF3i to the bullpen (held, not sold: it owns the only measured scoreboard, 8/10 from four feet on Jul 20). Setup reverts with the head: Pistol 0 means shaft vertical and hands ~1.35" behind the ball; the 'hands even' cue stays with the DF3i's Press Pistol 2°.

PUTTING — RUN THE TAPE TEST on the LINK.2.1 (~12 min, at home). Moved to the LINK on Aug 10 with the bag change, and it matters MORE on this head: a narrow blade carries less MOI than the DF3i mallet, so a heel strike twists the face closed harder for the same distance off centre — and the 1.5–1.7° LEFT start line on the grid was measured on this putter. Full protocol is in the 'Tape Test — Where You Actually Hit It' plan. Short version: (1) hang the putter from the top of the grip and tap the face heel-to-toe with an eraser — the spot with NO twist is the true sweet spot, mark it with tape and check it against the sight line. (2) Coat the face with foot-powder spray, hit 10 from 5 ft, photograph; re-coat, hit 10 from 30 ft, photograph. Don't wipe between putts. This is the last cheap untested thing on your card and it's the only candidate that explains BOTH open faults — a heel strike closes the face (starts it LEFT) and bleeds ball speed (lags SHORT). Send the two photos. If you want the comparison that settles the head question, run the same two sheets on the DF3i afterwards.

briefing.focus: Aug 10. The LINK.2.1 goes back in the bag and the DF3i goes to the bullpen — one day after the keep decision had the LINK down as the indoor practice head. This replaces the 'DF3i Confirmed' plan, which is now wrong in the one place it mattered most: the setup cue. The grip changes with the head, the start-line question re-opens with it, and the measurement work moves across. Nothing else about the project changes — the head is a preference call, the faults are still open, and the next thing that changes should be a number.

sections.t: The setup change that comes with the head
sections.k: Hands go BACK behind the ball again — carrying the DF3i's cue across would add lean this putter isn't built for.
sections.b:
This is the one thing in the swap that can actually cost you strokes, and it looks like nothing.

The LINK ships with a L.A.B. Pistol 0 — zero built-in press. The Jul 30 film measured exactly what that produces: shaft dead vertical at address, hands about 1.35" BEHIND the ball, repeatable to 0.3° across 59 frames. That is not a flaw in your setup. That is the geometry this putter is designed around: 69° lie, 2° effective loft, 0° shaft lean.

The DF3i's Press Pistol 2° leans the shaft for you, which is why the cue while it was in the bag was 'hands EVEN with the ball, the grip supplies the lean.' Leave that cue with the DF3i. On a Pistol 0 build, hands even with the ball is lean YOU are adding by hand, on a face carrying 2° of effective loft — there is almost nothing there to deloft before you're driving the ball into the turf.

So: let the shaft stand up. Hands behind the ball. Don't manufacture lean, and don't fight the vertical look — it's correct here.

The practical guard: don't roll a set on one head and walk straight to the other. Whichever one you're about to play, reset the hands on it first.

sections.t: What the swap re-opens
sections.k: The two reds on the grid were both measured on this head — going back to it puts start line back in play.
sections.b:
Read the evolution grid honestly before you take this putter to a card. The LINK's column is the ONLY one carrying two reds — face at impact, and the 1.5–1.7° LEFT start line — and both were measured on Jul 30, on this head. The DF3i's first filmed column carried none.

That is not a verdict against the LINK. The Jul 30 numbers came from by far the most-filmed day of this project, so some of what shows up there is measurement effort rather than a putter effect, and the DF3i's clean column is partly a clean column because less was measured in it. But it does mean the swap re-opens the start-line question instead of settling it. You are going back to the head the only hard left number was ever taken on.

The geometry gives that a mechanism, too. A narrow blade carries less MOI than a wide mallet, so a strike toward the heel twists the face closed MORE for the same distance off centre — and a closed face starts the ball LEFT, which is the signature miss of this entire project. The riser hosel means the shaft position isn't a reliable pointer to where the head's mass actually sits, so you can't eyeball it.

In the LINK's favour, and it's real: tempo measured 2.0:1 across seven of eight clips on this head against 2.4:1 on the DF3i, and 2:1 is the target.

sections.t: What the evidence actually supports
sections.k: This is a preference call, not a measurement call — own that, and it stays a good decision.
sections.b:
Neither head has a real scoreboard. The only one that exists in the whole project is the DF3i's 8/10 from four feet on Jul 20. No lag ladder, no 10-ball test on the LINK. The Aug 10 outdoor session was 23 clips, but with above-ground cups, no face-on angle and nothing overhead — good for feel and finish quality, not for face numbers.

So be straight about what this swap is: you like the putter, you roll it confidently, and nine of about twenty putts on Aug 10 finished dead. That's a preference call. Preference calls are allowed — a putter you want to look at gets rolled more, and reps taken beat better reps that aren't. What isn't allowed is calling it settled evidence, because that is the exact mistake that benched the DF3i on Jul 30 and then un-benched it on Aug 1, both times on one unmeasured round.

The decision stands. The FAULTS are still open. Those are two different things.

sections.t: The work moves with the head
sections.k: Every open measurement now runs on the LINK — same protocols, new putter.
sections.b:
Three things were queued on the DF3i. All of them move.

TAPE TEST — the tap test for the true sweet spot, then foot-powder spray, 10 from five feet and 10 from thirty, photographed. This is still the last cheap untested thing on your card and the only single candidate that explains BOTH open faults: a heel strike closes the face (starts it left) and bleeds ball speed (lags short). It matters more on a blade than it did on the mallet.

OVERHEAD FIVE — five putts, roll versus the mat centre line, median inside 0.5°. This is the direct re-measure of the 1.5–1.7° left number, on the head it was taken on. That makes it a genuine like-for-like this time.

FACE-ON CLIP — still not filmed, still the one angle that separates 'face aimed left' from 'face closing through impact', and now it also has to confirm the hands-behind address is holding through the stroke rather than pressing forward under pressure. White tape on the shaft.

If you want the comparison that would actually settle the head question rather than the preference question, run the tape test on both and put the two sheets side by side.

sections.t: The DF3i stays on the shelf, not on the market
sections.k: Hold it — it's the high-MOI control and the only head with a measured result behind it.
sections.b:
The redundancy argument that sent the LINK to storage on Aug 2 — you shouldn't own two zero-torque L.A.B. heads — now points the other way, and the answer is the same: don't act on it yet. Keep both.

The DF3i is worth holding for three reasons. It owns the only measured result in the project. It's the high-MOI control — if the blade's start line goes left again, swapping heads for a filmed set is the cleanest test you can run without buying anything. And it was never actually convicted: the pace complaint that benched it on Jul 30 was never tested against a single calibrated lag session.

No regrips on either. Lie Angle Balance is a property of the assembled club, grip included, so a local-shop swap risks putting a head out of spec with no way to verify it. If they're ever to be matched, that's a job for L.A.B.

And the standing rule survives the swap intact: that's now four putter movements in a month. The next thing that changes should be a NUMBER on the card, not a head in the bag.

club.note: RETURNED Aug 10, 2026. Reason given: distance control — too hard to get the pace under control with it. Bought Jul 18, gamed Jul 18–30 and Aug 1–10. Gone from the bag for good; the Press Pistol 2° went back with it, so the 'hands EVEN with the ball' cue is dead — do not carry it to the LINK. WHAT THIS COSTS, so it's on the record: the DF3i owned the only measured scoreboard in the entire project (8/10 from four feet, Jul 20), and it was the high-MOI control head — the one clean way to test whether a wide mallet fixed the left start line that a narrow blade was measured producing. Both of those are now unavailable. It also means the pace complaint has now decided this putter twice, in opposite directions, without one calibrated lag session behind either verdict.

THE PUTTER, and the ONLY zero-torque head left — the DF3i went back Aug 10 for distance control. This one is still inside its own return window (deadline unknown, find the receipt), so it is being ground on purpose rather than kept by default. SETUP: L.A.B. Pistol 0, zero built-in press — shaft DEAD VERTICAL at address, hands ~1.35" BEHIND the ball, measured on film Jul 30 and repeatable to 0.3°. That is this putter's designed geometry (69° lie, 2° effective loft, 0° lean), not a flaw. The Press Pistol 2° 'hands even' cue left with the DF3i. Don't manufacture lean. THE GRIND: distance control. Pace is what returned the last putter and it has never once been measured — the 30-ft ladder twice a week, logging shorts, spread and green speed, is the whole job. Tempo is already where it needs to be on this head: 2.0:1 measured across seven of eight clips against 2.4:1 on the DF3i, and 2:1 is the target, so the curve is buildable. WATCH: narrow blade, lower MOI than the mallet, so an off-centre strike bleeds more ball speed here than it did there — strike is a distance fault before it's a line fault, and the tape test is still unrun. Its column also carries the only two reds on the grid (face at impact, 1.5–1.7° left start line, both Jul 30, both on this head), and there is no control putter left to cross-check them against. If this one goes back too, what's left in the bag is the Newport 2 — a toe-hang blade against a confirmed SBST stroke, i.e. the exact mismatch that started the saga.

entries.text: L.A.B. DF3i RETURNED Aug 10, 2026 — distance control, too hard to get the pace under control. Gamed Jul 18–30 and Aug 1–10. The LINK.2.1 is now the only zero-torque putter in the bag and is itself still inside a return window. Lost with it: the only measured scoreboard in the project (8/10 from four feet, Jul 20) and the high-MOI control head.

EQUIPMENT — FIND THE LINK.2.1's RETURN DEADLINE. It is the only putter in the bag and it is still returnable, and right now nothing knows until when — the app is showing 'deadline unknown' because the old date belonged to the Phantom. Find the receipt, confirm the window with the shop, and set it on the Home card. Then treat it as a gate, not a countdown: two weeks of the 30-ft ladder at two different green speeds gives the keep-or-return call an actual scoreboard. Decide it on purpose — this is the second putter in three weeks to be judged on a feeling, and the first one that got sent back on one.

PUTTING — THE 30-ft LAG LADDER on the LINK.2.1, twice a week. This is now the main event: distance control is what sent the DF3i back on Aug 10, and in three weeks and four putters it has never once been measured. 10 balls from 30 feet. Log THREE numbers every time: (1) how many finish SHORT — target no more than 1 in 10, because a short putt has zero chance; (2) the SPREAD front-to-back of the ten stopping points — this is the actual measure of distance control, target inside 6 feet; (3) the GREEN SPEED or surface (that mat, this practice green, estimated stimp). The speed field is not optional — Aug 1 felt dialled on greens estimated 8–9 stimp, which is slow-to-medium, and the same stroke runs four to six feet past from 30 feet on an 11. Build the curve on at least TWO different speeds before trusting it. Then add the calibration set: 20, 30 and 40 feet, three balls each, and note where the BACKSTROKE ends for each one — that written-down mapping is the curve. Two weeks of this is what turns the LINK's keep-or-return call into a decision instead of a feeling.

PUTTING — Bed in the settled stroke on the LINK.2.1: deep bend / stand close, and the SOFT press moved with the body. GRIP CUE REVERTS AGAIN — the DF3i and its Press Pistol 2° went back Aug 10, so the 'hands EVEN with the ball, the grip supplies the lean' rule is retired. On the LINK's Pistol 0 there is no built-in lean: the shaft stands DEAD VERTICAL and your hands sit ~1.35" BEHIND the ball. Don't add lean by hand — with 2° of effective loft there is nothing to deloft before you're driving the ball into the turf, and a driven ball skids before it rolls, which costs you on exactly the long putts you're trying to control. Add ONE thing to this: fix your BALL POSITION with a mark and keep it there. Launch is sensitive to where the ball sits relative to the low point, and a ball position that wanders reads as bad distance control even when the stroke is fine. Confirm both on the face-on clip you already owe: shaft lean at address versus at impact, and the ball in the same place every rep. The stroke does NOT change because the head did.

Overhead filmed ✓ (Jul 30, on the LINK) — remaining: face-on clips for the lift and delivery verdicts + the 20-ball 5-footer baseline. Both now run on the LINK.2.1, since the DF3i went back Aug 10 and there is no second head to compare against. That makes the baseline more valuable, not less: it is the only scoreboard this putter would have before its return window closes.

PUTTING — RUN THE TAPE TEST on the LINK.2.1 (~12 min, at home). Promoted Aug 10: with the DF3i returned for distance control, strike location is the single best explanation left for the fault that just cost you a putter. An off-centre hit bleeds ball speed, so the same stroke comes up short — that is a DISTANCE fault before it is a line fault, and it explains both open faults with one cause, since a heel strike also closes the face and starts the ball LEFT. It matters more on this head than it did on the mallet: a narrow blade carries less MOI, so the same miss costs more speed and more face angle. Protocol: (1) hang the putter from the top of the grip and tap the face heel-to-toe with an eraser — the spot with NO twist is the true sweet spot; mark it with tape and check it against the sight line. (2) Coat the face with foot-powder spray, hit 10 from 5 ft, photograph; re-coat, hit 10 from 30 ft, photograph. Don't wipe between putts. The 30-footer sheet is the important one now — that's where a speed leak shows. Send both photos. Run this BEFORE the return window closes: if the strike is centred and the ladder spread is still wide, the head is a fair suspect; if it's heel-biased, the head isn't the problem and sending it back buys you nothing.

faults.why: NOW THE FAULT, and it has a receipt: it just cost you a putter. The DF3i went back Aug 10 because distance was too hard to control with it. Look at the run — benched Jul 30 for lags coming up short and short putts running hot; reprieved Aug 1 because pace felt dialled for a round; returned Aug 10 for distance control. Three verdicts on pace in eleven days, in two directions, and not one calibrated lag session behind any of them. That is the whole problem: a fault diagnosed only on feel can't be fixed, and it can't be ruled out either, so it follows you into the next head. It also has an unexamined asterisk — the one round it 'passed' was on greens estimated 8–9 on the stimp, slow-to-medium, where you swing bigger and hit firmer, and the same stroke runs four to six feet past from 30 feet on an 11. Fix: the 30-ft ladder on the LINK, twice a week, logging shorts, spread and green speed, plus the 20/30/40 calibration set that maps distance to BACKSTROKE LENGTH at a fixed tempo. Tempo is not the missing piece — 2.0:1 measured on this head, against a 2:1 target. Stroke length and strike are.

PROMOTED — still never measured on any putter, not once, and now it is the leading single explanation for the fault that just returned a putter. A strike off the middle bleeds ball speed, so the same stroke finishes short and the spread widens; a strike toward the HEEL also rotates the face closed and starts the ball LEFT. One cause, both open faults. The head swap raises the stakes rather than lowering them: the LINK is a narrow blade with less MOI than the mallet that just left, so the same miss costs more speed and more face angle here, and its riser hosel makes the true centre hard to find by eye. Twelve minutes settles it — tap test for the sweet spot, foot-powder sheets from 5 ft and 30 ft. The 30-ft sheet is the one that matters now. Run it before the return window closes, because it is the difference between 'the head is a fair suspect' and 'the head was never the problem'.

OPEN, and harder to settle than it was a week ago. The hard number — 1.5° and 1.7° LEFT on two of three overhead putts, 1.3–1.4" at 4 ft, ~2" at 6 ft — was measured Jul 30 on the LINK, which is the putter now in the bag. The Aug 1 round that softened this fault was on the DF3i, unmeasured, on slow greens, and that head has now been returned, so the cleanest test available a week ago — re-measure overhead on a high-MOI mallet and compare — is gone. What's left is the direct version, and it's still cheap: overhead, five putts, roll versus the mat centre line, on the LINK. Median inside 0.5° and this comes off the card. Note the honest read on the equipment question: the miss outlived three putters, which says it isn't the head; strike location has never been measured, which is the one way it still could be.

Reverted with the grip, and now it feeds the pace fault directly. The Press Pistol 2° left with the DF3i, so the LINK's Pistol 0 is back: no built-in lean, shaft vertical at address, hands ~1.35" behind the ball. The old 'don't double-count the lean' warning goes quiet again — but a new one replaces it. On a 2°-effective-loft face with the hands behind, launch is sensitive to ball position and to any press you add by hand: too far back or too much press and the ball is driven into the turf, skids before it rolls, and finishes short of where the stroke said it should. That is a distance-control leak hiding inside a delivery fault, which makes this worth measuring now rather than later. One slo-mo face-on set — white tape on the shaft, 240 fps, lights on — gives lean at address versus at impact AND ball position rep to rep, in the same clips.

CLOSED Jul 30 ✓. At 120 fps and 37.5 px/inch the sole held within 0.05–0.08" of its address height for the full 83 ms into impact, flat across ten consecutive frames, and never dropped below address height. The rise afterwards is the follow-through arc. Measured on the LINK, which is the head still in play, so this one carries cleanly. Wants two more slo-mo strokes on sample size, and the owed face-on set gives them for free.
CLOSED Jul 30 ✓ — overhead film measured the toe line 0.6°, 2.9° and 3.6° CLOSED to the target line across three reps. Never open. Measured on the LINK, so it stands unchanged by the DF3i going back.

metrics.name: Distance control
metrics.verdict: NEVER MEASURED — a full row of dashes, and that is the finding. Pace has now decided the fate of two putters and been quantified zero times: the DF3i was benched for it Jul 30, reprieved for it Aug 1, and RETURNED for it Aug 10. Every one of those calls was made on feel. This row fills in the moment the 30-ft ladder starts logging shorts, spread and green speed on the LINK. Until then, the most expensive fault on the card is also the only one with no data behind it.

metrics.name: Path
metrics.verdict: SETTLED — straight (SBST) across 20+ clips and four putters. Measured again Jul 30 on the LINK: ¼–½" inside at the top, back on the line by impact. Path is yours, not the putter's, which is why none of the head changes have reopened it.

metrics.name: Tempo / load
metrics.verdict: SETTLED — 2.0:1 measured on the LINK.2.1, seven of eight clips between 1.9 and 2.1, two independent ways, against a 2:1 target. It was 2.4:1 on the DF3i, but that head has gone back, so the number that counts is the one on the putter in the bag and it's the better of the two. Worth stating plainly for the pace grind: tempo is NOT your distance problem. Stroke length and strike are.

metrics.name: Face at impact
metrics.verdict: REOPENED Jul 30 — zero-torque guarantees the face won't TWIST, and it doesn't. It cannot guarantee where the face POINTS, and on 2 of 3 measured putts it pointed ~1.5° left at impact. Aimed there or closed through: only a face-on clip separates them, and that clip is owed on the LINK — the head it was measured on and the only one left.

metrics.name: Start line / aim
metrics.verdict: OPEN. Measured 1.5° and 1.7° LEFT on two of three overhead putts Jul 30 (1.3–1.4" at 4 ft, ~2" at 6 ft), one dead straight — on the LINK, which is the putter now in the bag. The Aug 1 round that softened this was on the DF3i and that head has been returned, so the mallet-versus-blade cross-check is no longer available. Re-measure directly: overhead, five putts, roll versus the mat centre line, on the LINK. Median inside 0.5° and this comes off the card.

metrics.name: Early lift
metrics.verdict: CLOSED Jul 30 ✓ — the sole held within 0.05–0.08" of address height for the full 83 ms into impact, flat across ten consecutive frames. The oldest open item on the card, finally shut, and measured on the head still in the bag. Take two more slo-mo strokes on sample size when the face-on set happens.

metrics.name: Stance line
metrics.verdict: CLOSED on arrival. Measured off the overhead frames: the toe line ran 0.6°, 2.9° and 3.6° CLOSED to the target line — never open on any rep. The trail-foot creep is fixed. Look higher for the aim leak.

briefing.focus: The DF3i went back on Aug 10 because distance was too hard to control with it. That makes pace the fault that has now decided two putters — and it has still never been measured, not one calibrated lag session in three weeks and four heads. The LINK.2.1 is the only zero-torque putter left and it is still inside its own return window. So the next two weeks are a grind with a number attached: build the pace curve on this head, and if it ends up going back too, let a scoreboard send it rather than a feeling.
rules: Pace has decided two putters and been measured zero times — that ends here
The ladder IS the grind: 10 balls from 30 ft, twice a week, three numbers logged
Log the green speed every session — a curve at one speed is one data point
Distance comes from stroke LENGTH at a fixed tempo, not from hitting it harder
Tempo is already right on this head (2.0:1) — stop looking there
Strike is the hidden speed leak — run the tape test before you judge the putter
Pistol 0 again: shaft vertical, hands ~1.35" behind, don't add lean by hand
Find the return deadline, then decide on numbers before it lapses

sections.t: Why the DF3i actually went back
sections.k: The complaint was pace — the one thing this project has never once measured.
sections.b:
Distance control is a completely fair reason to send a putter back. You have to trust the thing you're holding, and if the pace never came, it never came.

But look at the run before you carry the reasoning into this head. Jul 30: the DF3i gets benched after twelve days for lags coming up short and short putts running hot. Aug 1: it comes back in and gets reprieved because pace felt dialled for a full round. Aug 10: it gets returned for distance control. Three verdicts on the same fault in eleven days, in two different directions, and not one calibrated lag session behind any of them.

That's the thing worth naming. A fault judged only on feel can't be fixed, because there's nothing to move; and it can't be ruled out either, so it travels to the next putter. Pace is the most expensive item on your card — it has now cost you a head — and it's the only one with no data whatsoever behind it.

So this isn't a lecture about the return. The return is done. It's the reason the next two weeks look the way they do.

sections.t: The ladder — this is the grind
sections.k: Ten balls from thirty feet, twice a week, three numbers written down. That's the whole protocol.
sections.b:
Ten balls, 30 feet, on the LINK. Twice a week. Log three things every single time:

SHORTS — how many of the ten finish short of the hole. Target: no more than 1 in 10. A putt that finishes short had a zero per cent chance, and coming up short is the specific complaint that started all of this.

SPREAD — the front-to-back distance between the nearest and furthest of the ten stopping points. This is the actual measurement of distance control, and it's the number that will tell you whether anything is improving. Target: inside 6 feet.

GREEN SPEED — estimated stimp, or just name the surface honestly (that mat, this practice green). This field is not optional and it's the one most likely to get skipped. Aug 1 felt perfect on greens estimated 8–9 on the stimp, which is slow-to-medium; the same stroke runs four to six feet past from 30 feet on an 11. A curve built at one speed isn't a curve, it's a data point.

Then add the calibration set, five minutes: 20, 30 and 40 feet, three balls each, and note where the BACKSTROKE ENDS for each distance — inside the trail toe, at the toe, outside it, whatever landmark you can repeat. Written down, that mapping is your curve. It's the thing you've never had.

sections.t: Where distance control actually comes from
sections.k: Stroke length at a fixed tempo — if tempo moves with distance, the curve never stabilises.
sections.b:
Here's the good news, and it's genuinely good: the ingredient most people are missing, you already have. Tempo measured 2.0:1 on this putter across seven of eight clips, two independent ways, against a 2:1 target. Tempo is not your distance problem. Stop looking there.

What produces distance on a putt is how far back you take it while the tempo stays the same. The failure mode is the opposite — keeping the backstroke roughly constant and varying how hard you hit it. That works for one distance and falls apart everywhere else, because effort and tempo move together, and a stroke that accelerates differently every time can't have a curve.

So the discipline in every ladder session: same tempo, always. Count it, hum it, whatever gets it stable. Change the LENGTH. If you catch yourself hitting AT a long one, that rep is the fault showing up, and it's worth noting on the sheet.

This is also why the 20/30/40 calibration set matters more than it looks. Once three distances have a repeatable backstroke landmark attached, everything in between is interpolation, and lag putting turns into a reference you can consult instead of a feeling you have to summon.

sections.t: The hidden speed leak: strike
sections.k: An off-centre hit bleeds ball speed — that's a distance fault before it's ever a line fault.
sections.b:
This is the part that ties the whole card together, and it's twelve minutes of work you've now been carrying for eleven days.

A putt struck off the middle loses ball speed, so the same stroke finishes shorter — and inconsistently, because the miss isn't the same every time. That is exactly the symptom that just sent a putter back. And a strike toward the HEEL does a second thing: it rotates the face closed, which starts the ball LEFT, which is the signature miss of this entire project. One cause, both open faults. Nothing else on the card explains that much at once.

Strike location has never been measured on any putter you own. Not once, across four heads.

And the swap raises the stakes rather than lowering them. The DF3i was a wide, deep, high-MOI mallet — forgiving, and quiet about your misses. The LINK is a narrow blade with less MOI, so the same distance off centre costs more ball speed and more face angle. If strike is your leak, this head punishes it harder than the one that just went back, and the ladder will show it as a wide spread.

So run the tape test, and run it early: tap test for the true sweet spot, then foot-powder sheets from 5 feet and 30 feet. The 30-foot sheet is the one that matters now — a speed leak shows up on long putts, not short ones.

sections.t: Ball position, and the grip that came back
sections.k: Hands behind the ball is correct here — as long as ball position doesn't wander.
sections.b:
The Press Pistol 2° went back with the DF3i, so the cue reverts one more time and this is the last flip: the LINK's Pistol 0 has zero built-in press. Shaft DEAD VERTICAL at address, hands about 1.35" BEHIND the ball. Film measured exactly that on Jul 30, repeatable to 0.3° over 59 frames. It is the geometry this putter was designed around — 69° lie, 2° effective loft, 0° shaft lean — not something to correct. Don't add lean by hand.

The reason it belongs in a distance plan: with only 2° of effective loft and the hands behind, launch is sensitive. Ball creeping back in the stance delofts it further and drives it into the turf; the ball skids before it rolls, and a skidding putt finishes short of where the stroke said it should. Ball too far forward adds hop. Both read as bad distance control even when the stroke was fine.

So fix ball position with a mark and keep it there — same spot every rep, every session. And you can verify all of it in one set of clips: the face-on set you already owe gives you lean at address versus at impact AND ball position rep to rep, in the same footage.

sections.t: Before you send this one back too
sections.k: Give it a scoreboard first — and know what's actually behind it in the bag.
sections.b:
The LINK is still inside its own return window and nobody currently knows until when — the date the app was holding belonged to the Phantom, so it's been cleared and the Home card now says so. Find the receipt and set the real one. That's the first job this week, because everything else here is on a clock.

Then two things to hold while the ladder runs.

First, know what returning it would leave you. The only other putter in the bag is the Scotty Newport 2 — a toe-hang blade against your confirmed SBST stroke. That's the exact mismatch this whole project opened with, flagged as the equipment half of the left miss. That is NOT an argument for keeping the LINK. It's an argument for knowing what replaces it BEFORE the window closes, rather than after.

Second, set the gate now, while you're not deciding anything. Two weeks of the ladder at two different green speeds, plus the tape test. If the spread is still wide AND the tape shows a centred strike, the head is a fair suspect and you send it back with actual evidence — the first equipment decision in this project that would have any. If the tape shows a heel bias, the head was never the problem, and returning it buys you a fifth putter and the same fault.

sections.t: What none of this changes
sections.k: Path, tempo, lift and stance are settled — they belong to you, not to whatever is in the bag.
sections.b:
Worth keeping in view while the pace work runs, because four putters in a month makes it feel like everything is unstable. It isn't.

Path: settled, straight SBST across 20+ clips and four different heads. Tempo: 2.0:1 on this putter, inside the window. Early lift: closed Jul 30, measured, and measured on the head still in your hands. Stance line: square, never open across three reps.

All four of those were measured on the LINK, which means none of them walked out the door with the DF3i. What's open is start line, delivery, strike and pace — and the last two are the same twelve minutes and the same ladder away from having numbers.

The rule survives intact, and it's earned its keep: the next thing that changes should be a NUMBER on the card, not a head in the bag.

briefing.focus: UPDATED Aug 10, and this is the last grip flip — the DF3i and its Press Pistol 2° have been RETURNED, so 'hands even with the ball' is retired for good. The LINK.2.1's Pistol 0 has no built-in lean: shaft VERTICAL, hands ~1.35" BEHIND the ball. New this update and the biggest thing on the card in weeks — you've found that setting the face BARELY OPEN at address is the sweet spot. That is very likely not a compensation but a correction, and it points straight at the fault this project opened with. Everything that came off film of YOUR stroke is unchanged: GET LOW, TRAIL FOOT back, rock the shoulders.

sections.t: THE HEADLINE — get low
sections.b: Your words, and they go at the top of the plan rather than the bottom of a setup list: bending over is the most massive thing, and getting low is where you feel most comfortable. That is the feel to remember when everything else has drifted. If you only carry one thought to the practice green, carry this one — not the press, not the rehearsals, not the pace word. Deep bend, stand close, eyes down.
sections.k: Bend over and get low — that's the anchor feel everything else hangs off.

sections.t: Why the bend is more than comfort
sections.b:
Two real mechanisms sit under that feel. FIRST — the LINK.2.1 is Lie Angle Balanced, and that balance is only true when the shaft is presented at the lie angle it was built for. Stand too tall or too far away and the toe drops, the shaft leaves its designed lie, and the zero-torque property this whole project was built on quietly degrades. Posture is what delivers the technology. On this head the built spec is 69° lie, 2° effective loft and 0° shaft lean, with an aluminium riser hosel sized to the lie angle — still confirm the length is 34". SECOND — more bend lets the arms hang freer and tilts the shoulders onto a STEEPER plane, and a steeper shoulder plane is what produces a straight-back-straight-through stroke. Standing tall flattens that plane and builds an arc into the stroke you don't want.

This one carried across every head change, because it's a property of you and your posture rather than of whatever is in your hands.
sections.k: The bend isn't comfort: it presents the lie the putter needs, and steepens the shoulder plane that makes the stroke straight.

sections.t: The setup
sections.b:
BEND OVER, stand close, eyes down through the strike. Ball off the LEFT BREAST. Weight stacked ON the ball — pressure over it, not on the trail foot. TRAIL FOOT a touch BACK — it creeps forward on its own and opens you. Rock the shoulders, no hands. Loose grip. Face set BARELY OPEN — see the section below.

THE HANDS CUE, FINAL VERSION. HANDS ~1.35" BEHIND THE BALL, shaft DEAD VERTICAL. The DF3i went back on Aug 10 and its Press Pistol 2° went with it, so the 'hands even with the ball, the grip supplies the lean' rule is retired — there is no longer a grip in your bag that it describes.

The LINK's Pistol 0 has zero built-in press, and this is measured rather than assumed: overhead stills on Jul 30 put the shaft essentially vertical and repeatable to 0.3° across 59 frames, with the hands about 1.35" behind the ball. That is the geometry L.A.B. built this putter around — 69° lie, 2° effective loft, 0° lean — not a flaw in your address to be corrected. Don't manufacture lean with your hands to make it look like a normal putter. With only 2° of effective loft there is almost nothing to deloft before you're driving the ball into the turf, and a driven ball skids before it rolls, which costs you most on exactly the long putts you're trying to control.

ONE ADDITION, because pace is the live priority: fix your BALL POSITION with a mark and keep it there. Launch is sensitive to where the ball sits relative to the low point, and a ball position that wanders reads as bad distance control even when the stroke was fine.
sections.k: Hands ~1.35" BEHIND the ball and the shaft vertical — the Pistol 0 has no lean to borrow, and none to add.

sections.t: THE PRESS — settled from first principles
sections.b:
Start from what you are actually holding. The Pistol 0 is an UNPRESSED grip — zero built-in forward lean, shaft vertical, hands behind the ball. So unlike the DF3i era, the soft press is now the ONLY source of shaft lean in your stroke.

That changes the arithmetic in your favour and it's worth being precise about why, because the old rule was reasoned from real numbers. On the Press Pistol 2° there was already lean built in, so any press you added STACKED on top of it and could push effective loft below zero — a putter delivering negative loft drives the ball down into the green instead of rolling it. That is why 'keep it tiny' was a hard rule for the whole DF3i era.

With the Pistol 0 there is nothing to stack on. A small press cannot drive loft below zero, because it is starting from zero lean and 2° of loft. So the hard 'tiny or else' rule is genuinely suspended.

What replaces it is a softer rule with a different reason, and the reason is pace — see below. Do not read 'suspended' as 'manufacture some lean'. The putter is designed around 0° and there is very little loft to give away.
sections.k: The Pistol 0 has no lean to stack on, so the hard 'tiny or else' rule is suspended — but consistency replaces it, for pace.

sections.t: What this putter needs from the setup
sections.b:
A lie-angle-balanced putter makes one demand of you and it is not a stroke demand: present the shaft at the lie it was built for. Get that wrong — stand tall, reach for it — and the toe drops, the shaft leaves its designed lie, and the self-squaring property you bought degrades. That is why the deep bend matters mechanically here and not just for comfort.

Everything else in this routine came from film of YOUR stroke — path, shoulder plane, stance line, trigger — so none of it is putter-specific and none of it changed when the mallet went back. Two things ARE this head's business. The lie presentation above. And your AIM PICTURE: a narrow blade topline frames the target very differently from the wide mallet you spent nine days looking at, which is one reason the barely-open find is worth nailing down with a number now rather than trusting the eye through another head change.

One more that is specific to this head: the riser hosel. The shaft is NOT a reliable pointer to where the head's mass sits, so don't use it to judge the sweet spot by eye — that's what the tap test is for.
sections.k: Present the shaft at its built lie and re-check your aim picture. Leave the stroke alone.

sections.t: THE FACE — barely open is your square
sections.k: On a zero-torque head the face points where you set it, so this reads as an aim correction, not a compensation — which would make it the answer to the oldest fault on the card.
sections.b:
Your find, Aug 10: setting the face BARELY OPEN at address is the sweet spot. Take it seriously, because there is a clean mechanism underneath it and it lines up with everything already measured.

Start from what a zero-torque putter can and cannot do. Lie Angle Balance means the face does not TWIST during the stroke — and Jul 30 film confirmed exactly that, the face held. What it cannot do is decide where the face POINTS. A zero-torque head faithfully delivers whatever angle you set at address. So on this putter, face-at-impact is very close to face-at-address, by design.

Now put the two facts together. Overhead film measured the face pointing 1.5° and 1.7° LEFT at impact on two of three putts — the only hard number behind your signature miss. On a head that doesn't twist, a face pointing left at impact was almost certainly pointing left AT ADDRESS. That reframes the whole fault: it is an AIM error, not a delivery error. Nothing is closing through impact — you were aiming there the whole time.

And that is precisely what 'barely open feels right' means. What reads as barely open to your eyes is, on the actual target line, square. You are not compensating for a moving face; you are correcting a perception. That matters enormously for whether this holds up: compensations for timing drift and have to be re-found every week, but an aim offset is stable. This one should keep working.

It also answers the aim-check item directly. Your stance measured SQUARE on overhead film — the toe line ran 0.6°, 2.9° and 3.6° CLOSED across three reps, never open — so the leak was never in your feet. The instruction was to look higher. The face itself is higher, and here it is.

sections.t: The trap — don't stack the two fixes
sections.k: 'Barely open' is a feel calibrated to your current aim picture; retrain the picture as well and you'll start missing right.
sections.b:
This is the one way the discovery goes wrong, and it's worth reading before the next practice green.

'Barely open' is not a measurement. It is a FEEL, and it works because it is calibrated against your current, slightly-left aim perception. Which means there are two different fixes available for the same fault, and they do not combine:

LANE A — keep the feel. Aim what feels barely open, verify ONCE that it actually produces a square start line, then stop thinking about it. Cheap, fast, and it's already working.

LANE B — retrain the aim picture with a mirror or a laser until genuinely square LOOKS square, and drop the 'barely open' language entirely.

Do BOTH and you have applied the correction twice: a face that is genuinely open, and a new miss to the RIGHT. Pick a lane. Lane A is the recommendation — you found it yourself, on the course, and the cheapest fix is the one that's already in your hands.

The second hazard is drift, and this project has a documented history with it. A feel with no number attached wanders, and it wanders toward the exaggeration — 'barely open' quietly becomes 'open' over a few weeks, and the miss reappears on the other side without an obvious cause. So put a number on it once, then re-check it monthly. That's the new action item, and it's five putts long.

sections.t: THE TRAIL FOOT — the alignment leak
sections.b: Self-reported Jul 29 and worth taking seriously: your right foot creeps UP — forward, toward the target line — and it drags the stance line open with it. Open the feet and the shoulders follow, so you end up aimed LEFT of where you think you are. The fix is exactly what you said: set that trail foot a touch further back than feels natural. Expect it to feel CLOSED, like you're aimed right. That feeling is the correction, not an error — you're recalibrating off an open baseline, so square will read as closed until it beds in. Trust the line you set, not the feel, for the first few sessions.
sections.k: Your trail foot creeps forward, opens the stance and aims you left. Set it back — square will feel closed.

sections.t: Why it wrecks the takeaway specifically
sections.b: Because in an SBST stroke the shoulder line IS the track. There's no arc to absorb a misaligned setup — 'straight back' is straight back along whatever line your shoulders are on, so an open stance doesn't just aim you left, it points the whole stroke left. Then one of two things happens, and both are bad: you feel it immediately and manipulate the takeaway to save it, which puts the HANDS back in charge of a stroke built to have no hands in it — or you don't, and the ball starts left. That's why a stance error shows up as a takeaway problem. The takeaway is fine; it's obeying a line that's wrong.
sections.k: In a straight stroke the shoulder line IS the track, so an open stance points the whole stroke left.

sections.t: This is the miss the putter can't fix
sections.b:
Your signature miss is LEFT on short putts — the through-line of the entire putter saga, and it has now outlived four putters. That history is what rules the HEAD out: a fault that survives four different putters was never about the putter.

What it never ruled out was aim. A perfectly square face aimed at a target left of the hole produces exactly this miss, and no putter ever built will save you from it. Zero-torque guarantees the FACE stays square; it cannot guarantee the face is square TO THE RIGHT THING. That has been the standing line in this plan for two weeks, and the barely-open find is the first thing to actually act on it.

Note the split that always made the case: your 10-ball blocks started 10/10 on line on the MAT, where an alignment aid is doing the aiming for you, while the miss kept showing up on the COURSE, where nothing is. That pattern is an aim signature, not a stroke signature. It has been sitting in the data the whole time.
sections.k: A square face aimed at the wrong target still misses left — and the mat-versus-course split says that's exactly what's been happening.

sections.t: The check that costs nothing
sections.b: Lay a club or an alignment stick down the target line just outside the ball on the practice green and set up to it — your toes should run PARALLEL to it, not converging toward it. Ten seconds, and it recalibrates the feel. The structural safeguard is already in your routine: aim the FACE to the spot FIRST, then build the stance around it. Keep that order religiously. If you build the stance first, the face gets aimed to a crooked body; if you aim the face first and the stance then creeps, the mismatch shows up as discomfort — and discomfort you can feel is information you can act on.
sections.k: Alignment stick on the practice green: toes parallel, not converging. Ten seconds, recalibrates the feel.

sections.t: THE TRIGGER — settled: soft press, moved with the body
sections.b:
Keep the soft press — a genuinely small one, made as the body starts to move. Its JOB is rhythm: it breaks inertia so the stroke starts as a motion rather than a decision.

On the Pistol 0 it is also the only lean in the stroke, since the grip supplies none. That makes it more honest than it was during the DF3i era — what you feel is what the shaft is doing, with nothing built in underneath it — and it makes repeatability the whole game. Nothing is masking a press that grows.

It should pass THROUGH, not be held. Held presses were a real problem on Jul 29 and the mechanism that made them dangerous is gone, but the habit isn't, and on this grip a held press drags your hands forward out of the hands-behind address the putter is built around.
sections.k: Keep the soft press for rhythm — on this grip it's the only lean in the stroke, so make it the same size every time.

sections.t: The one rule — softness IS the safeguard
sections.b:
REWRITTEN Aug 10. The old version of this rule was arithmetic: the Press Pistol's 2° meant a firm press pushed effective loft below zero. That grip has gone back with the DF3i, so that specific danger is gone.

The rule survives anyway, for a better reason. SAME PRESS, SAME SIZE, EVERY PUTT. A press that varies is a shaft lean that varies, which is a launch that varies, which is a PACE that varies — and pace is now the priority fault on the card, the one that just cost you a putter. Consistency is no longer about protecting loft from going negative; it's about not injecting a random variable into the exact thing you're trying to measure on the ladder.

Two drift signals to watch, unchanged: if the press starts to feel FIRM, or like a POSITION you sit in rather than a motion you pass through, it has crept back toward a hold. A held press also quietly moves your hands forward of the 1.35"-behind address this putter wants.
sections.k: Same press, same size, every putt — a varying press is a varying pace, and pace is the fault that just cost you a putter.

sections.t: If it creeps back into a hold
sections.b: The alternatives stay on the shelf rather than getting deleted, because you may want one later: THE FLOAT — lift the head a hair off the turf before takeaway; no hand action at all and it removes ground friction. THE WHOLE-PUTTER WAGGLE — small forward-and-back from the shoulders, wrists silent. THE LEAD-SHOULDER SETTLE — a soft downward press of the shoulder that already runs the stroke. THE TRAIL-KNEE KICK — furthest from the hands, and the same trigger your full-swing routine uses. Any of them will break inertia without the hands touching shaft lean. You don't need one right now.
sections.k: Alternatives on the shelf if the press ever creeps back into a hold — float, waggle, shoulder settle, knee kick.

sections.t: How to tell it's releasing
sections.b: One face-on clip settles it: compare shaft lean at ADDRESS with shaft lean at IMPACT. Close to equal means the soft press is passing through the way it should. Meaningfully more at impact means it's being carried in, whatever it felt like — and feel is exactly what got this wrong the first time. The free check needs no camera: a purely rolling ball makes one clean click, a ball driven down into the green adds a faint scuff a beat later. Listen for the scuff.
sections.k: One face-on clip settles it: shaft lean at address versus at impact. No camera? Listen for the scuff.

sections.t: Stop shopping
sections.b:
Straight talk, because you called it yourself. Four putters in a month: the Phantom 7.5 returned Jul 20, the DF3i in Jul 18, out Jul 30, back in Aug 1, returned Aug 10, and the LINK.2.1 in and out and in again around it.

The LINK is now the only zero-torque head you own, and it is still inside its own return window. So 'stop shopping' is not quite available as advice — there is a real decision still to make. What IS available is the standard for making it: the DF3i was benched on a feeling, reprieved on a feeling, and returned on a feeling, without a single calibrated lag session behind any of the three. That is the pattern to break, not the putter.

So the rule from here, unchanged in spirit and sharper in practice: the next thing that changes should be a NUMBER on the card, not a head in the bag. And if this head does go back, let a scoreboard send it — two weeks of ladder data and a tape sheet — rather than a feeling. That would be the first equipment decision in this whole project with evidence under it.
sections.k: Four putters in a month, all judged on feel — break the pattern, not the putter: the next thing that changes should be a number.

sections.t: Why beside the ball and not behind it
sections.b: Rehearsing in your true putting posture — same deep bend, same arm hang, same shoulder plane — means the stroke that FEELS like 30 feet is the stroke you actually make. Magnitude transfers one-to-one. Rehearsing from behind the ball reads the break better, but you're standing upright there, so the size you feel is only an approximation. Your open fault is pace magnitude, not reading: path ✓, face ✓, start lines 10/10 twice over. Optimise the thing that's broken.
sections.k: Rehearse in your real posture beside the ball, because magnitude transfers one-to-one that way.

sections.t: Keep the order of the two rehearsals
sections.b: Ball-look first (path and contact), hole-look second (pace). The last thing you feel is the thing you carry in — so the pace stroke must be the last one. If the hole stroke ever drifts to first, the pace feel gets overwritten by the contact feel and you're back to guessing distance. Finish rehearsal 2 WITH the soft press, at its real size: it's the one part of the stroke that never used to get a practice rep, which is how it drifted last time without you noticing.
sections.k: Ball-look first, hole-look second — the last thing you feel is what you carry in.

sections.t: Two rules underneath it
sections.b: SAME BEAT COUNT, EVERY PUTT — a routine that varies in length is itself a pace variable, and the putts where you take an extra look are the ones that come up short. And a VERBAL BACKSTOP is worth testing: say the pace intention right before the press ('die it a foot past', 'back of the cup'). Feel decays, a word doesn't.
sections.k: Same beat count every putt, and try saying the pace intention out loud before the press.

sections.t: Still to test — lags
sections.b:
This is the top of the card, and it is the single thing that would have prevented the entire detour. The Jul 29 round was lags coming up SHORT and short putts running HOT, which is not two faults but one: a power curve you hadn't learned, so you under-hit the long ones and over-hit the short ones. That got the DF3i benched. It was never once tested. And on Aug 10 the same untested complaint sent that putter back for good.

So the curve gets built on the LINK, deliberately. The block test, twice a week: 10 balls from 30 feet. Log THREE numbers — how many finish SHORT (target no more than 1 in 10), the SPREAD front-to-back of the ten stopping points (target inside 6 feet), and the GREEN SPEED. Then the calibration set: 20, 30 and 40 feet, three balls each, noting where the BACKSTROKE ends for each distance. Written down, that mapping is the curve you have never had.

Two things make this more promising than it sounds. Tempo is already right on this head — 2.0:1 measured against a 2:1 target — so the missing ingredient is stroke LENGTH, not rhythm. And strike location has never been measured on any putter you own, which matters here because an off-centre hit bleeds ball speed and shows up as exactly this fault. The tape test is twelve minutes and it belongs at the front of this queue.

ONE WATCH ITEM from the barely-open find: if you were unconsciously steering the stroke to save a face aimed left, then fixing the aim removes the need for the steer — and a stroke that no longer steers can deliver different pace. So take a ladder reading EARLY, before the new aim beds in, and don't confuse a pace change caused by the aim fix with one caused by the putter.
sections.k: Build the power curve on the LINK — and take a reading early, because fixing the aim may move your pace too.

steps: Read it from BEHIND the ball — pick the line and a spot a few inches ahead of it
Step BESIDE the ball — BEND OVER, stand close, full putting posture
Rehearsal 1 — eyes on the BALL. Path and contact.
Rehearsal 2 — eyes on the HOLE. Pace. Finish it with the soft press.
Step in — set the FACE to the spot first and set it BARELY OPEN, then build the stance around it (trail foot a touch BACK)
Spot → ball → soft press with the body → putt
rules: GET LOW — the deep bend is what presents the lie this putter needs
Set the face BARELY OPEN — that's your square, and it's the first thing to move the left miss
Aim the FACE first, then build the stance to it
TRAIL FOOT back — square will feel closed
Hands ~1.35" BEHIND the ball — the Pistol 0 has no lean, so don't add any
Press SMALL and the SAME SIZE every putt — a varying press is a varying pace

entries.text: PUTTING — PUT A NUMBER ON 'BARELY OPEN'. You've found that setting the face barely open at address is the sweet spot, and on a zero-torque head that most likely means your aim picture reads square as slightly left — i.e. it's a real correction, not a compensation. Two jobs. (1) VERIFY, five putts: phone directly overhead the ball, set the face at what now feels barely open, roll five and measure the start line against the mat centre line. Median inside 0.5° and the oldest fault on the card comes off it. (2) QUANTIFY, so it can't drift: with the face set at your new 'barely open', photograph it against an alignment stick from directly above and note how open it actually is. A feel with no number attached wanders toward the exaggeration — 'barely open' quietly becomes 'open' and the miss reappears on the RIGHT. Re-check monthly. DON'T STACK FIXES: either keep the feel and verify it, OR retrain the aim picture with a mirror until square looks square — never both, or you'll apply the same correction twice.

PUTTING — Aim check above the feet. LIKELY ANSWERED Aug 10, pending measurement: your stance measured SQUARE on film (toe line 0.6°, 2.9°, 3.6° CLOSED across three reps, never open), so the left start line was never coming from your feet — the instruction was to look higher, and the barely-open find says the leak is the FACE, at address. On a zero-torque head the face points where you set it, so a face measured 1.5–1.7° left at impact was pointing there at address too. What's left is confirmation, not diagnosis: set up to an alignment stick, check the face against the line from directly above the ball, and see whether what feels 'barely open' is actually square. Keep the shoulder check in your pocket — a second club laid across the SHOULDERS — in case the face measures square and the ball still starts left.

PUTTING — ONE FACE-ON CLIP, on the LINK.2.1 (the DF3i went back Aug 10; this spec used to say the mallet). Its job has narrowed and got easier: the barely-open find already argues that the face was AIMED left rather than closing through impact, so this clip is now confirmation plus two things only it can give — shaft lean at address versus at impact on the Pistol 0 (expect ~0° at address, hands 1.35" behind, and the question is whether the press adds any), and ball position rep to rep, which feeds the distance grind. It also banks two more strokes of sample size on the closed early-lift verdict. NOT TICKED BY AUG 10 — that session ran 23 clips from five camera positions and every one was oblique, which is why it read pace beautifully and settled nothing else. The spec is narrow on purpose: camera at BALL HEIGHT, square to the target line (stand it behind the ball, walk to a spot 90° off the line, phone on the ground), white tape on the shaft ~6" above the head, 240 fps, 2–3 strokes. Indoors is fine — this clip does not need a green. One good clip beats twenty from the wrong angle. For the START LINE question, the overhead five is the test, not this one.

PUTTING — Before the next face-on set: wrap WHITE TAPE around the shaft ~6" above the head, switch Slo-Mo to 240 fps (Settings › Camera › Record Slo-mo › 1080p/240), lights on. The angle is already right — the only thing blocking the shaft-lean verdict is that a thin black shaft blurs out against a dim floor at impact speed. WHAT YOU'RE MEASURING CHANGED AGAIN on Aug 10: the DF3i and its Press Pistol 2° have been returned, so on the LINK's Pistol 0 expect roughly ZERO lean at address — shaft vertical, hands ~1.35" behind the ball — and the question is whether the soft press adds any by impact. Unlike the DF3i era there's no built-in 2° to subtract, so whatever the tape shows IS the press.

faults.why: BEST NEWS OF THE PROJECT, Aug 10 — and it needs five putts to confirm. Jack found that setting the face BARELY OPEN at address is the sweet spot. There is a clean mechanism under it: a zero-torque head does not TWIST (Jul 30 film confirmed the face held), but it cannot control where the face POINTS — it delivers whatever you set. So the 1.5° and 1.7° LEFT measured at impact were almost certainly 1.5–1.7° left AT ADDRESS. That reclassifies the whole fault from a DELIVERY error to an AIM error, which is the better of the two outcomes by a distance: aim offsets are stable, timing compensations drift. It also fits the oldest unexplained split in the data — 10/10 start lines on the MAT, where an alignment aid aims you, against a miss that kept appearing on the COURSE, where nothing does. And it fits the stance measurement: toes 0.6°, 2.9°, 3.6° CLOSED, never open, so the leak was never the feet. CONFIRM IT: overhead, five putts, face set at the new barely-open, roll versus the mat centre line. Median inside 0.5° and this comes off the card for the first time since the project began. TWO WARNINGS. Don't stack fixes — keep the feel OR retrain the aim picture with a mirror, never both, or you'll apply the correction twice and start missing RIGHT. And put a number on 'barely', because an unquantified feel drifts toward the exaggeration.

THE priority, and it has a receipt: it just cost you a putter. The DF3i went back Aug 10 because distance was too hard to control with it. Look at the run — benched Jul 30 for lags coming up short and short putts running hot; reprieved Aug 1 because pace felt dialled for a round; returned Aug 10 for distance control. Three verdicts on the same fault in eleven days, in two directions, and not one calibrated lag session behind any of them. A fault judged only on feel can't be fixed, because there's nothing to move, and it can't be ruled out either, so it follows you into the next head. It also has an asterisk: the one round it 'passed' was on greens estimated 8–9 on the stimp, where you swing bigger and hit firmer, and the same stroke runs four to six feet past from 30 feet on an 11. Fix: the 30-ft ladder on the LINK, twice a week, logging shorts, spread and green speed, plus the 20/30/40 set that maps distance to BACKSTROKE LENGTH at a fixed tempo. Tempo is not the missing piece — 2.0:1 measured on this head against a 2:1 target. Stroke length and strike are. NEW WATCH ITEM: if you were steering the stroke to rescue a face aimed left, fixing the aim removes the steer and may move your pace too — take a ladder reading early so the two don't get confused.

Still never measured on any putter, not once, across four heads — and now the last cheap thing standing between you and a complete diagnosis. A strike off the middle bleeds ball speed, so the same stroke finishes short and the spread widens; a strike toward the HEEL also rotates the face closed and starts the ball LEFT. With the aim question likely answered, this is the remaining candidate that could still be contributing to BOTH open faults. The head raises the stakes: the LINK is a narrow blade with less MOI than the mallet that just left, so the same miss costs more speed and more face angle here, and its riser hosel makes the true centre hard to find by eye. Twelve minutes — tap test for the sweet spot, foot-powder sheets from 5 ft and 30 ft, and the 30-ft sheet is the one that matters. RUN IT WITH THE NEW BARELY-OPEN ADDRESS, not the old one, since that's the setup you'll actually be using. Do it before the return window closes: centred strike plus a wide ladder spread makes the head a fair suspect; a heel bias means the head was never the problem.

Downgraded but still open, and now it feeds pace rather than line. The Press Pistol 2° left with the DF3i, so the LINK's Pistol 0 is back: no built-in lean, shaft vertical at address, hands ~1.35" behind the ball. The old 'don't double-count the lean' arithmetic is retired — there is nothing to stack on, so a small press can no longer push effective loft below zero. What remains is consistency: the press is now the ONLY lean in the stroke, so a press that varies is a launch that varies, which is a pace that varies, feeding straight into the priority fault. Same size every putt. One slo-mo face-on set — white tape on the shaft, 240 fps, lights on — gives lean at address versus at impact AND ball position rep to rep in the same clips. Whatever the tape shows IS the press now, with no built-in 2° to subtract.

CLOSED Jul 30 ✓. At 120 fps and 37.5 px/inch the sole held within 0.05–0.08" of its address height for the full 83 ms into impact, flat across ten consecutive frames, and never dropped below address height. The rise afterwards is the follow-through arc. Measured on the LINK, which is the head still in play, so it carries cleanly. Wants two more slo-mo strokes on sample size, and the owed face-on set gives them for free.

CLOSED Jul 30 ✓ — overhead film measured the toe line 0.6°, 2.9° and 3.6° CLOSED to the target line across three reps. Never open. Worth re-reading in light of the Aug 10 find: this measurement is what ruled the feet out and sent the search higher, which is exactly where the face turned out to be.

metrics.name: Start line / aim
metrics.verdict: OPEN — but for the first time there is a candidate fix, found Aug 10: setting the face BARELY OPEN at address. The measured fault is 1.5° and 1.7° LEFT on two of three overhead putts Jul 30 (1.3–1.4" at 4 ft, ~2" at 6 ft), one dead straight. Because a zero-torque head delivers the angle you set rather than twisting, a face pointing left at impact was pointing left at address — so this is an AIM error, and 'barely open' is you correcting it. Confirm the same way it was raised: overhead, five putts, new address, roll versus the mat centre line. Median inside 0.5° and this finally comes off the card.

metrics.name: Face at impact
metrics.verdict: REOPENED Jul 30, and Aug 10 supplies the likely answer. Zero-torque guarantees the face won't TWIST, and it doesn't. It cannot guarantee where the face POINTS, and on 2 of 3 measured putts it pointed ~1.5° left at impact. The two candidates were 'aimed there' and 'closed through' — and the barely-open find lands hard on AIMED THERE, since an address offset is exactly what a non-twisting head would carry to impact unchanged. Not confirmed until the overhead five says so, but this is no longer a coin flip.

metrics.name: Distance control
metrics.verdict: NEVER MEASURED — a full row of dashes, and that is the finding. Pace has now decided the fate of two putters and been quantified zero times: the DF3i was benched for it Jul 30, reprieved for it Aug 1, and RETURNED for it Aug 10. Every one of those calls was made on feel. This row fills in the moment the 30-ft ladder starts logging shorts, spread and green speed on the LINK. Until then, the most expensive fault on the card is also the only one with no data behind it.

metrics.name: Path
metrics.verdict: SETTLED — straight (SBST) across 20+ clips and four putters. Measured again Jul 30 on the LINK: ¼–½" inside at the top, back on the line by impact. Path is yours, not the putter's, which is why none of the head changes have reopened it — and why the left miss was never going to be explained by the stroke's shape.

metrics.name: Tempo / load
metrics.verdict: SETTLED — 2.0:1 measured on the LINK.2.1, seven of eight clips between 1.9 and 2.1, two independent ways, against a 2:1 target. It was 2.4:1 on the DF3i, but that head has gone back, so the number that counts is the one on the putter in the bag and it's the better of the two. Worth stating plainly for the pace grind: tempo is NOT your distance problem. Stroke length and strike are.

metrics.name: Early lift
metrics.verdict: CLOSED Jul 30 ✓ — the sole held within 0.05–0.08" of address height for the full 83 ms into impact, flat across ten consecutive frames. The oldest open item on the card, finally shut, and measured on the head still in the bag. Take two more slo-mo strokes on sample size when the face-on set happens.

metrics.name: Stance line
metrics.verdict: CLOSED on arrival — the toe line ran 0.6°, 2.9° and 3.6° CLOSED to the target line, never open on any rep. The trail-foot creep is fixed. This is the measurement that ruled the feet out and sent the search higher for the aim leak, and on Aug 10 that search found the face.

entries.setup: TWO BATCHES, ONE DAY. (1) AFTERNOON, 14:26–14:58 — 23 clips · 120 fps slo-mo · outdoor practice green with ABOVE-GROUND cups · L.A.B. DF3i (10 clips) + LINK.2.1 (13) · five ground-level camera positions, all oblique · two balls per rep (one blue, one white). (2) EVENING, ~19:54 — 5 clips · indoor mat with a printed centre line · 3 putts on the LINK.2.1 from TWO ANGLES, both ALONG the target line: down-the-line from floor level behind the ball (img0015/16/17, one per putt) and reverse down-the-line from the hole end (IMG_3476, img3478, slow-mo). A sixth clip — the third putt from the hole end — still to come.
entries.finding:
TWO SESSIONS, AND BETWEEN THEM THE FIRST START-LINE NUMBERS SINCE JUL 30. Afternoon, outdoors: about 20 putts scored off above-ground cups — NINE finished dead (touching the base or inside ~6 inches), the worst was ~4 feet, nothing went long, and both heads posted dead finishes at every distance sampled. The blue-ball question closed with Jack's answer that both balls were aimed at the same base: the blue sat parked across three clips, so it took three putts not five, and all three finished 1.2–1.5 ft from the base on both sides while the white died on the same putts — so pace work runs with the gamer ball model only. Direction went unscored, because every one of those 23 clips was oblique.

EVENING, INDOORS — and this is the new part. Five clips off a lined mat, three putts on the LINK, shot from two angles that are both ON the target line. Those are the right angles, and they make start line measurable for the first time since the barely-open find. Two putts tracked frame by frame against the mat's printed centre line, scaled by the ball's own 1.68" diameter; a stationary printed dash on that line reads 0.00" offset in both clips, which says the reference is unbiased. PUTT A rolled dead straight — inside ~0.1" of the line the whole way, about 0.8° and within the noise. PUTT B started on the line and drifted steadily LEFT, about 1.0–1.3" by the hole, call it 1°. One square, one a degree left, no consistent bias.

Against Jul 30's 1.5–1.7° LEFT on two of three, that is real improvement — with two large asterisks. It is two putts at roughly ±0.5° uncertainty. And it is a MAT WITH A PRINTED LINE, which is the one condition Jack has always passed: 10/10 start lines on the mat is the oldest line in this file, and the miss only ever appears on the course. A printed line does the aiming, so this tests the stroke, not the aim — and the aim is what the barely-open discovery is about. Consistent with the hypothesis; nowhere near confirming it. Face angle itself is not measurable here at all: the head spans ~70 pixels, where 1.5° is under two pixels.

metrics.n: one, set D · zero long all day
same base target — white died on same putts
off the printed line, whole roll
both cameras were ON the line

detail.story:
WHY THE RE-SCORE. These cups sit ON the green, not in it. A ball can't disappear, so the last frame of every clip is a scorecard — and that turned a session shot from diagnostic-useless angles into a ~20-putt pace ledger. Distances measured against the ball's own diameter at rest (1.68"), the one scale in a golf video that can't lie.

THE LEDGER, SET BY SET. Set A — DF3i, 14:26–14:47, medium-to-long: one long putt rolled the width of the green and stopped touching the base; a second finished dead from mid-range; one rep left both balls 2.5–3.5 ft short; one putt never reached the two-foot circle; one finished about a foot away. Set B — LINK, 14:48–14:49: the long right-to-left putt tracked ball-to-rest arrived at dying speed and stopped AT the base. Set C — DF3i, 14:51, five-footers: blue dead against the base, whites inside 8–14 inches, the whole cluster inside 2.5 ft. Set D — LINK, ~20 ft: one dead (2–4 in), one ~2 ft, one ~3.5–4 ft — the day's worst. Set E — LINK, 14:56–14:58, 6–8 ft: the white ball ran 2.3 ft, dead, 5 in, dead, dead across five putts; the blue took three putts and finished 1.2–1.5 ft every time.

WHAT THE TALLY SAYS. Nine of ~20 dead, most of the rest inside a foot and a half, worst ~4 ft, zero long. For a player whose pace card carries 'lags come up short' as the open conviction, the telling part is WHERE the short ones died: clustered around the base, not three feet before it. That is what calibrated-but-conservative looks like, and on the two speeds now sampled — Beekman's 8–9 stimp and this practice green — the curve is holding.

THE BLUE BALL, CLOSED AND REOPENED. The original oddity — 'blue finishes 1.2–1.5 ft in five straight finals' — was half camera artifact: frame-by-frame comparison shows the blue parked in the identical spot across clips 19–21, so it was putted three times, not five. The corrected fact is stranger: three blue putts, three finishes at 1.2–1.5 ft, spread across BOTH sides of the base, while the white died on the same putts from the same distance with the same putter. Jack confirms both were aimed at the same base, which rules out the easy explanation. Two remain. Small sample — three putts is three putts. Or the ball: a colored ball of a different model comes off the face at a different speed, and a repeating ~1.4 ft distance error at 7 feet is exactly what a firmer or softer cover does. Either way the operational rule is the same and it's cheap: pace work and the lag ladder happen with the gamer ball model only. And if that blue IS the same model as the white — then the scatter has no ball excuse, and the foot-powder strike test just became more interesting.

THE HONEST CAVEATS. An above-ground base STOPS a ball that touches it — some of the nine dead finishes would have trickled a foot past on a real green, so 'dead at base' means make-or-tap-in, not perfect dying weight; the tracked arrivals all came in soft with no ricochet, so none were hot. Balls can carry over between clips, and every parked ball was counted once — the set-E correction above is exactly that rule doing its job. And direction is still unscored: left/right of the base in any frame here is camera geometry, not a miss pattern.

THE EVENING MAT SESSION — DIRECTION, AT LAST. Five clips arrived from an indoor lined mat (19:54), three putts on the LINK.2.1 shot from two angles, both ALONG the target line: down-the-line from floor level behind the ball (img0015/16/17, one clip per putt) and reverse down-the-line from the hole end (IMG_3476, img3478). A sixth clip is still to come.

These are the RIGHT angles, and that is worth saying after a session of 23 oblique clips settled nothing. A camera on the target line is what makes start line measurable, and the mat supplies a printed centre line to measure against. Two putts were tracked frame by frame, with the ball's own 1.68" diameter setting the scale at every depth. The reference checks out: a stationary printed dash ON the centre line reads 0.00" offset in both clips, so the method is unbiased to about a thirtieth of an inch.

PUTT A (IMG_3476) rolled DEAD STRAIGHT — within about 0.1" of the printed line for its entire visible roll, which is roughly 0.8° and inside the measurement noise. PUTT B (img3478) started on the line and drifted steadily to the LEFT, reaching about 1.0–1.3" left by the time it got to the hole — call it 1°. So: one square, one a degree left, no consistent bias across the two.

Set that against the Jul 30 baseline of 1.5–1.7° LEFT on two of three overhead putts and it is a genuine improvement. It is also two putts, with an uncertainty of roughly ±0.5° once lens distortion and motion blur are allowed for, so it is encouraging rather than conclusive.
detail.compare:
Beekman (Aug 1) said pace felt dialled; it was a feeling, from a scramble, on slow greens, with no camera. This is ~20 measured finishes landing on the same side: the pace curve is real, and the LINK matched the DF3i from every distance it was given. What today adds that Beekman couldn't: the short range — the closing 6–8 ft set went dead three times out of five with a 5-incher besides, and the five-foot DF3i set clustered inside 2.5 ft.

Against the Jul 30 indoor sessions, the same trade as before: the mat measured DIRECTION but had no green; today measured DISTANCE but has no line. The two halves of the diagnosis still haven't been in the same shot.

On the head-to-head, the sets never played the same putt from the same spot, so nothing ranks the putters — but both heads posting dead finishes everywhere means neither head is the variable that mattered today. The stroke behind them did the work. The one variable that DID separate results was the ball.

AND THE HALVES MET — partly. The line above about the two halves of the diagnosis never being in the same shot is now half-answered: Jul 30 measured direction indoors, the Aug 10 afternoon measured distance outdoors, and the Aug 10 evening measured direction again, on the first putts filmed since the barely-open discovery. What is still true is that direction has only ever been measured INDOORS, on a mat with a printed line, and distance has only ever been measured OUTDOORS. Neither session has yet measured both at once, and the mat is the reason the direction half keeps looking better than the scorecard does.
detail.limits:
THE CAVEAT THAT DECIDES WHAT THIS IS WORTH: this was a mat with a printed target line, and a printed line does the AIMING for you. The oldest unexplained split in this whole project is 10/10 start lines on the mat against a left miss that only ever shows up on the course, and the barely-open discovery is an explanation for exactly that split — an AIM error, not a stroke error. So this session tests whether the stroke can send the ball down a line it has been handed. It cannot test whether Jack aims correctly when nothing is drawn on the ground, which is the open question. Two straight-ish putts on a lined mat are consistent with the aim hypothesis and do not confirm it.

FACE ANGLE IS NOT MEASURABLE IN THIS FOOTAGE. The putter head spans about 70 pixels in the reverse clip; a 1.5° rotation of the face would move its ends by under two pixels, well below the noise. So these clips cannot say what 'barely open' actually is in degrees — that still needs a close-up, phone directly above the ball with the head filling the frame, against a drawn line.

STILL OWED, and now the ONLY unshot angle: FACE-ON, square to the target line.
