The claw exists to take the trail hand OUT of the stroke — it's an anti-manipulation grip. So 'quiet hands' and 'claw' are the same instruction, and both are the same instruction as 'let a lie-angle-balanced head do its job'. Three things pointing one way.

IT MATCHES THE MISS IT'S AIMED AT. The trail hand is what steers and hits on short putts, and short putts are where your miss has always lived. Restricting it to short ones is the right scope, not a hedge.

AND THE OLD VERDICT DOESN'T BLOCK IT. The Grip Experiment closed with 'conventional confirmed, claw shelved, don't add complexity to a solved problem.' That was decided on a DIFFERENT PUTTER with a DIFFERENT GRIP and a left miss that was still live. All three have changed. Reopening it is legitimate.

TWO CAUTIONS, both cheap to respect. First, a claw can quietly introduce SHAFT LEAN — the trail hand sits on the grip differently and it's easy to end up pushing the handle forward without feeling it. The rule above doesn't relax: shaft vertical at address and at impact, on both grips. Get both in the same face-on clip and compare them.

Second, claw usually trades a little DISTANCE FEEL for a little line control — which is a bad trade for you right now, because pace is the open fault. Your own split already handles it: claw short, conventional for lags. Keep that split deliberately. It also keeps the lag ladder clean, so the pace numbers you're about to build aren't contaminated by a grip change.

sections.t: THE TRAIL FOOT — the alignment leak
sections.b: Self-reported Jul 29 and worth taking seriously: your right foot creeps UP — forward, toward the target line — and it drags the stance line open with it. Open the feet and the shoulders follow, so you end up aimed LEFT of where you think you are. The fix is exactly what you said: set that trail foot a touch further back than feels natural. Expect it to feel CLOSED, like you're aimed right. That feeling is the correction, not an error — you're recalibrating off an open baseline, so square will read as closed until it beds in. Trust the line you set, not the feel, for the first few sessions.
sections.k: Your trail foot creeps forward, opens the stance and aims you left. Set it back — square will feel closed.

sections.t: Why it wrecks the takeaway specifically
sections.b: Because in an SBST stroke the shoulder line IS the track. There's no arc to absorb a misaligned setup — 'straight back' is straight back along whatever line your shoulders are on, so an open stance doesn't just aim you left, it points the whole stroke left. Then one of two things happens, and both are bad: you feel it immediately and manipulate the takeaway to save it, which puts the HANDS back in charge of a stroke built to have no hands in it — or you don't, and the ball starts left. That's why a stance error shows up as a takeaway problem. The takeaway is fine; it's obeying a line that's wrong.
sections.k: In a straight stroke the shoulder line IS the track, so an open stance points the whole stroke left.

sections.t: This is the miss the putter can't fix
sections.b:
Your signature miss is LEFT on short putts — the through-line of the entire putter saga, and it has now outlived four putters. That history is what rules the HEAD out: a fault that survives four different putters was never about the putter.

What it never ruled out was aim. A perfectly square face aimed at a target left of the hole produces exactly this miss, and no putter ever built will save you from it. Zero-torque guarantees the FACE stays square; it cannot guarantee the face is square TO THE RIGHT THING. That has been the standing line in this plan for two weeks, and the barely-open find is the first thing to actually act on it.

Note the split that always made the case: your 10-ball blocks started 10/10 on line on the MAT, where an alignment aid is doing the aiming for you, while the miss kept showing up on the COURSE, where nothing is. That pattern is an aim signature, not a stroke signature. It has been sitting in the data the whole time.
sections.k: A square face aimed at the wrong target still misses left — and the mat-versus-course split says that's exactly what's been happening.

sections.t: The check that costs nothing
sections.b: Lay a club or an alignment stick down the target line just outside the ball on the practice green and set up to it — your toes should run PARALLEL to it, not converging toward it. Ten seconds, and it recalibrates the feel. The structural safeguard is already in your routine: aim the FACE to the spot FIRST, then build the stance around it. Keep that order religiously. If you build the stance first, the face gets aimed to a crooked body; if you aim the face first and the stance then creeps, the mismatch shows up as discomfort — and discomfort you can feel is information you can act on.
sections.k: Alignment stick on the practice green: toes parallel, not converging. Ten seconds, recalibrates the feel.

sections.t: THE TRIGGER — what starts the stroke now
sections.b:
The press was never mainly about lean. Its JOB was rhythm: it broke inertia, so the stroke started as a MOTION rather than as a decision. Take it out and that job doesn't disappear — it just needs doing another way.

Watch for the failure mode rather than assuming it: standing dead still over the ball and then having to DECIDE to go. That's where a stroke gets snatched, or steered, or quits halfway — and it tends to show up on short putts under pressure, not in practice. If your stroke starts cleanly from stillness, nothing here needs fixing and you should leave it alone.

If it doesn't, the shelf below has four inertia-breakers that don't touch shaft lean, which is the whole point of choosing from it rather than reinventing a press.

The one thing that has NOT changed: whatever starts the stroke, the shoulders run it. Quiet hands. That was true with the press and it is true without it.
sections.k: The press had one real job — breaking inertia. Removing it is right; just don't end up frozen over the ball.

sections.t: The rule that replaces it — nothing moves the shaft
sections.b:
REWRITTEN Aug 10. The old rule was 'same press, same size, every putt' — a rule for managing a variable you no longer have. What replaces it is cleaner: THE SHAFT IS VERTICAL AT ADDRESS AND VERTICAL AT IMPACT. Nothing you do moves it off vertical in either direction.

Both directions matter and they fail differently. Lean it FORWARD — hands drifting ahead of the head — and you deloft a face that has 2° to give, and you drive the ball. Let the hands fall BACK behind the head and the wrists want to save it, which is a flick, and the flick was the engine of the old blow-through left miss. Vertical is the target; both ways off it are misses.

This is easier to hold than the old rule, because 'don't move it' is a simpler instruction than 'move it a little, the same amount, every time'. And it's easier to check: one face-on clip, shaft angle at address versus at impact. Same number both times and it's done.
sections.k: One rule now, and it's simpler than the old one: the shaft is vertical at address and vertical at impact.

sections.t: The shelf — inertia-breakers that leave the shaft alone
sections.b:
Kept on the shelf rather than deleted, because with the press gone this is where you'd shop if the stroke ever starts feeling static. Every one of them breaks inertia WITHOUT the hands touching shaft lean, which is exactly why they're the right menu now.

THE FLOAT — lift the head a hair off the surface before takeaway. No hand action at all, and it removes ground friction as a bonus.

THE WHOLE-PUTTER WAGGLE — a small forward-and-back from the SHOULDERS, wrists silent.

THE LEAD-SHOULDER SETTLE — a soft downward press of the shoulder that already runs the stroke.

THE TRAIL-KNEE KICK — furthest from the hands of any of them, and the same trigger your full-swing routine already uses, which makes it the cheapest to learn.

You don't need one right now. Take one only if the 'decide to go' problem in the section above actually shows up.
sections.k: Four ways to start the stroke as a motion, none of which touch shaft lean. Only reach for one if you need it.

sections.t: How to tell the shaft stayed put
sections.b:
One face-on clip settles it: compare shaft angle at ADDRESS with shaft angle at IMPACT. With no press and a Pistol 0, both should read vertical. Equal is the pass. Meaningfully FORWARD at impact means lean is creeping in from somewhere — usually the trail hand — whatever it felt like, and feel is exactly what got this wrong before.

The free check needs no camera and it's the one to use tonight: a purely rolling ball makes ONE clean click; a ball driven down into the surface adds a faint scuff a beat later. Listen for the scuff. If you hear it, the shaft is leaning forward at impact no matter what your hands report.
sections.k: One face-on clip settles it, and the free version needs no camera: listen for the scuff.

sections.t: Stop shopping
sections.b:
Straight talk, because you called it yourself. Four putters in a month: the Phantom 7.5 returned Jul 20, the DF3i in Jul 18, out Jul 30, back in Aug 1, returned Aug 10, and the LINK.2.1 in and out and in again around it.

The LINK is now the only zero-torque head you own, and it is still inside its own return window. So 'stop shopping' is not quite available as advice — there is a real decision still to make. What IS available is the standard for making it: the DF3i was benched on a feeling, reprieved on a feeling, and returned on a feeling, without a single calibrated lag session behind any of the three. That is the pattern to break, not the putter.

So the rule from here, unchanged in spirit and sharper in practice: the next thing that changes should be a NUMBER on the card, not a head in the bag. And if this head does go back, let a scoreboard send it — two weeks of ladder data and a tape sheet — rather than a feeling. That would be the first equipment decision in this whole project with evidence under it.
sections.k: Four putters in a month, all judged on feel — break the pattern, not the putter: the next thing that changes should be a number.

sections.t: Why beside the ball and not behind it
sections.b: Rehearsing in your true putting posture — same deep bend, same arm hang, same shoulder plane — means the stroke that FEELS like 30 feet is the stroke you actually make. Magnitude transfers one-to-one. Rehearsing from behind the ball reads the break better, but you're standing upright there, so the size you feel is only an approximation. Your open fault is pace magnitude, not reading: path ✓, face ✓, start lines 10/10 twice over. Optimise the thing that's broken.
sections.k: Rehearse in your real posture beside the ball, because magnitude transfers one-to-one that way.

sections.t: Keep the order of the two rehearsals
sections.b: Ball-look first (path and contact), hole-look second (pace). The last thing you feel is the thing you carry in — so the pace stroke must be the last one. If the hole stroke ever drifts to first, the pace feel gets overwritten by the contact feel and you're back to guessing distance. Finish rehearsal 2 WITH the soft press, at its real size: it's the one part of the stroke that never used to get a practice rep, which is how it drifted last time without you noticing.
sections.k: Ball-look first, hole-look second — the last thing you feel is what you carry in.

sections.t: Two rules underneath it
sections.b: SAME BEAT COUNT, EVERY PUTT — a routine that varies in length is itself a pace variable, and the putts where you take an extra look are the ones that come up short. And a VERBAL BACKSTOP is worth testing: say the pace intention right before the press ('die it a foot past', 'back of the cup'). Feel decays, a word doesn't.
sections.k: Same beat count every putt, and try saying the pace intention out loud before the press.

sections.t: Still to test — lags
sections.b:
This is the top of the card, and it is the single thing that would have prevented the entire detour. The Jul 29 round was lags coming up SHORT and short putts running HOT, which is not two faults but one: a power curve you hadn't learned, so you under-hit the long ones and over-hit the short ones. That got the DF3i benched. It was never once tested. And on Aug 10 the same untested complaint sent that putter back for good.

So the curve gets built on the LINK, deliberately. The block test, twice a week: 10 balls from 30 feet. Log THREE numbers — how many finish SHORT (target no more than 1 in 10), the SPREAD front-to-back of the ten stopping points (target inside 6 feet), and the GREEN SPEED. Then the calibration set: 20, 30 and 40 feet, three balls each, noting where the BACKSTROKE ends for each distance. Written down, that mapping is the curve you have never had.

Two things make this more promising than it sounds. Tempo is already right on this head — 2.0:1 measured against a 2:1 target — so the missing ingredient is stroke LENGTH, not rhythm. And strike location has never been measured on any putter you own, which matters here because an off-centre hit bleeds ball speed and shows up as exactly this fault. The tape test is twelve minutes and it belongs at the front of this queue.

ONE WATCH ITEM from the barely-open find: if you were unconsciously steering the stroke to save a face aimed left, then fixing the aim removes the need for the steer — and a stroke that no longer steers can deliver different pace. So take a ladder reading EARLY, before the new aim beds in, and don't confuse a pace change caused by the aim fix with one caused by the putter.
sections.k: Build the power curve on the LINK — and take a reading early, because fixing the aim may move your pace too.

steps: Read it from BEHIND the ball — pick the line and a spot a few inches ahead of it
Step BESIDE the ball — BEND OVER, stand close, full putting posture
Rehearsal 1 — eyes on the BALL. Path and contact.
Rehearsal 2 — eyes on the HOLE. Pace. Finish it with the soft press.
Step in — set the FACE to the spot first and set it BARELY OPEN, then build the stance around it (trail foot a touch BACK)
Spot → ball → soft press with the body → putt

Ball 1–2 BALL-WIDTHS inside the lead heel
HANDS OVER THE HEAD OF THE PUTTER — that IS the straight shaft
NO PRESS. Nothing moves the shaft off vertical, at address or at impact
QUIET HANDS — the shoulders run the stroke, the hands just hold on
Set the face BARELY OPEN — that's your square
Aim the FACE first, then build the stance to it
TRAIL FOOT back — square will feel closed
CLAW for short ones, conventional for lags — keep the split clean

entries.text: PUTTING — THE CLAW TRIAL, kept honest. You're trialling a claw on short putts with the press removed and quiet hands. Two variables changed at once, so protect the split that already separates them: CLAW FOR SHORT ONES, CONVENTIONAL FOR LAGS. That keeps the 30-ft ladder clean, which matters because pace is the open fault and a grip change is exactly the kind of thing that would contaminate the curve you're about to build. THE ONE CHECK: a claw can introduce shaft lean without you feeling it — the trail hand sits differently and the handle creeps forward. Get BOTH grips into the same face-on set, 240 fps, white tape on the shaft, and compare shaft angle at address versus impact. Vertical on both is the pass; forward at impact on the claw means it's adding lean, and on a 2°-loft face that drives the ball. THE SCOREBOARD: the 20-ball 5-footer, one block claw, one block conventional, same session. Note that the old Grip Experiment closed with 'claw shelved' — that verdict was reached on the DF3i, with the Press Pistol 2°, and with the left miss still live. All three have changed, so it does not bind.

PUTTING — Bed in the settled stroke on the LINK.2.1: deep bend / stand close, HANDS OVER THE HEAD OF THE PUTTER, shaft straight up and down, QUIET HANDS. THE PRESS IS OUT as of Aug 10 — your call, and the arithmetic backs it: the LINK has 2° of effective loft built to be delivered at 0° lean, so any press subtracts from a budget that has nothing spare, and a press that varies in size is a launch that varies, which is a pace that varies. Your cue and the film agree exactly, which is new: hands over the putter HEAD means a vertical shaft, and a vertical shaft is what the Jul 30 stills measured as hands ~1.35" behind the BALL. Same position, two descriptions. THE RULE NOW: shaft vertical at address AND at impact — forward at impact delofts and drives it, hands falling back invites the old wrist flick. WATCH FOR: starting from dead stillness and having to decide to go, which is where a stroke gets snatched under pressure. If that shows up, take an inertia-breaker off the shelf in the routine plan (float, shoulder settle, trail-knee kick) — none of them touch shaft lean. Keep BALL POSITION marked: 1–2 ball-widths inside the lead heel.

briefing.focus: The routine as you run it now: get low, ball inside the lead heel, hands over the head of the putter, no press, quiet hands, face barely open, claw on the short ones, same beat count every putt. Standing work is the 30-ft ladder and one face-on clip. Everything historical — grip flips, putter changes, old measurements — is condensed in the Notes at the bottom; the sections above are only what you do.

sections.t: THE HEADLINE — get low
sections.k: Bend over and get low — the anchor feel everything else hangs off.
sections.b: Your words, and they go at the top: bending over is the most massive thing, and getting low is where you feel most comfortable. That is the feel to remember when everything else has drifted. If you carry one thought to the practice green, carry this one. Deep bend, stand close, eyes down.

sections.t: Why the bend is more than comfort
sections.k: It presents the lie the putter needs, and steepens the shoulder plane that makes the stroke straight.
sections.b:
Two mechanisms under the feel. FIRST — the LINK is Lie Angle Balanced, and that balance is only true when the shaft is presented at its built lie (69° lie, 2° effective loft, 0° lean, 34"). Stand tall or reach and the toe drops, the shaft leaves its lie, and the self-squaring property you bought quietly degrades. Posture is what delivers the technology.

SECOND — more bend hangs the arms freer and tilts the shoulders onto a STEEPER plane, and a steeper shoulder plane is what produces a straight-back-straight-through stroke. Standing tall builds in an arc you don't want.

sections.t: The setup
sections.k: Ball 1–2 widths inside the lead heel · hands over the head of the putter · quiet hands · face barely open.
sections.b:
BEND OVER, stand close, eyes down through the strike. BALL one to two ball-widths inside the lead heel — forward of centre so the head is a hair ASCENDING at contact, which is what produces true roll. Mark the spot and keep it; launch is sensitive to it, and a ball position that wanders reads as bad distance control even when the stroke was fine. Weight stacked ON the ball. TRAIL FOOT a touch back. Rock the shoulders, QUIET HANDS, loose grip. Face set BARELY OPEN — its own section below.

HANDS OVER THE HEAD OF THE PUTTER — shaft straight up and down. That is the entire hands instruction. Don't add lean to make it look like a normal putter: this face carries 2° of effective loft delivered at 0° lean, there is nothing to spare, and a driven ball skids before it rolls and finishes short.

(A vertical shaft photographs as hands ~1.35" behind the ball's centre — half a ball from face to centre plus the riser hosel's offset. Same position, the camera's description of it. Ball position is set by your FEET; the shaft is set by your HANDS.)

sections.t: THE FACE — barely open is your square
sections.k: Set what reads to you as barely open — that is square. Verify at a real target once; re-check monthly.
sections.b:
On this putter the face points where you set it — zero-torque means it doesn't twist through the stroke, so address IS impact. What reads to your eye as barely open is, on the actual line, square. Trust it and set it the same way every putt.

Two standing guards. DON'T STACK FIXES: keep this feel, or retrain the aim picture with a mirror — never both, or the correction gets applied twice and the miss flips right. PUT A NUMBER ON IT: once, photograph the face from directly above against an alignment stick, then re-check monthly — an unquantified feel drifts toward the exaggeration.

One check still owed, and it's the last one: five putts at a coin on a real green, nothing drawn on the ground, filmed from behind the ball. If the misses still fall on both sides, this closes for good.

sections.t: THE CLAW — short ones only
sections.k: It fits this putter's premise — keep it off the lags, and hold the shaft rule on both grips.
sections.b:
Scope: SHORT PUTTS. Conventional stays on the lags — a claw trades a little distance feel for line control, the wrong trade on a lag while pace is the open fault, and the split keeps the ladder numbers clean.

Why it fits: a zero-torque head is built on the premise that the face squares itself when the hands stop interfering, and the claw exists to take the trail hand OUT of the stroke. 'Quiet hands' and 'claw' are the same instruction.

The one check: a claw can push the handle forward without you feeling it. The shaft rule doesn't relax — vertical at address and impact, on BOTH grips. Get both into the same face-on set and compare. Scoreboard: the 20-ball 5-footer, one block claw, one block conventional, same session.

sections.t: THE TRAIL FOOT — set it back
sections.k: Trail foot back, square will feel closed — and always face first, then stance.
sections.b:
Set the trail foot a touch further back than feels natural, and expect square to feel CLOSED. You're recalibrating off an open baseline, so trust the line you set rather than the feel for the first few sessions.

Why it matters this much: in an SBST stroke the shoulder line IS the track. An open stance doesn't just aim you left — it points the whole stroke left, and then either the hands steer the takeaway to save it, or the ball starts left. A stance error shows up disguised as a takeaway problem.

Ten-second check: alignment stick down the line, toes PARALLEL, not converging. And keep the order religiously — aim the FACE to the spot first, then build the stance around it. Face-first means a creeping stance shows up as discomfort, and discomfort you can feel is information you can act on.

sections.t: THE SHAFT — vertical at address, vertical at impact
sections.k: One rule, checkable two ways: same shaft angle both ends, and no scuff in the sound.
sections.b:
The shaft is VERTICAL at address and VERTICAL at impact. Nothing you do moves it. Forward at impact delofts a face with 2° to give and drives the ball into the turf — it skids, then rolls, and finishes short. Hands falling BACK invite the wrist flick. Both directions off vertical are misses.

Check with a camera: one face-on clip, shaft angle at address versus impact, same number both times — pass. Check without one: LISTEN. A purely rolling ball makes one clean click; a driven ball adds a faint scuff a beat later. If you hear the scuff, the shaft leaned forward, whatever your hands report.

sections.t: THE TRIGGER — starting without a press
sections.k: The stroke must start as a motion, not a decision. If it does, leave this alone.
sections.b:
With no press, watch for one failure mode: standing dead still over the ball and having to DECIDE to go. That's where a stroke gets snatched or steered, and it shows up on short putts under pressure, not on the practice green. If your stroke starts cleanly from stillness, nothing here needs you — skip it.

If it does show up, take ONE off this shelf. Each starts the stroke without touching shaft lean: the FLOAT (lift the head a hair off the surface before takeaway), the WHOLE-PUTTER WAGGLE (small, from the shoulders, wrists silent), the LEAD-SHOULDER SETTLE, or the TRAIL-KNEE KICK — the same trigger your full-swing routine already uses, which makes it the cheapest to learn.

sections.t: THE REHEARSALS — beside the ball, pace last
sections.k: Rehearse in real posture beside the ball; ball-look first, hole-look second; same beat count every putt.
sections.b:
Read from BEHIND the ball — line, and a spot a few inches ahead of it. Then rehearse BESIDE the ball in full putting posture: same bend, same arm hang. Magnitude transfers one-to-one from that posture; behind-the-ball rehearsals read break better but run upright, so the size they teach is an approximation — and size is the thing you're training.

Order is fixed. Rehearsal 1, eyes on the BALL: path and contact. Rehearsal 2, eyes on the HOLE: pace. The last thing you feel is what you carry in, so the pace stroke goes last, always.

Same BEAT COUNT every putt — a routine that varies in length is itself a pace variable, and the putts that get an extra look are the ones that come up short. Backstop worth testing: say the pace intention out loud before stepping in ('die it a foot past', 'back of the cup'). Feel decays; a word doesn't.

Past 25 feet, test eyes ON THE HOLE through the stroke — as a block test on the practice green, not mid-round.

sections.t: THE LADDER — the standing work
sections.k: 10 from 30 ft, twice a week: shorts · spread · green speed. Gamer ball, conventional grip.
sections.b:
Twice a week on the LINK, gamer ball only, conventional grip: 10 balls from 30 feet. Log three numbers — SHORTS (target no more than 1 in 10; a short putt had zero chance), SPREAD front-to-back of the ten stopping points (target inside 6 feet; this is the actual measure of distance control), and GREEN SPEED or surface, every session, because a curve built at one speed is one data point.

Then the calibration set, five minutes: 20, 30 and 40 feet, three balls each, writing down where the BACKSTROKE ENDS for each. That written mapping is the power curve. Distance comes from stroke LENGTH at a fixed tempo — tempo is already right on this head (2.0:1 measured) — so if you catch yourself hitting AT a long one, that rep is the fault showing itself. Note it.

Full protocol and the keep-or-return gate live in The Distance Grind.

sections.t: Feel versus real — how this plan is written
sections.k: Your words set the intent; the film sets the positions. Where they disagree, the film wins.
sections.b: Standing rule, in your words: the film study is king. What you're DOING — grips, triggers, decisions — is yours and authoritative. Where a POSITION or a SENSATION is claimed, the measurement outranks the description, and where there's no measurement the plan says so instead of repeating the feel as if it were established.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: History, condensed. Nothing here changes what you do above.
sections.b:
Aug 10: the press came out (your call — the 2° loft budget has nothing to spare, and a varying press is a varying pace). The DF3i was returned for distance control; its Press Pistol 2° went with it, and every 'hands even / hands ahead' cue died with that grip. The claw reopened for shorts — the old 'claw shelved' verdict came from a different putter, a different grip and a live left miss, so it doesn't bind. 'Hands over the ball' was corrected to 'hands over the HEAD of the putter' — the corrected version matches the Jul 30 stills exactly (vertical shaft = hands ~1.35" behind the ball centre), the first time a feel and a measurement have landed on each other in this project.

Aug 10 pm film: three putts on a lined mat went 0.8° right / 1.0° left / 0.6° right — the one-way LEFT pull from Jul 30 (1.5°, 1.7°) did not reproduce. Start line downgraded; the residual dispersion points at strike, not aim; the old 0.5° gate is retired as too strict for the player and the method.

Jul 30 film, still standing: SBST path confirmed across four putters; tempo 2.0:1; early lift closed; stance line closed (toes never open); vertical shaft repeatable to 0.3°. Pace remains the open fault — it decided the fate of two putters without ever being measured, which is why the ladder is the standing work.

briefing.focus: One mechanism, four checks, one measuring protocol. Lead-side pressure pins the low point; the low point decides whether the ball rolls or hops; ball position and a vertical shaft decide where that low point meets the ball. Keep any feel that passes the four checks. History — including rules this plan used to carry — is in the Notes.
rules: Ball 1–2 ball-widths inside the lead heel — mark it
Pressure ~55/45 lead — its one job is pinning the low point
Low point at or just behind the ball = a hair ascending = true roll
Shaft returns to VERTICAL at impact — never ahead, never behind
The blade reports a bad strike — listen for the scuff, then measure

sections.t: What lead-side pressure is for
sections.k: It pins where the stroke bottoms out — that's the whole mechanism.
sections.b: Lead-side pressure does one job: it PINS THE LOW POINT of the stroke. Where your weight sits decides where the arc bottoms out, and where the arc bottoms out decides how the putter meets the ball. Everything below follows from that, on any head.

sections.t: The cost of hanging back
sections.k: Weight back = low point behind the ball = added loft = hop, skid, short.
sections.b:
Weight back moves the bottom of the arc BEHIND the ball, so the head arrives climbing hard with the shaft leaning away from the target. That adds loft you never asked for: the ball launches slightly, HOPS, SKIDS, and only then rolls. Every bit of hop is energy that was supposed to become roll, so the putt arrives soft — and skid distance changes with green speed and grain, so your pace stops being repeatable between surfaces.

The window on this head is narrow in both directions. The face carries 2° of effective loft — that's the whole budget. Lean away from the target and you add loft; lean toward it and you go below zero and drive the ball down. Both mistakes produce the same symptom: a skidding ball that finishes short of what the stroke intended.

sections.t: The four checks
sections.k: Ball inside the lead heel · low point just behind it · shaft back to vertical · 55/45. Pass all four, keep your feel.
sections.b:
(1) BALL one to two ball-widths INSIDE THE LEAD HEEL. Use the heel, not a body reference — a deep-bend posture moves your chest line; the heel doesn't move. Mark it on the mat.

(2) LOW POINT at or just behind the ball, so the head is a HAIR ascending at contact. This is what ball position is for.

(3) SHAFT RETURNS TO VERTICAL at impact — the same place it started.

(4) PRESSURE about 55/45 lead — enough to anchor the low point, not so much you start steering.

If a feel you're comfortable in delivers all four, keep the feel. The checks are the rule; the feel is yours.

sections.t: Ball position by the feet, lean by the hands
sections.k: A vertical shaft photographs as hands ~1.35" behind the ball — it happens by itself; don't set it.
sections.b:
Two different variables, two different controls. Ball position is set by your FEET (check 1). Shaft lean is set by your HANDS (check 3), and the target is zero.

A vertical shaft photographs as the hands sitting about 1.35" behind the ball's centre — half a ball (0.84") from face to centre, plus roughly half an inch from shaft axis to face on this riser-hosel blade. That's not a position to set; it's what 'hands over the head of the putter' produces on its own. If you try to put the hands somewhere, you're adding lean.

sections.t: The blade tells you
sections.k: This head reports a bad strike instead of muffling it — use that, then measure.
sections.b:
A narrow blade carries less MOI, so a strike off the middle bleeds real distance and you can FEEL it. That makes your hands a better instrument on this putter than on a big mallet — a mediocre low point won't hide.

Use it, but don't stop there. The sound check costs nothing: one clean click is a rolling ball; a faint scuff a beat later is a driven one. The measurement is the tape test — twelve minutes, its own plan — and it's the thing to run before drawing any conclusion about this putter's pace.

sections.t: Settle any change with data
sections.k: A/B it on the ladder and let the stopping points decide, not the feel.
sections.b:
A/B LAG LADDER — 30 feet, two blocks of 10. Block A: current feel. Block B: the change, everything else identical. Mark where each ball STOPS and measure the spread; tighter spread wins, and that's the answer, not anyone's opinion.

FACE-ON CLIP — the one measurement this plan keeps asking for: shaft angle at address versus impact (both vertical is the pass — with no press and no built-in lean, whatever the tape shows IS your hands), where the head bottoms out relative to the ball, and ball position rep to rep. White tape on the shaft, 240 fps, camera at ball height square to the line.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: History, condensed. Nothing here changes the checks above.
sections.b: The 'hands level or a touch ahead at impact' rule that used to be check 3 belonged to the DF3i's Press Pistol 2° — a grip with lean built in — and left with that putter on Aug 10; on a 0°-lean build, hands ahead delofts and drives it. The press was removed the same day, which also retired the old 'keep it tiny' arithmetic. The ball-forward, weight-on-the-ball question was settled on the mat back in July; what this plan adds is the number (1–2 widths inside the lead heel) and the ground reference. This plan's forgiveness section flipped twice with the bag — the mallet that muffled a wandering low point is gone, which raises the stakes and sharpens the feedback. And the reason the plan exists at all: pace decided the fate of two putters on feel alone, with zero calibrated lag sessions behind any verdict.

briefing.focus: Build this putter's power curve with numbers before its return window closes. The ladder twice a week, three numbers logged every time; the 20/30/40 backstroke map; the tape test early; then keep-or-return gets decided on a scoreboard. Setup for pace is four lines. History is in the Notes.
rules: Pace is the open fault — the ladder IS the grind
10 from 30 ft, twice a week: log SHORTS · SPREAD · GREEN SPEED
Distance = stroke LENGTH at a fixed tempo — 2.0:1 is already right
Tape test before you judge the putter — strike is a distance fault first
No press, hands over the head — nothing feeds a varying launch
Gamer ball only · conventional grip on lags
Find the return deadline, then let the scoreboard decide

sections.t: The ladder — this is the grind
sections.k: Ten balls from thirty feet, twice a week, three numbers written down.
sections.b:
Ten balls, 30 feet, on the LINK. Twice a week. Log three things every time:

SHORTS — how many of the ten finish short of the hole. Target: no more than 1 in 10. A putt that finishes short had a zero per cent chance.

SPREAD — front-to-back distance between the nearest and furthest stopping points. This is the actual measurement of distance control and the number that shows improvement. Target: inside 6 feet.

GREEN SPEED — estimated stimp, or name the surface honestly (that mat, this practice green). Not optional: a stroke that finishes perfectly on an 8–9 runs four to six feet past from 30 feet on an 11, so build the curve on at least TWO speeds before trusting it.

Then the calibration set, five minutes: 20, 30 and 40 feet, three balls each, noting where the BACKSTROKE ENDS for each distance — a landmark you can repeat. Written down, that mapping is the curve.

sections.t: Where distance comes from
sections.k: Stroke length at a fixed tempo — if tempo moves with distance, the curve never stabilises.
sections.b:
The ingredient most people are missing, you have: tempo measured 2.0:1 on this head against a 2:1 target. So the discipline in every ladder session is: same tempo, always — count it, hum it, whatever keeps it stable — and change the LENGTH.

The failure mode is the reverse: keeping the backstroke roughly constant and varying how hard you hit it. That works at one distance and falls apart everywhere else. If you catch yourself hitting AT a long one, that rep is the fault showing itself — note it on the sheet.

Once three distances have a repeatable backstroke landmark, everything between them is interpolation, and lag putting becomes a reference you consult instead of a feeling you summon.

sections.t: Strike — the hidden speed leak
sections.k: Off-centre contact bleeds ball speed. Twelve minutes of foot powder before any verdict on this putter.
sections.b:
A putt struck off the middle loses ball speed, so the same stroke finishes shorter — and inconsistently, because the miss moves. A heel strike also rotates the face closed. One cause, both faults, and it has never been measured on any putter you've owned.

This blade raises the stakes: less MOI than a mallet, so the same miss costs more speed and more face angle — and its riser hosel makes the true centre impossible to find by eye. If strike is your leak, the ladder will show it as a wide spread, and the tape test will show you where it's coming from.

So run the tape test EARLY — tap test for the true sweet spot, then foot-powder sheets from 5 and 30 feet, with the 30-footer as the verdict. Full protocol is its own plan. Use the barely-open address, since that's the setup you actually play.

sections.t: Setup for pace — four lines
sections.k: Marked ball position, vertical shaft, quiet hands, gamer ball. Pace has no other setup inputs.
sections.b:
BALL marked 1–2 ball-widths inside the lead heel, same spot every rep — launch is sensitive to it, and a wandering ball position reads as bad distance control even when the stroke was fine.

HANDS OVER THE HEAD OF THE PUTTER, no press, shaft vertical at address and impact — a varying launch is a varying pace, and with no press there's nothing to vary.

QUIET HANDS, shoulders run it.

GAMER BALL ONLY on all pace work, and conventional grip on the lags — the claw stays on short putts so the ladder numbers stay clean.

sections.t: The gate — before the window closes
sections.k: Find the deadline, run two weeks of numbers, and let the sheet decide keep-or-return.
sections.b:
First job: find the receipt and confirm the return deadline — the Home card is showing 'deadline unknown' until you set it. Everything here runs on that clock.

The gate, set now while nothing is being decided: two weeks of the ladder at two different green speeds, plus the tape test. If the spread is still wide AND the tape shows a centred strike, the head is a fair suspect — send it back with actual evidence, the first equipment decision in this project that would have any. If the tape shows a heel bias, the head was never the problem, and returning it buys a fifth putter and the same fault.

Know the fallback either way: the only other putter in the bag is the Newport 2, a toe-hang blade against your SBST stroke. That's not an argument for keeping the LINK — it's an argument for knowing the replacement BEFORE the window closes, not after.

sections.t: What's already settled
sections.k: Path, tempo, lift, stance — measured, closed, and none of them walked out with any putter.
sections.b:
Path: straight, SBST, confirmed across four heads. Tempo: 2.0:1 on this putter. Early lift: closed on film. Stance line: square, never open. Start line: downgraded — the one-way left pull did not reproduce across three measured putts.

What's open is pace and strike, and both are the same twelve minutes and the same ladder away from having numbers. The rule stands: the next thing that changes should be a NUMBER on the card, not a head in the bag.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: History, condensed. Nothing here changes the work above.
sections.b: The DF3i went back on Aug 10 for distance control — after being benched for pace Jul 30, reprieved Aug 1 and returned Aug 10: three verdicts in eleven days, all on feel, zero calibrated lag sessions. That pattern, not the putter, is what this plan exists to break. The Aug 1 'pace felt dialled' round was a scramble on 8–9 stimp greens — the friendliest read available. The Aug 10 outdoor session scored ~20 putts off above-ground cups: nine dead, worst ~4 ft, nothing long — first real evidence pace is closer than the returns implied. The blue ball scattered 1.2–1.5 ft on putts the white killed from the same spot — hence the gamer-ball rule. Both reds on the evolution grid (face at impact, start line) were measured on this head Jul 30; the start-line red was downgraded Aug 10 pm after the mat set came back 0.8° right / 1.0° left / 0.6° right — dispersion, no bias.

briefing.course: The Tape Test — Where You Actually Hit It
briefing.focus: Twelve minutes, at home, on the LINK.2.1. Strike location is the one cheap unmeasured thing left, and it's a DISTANCE fault before it's a line fault — an off-centre hit bleeds ball speed. Two steps: find the true sweet spot, then see where you actually hit it. The 30-foot sheet is the verdict.
rules: Step 1: hang the putter, tap the face — the no-twist point is the sweet spot; mark it
Check the mark against the sight line — the riser hosel fools the eye
Step 2: foot powder · 10 from 5 ft · re-coat · 10 from 30 ft · photograph both
Don't wipe between putts · barely-open address · conventional grip
The 30-ft sheet is the verdict — speed leaks show on long putts

sections.t: Step one — find the true sweet spot
sections.k: Hang it, tap it: the spot with no twist is the sweet spot. Mark it and check it against the sight line.
sections.b:
Hang the putter from the top of the grip so it swings free. Tap the face heel-to-toe with a pencil eraser and watch the head: everywhere off-centre it TWISTS, and at one spot it swings straight back with no twist. That spot is the true sweet spot. Mark it with a sliver of tape.

Then check the mark against the sight line. On this head the shaft is a poor pointer to where the mass sits — the riser hosel offsets it — so don't trust your eye on this one. If the mark and the sight line disagree, that disagreement is a finding on its own: you've been lining up a spot that isn't the middle.

sections.t: Step two — the powder sheets
sections.k: Two coats, two distances, two photos. Don't wipe between putts.
sections.b:
Coat the face with foot-powder spray. Hit 10 putts from 5 feet. Photograph the face. Re-coat, hit 10 from 30 feet, photograph again. Don't wipe between putts — the overlapping marks ARE the data.

Use the setup you actually play: barely-open face, hands over the head, conventional grip. If you want the claw's answer too, run it as a third coat on the 5-footers — separately, so the sheets don't mix.

sections.t: How to read the sheets
sections.k: Tight and centred clears the putter; a heel bias explains both faults at once; scatter explains the spread.
sections.b:
TIGHT CLUSTER ON THE MARK — strike isn't your leak. Pace work is pure stroke-length calibration, and the putter is cleared of the distance complaint.

CLUSTER OFF-CENTRE, especially toward the HEEL — one cause explaining both open faults at once: heel contact rotates the face closed (starts it left) and bleeds ball speed (finishes short). Fixable with setup distance-to-ball and eyeline, not with a new putter.

BROAD SCATTER — the ladder's spread has its cause: a strike that moves is a ball speed that moves. On this blade every miss costs more than it did on a mallet, so the sheet's stakes are real.

The 30-FOOT sheet is the one that matters — long putts are where a speed leak shows. The 5-foot sheet is the baseline that tells you whether the leak is stroke-length dependent.

sections.t: What the result feeds
sections.k: The keep-or-return gate and the pace grind both wait on these two photos.
sections.b:
This test is one of the two inputs to the LINK's keep-or-return gate: a wide ladder spread PLUS a centred sheet makes the head a fair suspect; a heel bias means the head was never the problem. It also de-noises the pace grind — until strike is measured, every ladder number carries an unknown inside it.

Send both photos when you run it.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: History, condensed.
sections.b: Written Aug 2 for the DF3i; moved to the LINK on Aug 10 when the mallet was returned. Still unrun — strike location has never been measured on any of the four putters owned this month. Two pointers from Aug 10 both aim here: the evening mat putts scattered ~0.8° either side of the line with no bias (a moving strike is the leading explanation on a head that can't twist), and the blue ball spread 1.2–1.5 ft on putts the white killed.

round.note: First 18 with full stats. 43/44, +15. 6/18 greens — 7 of the 12 misses SHORT. 6/14 fairways, five of the eight misses left. 38 putts: one 1-putt all day (the birdie on 3), fifteen holes at two putts or better, three 3-putts (9, 14, 16). Holes 14–17 cost +6.

entries.text: APPROACH — CLUB UP. Sterling Farms is the first round with a miss direction on every green, and it is not ambiguous: 12 greens missed, SEVEN of them short (1, 2, 6, 8, 10, 12, 17), against two left, one right, one long. That is the same pattern the GHIN archive shows (short 44 against long 0), now confirmed hole by hole, and it is the biggest tee-to-green lever you have — short is where the bunkers and the false fronts live, and a short miss is the one miss that can never end up close. TWO FIXES, both free. (1) Club to cover the BACK of the green, not the pin: take the number to the flag, add the yardage from flag to back edge, and pick the club that carries the middle of that window. (2) Stop clubbing off your best strike — your ladder numbers (PW 122 · 50° 108 · 56° 95 · 60° 80) are carries, and a 60% strike from the rough is 8–10 short of them. THE CHECK, next round: log the miss direction on every green again. If short drops under half the misses, this is working.

faults.why: THE priority — and Aug 12 is the first time it has been measured anywhere near a real green, by accident rather than by design. STERLING FARMS, 18 holes on the LINK.2.1: 38 putts, THREE 3-PUTTS (holes 9, 14 and 16), and exactly ONE 1-putt all day — the birdie on 3. Read it honestly in both directions. THE GOOD HALF IS REAL: with only 6 greens in regulation, twelve holes were chip-and-putt, and fifteen of eighteen still finished in two putts or fewer. That is the card's version of Jack's 'made a lot of 5 footers' — they were SECOND putts, holed come-backers, and they are what kept 87 from being 92. THE BAD HALF IS ALSO REAL: three 3-putts is three strokes handed back, and hole 9 was a green hit in regulation turned into a bogey. Jack's report was 'good lags, not dropping 10–20 feet yet'; the card agrees with the second half exactly (one 1-putt) and only partly with the first — lags good enough to two-putt from most places, not good enough to stop three of them running away. WHAT THIS DOES NOT REPLACE: the 30-ft ladder, still unrun. A round tells you the total; it cannot tell you the SPREAD, the green speed, or whether the misses were short or long — the three numbers the ladder exists to capture. Prior evidence stands: the DF3i went back Aug 10 for distance control after three verdicts in eleven days without one calibrated lag session, and the Aug 10 afternoon (~20 putts, nine dead, worst ~4 ft) said calibrated-but-conservative on a second green speed. Tempo is not the missing piece (2.0:1 against a 2:1 target). Stroke length and strike are. Run the ladder with the gamer ball model only.

The remaining candidate — but sized honestly now. Never measured on any putter, not once, across four heads. The Aug 10 evening start lines scattered ~0.8° either side of the line with no bias, and on a head that cannot twist, a face pointing a different way each rep is a face being MOVED by contact: heel closes it, toe opens it. That fits. What has changed is the STAKES: a 0.8° scatter still holes out to nearly eight feet, so as a LINE fault this is no longer costing strokes and does not need chasing. The reason to run the test anyway is PACE — an off-centre hit bleeds ball speed, so the same stroke finishes short and the lag spread widens, and pace is the fault that just cost a putter and has never been measured. Second nudge from the same day, also about pace, not line: the blue ball scattered 1.2–1.5 ft on putts the white killed from the same spot with the same putter. Twelve minutes — tap test for the sweet spot, foot-powder sheets from 5 ft and 30 ft, and the 30-footer is the one that matters. Run it with the barely-open address. Read the result as distance-control data. 

Aug 12 adds a reason to hurry: 38 putts and three 3-putts over 18 holes is the pace fault showing up on a scorecard, and the twelve-minute test is still the cheapest thing that could explain it. The LINK's return window is open and the deadline is still unknown.

Open, and Aug 10 could not touch it — twice in one day. The afternoon's 23 clips were all oblique; the evening's six were all ON the target line, which is right for start line and blind to shaft lean, because lean lives in the plane those cameras look straight down. Face-on is now the ONLY angle never shot. What it has to settle: the Press Pistol 2° went back with the DF3i, so the LINK's Pistol 0 supplies no lean at all — shaft vertical at address, hands ~1.35" behind the ball — and the soft press is now the ONLY lean in the stroke. The 'don't double-count the lean' arithmetic is retired; consistency replaces it, because a press that varies is a launch that varies, which is a pace that varies. One slo-mo face-on set gives lean at address versus impact AND ball position rep to rep in the same clips. Whatever the tape shows IS the press now, with no built-in 2° to subtract.

DOWNGRADED Aug 10 — off the top of the card, and the reasoning is worth keeping because the old gate on this line was wrong. THE CRUX IS THE SIGN, NOT THE SIZE. Jul 30: 1.5° LEFT, 1.7° LEFT, one straight — three putts pulling the SAME way. Aug 10 pm: 0.8° right, 1.0° left, 0.6° right — mean bias ≈0.1°, i.e. zero. Aim doesn't change between reps, so a one-way pull is what an aim error looks like, and it did not reproduce on any of the three. The founding premise of this entire putter saga was a DIRECTIONAL claim — 'signature miss: left on short putts' — and a directional claim is a claim about bias. On the evidence available, that bias is gone, and it went away after a setup change Jack found himself, not after any of the four putters.

IN STROKES, WHICH IS THE ONLY UNIT THAT MATTERS. Capture at the hole is ±1.29" (4.25" cup, 1.68" ball, dying speed). A 1.6° bias puts the ball outside that from 3.8 ft — so the old miss started costing strokes at four feet, which is exactly where the 'left on SHORT putts' signature came from. A 0.8° miss holes out to 7.7 ft. At 0.6° it's 10.2 ft. So the residual has moved start line out of the range where an 8.5 handicap loses shots to it: beyond eight feet, make rates are governed by pace and read, not by a degree of face angle.

THE 0.5° GATE IS RETIRED — it was a bad standard and it was mine. Half a degree is around the level tour putters hold, it was being applied to a phone-on-a-mat measurement carrying ±0.5° of its own error, and it implied a precision nobody should be chasing. Worse, it pointed at the wrong quantity: it gated on magnitude when the thing that was actually broken was direction.

AND THE RESIDUAL IS AN UPPER BOUND, not an estimate. Measurement noise can only ever INFLATE apparent dispersion — it cannot hide scatter that exists. So with ±0.5° of method error sitting inside an observed ~0.8°, the true dispersion is 0.8° or better, quite possibly nearer 0.6°. Jack's read that these are small numbers is correct and, if anything, understated.

WHAT'S LEFT TO DO, and it is small: confirm the bias stays gone away from a printed line — five putts at a coin on a real green, filmed from behind. That is a check, not an investigation. If the pull is still absent, this fault closes and start line stops being a thing this project tracks.

CLOSED Jul 30 ✓. At 120 fps and 37.5 px/inch the sole held within 0.05–0.08" of its address height for the full 83 ms into impact, flat across ten consecutive frames, and never dropped below address height. Measured on the LINK, the head still in play, so it carries cleanly. Wants two more slo-mo strokes on sample size — the owed face-on set gives them for free, which is one more reason to shoot it.

CLOSED Jul 30 ✓ — overhead film measured the toe line 0.6°, 2.9° and 3.6° CLOSED to the target line across three reps. Never open. Worth re-reading against the Aug 10 find: this measurement is what ruled the feet out and sent the search higher, which is exactly where the answer turned out to be.

club.spec: Zero-torque (Lie Angle Balanced) · narrow-body heel-shafted blade · 69° lie (70° fit target, in tolerance) · loft UNCONFIRMED · 0° shaft lean · riser hosel · L.A.B. Pistol 0 grip
club.note: Gamed from Jul 30. SPEC CORRECTED Aug 12. THE LOFT IS NOT CONFIRMED — L.A.B.'s own product pages, PGA Tour Superstore, Golf Galaxy, Fairway Jockey, Carl's Golfland, Golfio and two published reviews were all searched and none of them publish a loft for the LINK.2.1. The 2° this app has carried since Jul 30 went in as 'confirmed by research' and it wasn't; it's an estimate, and three plans have been reasoning off it — how much a press de-lofts, whether hands ahead drives the ball. Treat it as unknown until a loft/lie machine or L.A.B. support says otherwise. THE LIE IS SETTLED, and better than we knew: 69° is the as-built against a 70° target from the remote fitting, L.A.B. confirmed in tolerance — and the 1° gap is irrelevant. Face aim shift from a lie error is arcsin(sin(loft) × sin(lie error)); at 2° of loft that is 0.035°, about 0.07" at ten feet, smaller than a dimple. Lower loft makes it matter LESS, so the loft uncertainty can't rescue this as a problem either. What actually moves the number is HANDLE HEIGHT: one inch of hand lift on a 34" putter is arcsin(1/34) ≈ 1.7° of presentation change — roughly fifty times the build tolerance — and film already has you presenting ~68° against the 69° build, shaft dead vertical and repeatable to 0.3°. Heel shaft is made lie-angle-balanced by an aluminium riser hosel sized per lie angle, so the shaft position is NOT a reliable guide to where the head's centre of gravity sits. STILL UNKNOWN: as-built length (34" was the target, never confirmed) and head weight, never known on any putter you've owned. Also worth eyeballing: retailers list the stock grip as a Lamkin Deep Etched where this app carries a Pistol 0 — both are 0° lean so nothing downstream changes, but check what's actually on the shaft.

entries.text: EQUIPMENT — GET THE LINK.2.1's REAL NUMBERS. Three specs this project has been guessing at; one email to L.A.B. support, or one visit to a shop with a loft/lie machine. (1) LOFT — the important one. Nobody publishes it: L.A.B.'s own pages, PGA Tour Superstore, Golf Galaxy, Fairway Jockey, Carl's Golfland, Golfio and two published reviews all omit it. The 2° in this app is an estimate that got written down as fact, and it is load-bearing in three plans — how much a press de-lofts, whether hands ahead drives the ball, what 'delivered at 0° lean' actually delivers. Ask for the as-built loft on your order. (2) LENGTH — you targeted 34" and it has never been confirmed. It is also the denominator in the handle-height number (1" of lift = 1.7° at 34"), so it is worth having exactly. (3) HEAD WEIGHT — never known on any of the four putters, and head weight is the most direct lever on distance control there is, which is precisely the fault you are grinding. While you're asking: do they build lie in 1° increments? That tells you whether 69° against your 70° fit target was a choice or the nearest station. None of this is urgent for the keep-or-return call — the lie gap is already proven irrelevant, 0.035° of face aim — but the loft should stop being quoted as fact until someone measures it.

PUTTING — ONE FACE-ON CLIP, on the LINK.2.1, and it now answers FOUR things instead of two. Still not shot at a usable frame rate from a usable height: Jul 30's face-on set gave address shaft angle (dead vertical, repeatable to 0.3°) and then blurred out at impact; Aug 10 missed it twice in one day, 23 oblique clips in the afternoon and six on-line clips in the evening, and lean lives in the plane those cameras look straight down. WHAT THE CLIP OWES: (1) SHAFT LEAN at address versus impact — with the Press Pistol gone there is no built-in lean to subtract, so whatever the tape shows IS the stroke. (2) BALL POSITION rep to rep, which feeds the pace curve. (3) HANDLE HEIGHT rep to rep — NEW, and it is the sleeper. One inch of hand lift on a 34" putter is 1.7° of presentation change, about fifty times the entire 69°-vs-70° build tolerance, so hand height is the live variable and the fitting is not. Measure the spread across the reps, not the average. (4) LOW POINT and attack angle — NEW, and it is a distance-control input: where the head bottoms out relative to the ball decides launch, skid and rollout. THE FLAG TO SETTLE FIRST: an outside read of the face-on footage put your ball at or near stance CENTER rather than forward of it. That is medium confidence off 30 fps and it contradicts the live rule (1–2 ball-widths inside the lead heel), so it is a question, not a finding — but if it is true it is a PACE fault, because a low-loft putter met at or before low point launches down, skids, and rolls out inconsistently. THE SPEC, narrow on purpose: camera at BALL HEIGHT square to the target line — stand it behind the ball, walk to a spot 90° off the line, phone on the ground — white tape on the shaft ~6" above the head, 240 fps, 5–8 strokes at one distance. Indoors is fine; this clip does not need a green.

PUTTING — CAMERA PREP, and two of these are new rules that apply to every clip from now on. (1) WHITE TAPE around the shaft ~6" above the head — a thin black shaft blurs out against a dim floor at impact speed, and that single thing is what has blocked the shaft-lean verdict twice. (2) 240 fps (Settings › Camera › Record Slo-mo › 1080p/240), lights on, shoot near the window rather than the fireplace. A putting downstroke runs 0.2–0.3 s, so 30 fps gives you six to nine frames through the whole forward stroke — no tracker, human or automated, can pull low point or tempo out of that. (3) NEW — NEVER SHOOT ON THE 0.5× ULTRAWIDE. Use 1× or 2×. Barrel distortion on the ultrawide bends straight lines: the mat's parallel edges visibly converge, and any shaft angle, spine angle or lie angle read off such a frame is an artifact of the lens rather than the stroke. This is the cheapest single upgrade to the whole film library. (4) NEW — PUT A KNOWN-LENGTH REFERENCE OBJECT IN FRAME. A 12" ruler or an alignment stick, flat on the mat, parallel to the target line. This is what makes pixels convertible into inches and degrees; without it a clip can be described but not measured. (5) Tripod or a stable prop, never handheld. Start recording before you set up and stop after the ball finishes — do not trim. 5–8 strokes per angle at the same distance, no talking or repositioning between reps. WHAT YOU'RE MEASURING on the LINK's Pistol 0: expect roughly zero lean at address, shaft vertical, hands ~1.35" behind the ball, and with the press removed the question is whether anything adds lean by impact — the claw especially, since the trail hand sits differently and the handle can creep forward without you feeling it.

PUTTING — CONFIRM THE PULL STAYS GONE, then stop working on this. Scope cut Aug 10 after the three mat putts came back with no directional bias (0.8° right, 1.0° left, 0.6° right against Jul 30's 1.5–1.7° LEFT). The barely-open setup did what it was supposed to do. ONE CHECK LEFT: five putts at a real target — a coin or a tee on a practice green, nothing drawn on the ground — filmed from directly behind the ball on the line. You are looking for ONE thing: do the misses still fall on both sides? If yes, this closes and start line stops being tracked. Do NOT chase magnitude — a 0.8° miss still holes out to nearly eight feet, and the old 0.5° target was too strict for a phone measurement carrying ±0.5° of its own error. KEEP THE FEEL AS IT IS: don't retrain the aim picture with a mirror on top of it, or you apply the correction twice and the miss reappears on the right. IF THE PULL DOES COME BACK, here is your first hypothesis, and it is new. Plugged In Golf's reviewer — coming to the LINK.2.1 off other L.A.B. models — reported a run of highly repeatable PULLS in his first session with it, which resolved once he adapted to the conventional grip. Same model, same directional signature, and you switched to this head on Aug 10. So a returning left miss is an ADAPTATION pattern before it is anything else: not the fitting, not the head, not a reason to go shopping. Re-check the feel monthly so it doesn't drift, but it is no longer a priority item — pace is.

faults.why: THE priority — and Aug 12 is the first time it has been measured anywhere near a real green, by accident rather than by design. STERLING FARMS, 18 holes on the LINK.2.1: 38 putts, THREE 3-PUTTS (holes 9, 14 and 16), and exactly ONE 1-putt all day — the birdie on 3. Read it honestly in both directions. THE GOOD HALF IS REAL: with only 6 greens in regulation, twelve holes were chip-and-putt, and fifteen of eighteen still finished in two putts or fewer. That is the card's version of Jack's 'made a lot of 5 footers' — they were SECOND putts, holed come-backers, and they are what kept 87 from being 92. THE BAD HALF IS ALSO REAL: three 3-putts is three strokes handed back, and hole 9 was a green hit in regulation turned into a bogey. Jack's report was 'good lags, not dropping 10–20 feet yet'; the card agrees with the second half exactly (one 1-putt) and only partly with the first — lags good enough to two-putt from most places, not good enough to stop three of them running away. WHAT THIS DOES NOT REPLACE: the 30-ft ladder, still unrun. A round tells you the total; it cannot tell you the SPREAD, the green speed, or whether the misses were short or long — the three numbers the ladder exists to capture. Prior evidence stands: the DF3i went back Aug 10 for distance control after three verdicts in eleven days without one calibrated lag session, and the Aug 10 afternoon (~20 putts, nine dead, worst ~4 ft) said calibrated-but-conservative on a second green speed. Tempo is not the missing piece (2.0:1 against a 2:1 target). Stroke length and strike are. Run the ladder with the gamer ball model only.

The remaining candidate — but sized honestly now. Never measured on any putter, not once, across four heads. The Aug 10 evening start lines scattered ~0.8° either side of the line with no bias, and on a head that cannot twist, a face pointing a different way each rep is a face being MOVED by contact: heel closes it, toe opens it. That fits. What has changed is the STAKES: a 0.8° scatter still holes out to nearly eight feet, so as a LINE fault this is no longer costing strokes and does not need chasing. The reason to run the test anyway is PACE — an off-centre hit bleeds ball speed, so the same stroke finishes short and the lag spread widens, and pace is the fault that just cost a putter and has never been measured. Second nudge from the same day, also about pace, not line: the blue ball scattered 1.2–1.5 ft on putts the white killed from the same spot with the same putter. Twelve minutes — tap test for the sweet spot, foot-powder sheets from 5 ft and 30 ft, and the 30-footer is the one that matters. Run it with the barely-open address. Read the result as distance-control data. 

Aug 12 adds a reason to hurry: 38 putts and three 3-putts over 18 holes is the pace fault showing up on a scorecard, and the twelve-minute test is still the cheapest thing that could explain it. The LINK's return window is open and the deadline is still unknown.

Open, and Aug 10 could not touch it — twice in one day. The afternoon's 23 clips were all oblique; the evening's six were all ON the target line, which is right for start line and blind to shaft lean, because lean lives in the plane those cameras look straight down. Face-on is now the ONLY angle never shot. What it has to settle: the Press Pistol 2° went back with the DF3i, so the LINK's Pistol 0 supplies no lean at all — shaft vertical at address, hands ~1.35" behind the ball — and the soft press is now the ONLY lean in the stroke. The 'don't double-count the lean' arithmetic is retired; consistency replaces it, because a press that varies is a launch that varies, which is a pace that varies. One slo-mo face-on set gives lean at address versus impact AND ball position rep to rep in the same clips. Whatever the tape shows IS the press now, with no built-in 2° to subtract.

WIDENED Aug 12 — the same clip now owes four things, not two, and two of them are new. HANDLE HEIGHT: one inch of hand lift on a 34" putter is arcsin(1/34) ≈ 1.7° of presentation change, about fifty times the 69°-vs-70° build tolerance, which settles which of the two is worth thinking about — film already has you presenting ~68° against a 69° build. Measure the SPREAD across reps, not the average. LOW POINT and attack angle: where the head bottoms out relative to the ball is a distance-control input, and pace is the priority fault. And one flag to settle before anything else: an outside read of the face-on footage put the ball at or near stance CENTER rather than forward of it. Medium confidence off 30 fps, and it contradicts the live rule of 1–2 ball-widths inside the lead heel — so it is a question, not a finding. If it is true it is a PACE fault, not a line fault: a low-loft putter met at or before low point launches down, skids, and rolls out inconsistently. Related correction: the putter's loft is UNCONFIRMED. No retailer and no L.A.B. page publishes one, so the 2° this project quotes is an estimate. It does not change what the clip has to measure, but it does mean the de-lofting arithmetic downstream of it is softer than it reads.

DOWNGRADED Aug 10 — off the top of the card, and the reasoning is worth keeping because the old gate on this line was wrong. THE CRUX IS THE SIGN, NOT THE SIZE. Jul 30: 1.5° LEFT, 1.7° LEFT, one straight — three putts pulling the SAME way. Aug 10 pm: 0.8° right, 1.0° left, 0.6° right — mean bias ≈0.1°, i.e. zero. Aim doesn't change between reps, so a one-way pull is what an aim error looks like, and it did not reproduce on any of the three. The founding premise of this entire putter saga was a DIRECTIONAL claim — 'signature miss: left on short putts' — and a directional claim is a claim about bias. On the evidence available, that bias is gone, and it went away after a setup change Jack found himself, not after any of the four putters.

IN STROKES, WHICH IS THE ONLY UNIT THAT MATTERS. Capture at the hole is ±1.29" (4.25" cup, 1.68" ball, dying speed). A 1.6° bias puts the ball outside that from 3.8 ft — so the old miss started costing strokes at four feet, which is exactly where the 'left on SHORT putts' signature came from. A 0.8° miss holes out to 7.7 ft. At 0.6° it's 10.2 ft. So the residual has moved start line out of the range where an 8.5 handicap loses shots to it: beyond eight feet, make rates are governed by pace and read, not by a degree of face angle.

THE 0.5° GATE IS RETIRED — it was a bad standard and it was mine. Half a degree is around the level tour putters hold, it was being applied to a phone-on-a-mat measurement carrying ±0.5° of its own error, and it implied a precision nobody should be chasing. Worse, it pointed at the wrong quantity: it gated on magnitude when the thing that was actually broken was direction.

AND THE RESIDUAL IS AN UPPER BOUND, not an estimate. Measurement noise can only ever INFLATE apparent dispersion — it cannot hide scatter that exists. So with ±0.5° of method error sitting inside an observed ~0.8°, the true dispersion is 0.8° or better, quite possibly nearer 0.6°. Jack's read that these are small numbers is correct and, if anything, understated.

WHAT'S LEFT TO DO, and it is small: confirm the bias stays gone away from a printed line — five putts at a coin on a real green, filmed from behind. That is a check, not an investigation. If the pull is still absent, this fault closes and start line stops being a thing this project tracks.

ADDED Aug 12, for if it comes back. Plugged In Golf's reviewer, arriving at the LINK.2.1 from other L.A.B. models, reported a run of highly repeatable PULLS in his first session that resolved once he adapted to the conventional grip. Same model, same direction, and you changed to this head on Aug 10 — so a returning left miss is an ADAPTATION pattern first, ahead of the fitting or the head. One competing mechanism was examined and does not fit. Raising the handle presents the putter more upright (toe up), which on a lie-angle-balanced head breaks torque neutrality and is argued to close the face. But that argument is derived from L.A.B.'s design principle rather than any L.A.B. document, and the direction is wrong for you: film measured your presentation at ~68° against a 69° build — flatter, toe DOWN — which under the same mechanism predicts a miss RIGHT. Handle height still matters, but as consistency (1.7° per inch, measured as spread), not as an explanation of the old pull.

CLOSED Jul 30 ✓. At 120 fps and 37.5 px/inch the sole held within 0.05–0.08" of its address height for the full 83 ms into impact, flat across ten consecutive frames, and never dropped below address height. Measured on the LINK, the head still in play, so it carries cleanly. Wants two more slo-mo strokes on sample size — the owed face-on set gives them for free, which is one more reason to shoot it.

CLOSED Jul 30 ✓ — overhead film measured the toe line 0.6°, 2.9° and 3.6° CLOSED to the target line across three reps. Never open. Worth re-reading against the Aug 10 find: this measurement is what ruled the feet out and sent the search higher, which is exactly where the answer turned out to be.

500-yard par 5 from an elevated tee, and the green is well protected — the long second is the trap, not the tee shot. Lay up to a NUMBER off your wedge ladder (108 · 95 · 80) rather than chasing it. You found this fairway last time and still came up short of the green.

sections.t: The par 3s are the round
sections.k: They average 203 yards — these are wood holes, and bogey on all four is a par-72 round of 76.
sections.b:
Sterling Farms' par 3s average 203 YARDS. That is not a normal set of par 3s: it is four holes where a mid-handicapper is hitting the club he would hit into a par 4.

You bogeyed all four last time — 5, 8, 15 and 17 — and three of those misses finished short or long rather than beside the green. That is not a strike problem. It is a club problem: 221 on the 5th is past your 2-iron, and the 8th plays uphill on top of its number.

The rule for all four: club to cover the MIDDLE of the green, not the flag, and treat two putts as the plan. Four bogeys on these is +4 — that is a perfectly good outcome and it beats the double you get from short-siding yourself trying to make three.

sections.t: Driver is optional here
sections.k: Three of your green misses last time were tee shots that left you nothing, and the short holes don't need the big stick.
sections.b:
Your last card here lost more to tee shots than to any swing fault. On holes 1, 6 and 10 the drive left you with no realistic play at the green — three holes, +4 between them, and the approach club never had a say.

This is a 6,308-yard par 72 on 144 rolling acres. It is not long. The 1st is 337 downhill. A 5-wood or 2-iron off the tee on the short par 4s still leaves a wedge, and it takes the 'no play' outcome off the table entirely.

The 5-wood's carry is still unmeasured — this is a good round to learn it. Log the tee club on every hole and the by-club table will tell you whether it is actually finding more fairways than the driver, and whether those fairways are worth anything.

14 (SI 2) · 15 (par 3) · 16 (SI 16) · 17 (par 3) played +6 and turned a 41-ish back nine into 44.

The damaging pair are the ones that should have been easy: 16 is stroke index SIXTEEN and you made a six on it. A giveaway hole that gives nothing back is worth more than any birdie you chase on the hard ones.

Plan for this stretch: fairway, middle of the green, two putts, four bogeys at worst. +4 through there instead of +6 is two shots for no better ball-striking at all.

One caution kept on purpose: different copies of the tour shift the hole numbering, so every tip above was cross-checked against the pars and shapes on your Aug 12 card before it was pinned to a hole — and tips that could not be pinned were left out. The 232-yard figure on 17 is a reviewer's number for the back tees.

club.note: THE PUTTER — KEPT. The return window was closed on purpose Aug 12, 2026: this is the gamer, not a trial, and the equipment half of the left miss is now settled. The only zero-torque head in the bag and the last one standing after the DF3i went back Aug 10. SETUP: L.A.B. Pistol 0, zero built-in press — shaft DEAD VERTICAL at address, hands ~1.35" BEHIND the ball, measured on film Jul 30 and repeatable to 0.3°. That is this putter's designed geometry (69° lie, 2° effective loft, 0° lean), not a flaw. Don't manufacture lean. THE GRIND: distance control. Pace is what returned the last putter and it has never once been measured — the 30-ft ladder twice a week, logging shorts, spread and green speed, is the whole job. Tempo is already where it needs to be on this head: 2.0:1 measured across seven of eight clips against a 2:1 target. WATCH: narrow blade, lower MOI than a mallet, so an off-centre strike bleeds more ball speed here — strike is a distance fault before it's a line fault, and the tape test is still unrun. Its column carries the only two reds on the grid (face at impact, 1.5–1.7° left start line, both Jul 30, both on this head), and with no control putter left, re-measuring them on THIS head is the only thing that can move them. WHAT KEEPING IT MEANS: every remaining explanation for the left miss is aim or stroke, not gear.

(2) The same review calls the 3rd and 4th 'both very short' while his card has the 4th at stroke index 1 — an odd pairing, so the 4th's note leans on the course's own tip and his card rather than on the review's length claim. The bias that setup is supposed to produce is LEFT, which is your signature miss exactly, so dominance is a candidate EXPLANATION for why 'barely open' had to become your square. But the one peer-reviewed study on this says the dominance you measured standing up does not predict the one that operates when you're bent over a putt. So: re-measure it in posture, add one drop to a test you already owe, and change nothing about the stroke until the overhead five reports.
