sections.t: Why it fits — and how far that goes
sections.k: Same-side dominance predicts a left aim bias, which is your exact miss — but it can only ever be a partial explanation.
sections.b:
The teaching claim is that a right-handed, right-eye-dominant player lets the head turn so the dominant eye sits slightly INSIDE the ball-to-target line, the target then appears further left than it really is, and the putter gets aimed left to match. Same-side dominance, left bias. That is your miss and it has been your miss the whole way through.

It matters more on this putter than it would on any other. A zero-torque head doesn't twist, so address IS impact — a face measured 1.5–1.7° left at impact on Jul 30 was pointing there before the stroke started. That already reclassified the fault from delivery to AIM on Aug 10. Dominance is the first candidate that says where an aim error would come from.

And here is the honest strength of it: the left miss predates the LINK.2.1, predates the DF3i, predates the Phantom. A cause present through four putters fits a fact about your EYES far better than it fits any fact about a head. That is the real argument for taking it seriously — not the folklore, the persistence.

What it cannot do is prove itself. There are at least three live explanations on your card for a left aim bias and they all point the same direction, so a start line alone will never separate them.

sections.t: The study that says slow down
sections.k: The dominance you measured standing up is not the one that operates over a putt — measure the version that counts.
sections.b:
Dalton, Guillon & Naroo, Optometry and Vision Science, October 2015, 92(10):968–75. Thirty-one golfers — 14 amateurs, 7 club pros, 10 top professionals — with ocular dominance measured in BOTH primary gaze (standing, pointing at a target) and putting gaze (addressing the ball).

Four findings, and each one cuts against building anything on a standing test. Primary-gaze and putting-gaze dominance are NOT equal, and neither predicts the other. The magnitude of putting-gaze dominance is significantly WEAKER than primary-gaze. Dominance is NOT correlated with handedness in either position. And eye-hand dominance is not associated with better putting.

So 'I'm right-eye dominant' is almost certainly a primary-gaze fact — the Miles test, hands framed, standing up. The study's first finding says that number does not tell you what your eyes do in a putting stance, and its second says whatever dominance you do have down there is likely milder than the standing test made it look.

That is not a reason to ignore this. It is a reason to measure the version that matters before you act on the version you have.

sections.t: The one thing to actually do — the two-drop test
sections.k: Drop from the nose AND from under the right eye; the gap between the two marks is whether dominance is live for you at all.
sections.b:
You already owe an eyeline drop. Run it twice instead of once and it answers a much better question.

Full putting posture over a ball, as you'd really stand to it. Hold a second ball at the BRIDGE OF THE NOSE, let it go, mark where it lands relative to the ball. Re-set exactly, hold the second ball directly under the RIGHT EYE, let it go, mark that. Photograph both marks with the ball in frame.

Read it like this. Both marks in the same place — your head is square enough that dominance has no lever to pull, and you can cross this off permanently. An inch or more apart — dominance is live, and the gap IS the size of the effect, in the only units that matter.

Why from the eye and not just the nose: the standard check drops from the bridge of the nose, but for a strongly one-eyed player what governs aim is the 'vision centre', and the billiards literature — which has chased this harder than golf has — is clear that it can sit under the dominant eye, under the nose, or anywhere between, and it is individual. There is no formula. There is only your own two marks.

While you are down there, re-run the MILES TEST IN POSTURE: bent over the ball, hands framed around a small target across the room, close one eye then the other. That is the putting-gaze number the study says counts, and nobody has ever taken it.

sections.t: What it does NOT change
sections.k: Not the stroke, not the setup, not the putter — the barely-open feel already absorbs whatever this is.
sections.b:
Aug 10's mat putts came back 0.8° right, 1.0° left, 0.6° right, against Jul 30's 1.5–1.7° LEFT. Whatever was aiming you left is currently being cancelled. If dominance turns out to be the cause, the compensation you already found IS the fix — and knowing the mechanism only makes it trustworthy instead of superstitious, which is worth something, because an unexplained compensation is the one you talk yourself out of on the last green.

What you must not do is add a second correction. The standing rule is one at a time: the barely-open feel OR an aim-picture retrain, never both, or the correction lands twice and the miss flips right. Eye dominance would be a third layer of the same correction. It is knowledge, not an instruction.

Also not on the table: a different head, a different offset, a sight line chosen to suit an eye. The putter search closed Aug 12.

One thing your setup already does for you: GET LOW and STAND CLOSE puts your eyes more nearly over the ball, and the closer the eyes are to the line the less parallax either eye has to work with. The posture rule you kept for comfort was quietly the mitigation.

sections.t: Where it goes if the pull comes back
sections.k: Hypothesis two, behind the LINK adaptation pattern — with the head shape third and weakest.
sections.b:
If the overhead five shows the left miss returning, work the queue in order.

ONE — adaptation to the LINK.2.1 with a conventional grip. Plugged In Golf's reviewer, coming off other L.A.B. models, reported a run of highly repeatable PULLS in his first session that resolved once he adapted. Same model, same signature, and you switched heads on Aug 10.

TWO — eye dominance and vision centre, and by then you will have the two-drop marks to test it against instead of a folklore claim.

THREE — the head shape as an aim influencer. The reported rule of thumb is that round shapes and mallets bias aim RIGHT while straight lines and blades bias aim LEFT, and you moved from a high-MOI mallet to a narrow blade on Aug 10. Ranked last on purpose: your left miss predates the LINK, so head shape can be an amplifier at most and never the origin.

And hold this over all three — pace is the live fault, not line. The 30-ft ladder outranks every item on this page.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: One peer-reviewed source, several teaching claims, and a clear line between them.
sections.b:
FROM JACK (Aug 13, 2026): that he is right-eye dominant. Self-reported, and this project had never recorded it before today. Which test produced it, and whether it was taken standing, is unknown — that gap is exactly what the two-drop test closes.

PEER-REVIEWED: Dalton K, Guillon M, Naroo SA. 'Ocular Dominance and Handedness in Golf Putting.' Optometry and Vision Science 2015;92(10):968–75. n=31. The four findings quoted above are the study's own conclusions.

TEACHING CLAIM, NOT EVIDENCE: that same-side (right hand / right eye) players aim left, via the dominant eye drifting inside the line and shifting where the target appears. Widely taught — The Left Rough, Golf State of Mind, and attributed in places to David Orr's aim work. Consistent across sources on DIRECTION; no controlled study behind it that this project has found, and the Dalton study's findings argue the mechanism is weaker in a putting stance than in a standing one.

TEACHING CLAIM, NOT EVIDENCE: mallets/round shapes bias aim right, blades/straight lines bias aim left (GolfWRX, 'The Ultimate Putting Program' — aim). Reported as a rule of thumb, not a measurement of you.

FROM THE BILLIARDS SIDE: the 'vision centre' framing — that the correct sighting position ranges from under the dominant eye to under the nose and is individual with no general formula. Cue-sports coaching, carried across because the aiming problem is the same shape.

CARD FACTS: 1.5–1.7° left start line and face left at impact, measured Jul 30 on the LINK.2.1, overhead. Toe line 0.6°/2.9°/3.6° CLOSED across three reps — the feet were never the cause. Aug 10 mat putts 0.8° right, 1.0° left, 0.6° right — no directional bias since the barely-open change. Left miss on short putts present across the Phantom 7.5, the DF3i and the LINK.2.1.

STILL UNKNOWN: putting-gaze dominance, vision-centre offset, and whether any of the three left-bias candidates is doing the work. The overhead five and the two-drop test are what move those.

entries.text: PUTTING — THE TWO-DROP EYELINE TEST (2 minutes, at home). You're right-handed and right-eye dominant — same-side dominant, whose predicted aim bias is LEFT, which is the oldest fault on this card. Nothing in this project had recorded your eye dominance until Aug 13. Run it in full putting posture over a ball. (1) Hold a second ball at the BRIDGE OF THE NOSE, drop it, mark where it lands relative to the ball. (2) Re-set exactly, hold it directly under the RIGHT EYE, drop, mark that. Photograph both marks with the ball in frame. SAME SPOT = your head is square, dominance has no lever, cross it off for good. AN INCH OR MORE APART = dominance is live and that gap is the size of the effect. While you're down there, re-run the MILES TEST IN POSTURE — bent over the ball, hands framed on a small target across the room, close one eye then the other — because the only peer-reviewed study on this (Dalton, Guillon & Naroo, Optom Vis Sci 2015) found that standing dominance does not predict putting dominance, and that putting-gaze dominance is the weaker of the two. DELIBERATELY NOT A PRIORITY, and don't let it become one: it changes nothing about the stroke either way, the barely-open feel is already cancelling whatever aims you left, and pace is the live fault. Run it in the two minutes before a ladder session, never instead of one.

PUTTING — CONFIRM THE PULL STAYS GONE, then stop working on this. Scope cut Aug 10 after the three mat putts came back with no directional bias (0.8° right, 1.0° left, 0.6° right against Jul 30's 1.5–1.7° LEFT). The barely-open setup did what it was supposed to do. ONE CHECK LEFT: five putts at a real target — a coin or a tee on a practice green, nothing drawn on the ground — filmed from directly behind the ball on the line. You are looking for ONE thing: do the misses still fall on both sides? If yes, this closes and start line stops being tracked. Do NOT chase magnitude — a 0.8° miss still holes out to nearly eight feet, and the old 0.5° target was too strict for a phone measurement carrying ±0.5° of its own error. KEEP THE FEEL AS IT IS: don't retrain the aim picture with a mirror on top of it, and don't add an eye-dominance correction either — any second layer applies the fix twice and the miss reappears on the right. IF THE PULL DOES COME BACK, work the hypotheses in this order. ONE, ADAPTATION: Plugged In Golf's reviewer — coming to the LINK.2.1 off other L.A.B. models — reported a run of highly repeatable PULLS in his first session with it, which resolved once he adapted to the conventional grip. Same model, same directional signature, and you switched to this head on Aug 10. TWO, EYE DOMINANCE (new Aug 13): you're right-handed and right-eye dominant, and same-side dominance is taught to aim LEFT — which is the only candidate that predates every putter you've owned. The two-drop eyeline test gives you numbers to judge it with; the full read is in the 'Eye Dominance — What It Changes' plan. THREE, THE HEAD: blades and straight lines are reported to bias aim left where mallets bias right, and you moved from a mallet to a narrow blade — ranked last because your left miss is older than this putter. None of the three is a reason to go shopping. Re-check the feel monthly so it doesn't drift, but it is no longer a priority item — pace is.

Written Aug 13 2026 after you named the four that get you: slow play, random partners, not closing from in front, and letting anger or drift take the round. The finding that shapes the whole plan — over 63 of your own logged holes, neither the anger nor the fade shows up as strokes YET. The doubles do, and they are half of everything you have lost to par.
rules: Attention ON for the 30 seconds a shot takes — OFF on the walk
Anger gets ten yards, then the hole is filed
One target, named out loud, every tee

Closing three: same routine, one more club, middle of the green

steps: Before you leave: read the trigger list in the Mental tab and name the ONE most likely today — who you are playing with, what the pace looks like, how hot it is. Naming it in advance is most of the work.
First tee: say your one job out loud. It is the line you wrote in your last debrief, and it is the only swing-or-head thought you carry.
Every shot: attention ON when you start the read, OFF at the finish. You are not trying to concentrate for four hours — nobody can, and trying is what leaves you empty by the 15th.
Every dropped shot: ten yards of walking, then the club goes in the bag and the hole is filed. The anger is allowed. It just gets a container with an end you can see.
Every hole that starts badly: the club goes DOWN and the target moves to the fat of the green. This is the one that has your money on it.
The turn: eat something and drink, whether or not you want to, and say the one job again.
Last three holes: change nothing. Same routine, same target selection, one more club, middle of the green.
That evening: two minutes in the Mental tab — how locked in you were, what fired, and the one job for next time.

sections.t: The on/off switch
sections.k: Attention is a battery and the walk is where you spend it — so don't.
sections.b:
You do not have to concentrate for four hours, and the attempt is what leaves you flat on the back nine. A round is roughly 70 shots of about 30 seconds each: half an hour of actual golf inside a five-hour walk.

So the switch has two positions and a hard edge between them. ON starts when you begin the read and ends at the finish of the swing. OFF is everything else — talk, look at the trees, be somewhere else entirely. What breaks a round is not being distracted on the walk; it is standing over the ball with the walk still running, and standing over it early while you wait for the group ahead is the commonest way that happens.

The edge is what makes it work, and the edge is your routine. It has a fixed number of beats — read, one rehearsal, step in, go — so it is also a clock. If the beats are there, you were ON. If the rehearsal went missing, you were rushed, and that is the first thing to disappear every time.

sections.t: What your own cards say
sections.k: Neither the anger tax nor the fade shows up as strokes yet — the doubles do, and they are half of everything you have lost.
sections.b:
This is the honest part, and it points the work somewhere different from where you would have put it.

Across 63 holes logged hole by hole (six cards, Wianno and Sterling Farms, as of Aug 13 2026), you average +0.83 a hole. The hole AFTER a dropped shot plays +0.62 — BETTER than your average, with par or better on 43% of them. The closing three play +0.67 against +0.89 for everything before them. So on the evidence available, you neither tilt into the next tee nor fade at the finish.

What IS there: 13 holes of double bogey or worse, costing 26 strokes — 50% of everything you have lost to par. And the worst third of your rounds is the FIRST one (+1.05 a hole, against +0.71 for the middle and +0.71 for the closing), which is a warm-up problem, not a focus problem.

Two honest limits. Six rounds at two courses is a first read, not a verdict, and every one of those cards is stroke play — MATCH play is not in the data at all, so 'got to a lead and did not close it' is a claim these numbers cannot test either way. The Mental tab recomputes all of this on every card you log, so the read moves as the evidence does. Until it does: do not spend practice on a reset problem the scorecard cannot find.

sections.t: The hot decision — where the anger actually costs you
sections.k: The stroke anger costs you is the club you pick while still angry, during the hole, not the tee shot afterwards.
sections.b:
If the next tee is fine and the doubles are half your losses, then the damage is landing INSIDE the bad hole. That is where the hero recovery lives: the 3-wood out of the trees, the second aggressive club after a bad drive, the flop you would bet against. Every one of those is a decision made while hot, and every one turns a bogey into a double.

So the rule that matters is not about calming down afterwards. It is: from any recovery position, pick the club and the line you would bet a hundred dollars you can execute nine times out of ten. From trouble, that is nearly always the punch-out. When you are hot the club goes DOWN, never up.

A bogey is not an emergency. Par golf with no doubles beats birdie golf with four, and you already make par or better on a third of your holes — the base game is there. The tail is what costs you.

sections.t: Slow play and random partners
sections.k: Both are conditions, and the only response either one allows is where you stand.
sections.b:
You cannot speed up the group ahead and you cannot change how a stranger behaves. Treating either as something to be resolved is what converts an annoyance into four holes of stewing.

SLOW PLAY. The failure is standing over the ball early, because then the wait happens INSIDE your routine and the routine is the thing keeping you ON. So: wait away from the ball. Pick the club and the target while you wait — that is useful and it is not the routine. Start the routine only when it is genuinely your turn, and then run it at its normal speed. It has a fixed length; the waiting goes outside it.

PARTNERS. You get one comment in your head, and then it is a course condition — you do not argue with wind either. The one response available is physical: move so they are out of your eyeline and out of earshot for the thirty seconds the shot takes. On gimmes and rules noise, decide before the first tee what you are playing and say it once, pleasantly, on the tee. A thing agreed on the 1st is not an argument on the 9th.

sections.t: Closing
sections.k: Closing is the refusal to change anything, plus exactly one club.
sections.b:
There is no closing skill separate from playing. Everything that goes wrong with a lead is a CHANGE: a shorter routine because you want it over with, a smaller target because you are protecting, a bigger one because you want to finish it. Same routine, same target selection you used on the 2nd hole.

The single legitimate change is one more club, aimed at the middle of the green. That is what protecting a lead actually looks like — it takes the short-side miss out of play, which is your standing miss anyway. Steering is not protecting.

And if you catch yourself doing the arithmetic, convert it to the hole in front of you: what number makes THIS hole fine? Play that. The addition still works in the car park.

One caveat, because it is the honest one: your cards are stroke play and they say the last three holes are not where your strokes go. If the not-closing feeling is a MATCH-play thing, this section is a hypothesis, not a finding. Log the matches that matter and the Mental tab can start answering it properly.

sections.t: The debrief loop
sections.k: One job per round, chosen at the kitchen table, is the entire system.
sections.b:
The evening after you play — not on the drive home, when it is still a mood — spend two minutes in the Mental tab: how locked in you were out of five, which triggers fired and roughly when, one line on what actually happened, and one job for next round.

ONE job. A list of five is the same as none, and the tab shows the newest one at the top of the page so you read it before you play again.

What this buys you over time is the thing you cannot get from a single round: whether 'slow play gets me' is true every round or was true once, loudly. Eight triggers with counts against them turn a mood into a pattern, and a pattern is something you can rehearse against. It stays the softest evidence on the page — your own read, written after the fact — which is why it is ranked below everything your scorecard says, and why it is still the only witness for the parts a scorecard cannot see.

sections.b:
You gave three on Aug 13 2026. Two of them are attached to cards you had already logged hole by hole, so they can be checked rather than just recorded. Both are now in the debrief log.

WIANNO MATCH 1 (Jul 9, front, 46) — the opponent you found annoying. This is the worst card of the event by five shots, with four doubles on it. The part that matters: holes 1, 2 and 3 went +2, +2, +2 — SIX over in three holes. The other four Wianno nines cost +3 over their first three, every single one of them. Same course, same Blue tees, same week, same format, and the opening three cost double on the card where you say a person got into your head.

That also moves an existing finding. The Mental tab has been reporting that your worst stretch is the opening third (+1.05 a hole). Take this one card out and the opening third falls to +0.89 against a +0.76 baseline — the gap roughly halves. So a chunk of what has been filed as a warm-up problem may be a getting-into-my-head problem.

THE HONEST CAVEAT, and it is a big one: that card was ALSO the first nine of the whole event — the coldest start you had all week. Cold warm-up and an irritating opponent are perfectly confounded on a single card, and one card cannot separate them. The Swing Routine plan's warm-up primer is not refuted by this and neither is the trigger. What separates them is future data: log the trigger, and note whether you actually warmed up.

sections.k: The stroke anger costs you is the club you pick while still angry, during the hole, not the tee shot afterwards.
sections.b:
If the next tee is fine and the doubles are half your losses, then the damage is landing INSIDE the bad hole. That is where the hero recovery lives: the 3-wood out of the trees, the second aggressive club after a bad drive, the flop you would bet against. Every one of those is a decision made while hot, and every one turns a bogey into a double.

So the rule that matters is not about calming down afterwards. It is: from any recovery position, pick the club and the line you would bet a hundred dollars you can execute nine times out of ten. From trouble, that is nearly always the punch-out. When you are hot the club goes DOWN, never up.

A bogey is not an emergency. Par golf with no doubles beats birdie golf with four, and you already make par or better on a third of your holes — the base game is there. The tail is what costs you.

sections.k: Both are conditions, the only response either allows is where you stand — and the partner damage lands on holes 1–3.

SLOW PLAY. The failure is standing over the ball early, because then the wait happens INSIDE your routine and the routine is the thing keeping you ON. So: wait away from the ball. It has a fixed length; the waiting goes outside it.

This one now has the best evidence of any trigger you have, and it says the danger window is the START of the round: on the Jul 9 card the first three holes cost +6 against +3 on every other nine you played that week. sections.t: Closing

sections.t: The on/off switch
sections.k: Attention is a battery and the walk is where you spend it — so don't.
sections.b:
You do not have to concentrate for four hours, and the attempt is what leaves you flat on the back nine. A round is roughly 70 shots of about 30 seconds each: half an hour of actual golf inside a five-hour walk.

So the switch has two positions and a hard edge between them. ON starts when you begin the read and ends at the finish of the swing. OFF is everything else — talk, look at the trees, be somewhere else entirely. What breaks a round is not being distracted on the walk; it is standing over the ball with the walk still running, and standing over it early while you wait for the group ahead is the commonest way that happens.

The edge is what makes it work, and the edge is your routine. It has a fixed number of beats — read, one rehearsal, step in, go — so it is also a clock. If the beats are there, you were ON. If the rehearsal went missing, you were rushed, and that is the first thing to disappear every time.

You do not have to concentrate for four hours, and the attempt is what leaves you flat on the back nine. A round is roughly 70 shots of about 30 seconds each: half an hour of actual golf inside a five-hour walk.

So the switch has two positions and a hard edge between them. ON starts when you begin the read and ends at the finish of the swing. OFF is everything else — talk, look at the trees, be somewhere else entirely. What breaks a round is not being distracted on the walk; it is standing over the ball with the walk still running, and standing over it early while you wait for the group ahead is the commonest way that happens.

The edge is what makes it work, and the edge is your routine. It has a fixed number of beats — read, one rehearsal, step in, go — so it is also a clock. If the beats are there, you were ON. If the rehearsal went missing, you were rushed, and that is the first thing to disappear every time.

sections.t: What your own cards say
sections.k: Neither the anger tax nor the fade shows up as strokes yet — the doubles do, and they are half of everything you have lost.
sections.b:
This is the honest part, and it points the work somewhere different from where you would have put it.

Across 63 holes logged hole by hole (six cards, Wianno and Sterling Farms, as of Aug 13 2026), you average +0.83 a hole. The hole AFTER a dropped shot plays +0.62 — BETTER than your average, with par or better on 43% of them. The closing three play +0.67 against +0.89 for everything before them. So on the evidence available, you do not tilt into the next tee, and you fade at the finish once in six cards — see 'Your three examples' below for that one.

What IS there: 13 holes of double bogey or worse, costing 26 strokes — 50% of everything you have lost to par. And the worst third of your rounds is the FIRST one (+1.05 a hole, against +0.71 for the middle and +0.71 for the closing), which is a warm-up problem, not a focus problem.

Two honest limits. Six rounds at two courses is a first read, not a verdict, and every one of those cards is stroke play — MATCH play is not in the data at all, so 'got to a lead and did not close it' is a claim these numbers cannot test either way. The Mental tab recomputes all of this on every card you log, so the read moves as the evidence does. Until it does: do not spend practice on a reset problem the scorecard cannot find.

sections.t: The five Wianno matches, one at a time
sections.k: Three of the four things you filed as mental have a physical mechanism under them — and the cards can name it.
sections.b:
You walked through the whole event on Aug 13 2026. Every match is now in the debrief log against its own card, which is what lets each one be checked instead of just remembered.

MATCH 1 · Jul 9 front · 46. Threw the opening tee shot away, had to RE-TEE, made 6. An opponent you found annoying also got into your head. Four doubles, the worst card of the event, and holes 1–3 cost +6 against +3 on every other nine you played that week.

MATCH 2 · Jul 10 back · 44. The crumble: 10 through 16 at +6, right on your average, then bogey-double on 17 and 18.

MATCH 3 · Jul 10 front · 40. The SECOND thrown-away opening tee shot, same hard-left miss, another 6. Then you birdied the 2nd and played holes 2–9 in +3 — +0.38 a hole, the best stretch of golf in your whole logbook. Best score of the event.

MATCH 4 · Jul 11 front · 41. Played well. Missed short putts down the stretch. Zero doubles, zero birdies: six bogeys and three pars.

MATCH 5 · Jul 11 back · 41. The same again — played well, missed short putts down the stretch.

THE OPENING TEE SHOT DECIDES NOTHING. You threw it away twice and made 6 both times. Those two rounds went 46 and 40 — your worst card of the week and your best. Across everything you have logged the opening hole plays +1.5 a hole against a +0.83 baseline, the single most concentrated leak you own; the SECOND hole plays +0.83, your average exactly; and the rest of a round after a bad opening is no worse than after a clean one. So it costs you the opening hole and nothing after it. You do not need to recover better. You need to arrive with a swing, which makes it a warm-up problem, not a toughness one.

THE MISS ITSELF IS A SWING QUESTION, AND IT IS OPEN. Both were hard LEFT, and your usual bad one is a slice or push-slice — so your worst misses are going the opposite way to your normal one. Your own Golf Mind note already says the driver start line tends to PULL LEFT and that the straight ball needs the LONGER swing, which is at least consistent: the everyday slice curves a left start line back into play, and on a cold quick swing the curve never arrives. That is REASONING from your notes, not a diagnosis. A driver ball that finishes hard left can be a pull, a snap hook or a toe strike, and those want three different fixes; a genuine hosel strike starts RIGHT for a right-hander, so 'shank' is likely describing the feel rather than the contact. Film settles it, and there is a catch worth respecting: the swing that fails is the FIRST one. Film the first two swings of a session, cold, before you hit anything. The thirtieth ball will not show it.

"NOT CLOSING" IS TWO DIFFERENT THINGS, AND NEITHER IS NERVE. Match 2 lost strokes at the finish — bogey-double, a real fade, and the only one in your data. Matches 4 and 5 did not lose strokes at all; they lost SHORT PUTTS. That is not a mental failure, it is the headline project of this entire app: your signature miss is left on short putts. And the putter in your hands for all five matches was the Scotty Phantom 7.5 — max toe flow, arc-suited, against your overhead-confirmed straight stroke. That is the exact mismatch the putter saga opened with, and that putter went back on Jul 20.

So the honest version of "I get up and don't close" is: on the two rounds you played well, you closed badly on the GREENS, with the wrong putter for your stroke. What is NOT established is whether that is fixed. The gear changed — LINK.2.1, kept Aug 12 — but none of those five cards has putts on them, so "missed short putts when it mattered" cannot be measured, only recalled. Log putts per hole and this stops being a memory.

WHAT ACTUALLY CAME APART. One card in five, match 1, and it is the one carrying a person in your head. Same opening disaster as match 3, opposite outcome. Two rounds cannot prove that the partner is the difference, and match 1 was also the coldest start of the event — but it is the right thing to test, and it is why the partner plan now guards holes 1–3 rather than the finish.

sections.t: The match results — what actually decided them
sections.k: Only two of five were live at the finish, and both were lost on the greens.
sections.b:
You gave the results on Aug 13: LOST 2 down · LOST 2 down · WON 2 up · HALVED · LOST 1 down. 1-3-1, three holes down across the event. Both Jul 10 and Jul 11 were played back nine first, which is why match order is not date order.

Line the margins up against the cards and they track almost exactly:

Match 1 · Jul 9 front · 46 (+11) · lost 2 down
Match 2 · Jul 10 back · 44 (+9) · lost 2 down
Match 3 · Jul 10 front · 40 (+5) · WON 2 up
Match 4 · Jul 11 back · 41 (+6) · halved
Match 5 · Jul 11 front · 41 (+6) · lost 1 down

Best score won. Worst two scores lost by the most. The two 41s halved and lost by one. There is no match in this event where you played well and got beaten anyway, and none where a lead visibly evaporated into a bad number — the results are what the scores earned.

WHICH MEANS THE CLOSING QUESTION IS ABOUT TWO MATCHES, NOT FIVE. A match lost 2 down was decided by scoring; you cannot lose a two-hole margin at the last. Only the HALVE and the 1-down loss were live at the finish — and those are matches 4 and 5, the two you described as 'played well, missed short putts down the stretch'.

So the honest version of 'I get to a lead and don't close': on your own record it happened twice, both times on the last few greens, and the failure was SHORT PUTTS. That is not a nerve problem in the first instance — it is the headline project of this entire app. Your signature miss is left on short putts, and the putter in your hands for all five matches was the Scotty Phantom 7.5: max toe flow, arc-suited, against your overhead-confirmed straight stroke. The exact mismatch this whole saga opened with. It went back on Jul 20.

WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED, and it is the interesting part: whether that is now fixed. The gear changed — LINK.2.1, kept for good Aug 12 — but not one of those five cards has putts recorded on it, and none of them records what the match state was standing on the 8th tee. So 'I was up and let it go' is still not testable; what IS testable is whether the short putts keep falling out at the end. Log putts per hole, tell Claude the result of a match, and by the next event this section stops being a reconstruction.

AND KEEP THE THING THAT WORKED IN VIEW. Match 3 is the win: you threw the opening tee shot away, made 6, birdied the 2nd, and played the last eight holes in +3. That is the best stretch of golf in your logbook and it started with your worst swing of the week.

sections.t: The hot decision — where the anger actually costs you
sections.k: The stroke anger costs you is the club you pick while still angry, during the hole, not the tee shot afterwards.
sections.b:
If the next tee is fine and the doubles are half your losses, then the damage is landing INSIDE the bad hole. That is where the hero recovery lives: the 3-wood out of the trees, the second aggressive club after a bad drive, the flop you would bet against. Every one of those is a decision made while hot, and every one turns a bogey into a double.

So the rule that matters is not about calming down afterwards. It is: from any recovery position, pick the club and the line you would bet a hundred dollars you can execute nine times out of ten. From trouble, that is nearly always the punch-out. When you are hot the club goes DOWN, never up.

A bogey is not an emergency. Par golf with no doubles beats birdie golf with four, and you already make par or better on a third of your holes — the base game is there. The tail is what costs you.

sections.t: Slow play and random partners
sections.k: Both are conditions, the only response either allows is where you stand — and the partner damage lands on holes 1–3.
sections.b:
You cannot speed up the group ahead and you cannot change how a stranger behaves. Treating either as something to be resolved is what converts an annoyance into four holes of stewing.

SLOW PLAY. The failure is standing over the ball early, because then the wait happens INSIDE your routine and the routine is the thing keeping you ON. So: wait away from the ball. Pick the club and the target while you wait — that is useful and it is not the routine. Start the routine only when it is genuinely your turn, and then run it at its normal speed. It has a fixed length; the waiting goes outside it.

PARTNERS. This one now has the best evidence of any trigger you have, and it says the danger window is the START of the round: on the Jul 9 card the first three holes cost +6 against +3 on every other nine you played that week. Which means the pre-round naming matters most on the 1st tee, not the 15th. You get one comment in your head, and then it is a course condition — you do not argue with wind either. The one response available is physical: move so they are out of your eyeline and out of earshot for the thirty seconds the shot takes. On gimmes and rules noise, decide before the first tee what you are playing and say it once, pleasantly, on the tee. A thing agreed on the 1st is not an argument on the 9th.

sections.t: Closing
sections.k: Change nothing — and check whether your closing problem is actually a short-putt problem.
sections.b:
There is no closing skill separate from playing. Everything that goes wrong with a lead is a CHANGE: a shorter routine because you want it over with, a smaller target because you are protecting, a bigger one because you want to finish it. Same routine, same target selection you used on the 2nd hole.

The single legitimate change is one more club, aimed at the middle of the green. That is what protecting a lead actually looks like — it takes the short-side miss out of play, which is your standing miss anyway. Steering is not protecting.

And if you catch yourself doing the arithmetic, convert it to the hole in front of you: what number makes THIS hole fine? Play that. The addition still works in the car park.

Where the evidence now stands, and it has moved: two of the three rounds you flagged for closing lost SHORT PUTTS rather than strokes, with the arc-suited Phantom 7.5 in the bag. Before treating the finish as a nerve problem, see the Wianno section above. On the stroke side: one measured crumble, Jul 10 back nine, bogey-double on 17 and 18 after seven holes at your average. Every other card you have finishes its last two at +0.50 a hole or better. So this is a real failure mode with one instance, not a standing pattern — and the honest limit still applies, because these are stroke-play cards and losing a MATCH from in front does not have to show up as strokes at all. Log the matches and this can start answering the question you are actually asking.

sections.t: The debrief loop
sections.k: One job per round, chosen at the kitchen table, is the entire system.
sections.b:
The evening after you play — not on the drive home, when it is still a mood — spend two minutes in the Mental tab: how locked in you were out of five, which triggers fired and roughly when, one line on what actually happened, and one job for next round.

ONE job. A list of five is the same as none, and the tab shows the newest one at the top of the page so you read it before you play again.

What this buys you over time is the thing you cannot get from a single round: whether 'slow play gets me' is true every round or was true once, loudly. Eight triggers with counts against them turn a mood into a pattern, and a pattern is something you can rehearse against. It stays the softest evidence on the page — your own read, written after the fact — which is why it is ranked below everything your scorecard says, and why it is still the only witness for the parts a scorecard cannot see.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: Where every claim on this page came from.
sections.b:
FROM YOU (Aug 13 2026), and authoritative because nobody else can report it: you struggle to stay locked in for a full round; slow play and random partners set you off; you get to a lead or a good position and do not close it; and you let yourself get angry or distracted. You asked for this to be an OFF-COURSE tool, which is why nothing here is written to be tapped mid-round and why the live logger was left alone.

FROM YOUR CARDS (63 holes over 6 hole-by-hole rounds, Wianno Club and Sterling Farms, Jul 9 – Aug 12 2026): +0.83 a hole overall; +0.62 on the hole after a bogey or worse (37 holes, 43% par or better); +0.75 after a double or worse (12 holes); closing three +0.67 against +0.89 before them (18 vs 45 holes); thirds +1.05 / +0.71 / +0.71; 13 holes of double or worse costing 26 strokes, 50% of total strokes lost. All of it recomputes live in the Mental tab, so treat the figures quoted here as the Aug 13 snapshot.

NOT MEASURED, and said plainly rather than assumed: match play appears nowhere in these cards, so the closing claim is untested; six rounds at two courses is a thin sample; and the focus rating in the debrief is self-report, ranked below every number on the page.

STANDING CONTENT: the 10-yard reset, one-target-one-thought, practice-like-it-counts and 'bogey is not an emergency' already lived in the Coach lessons — this plan points at them rather than restating them. The if-then form (deciding the response in advance and attaching it to a named trigger) is the mechanism the trigger list is built on.

ADDED Aug 13 2026 — the three worked examples. FROM YOU: slow randoms at Sterling Farms today; an opponent you found annoying in the first Wianno match; crumbling on 17 and 18 in the Jul 10 back-nine match, which you identified from the two candidate cards when asked. FROM THE CARDS: Jul 9 front holes 1–3 = +6 against +3 on each of the other four Wianno nines; opening third +1.05 a hole with that card, +0.89 against a +0.76 baseline without it; Jul 10 back holes 10–16 = +6 (+0.86 a hole) then +1.50 a hole over 17–18; closing two across all six cards +0.58 against +0.88 for everything before, with Jul 10 back the only card above +0.50. NOT SEPARABLE: the Jul 9 card is both the annoying-opponent match AND the coldest start of the event, so cold warm-up and partner disruption are confounded on it and neither is established as the cause. NOT RATED: you did not give a focus score for any of the three, so all three are logged without one rather than with a guessed one.

ADDED Aug 13 2026 — the full Wianno walkthrough, superseding the earlier three-example note. FROM YOU: opening tee shot thrown away in matches 1 and 3, a re-tee in match 1, both misses hard LEFT and both described as atrocious, with your usual bad miss being a slice; matches 4 and 5 played well but lost short putts down the stretch; match numbering confirmed by you as Jul 9 front, Jul 10 back, Jul 10 front, Jul 11 front, Jul 11 back. FROM THE CARDS: opening hole +9 over 6 starts (+1.50 a hole) against a +0.83 baseline; second hole +5 over 6 (+0.83, baseline exactly); rest of round after a +2 opening +0.71 a hole against +0.88 after a better one; matches 1 and 3 both opened with a 6 and finished 46 and 40; match 3 holes 2-9 = +3 (+0.38 a hole); match 1 holes 1-3 = +6 against +3 on each of the other four nines. FROM THE PROJECT RECORD: the Phantom 7.5 was the gamer through Jul 9-11 and was returned Jul 20 — max toe flow against a confirmed SBST stroke, the mismatch this app was built around. INFERENCE, NOT FINDING: the left-start-line explanation for the driver miss is reasoned from your own Golf Mind note, not measured, and pull / snap hook / toe strike are not separable without film. NOT MEASURED: no putts are recorded on any of the five cards, so the short-putt story is recalled rather than counted; and two rounds cannot establish the partner as the difference between match 1 and match 3.

ADDED Aug 13 2026 — match results, from you: lost 2 down, lost 2 down, won 2 up, halved, lost 1 down, three down on totals. You also confirmed the running order — both Jul 10 and Jul 11 were played BACK nine first, so match 4 is the Jul 11 back and match 5 the Jul 11 front (an earlier version of this plan had those two the other way round). briefing.focus: The routine as you run it now: get low, ball inside the lead heel, hands over the head of the putter, no press, quiet hands, face barely open, claw on the short ones and a feel-only trail hand on the lags, same beat count every putt. Standing work is the 30-ft ladder and one face-on clip. Everything historical — grip flips, putter changes, old measurements — is condensed in the Notes at the bottom; the sections above are only what you do.
rules: GET LOW — the deep bend is what presents the lie this putter needs
Ball 1–2 BALL-WIDTHS inside the lead heel
HANDS OVER THE HEAD OF THE PUTTER — that IS the straight shaft
NO PRESS. Nothing moves the shaft off vertical, at address or at impact
QUIET HANDS — the shoulders run the stroke, the hands just hold on
TRAIL HAND senses the weight on LAGS — it never pushes, and nothing releases
Set the face BARELY OPEN — that's your square
Aim the FACE first, then build the stance to it
TRAIL FOOT back — square will feel closed
CLAW for short ones, conventional for lags — keep the split clean
steps: Read it from BEHIND the ball — pick the line and a spot a few inches ahead of it
Step BESIDE the ball — BEND OVER, stand close, full putting posture
Rehearsal 1 — eyes on the BALL. Path and contact.
Rehearsal 2 — eyes on the HOLE. Pace. This one goes last, always.
Step in — set the FACE to the spot, BARELY OPEN, then build the stance around it (trail foot a touch BACK)
Spot → ball → go. The stroke starts as a motion — quiet hands.

sections.t: THE HEADLINE — get low
sections.k: Bend over and get low — the anchor feel everything else hangs off.
sections.b: Your words, and they go at the top: bending over is the most massive thing, and getting low is where you feel most comfortable. That is the feel to remember when everything else has drifted. If you carry one thought to the practice green, carry this one. Deep bend, stand close, eyes down.

sections.t: Why the bend is more than comfort
sections.k: It presents the lie the putter needs, and steepens the shoulder plane that makes the stroke straight.
sections.b:
Two mechanisms under the feel. FIRST — the LINK is Lie Angle Balanced, and that balance is only true when the shaft is presented at its built lie (69° lie, 2° effective loft, 0° lean, 34"). Stand tall or reach and the toe drops, the shaft leaves its lie, and the self-squaring property you bought quietly degrades. Posture is what delivers the technology.

SECOND — more bend hangs the arms freer and tilts the shoulders onto a STEEPER plane, and a steeper shoulder plane is what produces a straight-back-straight-through stroke. Standing tall builds in an arc you don't want.

sections.t: The setup
sections.k: Ball 1–2 widths inside the lead heel · hands over the head of the putter · quiet hands · face barely open.
sections.b:
BEND OVER, stand close, eyes down through the strike. BALL one to two ball-widths inside the lead heel — forward of centre so the head is a hair ASCENDING at contact, which is what produces true roll. Mark the spot and keep it; launch is sensitive to it, and a ball position that wanders reads as bad distance control even when the stroke was fine. Weight stacked ON the ball. TRAIL FOOT a touch back. Rock the shoulders, QUIET HANDS, loose grip. Face set BARELY OPEN — its own section below.

HANDS OVER THE HEAD OF THE PUTTER — shaft straight up and down. That is the entire hands instruction. Don't add lean to make it look like a normal putter: this face carries 2° of effective loft delivered at 0° lean, there is nothing to spare, and a driven ball skids before it rolls and finishes short.

(A vertical shaft photographs as hands ~1.35" behind the ball's centre — half a ball from face to centre plus the riser hosel's offset. Same position, the camera's description of it. Ball position is set by your FEET; the shaft is set by your HANDS.)

sections.t: THE FACE — barely open is your square
sections.k: Set what reads to you as barely open — that is square. Verify at a real target once; re-check monthly.
sections.b:
On this putter the face points where you set it — zero-torque means it doesn't twist through the stroke, so address IS impact. What reads to your eye as barely open is, on the actual line, square. Trust it and set it the same way every putt.

Two standing guards. DON'T STACK FIXES: keep this feel, or retrain the aim picture with a mirror — never both, or the correction gets applied twice and the miss flips right. PUT A NUMBER ON IT: once, photograph the face from directly above against an alignment stick, then re-check monthly — an unquantified feel drifts toward the exaggeration.

One check still owed, and it's the last one: five putts at a coin on a real green, nothing drawn on the ground, filmed from behind the ball. If the misses still fall on both sides, this closes for good.

sections.t: THE CLAW — short ones only
sections.k: It fits this putter's premise — keep it off the lags, and hold the shaft rule on both grips.
sections.b:
Scope: SHORT PUTTS. Conventional stays on the lags — a claw trades a little distance feel for line control, the wrong trade on a lag while pace is the open fault, and the split keeps the ladder numbers clean. The other half of that split — what the trail hand does once it is back on the club — is its own section below.

Why it fits: a zero-torque head is built on the premise that the face squares itself when the hands stop interfering, and the claw exists to take the trail hand OUT of the stroke. 'Quiet hands' and 'claw' are the same instruction.

The one check: a claw can push the handle forward without you feeling it. The shaft rule doesn't relax — vertical at address and impact, on BOTH grips. Get both into the same face-on set and compare. Scoreboard: the 20-ball 5-footer, one block claw, one block conventional, same session.

sections.t: THE TRAIL HAND — the feel hand, on lags only
sections.k: Let the right hand sense the weight of the head on lags and never push it — and remember the claw leaves you no feel hand at all on the short ones.
sections.b:
On LAGS, conventional grip: let the RIGHT hand be the one that senses the weight of the head, and let the left just ride along. Keep that — it is a good cue and it is pointed at the right fault. Pace is the open one, distance on this putter is stroke LENGTH at a fixed tempo, and a hand that reports how heavy the head feels going back is reporting the exact thing the ladder exists to calibrate.

The whole cue lives in one word, though: SENSE the weight, never PUSH the club. A trail hand that drives through the ball is a second pace input stacked on top of stroke length, which is how a power curve stops being repeatable. It also has a quiet way of shoving the handle forward, and that breaks the vertical-shaft rule without ever feeling like it did. If a lag finishes short, the fix is committing to the LENGTH you rehearsed, not squeezing harder.

The scope is not a preference. The claw exists to take the trail hand OUT of the stroke — it moves the pressure into the lead hand and leaves the right as a guide. So on the short ones there is no feel hand, and there should not be. 'Right hand feels it, left hand rides along' is a CONVENTIONAL-GRIP cue, and it runs on exactly the putts the conventional grip already runs on. Claw short, conventional long, feel hand on the long ones.

One thing this is NOT, and on this putter it matters: a release. A release means the face rotating through impact, and this head is built so it does not — L.A.B.'s own coaching is that your job is just to LET IT STAY SQUARE, which is why their first drill is putting with your thumbs off the grip. Your stroke is straight back and straight through, confirmed across four heads, so there is no rotation to time even if you wanted one. And where the marketing says 'square to your arc', read LINE — you do not have an arc. Feel the weight; leave the face where you set it.

Two things to notice on the next ladder session, because the answers change what belongs in here. When a lag comes off right, does the head just swing while you sense the weight, or are you consciously pushing it through the ball? And on the lags, is the grip fully conventional, or has something crept over from the claw?

sections.t: THE TRAIL FOOT — set it back
sections.k: Trail foot back, square will feel closed — and always face first, then stance.
sections.b:
Set the trail foot a touch further back than feels natural, and expect square to feel CLOSED. You're recalibrating off an open baseline, so trust the line you set rather than the feel for the first few sessions.

Why it matters this much: in an SBST stroke the shoulder line IS the track. An open stance doesn't just aim you left — it points the whole stroke left, and then either the hands steer the takeaway to save it, or the ball starts left. A stance error shows up disguised as a takeaway problem.

Ten-second check: alignment stick down the line, toes PARALLEL, not converging. And keep the order religiously — aim the FACE to the spot first, then build the stance around it. Face-first means a creeping stance shows up as discomfort, and discomfort you can feel is information you can act on.

sections.t: THE SHAFT — vertical at address, vertical at impact
sections.k: One rule, checkable two ways: same shaft angle both ends, and no scuff in the sound.
sections.b:
The shaft is VERTICAL at address and VERTICAL at impact. Nothing you do moves it. Forward at impact delofts a face with 2° to give and drives the ball into the turf — it skids, then rolls, and finishes short. Hands falling BACK invite the wrist flick. Both directions off vertical are misses.

Check with a camera: one face-on clip, shaft angle at address versus impact, same number both times — pass. Check without one: LISTEN. A purely rolling ball makes one clean click; a driven ball adds a faint scuff a beat later. If you hear the scuff, the shaft leaned forward, whatever your hands report.

sections.t: THE TRIGGER — starting without a press
sections.k: The stroke must start as a motion, not a decision. If it does, leave this alone.
sections.b:
With no press, watch for one failure mode: standing dead still over the ball and having to DECIDE to go. That's where a stroke gets snatched or steered, and it shows up on short putts under pressure, not on the practice green. If your stroke starts cleanly from stillness, nothing here needs you — skip it.

If it does show up, take ONE off this shelf. Each starts the stroke without touching shaft lean: the FLOAT (lift the head a hair off the surface before takeaway), the WHOLE-PUTTER WAGGLE (small, from the shoulders, wrists silent), the LEAD-SHOULDER SETTLE, or the TRAIL-KNEE KICK — the same trigger your full-swing routine already uses, which makes it the cheapest to learn.

sections.t: THE REHEARSALS — beside the ball, pace last
sections.k: Rehearse in real posture beside the ball; ball-look first, hole-look second; same beat count every putt.
sections.b:
Read from BEHIND the ball — line, and a spot a few inches ahead of it. Then rehearse BESIDE the ball in full putting posture: same bend, same arm hang. Magnitude transfers one-to-one from that posture; behind-the-ball rehearsals read break better but run upright, so the size they teach is an approximation — and size is the thing you're training.

Order is fixed. Rehearsal 1, eyes on the BALL: path and contact. Rehearsal 2, eyes on the HOLE: pace. The last thing you feel is what you carry in, so the pace stroke goes last, always.

Same BEAT COUNT every putt — a routine that varies in length is itself a pace variable, and the putts that get an extra look are the ones that come up short. Backstop worth testing: say the pace intention out loud before stepping in ('die it a foot past', 'back of the cup'). Feel decays; a word doesn't.

Past 25 feet, test eyes ON THE HOLE through the stroke — as a block test on the practice green, not mid-round.

sections.t: THE LADDER — the standing work
sections.k: 10 from 30 ft, twice a week: shorts · spread · green speed. Gamer ball, conventional grip.
sections.b:
Twice a week on the LINK, gamer ball only, conventional grip: 10 balls from 30 feet. Distance comes from stroke LENGTH at a fixed tempo — tempo is already right on this head (2.0:1 measured) — so if you catch yourself hitting AT a long one, that rep is the fault showing itself. Note it.

sections.k: History, condensed. Nothing here changes what you do above.

briefing.focus: The routine as you run it now: get low, ball inside the lead heel, hands over the head of the putter, no forward press, a light trail-thumb press to start it, quiet hands, face barely open, claw on the short ones and a feel-only trail hand on the lags, same beat count every putt. Everything historical — grip flips, putter changes, old measurements — is condensed in the Notes at the bottom; the sections above are only what you do.
rules: GET LOW — the deep bend is what presents the lie this putter needs
Ball 1–2 BALL-WIDTHS inside the lead heel
HANDS OVER THE HEAD OF THE PUTTER — that IS the straight shaft
NO FORWARD PRESS. Nothing moves the shaft off vertical, at address or at impact
TRIGGER = a light TRAIL-THUMB press, then go — it ENDS before the stroke does
QUIET HANDS — the shoulders run the stroke, the hands just hold on
TRAIL HAND senses the weight on LAGS — it never pushes, and nothing releases
Set the face BARELY OPEN — that's your square
Aim the FACE first, then build the stance to it
TRAIL FOOT back — square will feel closed
CLAW for short ones, conventional for lags — keep the split clean
steps: Read it from BEHIND the ball — pick the line and a spot a few inches ahead of it
Step BESIDE the ball — BEND OVER, stand close, full putting posture
Rehearsal 1 — eyes on the BALL. Path and contact.
Rehearsal 2 — eyes on the HOLE. Pace. This one goes last, always.
Step in — set the FACE to the spot, BARELY OPEN, then build the stance around it (trail foot a touch BACK)
Spot → ball → go. The stroke starts as a motion — quiet hands.

sections.t: THE HEADLINE — get low
sections.k: Bend over and get low — the anchor feel everything else hangs off.
sections.b: Your words, and they go at the top: bending over is the most massive thing, and getting low is where you feel most comfortable. That is the feel to remember when everything else has drifted. If you carry one thought to the practice green, carry this one. Deep bend, stand close, eyes down.

sections.t: Why the bend is more than comfort
sections.k: It presents the lie the putter needs, and steepens the shoulder plane that makes the stroke straight.
sections.b:
Two mechanisms under the feel. FIRST — the LINK is Lie Angle Balanced, and that balance is only true when the shaft is presented at its built lie (69° lie, 2° effective loft, 0° lean, 34"). Stand tall or reach and the toe drops, the shaft leaves its lie, and the self-squaring property you bought quietly degrades. Posture is what delivers the technology.

SECOND — more bend hangs the arms freer and tilts the shoulders onto a STEEPER plane, and a steeper shoulder plane is what produces a straight-back-straight-through stroke. Standing tall builds in an arc you don't want.

sections.t: The setup
sections.k: Ball 1–2 widths inside the lead heel · hands over the head of the putter · quiet hands · face barely open.
sections.b:
BEND OVER, stand close, eyes down through the strike. BALL one to two ball-widths inside the lead heel — forward of centre so the head is a hair ASCENDING at contact, which is what produces true roll. Mark the spot and keep it; launch is sensitive to it, and a ball position that wanders reads as bad distance control even when the stroke was fine. Weight stacked ON the ball. TRAIL FOOT a touch back. Rock the shoulders, QUIET HANDS, loose grip. Face set BARELY OPEN — its own section below.

HANDS OVER THE HEAD OF THE PUTTER — shaft straight up and down. That is the entire hands instruction. Don't add lean to make it look like a normal putter: this face carries 2° of effective loft delivered at 0° lean, there is nothing to spare, and a driven ball skids before it rolls and finishes short.

(A vertical shaft photographs as hands ~1.35" behind the ball's centre — half a ball from face to centre plus the riser hosel's offset. Same position, the camera's description of it. Ball position is set by your FEET; the shaft is set by your HANDS.)

sections.t: THE FACE — barely open is your square
sections.k: Set what reads to you as barely open — that is square. Verify at a real target once; re-check monthly.
sections.b:
On this putter the face points where you set it — zero-torque means it doesn't twist through the stroke, so address IS impact. What reads to your eye as barely open is, on the actual line, square. Trust it and set it the same way every putt.

Two standing guards. DON'T STACK FIXES: keep this feel, or retrain the aim picture with a mirror — never both, or the correction gets applied twice and the miss flips right. PUT A NUMBER ON IT: once, photograph the face from directly above against an alignment stick, then re-check monthly — an unquantified feel drifts toward the exaggeration.

One check still owed, and it's the last one: five putts at a coin on a real green, nothing drawn on the ground, filmed from behind the ball. If the misses still fall on both sides, this closes for good.

sections.t: THE CLAW — short ones only
sections.k: It fits this putter's premise — keep it off the lags, and hold the shaft rule on both grips.
sections.b:
Scope: SHORT PUTTS. Conventional stays on the lags — a claw trades a little distance feel for line control, the wrong trade on a lag while pace is the open fault, and the split keeps the ladder numbers clean. The other half of that split — what the trail hand does once it is back on the club — is its own section below.

Why it fits: a zero-torque head is built on the premise that the face squares itself when the hands stop interfering, and the claw exists to take the trail hand OUT of the stroke. 'Quiet hands' and 'claw' are the same instruction.

The one check: a claw can push the handle forward without you feeling it. The shaft rule doesn't relax — vertical at address and impact, on BOTH grips. Get both into the same face-on set and compare. Scoreboard: the 20-ball 5-footer, one block claw, one block conventional, same session.

sections.t: THE TRAIL HAND — the feel hand, on lags only
sections.k: Let the right hand sense the weight of the head on lags and never push it — and remember the claw leaves you no feel hand at all on the short ones.
sections.b:
On LAGS, conventional grip: let the RIGHT hand be the one that senses the weight of the head, and let the left just ride along. Keep that — it is a good cue and it is pointed at the right fault. Pace is the open one, distance on this putter is stroke LENGTH at a fixed tempo, and a hand that reports how heavy the head feels going back is reporting the exact thing the ladder exists to calibrate.

The whole cue lives in one word, though: SENSE the weight, never PUSH the club. A trail hand that drives through the ball is a second pace input stacked on top of stroke length, which is how a power curve stops being repeatable. It also has a quiet way of shoving the handle forward, and that breaks the vertical-shaft rule without ever feeling like it did. If a lag finishes short, the fix is committing to the LENGTH you rehearsed, not squeezing harder.

The scope is not a preference. The claw exists to take the trail hand OUT of the stroke — it moves the pressure into the lead hand and leaves the right as a guide. So on the short ones there is no feel hand, and there should not be. 'Right hand feels it, left hand rides along' is a CONVENTIONAL-GRIP cue, and it runs on exactly the putts the conventional grip already runs on. Claw short, conventional long, feel hand on the long ones.

One thing this is NOT, and on this putter it matters: a release. A release means the face rotating through impact, and this head is built so it does not — L.A.B.'s own coaching is that your job is just to LET IT STAY SQUARE, which is why their first drill is putting with your thumbs off the grip. Your stroke is straight back and straight through, confirmed across four heads, so there is no rotation to time even if you wanted one. And where the marketing says 'square to your arc', read LINE — you do not have an arc. Feel the weight; leave the face where you set it.

Two things to notice on the next ladder session, because the answers change what belongs in here. When a lag comes off right, does the head just swing while you sense the weight, or are you consciously pushing it through the ball? And on the lags, is the grip fully conventional, or has something crept over from the claw?

sections.t: THE TRAIL FOOT — set it back
sections.k: Trail foot back, square will feel closed — and always face first, then stance.
sections.b:
Set the trail foot a touch further back than feels natural, and expect square to feel CLOSED. You're recalibrating off an open baseline, so trust the line you set rather than the feel for the first few sessions.

Why it matters this much: in an SBST stroke the shoulder line IS the track. An open stance doesn't just aim you left — it points the whole stroke left, and then either the hands steer the takeaway to save it, or the ball starts left. A stance error shows up disguised as a takeaway problem.

Ten-second check: alignment stick down the line, toes PARALLEL, not converging. And keep the order religiously — aim the FACE to the spot first, then build the stance around it. Face-first means a creeping stance shows up as discomfort, and discomfort you can feel is information you can act on.

sections.t: THE SHAFT — vertical at address, vertical at impact
sections.k: One rule, checkable two ways: same shaft angle both ends, and no scuff in the sound.
sections.b:
The shaft is VERTICAL at address and VERTICAL at impact. Nothing you do moves it. Forward at impact delofts a face with 2° to give and drives the ball into the turf — it skids, then rolls, and finishes short. Hands falling BACK invite the wrist flick. Both directions off vertical are misses.

Check with a camera: one face-on clip, shaft angle at address versus impact, same number both times — pass. Check without one: LISTEN. A purely rolling ball makes one clean click; a driven ball adds a faint scuff a beat later. If you hear the scuff, the shaft leaned forward, whatever your hands report.

sections.t: THE TRIGGER — the trail thumb press, and the whole shelf
sections.k: Your live trigger is a light trail-thumb press; it must end before the stroke does, and everything else stays on the shelf below.
sections.b:
LIVE, your call, Aug 13: a light downward press of the TRAIL THUMB on the grip, then go. It fits this putter and this plan for one reason above all the others — it is a change in PRESSURE, not a change in POSITION. Every other rule here exists to keep the shaft vertical and the 2° of loft intact, and a thumb that presses without moving the handle leaves both alone. That is precisely the promise a forward press cannot make.

THREE GUARDS, and they are the whole difference between this working and this quietly becoming a forward press. IT ENDS — the press is a start signal, not a stroke input: it happens, then the stroke happens. Pressure that carries through the ball is the trail hand steering, which the section above rules out. IT STAYS LIGHT — a light grip is the manufacturer's instruction on this head, so a trigger that resets you to a firm grip has cost more than it bought. Press, release to stroke pressure, go. IT PRESSES DOWN THE SHAFT, NOT ACROSS IT — this is the one with a mechanism under it: trail-hand pressure aimed along the putter's plane leaves the face stable, while pressure arriving at an angle tends to rotate it. On the conventional grip your thumb sits down the top of the handle, so 'down' is along the shaft and you are fine.

CHECK IT ON THE CLAW. In a claw the trail hand is turned and the thumb is no longer where it was, so 'press down' can quietly become 'press across'. And the claw is on the SHORT putts — exactly where a freeze shows up under pressure. Look at where your trail thumb actually sits in the claw before you trust the same trigger on both grips; if it is not on top, run a sensory trigger on the short ones instead. One face-on clip settles it: shaft angle at address against the frame before the takeaway. Same number, and the press is clean.

RULED OUT, permanently: the FORWARD PRESS. It is the most common trigger in golf and the strongest cure for a jerky takeaway, and it still stays out. This face carries 2° of effective loft delivered at 0° lean, a forward press delofts it, and a delofted putt skids before it rolls and finishes short — with pace as your open fault, that is the last thing to buy. The only honest version of it builds the lean into the ADDRESS position so the angle you set is the angle you deliver, and that is a different putter's conversation.

THE SHELF — KINETIC (a small movement starts the chain). MICRO-WAGGLE: a tiny back-and-forth of the head, or one small forward-and-back, run from the shoulders with the wrists silent. TOE TAP or HEEL LIFT: the trail foot taps, or a heel lifts and resets — it releases a lower-body freeze without touching the arms, which makes it the safest kinetic option here. HOVER-AND-SET: the head hovers and then settles, or simply stays hovering. Nicklaus never grounded his putter, and his own reason was that a grounded club let his grip and arms go slack while hovering made the pressure uniform — it also lets you feel the head's full WEIGHT, which is the same currency as the lag cue in the section above. GRIP SQUEEZE-AND-RELEASE: a brief tighten, then relax to stroke pressure — the same family as your thumb press, one step cruder. TRAIL-KNEE KICK: the trigger your full-swing routine already runs, which makes it the cheapest to learn. LEAD-SHOULDER SETTLE.

THE SHELF — SENSORY (no movement at all, so nothing on this list can touch face angle or loft — the safer default if freezing is the real problem). LAST LOOK: the eyes go to the hole and the stroke starts the instant they arrive back at the ball. Nearly free for you, because your rehearsal order already ENDS on a look at the hole. EXHALE: the stroke starts on the out-breath. This is the one to reach for under pressure specifically — breath-holding and tension arrive together, and a long exhale is the standard way of pulling that back. Note where your failure actually lives: short putts under pressure, not the practice green. COUNT or BEAT: an internal 'one... two' that starts before the putter moves — you already run a fixed beat count, so this is the smallest addition on the shelf.

FOUR RULES FOR WHICHEVER ONE YOU RUN. ONE trigger, never two — stacking triggers is the same error as stacking an aim fix onto the barely-open feel. SAME SLOT every putt: the trigger is the LAST thing before the stroke, and where it sits in the routine matters as much as what it is. IT MUST SHORTEN THE DWELL — the real variable is how long you stand still over the ball, so count it; a trigger that hasn't shortened it isn't working, whatever it feels like. AND IF YOU FREEZE ANYWAY, STEP OFF — no trigger rescues a freeze you are already inside. Walk back behind the ball and restart from the top. Eight seconds, and always cheaper than the putt.

Settle any swap the way you settle everything else here: the 20-ball five-footer, one block with the trigger and one without, same session — and write down the dwell time on both.

sections.t: THE REHEARSALS — beside the ball, pace last
sections.k: Rehearse in real posture beside the ball; ball-look first, hole-look second; same beat count every putt.
sections.b:
Read from BEHIND the ball — line, and a spot a few inches ahead of it. Then rehearse BESIDE the ball in full putting posture: same bend, same arm hang. Magnitude transfers one-to-one from that posture; behind-the-ball rehearsals read break better but run upright, so the size they teach is an approximation — and size is the thing you're training.

Order is fixed. Rehearsal 1, eyes on the BALL: path and contact. Rehearsal 2, eyes on the HOLE: pace. The last thing you feel is what you carry in, so the pace stroke goes last, always.

Same BEAT COUNT every putt — a routine that varies in length is itself a pace variable, and the putts that get an extra look are the ones that come up short. Backstop worth testing: say the pace intention out loud before stepping in ('die it a foot past', 'back of the cup'). Feel decays; a word doesn't.

Past 25 feet, test eyes ON THE HOLE through the stroke — as a block test on the practice green, not mid-round.

sections.k: 10 from 30 ft, twice a week: shorts · spread · green speed. Gamer ball, conventional grip.
sections.b:

History is in the Notes.

sections.t: The ladder — this is the grind
sections.k: Ten balls from thirty feet, twice a week, three numbers written down.
sections.b:
Ten balls, 30 feet, on the LINK. Twice a week. Log three things every time:

SHORTS — how many of the ten finish short of the hole. Target: no more than 1 in 10. A putt that finishes short had a zero per cent chance.

SPREAD — front-to-back distance between the nearest and furthest stopping points. This is the actual measurement of distance control and the number that shows improvement. Target: inside 6 feet.

GREEN SPEED — estimated stimp, or name the surface honestly (that mat, this practice green). Not optional: a stroke that finishes perfectly on an 8–9 runs four to six feet past from 30 feet on an 11, so build the curve on at least TWO speeds before trusting it.

Then the calibration set, five minutes: 20, 30 and 40 feet, three balls each, noting where the BACKSTROKE ENDS for each distance — a landmark you can repeat. Written down, that mapping is the curve.

sections.t: Where distance comes from
sections.k: Stroke length at a fixed tempo — if tempo moves with distance, the curve never stabilises.
sections.b:
The ingredient most people are missing, you have: tempo measured 2.0:1 on this head against a 2:1 target. So the discipline in every ladder session is: same tempo, always — count it, hum it, whatever keeps it stable — and change the LENGTH.

The failure mode is the reverse: keeping the backstroke roughly constant and varying how hard you hit it. That works at one distance and falls apart everywhere else. If you catch yourself hitting AT a long one, that rep is the fault showing itself — note it on the sheet.

Once three distances have a repeatable backstroke landmark, everything between them is interpolation, and lag putting becomes a reference you consult instead of a feeling you summon.

sections.t: Strike — the hidden speed leak
sections.k: Off-centre contact bleeds ball speed. Twelve minutes of foot powder before any verdict on this putter.
sections.b:
A putt struck off the middle loses ball speed, so the same stroke finishes shorter — and inconsistently, because the miss moves. A heel strike also rotates the face closed. One cause, both faults, and it has never been measured on any putter you've owned.

This blade raises the stakes: less MOI than a mallet, so the same miss costs more speed and more face angle — and its riser hosel makes the true centre impossible to find by eye. If strike is your leak, the ladder will show it as a wide spread, and the tape test will show you where it's coming from.

So run the tape test EARLY — tap test for the true sweet spot, then foot-powder sheets from 5 and 30 feet, with the 30-footer as the verdict. Full protocol is its own plan. Use the barely-open address, since that's the setup you actually play.

sections.t: Setup for pace — four lines
sections.k: Marked ball position, vertical shaft, quiet hands, gamer ball. Pace has no other setup inputs.
sections.b:
BALL marked 1–2 ball-widths inside the lead heel, same spot every rep — launch is sensitive to it, and a wandering ball position reads as bad distance control even when the stroke was fine.

HANDS OVER THE HEAD OF THE PUTTER, no FORWARD press, shaft vertical at address and impact — a varying launch is a varying pace, and with nothing leaning the shaft there is nothing to vary. (The trail-thumb trigger you started Aug 13 is a pressure change, not a position change, so it does not touch this. Its rules live in the Routine plan.)

QUIET HANDS, shoulders run it.

GAMER BALL ONLY on all pace work, and conventional grip on the lags — the claw stays on short putts so the ladder numbers stay clean.

sections.t: The gate — before the window closes
sections.k: Find the deadline, run two weeks of numbers, and let the sheet decide keep-or-return.
sections.b:
First job: find the receipt and confirm the return deadline — the Home card is showing 'deadline unknown' until you set it. Everything here runs on that clock.

The gate, set now while nothing is being decided: two weeks of the ladder at two different green speeds, plus the tape test. If the spread is still wide AND the tape shows a centred strike, the head is a fair suspect — send it back with actual evidence, the first equipment decision in this project that would have any. If the tape shows a heel bias, the head was never the problem, and returning it buys a fifth putter and the same fault.

Know the fallback either way: the only other putter in the bag is the Newport 2, a toe-hang blade against your SBST stroke. That's not an argument for keeping the LINK — it's an argument for knowing the replacement BEFORE the window closes, not after.

What's open is pace and strike, and both are the same twelve minutes and the same ladder away from having numbers. The rule stands: the next thing that changes should be a NUMBER on the card, not a head in the bag.
