SHAFT STILL VERTICAL — a rap that leans forward delofts a face with 2° to give
It cures DECELERATION, not AIM — barely open still does the aiming
SHORT ≠ QUITTING. If the short ones come up short, that is deceleration, not the plan

sections.t: WHAT THE POP STROKE ACTUALLY IS
sections.k: A short backstroke and a firm rap with little follow-through — and it was invented for slow greens, which is what you play.
sections.b:
The pop stroke is a short backstroke, a firm accelerating rap at the ball, and an abbreviated follow-through. Gary Player played it, rapping the ball with almost no finish. Billy Casper is the purest example — compact, hands close to the body, the face hooded going back, and then a pop; the standard description is that it looks like tapping a tack with a hammer, which is why it is also called the tap stroke.

The part worth knowing before you adopt it: this stroke came out of SLOW GREENS. It was developed by players who needed extra pop to get the ball to the hole on surfaces that did not run. That is a genuine argument in its favour for you — your pace is calibrated at an estimated 8-9 stimp, which is exactly that world. It is also the warning that comes with it. On a fast green a stroke built to add force is the wrong instinct, and you will find that out on a downhill four-footer before you find it out anywhere else.

Your own description of it — short back, straight through — is already the safe half of the idea. It describes the LENGTH and the DIRECTION of the stroke, which is all you want from it.

sections.t: THE ONE THING YOU CANNOT COPY — the wrists
sections.k: Casper's pop was a wrist stroke; on this putter it has to be a short shoulder stroke instead, or it fights everything else you do.
sections.b:
This is the whole adaptation, and it is not a small one. The classic pop stroke is a WRIST stroke. Casper cocked his wrists to keep the face square going back and then released them into the ball. The technique's own history says as much: it was right-wrist action that supplied the extra pop on slow greens.

That mechanism is not available to you, for two reasons that point the same way. Your whole method is QUIET HANDS with the shoulders running the stroke. And the head you play is built on the premise that the face squares ITSELF when the hands stop interfering — L.A.B.'s own instruction is that your job is only to let it stay square. A wrist-released pop is the single most hand-active stroke in putting. Bolting it onto a zero-torque putter is asking the club to undo what you are doing to it.

So take the GEOMETRY, not the MECHANISM. Short backstroke, short through-stroke — your call, and it is the authentic shape; Casper's finish stopped dead. Both halves run from the shoulders, with the wrists silent — exactly the stroke you already make, just shorter and more committed. What you are borrowing from Casper is the SIZE and the INTENT, and nothing else.

The tell that you have drifted into the real thing is the putter head PASSING YOUR HANDS. That is the wrist releasing, and it is the one thing to watch for — more so now that the claw is out of play, because the claw was the physical guard against it and discipline is what replaces it.

sections.t: SHORT THROUGH IS NOT THE SAME AS QUITTING
sections.k: A short finish that accelerated and a short finish that decelerated look identical afterwards — the ball's roll-out is what tells them apart.
sections.b:
This is the one thing to get right about a short finish, because the good version and the bad version leave the same picture.

THE GOOD ONE: the head accelerates through the ball and then stops, because the stroke was small and the energy went into the ball. That is Casper's stroke, and it is what you have asked for.

THE BAD ONE: the head slows down BEFORE the ball and the finish is short because there was nothing left. That is deceleration — the classic short-putt killer, and the thing a short backstroke makes easy to fall into, since a small backstroke gives you less room to build any speed at all.

Afterwards they look the same. So do not judge it by the finish. JUDGE IT BY THE ROLL-OUT: a stroke that accelerated gets the ball consistently to 17 inches past. A stroke that quit leaves putts short and, worse, leaves them short by a varying amount. If your short putts start finishing at the front edge, the through-stroke is quitting, and the fix is committing to the pace rather than lengthening the backstroke.

The useful mental version: the backstroke sets the size, the through-stroke sets the INTENT. Short is a size. Quitting is a loss of intent, and it is a different thing entirely.

sections.t: SPEED — 17 inches past, and why firm is right on the short ones
sections.k: The ring around the hole is trodden flat, so a dying ball wobbles through it — 17 inches past is the researched target.
sections.b:
There is a real reason a firmer short putt works, and it is not toughness. The area roughly one to six feet all around a hole takes all the foot traffic on a green, so it is depressed and bumpy — Dave Pelz's 'lumpy donut'. A ball arriving with barely any pace wobbles through exactly the bit of green that is in the worst condition. A ball with a little more speed pushes through it.

Pelz's number is 17 INCHES PAST the hole. That is the target: enough pace to hold the line through the trodden ring and take some break out, not so much that you shrink the effective hole and leave yourself the one coming back.

The honest counter-argument, because it is real physics: a ball dying into the hole can fall in off the edges, so a softer putt has a bigger effective target and more room for a stroke error. Both things are true. The reason firm wins on a SHORT putt specifically is that inside six feet you are not solving a distance problem — you are trying to start it on line and get it there before the green can do anything to it. That balance flips as soon as the putt gets long, which is why this stroke is quarantined.

17 inches is a specific number, so treat it as one: on the practice green, put a tee 17 inches behind the hole and putt to leave it between the hole and the tee.

sections.t: THE LOFT TRAP — when the rap becomes a jab
sections.k: A firm short stroke is the easiest way to lean the shaft forward, and this face has 2° to give before the ball is being driven into the turf.
sections.b:
This is the specific way the pop stroke can hurt you on THIS putter, and it is worth more attention than the stroke shape.

Casper's pop hit the ball and then the turf, clubhead stopping abruptly. That is a descending, forward-leaning delivery. Your putter carries 2° of effective loft delivered at 0° shaft lean, and there is essentially nothing to spare. A rap that arrives with the shaft leaning forward delofts a face that has no loft to lose, and a delofted putt is driven into the turf: it skids, then rolls, and finishes short and off line.

The rule does not relax because the stroke got shorter. SHAFT VERTICAL at address, SHAFT VERTICAL at impact — the same on this stroke as on every other one.

The check needs no camera: LISTEN. A purely rolling ball makes one clean click. A driven ball adds a faint scuff a beat later. If you start hearing the scuff on short putts, the pop has turned into a jab and the shaft is leaning. The camera version is the same face-on clip you already owe — shaft angle at address against shaft angle at impact, same number both times.

sections.t: THE CLAW — the safety net, and the trip-wire that deploys it
sections.k: Out of play by your call, kept in reserve — and the number that brings it back is set now, while nothing is going wrong.
sections.b:
NOT IN PLAY. As of Aug 13 you are putting conventional on the short ones. The claw is the reserve, and that is a reasonable place for it — a grip you can reach for is worth more than a grip you are grinding on.

SET THE TRIP-WIRE NOW, while nothing is going wrong. 'If short putts aren't falling' is exactly the kind of judgement that never quite triggers in the moment, and then triggers three bad rounds too late. So make it a number, using the scoreboard this plan already runs: TWO consecutive 20-ball five-footer blocks below your conventional baseline, or more than 2 LEFT misses in a block. Either one, and the claw goes back on for a block to see whether it answers it.

WHY IT IS THE RIGHT SAFETY NET, specifically. A firm, short, hitting stroke is the exact shape that invites the trail hand to take over, and the claw physically removes it — pressure moves to the lead hand, the right becomes a guide, and flipping the wrists gets awkward rather than merely discouraged. So if the pop stroke ever goes wrong, the claw is aimed at the most likely way it will have gone wrong. That is a better reason to hold it in reserve than habit.

WHAT CHANGES WHEN IT COMES BACK. On the claw there is no feel hand and there should not be — the lag cue about the trail hand sensing weight is a conventional-grip cue and it does not come in. And the shaft rule does not relax on either grip: a claw can push the handle forward without you feeling it.

sections.t: WHY THIS STAYS INSIDE SIX FEET
sections.k: The pop holds the backstroke short and varies force, which is the exact failure the lag plan exists to prevent.
sections.b:
Your distance system says DISTANCE COMES FROM STROKE LENGTH AT A FIXED TEMPO. The Lag Putts plan names the opposite as the failure mode by name: keeping the backstroke roughly constant and varying how hard you hit it works at one distance and falls apart everywhere else.

A pop stroke is that failure mode, deliberately. It holds the length short and supplies the rest with force.

On a short putt that is not a flaw, because there is no meaningful distance problem to solve inside six feet — the ball has one job, which is to reach the hole on line. On anything longer it is exactly the thing that produced a round of short lags and hot short putts, and it is why pace has never been calibrated in this project.

So the split is hard: POP inside about six feet, FULL STROKE LENGTH outside it — same grip on both for now, so the stroke shape is the only thing that changes. Keeping them apart is also what keeps the ladder numbers clean — the ladder is measuring the long stroke, and a pop rep on it is a corrupted data point.

sections.t: WHAT IT FIXES, AND WHAT IT DOESN'T
sections.k: It is a cure for deceleration and for standing frozen over a short putt — it is not a cure for your aim.
sections.b:
WHAT IT GENUINELY HELPS. Deceleration, which is the classic short-putt killer, and the freeze — a short committed stroke gives the conscious mind less time and less room to intervene. That connects to the trigger work: your failure lives on short putts under pressure, not on the practice green, and a stroke with less dwell and less distance to travel is a real answer to that.

WHAT IT DOES NOT TOUCH, and this matters because it would be easy to expect otherwise. Your left miss is an AIM error, not a delivery error — reclassified Aug 10, and the Aug 10 pm mat set came back 0.8° right / 1.0° left / 0.6° right with no bias at all. Face angle decides about 80% of where a putt starts. A pop stroke changes how the face is DELIVERED; it does not change where you have AIMED it. Barely open is still what does the aiming, and it is untouched by any of this.

So do not adopt this expecting the left ones to stop. Adopt it because a short committed stroke under pressure is worth having, and then measure it.

sections.t: THE SCOREBOARD — the 20-ball five-footer
sections.k: Two blocks in the same session, A against B, and the pass mark is the one the grip experiment already used.
sections.b:
This does not get decided on feel. The whole project's record on deciding putting things by feel is four putter movements in twelve days.

THE TEST. 20 balls from five feet, in two blocks in the SAME session: one block with the pop stroke, one with your normal short-putt stroke. Same grip on both (conventional), same green, same day — the green speed changes everything and a comparison across two sessions compares two greens.

WHAT TO LOG. Makes out of 20, and the direction of every miss. The pass mark is the one the grip experiment already set: 2 or fewer LEFT misses per 20. Note the green speed too.

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CONVICT IT. More makes is the headline, but watch three other things. If the misses get LONGER — running well past — the pop is a jab and the loft trap has you. If putts come up SHORT, the through-stroke is quitting rather than merely being short, which is the failure mode a short finish invites. And if you start hearing the scuff, stop and check the shaft before you read the scores at all.

Run it at two green speeds before you commit. A stroke built for slow greens will flatter itself on a slow one.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: Where the stroke came from, what was adapted, and what has not been measured.
sections.b:
FROM YOU, Aug 13 2026, and authoritative: a pop stroke on the short ones — short back, SHORT through, and no wrists. Also from you, same day: the claw is out of play, held as the safety net if the short ones stop falling.

RESEARCHED. The pop stroke's history and mechanics: Gary Player rapped it with no follow-through; Billy Casper is the canonical version — compact, hands close to the body, face hooded going back, ball-then-turf contact and an abbreviated finish, described as tapping a tack with a hammer. Its origin is slow greens, where right-wrist action supplied the extra pop. The speed target comes from Dave Pelz's research: the 'lumpy donut' of trodden ground one to six feet around the hole, and 17 inches past as the optimal pace. The counter-argument — that a dying ball has a bigger effective hole — is real physics and is stated rather than buried.

ADAPTED, and this is the significant edit. The classic pop is a WRIST stroke, which contradicts both quiet hands and the zero-torque premise of the LINK. What survives here is the geometry — short backstroke, positive through-stroke — run from the shoulders. That is a reasoned adaptation, not something anyone measured.

REVISED SAME DAY. An earlier version of this plan had the through-stroke 'at least as long as the backstroke' and the claw running as the guardrail. Both were corrected by you: the finish is short, and the grip is conventional. The anti-deceleration guard therefore moved from LENGTH to ACCELERATION, which is the honest version anyway — and with the claw out, the wrist-flick guard is discipline rather than geometry, so the tell matters more.

NOT MEASURED. All of it. No pop-stroke rep has ever been filmed or scored, the 20-ball five-footer has not been run on the LINK, and the face-on clip that would catch the shaft leaning forward is still owed. Until the scoreboard exists this plan describes an experiment, not a finding.

briefing.focus: Everything past about six feet. Build this putter's power curve with numbers: the ladder twice a week, three numbers logged every time, the 20/30/40 backstroke map, and the tape test whose full protocol is in here. Conventional grip and full stroke length — the pop stroke belongs to the Short Putts plan and must not come out here.
rules: PAST ~6 FEET — conventional grip, full stroke length, no pop
Pace is the open fault — the ladder IS the grind
10 from 30 ft, twice a week: log SHORTS · SPREAD · GREEN SPEED
Distance = stroke LENGTH at a fixed tempo — 2.0:1 is already right
Run the TAPE TEST — strike is a distance fault before it is a line fault
No FORWARD press, hands over the head — nothing feeds a varying launch
Gamer ball only · conventional grip

sections.t: The ladder — this is the grind
sections.k: Ten balls from thirty feet, twice a week, three numbers written down.
sections.b:
Ten balls, 30 feet, on the LINK. Twice a week. Log three things every time:

SHORTS — how many of the ten finish short of the hole. Target: no more than 1 in 10. A putt that finishes short had a zero per cent chance.

SPREAD — front-to-back distance between the nearest and furthest stopping points. This is the actual measurement of distance control and the number that shows improvement. Target: inside 6 feet.

GREEN SPEED — estimated stimp, or name the surface honestly (that mat, this practice green). Not optional: a stroke that finishes perfectly on an 8–9 runs four to six feet past from 30 feet on an 11, so build the curve on at least TWO speeds before trusting it.

Then the calibration set, five minutes: 20, 30 and 40 feet, three balls each, noting where the BACKSTROKE ENDS for each distance — a landmark you can repeat. Written down, that mapping is the curve.

sections.t: Where distance comes from
sections.k: Stroke length at a fixed tempo — if tempo moves with distance, the curve never stabilises.
sections.b:
The ingredient most people are missing, you have: tempo measured 2.0:1 on this head against a 2:1 target. So the discipline in every ladder session is: same tempo, always — count it, hum it, whatever keeps it stable — and change the LENGTH.

The failure mode is the reverse: keeping the backstroke roughly constant and varying how hard you hit it. That works at one distance and falls apart everywhere else. If you catch yourself hitting AT a long one, that rep is the fault showing itself — note it on the sheet.

Once three distances have a repeatable backstroke landmark, everything between them is interpolation, and lag putting becomes a reference you consult instead of a feeling you summon.

sections.t: Strike — the hidden speed leak
sections.k: Off-centre contact bleeds ball speed. Twelve minutes of foot powder before any verdict on this putter.
sections.b:
A putt struck off the middle loses ball speed, so the same stroke finishes shorter — and inconsistently, because the miss moves. A heel strike also rotates the face closed. One cause, both faults, and it has never been measured on any putter you've owned.

This blade raises the stakes: less MOI than a mallet, so the same miss costs more speed and more face angle — and its riser hosel makes the true centre impossible to find by eye. If strike is your leak, the ladder will show it as a wide spread, and the tape test will show you where it's coming from.

So run the tape test EARLY — tap test for the true sweet spot, then foot-powder sheets from 5 and 30 feet, with the 30-footer as the verdict. The full protocol is the next section. Use the barely-open address, since that's the setup you actually play.

sections.t: The tape test — the whole protocol, twelve minutes
sections.k: Hang it and tap it to find the true sweet spot, then two powder sheets at two distances — the 30-footer is the verdict.
sections.b:
STEP ONE — FIND THE TRUE SWEET SPOT. Hang the putter from the top of the grip so it swings free. Tap the face heel-to-toe with a pencil eraser and watch the head: everywhere off-centre it TWISTS, and at one spot it swings straight back with no twist. That spot is the true sweet spot. Mark it with a sliver of tape.

Then check the mark against the sight line. On this head the shaft is a poor pointer to where the mass sits — the riser hosel offsets it — so don't trust your eye. If the mark and the sight line disagree, that disagreement is a finding on its own: you have been lining up a spot that isn't the middle.

STEP TWO — THE POWDER SHEETS. Coat the face with foot-powder spray. Hit 10 putts from 5 feet. Photograph the face. Re-coat, hit 10 from 30 feet, photograph again. Don't wipe between putts — the overlapping marks ARE the data. Use the setup you actually play: barely-open face, hands over the head, conventional grip. If you want the claw's answer too, run it as a third coat on the 5-footers, separately, so the sheets don't mix.

HOW TO READ THEM. TIGHT CLUSTER ON THE MARK — strike isn't your leak, and pace work is pure stroke-length calibration. CLUSTER OFF-CENTRE, especially toward the HEEL — one cause explaining both open faults at once, since heel contact rotates the face closed (starts it left) and bleeds ball speed (finishes short); fixable with distance-to-ball and eyeline, not with a new putter. BROAD SCATTER — the ladder's spread has its cause, because a strike that moves is a ball speed that moves.

The 30-FOOT sheet is the one that matters — long putts are where a speed leak shows. The 5-foot sheet is the baseline that says whether the leak is stroke-length dependent. Send both photos when you run it.

sections.t: Setup for pace — four lines
sections.k: Marked ball position, vertical shaft, quiet hands, gamer ball. Pace has no other setup inputs.
sections.b:
BALL marked 1–2 ball-widths inside the lead heel, same spot every rep — launch is sensitive to it, and a wandering ball position reads as bad distance control even when the stroke was fine.

HANDS OVER THE HEAD OF THE PUTTER, no FORWARD press, shaft vertical at address and impact — a varying launch is a varying pace, and with nothing leaning the shaft there is nothing to vary. (The trail-thumb trigger you started Aug 13 is a pressure change, not a position change, so it does not touch this. Its rules live in the Routine plan.)

QUIET HANDS, shoulders run it.

GAMER BALL ONLY on all pace work, and conventional grip — which is now the grip on every length, so the ladder numbers and the short-putt numbers are directly comparable. What must NOT come out here is the pop stroke: a short backstroke with force added is the exact failure this plan exists to prevent.

sections.t: What the numbers are for now
sections.k: The putter is settled, so the ladder stopped being a trial and became a calibration.
sections.b:
The keep-or-return gate this section used to hold is CLOSED — you kept the LINK by decision on Aug 12 and shut the return window yourself. That changes what the numbers are for, and it is a better job than the one they had.

They are no longer evidence in a trial. Nothing on the ladder can now send a head back, which means nothing on the ladder needs defending. Two weeks of numbers at two different green speeds plus the tape test now buy you a power curve you can consult instead of a feeling you summon — and if the spread stays wide with a centred sheet, the answer is head WEIGHT or reps, not a fifth putter.

Head weight is the dial, and it is the cheapest one left. A heavier head produces a shorter, more repeatable stroke for a given distance, which usually helps lag control; a lighter head asks for a longer stroke and gives more feel on the short ones. Don't touch it before you have baseline numbers, or you will be changing two things at once and learn nothing.

And the standing rule survives everything: the next thing that changes should be a NUMBER on the card, not a head in the bag.

sections.t: What's already settled
sections.k: Path, tempo, lift, stance — measured, closed, and none of them walked out with any putter.
sections.b:
Path: straight, SBST, confirmed across four heads. Tempo: 2.0:1 on this putter. Early lift: closed on film. Stance line: square, never open. Start line: downgraded — the one-way left pull did not reproduce across three measured putts.

What's open is pace and strike, and both are the same twelve minutes and the same ladder away from having numbers. The rule stands: the next thing that changes should be a NUMBER on the card, not a head in the bag.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: History, condensed. Nothing here changes the work above.
sections.b:
The DF3i went back on Aug 10 for distance control — after being benched for pace Jul 30, reprieved Aug 1 and returned Aug 10: three verdicts in eleven days, all on feel, zero calibrated lag sessions. That pattern, not the putter, is what this plan exists to break. The Aug 1 'pace felt dialled' round was a scramble on 8–9 stimp greens — the friendliest read available. The Aug 10 outdoor session scored ~20 putts off above-ground cups: nine dead, worst ~4 ft, nothing long — first real evidence pace is closer than the returns implied. The blue ball scattered 1.2–1.5 ft on putts the white killed from the same spot — hence the gamer-ball rule. Both reds on the evolution grid (face at impact, start line) were measured on this head Jul 30; the start-line red was downgraded Aug 10 pm after the mat set came back 0.8° right / 1.0° left / 0.6° right — dispersion, no bias.

Aug 13: the Tape Test folded in from its own plan — it was always the same subject as this one, since strike is a distance fault before it is a line fault. Written Aug 2 for the DF3i, moved to the LINK Aug 10, still unrun on any of the four putters owned this month. Two Aug 10 pointers both aim at it: the evening mat putts scattered ~0.8° either side with no bias (a moving strike is the leading explanation on a head that cannot twist), and the blue ball spread 1.2-1.5 ft on putts the white killed. The keep-or-return gate closed Aug 12 when you kept the putter by decision.

briefing.focus: Every putting question worked through end to end, one per section, newest first. This is the reference shelf, not the routine — nothing here tells you what to do on a putt. Tap a section to open it; each one says what was asked, what checked out, what did not, what changed in the other plans, and what is still unmeasured.
rules: One section per workshop, NEWEST FIRST — tap to open, they stay shut otherwise
Every section says WHAT CHANGED in the other plans, so nothing here is orphaned
Sourced claims and reasoned ones are labelled differently — on purpose
