(Rewritten Aug 14: this drill used to send you to a demo with the Phantom 7.5, which went back on Jul 20 — the putter search is over and the only toe-hang head left is the one in your own bag.)

briefing.focus: The shot into a green — from the fairway, from the rough, and every par 3, because there the tee shot IS the approach. One measured tendency runs through all of it: you miss SHORT. On the only round with a direction recorded on every green, 7 of 12 missed greens finished short of it. That is a flag, not a rate — one round — but it points at something systematic rather than random, and the first suspect is not your swing. It is that every carry number in this app is an ESTIMATE you have never measured.
rules: CLUB FOR THE MIDDLE of the green. Never for the pin
YOU MISS SHORT — 7 of 12. Take the club that COVERS the green, not the one that just reaches it
Your ladder is ESTIMATED, not measured. Treat every number as optimistic until you calibrate
A PAR 3 IS AN APPROACH — and it is the cleanest test you have, with no drive to blame
LOG THE CLUB you hit in. One tap, and the table in Scores is sitting empty waiting for it
The 5-wood has NO carry number at all. The 2-iron at least has an estimate
SHORT-SIDING yourself is an approach error — the short game just pays for it

sections.t: WHAT YOUR OWN CARDS SAY — and how thin it is
sections.k: Seven of twelve missed greens finished SHORT, and the sample is essentially one round — a direction worth acting on, a rate worth ignoring.
sections.b:
THE NUMBERS, all of them. Eighteen holes carry a green result: 6 hit, 12 missed, so 33%. Of the 12 misses — SHORT 7 · LEFT 2 · RIGHT 1 · LONG 1 · other 1. Three of the misses were conceded by the tee shot (the noshot flag), meaning the approach never had a real play at the green and the club was not the problem on those.

WHAT IS AND ISN'T SIGNAL HERE. The RATE is unremarkable — published figures put a 5-handicap around 46% of greens and a 10-handicap around 37%, so 33% off eighteen holes is roughly where your index says you should be, and it is not the thing to work on. The DIRECTION is the signal. Seven of twelve in one direction is not scatter; a swing that is simply missing greens sprays them, and yours land consistently on the near side.

THE HONEST LIMITS, stated up front because the rest of this plan leans on that one number. It is one round. Four of the twelve misses were on par 3s and eight on par 4s and 5s, which are different shots from different lies. And the single most useful column — WHICH CLUB you hit — is empty on every one of them, so nothing here can yet name the club that comes up short.

sections.t: THE FIRST SUSPECT — your ladder is a guess
sections.k: Every carry number in this app is an estimate you have never measured, and estimates run long, which produces exactly the miss you have.
sections.b:
Open the Bag and the ladder says ESTIMATED, not calibrated. That is thirteen numbers nobody has checked with a launch monitor or a marked range, and one of them — the 5-wood — is blank entirely.

WHY THAT IS THE FIRST PLACE TO LOOK. A miss that is systematic wants a systematic cause, and an estimated ladder is exactly that: it applies the same error to every club, every time, on every hole. A swing fault would not be so tidy.

WHY ESTIMATES RUN LONG — and this part is REASONING, not something measured about you. Golfers build their carry numbers from memorable shots, and the memorable ones are the good ones: the flushed 7-iron, downwind, in July, that finished pin high. The mishits do not get filed. So a ladder assembled from memory sits a few yards optimistic on every rung, and a few yards optimistic on every rung is a ball that lands on the front edge instead of the middle. That mechanism fits your data. It is not proven by it.

WHAT IT WOULD TAKE TO SETTLE IT. A calibrated ladder — one range session with a launch monitor, five balls a club, average the middle three. Until then the honest reading of every yardage in this app is 'about this, probably a bit less'.

AND THE ONE HOLE IN THE LADDER. The 5-wood came back into the bag on Aug 12 with NO carry number, and at 16.5° it sits about half a degree off the 2-iron utility. So on a hole where the number actually matters, the 2-iron is the club you have a figure for, even if it is an estimated one. Do not guess the 5-wood into a green and then call the result a club-selection lesson.

sections.t: CLUB FOR THE MIDDLE — the rule that does not move
sections.k: You cannot know where the flag is when you plan the shot, and aiming at one sends you at an edge on a day your miss is already short.
sections.b:
Take the yardage to the MIDDLE of the green and pick the club that covers the middle with a normal strike — not your best one. This is the same rule the round-prep plans are written to, so there is one instruction and not two.

WHY THE MIDDLE WINS TWICE FOR YOU SPECIFICALLY. A green has depth, and the middle is the only target where BOTH a slightly heavy strike and a slightly thin one still finish on the putting surface. Aim at a front pin and your good shot is fine while your normal one is in the fringe. Aim at the middle and your normal one is a putt. Given a documented short bias, the middle also quietly corrects it — the club that covers the centre is usually the one that would have covered a front pin comfortably.

WHAT 'NORMAL STRIKE' MEANS IN PRACTICE. If you are between clubs, the longer one is the answer far more often than it feels — because the miss you are protecting against is the one you actually have. The exception is a genuine hazard long, and long hazards are rarer than short ones: front bunkers, false fronts and uphill approaches are the standard defence of a golf hole.

Back pin, front pin, tucked, short-sided: those words are smells in a plan, because none of them are knowable in advance. Where the trouble sits does not move; where the flag sits does.

sections.t: PAR 3s ARE THE CLEAN TEST
sections.k: No drive to blame, so a par-3 green missed short is a club-choice error and nothing else — four of your twelve misses were exactly that.
sections.b:
On a par 3 the tee shot IS the approach. There is no fairway to have missed, no lie to explain it away, no awkward number left by a drive. You stand on a tee with a known yardage and a flat lie and choose a club.

That makes every par 3 a free, controlled experiment in the exact thing this plan is about — and four of your twelve missed greens came on them. It is also why the app deliberately does NOT record an approach club on a par 3: the tee club already is it.

HOW TO USE THEM. Yardage to the middle, club that covers the middle, and note afterwards whether it finished short, middle or long. Four par 3s a round is four data points on one question, and after three rounds you will have twelve — which is more green-direction data than this entire plan is currently built on.

sections.t: THE COLUMN YOU HAVE NEVER FILLED IN
sections.k: You have not once logged the club you hit into a green, so the app's approach table is empty and the 'which club' question cannot be answered at all.
sections.b:
The live logger takes an approach club in ONE TAP on every par 4 and par 5. You have logged 63 holes and the count of recorded approach clubs is zero.

WHAT THAT COSTS. Scores already contains an INTO THE GREEN · BY CLUB table, built and waiting, that turns on at ten recorded approaches. With it, 'you miss short' becomes 'you miss short with the 8-iron and below' or 'you miss short with everything', and those have completely different fixes — the first is a strike or a gapping problem in one part of the bag, the second is the ladder. Without it, this plan can tell you the direction of your miss and never the cause.

It is the cheapest data in the app: one chip, on the hole you are already logging. Two rounds and the table has something to say.

sections.t: WHERE THIS ENDS AND THE SHORT GAME BEGINS
sections.k: Short-siding yourself is decided by the approach club, and the short game only pays the bill afterwards.
sections.b:
The Short Game plan has a rule in it — never short-side yourself on the approach — and this is the plan that actually controls it. A ball that finishes on the near side of a green is usually a straightforward chip; a ball short and on the wrong side of the hole is the shot that plan calls the medicine rule, where the honest target stops being 'close' and becomes 'on the green'.

So the two plans meet here. Club for the middle and the short game gets easy shots. Chase a flag and the short game inherits hard ones — and on the one round with a full record, it converted none of them.

One boundary worth keeping straight: how you hit the iron lives in Swing Thoughts and Swing Focus. WHICH iron lives here.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: What came off your cards, what is researched, and what is reasoning that has not been tested.
sections.b:
FROM YOUR OWN CARDS: 18 holes with a green result (6 hit / 12 missed, 33%); the miss split S7 · L2 · R1 · Lg1 · X1; 3 misses flagged as conceded by the tee shot; 4 of the 12 on par 3s; 63 logged holes with zero recorded approach clubs; the carry ladder flagged ESTIMATED with the 5-wood blank.

RESEARCHED: greens-in-regulation benchmarks by handicap — a 5-handicap around 46% and a 10-handicap around 37% — from published handicap-stat summaries (TheGrint, Golf.com, Golf Monthly). Used only to say your RATE is unremarkable, which is the point.

REASONING, NOT MEASUREMENT: that self-estimated carry numbers skew long because good strikes are the memorable ones. It fits the data and it is the first thing to test; it is not established for you. Nothing in this plan has been checked against a launch monitor.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THIS PLAN: a calibrated ladder, and ten logged approach clubs. Either one on its own would say more than everything above.

briefing.course: Reading the Green — Before You Aim
briefing.focus: The step that happens BEFORE the routine aims anything: what the putt is going to do. Written as general best practice and labelled that way throughout, because nothing in your record measures your green reading — no fault, no film, no number. It earns a plan anyway for one reason: SPEED PICKS THE LINE, and pace is your one open putting fault. Read and pace are not two subjects; they are the same one approached from different ends.
rules: FIRST THREE MINUTES of every round: two long putts, call the finish OUT LOUD
Read from BEHIND the ball, and from the LOW side
FEET FIRST — they feel slope your eyes talk you out of
SPEED PICKS THE LINE — choose the pace, and the line follows from it
Miss on the PRO SIDE. The high side keeps the hole in play as the ball dies
Inside six feet: find the FALL LINE and most short putts get simpler
This is BEST PRACTICE, not a diagnosis — nothing here has been measured on you

sections.t: THE FIRST THREE MINUTES — buy the day's speed
sections.k: Green speed changes every round and everything else is downstream of it, so calibrate before the first tee rather than on the fourth green.
sections.b:
Two long putts on the practice green, looking at the HOLE rather than the ball, and call out where each one will finish before it stops. Then a third if the first two were wrong.

WHY THIS AND NOT TEN MINUTES OF FIVE-FOOTERS. You are not there to groove a stroke — the stroke is settled and lives in its own plans. You are there to buy one number: how far this golf course's greens run today. Everything on this page depends on it, because the amount a putt breaks is a function of how fast it is travelling when it gets there.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE FOR YOU THAN FOR MOST. Pace is your one open putting fault — the ladder logs green speed as one of its three numbers precisely because it is a variable, not a constant. Arriving without it means the first few greens are spent guessing, and the first few greens are where a round's three-putts cluster.

HONEST NOTE: your pace work is calibrated against an estimated 8–9 stimp. That estimate has never been checked against a measured green.

sections.t: WHERE TO STAND — behind, and low
sections.k: Read from behind the ball for the line and from the low side for the amount, because slope reads bigger from below than above.
sections.b:
BEHIND THE BALL, crouched, is where the line lives: you see the whole path from where the ball is to where it is going, which is the only view that shows the putt as the ball will experience it.

THE LOW SIDE is where the AMOUNT lives. Standing below the hole, the slope presents itself against the horizon and reads honestly; standing above it, the same slope flattens out and gets under-read. That is why the standard advice is to walk to the low side of the putt rather than reading from wherever you happen to be standing — and the cost is about ten seconds.

WHAT NOT TO DO: read from four places. More views do not average out into a better answer, they produce a committee. Behind, then low, then go — and the routine takes it from there.

GENERAL BEST PRACTICE. This is standard instruction, not something derived from your film.

sections.t: FEET FIRST — the sense your eyes argue with
sections.k: Your feet register slope your eyes miss, especially the subtle tilts that decide a putt inside fifteen feet.
sections.b:
Standing mid-putt, roughly halfway between ball and hole, your feet tell you which way the ground falls before your eyes have finished arguing about it. On a green with no obvious feature, that is often the only honest input available.

WHY THE EYES ARE THE UNRELIABLE ONE. Greens are built inside a landscape, and the landscape lies: a green that sits on a hillside reads flat because everything around it slopes the same way, and a green ringed by mounding reads tilted when it is not. Your inner ear and the pressure under your feet are not fooled by scenery.

WHERE THIS PAYS. The subtle putt — the eight-footer that looks dead straight. Those are the ones that get missed on the low side all day, because 'looks straight' is exactly what a small tilt looks like.

GENERAL BEST PRACTICE, and there is a drill for it on the bench in Coach rather than here.

sections.t: GRAIN — the read under the read
sections.k: On grainy surfaces the grass direction can outweigh the slope on short putts, and it shows up as a putt that will not hold its line.
sections.b:
Grain is which way the grass lies, and it is a real force on the ball: down-grain putts run out, into-grain putts brake, and cross-grain putts drift on top of whatever the slope is already doing.

HOW TO SEE IT. Shiny, silvery grass ahead of you is down-grain and fast. Dull, darker grass is into-grain and slow. Grain tends to grow toward water and toward the setting sun, and it grabs hardest around the hole, where you can often see one side of the cup edge looking ragged and the other clean — the ragged side is where the grain is growing over.

WHERE IT DOES AND DOESN'T MATTER. It is a large effect on warm-season grasses (bermuda) and a small one on the bent and poa greens you play most of the time in the Northeast, where slope dominates. So this is a section to remember when you travel — Florida, and the Bonita Bay and Old Corkscrew type of course on your list — rather than a daily input.

GENERAL BEST PRACTICE.

sections.t: SPEED PICKS THE LINE — the one that connects to your open fault
sections.k: A putt has a different line at every speed, so deciding the pace first is what makes the read a single answer instead of a range of them.
sections.b:
The same putt breaks a lot when it dies at the hole and very little when it is rammed. So 'how much does this break' has NO answer until you have decided how hard you are hitting it. Read the break first and you are guessing at both variables at once.

THE ORDER, THEREFORE: choose the pace, then read the break that pace produces, then aim. Your routine already puts the pace look LAST for exactly this reason — the final rehearsal beside the ball is a pace rehearsal, and it is the one you walk into the putt with.

WHY THIS IS THE SECTION THAT EARNS THE PLAN. Pace is your one open putting fault, and every mis-read that comes from indecision about speed gets recorded as a bad line. If a putt keeps missing low, the honest first question is not 'did I under-read it' but 'did I hit it softer than I read it'.

WHAT THE PACE SHOULD BE. Past six feet, the Lag Putts plan owns it and the target is a six-foot circle. Inside six feet, the Short Putts plan owns it and the target is seventeen inches past. This plan does not set a pace of its own — it just insists you pick one before you read.

sections.t: THE PRO SIDE — where to miss
sections.k: Amateurs miss the vast majority of breaking putts on the low side, where the ball is dying away from the hole rather than toward it.
sections.b:
A ball above the hole is still falling toward it as it slows, so it keeps a chance of dropping right up to the last roll. A ball below the hole is falling away, and it was never going in from the moment it started curving.

THE PRACTICAL VERSION: whatever break you see, play a touch more of it. The error you are correcting is not random — under-reading is the standard human bias, and it is why 'amateur side' and 'low side' mean the same thing.

AND THE INTERACTION WITH SPEED, which is the whole reason this section sits after that one: playing more break only works with dying pace. More break plus a firm stroke is just a miss on the high side. Pick the pace, then give the read the benefit of the doubt on the high side of it.

GENERAL BEST PRACTICE — this one has decades of tour-stat support behind it, but none of it is about you specifically.

sections.t: INSIDE SIX FEET — find the fall line and stop reading
sections.k: Short putts get simpler when you locate straight-uphill and straight-downhill first, because every other short putt is a small fraction of that.
sections.b:
The FALL LINE is the direction water would run off the hole — straight downhill one way, straight uphill the other. Find it and you have found the two putts on that hole with no break at all, and you now know that a putt from anywhere near those two lines has almost none either.

WHY THIS BELONGS IN A READING PLAN AND NOT IN SHORT PUTTS. It is a READ, not a stroke. The Short Putts plan owns what you do with the putter inside six feet — the short stroke, the pace, the scoreboard. What the putt is going to do before you make that stroke is this page.

AND THE DISCIPLINE THAT MATTERS MOST HERE: inside six feet, once you have the fall line, STOP READING. Your miss inside six feet is an aim problem, currently being measured with the laser, and a long read over a short putt is the ideal environment for talking yourself off your aim. Read it once, set the face, go.

GENERAL BEST PRACTICE, with one piece that is yours: the 'stop reading' instruction exists because of your own documented short-putt history, not because it is standard advice.

sections.t: WHERE THIS SITS — the plan boundaries
sections.k: Reading ends the moment you set the face; from there the Routine plan takes over and nothing on this page speaks again.
sections.b:
THE ORDER, end to end. Read it (this plan) → set the face barely open and build the stance to it (Routine) → the stroke itself, short or long (Short Putts / Lag Putts) → and everything about how you stand and hold it (Grip & Posture).

WHAT THIS PLAN DELIBERATELY DOES NOT DO. It does not set a pace — the two stroke plans do. It does not touch aim: your aim is a settled feel with a measurement pending, and a read that keeps second-guessing the face is how that gets undone.

If you find yourself re-reading while standing over the ball, the read failed and the answer is to step off and start the routine again, not to fix it from there.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: Almost all of this is standard instruction rather than anything measured about you, and the plan says so on every section.
sections.b:
WHAT IS MEASURED ABOUT YOU: nothing on this page. There is no filmed read, no logged mis-read, and no fault in the diagnosis card about green reading. Your putting record measures stroke, aim and pace — not what you decided before any of them.

WHY IT EXISTS ANYWAY. Two reasons, and neither is 'it completes the set'. First, the Routine plan opens with 'read it from behind' and then handed off to nothing, so the first step of your own routine was the only one without a page. Second, speed picks the line, which makes reading the front half of the pace problem that IS your open fault.

GENERAL BEST PRACTICE SOURCES: standard green-reading instruction — low-side reading, feet-first slope sensing, grain identification by sheen and by the cup edge, the amateur-side miss bias, and fall-line location for short putts. The Green Reading shelf in Coach carries the drills for all of it; the drills are deliberately not repeated here.

WHAT WOULD MAKE THIS PLAN YOURS: logging which side your missed putts finish on. If they cluster low, the read is under-done. If they cluster left inside six feet, that is aim and it belongs to the laser audit, not to this page.

ONE UNMEASURED NUMBER carried from elsewhere: the 8–9 stimp your pace work is calibrated against is an estimate and has never been checked.

briefing.focus: The routine as you run it now: read it from behind, rehearse beside the ball with the pace look last, aim the FACE barely open and build the stance to it, trail-thumb press, and go — same beat count every putt. How you stand and what is in your hands is the GRIP & POSTURE plan; the short ones and the lags each have their own.
rules: READ IT FIRST — pace before break. The how lives in the Reading plan
Aim the FACE first, then build the stance to it
Set the face BARELY OPEN — that's your square
Rehearse BESIDE the ball — ball-look first, HOLE-look last, always
TRIGGER = a light TRAIL-THUMB press, then go — it ENDS before the stroke does
Same BEAT COUNT every putt — a routine that varies in length is a pace variable
POP on the short ones, full length on the lags — each has its own plan
Setup and grip live in GRIP & POSTURE — get low, ball inside the lead heel, shaft vertical
steps: Read it from BEHIND the ball — pick the line and a spot a few inches ahead of it
Step BESIDE the ball — BEND OVER, stand close, full putting posture
Rehearsal 1 — eyes on the BALL. Path and contact.
Rehearsal 2 — eyes on the HOLE. Pace. This one goes last, always.
Step in — set the FACE to the spot, BARELY OPEN, then build the stance around it (trail foot a touch BACK)
Spot → ball → go. The stroke starts as a motion — quiet hands.

sections.t: THE READ — its own plan now
sections.k: What the putt is going to do, before you aim anything at it, moved to the Reading the Green plan.
sections.b:
Step one of this routine is still read it from behind — but the HOW moved out on Aug 14, the same way grip and the short stroke did.

The short version, so you are not left with nothing: behind the ball for the line, the low side for the amount, feet first on a green that looks flat, and pick the PACE before you read the break, because a putt has a different line at every speed. Past six feet the pace target is the Lag Putts circle; inside six it is seventeen inches past.

Everything else — grain, the pro side, the fall line, and the three minutes on the practice green that buy you the day's speed — is in Reading the Green.

sections.t: THE FACE — barely open is your square
sections.k: Set what reads to you as barely open — that is square. Verify at a real target once; re-check monthly.
sections.b:
On this putter the face points where you set it — zero-torque means it doesn't twist through the stroke, so address IS impact. What reads to your eye as barely open is, on the actual line, square. Trust it and set it the same way every putt.

Two standing guards. DON'T STACK FIXES: keep this feel, or retrain the aim picture with a mirror or a laser — never both, or the correction gets applied twice and the miss flips right. That guard got sharper on Aug 13, because a laser is a Lane B instrument by nature: watch a green line on the carpet long enough and your eye recalibrates whether you asked it to or not. Use it to MEASURE and look at the number afterwards. PUT A NUMBER ON IT: the laser does this properly now — at six feet, 1.26 inches of offset is one degree, so ten balls filmed against a marked scale turns barely open into an average you can re-check monthly. An unquantified feel drifts toward the exaggeration.

One check still owed, and it's the last one: five putts at a coin on a real green, nothing drawn on the ground, filmed from behind the ball. If the misses still fall on both sides, this closes for good. The indoor half of it can now be done any evening — the PUTTLAZR (Aug 13) reads the aim directly once it is calibrated to the FACE rather than the shaft, and the whole protocol is in Coach → At-Home Putting. Aim by feel, never at the beam.

Run the TWO-DROP TEST in the same session, since you are already in posture: drop a ball from your nose, then drop one from directly under your right eye, and measure the gap between the two marks. You are same-side dominant — right hand, right eye — and that predicts a LEFT aim bias, which is your miss exactly. The gap says whether that is live for you at all, measured bent over rather than standing up, which is the only version that counts. It is a reading, NOT a second correction: barely-open already cancels whatever aims you left, and stacking a fix on top misses right. Full write-up is in the Workshop Log.

sections.t: GRIP & POSTURE — its own plan now
sections.k: How you stand, what is in your hands, ball position, the shaft and the low point all moved to one plan.
sections.b:
Everything that is true BEFORE the putter moves now lives in GRIP & POSTURE — THE SETUP: get low and why the bend matters, the conventional grip and light pressure, ball one to two widths inside the lead heel, hands over the head of the putter, the vertical shaft at both ends, the trail foot back, lead-side pressure and the low point, and the trail hand's job on lags.

What stayed here is the ROUTINE: the read, the rehearsals, the aim, the trigger and the beat count. Those are the things you do in an order, every putt, and they are what this plan is for.

sections.t: SHORT PUTTS — they have their own plan now
sections.k: Everything inside about six feet — the claw, the pop stroke, the speed target and the scoreboard — lives in the Short Putts plan.
sections.b:
This plan is the stroke and the routine you run on every putt. The short ones have enough of their own content — a different grip, a different stroke shape and a different speed target — that they now have their own plan: SHORT PUTTS — THE POP STROKE.

What moved there: the pop stroke (short back, short through), the claw as a reserve grip, the 17-inch speed target, the loft trap that comes with rapping a ball on this face, and the 20-ball five-footer that settles whether any of it is better.

What stayed here, because it is true on every putt regardless of length: get low, ball position, the vertical shaft, barely open, trail foot back, the trigger, and the rehearsals.

sections.t: THE TRIGGER — the trail thumb press
sections.k: Your live trigger is a light trail-thumb press; it must end before the stroke does, and the full shelf of alternatives is in the Workshop Log.
sections.b:
LIVE, your call, Aug 13: a light downward press of the TRAIL THUMB on the grip, then go. It fits because it is a change in PRESSURE, not a change in POSITION — every other rule here exists to hold the shaft vertical and what little loft this face has intact, and a thumb that presses without moving the handle leaves both alone.

THREE GUARDS. IT ENDS — a start signal, not a stroke input; pressure that carries through the ball is the trail hand steering, which the section above rules out. IT STAYS LIGHT — press, release to stroke pressure, go; a trigger that resets you to a firm grip has cost more than it bought on this head. IT PRESSES DOWN THE SHAFT, NOT ACROSS IT — pressure along the putter's plane leaves the face stable, pressure arriving at an angle tends to rotate it. On the conventional grip your thumb is on top, so 'down' is along the shaft.

CHECK IT ON THE CLAW. There the trail hand is turned and the thumb is no longer on top, so 'press down' can quietly become 'press across' — and the claw is on the SHORT putts, which is where a freeze shows up under pressure. If it is not on top, run a sensory trigger on the short ones instead. One face-on clip settles it: shaft angle at address against the frame before the takeaway.

FORWARD PRESS stays out permanently. It delofts a face with little to give, and a delofted putt skids before it rolls and finishes short. (The 2° this project quotes is an estimate — L.A.B. publishes no loft for this head — so the mechanism is solid but the margin is not measured.)

FOUR RULES for whichever trigger you run. ONE trigger, never two. SAME SLOT every putt — it is the last thing before the stroke. IT MUST SHORTEN THE DWELL — count the seconds you stand still over the ball; if a trigger hasn't shortened it, it isn't working, whatever it feels like. AND IF YOU FREEZE ANYWAY, STEP OFF — no trigger rescues a freeze you are already inside; walk back behind the ball and restart. Eight seconds, always cheaper than the putt.

The full shelf of alternatives — kinetic and sensory, and what each one costs — is in the Putting Workshop Log under Aug 13, along with everything that was checked to get here.

sections.t: THE REHEARSALS — beside the ball, pace last
sections.k: Rehearse in real posture beside the ball; ball-look first, hole-look second; same beat count every putt.
sections.b:
Read from BEHIND the ball — line, and a spot a few inches ahead of it. Then rehearse BESIDE the ball in full putting posture: same bend, same arm hang. Magnitude transfers one-to-one from that posture; behind-the-ball rehearsals read break better but run upright, so the size they teach is an approximation — and size is the thing you're training.

Order is fixed. Rehearsal 1, eyes on the BALL: path and contact. Rehearsal 2, eyes on the HOLE: pace. The last thing you feel is what you carry in, so the pace stroke goes last, always.

Same BEAT COUNT every putt — a routine that varies in length is itself a pace variable, and the putts that get an extra look are the ones that come up short. Backstop worth testing: say the pace intention out loud before stepping in ('die it a foot past', 'back of the cup'). Feel decays; a word doesn't.

Past 25 feet, test eyes ON THE HOLE through the stroke — as a block test on the practice green, not mid-round.

sections.t: THE STANDING WORK — where it lives
sections.k: Ten balls from thirty feet twice a week, and the whole protocol is in the Lag Putts plan.
sections.b:
Twice a week on the LINK, gamer ball only: 10 balls from 30 feet, logging SHORTS, SPREAD and GREEN SPEED, plus the 20/30/40 backstroke map. That is the standing work, and it belongs to pace rather than to the routine.

The full protocol, the targets and the tape test all live in the LAG PUTTS plan. The short-putt scoreboard — the 20-ball five-footer — lives in SHORT PUTTS.

sections.t: Feel versus real — how this plan is written
sections.k: Your words set the intent; the film sets the positions. Where they disagree, the film wins.
sections.b: Standing rule, in your words: the film study is king. What you're DOING — grips, triggers, decisions — is yours and authoritative. Where a POSITION or a SENSATION is claimed, the measurement outranks the description, and where there's no measurement the plan says so instead of repeating the feel as if it were established.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: History, condensed. Nothing here changes what you do above.
sections.b:
Aug 10: the press came out (your call — the 2° loft budget has nothing to spare, and a varying press is a varying pace). The DF3i was returned for distance control; its Press Pistol 2° went with it, and every 'hands even / hands ahead' cue died with that grip. The claw reopened for shorts — the old 'claw shelved' verdict came from a different putter, a different grip and a live left miss, so it doesn't bind. 'Hands over the ball' was corrected to 'hands over the HEAD of the putter' — the corrected version matches the Jul 30 stills exactly (vertical shaft = hands ~1.35" behind the ball centre), the first time a feel and a measurement have landed on each other in this project.

Aug 10 pm film: three putts on a lined mat went 0.8° right / 1.0° left / 0.6° right — the one-way LEFT pull from Jul 30 (1.5°, 1.7°) did not reproduce. Start line downgraded; the residual dispersion points at strike, not aim; the old 0.5° gate is retired as too strict for the player and the method.

Jul 30 film, still standing: SBST path confirmed across four putters; tempo 2.0:1; early lift closed; stance line closed (toes never open); vertical shaft repeatable to 0.3°. Pace remains the open fault — it decided the fate of two putters without ever being measured, which is why the ladder is the standing work.

Aug 13 — two workshops, both written up in full in the PUTTING WORKSHOP LOG rather than here. THE TRAIL HAND: the L.A.B. framing checked out, 'let the head release' did not and was cut, and the lead-hand half was scoped to the lags because the claw inverts it. THE TRIGGER: the trail thumb press is yours by decision, and the old 'NO PRESS' rule was renamed NO FORWARD PRESS to kill the collision. Neither has been filmed — that the thumb press leaves the shaft alone is reasoning from where your thumb sits, not a measurement.

Aug 13, later: the setup and grip sections moved out to GRIP & POSTURE and the claw section moved to SHORT PUTTS, leaving this plan as the routine alone. Also Aug 13 — the claw came out of play by your call; conventional on every length now, with the claw held as the reserve.

briefing.focus:
Your own swing thoughts and setup keys, club by club, in your words — the go-to reference before a round or a range session. Grip settled: conventional. Everything about putting lives in the Putting lab, so there is one source for it rather than two.

Renamed from ‘Golf Mind’ on Aug 14 2026: the page has always been driver / 5-wood / irons / wedges, and the old title read as the mental game, which now has a lab of its own.

sections.t: Driver — the big stick
sections.b: Aim the CENTER of the fairway — the start line tends to pull left, so center-aim leaves room. The straight ball comes from a LONGER, fuller swing — commit to that one. A tighter, shorter swing turns it into a cut, and when that goes wrong the miss is a PUSH-SLICE. So: full swing for straight; if you shorten it, expect the cut and know the push-slice is the bad one.
sections.k: Aim centre — your start line pulls left, and the straight ball needs a LONGER swing, not a tighter one.

sections.t: The fairway finder — 5-wood
sections.b:
The mini driver came OUT of the bag on Aug 12 and the Cobra Darkspeed X 5-wood (16.5°, bumped down from stock) took its slot as the fairway finder. Same job as before: a club you can put in play when the driver is the wrong risk.

One honest gap — its CARRY is unmeasured. It has been out of the bag a year, and there is no number for it on the ladder. Leave that blank until you hit some; a guessed number on a calibrated ladder reads exactly like a measured one, and that is how you end up short of a green with the right club in your hands.

And an open question worth knowing you have: at 16.5° it sits about half a degree off the 2-iron utility, so whether both belong in the bag is genuinely unsettled.

(The mini driver was kept, not sold — teed LOW with the weights back for the piercing ball, if it ever comes back.)
sections.k: The Cobra Darkspeed X 16.5° took this slot on Aug 12; its carry is unmeasured, so don't guess a number.

sections.t: Irons
sections.b:
Ball position right of center, toward the trail (right) thigh. The new KING TECs fly HIGHER and longer than the old set — trust the extra height. When you need to flight it down or take something off, CHOKE DOWN and hit the control shot rather than just swinging soft.

WHICH iron is a different question from how to hit one, and it moved to its own plan on Aug 14: APPROACH PLAY — CLUB UP. Short version — club for the MIDDLE of the green, and lean to the longer club, because 7 of your 12 recorded green misses finished short.
sections.k: Ball back toward the trail thigh; the KING TECs fly higher than the old set, so trust the height.

sections.t: Wedges
sections.b: (Open — fill in as you dial the Vokeys: your go-to feels for full vs. partial, and any open-face/flop keys. Ladder to stay honest: 60°→80 · 56°→95 · 50°→108 · PW→122.)
sections.k: Open — fill in your Vokey feels as you dial them. Ladder: 60°→80 · 56°→95 · 50°→108 · PW→122.

sections.t: Putting — it lives in the Putting lab
sections.b:
This section used to carry a putting key, and it went stale the moment the putter changed — it still said 'hands EVEN with the ball, press stays tiny', which was the DF3i's Press Pistol 2° geometry. The DF3i went back on Aug 10, and on the LINK's Pistol 0 that same cue is lean YOU are adding to a face with 2° to give.

That is the argument for not keeping it here at all. Two plans describing one stroke is exactly how a retired cue survives a putter change, and this one did for three days.

So: putting lives in the PUTTING LAB. The Routine plan is the whole stroke, the Setup plan is the low point and the weight, and the Distance Grind is the pace work. Nothing about putting gets written here again.
sections.k: Deliberately empty: two places describing one stroke is how a retired cue survives.

rules: Driver: aim centre, swing LONGER not tighter
5-wood: the fairway finder now — the mini driver came out Aug 12
Irons: trust the extra height, choke down to flight it

entries.text: APPROACH — CLUB UP. Sterling Farms is the first round with a miss direction on every green, and it is not ambiguous: 12 greens missed, SEVEN of them short (1, 2, 6, 8, 10, 12, 17), against two left, one right, one long. That is the same pattern the GHIN archive shows (short 44 against long 0), now confirmed hole by hole, and it is the biggest tee-to-green lever you have — short is where the bunkers and the false fronts live, and a short miss is the one miss that can never end up close. TWO FIXES, both free. (1) Club to cover the BACK of the green, not the pin: take the number to the flag, add the yardage from flag to back edge, and pick the club that carries the middle of that window. (2) Stop clubbing off your best strike — your ladder numbers (PW 122 · 50° 108 · 56° 95 · 60° 80) are carries, and a 60% strike from the rough is 8–10 short of them. THE CHECK, next round: log the miss direction on every green again. If short drops under half the misses, this is working. (Aug 14: this now has a plan of its own — APPROACH PLAY — CLUB UP in the Swing lab, which carries the numbers, the ladder suspicion and the par-3 test.)

LOG THE APPROACH CLUB. 63 holes logged and not one recorded approach club, which means the INTO THE GREEN · BY CLUB table in Scores has never had anything to show. It is one chip on every par 4 and par 5 in the live logger. This is the cheapest data left in the app and it is the difference between 'you miss short' and 'you miss short with the 8-iron and below' — those have different fixes, and right now nothing can tell them apart. Ten recorded approaches turns the table on; two rounds gets you there.

briefing.focus: Every full-swing and scoring question worked through end to end, one per section, newest first. This is the reference shelf — what you actually do lives in Swing Focus, Swing Positions, the Pre-Shot routine and Miracle 201.
rules: One section per workshop, NEWEST FIRST — tap to open
Every section says WHAT CHANGED in the swing plans as a result
This is a REFERENCE. What you actually do lives in Swing Focus and the Pre-Shot routine

sections.t: Aug 14 2026 — What each lab is missing, and what was deliberately not built
sections.k: Both labs cover TECHNIQUE thoroughly and neither covered DECIDING — which club, and what the putt will do — so two plans were built and four were rejected for lack of evidence.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. The short-game plan went in on Aug 13. Is there more worth building in the full swing and putting, or is the shelf full?

HOW IT WAS ASSESSED. Not by asking what a golf app usually has, but by listing the SITUATIONS each lab already owns and looking for ones with real evidence behind them and no page.

WHAT WAS ALREADY COVERED. Putting had five plans and a clean situation split: before the putter moves (Grip & Posture), the order you do it in (Routine), inside six feet, past six feet, and the log. Swing had five: the pre-shot order, a body-position reference, the fault fix, club-by-club keys, and the log. Both are thorough on TECHNIQUE — what the body does.

WHAT THEY BOTH MISSED, and it is the same shape in each. Neither lab had a plan for DECIDING. In the swing that is WHICH CLUB goes into a green; in putting it is WHAT THE PUTT IS GOING TO DO before you aim at it. Both are decisions made before a technique plan becomes relevant, and both had evidence sitting unused.

BUILT #1 — APPROACH PLAY, and the evidence is the strongest in the app. 7 of 12 recorded green misses finished SHORT, there is an open action about it, and there was no plan owning it — the Irons section of Swing Thoughts is about how to hit one, not which to pull. Writing it surfaced two things worth more than the plan. The carry ladder is flagged ESTIMATED and never has been calibrated, which is a systematic error that would produce exactly a systematic short miss. And the approach-club column has NEVER been filled in on any of 63 logged holes, so the app's own INTO THE GREEN table has never had data — which is why 'you miss short' cannot yet be narrowed to a club. New action for it.

BUILT #2 — READING THE GREEN, on weaker evidence, and it says so on every section. Nothing measures Jack's reading. It earns the page on two structural grounds instead: the Routine plan's first step is 'read it from behind' and handed off to NOTHING, and speed picks the line — which makes reading the front half of the pace problem that is the one open putting fault.

WHAT WAS REJECTED, which matters as much. A TROUBLE / RECOVERY plan — the lesson exists in Coach and there is no measured recovery problem, so it would be a page of generic advice. A WIND AND UNEVEN LIES plan — same, with no data at all. A TEE-SHOT STRATEGY plan — genuinely tempting, but it is already split between Swing Thoughts, the round-prep briefings that carry per-hole tee calls, and the Off-the-tee-by-club table, and a fourth home would create the exact duplication this project keeps having to undo. A separate WARM-UP plan — the evidence is real (two Wianno openers went hard left, and the Locked In plan already reads that as a warm-up problem rather than a resilience one) but it is ALREADY in two places: the Swing Routine's warm-up primer and Locked In's opening-hole section. A third would be worse than either. That one is flagged for Jack rather than built, because consolidating it means deciding which existing plan loses a section.

THE RULE THAT CAME OUT OF IT. A new plan needs a SITUATION and EVIDENCE. A situation with no evidence is a page of best practice, which is worth writing only where nothing else covers it and the plan admits what it is — the short-game plan and now the reading plan are both that, explicitly. A gap with neither is not a gap.

NOT MEASURED. The approach plan's central mechanism — that self-estimated carries skew long — is reasoning that fits the data, not a finding. It costs one range session to test and nothing in the app can settle it without one.

SOURCES. Greens-in-regulation benchmarks by handicap (roughly 46% at a 5-handicap, 37% at a 10) from published handicap-stat summaries — TheGrint, Golf.com, Golf Monthly. Used only to establish that the 33% RATE is unremarkable and the miss DIRECTION is the signal. Everything else came off Jack's own cards.

sections.t: Jul 28–29 2026 — The scoring record: the member-guest and three years of GHIN
sections.k: Two independent data sets reach one conclusion — par 5s and doubles are the entire gap, and 2024 already proves the better number is in you.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. Two analyses a day apart, and they were kept as separate plans until Aug 13 even though they answer the same thing: where do the strokes actually go?

THE MEMBER-GUEST (Wianno Club, Osterville MA, Jul 9-11 2026 — five 9-hole matches with your brother, Blue tees, par 35). 45 holes, 212 strokes, +37, every total reconciled against the hole-by-hole and the bogey/double markings. The mix: 1 birdie, 16 pars, 18 bogeys, 10 DOUBLES. The doubles are more than a quarter of the damage, and the cleanest illustration is the same golfer two days apart — 41 with no doubles against 46 with four. Three more findings. You never parred an opening hole all week: +7 across five of them. Par 3s bled +11 with no driver involved, so that is iron control rather than a driving miss. Holes 1 and 3 alone accounted for +10 of the +37, from six of the forty-five holes played. And eight par-5 plays produced zero birdies.

THREE YEARS OF GHIN (44 posted scores, 38 rounds of hole-by-hole detail). Scoring average went 85.2 → 83.6 → 86.7. The one metric that has worsened every single year without exception is the par-5 average: 5.46 → 5.72 → 5.88. That is the same finding the member-guest produced independently a day earlier — two sources, different data, one conclusion.

WHAT ELSE THE THREE YEARS SAY. 2025 gave back everything 2024 gained, with nine points of pars converting almost one-for-one into bogeys. The spread narrowed from 21 shots to seven — the bad days improved, but the good days vanished with them. 2024 was not a fluke: 39% pars and a 4.65 par-4 average is genuinely good golf you have already played, which makes 83.6 a number to return to rather than aspire to. And par 3s improved and stayed improved, so 2025 was not a general ball-striking collapse.

THE ONE JOB. Don't fix all of it. Par 5s have the most evidence, the clearest mechanism and a free fix: take the LADDER NUMBER on the lay-up instead of the hopeful one.

READ THE SAMPLES HONESTLY. Nine scores in 2024 against 23 in 2023 — small samples move, and none of it adjusts for course or tees. The member-guest cards were MATCHES, so some scores are most-likely-score postings: the trend holds, but the doubles are softer than they look.

WHAT CHANGED, AND WHAT SINCE SUPERSEDED IT. The opening-hole finding is what the warm-up primer in the Swing Routine plan is for. The member-guest's match-play side has since been overtaken entirely — all five matches now carry results and margins on the rounds themselves, and the reframe (two of the three rounds flagged for closing lost SHORT PUTTS rather than strokes) lives in the Mental tab's Locked In plan. One loose end kept from the original debrief: GHIN had your index at 11.1 while the app still said 8.5.

sections.t: How this log works
sections.k: Anything worked through end to end lands here as one section, so the doing-plans stay short.
sections.b:
When a question gets worked through properly — research, a claim checked, a decision reached — it lands here as ONE section rather than being spread through the plans that tell you what to do.

That keeps the split clean. Swing Focus, Swing Positions, the Pre-Shot routine, Miracle 201 and Golf Mind say what you do NOW. This log says how those instructions were arrived at and what was rejected on the way.

Each section carries the same skeleton: the question, what checked out, what did not, what changed in the other plans, what remains unmeasured, and the sources. The unmeasured line is not optional — a workshop that cannot say what it still does not know is a sales pitch.

briefing.focus: Every putting question worked through end to end, one per section, newest first. This is the reference shelf, not the routine — nothing here tells you what to do on a putt. Tap a section to open it; each one says what was asked, what checked out, what did not, what changed in the other plans, and what is still unmeasured.
rules: One section per workshop, NEWEST FIRST — tap to open, they stay shut otherwise
Every section says WHAT CHANGED in the other plans, so nothing here is orphaned
Sourced claims and reasoned ones are labelled differently — on purpose
This is a REFERENCE. What you actually do lives in the Routine plan

sections.t: Aug 14 2026 — Why reading got a plan when nothing measures it
sections.k: The routine's first step handed off to nothing, and reading is the front half of the pace problem — two structural reasons, and no measured one.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. The putting lab already had five plans in a clean situation split. Was green reading a real gap or just a missing chapter?

WHAT ARGUED AGAINST IT. Nothing in the record measures Jack's reading. No fault, no film, no logged mis-read. By the standard this project usually applies, that is thin ground for a page — and a plan built to complete a set is exactly the kind of padding the round-prep rules warn about.

WHAT DECIDED IT, and neither reason is 'greens get read'. First, the Routine plan opens with READ IT FROM BEHIND and then handed off to nothing at all — the first step of his own routine was the only one without a page behind it, while grip, the short stroke and the long stroke had all been split out. Second, SPEED PICKS THE LINE: a putt has a different line at every pace, so the read cannot be settled before the pace is chosen. That makes reading the front half of the pace problem, and pace is the one open putting fault on the card.

HOW IT IS WRITTEN AS A RESULT. Labelled general best practice on every section, with the one exception called out — 'inside six feet, stop reading once you have the fall line' exists because of his documented short-putt history, not because it is standard advice. It deliberately sets NO pace of its own; the two stroke plans own that, and a third source for pace is how a retired cue survives.

WHAT WOULD MAKE IT HIS. Logging which SIDE missed putts finish on. Clustering low means the read is under-done. Clustering left inside six feet is aim, and that belongs to the laser audit rather than to this page.

NOT MEASURED: everything on that plan, plus the 8–9 stimp its speed talk is calibrated against, which remains an estimate. Full cross-lab reasoning — including the four plans that were rejected — is in the SWING workshop log, since the review covered both labs at once.

sections.t: Aug 14 2026 — The laser: what it can measure, and the trap that came in the box
sections.k: It can finally put a number on ‘barely open’ — but only as a measuring device, only after it is calibrated to the face, and only if you never look at the beam.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. Jack bought a PUTTLAZR green-line indoor putting trainer (Aug 13). What can it actually settle, and what should it be kept away from?

WHAT IT IS. A laser module that clamps to the putter shaft with a 360° adjustable head and throws a green line forward; the kit also carries a small tripod stand so the beam can be used as a fixed reference instead of a club-mounted one. NOTE ON SOURCING: the product's own listing was unreachable from here (blocked at the network), so these specs come from retailer and review pages for the same device plus the box in his hands — anything the user guide contradicts, the user guide wins.

WHAT IT CAN GENUINELY SETTLE, and it is the biggest open question in the project. Aug 10 reclassified the left miss from a delivery error to an AIM error: a zero-torque head does not twist through the stroke, so 1.5–1.7° left at impact on Jul 30 was almost certainly 1.5–1.7° left at ADDRESS. ‘Barely open’ is the fix, it was found on the course, and it has never had a number on it — which the plans have flagged as a drift risk since Aug 10. A calibrated beam reads that aim directly. The conversion that makes it a measurement rather than an impression: at six feet, 1.26 INCHES of offset is one degree, so the old bias would land about two inches left of target. That is readable off a phone screen against a taped half-inch scale.

AND IT WORKS ON CARPET, which is the part worth noticing. Carpet cannot measure pace and never will — the open fault stays a practice-green job. But the angle you set the face at does not care what the surface is, so aim is the one thing a living room can measure honestly.

WHAT DIDN'T CHECK OUT — three limits, all worth stating plainly. THE CLAMP IS ON THE SHAFT, NOT THE FACE: out of the box the beam points wherever the clamp sits, and until the two are tied together the number is confident and wrong, which is worse than no number. Calibration is a book corner and three minutes, in real posture, because the beam is fixed in the SHAFT'S frame — calibrate standing up, measure bent over, and you have measured your posture. THE BEAM IS NOT THE START LINE: it reports face aim, and the ball's actual start line is face plus path plus strike, so an off-centre hit still bends a putt the laser called square (that is the tape test's job, and it is still unrun). AND A CLAMP SLIPS — so the calibration is re-checked at the END of a session, and a failed end-check voids the session's numbers rather than half of them.

THE TRAP, and it is the reason this section exists. The plans have carried a two-lane warning since Aug 10: LANE A keeps the barely-open feel and verifies it once; LANE B retrains the aim picture with a mirror or a laser until genuinely square looks square, and drops the barely-open language entirely. Doing both applies the correction twice and flips the miss RIGHT. The device that just arrived is a Lane B instrument by nature — stand over enough putts watching a green line and the eye recalibrates unasked. So the standing rule is that it MEASURES: set up without looking at the beam, let the camera read the floor, look at the number afterwards. If the audit says barely-open aims square, the laser has done its whole job and goes back in the box until the monthly re-check.

WHAT CHANGED. Four new At-Home Putting lessons in Coach — calibration, the ten-ball aim audit, the measure-don't-retrain rule, and the three filming angles with the scale that makes them measurable. The Routine plan's FACE section now names the laser as the instrument for the check it has been owing and for the monthly number, with the Lane A/B guard widened to name it. A new action item says run the audit BEFORE practising with the thing.

NOT MEASURED — all of it, and that is the point. Not one ball has been struck with this device. ‘Barely open’ remains an unquantified feel; the two-drop eye-dominance test is still owed; the overhead five on a real green is still owed; the tape test is still unrun. What changed on Aug 13 is that the instrument exists, not that anything has been established.

SOURCES. Retailer and review pages for the same green-line shaft-clamp trainer (360° adjustable head, green beam for contrast indoors); the geometry is plain trigonometry — 72 inches × tan(1°) = 1.26 in. The Jul 30 impact figures and the Aug 10 reclassification are this project's own record.

sections.t: Aug 13 2026 — The pop stroke, adapted for a zero-torque head
sections.k: The geometry survives and the wrist mechanism does not — which is the whole reason the version in your plan is not the version Casper played.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. You wanted a pop stroke on the short ones: short back, short through. Does it hold up on a Lie Angle Balanced blade, and what has to change?

WHAT THE STROKE ACTUALLY IS. A short backstroke, a firm accelerating rap, and an abbreviated follow-through. Gary Player rapped it with almost no finish. Billy Casper is the canonical version — compact, hands close to the body, the face hooded going back, ball-then-turf contact and a finish that stopped dead, standardly described as tapping a tack with a hammer. Arnold Palmer and Nicklaus are named in the same tradition.

WHAT CHECKED OUT, AND IS GENUINELY IN ITS FAVOUR. The stroke came out of SLOW GREENS — it was developed by players who needed extra pop to reach the hole on surfaces that did not run. Your pace is calibrated at an estimated 8-9 stimp, which is exactly that world, so the historical fit is real. It is also the warning that comes with it: on a fast downhill four-footer a stroke built to add force is the wrong instinct. And the speed target has research behind it rather than folklore — the ring roughly one to six feet around any hole takes all the foot traffic, so it is trodden flat and bumpy (Dave Pelz's 'lumpy donut'), and a ball arriving with no pace wobbles through the worst-conditioned part of the green. Pelz's number is 17 INCHES PAST.

WHAT DIDN'T, and it is the core of the whole thing. THE CLASSIC POP IS A WRIST STROKE. Casper cocked the wrists to hold the face square going back and released them into the ball, and the technique's own history says right-wrist action is what supplied the pop. That mechanism is unavailable to you twice over: your method is quiet hands with the shoulders running the stroke, and the head you play is built on the premise that the face squares ITSELF once the hands stop interfering. A wrist-released pop is the most hand-active stroke in putting, and bolting it onto a zero-torque putter asks the club to undo what you are doing to it. So the plan takes the GEOMETRY and not the MECHANISM — short backstroke, short through-stroke, both run from the shoulders.

THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT, kept rather than buried. A ball dying into the hole can fall in off the edges, so a softer putt has a genuinely bigger effective target and more room for a stroke error. That is real physics. Firm wins on a SHORT putt specifically because inside six feet there is no distance problem to solve — the ball has one job, which is to reach the hole on line before the green can do anything to it. The balance flips as the putt lengthens, which is why the stroke is quarantined inside six feet.

THE TRAP THAT EARNED THE MOST WORDS. Casper's pop hit ball-then-turf: a forward-leaning, descending delivery. Your face carries 2° of effective loft at 0° lean with nothing to spare, so a rap arriving with the shaft leaning forward delofts a face that has no loft to lose and drives the ball into the turf — skid, then roll, then short. The vertical-shaft rule does not relax because the stroke got shorter, and the no-camera check is the scuff in the sound.

WHAT IT FIXES AND WHAT IT DOESN'T. It is a real answer to deceleration and to the freeze, and it connects to the trigger work — a short committed stroke gives the conscious mind less time to intervene, and your failure lives on short putts under pressure. It does NOT touch AIM. The left miss was reclassified Aug 10 as an aim error, the Aug 10 pm mat set came back 0.8° right / 1.0° left / 0.6° right with no bias, and face angle decides about 80% of where a putt starts. Barely open still does the aiming.

TWO CORRECTIONS FROM YOU, same day, both of which changed the plan. The through-stroke is SHORT, not 'at least as long as the backstroke' — your version is the authentic one, so the anti-deceleration guard moved from LENGTH to ACCELERATION, which is the honest version anyway: a finish that accelerated and a finish that quit look identical afterwards, and the roll-out is what separates them. And the CLAW came out of play, held as the safety net. That one had structural consequences, because the claw was the PHYSICAL guard against the trail hand taking over a short hitting stroke; with it gone the guard is discipline, so the tell — the head passing your hands — matters more, and the trip-wire that brings the claw back was set as a number while nothing was going wrong.

WHAT CHANGED. A new plan, SHORT PUTTS — THE POP STROKE, which also took the claw section from the Routine plan. The Distance Grind was retitled LAG PUTTS so the pair reads as a split. A new At-Home Putting lesson in Coach trains the stroke and the 17-inch pace on carpet.

NOT MEASURED — all of it. No pop-stroke rep has been filmed or scored, the 20-ball five-footer has not been run on the LINK, and the face-on clip that would catch the shaft leaning forward is still owed. Until the scoreboard exists, that plan describes an experiment rather than a finding.

SOURCES. Australian Golf Digest on the shorter, firmer stroke; Kermit Zarley on Billy Casper's mechanics; The Recreational Golfer on the pop stroke's slow-green origins; Golf Digest and Golf.com on Pelz's lumpy donut and the 17-inch target, including the soft-putt counter-argument.

SINCE UPDATED, same day: the claw is not a safety net, it is a second short-putt SOLUTION on trial alongside the pop stroke — Jack's correction, and it stands. The plan was retitled Short Putts — Inside Six Feet so it is not named after one of two candidates. The finding above is unchanged; what changed is that grip and stroke shape are now treated as two independent dials with a test order, rather than one adopted stroke plus a contingency.

SINCE UPDATED: the 2° of effective loft quoted above is an ESTIMATE — no retailer and no L.A.B. page publishes a loft for this head. The finding stands (a forward-leaning rap delofts and drives the ball down) but the margin was stated more precisely than the evidence supports, and the language in the plans was softened on Aug 13.

sections.t: Aug 13 2026 — The trigger: what starts the stroke
sections.k: The trail thumb press is live by your decision; it survives because it changes pressure rather than position, and the full shelf of alternatives is here.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. With the forward press out, what starts the stroke? You brought a full taxonomy — kinetic triggers (a small movement starts the chain) and sensory ones (a cue that is not a movement at all) — and decided on the TRAIL THUMB PRESS.

WHY IT SURVIVES. It is a change in PRESSURE, not a change in POSITION. Everything in the Routine plan exists to hold the shaft vertical and the 2° of effective loft intact, and a thumb that presses without moving the handle leaves both alone. That is the promise a forward press cannot make.

WHAT CHECKED OUT. The forward-press objection is real and it is why that one stays out: a forward press delofts the face, and a delofted putt skids before it rolls and finishes short — on a head with 2° to give, with pace as the open fault, that is the last thing to buy. Nicklaus genuinely never grounded his putter, and his own stated reason was that a grounded club let his grip and arms go slack while hovering made the pressure uniform — he also described feeling the head's full weight, which is the same currency as the lag cue. And the physiology behind the exhale trigger is sound: breath-holding and tension arrive together, so a long exhale is the standard way of pulling that back.

THE ONE MECHANISM WORTH CARRYING. Trail-hand pressure directed ALONG the putter's plane leaves the face stable; pressure arriving at an angle tends to rotate it. That is the entire reason the instruction is 'down the shaft' rather than just 'press', and the reason the claw needs checking on its own — in a claw the trail thumb is not on top, so the same press can arrive across the handle instead of down it. The claw is on the short putts, which is exactly where a freeze shows up under pressure, so that is the half genuinely worth filming.

THE SHELF — KINETIC. MICRO-WAGGLE: a tiny back-and-forth of the head, or one small forward-and-back, run from the shoulders with the wrists silent. TOE TAP or HEEL LIFT: the trail foot taps, or a heel lifts and resets — releases a lower-body freeze without touching the arms, the safest kinetic option. HOVER-AND-SET: the head hovers then settles, or stays hovering (see Nicklaus above). GRIP SQUEEZE-AND-RELEASE: brief tighten, then relax to stroke pressure — the same family as your thumb press, one step cruder. TRAIL-KNEE KICK: the trigger your full-swing routine already runs, so the cheapest to learn. LEAD-SHOULDER SETTLE. FORWARD PRESS: ruled out here, and the only honest version builds the lean into address so the angle you set is the angle you deliver.

THE SHELF — SENSORY. No movement at all, so none of these can touch face angle or loft — the safer default if freezing is the real problem. LAST LOOK: eyes go to the hole, the stroke starts the instant they arrive back at the ball; nearly free for you, because your rehearsal order already ends on a look at the hole. EXHALE: the stroke starts on the out-breath — the one to reach for under pressure specifically. COUNT or BEAT: an internal 'one... two' before the putter moves; you already run a fixed beat count, so it is the smallest addition on the shelf.

ADDED TO YOUR LIST, all four about the freeze rather than the trigger: step off and restart if you freeze anyway, since no trigger rescues a freeze you are already inside; the dwell-time test, because the real variable is how long you stand still and a trigger that hasn't shortened it isn't working; one trigger never two; and same slot every putt, since where it sits matters as much as what it is.

WHAT CHANGED. The Routine plan carries the live trigger and its three guards. Its old 'NO PRESS' rule now reads NO FORWARD PRESS in both the Routine plan and the Distance Grind — you now have a press that is allowed, and the collision would have read as a contradiction on the practice green.

NOT MEASURED. Nothing about the thumb press has been filmed. That it leaves the shaft alone is reasoning from where your thumb sits, not a measurement.

SOURCES. MyGolfSpy on the forward press and deloft; Golf Digest (Jim Flick / Jack Nicklaus) on hovering the club; Golf Smart Academy on trail-hand pressure direction and face stability; MyGolfSpy on breathing under pressure.

SINCE UPDATED: the 2° of effective loft quoted above is an ESTIMATE — L.A.B. publishes no loft for this head. The conclusion is unchanged (the forward press stays out, the thumb press changes pressure rather than position); only the precision of the margin was overstated.

sections.t: Aug 13 2026 — The trail hand, and what L.A.B. actually claims
sections.k: Making the right hand the feel hand is a good cue on lags, but 'let the head release' contradicts the putter and was cut.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. Is 'right hand feels the speed, left hand just rides along' a sound cue on a zero-torque head?

WHAT HELD. L.A.B.'s premise is as advertised: the head is balanced to the shaft's lie, so it resists twisting and needs no hand manipulation. Light grip pressure and quiet hands are the manufacturer's own coaching here, not a teaching preference — Sam Hahn's line is that his job was just to LET IT STAY SQUARE, and the company's first drill is putting with your thumbs off the grip. Face angle is also the right thing to protect: over 1301 putts from 4 m by 71 elite players, face angle decided 80% of direction consistency, against 17% for path and 3% for strike (Karlsen, Smith & Nilsson, J Sports Sci 2008).

WHAT DIDN'T, and this is the one that would have changed what you do. 'LET THE HEAD RELEASE' was cut. A release means the face rotating through impact, and this head is built so it does not — the instruction is the opposite of a release. It also contradicted the paragraph it sat in. And your stroke is straight back and straight through, confirmed across four heads, so there is no rotation to time even if you wanted one.

THREE SMALLER CORRECTIONS. 'Square to your arc' is L.A.B.'s own wording and fine generically, but you do not have an arc — on your stroke it is square to the LINE, and arc language is what put a toe-hang blade in the bag in the first place. 'Passive lead hand' was scoped to the LAGS, because the claw inverts the pressure hierarchy: the claw exists to take the trail hand out, moving pressure into the lead hand and leaving the right as a guide, so on short putts there is no feel hand and there should not be. And 'most face-control trouble is anxiety and deceleration' was dropped — an unmeasured teaching claim, and not your diagnosis anyway now the left miss reads as an AIM error and the Aug 10 pm mat set (0.8° right / 1.0° left / 0.6° right) failed to reproduce a pull.

ONE GUARD ADDED. An active trail hand has a quiet way of shoving the handle forward, which breaks the vertical-shaft rule without ever feeling like it did.

WHAT CHANGED. The Routine plan gained the rule 'TRAIL HAND senses the weight on LAGS — it never pushes, and nothing releases' and a section beside the claw section carrying the cue, its scope and its guards.

STILL UNMEASURED. Whether an active trail hand was ever in your stroke to begin with. No film has been asked that question.

SOURCES. Outtabounds on lie angle balance; MyGolfSpy on Sam Hahn's instruction; Karlsen, Smith & Nilsson 2008 (PubMed 17917952); Golf Monthly on the claw grip.

SINCE UPDATED, same day: the claw came out of play by his call, so the scoping conclusion still stands but is currently dormant — conventional on every length, with the claw held as the short-putt reserve. What survives unchanged is the reasoning: whenever the claw IS on, there is no feel hand.

sections.t: Aug 13 2026 — Eye dominance: an explanation, not a second fix
sections.k: Same-side dominance predicts a left aim bias — your exact miss — but the standing measurement doesn't predict the putting one, so nothing changes until the overhead five reports.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. You are right-eye dominant and right-handed — SAME-SIDE dominant, the group taught to aim left. Does that explain the signature miss?

WHY IT FITS. The bias that setup is supposed to produce is LEFT, which is your miss exactly, and it is the only candidate cause that predates every putter you have owned. That makes it a real explanation for why 'barely open' had to become your square.

THE STUDY THAT SAYS SLOW DOWN. The dominance you measured standing up is almost certainly a primary-gaze result, and the only peer-reviewed work here (Dalton, Guillon & Naroo, Optom Vis Sci 2015;92(10):968–75, n=31) found primary-gaze and putting-gaze dominance are neither equal nor predictive of each other, with putting-gaze the weaker. So your PUTTING dominance is unmeasured. Everything else on this topic is teaching claim, not evidence.

THE ONE THING TO ACTUALLY DO — THE TWO-DROP TEST. Add one drop to the overhead five you already owe: drop a ball from the nose, then drop one from directly under the right eye, and measure the gap between the two marks. That gap is whether dominance is live for you at all, measured in the posture that counts rather than standing up.

THE GUARD THAT MATTERS MOST. DON'T STACK IT. The barely-open feel already cancels whatever aims you left. Adding an eye-dominance correction on top applies the fix twice and the miss flips RIGHT. This is an explanation, never a second correction. Getting low and standing close already shrinks it too — eyes over the ball leaves less parallax to have.

WHERE IT RANKS. Hypothesis two behind the LINK adaptation pattern, with head shape third and weakest.

WHAT CHANGED. Nothing about the stroke, the setup or the putter — that was the finding. The two-drop test rides along with the overhead five in the Routine plan's FACE section.

STILL UNMEASURED. Putting-gaze dominance, and the overhead five itself.

sections.t: Jul 30 – Aug 12 2026 — The putter saga, end to end
sections.k: Four head movements in a month, every one decided on an unmeasured round — and the LINK.2.1 is the one that stayed.
sections.b:
THE SEQUENCE. Jul 30: DF3i out, LINK.2.1 in, after a round of short lags and hot short putts. Aug 1: a Beekman scramble where pace felt dialled put the DF3i straight back in and sent the LINK to storage on redundancy. Aug 10: the LINK came back and the DF3i was returned for distance control. Aug 12: you closed the return window by decision and KEPT the LINK for good. Four movements in twelve days.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY DECIDED, AND ON WHAT. Every one of those calls was made on feel, on a single unmeasured round, and not one of them was tested against a calibrated lag session. The Aug 1 reprieve came off a SCRAMBLE — where a teammate has often already shown you the line and the pace — on greens running an estimated 8-9 stimp, the friendliest putting environment that exists. Slow greens flatter you twice: you swing bigger, which forgives an off-centre strike, and you hit firmer, and firm takes the break out. That pattern, not any putter, is the thing the Distance Grind exists to break.

THE LEGAL-MOVE POINT, which still holds. The LINK.2.1 is Lie Angle Balanced — the same zero-torque technology as the DF3i, in a narrow heel-shafted blade. The thing that made the Phantom 7.5 wrong for you, toe flow against a straight-back-straight-through stroke, stayed absent throughout. So the whole saga was a SHAPE argument, not a technology one, and it never reopened the mismatch it started with.

WHAT YOU TRADED. The DF3i was a wide, deep, high-MOI mallet; the LINK is a narrow blade with far less MOI, so an off-centre strike costs more speed and more face angle. You moved to a head that is less tolerant of PACE, which is your one open fault. The counter-argument is real and it is the reason to keep going: a forgiving head HIDES strike quality, a blade reports it. The blade is more punishing and more informative.

THE SETUP CUE THAT MOVES WITH THE HEAD — the one thing in any swap that can cost strokes. The DF3i's Press Pistol 2° leaned the shaft for you, so its cue was 'hands EVEN with the ball, the grip supplies the lean'. The LINK ships a Pistol 0 — zero built-in lean — and Jul 30 film measured exactly what that produces: shaft dead vertical, hands about 1.35" BEHIND the ball, repeatable to 0.3° across 59 frames. That is not a flaw, it is the geometry the putter is built around (69° lie, 2° effective loft, 0° lean). The 'hands even' cue died with the DF3i and must never be carried across — on a Pistol 0 it is lean YOU are adding, on a face with almost nothing to deloft.

WHAT THE NUMBERS SAY, read fairly. AMBIGUOUS, not favourable. The LINK's column holds the only two reds on the evolution grid — face at impact and the 1.5-1.7° left start line, both measured Jul 30, on this head — while the DF3i's first filmed column carries none. But Jul 30 was by far the most-filmed day of the project (three sessions, fourteen clips, the first face-on at 120 fps), so some of that is measurement effort rather than a putter effect, and the DF3i's clean column is partly clean because less was measured in it. In the LINK's favour: tempo 2.0:1 across seven of eight clips against the DF3i's 2.4:1, with 2:1 the target. The only real scoreboard in the entire project is the DF3i's 8/10 from four feet on Jul 20 — and it went back with the mallet.

WHAT THE SAGA PROVED. That the left miss travels. It reappeared while you were holding a zero-torque putter, which is the cleanest evidence available that the head was never the cause — and it is why the miss was eventually reclassified as an AIM error rather than a delivery one. Also that lags finishing short and short putts running hot are not two faults but one: an uncalibrated power curve, where you default to too-small on the big number and too-big on the small one.

WHAT CHANGED. The LINK is the putter, permanently — `returnWindow` is off, the Home return-window card is gone, and Decisions reads DECIDED. The Routine plan carries the Pistol 0 geometry as its hands instruction. The Distance Grind owns the calibration work the whole saga skipped.

STILL UNMEASURED. Strike location, on any of the four putters owned this month — which remains the single candidate that explains both open faults at once, since a heel strike closes the face and bleeds ball speed. The tape-test protocol now lives in the Lag Putts plan.

sections.t: How this log works
sections.k: Anything worked through end to end lands here as one section, so the doing-plans stay short.
sections.b:
The rule going forward: when a question gets worked through properly — research, a claim checked, a decision reached — it lands here as ONE section rather than being spread through the plans that tell you what to do.

That keeps the split clean. The Routine plan, the Setup plan and the Distance Grind say what you do NOW, in as few words as they can. This log says how each of those instructions was arrived at, what was rejected on the way, and where the sources were. When an instruction changes, the reasoning does not have to be re-derived and it does not have to sit in the middle of a plan you read on the practice green.

Each section carries the same skeleton: the question, what checked out, what did not, what changed in the other plans, what remains unmeasured, and the sources. The unmeasured line is not optional — a workshop that cannot say what it still does not know is a sales pitch.

briefing.focus: Every putting question worked through end to end, one per section, newest first. This is the reference shelf, not the routine — nothing here tells you what to do on a putt. Tap a section to open it; each one says what was asked, what checked out, what did not, what changed in the other plans, and what is still unmeasured.
rules: One section per workshop, NEWEST FIRST — tap to open, they stay shut otherwise
Every section says WHAT CHANGED in the other plans, so nothing here is orphaned
Sourced claims and reasoned ones are labelled differently — on purpose
This is a REFERENCE. What you actually do lives in the Routine plan

sections.t: Aug 14 2026 — The pre-LINK film was deleted. Everything it measured is here.
sections.k: Eight putting sessions on three putters you no longer play were cleared out — this section keeps every number they produced, because two of them still underpin decisions you are living with.
sections.b:
WHAT HAPPENED. Jack cleared the film room of every putting session shot on a putter that is not the LINK.2.1 — the Phantom 7.5, the Newport 2 and the DF3i. Eight sessions, Jul 17 through Jul 21. His call and a reasonable one: he plays one putter now and frame-by-frame breakdowns of retired gear are not what the film room is for.

WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS ANYWAY. Two of those sessions are still load-bearing. The conclusions live on in the evolution grid, the faults and the plans, but the EVIDENCE lived only on the rows that were deleted, and a claim whose source has been thrown away quietly becomes folklore. So the numbers are written out here in full.

THE TWO THAT MATTER MOST.

(1) THE SBST CONFIRMATION — the reason you play a zero-torque putter at all. Jul 18, 9 clips overhead + down-the-line: path confirmed STRAIGHT, straight-back-straight-through. Same day, 5 more overhead clips across 3× Phantom 7.5 and 2× Newport 2: path straight on BOTH putters, face square through impact, no visible toe-over, balls starting dead on the centre line. That is the finding the whole equipment case was built on — an arc-balanced head fights a straight stroke — and it was measured on the two arc putters, which is precisely what made it convincing. It has never been re-run on the LINK because it has never needed to be.

(2) 8 OUT OF 10 FROM FOUR FEET — Jul 20, DF3i, conventional grip, 10 balls on the return mat. All 10 start lines clean, no face-flip. The signal was at ARRIVAL: 2 misses and 2 lip-hangs, all four on dying pace, both misses on the pull side. Read at the time as soft-pace drift rather than a stroke fault.
