THE SEQUENCE. Jul 30: DF3i out, LINK.2.1 in, after a round of short lags and hot short putts. Aug 1: a Beekman scramble where pace felt dialled put the DF3i straight back in and sent the LINK to storage on redundancy. Aug 10: the LINK came back and the DF3i was returned for distance control. Aug 12: you closed the return window by decision and KEPT the LINK for good. Four movements in twelve days.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY DECIDED, AND ON WHAT. Every one of those calls was made on feel, on a single unmeasured round, and not one of them was tested against a calibrated lag session. The Aug 1 reprieve came off a SCRAMBLE — where a teammate has often already shown you the line and the pace — on greens running an estimated 8-9 stimp, the friendliest putting environment that exists. Slow greens flatter you twice: you swing bigger, which forgives an off-centre strike, and you hit firmer, and firm takes the break out. That pattern, not any putter, is the thing the Distance Grind exists to break.

THE LEGAL-MOVE POINT, which still holds. The LINK.2.1 is Lie Angle Balanced — the same zero-torque technology as the DF3i, in a narrow heel-shafted blade. The thing that made the Phantom 7.5 wrong for you, toe flow against a straight-back-straight-through stroke, stayed absent throughout. So the whole saga was a SHAPE argument, not a technology one, and it never reopened the mismatch it started with.

WHAT YOU TRADED. The DF3i was a wide, deep, high-MOI mallet; the LINK is a narrow blade with far less MOI, so an off-centre strike costs more speed and more face angle. You moved to a head that is less tolerant of PACE, which is your one open fault. The counter-argument is real and it is the reason to keep going: a forgiving head HIDES strike quality, a blade reports it. The blade is more punishing and more informative.

THE SETUP CUE THAT MOVES WITH THE HEAD — the one thing in any swap that can cost strokes. The DF3i's Press Pistol 2° leaned the shaft for you, so its cue was 'hands EVEN with the ball, the grip supplies the lean'. The LINK ships a Pistol 0 — zero built-in lean — and Jul 30 film measured exactly what that produces: shaft dead vertical, hands about 1.35" BEHIND the ball, repeatable to 0.3° across 59 frames. That is not a flaw, it is the geometry the putter is built around (69° lie, 2° effective loft, 0° lean). The 'hands even' cue died with the DF3i and must never be carried across — on a Pistol 0 it is lean YOU are adding, on a face with almost nothing to deloft.

WHAT THE NUMBERS SAY, read fairly. AMBIGUOUS, not favourable. The LINK's column holds the only two reds on the evolution grid — face at impact and the 1.5-1.7° left start line, both measured Jul 30, on this head — while the DF3i's first filmed column carries none. But Jul 30 was by far the most-filmed day of the project (three sessions, fourteen clips, the first face-on at 120 fps), so some of that is measurement effort rather than a putter effect, and the DF3i's clean column is partly clean because less was measured in it. In the LINK's favour: tempo 2.0:1 across seven of eight clips against the DF3i's 2.4:1, with 2:1 the target. The only real scoreboard in the entire project is the DF3i's 8/10 from four feet on Jul 20 — and it went back with the mallet.

WHAT THE SAGA PROVED. That the left miss travels. It reappeared while you were holding a zero-torque putter, which is the cleanest evidence available that the head was never the cause — and it is why the miss was eventually reclassified as an AIM error rather than a delivery one. Also that lags finishing short and short putts running hot are not two faults but one: an uncalibrated power curve, where you default to too-small on the big number and too-big on the small one.

WHAT CHANGED. The LINK is the putter, permanently — `returnWindow` is off, the Home return-window card is gone, and Decisions reads DECIDED. The Routine plan carries the Pistol 0 geometry as its hands instruction. The Distance Grind owns the calibration work the whole saga skipped.

STILL UNMEASURED. Strike location, on any of the four putters owned this month — which remains the single candidate that explains both open faults at once, since a heel strike closes the face and bleeds ball speed. The tape-test protocol now lives in the Lag Putts plan.

SINCE UPDATED (Aug 14 2026) — the grip named above is a LAMKIN DEEP ETCHED, not a Pistol 0. The app carried the wrong name from Jul 30 to Aug 14. Both are 0° built-in lean, so every word of the geometry in this section stands, including the 59-frame film measurement. Left unedited on purpose: a log records what was believed at the time. Full correction in the Aug 14 section at the top of this log.

sections.t: How this log works
sections.k: Anything worked through end to end lands here as one section, so the doing-plans stay short.
sections.b:
The rule going forward: when a question gets worked through properly — research, a claim checked, a decision reached — it lands here as ONE section rather than being spread through the plans that tell you what to do.

That keeps the split clean. The Routine plan, the Setup plan and the Distance Grind say what you do NOW, in as few words as they can. This log says how each of those instructions was arrived at, what was rejected on the way, and where the sources were. When an instruction changes, the reasoning does not have to be re-derived and it does not have to sit in the middle of a plan you read on the practice green.

Each section carries the same skeleton: the question, what checked out, what did not, what changed in the other plans, what remains unmeasured, and the sources. The unmeasured line is not optional — a workshop that cannot say what it still does not know is a sales pitch.

briefing.focus: First look at a hill course: rolling ground above Keuka Lake, five elevated greens, blind approaches, long uphill par 4s and a creek on five holes. Every one of those pushes the ball SHORT, which is already your standing miss. Club up, cover the middle, and take bogey on the climbs without an argument.
rules: Club up — greens here play long
Cover the middle, never the flag
Blind shot? Pick the target first
Creek on 5 holes — ask which
Ball above your feet goes LEFT
1 is a hard opener: par is a bonus
Four 30-ft lags before you tee off

holes.avoid: *A big number on a cold swing.* Bogey on the 1st costs one shot; the tee shot you try to rescue costs three

So it climbs — that is *INFERRED* from the view direction, not stated anywhere. If it does climb, the approach is a *club more* than the number

No sourced yardage, par or stroke index for this hole or any other — see the last section for why

sections.t: Every green plays long here
sections.k: Five elevated greens, blind approaches and uphill par 4s all leave the ball short — and short is already your miss.
sections.b:
The course description is unusually specific about this: five ELEVATED greens, many holes needing a BLIND approach, and long uphill par 4s with steep approaches to the greens. That is three separate reasons for the ball to finish short of the putting surface.

And short is your standing miss on approach — it is the loudest finding in your own hole data, and it is why the carry ladder keeps coming up. So the correction is not subtle here: take the yardage to the MIDDLE of the green, then add a club for the climb. On an elevated green the flag is often all you can see, which makes the front edge look like the middle; it isn't.

Why that trade is cheap: past the middle of an elevated green you are usually putting. Short of it, you are chipping up a steep bank from below the surface, which is the hardest shot on this kind of course and the one that turns a bogey into a double.

The blind ones need a separate discipline: do not swing at a target you have not chosen. Walk to the crest or the marker post, pick a tree, a pole or a skyline notch, aim at THAT, and go. A blind approach played at a vague 'up there' is how you end up short and left of everything.

sections.t: Very few level lies
sections.k: The slope aims the ball — read the lie before you read the yardage.
sections.b:
Built on rolling terrain overlooking the lake, so 'expect very few level lies' is the course's own summary of itself. That is a sourced fact about the ground. What follows below is standard ball-flight, not Lakeside research — it is true everywhere, it just matters more here.

Ball ABOVE your feet: the club sits toe-down, the face points left, and the ball starts and curves LEFT. Stand a touch taller, grip down, aim right of the target. This is the lie you will get most often on a hillside course and it is the one to have in your head.

Ball BELOW your feet: the opposite — the ball leaks RIGHT. More knee flex, stay down through it, aim left, and take one more club because you will catch it thinner than you want.

UPHILL lie: the slope adds loft. Higher, shorter, and it can be a full club or more. Club up, ball slightly forward, swing with the slope rather than into it.

DOWNHILL lie: the slope takes loft off. Lower, longer, and it is the hardest of the four. Take more loft than the number says, play the ball back, and let the club chase down the hill.

The compounding case is the one that will actually cost you a shot tomorrow: an uphill lie into an elevated green is two clubs, not one. On a hill course the errors stack in the same direction, and that direction is short.

sections.t: The tee shot: trees, a creek, and no local knowledge
sections.k: The drive that leaves no play is the shot that has cost you most — and this is a blind, wooded course you have never seen.
sections.b:
What is sourced: heavily wooded landscaping, with many of the tees sitting inside tunnels of trees, and a creek that comes into play on FIVE holes. Which five is not published anywhere reachable. That is a ten-second question on the first tee and it is worth asking the pro shop or whoever you are playing with — where the water crosses is the single most valuable fact about a course you have never played, because unlike a pin it never moves.

The course also changes character halfway through. The original nine dates from 1950 and is the tight, wooded half; the holes added in 1995 were built on wide-open terrain and are described as a deliberate contrast. So do not carry a driver decision made on the open holes back onto the tree tunnels.

Your own evidence for the club choice: at Sterling Farms three tee shots left you with NO realistic play at the green — three holes, +4 between them, and the approach club never got a say. That is exactly what a blind, tree-lined tee shot on an unknown course produces. When you cannot see where the fairway goes, the 5-wood or the 2-iron is the honest club, and neither of them costs you a wedge into a 6,600-yard par 72.

Two things to log while you are out there. Tap the TEE CLUB on every hole — the by-club table is the only thing that will ever settle the driver-versus-5-wood question, and the 5-wood's carry is still unmeasured. And use the DEAD chip on any hole where the drive took the green away, so those holes get charged to the tee shot rather than to your irons.

sections.t: Greens you have never putted
sections.k: Medium speed and unknown to you, so the round turns on lag — which is the fault you are already working on.
sections.b:
Sourced: the greens are well bunkered and described as medium speed; one review calls them medium-fast with a very true roll, which is the good version of unknown. Bent grass, per one listing.

Distance control is your open putting fault and it has never been measured. A course you have never putted is where it will show, so give it the ten minutes before you tee off rather than finding out on the 3rd green: four lags from 30 feet and one from 40, scoring nothing but whether the ball finishes inside a six-foot circle, then five from three feet with the full routine. That is your standing grind, done on the greens you are about to play.

On the LINK the aim picture is unchanged and does not get a second correction: face BARELY OPEN at address, shaft vertical, hands about 1.35 inches behind the ball. Do not add an aim-picture adjustment on top of the barely-open feel — that applies the fix twice and misses right.

One green-reading note that follows from the terrain rather than from research: on ground that rolls this much, the big break is usually the one you cannot see from beside the ball. Read the putt from below the hole, where the slope shows itself, and if you are guessing, miss on the HIGH side — a low miss was never going in.

sections.t: The first three holes
sections.k: Your record says a round gets away EARLY, not at the finish — and the 1st here is a hard opener.
sections.b:
This is the one place where your mental data and the course description point at the same holes. Reviewers call the 1st one of the hardest starting holes on the course. Your own cards say the Wianno match where a partner got into your head cost +6 over holes 1–3, against +3 on each of the other four nines out there — partner disruption lands at the START, not at the finish. Honest caveat, the same one that is in the Locked In plan: that was also the coldest start of the event, so warm-up and partner are confounded on that card and neither is established.

What the same data says you do NOT have: a closing fade. Your last three holes run +0.67 against +0.89 for everything before them. So the job tomorrow is the beginning, not the end.

Practical version: get there early enough to do the lag ladder above, treat the first three holes as the ones to protect, and take par-or-bogey on the 1st without a second thought. Slow play and random partners are two of your named triggers — if either shows up, the if-then responses are in the Mental tab, and the debrief afterwards is where they get counted.

sections.t: Nobody publishes this course hole by hole — so log it
sections.k: One live round with tee clubs and stroke indexes turns the next Lakeside plan into a real hole-by-hole briefing.
sections.b:
This plan has ONE hole note instead of eighteen, and that is deliberate. The club's own site and every scorecard database that carries Lakeside were unreachable from here, so nothing per-hole could be pinned: no yardages, no pars, no stroke indexes, no idea which five holes the creek crosses or which five greens are the elevated ones. Writing tee-shot lines for holes nobody could see would read exactly like researched ones, and that is the failure worth avoiding.

So the round itself is the research. Log it live: par and stroke index off the card, putts, greens hit and where the misses finished, fairways, the tee club on every hole, the approach club on the par 4s and 5s, and the DEAD chip where the drive left nothing. That card prefills every future round here — par and stroke index come straight off the newest card at the same course, so the second Lakeside round needs almost no typing.

And photograph the scorecard. Tees played, rating, slope, the yardage column and the stroke indexes. Rating and slope get backfilled onto the card so the round produces a handicap differential, and the yardage column is what a proper hole-by-hole plan is built from.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: Course-level facts came from search summaries of blocked sites; nothing per-hole could be sourced, and the numbers below disagree with each other.
sections.b:
RESEARCHED (searched Aug 19 2026). Every course site and scorecard database — lccpy.com, BlueGolf, GolfLink, GolfPass, Golfify, GolfTraxx, foretee — was blocked outright from this session, so these come from search-result summaries OF those pages rather than the pages themselves. Treat them as good but second-hand.

- Rating and slope CONFLICT across sources: 71.6 / 131 from the Blue (the club's own listing); 72.3 / 131 Blue and 70.5 / 129 White (GolfLink summary); 71.4 / 129 unattributed to a tee elsewhere. UNCONFIRMED — read the card, and send me the tees you played so the round gets the right pair.
- Terrain: built on rolling terrain overlooking Keuka Lake, 'expect very few level lies'.
- Heavily wooded; many tees sit inside tunnels of trees.
- A creek comes into play on FIVE holes. Which five: not published anywhere reachable.
- FIVE elevated greens; many holes need a blind approach.
- Greens well bunkered, medium speed; one review says medium-fast with a very true roll. Where the bunkers sit, hole by hole: unknown.
- Long uphill par 4s with steep approaches to the greens (review summary).
- Hole 1: 'one of the hardest starting holes', with views back down the hill toward Keuka Lake. That it plays UPHILL is my inference from the view direction, not a sourced statement.
- Lake views from behind the 5th and 10th greens (review summary). That is scenery, not a playing instruction, so neither hole is written up — there is nothing about how to play them.
- History: club established 1923; the golf course opened in 1950 as nine holes and went to 18 in 1995, the new holes built on open ground in deliberate contrast to the wooded originals.
- Semi-private. 145 Rt 54 E Lake Road, Penn Yan NY 14527. Opens 8am (from the listing on the map card you sent).

FROM YOUR OWN CARDS. Approach misses finish short more than any other direction. Three tee shots at Sterling Farms left no realistic play at the green, +4 between them. Wianno holes 1–3 played +6 on the disrupted card against +3 on each of the other four nines. Closing three holes +0.67 a hole against +0.89 before them. Putting distance control is open and unmeasured; tempo is closed at 2.0:1.

NOT SOURCED, THEREFORE NOT WRITTEN: per-hole yardages, pars and stroke indexes; which holes the creek crosses; which greens are the elevated ones; where the bunkers sit; any dogleg direction. If you can grab the course's own hole-by-hole tour or a scorecard photo, all of that becomes writable.

lesson.title: Play the hill before you play the yardage
lesson.body:
On a course built across a hillside you will hit more sloping lies than flat ones, and the slope decides both the number and the start line before you have made a decision about either. Four lies, four rules.

BALL ABOVE FEET: the club sits toe-down, the face aims left, the ball starts and curves LEFT. Stand taller, grip down, aim right.

BALL BELOW FEET: the ball leaks RIGHT. More knee flex, stay down through it, aim left, one more club — you will catch it thin.

UPHILL LIE: the slope adds loft. Higher and shorter, often a full club. Club up, ball a touch forward, swing along the slope.

DOWNHILL LIE: the slope removes loft. Lower and longer, and the hardest of the four to strike. More loft than the number, ball back, chase the club down the hill.

The reason this is a course-management lesson rather than a swing one: the errors STACK. An uphill lie into an elevated green is two clubs, not one, and both mistakes push the ball the same way you already miss — short. The saving is not in a better swing off the slope, it is in reading the lie and the green together before you pull a club.
lesson.drill: Nine holes of naming it out loud. Before every full shot off a slope, say the lie and the correction — 'above my feet, it goes left, aim right' — then pick the club, then swing. Note on the card where each miss actually finished. Score the CALLS, not the shots: you are looking for the lies where your prediction and the ball disagreed, because those are the two you have to work on.

sections.t: The par 3s are the round
sections.k: They average 203 yards — these are wood holes, and bogey on all four is a par-72 round of 76.
sections.b:
Sterling Farms' par 3s average 203 YARDS. That is not a normal set of par 3s: it is four holes where a mid-handicapper is hitting the club he would hit into a par 4.

You bogeyed all four last time — 5, 8, 15 and 17 — and three of those misses finished short or long rather than beside the green. That is not a strike problem. It is a club problem: 221 on the 5th is past your 2-iron, and the 8th plays uphill on top of its number.

The rule for all four: club to cover the MIDDLE of the green, not the flag, and treat two putts as the plan. Four bogeys on these is +4 — that is a perfectly good outcome and it beats the double that comes from chasing an edge of the green. You will not know where the flag is until you are standing there, and it should not change the club: the middle is the target on all four.

sections.t: Driver is optional here
sections.k: Three of your green misses last time were tee shots that left you nothing, and the short holes don't need the big stick.
sections.b:
Your last card here lost more to tee shots than to any swing fault. On holes 1, 6 and 10 the drive left you with no realistic play at the green — three holes, +4 between them, and the approach club never had a say.

This is a 6,308-yard par 72 on 144 rolling acres. It is not long. The 1st is 337 downhill. A 5-wood or 2-iron off the tee on the short par 4s still leaves a wedge, and it takes the 'no play' outcome off the table entirely.

The 5-wood's carry is still unmeasured — this is a good round to learn it. Log the tee club on every hole and the by-club table will tell you whether it is actually finding more fairways than the driver, and whether those fairways are worth anything.

sections.t: 14 through 17

sections.b:
14 (SI 2) · 15 (par 3) · 16 (SI 16) · 17 (par 3) played +6 and turned a 41-ish back nine into 44.

The damaging pair are the ones that should have been easy: 16 is stroke index SIXTEEN and you made a six on it. A giveaway hole that gives nothing back is worth more than any birdie you chase on the hard ones.

Plan for this stretch: fairway, middle of the green, two putts, four bogeys at worst. +4 through there instead of +6 is two shots for no better ball-striking at all.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: Where the course facts come from, and where your own card does.
sections.b:
Course facts here are researched: Geoffrey Cornish design opened 1972, renovated by Robert McNeil in 2005, 6,308 yards, par 72, 71.1/118, 144 acres of a former dairy farm, par 3s averaging 203 yards. Hole detail comes from two sources. GOLFCT's review covers the front nine: 1 (337, downhill), 2 (500, elevated tee, protected green), 4 (sharp dogleg left), 5 (221-yard par 3), 7 (dogleg right), 8 (uphill par 3), 9 (short straightaway par 4).

The course's OWN pro tips (from its video tour) cover more: 4 (long iron or fairway wood, high second), 6 (large tree right of the fairway), 8 (bunker in front of the green), 10 (large bunkers right of fairway and green; left-center; don't be long), 11 (mid-iron tee shot, small green), 12 (left-center; a fade helps the second), 13 (the signature hole: water, long iron or fairway wood, right-center), 18 (driver; reachable in two). One caution kept on purpose: different copies of the tour shift the hole numbering, so every tip above was cross-checked against the pars and shapes on your Aug 12 card before it was pinned to a hole — and tips that could not be pinned were left out. The 232-yard figure on 17 is a reviewer's number for the back tees. CONFIRMED BY JACK Aug 12: the water is on 13, so that pin is no longer a research guess.

Everything else about 10–18 comes from YOUR card of Aug 12, 2026 (87, 43/44, +15). Where a note names a yardage or a hazard it is researched; where it names a score, a miss or a stroke index it is measured off your own round. No hole here has been described from imagination.

Aug 12 also swapped the mini driver out for the Cobra Darkspeed X 5-wood at 16.5°, which made its debut on the 4th: fairway, green, par, on stroke index 1.

KNOWN HAZARDS, so they never have to be rediscovered: water on 13 (confirmed); large bunkers right of both the fairway and the green on 10; a bunker fronting the green on the uphill 8th; a large tree right of the fairway on 6; the 2nd green described only as 'well protected', which is unspecified and stays that way until it can be seen. Nothing on 3 or 15 — those two carry only your own record, and if you notice what guards them, say so and they get a note.

TWO SOFT SPOTS, flagged rather than buried. (1) The 2014 review calls the 7th 'a dogleg right handicap 1 hole', but Jack's card puts stroke index 1 on the 4th and 9 on the 7th. The SHAPE is kept because shapes outlast re-ratings; the 'handicap 1' claim is dropped. (2) The same review calls the 3rd and 4th 'both very short' while his card has the 4th at stroke index 1 — an odd pairing, so the 4th's note leans on the course's own tip and his card rather than on the review's length claim. Neither is a numbering error big enough to move a tip to another hole, but if the 7th turns out not to bend right, that note is the one to bin.

The 7th's tee line is REASONING, not a sourced tip: on a hole running right, a ball started left finishes through the fairway, which is exactly the miss on his card. No source says the right side is safe, so the note says right-centre and says why.

sections.t: What the card actually says
sections.k: 6,189 yards from the whites, eight of ten par 4s under 400 and no par 3 over 180 — this is a position course.
sections.b:
WHITE TEES: 6,189 yards, par 72, 70.5 / 129. Out 3,034 · In 3,155. Everything below is built on that card rather than on a database, because you photographed it.

It is a SHORT course. There are ten par 4s and eight of them are under 400 yards — 275 (7th), 327 (10th), 345 (4th), 346 (11th), 378 (8th), 385 (18th), 387 (2nd), 393 (15th). Only the 3rd at 399 and the 16th at 441 are longer, and only the 16th is out of reach for a fairway finder.

Four par 3s, and not one is long: 137 (17th), 144 (5th), 158 (14th), 177 (9th). On your estimated ladder that is a 9-iron, an 8-iron, a 7-iron and a 5-iron — four clubs you can control.

Four par 5s, all under 500: 439 (6th), 482 (12th), 486 (13th), 490 (1st). The 12th and 13th are back to back.

WHERE THE CARD SAYS THE SHOTS ARE. The five hardest holes by stroke index are the 3rd (1), the 16th (2), the 1st (3), the 15th (4) and the 2nd (5) — four par 4s and the opening par 5. The five easiest are the 17th (18), the 5th (17), the 12th (16), the 7th (15) and the 14th (14) — two par 3s, a par 5 and the shortest par 4 on the course.

That split is the whole plan in one line. The hard five are holes you protect and take bogey on; the easy five are where the round is actually made. A 482-yard par 5 rated stroke index 16, and a 275-yard par 4 rated 15, are the two the card is openly handing you.

sections.t: Every green plays long here
sections.k: Five elevated greens, blind approaches and uphill par 4s all leave the ball short — and short is already your miss.
sections.b:
The course description is unusually specific about this: five ELEVATED greens, many holes needing a BLIND approach, and long uphill par 4s with steep approaches to the greens. That is three separate reasons for the ball to finish short of the putting surface.

And short is your standing miss on approach — it is the loudest finding in your own hole data, and it is why the carry ladder keeps coming up. So the correction is not subtle here: take the yardage to the MIDDLE of the green, then add a club for the climb. On an elevated green the flag is often all you can see, which makes the front edge look like the middle; it isn't.

Why that trade is cheap: past the middle of an elevated green you are usually putting. Short of it, you are chipping up a steep bank from below the surface, which is the hardest shot on this kind of course and the one that turns a bogey into a double.

The blind ones need a separate discipline: do not swing at a target you have not chosen. Walk to the crest or the marker post, pick a tree, a pole or a skyline notch, aim at THAT, and go. A blind approach played at a vague 'up there' is how you end up short and left of everything.

sections.t: Very few level lies
sections.k: The slope aims the ball — read the lie before you read the yardage.
sections.b:
Built on rolling terrain overlooking the lake, so 'expect very few level lies' is the course's own summary of itself. That is a sourced fact about the ground. What follows below is standard ball-flight, not Lakeside research — it is true everywhere, it just matters more here.

Ball ABOVE your feet: the club sits toe-down, the face points left, and the ball starts and curves LEFT. Stand a touch taller, grip down, aim right of the target. This is the lie you will get most often on a hillside course and it is the one to have in your head.

Ball BELOW your feet: the opposite — the ball leaks RIGHT. More knee flex, stay down through it, aim left, and take one more club because you will catch it thinner than you want.

UPHILL lie: the slope adds loft. Higher, shorter, and it can be a full club or more. Club up, ball slightly forward, swing with the slope rather than into it.

DOWNHILL lie: the slope takes loft off. Lower, longer, and it is the hardest of the four. Take more loft than the number says, play the ball back, and let the club chase down the hill.

The compounding case is the one that will actually cost you a shot tomorrow: an uphill lie into an elevated green is two clubs, not one. On a hill course the errors stack in the same direction, and that direction is short.

sections.t: The tee shot: trees, a creek, and no local knowledge
sections.k: The drive that leaves no play is the shot that has cost you most — and this is a blind, wooded course you have never seen.
sections.b:
What is sourced: heavily wooded landscaping, with many of the tees sitting inside tunnels of trees, and a creek that comes into play on FIVE holes. Which five is not published anywhere reachable. That is a ten-second question on the first tee and it is worth asking the pro shop or whoever you are playing with — where the water crosses is the single most valuable fact about a course you have never played, because unlike a pin it never moves.

The course also changes character halfway through. The original nine dates from 1950 and is the tight, wooded half; the holes added in 1995 were built on wide-open terrain and are described as a deliberate contrast. So do not carry a driver decision made on the open holes back onto the tree tunnels.

Your own evidence for the club choice: at Sterling Farms three tee shots left you with NO realistic play at the green — three holes, +4 between them, and the approach club never got a say. That is exactly what a blind, tree-lined tee shot on an unknown course produces. When you cannot see where the fairway goes, the 5-wood or the 2-iron is the honest club, and on this card neither of them costs you much: from the whites the 2-iron leaves 141 or less into four of the ten par 4s and a long-to-mid iron into five more, and only the 441-yard 16th genuinely needs the driver.

Two things to log while you are out there. Tap the TEE CLUB on every hole — the by-club table is the only thing that will ever settle the driver-versus-5-wood question, and the 5-wood's carry is still unmeasured. And use the DEAD chip on any hole where the drive took the green away, so those holes get charged to the tee shot rather than to your irons.

sections.t: The greens
sections.k: Medium speed, and the round turns on lag — which is the fault you are already working on.
sections.b:
Sourced: the greens are well bunkered and described as medium speed; one review calls them medium-fast with a very true roll, which is the good version of unknown. Bent grass, per one listing.

Distance control is your open putting fault and it has never been measured. You have putted them once now, on Aug 20, so the next round here is not a blind one — but the fault is still open, so give it the ten minutes before you tee off rather than finding out on the 3rd green: four lags from 30 feet and one from 40, scoring nothing but whether the ball finishes inside a six-foot circle, then five from three feet with the full routine. That is your standing grind, done on the greens you are about to play.

On the LINK the aim picture is unchanged and does not get a second correction: face BARELY OPEN at address, shaft vertical, hands about 1.35 inches behind the ball. Do not add an aim-picture adjustment on top of the barely-open feel — that applies the fix twice and misses right.

One green-reading note that follows from the terrain rather than from research: on ground that rolls this much, the big break is usually the one you cannot see from beside the ball. Read the putt from below the hole, where the slope shows itself, and if you are guessing, miss on the HIGH side — a low miss was never going in.

sections.t: The first three holes
sections.k: Your record says a round gets away EARLY, not at the finish — and the 1st here is a hard opener.
sections.b:
This is the one place where your mental data and the course description point at the same holes. Reviewers call the 1st one of the hardest starting holes on the course, and the card backs them: it is a 490-yard par 5 at stroke index 3. Your own cards say the Wianno match where a partner got into your head cost +6 over holes 1–3, against +3 on each of the other four nines out there — partner disruption lands at the START, not at the finish. Honest caveat, the same one that is in the Locked In plan: that was also the coldest start of the event, so warm-up and partner are confounded on that card and neither is established.

What the same data says you do NOT have: a closing fade. Your last three holes run +0.67 against +0.89 for everything before them. So the job here is the beginning, not the end.

Practical version: get there early enough to do the lag ladder above, treat the first three holes as the ones to protect, and take par-or-bogey on the 1st without a second thought. Slow play and random partners are two of your named triggers — if either shows up, the if-then responses are in the Mental tab, and the debrief afterwards is where they get counted.

entries.setup: FULL SWING · Driver · 7 phone stills (address → finish) · ON COURSE, elevated tee · rear-quarter angle (behind and off the rear shoulder — NOT square DTL)
entries.finding: First driver film taken on the course rather than in a bay, and the first of any swing on file that catches the FINISH — which changes the read. The finish is complete: trail toe up, weight fully on the lead side, chest and hips turned through, held in balance. That argues against the strong 'hips stall' story on the card, because a stalled, all-arms swing does not finish there. What these frames DO show is a posture problem — a rounded upper back and chin on the chest at address, a trail leg that straightens at the top, and a body visibly taller through delivery than at address. So the fault is refined rather than restated: the rotation happens, the tilt is what gets lost. The angle cannot read shaft plane, path, face or attack angle, so the across-the-line top and the slice both stay exactly where Jul 27 left them.

clubhead still well behind at hands-hip-high — no cast

detail.story:
Seven stills spanning address, early takeaway, top, transition, past impact and a held finish. The bones are the same ones Jul 26 found and they are good: a genuinely full coil with the head behind the ball, and a transition that starts from the ground — at hands-hip-high the clubhead is still well behind him, which is the opposite of a cast.

The new frame is the finish, and it is the best one in the set. Fully up on the trail toe, weight completely on the lead side, chest and hips turned past the target, hands high with the club wrapped behind the lead shoulder, and he holds it. Post-impact backs it up: head still down and behind the ball well past the strike.

That finish is what forces the refinement. The open fault said the hips stall and slide instead of clearing. A swing that truly stalls does not finish like this — it hangs back on the trail foot or the lead arm collapses. So the rotation is not what is missing. What IS missing is the posture it rotates around: the upper back is rounded and the chin is down at address, the trail leg straightens at the top so the pelvis loses its forward tilt before the downswing begins, and by the delivery frame the body is plainly taller than it was at address. Three frames, one story — he turns around a rising spine rather than the one he set. The useful consequence is that the cheapest entry point is now the earliest one: address posture and a little trail-knee flex, both checkable in a mirror before a ball is hit.
detail.compare: Third full-swing entry on record, after the Jul 19 sim baseline and the Jul 26 driver/wedge stills. Confirms Jul 26's three positives a second time and on the course rather than in a bay — coil, head behind the ball, ground-up transition, balanced finish. Revises Jul 26's 'hips slide level through impact' from a rotation fault to a posture fault. Does NOT re-grade Jul 26's across-the-line top, which needs an angle this film does not have.
detail.limits: Rear-quarter camera — behind and off the rear shoulder, elevated — so shaft plane at the top, club path, face-to-path and attack angle are all unreadable, and nothing here can confirm or refute the over-the-top slice. No true impact frame: the sequence jumps from hands-hip-high to well past the strike. The apparent standing-up in the delivery frame is partly perspective, since a rear-quarter lens exaggerates it as the body rotates toward the camera — the ADDRESS frames are the solid evidence, because a static position does not depend on rotation. DATE AND COURSE ARE AN INFERENCE, not Jack's report: he described the film only as recent, and it is dated to the Aug 20 Lakeside Country Club round on the strength of the terrain and the day it arrived. Correct it and this row gets removed and re-added.

faults.why: Open — filmed Jul 26, both clubs. At the top the shaft points RIGHT of target, which is ACROSS THE LINE. TERMINOLOGY CORRECTED Aug 20: this fault was tagged 'laid-off-top' and its text called the same position 'across the line / laid off'. Those are opposite positions — laid off is the shaft pointing LEFT of target — and the Jul 26 metrics say right, so across the line is the observation and always was. The fix is one thought: the trail elbow points DOWN and stays IN FRONT of the hip seam. WORKING (Jul 27): one-handed Miracle 201 swings land the drop into the slot, and that is the confirmed fix-feel rather than a theory. NOT RE-GRADED Aug 20: the on-course driver film was shot from behind and off the rear shoulder, and a rear-quarter angle cannot read the shaft against the target line — so this is still a Jul 26 reading, not a current one. NOT MEASURED: no sim numbers. Video shows a position; it cannot give club path or face-to-path, and until those exist the root cause is reasoned rather than established.

Open — and REFINED Aug 20 by the first film that caught a finish. This was tagged 'hips-stall' and read as the hips sliding toward the target instead of clearing back and up. The Aug 20 on-course driver stills argue against the strong version of that: the finish is complete — trail toe up, weight fully on the lead side, chest and hips turned through, held in balance — and a genuinely stalled, all-arms swing does not finish there. It hangs back or the lead arm collapses. So the rotation is not the missing piece. WHAT IS: the posture set at address is not the posture he turns around, and it goes in three places — the upper back is rounded and the chin is down at ADDRESS; the trail leg straightens at the TOP, so the pelvis gives up its forward tilt before transition starts; and the body is visibly taller through DELIVERY than at address. The instruction is unchanged in spirit — turn around a post, do not slide — but the entry point moves earlier: a long spine at address and a little trail-knee flex to the top, and the pelvis has somewhere to stay. HONESTY GUARD: a rear-quarter camera exaggerates apparent standing-up as the body rotates toward the lens, so the delivery frame is a candidate rather than a measurement; the address frames are the solid ones, because a static position does not depend on rotation. GOOD and to be protected, now confirmed twice and on the course rather than in a bay: the coil, the head behind the ball, the ground-up transition, and the balanced held finish.

Open — the lifelong miss, and the reason the two above matter. Same root: arms come over the top when the body cannot deliver from the inside, producing an out-to-in path and the slice. Drill that isolates it: a headcover just outside the ball forces an in-to-out path. NOT ADVANCED Aug 20 — seven stills of a live tee shot neither confirm nor refute it. A finish that swings around and left is what a normal rotational finish looks like too, and no still from a rear-quarter angle can give a path. NOT MEASURED, and this is the honest limit — no launch monitor session exists, so path and face-to-path are inferred from video and from the shape of the miss. The next sim session settles it; until then this is the best-supported explanation rather than a measurement, and it has been waiting three and a half weeks.

briefing.focus: Good ground-up sequencing and a complete, balanced finish (keep both) and a posture that does not survive the swing (fix). Your read — 'great at the top, lose it through contact' — was written up here as stalling hips; the Aug 20 on-course driver film says the rotation DOES finish, and what you lose is the tilt you set at address. Same instruction, earlier entry point. Standing swing plan until the next filmed check.

sections.t: ✓ What's working — one-handed Miracle 201 drop
sections.b: CONFIRMED (Jul 27): swinging the MIRACLE 201 ONE-HANDED (trail/right hand only) tonight really helped you FEEL the club drop into the slot in transition. Make it your go-to reset — the heavy, whippy head with just the trail hand forces the elbow to lead DOWN (in front of the trail-hip seam) and shallows the shaft, so the hips can clear instead of the club laying off. Use it as a warm-up primer and any time the top gets across the line: a few slow one-handed 201 reps feeling the drop, then blend it into your two-hand swing. A club held trail-arm-only works as a stand-in when the trainer isn't handy.
sections.k: One-handed Miracle 201 swings are the confirmed fix-feel for the transition drop.

sections.t: The one connection: the top, the posture AND the over-the-top slice are one story
sections.b:
When the club gets across the line / laid off at the top (shaft pointing right of target, trail elbow drifting behind you), the downswing has to re-route the club to save the shot. Two re-routes usually happen together: the hips SLIDE toward the target and the chest hangs back (the 'lose it through contact' feel), AND the trail shoulder throws the club OUT over the plane so it cuts across the ball — that's the over-the-top slice. One cause, three symptoms. So we don't chase three fixes: clean up the top, drop the club into the slot (shallow), and let the hips CLEAR — and all three symptoms go with it.

UPDATED Aug 20: two corrections to the WORDS, not to the mechanism. (1) The top position filmed on Jul 26 is ACROSS THE LINE — shaft pointing RIGHT of target. 'Laid off' is the opposite position, shaft pointing LEFT of target, and the two were being used interchangeably here. They are not the same thing. (2) The middle symptom is better described as LOSING POSTURE than as stalling hips: the Aug 20 finish is complete and balanced, so the hips do get there. The one-cause reading survives both corrections.
sections.k: The top, the lost posture and the lifelong slice are one fault, not three.

sections.t: What the film showed (both clubs, Jul 26)
sections.b: GOOD, protect it: full coil, head behind the ball (driver), lower-body-led transition on both, and a balanced held finish. WEDGE bonus: spine angle stayed, you covered the ball — a proper descending strike. TO FIX: (1) slightly across-the-line top on BOTH clubs — one feel fixes both; (2) driver hips look to slide level through impact instead of clearing up-and-around. No launch numbers were in frame, so path/attack-angle/spin are still unmeasured — that's the next data to grab.
sections.k: Film says: coil, head behind the ball and lower-body-led transition are all good — protect them.

sections.t: What the on-course film showed (driver, Aug 20)
sections.k: The finish is complete — so what you lose through contact is posture, not rotation.
sections.b:
Seven phone stills of a live tee shot, address to finish — the first driver film taken ON THE COURSE rather than in a bay, and the first of any driver swing that catches the FINISH.

GOOD, and now confirmed twice: a full coil with the head behind the ball; a ground-up transition (at hands-hip-high the clubhead is still well behind you — no cast); and a finish that is genuinely complete — trail toe up, weight fully on the lead side, chest and hips turned through, held in balance.

That finish is why this plan changed. A swing whose hips truly stall does not finish there — it hangs back on the trail foot or collapses the lead arm. Yours does not. So rotation is not the missing piece.

WHAT IS: posture. The upper back is rounded and the chin is down on the chest at ADDRESS. The trail leg straightens at the TOP. And through DELIVERY the body is visibly taller than it was at address. One story across three frames — you turn around a rising spine instead of the one you set.

WHAT THE FRAMES CANNOT SAY: the camera sat behind you and off the rear shoulder, so shaft plane at the top, club path, face-to-path and attack angle are all unreadable, and there is no true impact frame. The across-the-line top and the slice are both exactly where Jul 27 left them. Next film: phone on the ground ON the target line behind the ball, at hand height, plus one face-on.

sections.t: Fix 0 · Keep the posture you set
sections.k: Set a long spine and hold a little trail-knee flex to the top; the pelvis then has somewhere to stay.
sections.b:
This one happens before the club moves, which is why it is Fix 0 rather than Fix 4 — and it is the cheapest thing on this page, because it is static and you can check it in a mirror.

AT ADDRESS: hinge from the HIPS, not from the middle of your back. Chest tall, shoulder blades down, room for a fist between your chin and your chest, arms hanging under the shoulders. The rounded-back, chin-down setup in the Aug 20 stills costs you twice: it caps the shoulder turn, so the arms lift to make up the difference, and a chest already folded at address is the setup most likely to stand up in transition.

TO THE TOP: keep a little flex in the TRAIL knee. If the trail leg straightens going back — which it does in the Aug 20 film — the pelvis has already given up its forward tilt before the downswing starts, and coming down there is nowhere to go but up. Holding it at the top is cheaper than fighting it at the bottom.

THE CHECK: phone on the ground, square down the line, at hand height. Freeze address and freeze delivery and put the two side by side. Your belt line should sit at roughly the same height in both. That is the whole test.

sections.t: Fix 1 · Clean up the top (trail elbow in front)
sections.b: FEEL: at the top, the trail (right) elbow points more DOWN at the ground and stays in FRONT of your trail-hip seam, keeping the club a hair more in front of your chest. Right now the elbow drifts behind you, which lays the shaft off. DRILL — the one-handed Miracle 201 (or club trail-arm-only): make slow half-swings feeling the trail elbow lead down into the slot; pause at the top and check the shaft points AT the target line, not right of it. Mirror or a phone on a tripod DTL at the top confirms it. 10 slow reps before you hit balls. (This is the drill that's working for you — see 'What's working' above.)
sections.k: Fix 1: trail elbow points down and stays in FRONT of the hip seam at the top.

sections.t: Fix 2 · Clear the hips, don't slide them
sections.b:
FEEL: from the top, the lead (left) hip clears BACK and UP — belt buckle turning left and rotating open — while your chest stays over the ball a beat longer. Not a slide toward the target; a turn around a post. This is where your speed and your 'through contact' consistency live. DRILLS: (a) Trail-foot-back / step-through: hit half wedges stepping the trail foot back through impact — forces rotation over slide. (b) Lead-hip-to-the-wall: set up with your lead hip a few inches off a wall/bag; on the downswing the hip should clear so it just brushes back and up, not bump forward into it. (c) Chair/impact-bag: feel the trail glute fire and the hips deepen (not thrust toward the ball) so you don't early-extend. 2–3 sets of 10 each, twice a week.

UPDATED Aug 20: the on-course driver film says the clearing itself IS happening — the finish is complete and balanced, which a stalled swing cannot produce. So read this section as being about HEIGHT more than about turn: the lead hip clears back and UP around a spine angle you have KEPT, and the drills that earn their time here are the two that stop you standing up — lead-hip-to-the-wall and the chair/impact-bag feel. Start at Fix 0 though; by the time this section gets its chance the tilt has usually already gone.
sections.k: Fix 2: the lead hip clears BACK and UP while the chest stays over the ball a beat longer.

sections.t: Fix 3 · Your over-the-top slice — same root, plus the path & face piece
sections.b: The lifelong slice comes from the SAME move: OVER THE TOP means in transition the upper body (trail shoulder) takes over and throws the club OUT and over the plane, so it swings across the ball OUT-TO-IN; with an open face that start-left, curve-right is your slice (a square face on that same path is a pull). Everything in this plan already fixes the CAUSE — the one-handed drop shallows the club, the trail elbow leading down puts it on line, and the hips CLEARING makes room so the arms deliver from the INSIDE instead of over the top. The extra piece is PATH then FACE. (1) PATH feel: from the top, feel the club fall behind you and swing OUT toward right-center field (in-to-out). DRILL — put a headcover/water bottle a few inches OUTSIDE the ball on the target line; swing so you miss it (coming over the top clips it). (2) FACE: a slice also needs an open face — once your path comes from the inside, if the ball still fades or you start pulling, the face is open to the path; with your conventional grip, let the trail forearm rotate/release through and check the grip isn't too weak. Fix PATH FIRST — chasing the face while still coming over the top just makes a bigger slice or a smother-hook.
sections.k: Fix 3: the slice is the same root — a headcover outside the ball forces the in-to-out path.

sections.t: Driver vs wedge — keep them different on purpose
sections.b: DRIVER: ball forward, hips clearing up-and-around so you hit slightly UP — that's carry and less spin. WEDGE: keep exactly what the film showed — stay down, cover the ball, hit DOWN; don't let 'clear the hips' turn into standing up out of a wedge. Same sequencing engine, opposite low-point. If a swing thought bleeds the wrong way, park it — the wedge is already good.
sections.k: Keep driver and wedge deliberately different: up on the driver, down and covering on the wedge.

sections.t: How to test it at the sim (get the numbers this time)
sections.b: The visual read can only go so far without data. Next session, capture and log these: DRIVER — attack angle (want positive / hitting up), CLUB PATH (over-the-top shows as a negative/left number — you want it near zero to slightly positive/right), FACE-TO-PATH (that's what curves it), spin, and ball speed. WEDGES — carry, spin, launch, and gap-check 60/56/50 against the ladder (80/95/108). Film one DTL clip at hand height + one face-on per club. Bring those back and we can prove whether the path is actually coming from the inside now.
sections.k: Stop guessing from video — get attack angle, club path and face-to-path at the next sim session.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: Where each instruction here came from, and what is still unmeasured.
sections.b:
JUL 26 — five phone stills each of driver and wedge, simulator bay. Source of the full coil, the head behind the ball, the ground-up transition and the balanced finish (all GOOD), and of the across-the-line top on BOTH clubs.

JUL 27 — one-handed Miracle 201 swings confirmed as the fix-feel for the transition drop. Your own report of what you did, so it stands on its own.

AUG 20 — seven phone stills of a live tee shot with the driver, address to finish, rear-quarter angle. First film to catch a finish. Source of the posture reading and of the correction to the hips-stall framing. The plan was retitled here: it was 'Swing Focus — Hips & the Laid-Off Top', and both halves of that name had gone wrong — 'laid off' was the wrong term for an across-the-line top, and the hips are not the part that fails.

STILL UNMEASURED, and it has been since Jul 27: club path, face-to-path, attack angle and spin. No launch-monitor session exists, so everything this plan says about the slice is the best-supported explanation rather than a measurement. The Aug 20 film could not advance it — a rear-quarter camera cannot read a path — and there is still no true impact frame on any driver swing on file.

rules: Long spine at address — chin off the chest
Keep a little trail-knee flex to the top
Trail elbow DOWN and in FRONT — the one thought
Turn around the post — the finish is already right
Next film: SQUARE down the line, at hand height
Next sim session: get path and face-to-path numbers

entries.text: SWING — POSTURE, and the film that can actually grade it. The Aug 20 driver stills show a rounded upper back and chin on the chest at address, a trail leg that straightens at the top, and a body taller through delivery than at address — so the 'lose it through contact' feel is posture, not stalling hips: the finish is complete. Two things. (1) MIRROR CHECK at address: hinge from the hips, chest tall, a fist between chin and chest, and hold a little trail-knee flex to the top. (2) NEXT RANGE SESSION, film SQUARE down the line — phone on the ground ON the target line behind the ball, at hand height — plus one face-on. The Aug 20 angle was rear-quarter, which is why the across-the-line top still has not been re-graded since Jul 26.

lesson.title: The first two balls are the only cold ones you get
lesson.body: Every swing fault in this app was filmed off a ball somewhere in the middle of a session — warm, loose, third club of the day. That is not the swing that starts your round. Two opening tee shots at Wianno went hard LEFT, badly enough to re-tee once, and your normal bad miss is a slice or push-slice, so the worst swings you make are going the OPPOSITE way to the diagnosed ones. Nothing in the library grades that swing, because by ball thirty it has gone. A range session is the only place you can film it on purpose: you arrive cold once per session, and if you spend that arrival on a wedge you have spent the only cold driver swing of the day. So the first two balls of a range session are not warm-up. They are data, and they are the only data of their kind you can collect.
lesson.drill: First two balls of the session, before anything else and before any stretching that changes what you are: driver, full routine, real target. Film both — phone on the ground ON the target line behind the ball at hand height, then one face-on. Do not re-hit them, do not judge them, and do not fix anything. Note the start line and the curve of each in one line, then warm up normally. Send the clips. Do it on three separate range sessions before you draw any conclusion: two hard-left openers is a pattern worth filming, not a diagnosis, and a pull, a snap hook and a toe strike all finish left with three different fixes.

lesson.title: Put a number on every club before the ladder claims one
lesson.body: Your loudest scoring pattern is that you miss greens SHORT — Sterling Farms missed twelve greens and seven of them were short, against two left, one right and one long, and the GHIN archive says the same thing across a season. There are exactly two causes and this drill separates them: either you are picking the wrong club, or your ladder numbers are wrong. Right now one club in the bag has no number at all. The Cobra Darkspeed X 5-wood at 16.5 degrees went back in the bag on Aug 12 and has never been measured, and it sits about half a degree off the 2-iron utility — so the ladder cannot say whether both clubs belong in there. The 7-wood in the bullpen is in the same position. And a carry number is a CARRY off a good strike; a 60 percent strike from rough finishes eight to ten yards shorter, which is most of the short miss right there. Measure the number, then club off the number, then stop guessing.
lesson.drill: Bring a rangefinder and pick a target with something behind it you can shoot. Five balls per club, alternating clubs rather than raking a bucket with one — ignore the best and the worst, average the middle three, and write that number down as the CARRY. Do the whole ladder over two sessions: driver, 5-wood, 2-iron, 4 through 9 iron on the first; PW, 50, 56, 60 and a second pass at the 5-wood on the second. Enter them in the carry ladder in the app. Two things to record beside each number: how many of the five you actually struck, and how big the gap is to the club either side. Any gap under six yards is two clubs doing one job, and any gap over eighteen is a hole in the bag — those two answers are the whole 5-wood-versus-2-iron question.

lesson.title: The gate outside the ball — path before face
lesson.body: Over the top is the open fault with the longest record: it is the lifelong miss, it was filmed on Jul 26 on both clubs, and it is the reason the other two swing faults matter. The arms come over the top when the body cannot deliver from the inside, and the ball starts left of target and curves right. The fix is not a feel, it is an obstacle. If there is something just outside the ball on the target line, an over-the-top move hits it and an inside delivery misses it — the feedback arrives before you have finished the swing, which is the only kind of feedback that changes a pattern. Two rules keep this honest. PATH FIRST, FACE SECOND: while you are learning to come from the inside the ball will start right and stay right, and that is a pass, not a failure — you release the face once the path is repeatable, not at the same time. And do it at HALF SPEED to begin with, because a full-speed swing at an object you are trying to miss is how the object gets hit.
lesson.drill: A headcover or a water bottle on the ground just outside the ball, on the target line, level with the ball. Aim at right-center field. 3 sets of 8 with a 7-iron: swing to miss the object, from the inside, ball starting at the right half of the target. Score each set out of 8 for clean misses of the object — under 6 and you slow down, you do not swing harder. Once a set of 8 comes back clean at full speed, hit five with the driver, then STOP: this drill is worth more in 25 balls twice a week than in a hundred once a month. Warm into it with the one-handed Miracle 201 reps so the slot feel is already there before a ball is involved.

lesson.title: Film it SQUARE, or it cannot be graded
lesson.body: Film is king in this project, but only a square camera is film — everything else is an opinion with a timestamp. The across-the-line top was measured on Jul 26 on both clubs and it has NOT been re-graded since, not because nobody filmed the swing but because the Aug 20 driver angle was rear-quarter. A shaft that points right of target at the top and a camera that sits right of the target line produce the same picture, so an off-line angle cannot tell you which one you are looking at. The setup is worth more than the swing you put in front of it: phone on the ground, ON the target line, directly behind the ball, lens at hand height. Face-on means level with the ball, square to the target line, hips height. Get those two right once and every session afterwards is comparable to every other one, which is the entire point of filming at all.
lesson.drill: Set the phone on the ground on the target line behind the ball at hand height, with an alignment stick or a club laid on the line so you can see in the frame whether the camera is honest. Ten swings, 7-iron, 60 fps or better. Then move to face-on, level with the ball, and shoot five more. Watch one thing only: at the top, does the shaft point AT the target line, right of it (across the line) or left of it. Say the answer out loud, then send the clips. Re-shoot from the same two positions every fortnight — the value is in the comparison, and a rear-quarter clip is worth nothing to it.

lesson.title: Stay in your posture — with balls in the way
lesson.body: The Aug 20 driver stills changed what this fault IS. It used to be read as the hips stalling; the film says the finish is complete, so it is not a stall — it is posture. Rounded upper back and chin on the chest at address, the trail leg straightening at the top, and a body standing TALLER through delivery than it was at address. That last one is the one that costs shots: if you rise between address and impact the club has to find a ball that is now further away than it was when you set the low point, and thin, heel and a face that never squares all come out of the same rise. The at-home mirror check gets the address position right. What it cannot do is prove the position survives a ball, and the position surviving a ball is the entire fault.
lesson.drill: Set up at address and check three things: hinge from the hips, chest tall, a fist of room between chin and chest, and a little trail-knee flex you intend to hold to the top. Then 3 sets of 8 with a 7-iron at 80 percent, holding the finish upright for a count of three on every ball — a swing you cannot hold is a swing that came out of posture. Film the last set square down the line at hand height and look at ONE thing: the height of your head at address versus at impact. Grade the set out of 8 for balls where it did not rise. Under 5 means drop to 60 percent speed rather than trying harder; posture does not respond to effort.

lesson.title: Aim is a measurement, not a feel
lesson.body: This project has already learned this lesson once, on the green. The whole putter saga turned out to be an AIM question rather than a delivery one, and it took a laser to find out — because how the face LOOKS is a habit, and a habit feels correct by definition. Nothing has ever checked the same thing on your full swing. That matters more than it sounds: if your feet and shoulders are aimed right of target, a perfectly delivered swing produces a push, and every fix you then apply is a fix for a swing that was fine. Over the top is exactly the compensation a body makes to get a ball back at a target it is not aimed at, so an unmeasured aim can quietly manufacture the fault you are working on. Sticks on the ground cost nothing and answer it in one look. The rule from the putting side applies here too: MEASURE with them, do not let them retrain you. If you find you are aimed right, that is a fact about your setup, not a new swing thought to carry to the first tee.
lesson.drill: One stick on the ground along your toe line, a second pointing at the target just outside the ball. Set up to the target the way you normally would, WITHOUT looking down, then step back and look at where the toe stick actually points. That first look is the measurement — write down which way you were off and by roughly how much. Then hit 15 balls with the sticks down, then TAKE THEM AWAY and hit 10 more, checking your aim on every third one by stepping behind the ball. Ten balls without the sticks is the real test: aim only counts when nothing on the ground is holding it.

lesson.title: Driver, 5-wood or 2-iron — settle it with a fairway-width target
lesson.body: The bag currently carries three answers to the same question. The mini driver came out on Aug 12 and the 5-wood took its fairway-finder slot without ever being measured, and the 2-iron utility sits about half a degree away from it. Meanwhile the app now counts something better than a fairway percentage: the DEAD column on the off-the-tee table, which is how often a club left you no realistic play at the green. Most rough is playable and none of those are, and that is the real driver-versus-fairway-finder question. What the round data cannot do is give you a fair sample quickly — you hit maybe four drivers a round off holes that all differ. A range bay can put all three clubs on the same target on the same day, which is the only way the comparison is clean.
lesson.drill: Pick two objects on the range roughly 30 yards apart at your tee-shot distance — that is a generous fairway, and generous is right, because the question is not accuracy, it is trouble. 10 balls with each of driver, 5-wood and 2-iron, rotating one ball at a time rather than a block per club, full routine on every one. Score three columns per club: IN the gap, outside it, and DEAD — a ball so far off it would have been behind trees or out of bounds. Carry the numbers over two sessions before reading them, then compare the dead rate against what the off-the-tee table in Scores says about the same clubs on the course. If the 5-wood and the 2-iron score the same on every column, that is your answer about whether both belong in the bag.

lesson.title: Play nine holes on the range
lesson.body: A bucket of balls is the least golf-like activity in golf: same club, same target, same lie, no consequence, and a rehearsal between every ball. The course gives you one swing, then a four-minute walk, then a different club at a different target. Everything you practise in a block gets easier as the block goes on, which is precisely why block work flatters you and then does not transfer. The fix is not to stop hitting balls, it is to spend the LAST part of every session doing what the course actually asks. This also gives you somewhere to rehearse the thing the Mental tab keeps pointing at: your reset. A bad ball in a block costs nothing, so a block cannot train what you do after one. Nine imaginary holes can — a duffed tee shot means you are now playing a recovery, exactly like a Tuesday.
lesson.drill: Last 20 balls of every range session, no exceptions. Play nine holes of a course you know — say each hole out loud before you hit: the hole, the club, the target, the miss you will not take. Tee shot, then the approach from wherever you honestly judge that ball finished, with the club that distance would actually ask for. One ball per shot, full routine, no re-hits and no rehearsal of the swing you just made. Score it against par and write the number in your phone. Two rules that make it work: never hit two balls at the same target, and when one goes badly, walk the ten yards behind the mat and start the next hole properly. Compare the score to the last three sessions — that number moves with your golf, and a block of 7-irons never does.

lesson.title: Find out where on the face you are actually hitting it
lesson.body: This is the one row on the evolution grid that is nothing but question marks, and a row of question marks is the most useful row on that page: it says what to go and film next. Strike location has NEVER been measured, on any of the four putter heads you have owned. It matters because it is a DISTANCE fault before it is a line fault — an off-centre strike bleeds ball speed, so the same-looking stroke rolls two different distances, and distance control is the open priority that has now decided the fate of two putters. It is also the leading candidate for the Aug 10 scatter. The at-home tape test answers the question indoors on a flat carpet; this is the version that answers it on a real green at the distance where a bad strike actually costs you a hole, because a heel strike from four feet still goes in and a heel strike from thirty feet is a three-putt.
lesson.drill: Foot powder or impact tape on the LINK's face — a light even coat, and re-coat every five balls, because a smeared face reads as a wide pattern that is not there. 10 balls from 30 feet at a hole, then 10 from 20. Photograph the face after each set of five before you wipe it. What you are reading is not whether a strike was centred; it is whether the pattern is TIGHT and whether it is CENTRED, and those are two different answers with two different fixes. Write both in the Putting Lab alongside how far each ball finished from the hole. Do the whole thing again a fortnight later before you conclude anything — one session is a session, not a measurement.

lesson.title: Never the same putt twice
lesson.body: Every lag drill you own is a ladder: fixed distances, several balls from each, working up and back down. Ladders are the right way to CALIBRATE, and the 30-foot grind stays the main event. But a ladder cannot test what the course tests, because on the course you never get a second ball from the same spot — the putt that produces a three-putt is always a first putt from a distance you have not just rehearsed. That is exactly what the app now records: where the first putt started, and how often a hole that started past 21 feet turned into three. This drill is the practice-green version of that number, and it is the honest one. The pass mark is not makes. From 25 feet a make is luck; finishing inside three feet is a skill, and three feet is the distance where the next putt stops being a question.
lesson.drill: One ball. Walk to a spot on the green, no measuring and no aiming practice, and hit ONE putt with your full routine. Then walk to wherever it finished, pick a new hole, and putt from there — so every putt is a first putt from a distance you did not choose in advance. 20 putts. Score one point for every ball finishing inside three feet and subtract one for anything that finishes past six, and estimate the distance of each putt as you walk to it so you are training the read as well as the stroke. Anything above +10 out of 20 is a good day. Log the score and the green speed each time: this number is directly comparable to the three-putt rate from 21 feet and up on your round cards, which is the on-course version of the same question.

lesson.title: Uphill and downhill are two different putts from one distance
lesson.body: Distance control gets practised as if a green were flat, and no green is. The same 25 feet can need two very different strokes, and the miss is not symmetrical: leave an uphill putt short and you have a straightforward eight-footer, but run a downhill putt six feet past and you have the exact putt this whole project is about — a short one, breaking, that you have to hole. That is how a pace error turns into the fault you already have. Most players learn the uphill number and apply it to everything, which is why downhill lags finish long far more often than uphill ones finish short. What you want out of this is not a feel but a RATIO you can carry: how much less stroke a downhill putt of the same length needs on this green today, and how much more an uphill one takes.
lesson.drill: Find a slope you can putt straight up and straight down — same line, same length, about 25 feet. 5 balls up, 5 balls down, alternating rather than in blocks. Measure how far past or short each one finishes in paces and write down the two averages. Then repeat at 12 feet. What you are after is one sentence you can say on the course: on a green this speed, downhill takes about X less and uphill about Y more. Re-run it in the first three minutes of any round on a green you do not know, at one distance only — the ratio changes with green speed, and a number from a fast green applied to a slow one is worse than no number.

sections.t: Your two most expensive holes
sections.k: The 1st and the 3rd cost you a quarter of everything you lost at Wianno, and neither is a hard hole.
sections.b:
Across the five nines of the Jul 9-11 member-guest you played the 1st three times for 6, 6, 5 and the 3rd three times for 5, 5, 4. That is +10 between them, out of +37 for the whole event, off six of the forty-five holes you played.

What makes it worth a plan rather than a shrug is what those holes ARE. The 1st is 319 yards and stroke index 15 - the fourth-easiest hole on the card. The 3rd is a 150-yard par 3 at stroke index 17 - the second-easiest. You are not being beaten by the hard holes here. The 2nd (stroke index 1) you have played in 6, 3, 5, and the 8th (stroke index 3) in three straight pars.

So the two fixes are small and specific. On the 1st, take the driver out of it: 2-iron leaves 114 yards, which is a full 50-degree, and it takes the left miss out of play - both opening drives that got away from you here went hard left, which is the fault the driver film is already chasing. On the 3rd, take one more club than the yardage says and aim at the middle: three plays, no par, and every miss was a dropped shot rather than a disaster.

One honest caveat on the 1st: your record there is also the coldest swing of every round, and the Mental tab has been reporting the opening third as your worst. Warm-up and hole difficulty are confounded on that tee. The 2-iron helps either way.
