Blue tees: OUT 3,031, IN 3,055, 6,086 total, par 35-35-70. Rating and slope off your own GHIN cards from July: 35.4/125 front, 35.1/125 back.

The shape of it: TEN par 4s, FIVE par 3s and THREE par 5s. Five par 3s is unusual and it matters - a third of your scoring chances here are tee shots to a green, in wind, off a Cape links-ish turf. They are 150, 210, 160, 118 and 192 yards, so they ask for an 8-iron, a 4-iron, a 7-iron, a pitching wedge and a 4-iron on your estimated ladder. Nothing longer than a 4-iron, and two of them are wedges or short irons.

Your record on the five: 3rd +1.67, 5th +0.67, 9th +0.67, 11th +1.00, 14th 0.00. So the two SHORTEST of them (the 150-yard 3rd and the 118-yard 11th) are the two you play worst, and the 210-yard 5th - the hardest par 3 on the card - you play better than your average hole. That is a straight aiming-and-commitment read, not a distance one.

The stroke indexes run odds on the front and evens on the back, which is the standard convention and a good sign the card is a real one. Hardest four: 2, 10, 8, 18. Easiest four: 11, 3, 13, 1 - and you have lost eight shots on three of those four.

sections.t: Wind, square greens and firm turf
sections.k: Middle of the green, always - a compact square green in a crosswind has no safe short side.
sections.b:
Sourced, from the course write-ups: a compact, wind-exposed Cape layout with short walking connections, modest elevation change and frequent cross-winds off Nantucket Sound. Fast and firm conditions, a handful of heavily-sloped greens, and a set of square-edged green pads - the 7th is named as one of many square greens on the course. Hole variety leans to shorter par 4s that reward placement and two reachable-for-some par 5s.

What that means for how you play it. A compact green pad with square edges and firm turf is a target that does not hold a shot coming in on a bad line - which is the case for the middle of the green on every approach, and against ever aiming at an edge. Add a crosswind and the short side stops being a place you can get up and down from.

It also means the ball runs. On a firm Cape course the number is not the carry number, and a 3 that lands pin-high finishes long. Where you have a choice between two clubs on a downwind approach, the smaller one lands short and runs on; the bigger one is over the back and dead.

What is NOT sourced and should not be guessed: the individual green slopes, the bunker positions on fifteen of the eighteen holes, and where the wind normally comes from. Wianno is private, there is no published hole-by-hole tour, and no plan can invent them.

sections.t: The holes you already own
sections.k: The 8th, the 14th and the 16th - five plays between them, five pars, and two are rated top-eight hardest.
sections.b:
The 8th: 555 yards, par 5, stroke index 3 - the longest hole on the card and the third-hardest. You have played it three times for 5, 5, 5. That is the only hole at Wianno you have never dropped a shot on, and it is the hardest par 5 out there.

The 14th: 192-yard par 3, stroke index 12. Two plays, two 3s.

The 16th: 402-yard par 4, stroke index 8 - the eighth-hardest hole on the card. Two plays, two 4s.

This is in the plan for one reason: nothing in the app tells you to keep doing something, and it should. Whatever club and whatever line you have been using on those three, that is the pattern to repeat, not to review. The prep list is the 1st, the 3rd, the 12th and the 15th - and none of the three above.

sections.t: Match play, and what your five matches actually said
sections.k: Two of the five were still live at the finish, and both were lost on short putts with a putter that has since gone back.
sections.b:
You played five 9-hole matches here with your brother, Jul 9-11 2026, Blue tees. Of those five, only two were live at the finish - a halve and a one-hole margin. A match lost 2 down was decided by scoring, not by nerve, and the Mental tab is deliberate about not turning those into a closing story.

The two that WERE live are both matches you lost short putts in, with the arc-suited Phantom 7.5 in the bag - a putter that mismatched your straight-back-straight-through stroke and went back on Jul 20. That reframe is the most useful thing the Mental tab has produced: on your own record, your closing problem is a short-putt problem. The LINK is in the bag now and the Short Putts plan is the thing to have read on the way up.

The other card-checked example: the first match (Jul 9 front, 46) is the worst card of the event by five shots, and holes 1-3 went +2, +2, +2 - six over in three holes, against +3 over the first three on each of the other four nines. That is the match where an opponent got into your head. The honest caveat, unchanged: it was also the coldest start of the week, so warm-up and partner are confounded on that one card and neither is established.

Nothing here needs doing on the course. It is here because the Mental tab is off-course by design and this is the course it is about.

sections.t: What is not published, and what to log
sections.k: Twelve of the eighteen holes have no researched note at all - Wianno is private and the hole tours do not exist.
sections.b:
Sourced hole facts, all of them, in full: the 2nd and 8th share a fairway separated by four crescent-shaped bunkers; the 7th is a short left dogleg to a squared-edge green; the 9th carries the northeast corner of Parker Pond; the 12th and 13th have centreline bunkers. That is five holes. Everything else on the hole notes above is your own scorecard.

That is not a gap that more searching fixes. Wianno is a private club with no public hole-by-hole tour, no course-tour video and no published yardage book. Rather than describe holes nobody has written about, those holes carry your record and nothing else - which is the rule this app runs on.

So the way this plan gets better is you. Log the round in the live logger and write a hole note on the 1st, the 3rd, the 12th and the 15th - where the trouble actually is, which side the pin tends to be cut, what the wind was doing. Notes are carried, never parsed: nothing in the app reads them for keywords, but the next time you stand on that tee, the logger prints what you wrote last time under your record for the hole. Four notes turns the twelve blank holes into a real plan over two visits.

Also worth logging in one tap each: putts per hole and how long the putt you holed was. Two of your five matches here turned on short putts and there is no putt data on any of those five cards, so 'missed short putts when it mattered' can be remembered but not checked.

FROM YOUR CARDS. Five 9-hole matches, Jul 9-11 2026, Blue tees, 45 holes, 212 strokes, +37, transcribed from the GHIN cards. briefing.focus: Pete Dye's only New York design, ranked 7th-toughest public course in the country by Golf Advisor's readers, and you have never played it. 6,261 from the Granite tees is the card for your game. Water is in play on six holes, pot bunkers and 14,000 feet of rock wall are in play everywhere, and the greens are small and often crowned — so the whole plan is position off the tee and the middle of every green. There is no record here to lean on: this is research only, and it says take bogey on 2, 18, 8 and 17 without an argument.

sections.t: The tee sheet decision: Granite, not Oak
sections.k: 6,261 from the Granite tees is your card here — the Oak at 6,773 is a different golf course.
sections.b:
Five sets: Black 7,165, Oak 6,773, Granite 6,261, Sand 5,683, Pine 5,151.

Granite is the one. It is the same length as the courses you play well - Lakeside is 6,189, Richter Park 6,547 - and it is the set the hole-by-hole yardages in this plan appear to come from: they sum to roughly 6,270 with two holes estimated, which lines up with the published Granite figure of 6,261. That is an inference from arithmetic, not a sourced tee assignment, so check the card in the pro shop.

Why it matters more here than elsewhere. This course was ranked no. 7 in Golf Advisor's 2020 Top 50 Toughest Golf Courses in the U.S., off 350,000 reader ratings. From the Black tees it is 76.0/150. An extra 500 yards on a Pete Dye course with forced carries is not a stretch, it is a different game - and the holes where you would feel it (the 2nd, the 9th, the 18th) are already the hardest ones on the card.

sections.t: The water, hole by hole
sections.k: Six holes have water, and on four of them it is the approach rather than the drive.
sections.b:
Hunted specifically, because unlike a pin a pond does not move:

1st - water BEHIND the green, behind the horseshoe bunker. Only in play if you air-mail the approach, which makes the long miss the expensive one.
2nd - water on the APPROACH, short of the green, with a bail-out area left. Stroke index 1. Take the bail-out.
3rd - water on the DRIVE. The tee shot has to carry it.
4th - water RIGHT of the green, beyond the right-hand bunkers. Par 3, 139 yards.
15th - a reed-lined POND fronting the green. Par 3, and the green is a shallow sliver, so the front edge is the water.
18th - a LAKE left of the green, at the end of a left-hand bunker chain that runs the whole fairway.

Not water but the same conversation: the 13th green has a deep ravine left with a bunker in the floor of it, and there are wetlands through the property that the 14,000 feet of rock wall runs around.

What is NOT confirmed: whether any of the remaining twelve holes carry water. Absence of a mention in a review is not absence of a hazard, and no published hole-by-hole for this course could be opened directly from here - everything above is from reviews and course write-ups. Treat this list as 'water certainly here' rather than 'water nowhere else', and log what you find.

sections.t: Pete Dye bunkering: position beats distance
sections.k: Missing a bunker into the mounded grass around it is worse than being in the bunker.
sections.b:
Sourced: Pete and Perry Dye's signature volcanic bunkers and mounds work with the natural wetlands, trees and exposed rock; pot bunkers dot whole holes (the 5th and the 16th are both named); bunkers are built with mounds around them, so missing a bunker into thick grass makes the approach harder than being in the sand; and rock walls, two to seven feet high in places, are used as both natural and man-made barriers - the 11th tee is walled on three sides.

The practical version for your game, off your own numbers. Your standing miss off the tee is the drive that leaves no play at the green - the 'Dead' column on the tee-club table exists because of it - and this is the course where that miss costs the most. Four holes on this card have an answer that is not a driver: the 5th (290, pot bunkers everywhere), the 10th (340, woods left and mounded bunkers right), the 12th (337, a fairway bunker to clear) and the 13th (a lay-up after the drive). Take the answer.

The other half is the greens. Two are described as crowned (the 6th and the 9th), one as tiny and perched (13th), one as a shallow sliver (15th), one as long and narrow (11th's neighbourhood). A crowned or perched green does not hold an off-centre shot, which is the case for the middle on every single approach here - and it is the same instruction the Lakeside plan gives for a different reason.

sections.t: The four par 5s are the round
sections.k: 7, 9, 13 and 16 — the only four holes here where a full wedge into a green is a realistic ask.
sections.b:
You carry a finding from two independent sources - your GHIN history and the Wianno member-guest - that you make no birdies on par 5s. This course gives you four of them, and three are gettable in three sensible shots:

7th, 480, sourced as 'a fairly easy par 5'. Driver, 7-iron, 87 yards - a full 56°.
9th, 521, narrow on the second and a crowned green. Driver, 5-iron, 106 yards - a full 50°. This one is a par hole.
13th, 448, drive over Pete's Rock then a PW to 91 - a full 56° into a tiny green.
16th, 494, driver then a 7-iron to 101 - a full 50°, to an elevated green, so club up.

The pattern is deliberate and it is the whole tactic: on every one of them the lay-up club is chosen to leave a FULL wedge, not the shortest possible shot. A 40-yard pitch is the hardest shot in golf and a 90-yard 56° is one of your best. All four numbers come off the estimated ladder, which is not calibrated - so treat them as the shape of the plan rather than as exact.

sections.t: You have never played here
sections.k: No card, no hole record, no notes — everything in this plan is research, and the app will say so.
sections.b:
Pound Ridge went into your Courses list on Jul 29 2026 and you have not logged a round there. That has three consequences worth stating.

The hole cards in the live logger will show this plan's note and NOTHING under 'Last' - there is no record to print. That is expected, not a bug.

The par and stroke index will still prefill, because a reconciled scorecard for Pound Ridge has been on file since Aug 20: par 72, and stroke indexes for all eighteen. Every one of those eighteen pars is independently confirmed by the hole-by-hole review this plan is built from - a par 3 on 4, 6, 11 and 15, a par 5 on 7, 9, 13 and 16, par 4s everywhere else - which is a real check on a card that was assembled rather than photographed.

And the plan gets its second draft from you. Blind tee shots are the specific thing to write a note about here: the 13th over Pete's Rock is blind by design, the 12th needs a carry number nobody publishes, and the 14th needs one too. Write down what you actually took and where it finished, and the next visit starts with your own numbers instead of a reviewer's adjectives.

lesson.title: Your wedge numbers assume a good strike — go and check the strike
lesson.body: The clock system gives you nine numbers and the carry ladder writes them down: PW 122, 50 at 108, 56 at 95, 60 at 80. Every one of those is a CARRY off a good strike, and that is the quiet assumption underneath the biggest scoring pattern you have. Sterling Farms missed twelve greens and seven of them finished SHORT, and a fat wedge is short by a distance nobody can predict — half a groove low costs more yards than a whole club does. So there are two completely different reasons a 95-yard shot finishes at 88, and the wedge matrix cannot tell them apart: either the number is wrong, or the strike was. This drill answers the second one, which is worth doing FIRST, because re-baselining a ladder off a session of thin and fat contact just writes bad numbers down more carefully. The bounce is on your side here — the 50 is an 8-degree F grind, the 56 a 10-degree S, the 60 an 8-degree M — and bounce only works if the club is still travelling down when it reaches the ball.
lesson.drill: Lay a club or an alignment stick on the ground perpendicular to your target line and put the ball just ahead of it, or spray a line in the turf if the range lets you. 10 balls each with the 56 and the PW at a three-quarter swing: the divot has to START at or AFTER the line. Score each set out of 10 for ball-first contact — not for where it finished, and not for how it felt. Under 7 and you have found the short miss, and no amount of clubbing up fixes it. Then hit five more of whichever club scored worse, this time calling out loud before each one whether the last strike was ball-first, fat or thin, and check yourself against the divot: knowing which one you just hit is the skill that lets you trust a yardage on the course.
Two balls, driver, filmed from two angles — before you have hit anything else.
steps: Set the phone on the ground ON the target line behind the ball, lens at hand height.
Ball one: full routine, real target. Do not re-hit it.
Move the phone square to the line, level with the ball. Ball two, same routine.
Write one line on each — start line and curve. Then warm up normally and leave it alone.
Send both clips. Repeat on three separate sessions before concluding anything.
lesson.score: Two clips, both from the FIRST two swings of the day. A warm swing is not the swing that is failing.

steps: Five balls with one club, then switch — never rake a bucket with one club.
Throw out the best and the worst. Average the middle three. That is the CARRY.
Session one: driver, 5-wood, 2-iron, 4 through 9 iron. Session two: PW, 50, 56, 60, and the 5-wood again.
Beside each number write how many of the five you actually struck.
Enter them in the carry ladder, then read the GAPS between neighbours.

Half speed to start. Swing to miss the headcover, from the inside.
The ball will start RIGHT and stay right. That is a pass — path first, face second.

lesson.drill: Address check, then 3 sets of 8 at 80 percent, holding the finish for three.
steps: At address: hinge from the hips, chest tall, a fist between chin and chest.
Hold a little trail-knee flex all the way to the top.
3 sets of 8 with a 7-iron at 80 percent. Hold every finish upright for a count of three.
Film the last set square down the line at hand height.
Compare head height at address against head height at impact. That is the whole fault.
lesson.score: Grade the set out of 8 for balls where the head did not rise. Under 5, drop to 60 percent — posture does not respond to effort.

viz.cap: Side on · the head must not rise between address and impact

lesson.drill: Two sticks: one on the target line outside the ball, one along your toes.
steps: Lay stick 1 just outside the ball, pointing at the target.
Set up to the target the way you normally would, WITHOUT looking down.
Lay stick 2 along your toe line, step back, and look at where it actually points.
That first look is the measurement. Write down which way you were off.
Hit 15 with the sticks down, then take them away and hit 10 more, checking every third.
lesson.score: The ten without the sticks are the real test. Aim only counts when nothing on the ground is holding it.

viz.cap: Top down · set up as normal, THEN look

parts.t: STICK 2 · your toe line — aimed RIGHT?

lesson.drill: Two range markers about 30 yards apart. 10 balls each with driver, 5-wood, 2-iron.
steps: Pick two objects roughly 30 yards apart at your tee-shot distance. That is a generous fairway.
Rotate ONE ball at a time between the three clubs, never a block per club.
Full routine on every ball.
Score three columns per club: IN the gap, OUT of it, and DEAD — behind trees or out of bounds.
Carry the numbers over two sessions, then compare them to the Dead column in Scores.
lesson.score: If the 5-wood and the 2-iron score the same on all three columns, that is your answer about whether both belong in the bag.

viz.cap: Looking down the range · a generous fairway

parts.t: dead — no play at the green

lesson.drill: The last 20 balls of every range session are nine holes, one ball per shot.
steps: Say the hole out loud first: the club, the target, and the miss you will not take.
Tee shot, then the approach from wherever you honestly judge that ball finished.
One ball per shot. No re-hits, no rehearsal of the swing you just made.
Never two balls at the same target.
After a bad one, walk the ten yards behind the mat before starting the next hole.
lesson.score: Score it against par and keep the number. It moves with your golf — a block of 7-irons never does.

viz.cap: Every range session · the last fifth is golf

parts.t: 1 ball per shot · a new target every time

lesson.drill: A club laid across the target line, ball just ahead of it. 10 each with the 56 and the PW.
steps: Lay a club or a stick on the ground square across the line, ball just ahead of it.
Three-quarter swings. The divot has to START at or after the line.
10 with the 56, then 10 with the PW.
Score for ball-first contact — not for where it finished and not for how it felt.
Then five more with whichever scored worse, calling fat, thin or ball-first BEFORE you look at the divot.
lesson.score: Under 7 out of 10 and you have found the short miss. Clubbing up does not fix a fat wedge.

viz.cap: Side on · the divot starts AT or AFTER the line

lesson.drill: Foot powder on the LINK's face. 10 balls from 30 ft, 10 from 20.
steps: Light, even coat of powder or impact tape on the face.
Re-coat every five balls — a smeared face reads as a wide pattern that is not there.
10 balls from 30 ft at a hole, then 10 from 20. Photograph the face before each wipe.
Log how far each ball finished from the hole beside the strike pattern.
Run the whole thing again a fortnight later before concluding anything.
lesson.score: Two separate answers: is the pattern TIGHT, and is it CENTRED. They have different fixes.

viz.cap: The two answers a powdered face gives you

parts.t: An off-centre strike bleeds ball speed — distance before line.

lesson.drill: One ball. Putt, walk to where it finished, pick a new hole, putt again. 20 putts.
steps: One ball only. Walk to a spot — no measuring, no practice putt from there.
Estimate the distance as you walk to it. You are training the read too.
Full routine, one putt.
Walk to wherever it finished, pick a DIFFERENT hole, and putt from there.
20 putts. Log the score and the green speed.
lesson.score: +1 for every ball finishing inside 3 ft, −1 for anything past 6 ft. Above +10 out of 20 is a good day.

viz.cap: Every putt is a FIRST putt from a distance you did not choose

lesson.drill: One slope, one line: 5 balls straight down, 5 straight up, alternating. 25 ft.
steps: Find a slope you can putt straight up and straight down on the same line, about 25 ft.
Alternate — 1 down, 1 up, 1 down — never in blocks.
Measure how far past or short each one finishes, in paces.
Write the two averages down. Then repeat the whole thing at 12 ft.
Re-run it at one distance in the first three minutes of any round on a green you do not know.
lesson.score: One sentence to carry: on a green this speed, downhill takes about X less and uphill about Y more.

viz.cap: Same line, same length · the ratio changes with green speed

parts.t: Run one 6 ft past and it is the putt this whole project is about.

lesson.drill: Balls at 20, 30 and 40 ft. Two putts from each, up the ladder and back.
steps: Drop balls at 20, 30 and 40 ft from one hole.
Two putts from 20, two from 30, two from 40 — then back down. That is 12 balls.
You are not trying to hole them. You are trying to finish inside six feet.
Score a point per ball that finishes inside six feet.
Log the score and the green speed each time.
lesson.score: 9 or better out of 12. This is the main event — pace has decided the fate of two putters.

viz.cap: The ladder · three distances, up and back

parts.t: 2 putts from each · up and back = 12 balls

lesson.drill: A check, not a fix. Metronome at 70–76, 20 strokes at mixed lengths.
steps: Metronome at 70–76 bpm. One click at the top of the stroke, one at impact.
20 strokes at mixed lengths — short, medium, long, in no order.
Every length must take the SAME beat. Only the size of the stroke changes.
Any length that needs a different beat is the one to watch on the ladder.
Once a fortnight is enough. Your tempo is already 2.0:1 — this protects it.
lesson.score: Same two clicks at every length. A length that will not fit the beat is a distance-control fault, not a tempo one.

viz.cap: One beat, three sizes

parts.t: metronome 70–76 · click at the top, click at impact
every length takes the SAME beat — only the size changes

lesson.drill: A tee six inches ahead of the ball on the line. The head must pass over it.
steps: Put a tee in the ground six inches ahead of the ball, on your line.
Make your normal stroke.
After impact the head must pass OVER the tee — and stay below shin height doing it.
15 reps, every session.
It quiets the toe-over release at the same time.
lesson.score: 15 clean passes. This fault closed on film Jul 30 and has stayed closed — this is maintenance, not a repair.

viz.cap: Side on · low and long past the tee

lesson.drill: 20 balls from five feet with the FULL routine on every one.
steps: Five feet, one hole, 20 balls.
Full routine on every ball — the beat count and the trigger included. No raking.
Log makes AND miss direction in the Putting Lab.
Count the LEFT misses separately. That number is the one that matters.
Compare it to your 4–6 ft conversion on the round cards — mat against grass.
lesson.score: 2 or fewer LEFT misses in 20. That is the scoreboard for the whole short-putt project.

viz.cap: Five feet · the left miss is the number

parts.t: 20 balls · full routine on every one

lesson.drill: Around the clock at 5 ft on a sloped hole. Eight positions, one ball each.
steps: Find the fall line through the hole first.
Place 8 balls in a circle at 5 ft — the clock positions.
Before each putt, say the clock position and the break you expect out loud.
Work round the clock. One ball per position.
Note which positions you miss LOW.
lesson.score: The positions you miss low are your read-bias putts. That is the finding, not the make count.

viz.cap: Eight positions · find the fall line first

parts.t: the ones you miss LOW are your read-bias putts
say the position and the break out loud

lesson.drill: Two coin gates on carpet, a target six feet away, 20 putts.
steps: Gate 1 at the ball: two coins just wider than the putter head.
Gate 2 one putter-length ahead: two coins barely wider than the ball.
Target six feet away — a coaster, a table leg, anything.
Set the face BARELY OPEN, exactly as you do on the course. That is the aim picture being tested.
20 putts. Count clean passes through both gates.
lesson.score: Under 15 clean, slow down and watch the FACE, not the ball. Clip the far gate's left coin and you aimed left.

viz.cap: Top down · the far gate is the aim test

parts.t: clip the LEFT coin here = you aimed left
20 putts · count clean passes through both

lesson.drill: Ten balls down a metal yardstick. Streak scoring.
steps: Lay the yardstick on the carpet, ball on one end.
Roll ten balls down it. A ball that stays on for the full length is a hold.
Count CONSECUTIVE holds. One fall-off restarts the streak.
Before work or after dinner — it takes three minutes.
Write the longest streak down.
lesson.score: Beat yesterday's streak. Nothing else on this drill is worth measuring.

viz.cap: The $3 start-line machine

parts.t: a ball that holds the full length is a hold
count consecutive holds · one fall-off and you restart

lesson.drill: Putter head a half-inch off the baseboard, and it stays there — back and through.
steps: Set up with the putter head a half-inch from the baseboard.
15 slow-motion strokes keeping the HEEL that same half-inch away, back and through.
Then 10 at full speed.
Then 5 with a ball rolled at a target along the wall.
Three minutes, every day you don't see a green.
lesson.score: Heel drifts INTO the wall going back = you are pulling inside. Drifts AWAY coming through = an arc is sneaking into a straight stroke.

viz.cap: Top down · the wall does not flatter you

parts.t: half an inch, the whole way
15 slow · 10 at speed · 5 with a ball

lesson.drill: Weekly: five putts face-on, five overhead. Watch them back at half speed.
steps: Film 5 putts FACE-ON — phone at shin height, square to you.
Film 5 OVERHEAD — phone directly over the ball.
Watch them back once at half speed. Once, not five times.
Write one note per session — 'head stayed down 4/5'.
Since Aug 13 there is a third angle: from BEHIND on the line with the laser on and a marked scale at the target. That one measures your AIM, not your stroke.
lesson.score: One note per session and the clips sent in. They land in the Putting Lab like any other filmed session.

viz.cap: Three angles · the third one measures aim

lesson.drill: Metronome at 72. No target, no hole. 20 strokes without a ball, 20 with.
steps: Metronome at 72 bpm. No target and no hole — this is not about where it goes.
20 strokes with no ball at all.
Then 20 with a ball rolled nowhere in particular.
Eyes on tempo only.
If a stroke feels rushed, it was. Restart the count of 20.
lesson.score: 40 strokes on the beat. A restart is not a failure — it is the drill working.

viz.cap: No ball, no target, no result to chase

parts.t: a stroke that felt rushed was rushed — restart the 20

lesson.drill: Ten putts to a target 15 ft +, eyes closed at impact. Call each one before you look.
steps: Target 15 ft or more away. Full routine.
Close your eyes at impact and keep them closed.
Call the finish out loud — short, on it, or past — BEFORE you look.
Score your CALLS, not your putts.
Move the target and do it again.
lesson.score: 8 out of 10 correct calls. If you cannot feel where it finished, you cannot control the distance.

viz.cap: Call it before you look

parts.t: score the CALLS, not the putts

lesson.drill: A target five feet away and a second marker 17 INCHES past it.
steps: Target at 5 ft on the carpet. Second marker 17 inches beyond it.
17 inches is the researched pace for a short putt — firm enough to hold its line through the trodden ring round a real hole.
20 balls. The win is finishing BETWEEN the two, not hitting the target.
Short back, short through, run from the shoulders with the wrists silent.
Watch for the putter head passing your hands — that is the wrist releasing, and it is the half of the pop stroke you are NOT copying.
lesson.score: Balls dying short means the through-stroke is quitting, not that it was merely small. A short stroke that accelerated and one that quit look identical afterwards.

viz.cap: Carpet · finish in the window, do not hit the target

parts.t: 20 balls · still accelerating when it stops

lesson.drill: 20 consecutive hits on a coin-sized target from four feet.
steps: Coin-sized target, four feet away.
Hit it 20 times in a row. A miss restarts the count.
Full routine on the last five — those are the ones with real pressure.
Track the longest streak in your notes.
Mark the streak day done when you finish.
lesson.score: 20 in a row, or the longest streak you got to. The last five are the whole point.

viz.cap: Twenty in a row · a miss restarts it

parts.t: the last five carry the pressure

lesson.drill: Three blocks of ten at five feet on carpet, one dial changed at a time.
steps: Block 1 — conventional grip, your normal stroke. This is the BASELINE.
Block 2 — claw grip, your normal stroke.
Block 3 — conventional grip, the pop stroke.
All three in one sitting, at 5 ft, same target. Write all three numbers down.
Whichever wins gets taken to the 20-ball five-footer on a real green.
lesson.score: Carpet picks the candidate; the green decides it. Changing two dials at once tells you nothing.

viz.cap: One dial at a time, or it proves nothing

parts.t: the winner goes to a real green before you adopt it

lesson.drill: Three minutes, before every laser session. A hardcover book is the square edge.
steps: Lay a hardcover book flat on the carpet, one long edge running at your target.
Set up in your real posture. Put the putter FACE flush against the book's end edge.
Rotate the LASER HEAD until the beam runs down the line onto the target. That is the face, not the shaft.
Mark the clamp with a strip of tape so any movement is visible.
Re-check at the END of the session — 30 seconds.
lesson.score: If the end check fails, throw the session's numbers out. Half-believing them is worse than not measuring.

viz.cap: Top down · square the beam to the FACE

parts.t: tape the clamp · re-check at the end

lesson.drill: Ten balls at a coin six feet away, laser calibrated, a taped scale at the target.
steps: Calibrate the laser to the face first. Always first.
Tape a strip of paper across the line AT the target, marked in half-inches out to four each way. The scale is what turns a clip into a measurement.
Phone behind the ball, low, on the line.
Full routine every ball. Aim by the barely-open feel. Hold still two seconds at address so the beam is readable, then putt.
Log every ball's offset in inches, L or R. Ten numbers and one average.
lesson.score: An average, in inches, for 'barely open' — measured for the first time. Send the clip.

viz.cap: The scale is what makes it a measurement

parts.t: 10 balls · log every offset in inches

lesson.drill: The monthly re-check. Five balls, and most months you do nothing about it.
steps: Calibrate. Target at six feet. Phone behind, on the line.
Five putts with the full routine.
Eyes on the ball and the face — never on the floor. You are measuring, not aiming at a beam.
Read the average offset off the film afterwards.
Under an inch either way is nothing to act on. Put it away for another month.
lesson.score: A bias in the SAME direction across all five is drift — log it in the app before you change anything in the routine.

viz.cap: Under an inch is not a finding

parts.t: five in the same direction is drift — log it

lesson.drill: Every laser session: three clips, about four minutes.
steps: BEHIND — 10 balls, scale taped at the target, phone low and on the line.
OVERHEAD — 5 balls, phone directly over the ball.
FACE-ON — 5 balls, shin height, square to you.
Call the ball number out loud on the behind clips so numbers can be matched to film later.
Send all three.
lesson.score: Three clips is a filmed session and it lands in the Putting Lab like any other. Two clips is a note.

viz.cap: Three angles, four minutes

lesson.drill: Clear the space, check the grip, warm up. Every session, before anything else.
steps: About 8 ft clear all round and a high ceiling. Never near people, lights or a TV.
Normal conventional grip and your REAL posture — it only transfers if the setup matches.
20–30 slow smooth swings before anything hard. At 550 g it is heavier than your driver.
Add a few LEFT-handed swings each session to balance the body.
A cold max swing is how you tweak a back. There is no version of this that skips the warm-up.
lesson.score: Space checked and 20–30 easy swings in before the first hard one. Every session, no exceptions.

viz.cap: About 8 ft clear, all the way round

lesson.drill: 6–8 slow one-handed trail-arm swings to open, then again before every two-handed set.
steps: 6–8 slow one-handed trail-arm swings to open the session.
Then repeat them inside Drill 1, before each two-handed set.
Slow. There is no speed in this one.
Any session where the top feels across the line, go back to one-handed until the drop returns.
lesson.score: One-handed reps between every set, not just at the start. This is the reset that is already working.

viz.cap: Between every set, not just at the start

parts.t: 6–8 SLOW REPS TO OPEN, THEN BEFORE EVERY SET
top feels across the line? back to one-handed until the drop returns

lesson.drill: Warm in one-handed, then 2 sets of 10 two-handed, both directions, dial low.
steps: Warm in with the one-handed reps.
2 sets of 10 two-handed, both directions, dial LOW.
Every session without exception — this one outranks the rest.
If the click is firing early, the load was not patient enough.
Slow the TRANSITION, not the backswing. They are not the same thing.
lesson.score: Two sets of ten, every session. An early click means go back and be more patient at the top, not slower going back.

viz.cap: Which part to slow down

parts.t: 2 sets of 10 · both directions · dial LOW

lesson.drill: 3 sets of 8, listening every rep. The click must live at or past the bottom.
steps: 3 sets of 8. Listen on every rep.
The click should crack at the BOTTOM of the arc, at or just past your lead leg.
A click up in the downswing is casting — the speed is spent above the ball.
Keep the wrists hinged and let the head release LATE.
Log whether the click is firing past the ball yet.
lesson.score: The click at or past the bottom, consistently. You do not need a camera or an opinion for this one — you need to listen.

viz.cap: You can hear this one

parts.t: ✓ at or just past the ball
wrists hinged · let the head release LATE

lesson.drill: 2 sets of 8, straight after the wall and trail-foot-back drills.
steps: Run the wall drill and the trail-foot-back drill from your swing plan first.
Then 2 sets of 8 here, while the feel is still fresh.
Feel the lead hip clear BACK and UP through impact — not sliding toward the target.
The order is the drill. On its own it trains half of it.
lesson.score: Two sets of eight, run immediately after the other two. Doing it cold on another day is a different exercise.

viz.cap: The order is the drill

parts.t: RUN IT WHILE THE FEEL IS FRESH

lesson.drill: 10 slow reps to a PAUSE at the top. No speed at all.
steps: Slow reps to a full PAUSE at the top. There is no speed in this drill.
At the pause, feel the trail elbow point DOWN and stay IN FRONT of your trail-hip seam.
Check in a mirror, or a phone on a tripod: the shaft must point AT the target line, not right of it.
10 reps. Pause and check on every one.
The whippy shaft is why this is worth doing on the 201 — a normal club hides an off-plane top well enough to need film.
lesson.score: Shaft pointing at the line, not right of it, on 10 out of 10. Pointing right is across the line — the fault filmed Jul 26 on both clubs.

viz.cap: Top down at the top · across the line points RIGHT of target

parts.t: trail elbow down and IN FRONT of the trail-hip seam
10 slow reps to a PAUSE · no speed at all

lesson.title: Kill the across-the-line top

lesson.drill: 3 sets of 5 max-effort swings, full rest between sets.
steps: 3 sets of 5 max-effort swings. FULL rest between sets — this is speed work, not conditioning.
Add a few non-dominant-side swings.
Benchmark: the highest dial setting you can consistently trigger. Track it week over week.
Alternate a tempo day (low dial, Drills 1–4) with a speed day. Do not grind both.
Pre-round: 15–20 EASY swings only — a warm-up and a tempo primer, never a speed session.
lesson.score: The highest dial you can consistently trigger, climbing week over week. That is the only number on this drill.

viz.cap: Alternate the days · never grind both

parts.t: 3 × 5 max effort · full rest between sets
pre-round is 15–20 EASY swings, never this

lesson.drill: First 3 minutes of every round: two long putts, looking at the hole.
steps: Two long putts on the practice green. Look at the HOLE, not the ball.
Call the finish spot out loud before the ball stops.
That is it. Two putts, three minutes.
It calibrates the day's speed better than ten mechanical reps do.
lesson.score: Two called finishes before you tee off. Speed is the one thing that changes green to green and day to day.

viz.cap: Three minutes, two putts, before every round

parts.t: eyes on the HOLE, not the ball

lesson.drill: The same flat 10-footer in both directions, with the same stroke.
steps: Find a flat 10-footer on the practice green.
Putt it one way with your normal stroke. Note where it finishes.
Putt it back the other way with the SAME stroke. Note where that finishes.
The gap between the two is the day's grain strength.
Remember it on the course — it is the read under the read.
lesson.score: One number: how much further the ball runs downgrain. Same stroke both ways, or it measures nothing.

viz.cap: Same stroke, both directions

parts.t: same flat 10-footer, both ways, same stroke
the gap between the finishes is the grain

lesson.drill: Nine holes of guessing the break with your feet before you read it.
steps: Stand halfway along the putt, level with the middle of it.
Close your eyes. Feel which foot is lower. That is the break.
Say it out loud BEFORE you do your normal read.
Then read it normally and putt as usual.
Count how often the feet-read was right.
lesson.score: Most players start trusting their feet by hole five. Count the hits — the count is the whole drill.

viz.cap: Read from the low side, feet only

parts.t: count how often the feet-read was right
stand halfway · eyes closed · then read it normally

lesson.drill: The same 12-foot breaker at three different speeds.
steps: Pick one 12-foot breaker and stay on it.
One putt that dies at the front edge. Watch the line it needed.
One that finishes a foot past. Then one two feet past.
Watch how much the line changes between them. Dying speed doubles the break.
Then three at CAPTURE speed on the capture-speed line. That pairing is the one to groove.
lesson.score: Capture speed is about a foot past — it keeps the hole biggest and matches how you practise. Pick the speed first, then the line.

viz.cap: One putt, three correct lines

parts.t: ✓ capture speed: a foot past. Speed first, then line.

lesson.drill: Around the clock at four feet — but find the fall line before you start.
steps: Find the fall line through the hole FIRST. Everything else follows from it.
Place 8 balls in a circle at 4 ft.
Before each putt, say its clock position and the break you expect out loud.
The two balls sitting ON the fall line are dead straight. Know which they are.
This stacks straight onto your 20-ball five-footer test.
lesson.score: Saying the break out loud before each one. A putt you cannot describe is a putt you guessed.

viz.cap: Find the fall line first

parts.t: the two putts ON the fall line are straight
say the position and the break out loud, every ball

lesson.drill: Three swing lengths per wedge, five balls each, at the range.
steps: Feel the three swings as a clock: hands to 9 o'clock (half), 10:30 (three-quarter), and full.
5 balls per swing length per wedge. Ignore the best and the worst; average the middle three.
Three wedges × three swings = nine numbers covering 45 to 110 yards.
Enter them in the wedge matrix in the Bag tab.
Re-check twice a season.
lesson.score: Nine numbers in the matrix. Six of them do not exist yet — only the full swings have ever been written down.

viz.cap: Nine numbers · six of them are still blank

parts.t: six of the nine numbers have never been measured
5 balls per cell · average the middle three

lesson.drill: No ball. Chipping swings that brush the grass with the SOLE. Listen for it.
steps: No ball. Make chipping swings that brush the grass with the sole of the club.
Listen. You want a THUMP, not the scrape of the leading edge.
Your 56° has 10° of bounce and the 50° has 8° — let the sole skid, do not dig.
Then hit 10 chips trying to reproduce that same thump.
Judge it by the sound, not by the shot.
lesson.score: Ten chips that sounded like the practice swings. A scrape means the leading edge got there first.

viz.cap: Listen, do not look

parts.t: no ball first · listen for the sound

lesson.drill: One lie, three clubs, one pin. 50° runner, 56° standard, 60° pitch.
steps: Same greenside lie for all three. Do not improve it between clubs.
Play a 50° runner, a 56° standard and a 60° pitch — all to the same pin.
Note which finishes closest.
Repeat from two more lies before you believe the answer.
The 60° is the one that feels best and finishes worst. That is the lesson.
lesson.score: Nine times out of ten it is the LOWEST-lofted option that was available. Pick the boring one.

viz.cap: Same lie, same pin, three clubs

parts.t: the lowest loft that was available usually wins

lesson.drill: A towel three paces onto the green. Five balls each with all three wedges.
steps: Lay a towel 3 paces onto the green. That is your landing spot, not the pin.
5 balls with the 50°, all landing on the towel.
5 with the 56°, then 5 with the 60° — same towel every time.
Watch how differently they finish from the SAME landing spot.
That difference is what club selection around the green actually is.
lesson.score: Fifteen balls on one towel. If you are chasing the flag instead of the towel, the drill is not running.

viz.cap: One landing spot, three finishes

parts.t: same landing spot · watch how differently they finish

lesson.drill: On every tee next round, say the dead side out loud before you pick a club.
steps: Stand on the tee and find the DEAD side first — OB, water, trees, the drop.
Say it out loud. 'Dead right.'
Only then pick the club and the target, biased away from it.
The fat side is wherever a miss still leaves you a shot.
Log how many penalty strokes you take off the tee, and compare to your average.
lesson.score: Penalty strokes off the tee, down. The order matters — naming the trouble before choosing the club is the whole drill.

viz.cap: Name the dead side before you choose

parts.t: say the dead side out loud BEFORE you pick a club

lesson.drill: One round: aim at the dead centre of every green, whatever the pin is doing.
steps: Every approach, every par 3, for one full round.
Take the number to the MIDDLE of the green. Not the flag.
Club to cover the middle — your standing miss is short, so this is where the two findings meet.
Ignore where the pin is. Completely.
Count greens hit and compare to your average.
lesson.score: Greens in regulation, up. A tucked pin is a way to turn a good shot into a bad score.

viz.cap: The middle, whatever the flag is doing

lesson.drill: Pick your money number. For three rounds, every lay-up finishes at it.
steps: Pick the number — for most players a full gap wedge. For you the PW at 122 or the 50° at 108.
Next three rounds, every single lay-up finishes at that number.
That sometimes means hitting LESS club than you want to. Do it anyway.
A half wedge is the hardest shot in the bag and you have never measured one.
Track proximity from that number.
lesson.score: Proximity from your money number. Three rounds of laying up to a full swing beats three rounds of laying up 'near the green'.

viz.cap: Lay up to a full swing, not to the green

parts.t: next three rounds · track proximity from that number

lesson.drill: From any trouble, play the shot you would bet $100 you can pull off 9 times in 10.
steps: You are in trouble. Before anything else, accept that the score for this hole just went up.
List the options honestly, including the sideways one.
Pick the club and line you would bet $100 you can execute 9 times out of 10.
Nothing fancier. A hero shot that comes off once in four costs more than the bogey did.
Run this rule for one month.
lesson.score: Doubles and others, down. Bogey is not an emergency — the shot that turns it into a triple is.

viz.cap: The $100 question

parts.t: the score already went up — do not let it go up twice

lesson.drill: Nine holes of naming the lie and the correction out loud before every shot.
steps: Before every full shot off a slope, say the lie out loud.
Then say the correction — 'above my feet, it goes left, aim right'.
THEN pick the club. Then swing.
Note on the card where each miss actually finished.
Score the CALLS, not the shots.
lesson.score: The lies where your prediction and the ball disagreed. Those two are the ones to work on — the rest you already know.

viz.cap: Four lies, four corrections

parts.t: say it out loud BEFORE you pick a club

lesson.drill: Never hit two balls at the same target. Twenty balls, twenty targets.
steps: Every ball gets a NEW small target. A specific one — a flag, a post, a patch of grass.
Full routine on every ball, including the walk-in.
No re-hits. A bad one is gone, same as on the course.
20 balls = 20 first swings.
This is the only range format that trains what the course asks.
lesson.score: Twenty different targets in twenty balls. The moment you hit two at the same thing, it has become block practice.

viz.cap: Twenty first swings

parts.t: a new target and a full routine, every ball

lesson.drill: Ten yards to review it. After that, present tense only.
steps: The shot is hit. You get ten yards of walking to be annoyed about it.
In those ten yards: what happened, what you'd do differently. Once.
At the ten-yard mark it is over. From there it is present tense only — this lie, this number, this shot.
Practise it on GOOD holes too, not just after a bad one.
The ritual has to be automatic before it is needed.
lesson.score: Used on a good hole as often as a bad one. A reset you only reach for when you're angry is a reset you have never rehearsed.

viz.cap: Ten yards, then it is over

parts.t: practise it on GOOD holes too

lesson.drill: Three straight five-footers with the full routine. Miss one and start over.
steps: End every practice session with this. Every one.
Three five-footers in a row, full routine on each.
Miss one and you start again at one.
You are not allowed to leave until it is done.
That is the only pressure available to you in practice — use it.
lesson.score: Three in a row, or you are still there. The value is entirely in not being allowed to walk away.

viz.cap: Three to leave

parts.t: three straight 5-footers · full routine on each
✗ miss one and you start again at one
you are not allowed to leave until it is done

lesson.drill: The full pre-shot routine twenty times, at home, with no ball.
steps: Read, one rehearsal beside the ball, step in, trail-thumb press, go.
No ball. Nothing to hit and nothing to judge it by.
Twenty reps, with the SAME beat count on every one.
Time them if you have to. Any rep that runs a different length is the one to watch.
A routine that varies in length is a pace variable, and pace is the open fault.
lesson.score: Twenty reps of the same length. This is the only place the routine can be trained without a result to react to.

viz.cap: The same beat, twenty times

parts.t: READ · REHEARSE · STEP IN · PRESS · GO
no ball · a routine that varies in length is a pace variable

lesson.drill: Putt and chip at home with the thing that grates actually running.
steps: Music on, a timer counting, someone talking — whatever actually gets to you.
Ten balls with the interference for every ten in silence.
Then rehearse the WAIT specifically: stand over the ball doing nothing for a full minute before the stroke.
A full minute. That is slow play in its pure form, and it is what you said sets you off.
The point is not to enjoy it. It is to have done it before it happens to you.
lesson.score: Ten noisy for every ten quiet, and one full minute of standing still. Practising only in silence is practising the easy version.

viz.cap: Practise the version that annoys you

parts.t: then stand over the ball doing NOTHING for a full minute
that is slow play in its pure form

lesson.drill: Draw a line in the practice bunker. Splash sand starting at the line, no ball.
steps: Draw a line in the sand. No ball at all to begin with.
Make swings that splash sand starting AT the line — the club never digs, it skids.
Face slightly open before you grip, ball forward of centre, weight on the front foot.
Then put balls two inches ahead of the line and keep hitting the line.
The club never touches the ball. The sand throws it out.
lesson.score: Sand starting at the line every time, with the ball two inches in front untouched. Your 56° has 10° of bounce — it is built for exactly this.

viz.cap: Side on · hit the line, not the ball

parts.t: the club never touches the ball
let the sole SKID — do not dig the leading edge

lesson.drill: Three targets from one bunker. Five balls each, changing only the follow-through.
steps: Pick a short, a middle and a long target from the same bunker.
5 balls at each.
Same swing, same speed, same entry point, same everything.
The ONLY thing that changes is how far through you go.
Short finish, short shot. Full finish, long shot.
lesson.score: Three distances out of one swing. If you are changing speed to change distance, the drill is not running.

viz.cap: Same swing · three follow-throughs

parts.t: same speed · same entry point · same everything
5 balls each · only the follow-through length changes

lesson.drill: Step on three balls in the practice bunker and play them out.
steps: Tread three balls into the sand until they are half buried.
Close the face — the opposite of a normal splash shot — and set up ball back.
Swing steeply and DIG. Commit to it.
It comes out low and running, with no spin. Expect that and plan where it finishes.
Walk away. There is no version of this shot that stops by the flag.
lesson.score: Three plugged lies played out where it does not count. Learning the shot in advance is what removes the panic when it turns up.

viz.cap: Steep, closed, and it will run

parts.t: it comes out low with no spin — plan for that
learn it where it does not count

lesson.drill: Ten balls from five feet with the Newport 2, then ten with the LINK.2.1.
steps: Five feet, same hole, full routine on every ball.
10 with the Newport 2 — the toe-hang blade. Then 10 with the LINK.2.1.
Read MISS DIRECTION, not feel. Feel is what got the Phantom 7.5 bought.
The arc-suited head should start more of them LEFT against your straight stroke.
Log both numbers, then put the Newport back in the bullpen.
lesson.score: Two miss-direction tallies. You own both sides of this experiment, so it costs nothing to check once and never re-open it.

viz.cap: Miss direction decides it, not feel

parts.t: 10 balls each · then the Newport goes back in the bullpen

lesson.drill: Drag a fingernail across the face. Compare the centre against the heel.
steps: Take the 56° — it does the most work, so it wears first.
Drag a fingernail across the grooves at the CENTRE of the face.
Now do the same out on the heel, where you never hit it.
Grooves the nail does not catch in are worn.
The difference between the two spots is how much life the club has lost.
lesson.score: A nail that catches on the heel and slides at the centre. Worn grooves do not look worn — that is why nobody replaces them in time.

viz.cap: The heel is your control sample

parts.t: grooves a nail does not catch in are done

lesson.drill: At address, hold the club at 3 out of 10. See whether it feels like it could slip.
steps: Take your normal address position.
Deliberately soften the grip to about 3 out of 10 — light enough to feel odd.
That is the pressure you should be able to hold a full swing at.
If at 3 it feels like the club could slip out of your hands, the grips are done.
Check it on the driver and a wedge — they wear at different rates.
lesson.score: A club that stays put at 3 out of 10. Worn grips do not fail by slipping — they fail by making you squeeze, and squeezing kills speed.

viz.cap: Three out of ten

parts.t: feels like it could slip at 3? the grips are done

lesson.drill: Two weeks of noting every approach where you were 'between clubs', and the yardage.
steps: Every time you are between clubs, write the yardage down. On the card, in the moment.
Two weeks. Do not filter — write down every one.
Then look at the numbers. Three or more at the SAME yardage is a real gap.
One at 103 and one at 118 is not a gap; it is two ordinary shots.
A real gap gets fixed by a loft, not by trying harder.
lesson.score: Three or more at one number. Anything less is a bad day, and re-lofting a wedge for a bad day is how bags get worse.

viz.cap: Where the numbers cluster

parts.t: three or more at one number is a gap, not a bad day

lesson.title: The AirBreak: an 8-foot green with the slopes built in
lesson.body:
The mat you just added is closer to a small green than to carpet, and three of its facts change how home practice reads. THE SPEED: it runs about 10 on the stimp meter — one known, repeatable pace, where carpet was always a guess. THE HOLE: a real 4.25-inch cup sunk into the base, so a putt hit too hard lips out the way it would outdoors. A coaster on carpet could never reject a putt, and rejection is the feedback that teaches dying pace. THE PUMPS: eight of them under the turf. Step on one and that section rises; press its release and it drops. Up to about 7.5% of side slope and about 3% of continuous uphill or downhill — more break than most greens you play.

Three standing rules for it. FIRST: flat is a setting. Open every session flat, ten putts with the full routine, before touching a pump — the flat baseline is what makes a missed breaker readable afterwards, because if you miss the flat ones too, the problem is the stroke, not the read. SECOND: it is ONE green speed. Pace learned here is mat pace — carry the habit, not the number, and say ‘on the mat’ when you log a session so a 10-stimp result never masquerades as a reading from a real green. THIRD: eight feet is its whole world. It trains exactly your scoring zone — the left miss, the tap-in band, and the short third putt that turns a lag into a three-putt — and it cannot train the lag itself. The 30-ft ladder still lives on a real green; the mat protects the putts that come after it.

Everything already on this shelf transfers: the coin gate, the yardstick, 20-in-a-row and the pop stroke all run on the mat as written, now with a real hole for a target. The specs above are the maker’s numbers (PuttOut’s product page, confirmed by the review press), not measured here.
lesson.drill: The session opener — flat mat, ten balls, before any pump is touched.
steps: Mat flat: every pressure release pressed, surface checked by eye down its length.
Ball at 6 ft — the middle of your scoring zone. Full routine on every putt, barely-open face exactly as on the course.
Ten putts. Count makes, and note the miss side of every miss.
Only now pump in whatever the session is about — breakers, slope, or the nine-hole game.
lesson.score: 7 of 10 or better flat says the stroke is travelling — go build breaks on it. Under that, or two misses on the same side, stay flat and run the coin gate instead: a break added on top of a leak just hides it.

viz.cap: Side on · step a pump and that section rises

lesson.title: Breakers both ways: the pair that catches a left aim
lesson.body:
A green never gives you the same breaking putt twice — the mat gives you nothing else, and that repeatability is the whole edge. The method does not change from the green-reading shelf: pick the spot where the ball has to enter the break — the apex, or the point on the lip — and hit a STRAIGHT putt at that spot, barely-open face and all. The feel you calibrated is about your start line, never about the hole; on a breaker those are two different directions, which is exactly why a breaker is where an aim bias hides. ‘I misread it’ and ‘I aimed left again’ produce the same miss, and on a course you can never replay the putt to find out which it was.

The mat can split them, because the two break directions treat a left leak differently. On a RIGHT-TO-LEFT putt you borrow to the right; an aim-left leak eats the borrow, the ball starts low and the break drags it further low — the miss is amplified. On a LEFT-TO-RIGHT putt the same leak just adds borrow and half hides. So run them as a PAIR with the same borrow, and read the gap between the two make counts: a stroke problem misses both directions roughly equally, a left-aim leak shows up as right-to-left lagging far behind. That is a diagnosis a practice green can’t run and film can’t see.
lesson.drill: Same borrow, both directions, ten putts each — the gap between the counts is the reading.
steps: Two pumps up on one side, mid-mat. Ball 6–7 ft out: a right-to-left breaker.
Stand behind it and pick the entry spot. Putt STRAIGHT at the spot — full routine, barely-open face on that start line, then let the slope do the rest.
Ten putts. Count makes, and count low-side misses separately.
Release those pumps and pump the mirror side to the same height. Ten more, left-to-right, same distance, same routine.
Write both counts in your notes — the PAIR is the result, not either number.
lesson.score: Counts within 2 of each other: the face is holding on both start lines, so your misses are reads — and reads improve fast here. Right-to-left trailing by 3+ with low misses: the left aim is leaking back. Stop reading break and run the coin gate flat until it passes.

viz.cap: Top down · right-to-left: a straight putt at the spot

parts.t: the spot — aim at THIS, not the hole
aim-left here eats the borrow → low miss, amplified

lesson.title: Downhill is the putt the mat was bought for
lesson.body:
Pace is the open fault — it retired a putter, and at Sterling Farms it handed back three strokes in three-putts. But look at where a three-putt actually ENDS: with a short putt, usually with slope in it, hit by someone still annoyed about the lag. That last putt fits on eight feet of mat, and the mat can tilt it — about 3% of continuous slope either way. Downhill is the direction to overweight, because the cost is asymmetric: leave an uphill putt short and the next one is a flat tap; run a downhill putt three feet past and the next one is another slick breaker coming back. Most players learn one stroke and apply it to both directions, which is why downhill putts race past far more often than uphill ones die short.

The target on a downhiller is DYING pace. A ball arriving dead uses the full width of the cup; one arriving hot has only the middle couple of inches, and this mat will actually lip it out and tell you — feedback a target on carpet was never able to give. Vary the distance putt to putt rather than grooving one number — a groove flatters, variation trains. Two honesty guards. The up-versus-down ratio you learn is a 10-stimp mat ratio, not your Saturday green’s: what transfers is the HABIT of asking ‘up or down?’ before every putt, and the downhill die itself, which is a skill rather than a number. And this drill does not touch the lag — the 30-ft ladder is still unrun and still lives on a real green.
lesson.drill: Five up, five down from mixed distances — and call every putt before you look.
steps: Pump the hole end up: every putt is now uphill. Five balls at 5, 6, 7, 8, then 6 ft — never the same distance twice in a row.
Call each one ‘long’, ‘short’ or ‘flush’ at contact, eyes still down, before you watch it. The call is the rep — being wrong is what recalibrates.
Release, pump the BALL end up the same amount: now every putt is downhill. Same five distances, same calls, dying pace — fall in the front door or stop beside the cup.
Finish with one sentence in your notes: ‘on this tilt, downhill takes about X less.’ The asking is the part that goes to the course.
lesson.score: 8 of 10 calls correct is the pass — you are grading the calls, not the makes. And nothing downhill finishes more than a foot past: a downhiller that races 3 ft by is the lag-into-three-putt pattern, run indoors.

viz.cap: Side on · the same 7-footer is two different putts

parts.t: UPHILL · more stroke · short miss is safe
DOWNHILL · dying pace — a dead ball uses the whole cup

lesson.title: The pump game: nine holes, never the same putt twice
lesson.body:
Block practice flatters you: by the tenth ball from the same spot you are not putting, you are repeating, and the course never asks the same question twice. Random practice tests worse in the session and transfers better to the round — the same reason the practice-green drills say to change something every few balls. The pumps make random practice effortless at home for the first time: one step changes the hole you are playing.

So play nine. Before every hole, change exactly ONE thing — a pump up, a release down, the distance, the line you play down the mat. One change keeps the setup honest (you cannot drift back to a favourite putt) and keeps the game moving. Every ball gets the full routine, because the routine under a FRESH read is precisely the on-course skill — a new putt, read from behind, spot picked, committed. And the game is scored, because consequences are what turn rolling balls into practice: the same muscle as 20-in-a-row, asked a different question. One loud result to watch for: three-putting a hole on an eight-foot mat means the first putt ignored the slope entirely. Whatever that hole’s setting was, it opens your next session.
lesson.drill: Nine holes on the mat, par 18, one pump change between each. Log the total, beat your best.
steps: Hole 1: mat flat, 6 ft. Hole everything out from wherever it finishes — no gimmes here.
Between holes, change exactly one thing: a pump, a release, the distance (4–8 ft), or the line down the mat.
Full routine on every ball — read the new putt from behind, pick the spot, then go.
Count every putt, cap a hole at 3. Par is 18.
Write the total in your notes with the date. The number only means anything against your own last one.
lesson.score: 18 is a par round; 15 or better is a good night. Any 3 gets its setting named in your notes — that configuration is your next session’s opener.

viz.cap: Top down · one hole, nine different questions

entries.note: Face-on is the angle the putting lab has never shot, and this is the drill that shoots it — so it now answers the delivery-unverified fault directly.
Filming the beam is a face-on set, which is exactly what the open delivery-unverified fault is waiting on.
The pace fault names the 30-ft ladder by name as the thing still unrun. This is that ladder, so it is now flagged against the fault.
Calling a putt before you look is distance-control training, which is the open fault — it now says so.
One-handed reps are the confirmed fix-feel for the across-the-line top and the anti-cast move for the over-the-top miss. Both faults are open; neither reached this drill.
Load and wait is the sequencing drill for the over-the-top miss.
The transition drill starts the downswing from the ground, which is the entry point the refined posture fault asks for.
The drill is literally named for this fault and was not tagged with it.
Nought up-and-downs from twelve missed greens is the open short-game fault; using the bounce is the first thing that changes it.
Pick the boring shot — the scrambling decision itself.
Landing-spot control is what turns a chip into a one-putt.
A greenside bunker is an up-and-down chance like any other.
Seven of twelve green misses finished short, and the club candidate for it is exactly this lesson: enough club, middle of the green.

entries.setup: 4 clips · slo-mo · L.A.B. LINK.2.1 · first film on the PuttOut AirBreak. TWO CAMERA POSITIONS, both ON the target line: (1) one clip from the TARGET end, phone flat on the mat looking back — the whole roll and the target disc in frame; (2) three clips on the long strip mat, phone flat directly behind the ball at ball height
entries.finding: One scorable putt, and it is a good one. On the AirBreak the ball starts dead on the mat's own centre line, curves about 1.35 ball-widths — roughly two inches — to HIS LEFT over the back half of the roll, catches the right shoulder of the target disc and dies about a ball past it. That is a break read, started high and paced correctly; it is NOT the old left miss returning, because the curve ACCELERATES as the ball slows, which is what a tilt does and what an off-line start cannot do. The other three clips document the stroke and measure nothing — the ball crests the strip mat within a few frames and there is no line, cup or gate in the picture to measure against. Both positions again look along the target line, so shaft lean, face angle and strike location are all untouched: a third filming day running without the face-on angle they need.
