detail.story:
THE CORRECTION FIRST. This entry was written from ONE clip and said the opposite. On that single putt the ball started on the mat's centre line, curved left and finished near the trainer, and it was written up as a break read and paced correctly. Two more clips of the same setup arrived and inverted it: that putt did not go in, it caught the trainer's left edge and ran on, and it is the middle of three, not the whole of the evidence. The lesson is one this project has learned before on a recounted round — check the example against the record before writing it up, because a sample of one can invert.

WHAT THE THREE PUTTS DID. The mat is in the identical place in all three clips, to within a pixel across ten sampled rows, and the ball is set down within five pixels of the same spot each time. So the three are directly comparable.

C — curves to his RIGHT for most of the roll, then flattens and turns back left, and finishes IN the trainer. A make.
A — starts barely right, is taken left, catches the trainer's LEFT shoulder and runs around the outside of the rim. Comes to rest 0.5 inches left of centre and about 6 inches past it.
B — never moves right at all. Goes left from the first frame and keeps going, still curving when the clip ends. Comes to rest 6.3 inches LEFT and about 5 inches past.

WHY THAT IS A TILT AND NOT A PULL. A ball started off-line runs STRAIGHT, and its distance from the centre grows at a CONSTANT rate. A and B both accelerate away from it: A goes from 0.009 ball-widths per unit of roll in the first half to 0.089 in the second, B from 0.009 to 0.14. Sideways movement per foot rising as the ball slows is a surface, not a stroke. And a fixed tilt is the only thing that explains all three at once — C went the other way because it was STARTED further right, which is what playing the break looks like.

HOW THE NUMBERS WERE GOT, so they can be argued with. Sideways distances are measured against the mat's own centre, which holds one place in the frame for the whole visible run, and are quoted against the ball's own apparent size in the same frame, so perspective cancels and no lens assumption is needed. One check falls out of it and comes back sensible: the mat measures about 25 inches across, which is what a PuttOut mat is. The ALONG-the-mat distances need one real length to anchor them and the mat supplies it: the AirBreak is 8 ft, which read through the perspective makes this a putt of about SIX FEET, with A finishing about 6 inches past the trainer and B about 5. A third check falls out of the same arithmetic and also holds — it puts the phone 25 inches beyond the near end of the mat and 31 inches above it, which is exactly the table you can see at the bottom of the frame. The sideways numbers need no assumption at all; the depth ones are good to about a tenth.

THE PACE READ, which is the useful one. Nothing ran long. Both misses finished five to six inches by on a SIX-FOOT putt — a dying pace, not a firm one — and the holed one stayed in the cup rather than being thrown back out. Worth noticing how that couples to the break: a dying ball takes the most break there is, which is the other half of why A and B got eaten by it. Firmer, or more allowance. That is an inference off three putts, not an instruction. That is the same answer the Aug 10 afternoon gave from a different surface — calibrated, if anything a shade conservative — and it is the first time an INDOOR batch has said it, because it is the first indoor surface in the record that makes the ball curve. A breaking putt is decided by speed. A straight strip hides the error; this mat does not.
detail.limits:
START LINE CANNOT BE SCORED ON THIS MAT. Not with the tilt unrecorded. Aim and break are the same measurement here and there is no way to separate them, so the AirBreak is the wrong tool for the aim question and the right one for pace. If you want start line, film on a flat mat with a printed line; if you want pace, use this.

EVERY CAMERA POSITION TODAY WAS ON THE TARGET LINE — all six clips. That is the plane shaft lean lives in, so the lens looks straight down it and sees nothing. FACE-ON REMAINS THE ONLY ANGLE NEVER SHOT ON THE LINK.2.1, three filming days running.

NO VIEW OF THE FACE, so strike location is untouched for a fourth filming day. Still never measured on any of four putters.

THE THREE BALL-HEIGHT CLIPS SCORE NOTHING. Phone flat behind the ball on the strip mat, slow motion: the head fills the frame, the mat crests a few feet out and the ball vanishes over it within a few frames. No line, no cup, no gate to measure against.

n=3, at one distance, on one tilt that was never written down.
detail.compare:
VERSUS AUG 10 PM (about 20 putts off above-ground cups, nine finishing dead, worst about 4 ft, nothing long): today agrees and adds an indoor voice to it. Two misses finishing five to six inches past a six-footer and one holed is the same 'calibrated, slightly conservative' shape on a fourth surface.

VERSUS AUG 10 MAT (3 putts, 0.8 right / 1.0 left / 0.6 right against a printed line): that batch could score aim because the mat was flat and lined. This one cannot, for the opposite reason. The two are complements, not a series — do not read today's two left finishes as a worsening of that number, because they are not measuring the same thing.

VERSUS JUL 30 (1.5 and 1.7 degrees left on two of three, overhead): no overhead clip today, so nothing here re-tests it.

metrics.name: Path
metrics.verdict: SETTLED — straight back, straight through. Measured on the LINK on Jul 30 from three overhead clips: a quarter to a half inch inside at the top, back on line by impact. Neither Aug 10 batch could see it (the afternoon clips were all oblique, the mat set had no overhead), and it does not need re-testing — this is the finding the whole zero-torque case rests on, and nothing since has argued with it.

metrics.name: Tempo / load
metrics.verdict: SETTLED at 2.0:1 against a 2:1 target — 7 of 8 down-the-line clips landed 1.9–2.1 on Jul 30. Not measured since, and it is now a thing to hold still rather than fix. If you ever catch yourself hitting AT a long putt, that is this drifting, and it will show up as pace before it shows up as anything else.

metrics.name: Early lift
metrics.verdict: CLOSED Jul 30 — at 120 fps the sole held within 0.05–0.08 inches of its address height for the full 83 ms into impact, flat across ten consecutive frames, and never dropped below address height. This was fault number one in every early session. It is the classic fault that comes back quietly under pressure, so it stays on the grid as maintenance, not as a repair.

metrics.name: Start line / aim
metrics.verdict: THE BIAS IS GONE. THE SCATTER IS NOT. Jul 30: 1.5° and 1.7° LEFT on two of three measured putts with one straight — three putts pulling the same way, which is what an AIM error looks like, because aim does not vary between reps. Aug 10 on the mat: 0.8° right, 1.0° left, 0.6° right — mean bias about 0.1° right, which is zero, and the one-way pull did not reproduce once. But the median miss is 0.8° against this project's own 0.5° gate, so it does NOT come off the card. Three caveats stand: n=3, at roughly ±0.5° each; the absence of the bias is the robust part, not the size of what is left; and it was a mat with a printed line, which does the aiming for you. Aug 24 could not score it at all and the reason is worth keeping: the AirBreak makes the ball CURVE, so on it aim and break are the same number and there is no way to separate them. Three putts finished left, left and in — which on a surface falling left is a break-reading result, not an aim one. If you want this row moved, it has to be a FLAT mat with a printed line.

metrics.name: Face at impact
metrics.verdict: NEVER DIRECTLY MEASURED — every reading here is inferred. Jul 30 was a red by deduction: neutral path, square stance, and the ball still starting left, so the face was pointing left at impact. On Aug 10 it was not measurable at all — the head spans about 70 pixels in those clips and 1.5° is under two of them. On a zero-torque head this is the same question as AIM, since the face you set is the face you deliver, which is exactly what the laser audit exists to put a number on. Aug 24 adds nothing: all six clips were shot along the target line, none overhead, none face-on.

metrics.name: Strike location
metrics.verdict: NEVER MEASURED, on any of the four putters owned this month, and since Aug 10 it is the leading candidate for what is left. Heel and toe contact rotate the face in opposite directions, which produces scatter with NO bias — which is the exact shape the mat set came back in. That is an inference, not a finding. The foot-powder tape test settles it in twelve minutes and has been owed since Jul 30. A fourth column of question marks. Aug 24 put six clips on the card and not one of them shows the face. The twelve-minute powder test remains the only thing that settles it.

metrics.name: Pace / distance
metrics.verdict: THE OPEN FAULT, and still the least-measured thing on this page — it has decided the fate of two putters and has never had a number. The one piece of real evidence is Aug 10 afternoon: about 20 putts scored off above-ground cups, NINE finishing dead, the worst about 4 feet, and nothing long all day. That is encouraging and it is not a baseline. The 30-foot ladder — shorts, spread and green speed, twice a week — is what turns this row into a number. Aug 24 is the second real piece, and the first from indoors: three putts at a PuttOut trainer on the AirBreak, one holed and left in the cup, the two misses finishing five to six inches past on a putt of about six feet, which is a dying pace rather than a firm one. Nothing short, nothing long, which is the same answer the Aug 10 afternoon gave on a different surface. Two agreeing reads is not a baseline, and the ladder still has never been run — but the AirBreak is now the practice surface for this fault, because a breaking putt is decided by speed and a straight strip hides the error.

faults.why:
THE priority — and Aug 12 is the first time it has been measured anywhere near a real green, by accident rather than by design. STERLING FARMS, 18 holes on the LINK.2.1: 38 putts, THREE 3-PUTTS (holes 9, 14 and 16), and exactly ONE 1-putt all day — the birdie on 3. Read it honestly in both directions. THE GOOD HALF IS REAL: with only 6 greens in regulation, twelve holes were chip-and-putt, and fifteen of eighteen still finished in two putts or fewer. That is the card's version of Jack's 'made a lot of 5 footers' — they were SECOND putts, holed come-backers, and they are what kept 87 from being 92. THE BAD HALF IS ALSO REAL: three 3-putts is three strokes handed back, and hole 9 was a green hit in regulation turned into a bogey. Jack's report was 'good lags, not dropping 10–20 feet yet'; the card agrees with the second half exactly (one 1-putt) and only partly with the first — lags good enough to two-putt from most places, not good enough to stop three of them running away. WHAT THIS DOES NOT REPLACE: the 30-ft ladder, still unrun. A round tells you the total; it cannot tell you the SPREAD, the green speed, or whether the misses were short or long — the three numbers the ladder exists to capture. Prior evidence stands: the DF3i went back Aug 10 for distance control after three verdicts in eleven days without one calibrated lag session, and the Aug 10 afternoon (~20 putts, nine dead, worst ~4 ft) said calibrated-but-conservative on a second green speed. Tempo is not the missing piece (2.0:1 against a 2:1 target). Stroke length and strike are. Run the ladder with the gamer ball model only.

Aug 24 — CORRECTED, same day, after three more clips of the same session arrived. The first read here was built on one putt and said it finished at the target; it did not. THE FULL BATCH: three putts on the PuttOut AirBreak at a PuttOut trainer — one holed and left sitting in the cup, one caught the trainer's left edge and ran about 6 inches past, one missed 6.3 inches left and finished about 5 inches past — on a putt of about six feet, so a DYING pace rather than a firm one. Nothing short, nothing long. That is the same shape as the Aug 10 afternoon on a completely different surface, which makes two agreeing reads and still not a baseline. The lasting change is the practice surface: the AirBreak is the first indoor mat in the record that makes the ball CURVE, and a breaking putt is decided by speed while a straight strip hides the error. Run the 30-ft ladder outdoors; run the short work on this.

The remaining candidate — but sized honestly now. Never measured on any putter, not once, across four heads. The Aug 10 evening start lines scattered ~0.8° either side of the line with no bias, and on a head that cannot twist, a face pointing a different way each rep is a face being MOVED by contact: heel closes it, toe opens it. That fits. What has changed is the STAKES: a 0.8° scatter still holes out to nearly eight feet, so as a LINE fault this is no longer costing strokes and does not need chasing. The reason to run the test anyway is PACE — an off-centre hit bleeds ball speed, so the same stroke finishes short and the lag spread widens, and pace is the fault that just cost a putter and has never been measured. Second nudge from the same day, also about pace, not line: the blue ball scattered 1.2–1.5 ft on putts the white killed from the same spot with the same putter. Twelve minutes — tap test for the sweet spot, foot-powder sheets from 5 ft and 30 ft, and the 30-footer is the one that matters. Run it with the barely-open address. Read the result as distance-control data. 

Aug 12 adds a reason to hurry: 38 putts and three 3-putts over 18 holes is the pace fault showing up on a scorecard, and the twelve-minute test is still the cheapest thing that could explain it. The LINK's return window is open and the deadline is still unknown.

Aug 24 adds nothing, and that is the finding. Four more clips, not one of them showing the face: both camera positions sat ON the target line. This is now four filming days without a view of contact on a fault that has never been measured on any of four putters. The twelve-minute test — tap for the sweet spot, foot-powder sheets from 5 ft and 30 ft — is still the only thing that settles it, and it is still cheaper than any of the film shot since.

Aug 24 adds nothing, and that is the finding. Six clips, not one showing the face — both camera positions sat ON the target line. Four filming days now without a view of contact, on a fault never measured across four putters. The twelve-minute test — tap for the sweet spot, foot-powder sheets from 5 ft and 30 ft — is still the only thing that settles it, and it is still cheaper than any of the film shot since.

Open, and Aug 10 could not touch it — twice in one day. The afternoon's 23 clips were all oblique; the evening's six were all ON the target line, which is right for start line and blind to shaft lean, because lean lives in the plane those cameras look straight down. Face-on is now the ONLY angle never shot. What it has to settle: the Press Pistol 2° went back with the DF3i, so the LINK's Pistol 0 supplies no lean at all — shaft vertical at address, hands ~1.35" behind the ball — and the soft press is now the ONLY lean in the stroke. The 'don't double-count the lean' arithmetic is retired; consistency replaces it, because a press that varies is a launch that varies, which is a pace that varies. One slo-mo face-on set gives lean at address versus impact AND ball position rep to rep in the same clips. Whatever the tape shows IS the press now, with no built-in 2° to subtract.

WIDENED Aug 12 — the same clip now owes four things, not two, and two of them are new. HANDLE HEIGHT: one inch of hand lift on a 34" putter is arcsin(1/34) ≈ 1.7° of presentation change, about fifty times the 69°-vs-70° build tolerance, which settles which of the two is worth thinking about — film already has you presenting ~68° against a 69° build. Measure the SPREAD across reps, not the average. LOW POINT and attack angle: where the head bottoms out relative to the ball is a distance-control input, and pace is the priority fault. And one flag to settle before anything else: an outside read of the face-on footage put the ball at or near stance CENTER rather than forward of it. Medium confidence off 30 fps, and it contradicts the live rule of 1–2 ball-widths inside the lead heel — so it is a question, not a finding. If it is true it is a PACE fault, not a line fault: a low-loft putter met at or before low point launches down, skids, and rolls out inconsistently. Related correction: the putter's loft is UNCONFIRMED. No retailer and no L.A.B. page publishes one, so the 2° this project quotes is an estimate. It does not change what the clip has to measure, but it does mean the de-lofting arithmetic downstream of it is softer than it reads.

Aug 24 — blind for the third filming day running. All six clips were shot ALONG the target line: three from the target end looking back, three from directly behind the ball at ball height. That is the exact plane shaft lean lives in, so the lens looks straight down it and sees nothing. FACE-ON REMAINS THE ONLY ANGLE NEVER SHOT ON THE LINK.2.1. Phone on the floor beside the mat, level with the ball, square to the stance line, one slo-mo set — that single clip gives lean at address versus impact AND ball position rep to rep, and nothing else on the filming list is owed as long.

DOWNGRADED Aug 10 — off the top of the card, and the reasoning is worth keeping because the old gate on this line was wrong. THE CRUX IS THE SIGN, NOT THE SIZE. Jul 30: 1.5° LEFT, 1.7° LEFT, one straight — three putts pulling the SAME way. Aug 10 pm: 0.8° right, 1.0° left, 0.6° right — mean bias ≈0.1°, i.e. zero. Aim doesn't change between reps, so a one-way pull is what an aim error looks like, and it did not reproduce on any of the three. The founding premise of this entire putter saga was a DIRECTIONAL claim — 'signature miss: left on short putts' — and a directional claim is a claim about bias. On the evidence available, that bias is gone, and it went away after a setup change Jack found himself, not after any of the four putters.

IN STROKES, WHICH IS THE ONLY UNIT THAT MATTERS. Capture at the hole is ±1.29" (4.25" cup, 1.68" ball, dying speed). A 1.6° bias puts the ball outside that from 3.8 ft — so the old miss started costing strokes at four feet, which is exactly where the 'left on SHORT putts' signature came from. A 0.8° miss holes out to 7.7 ft. At 0.6° it's 10.2 ft. So the residual has moved start line out of the range where an 8.5 handicap loses shots to it: beyond eight feet, make rates are governed by pace and read, not by a degree of face angle.

THE 0.5° GATE IS RETIRED — it was a bad standard and it was mine. Half a degree is around the level tour putters hold, it was being applied to a phone-on-a-mat measurement carrying ±0.5° of its own error, and it implied a precision nobody should be chasing. Worse, it pointed at the wrong quantity: it gated on magnitude when the thing that was actually broken was direction.

AND THE RESIDUAL IS AN UPPER BOUND, not an estimate. Measurement noise can only ever INFLATE apparent dispersion — it cannot hide scatter that exists. So with ±0.5° of method error sitting inside an observed ~0.8°, the true dispersion is 0.8° or better, quite possibly nearer 0.6°. Jack's read that these are small numbers is correct and, if anything, understated.

WHAT'S LEFT TO DO, and it is small: confirm the bias stays gone away from a printed line — five putts at a coin on a real green, filmed from behind. That is a check, not an investigation. If the pull is still absent, this fault closes and start line stops being a thing this project tracks.

ADDED Aug 12, for if it comes back. Plugged In Golf's reviewer, arriving at the LINK.2.1 from other L.A.B. models, reported a run of highly repeatable PULLS in his first session that resolved once he adapted to the conventional grip. Same model, same direction, and you changed to this head on Aug 10 — so a returning left miss is an ADAPTATION pattern first, ahead of the fitting or the head. One competing mechanism was examined and does not fit. Raising the handle presents the putter more upright (toe up), which on a lie-angle-balanced head breaks torque neutrality and is argued to close the face. But that argument is derived from L.A.B.'s design principle rather than any L.A.B. document, and the direction is wrong for you: film measured your presentation at ~68° against a 69° build — flatter, toe DOWN — which under the same mechanism predicts a miss RIGHT. Handle height still matters, but as consistency (1.7° per inch, measured as spread), not as an explanation of the old pull.

CLOSED Jul 30 ✓. At 120 fps and 37.5 px/inch the sole held within 0.05–0.08" of its address height for the full 83 ms into impact, flat across ten consecutive frames, and never dropped below address height. Measured on the LINK, the head still in play, so it carries cleanly. Wants two more slo-mo strokes on sample size — the owed face-on set gives them for free, which is one more reason to shoot it.

CLOSED Jul 30 ✓ — overhead film measured the toe line 0.6°, 2.9° and 3.6° CLOSED to the target line across three reps. Never open. Worth re-reading against the Aug 10 find: this measurement is what ruled the feet out and sent the search higher, which is exactly where the answer turned out to be.

briefing.focus: Every putting question worked through end to end, one per section, newest first. This is the reference shelf, not the routine — nothing here tells you what to do on a putt. Tap a section to open it; each one says what was asked, what checked out, what did not, what changed in the other plans, and what is still unmeasured.

sections.t: Aug 24 2026 — Three putts on the AirBreak: a mat that falls left, and a one-putt conclusion that had to be withdrawn
sections.k: Two of three missed LEFT and it is still not the signature miss — the surface falls that way, and the one putt he started far enough right went in; the section also records how a read written off ONE clip inverted when two more arrived.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. Six clips arrived on the LINK.2.1 — three of them the first film ever shot on the PuttOut AirBreak mat, at a PuttOut Pressure Putt Trainer. What do they measure?

WHAT CHECKED OUT. The three AirBreak clips are one comparable set: the mat sits in the identical place in all three, to within a pixel across ten sampled rows, and the ball is set down within five pixels of the same spot each time. Nothing moved. Three putts, three outcomes:

C — runs to his RIGHT for most of the roll, then flattens and turns back, and finishes IN the trainer. A make.
A — starts barely right, is taken left, catches the trainer's LEFT shoulder and runs around the outside of the rim, coming to rest half an inch left of centre and about 6 inches past it.
B — never moves right at all. Left from the first frame, still curving when the clip ends, and comes to rest 6.3 inches LEFT and about 5 inches past.

ONE SURFACE EXPLAINS ALL THREE. A ball started off-line travels a STRAIGHT line and its distance from the centre grows at a CONSTANT rate. A and B both accelerate away: A from 0.009 ball-widths per unit of roll in the first half to 0.089 in the second, B from 0.009 to 0.14. Sideways movement per foot rising as the ball slows is a surface, not a stroke. And a single tilt falling to his LEFT is the only thing that fits all three at once, because C only went the other way after being STARTED further right — which is what allowing for break looks like. So the difference between the three is how much of it he played: C enough, A not quite, B none.

WHY THIS IS NOT THE SIGNATURE MISS. Two of three finished left, on a project whose whole story is a left miss, and the temptation is obvious. But on a surface that falls left, finishing left is what UNDER-READING THE BREAK looks like, and the one putt that allowed enough went in. The tilt was never recorded, so aim and break cannot be separated on this mat at all — which is the real conclusion below.

WHAT WAS WITHDRAWN, and why it is left on the record. The first version of this section was written from ONE of the three clips, before the other two arrived. It said the ball started on the centre line, took the break and finished at the target, and it called that a putt read and paced correctly. It was wrong on the outcome — that ball never went in, it caught the left edge and ran on — and wrong on the conclusion, because one putt cannot tell a played break from an under-read one. The same trap is already in this log's Aug 13 mental-game work under a different name: check the example against the record before writing it up, because a sample of one can invert. Here the record arrived four minutes later.

HOW THE NUMBERS WERE GOT. Sideways distances are measured against the mat's own centre, which holds one place in the frame for the whole visible run — which is also what proves the phone was square rather than cocked — and are quoted against the ball's own apparent size in the same frame, so perspective cancels and no lens assumption enters. Two checks fell out and both came back sensible: the mat measures about 25 inches across and the phone sat about 30 inches above it. ALONG-the-mat distances need one real length to anchor them, and the mat itself supplies it: the AirBreak is 8 ft, which read through the perspective makes this a putt of about SIX FEET and both misses five to six inches past. A third check falls out of the same arithmetic and also holds — it puts the phone 25 inches beyond the near end of the mat and 31 inches above it, which is exactly the table visible at the bottom of the frame. The sideways numbers need no assumption at all; the depth ones are good to about a tenth. And the pace that follows is worth stating: five to six inches past a six-footer is a DYING ball, which is also the ball that takes the most break — the other half of why A and B were eaten by it.

WHAT CHANGED IN THE OTHER PLANS. The stroke instructions are untouched — nothing here changes what he does over a putt. Three things moved instead. The session entry was rewritten in place rather than duplicated, per the one-session-per-day rule. The evolution grid gained a fourth column, 'Aug 24 AirBreak' — a tick on nothing, a dash on five rows, a question mark on strike location, and a '~' on Pace, which is the one row that moved. And the diagnosis card's pace fault now carries the AirBreak result and, more usefully, a change of practice surface: this mat is the first indoor one in the record that makes the ball curve, and a breaking putt is decided by speed while a straight strip hides the error.

THE STRUCTURAL FINDING, which outlives the three putts. ALL SIX clips were shot ALONG the target line — three from the target end looking back, three from directly behind the ball. Shaft lean lives in the plane those lenses stare down, so all six are blind to it; strike location needs a view of the face and got none; face angle needs an overhead or a printed line and got neither. Three filming days running have now missed the one angle the open faults ask for. And the AirBreak adds a rule of its own: it is the WRONG mat for the aim question, because on a breaking surface aim and break are one number, and the RIGHT one for pace, for exactly the same reason. Flat mat with a line for start line; this one for speed.

NOT MEASURED: the mat's tilt, never recorded, which is why the two inches of break has no scale behind it and why start line cannot be scored here; the putt's length, estimated only; strike location, still zero for zero across four putters; shaft lean at impact; face angle at impact; and the 30-ft ladder, unrun since it was written.

sections.t: Aug 14 2026 — The loft is confirmed at 2°, and the grip was never a Pistol 0
sections.k: Two of the three specs flagged as guesses got settled off L.A.B.'s own page and a look at the putter — the loft estimate was right, the grip name was wrong, and neither one changes an instruction.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. Aug 12 flagged three specs this project had been treating as fact without a source — loft, as-built length, head weight — and one contradiction: the app named an L.A.B. Pistol 0 grip while retailers listed a Lamkin Deep Etched, left as something to go and look at. Two of the four got answered on Aug 14, off L.A.B.'s own LINK.2.1 custom build page and a direct look at the putter.

WHAT CHECKED OUT — THE LOFT. L.A.B. publish it in the SPECIFICATIONS panel of the custom page: EFFECTIVE LOFT: 2 DEGREES. The 2° this app has carried since Jul 30 was right.

Be precise about what that vindicates. The Aug 12 audit was still correct to flag it — at the time the number had no locatable source, and a claim whose source cannot be found is folklore whether or not it happens to be true. What was wrong was the SEARCH, not the scepticism: the figure sits in a collapsed accordion on the CUSTOM page, and every search on Aug 12 went at the stock page and the retailers. The lesson is where to look, not to trust an unsourced number next time.

Three plans were hedging that figure — how much a press de-lofts, whether hands ahead drives the ball, what '0° lean delivered' actually delivers. They can stop hedging.

THE SAME PANEL, THREE MORE FACTS. 303 stainless head, black PVD finish. Lengths 28–38" (shaft dependent). Lie angles 65–74°. That last one partly answers an Aug 12 sub-question: 70° was orderable, so 69° as-built was not L.A.B. reaching for the nearest available station. Whether it was a deliberate build choice or a tolerance outcome against the 70° target is still unanswered — and still irrelevant, at 0.035° of face aim.

WHAT DID NOT — THE GRIP. It is a LAMKIN DEEP ETCHED, confirmed by looking at the putter. The app said L.A.B. Pistol 0 from Jul 30 to Aug 14, written down as 'stock spec confirmed by research'. Fifteen days wrong.

NOTHING DOWNSTREAM CHANGES, and it is worth saying WHY rather than just asserting it. Every use of that name in this project was a stand-in for exactly one property: zero built-in lean. The Lamkin Deep Etched has zero built-in lean too. So the geometry the plans describe — shaft vertical, hands about 1.35" behind the ball's centre, the DF3i's 'hands EVEN with the ball' cue dead and never to be carried across — is untouched. And it was never resting on the label in the first place: Jul 30 film measured the shaft dead vertical and repeatable to 0.3° across 59 frames. Film is king, and here the film was right while the label was wrong — which is the cleanest demonstration of that rule this project has produced.

WHAT CHANGED IN THE PLANS. The bag spec and a dated history row carry the corrected grip and the confirmed loft. GRIP & POSTURE and SWING THOUGHTS both named the Pistol 0 and now don't — text only, no instruction moved. The saga section of this log keeps its original wording with a SINCE UPDATED line appended, because a log records what was believed at the time.

STILL UNMEASURED — and these two matter more than the loft did. AS-BUILT LENGTH: 34" was targeted and has never been confirmed, and it is the denominator in the handle-height number (1" of hand lift = 1.7° at 34", roughly fifty times the lie tolerance). HEAD WEIGHT: never known on any of the four putters owned this month, and the most direct lever there is on distance control, which is the open fault. Neither is a catalogue fact. That is precisely why a product page could settle the loft and cannot settle these — they are build-order facts, and they need L.A.B. support or a shop with a scale.

SOURCES. RESEARCHED — labgolf.com, LINK.2.1 custom putter page, SPECIFICATIONS panel: loft, head material, finish, length range, lie range; read Aug 14 2026. OBSERVED — the grip, by looking at the putter.

sections.t: Aug 14 — THE FORWARD PRESS, BACK BY DECISION
sections.k: The press is yours again by choice; it is only compatible with this putter if it RECOVERS, and that it recovers is unmeasured.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. Jack: "I'm gonna go with the forward press for putting trigger again — feels the best of them all, before the takeaway." He had run the shelf of triggers from the Aug 13 workshop and picked one. Which trigger he runs is his call and is not overridable by film; whether it costs him anything is not.

WHAT IT COLLIDED WITH. Three live rules said the opposite, in three different plans: GRIP & POSTURE's "NO FORWARD PRESS. Shaft VERTICAL at address and VERTICAL at impact"; the ROUTINE plan's "FORWARD PRESS stays out permanently"; and SHORT PUTTS' "SHAFT STILL VERTICAL — a rap that leans forward delofts a face with little to give." Leaving any of those standing would have left two live sources for one instruction, so all three were changed in the same pass.

WHAT CHECKED OUT — the distinction that resolves it. A forward press is two different moves sharing a name. A press that RECOVERS is a trigger: the hands go forward, the shaft returns to vertical as the stroke starts, and the ball is struck with zero lean. A press that is HELD — where the stroke begins from the pressed position — leaves the shaft leaning at impact, which delofts and drives the ball into the turf. Jack described a trigger run BEFORE the takeaway, which is the recovering kind, and that version conflicts with nothing the film has established. So the rule did not have to be abandoned, only re-scoped: the vertical-shaft requirement was always really about IMPACT, and 'vertical at address' was a proxy for it that only held while nothing moved.

WHAT DID NOT CHECK OUT — the ban's own footing. The Aug 10 removal was not measured either. It rested on two things: the deloft arithmetic, which this project already corrected on Aug 13 when it found that the ~2° of loft is an ESTIMATE (no retailer and no L.A.B. page publishes a figure for this head), and the observation that a VARYING press is a varying pace. The second one survives intact and is the strongest guard on the new trigger; the first is directional rather than exact. So this is not film being overturned by feel — it is one unfilmed preference replacing another, which is worth stating plainly.

WHAT CHANGED ELSEWHERE. ROUTINE: the trigger rule, the trigger section and step 6 now name the forward press, and the trail-thumb press is out (one trigger, never two). GRIP & POSTURE: the NO FORWARD PRESS rule is retired and THE SHAFT section re-scoped to impact. SHORT PUTTS: same re-scope, plus a new warning that press-plus-pop is the highest-risk pairing on the card — a short firm rap is the stroke with the least time to give the lean back, so if a scuff shows up anywhere it shows up inside six feet first.

WHAT IS STILL UNMEASURED. That the press recovers at all — nobody has filmed it. The size of the press, which has no number on it and will drift exactly the way 'barely open' has drifted for weeks. Whether it changes pace, which matters more than usual because PACE CALIBRATION is the open fault and a leaked lean finishes putts SHORT. Two detectors already exist and neither needs new equipment: the face-on clip (shaft angle at address, at the top of the press, and at impact — matching address and impact is the pass) and the 30-ft ladder that is already the standing work, where a press leaking lean shows up as shorts that were not there before.

SOURCES. Jack's own decision, Aug 14, reported as a feel ('feels the best of them all'). Everything else here is prior project record: the Aug 10 press removal and the Press Pistol 2° that left with the DF3i; the Aug 13 loft-estimate correction; the Jul 30 film establishing a vertical shaft repeatable to 0.3°; and the open pace fault. No new measurement was taken today.

SINCE UPDATED (Aug 14, later the same day): this section leans on the loft being an ESTIMATE when it weighs the old ban's footing. It was confirmed at 2° hours afterwards — L.A.B. publishes 2° effective loft for this head in the SPECIFICATIONS panel of the LINK.2.1 custom build page — confirmed Aug 14, so this is a spec now, not an inference. The estimate turned out to be correct, so the reasoning above is unaffected: the ban rested on arithmetic that is now sourced rather than inferred, and the decision to run a press that RECOVERS is the same decision either way. What changes is that 'the margin is not measured' is no longer true, and the ROUTINE and SHORT PUTTS plans were updated to stop saying it.

sections.t: Aug 14 2026 — The pre-LINK film was deleted. Everything it measured is here.
sections.k: Eight putting sessions on three putters you no longer play were cleared out — this section keeps every number they produced, because two of them still underpin decisions you are living with.
sections.b:
WHAT HAPPENED. Jack cleared the film room of every putting session shot on a putter that is not the LINK.2.1 — the Phantom 7.5, the Newport 2 and the DF3i. Eight sessions, Jul 17 through Jul 21. His call and a reasonable one: he plays one putter now and frame-by-frame breakdowns of retired gear are not what the film room is for.

WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS ANYWAY. Two of those sessions are still load-bearing. The conclusions live on in the evolution grid, the faults and the plans, but the EVIDENCE lived only on the rows that were deleted, and a claim whose source has been thrown away quietly becomes folklore. So the numbers are written out here in full.

THE TWO THAT MATTER MOST.

(1) THE SBST CONFIRMATION — the reason you play a zero-torque putter at all. Jul 18, 9 clips overhead + down-the-line: path confirmed STRAIGHT, straight-back-straight-through. Same day, 5 more overhead clips across 3× Phantom 7.5 and 2× Newport 2: path straight on BOTH putters, face square through impact, no visible toe-over, balls starting dead on the centre line. That is the finding the whole equipment case was built on — an arc-balanced head fights a straight stroke — and it was measured on the two arc putters, which is precisely what made it convincing. It has never been re-run on the LINK because it has never needed to be.

(2) 8 OUT OF 10 FROM FOUR FEET — Jul 20, DF3i, conventional grip, 10 balls on the return mat. All 10 start lines clean, no face-flip. The signal was at ARRIVAL: 2 misses and 2 lip-hangs, all four on dying pace, both misses on the pull side. Read at the time as soft-pace drift rather than a stroke fault. This is the ONLY scored putting benchmark in the entire project, and it is on a putter that went back — so the 20-ball five-footer in the Short Putts plan has no prior number to beat, only this one for context, and it was hit from four feet rather than five with a different head in hand. Treat it as a marker, not a baseline.

THE REST, in one line each. JUL 17, ground-level close-up, 3 strokes: tempo ~1:1, face closing, early lift, contact centred. JUL 18, face-on / near-DTL, 2 strokes: path near-neutral, start line on centre, early lift PRONOUNCED. JUL 18 baseline re-analysis of all 10 original clips (Phantom 7.5, three angles): early lift documented from all three — steep rise going back, head hanging high after impact, exiting the frame upward in the side view; old backswing ≈0.40s against ≈0.65s later the same week, a ~60% longer load; path straight and on-line in every old overhead, so the stroke's bones were always good; face-closing too subtle to confirm at that frame rate. JUL 18, DF3i first filmed reps, 5 eye-level overhead clips: start line dead centre 5 of 5, no left pull anywhere, tempo 0.55s back / 0.23s down ≈ 2.4:1. JUL 21, DF3i, 5 ground-level DTL clips through a tunnel-and-gate drill: start line on the centre line 5 of 5, gated centre every time with no left leak, face square through impact, and the first ground-level look at head height — the head stayed low and extended down the line, none of the abrupt lift-and-hang from the baseline clips.

WHAT THIS CHANGES ABOUT LIVE FINDINGS: nothing. Path SETTLED, tempo FIXED at 2.0:1, early lift CLOSED — all three were re-measured on the LINK on Jul 30, which is a session that survives. The pre-LINK film was the road to those answers, not the answers themselves.

ONE THING TO KNOW ABOUT THE EVOLUTION GRID. Its five columns — S1, S2, S3, S4, BL — ARE these deleted sessions, so the Putting Lab's stroke-evolution table is now entirely pre-LINK and stops before the putter you play. It still reads correctly as history. Rebuilding it on the Jul 30 and Aug 10 LINK sessions is a separate decision and has not been made.

ALSO KEPT ON PURPOSE, and worth saying since they involve retired putters: the AUG 1 Beekman entry (DF3i, ON COURSE, no film — it is the 'pace felt dialled' report that un-benched a putter returned nine days later, and this project keeps that as a standing counter-example to trusting feel), and the AUG 10 session, which is a DF3i-vs-LINK A/B and therefore the comparison that decided the putter, as well as the source of the current start-line numbers.

sections.t: Aug 14 2026 — Why reading got a plan when nothing measures it
sections.k: The routine's first step handed off to nothing, and reading is the front half of the pace problem — two structural reasons, and no measured one.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. The putting lab already had five plans in a clean situation split. Was green reading a real gap or just a missing chapter?

WHAT ARGUED AGAINST IT. Nothing in the record measures Jack's reading. No fault, no film, no logged mis-read. By the standard this project usually applies, that is thin ground for a page — and a plan built to complete a set is exactly the kind of padding the round-prep rules warn about.

WHAT DECIDED IT, and neither reason is 'greens get read'. First, the Routine plan opens with READ IT FROM BEHIND and then handed off to nothing at all — the first step of his own routine was the only one without a page behind it, while grip, the short stroke and the long stroke had all been split out. Second, SPEED PICKS THE LINE: a putt has a different line at every pace, so the read cannot be settled before the pace is chosen. That makes reading the front half of the pace problem, and pace is the one open putting fault on the card.

HOW IT IS WRITTEN AS A RESULT. Labelled general best practice on every section, with the one exception called out — 'inside six feet, stop reading once you have the fall line' exists because of his documented short-putt history, not because it is standard advice. It deliberately sets NO pace of its own; the two stroke plans own that, and a third source for pace is how a retired cue survives.

WHAT WOULD MAKE IT HIS. Logging which SIDE missed putts finish on. Clustering low means the read is under-done. Clustering left inside six feet is aim, and that belongs to the laser audit rather than to this page.

NOT MEASURED: everything on that plan, plus the 8–9 stimp its speed talk is calibrated against, which remains an estimate. Full cross-lab reasoning — including the four plans that were rejected — is in the SWING workshop log, since the review covered both labs at once.

sections.t: Aug 14 2026 — The laser: what it can measure, and the trap that came in the box
sections.k: It can finally put a number on ‘barely open’ — but only as a measuring device, only after it is calibrated to the face, and only if you never look at the beam.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. Jack bought a PUTTLAZR green-line indoor putting trainer (Aug 13). What can it actually settle, and what should it be kept away from?

WHAT IT IS. A laser module that clamps to the putter shaft with a 360° adjustable head and throws a green line forward; the kit also carries a small tripod stand so the beam can be used as a fixed reference instead of a club-mounted one. NOTE ON SOURCING: the product's own listing was unreachable from here (blocked at the network), so these specs come from retailer and review pages for the same device plus the box in his hands — anything the user guide contradicts, the user guide wins.

WHAT IT CAN GENUINELY SETTLE, and it is the biggest open question in the project. Aug 10 reclassified the left miss from a delivery error to an AIM error: a zero-torque head does not twist through the stroke, so 1.5–1.7° left at impact on Jul 30 was almost certainly 1.5–1.7° left at ADDRESS. ‘Barely open’ is the fix, it was found on the course, and it has never had a number on it — which the plans have flagged as a drift risk since Aug 10. A calibrated beam reads that aim directly. The conversion that makes it a measurement rather than an impression: at six feet, 1.26 INCHES of offset is one degree, so the old bias would land about two inches left of target. That is readable off a phone screen against a taped half-inch scale.

AND IT WORKS ON CARPET, which is the part worth noticing. Carpet cannot measure pace and never will — the open fault stays a practice-green job. But the angle you set the face at does not care what the surface is, so aim is the one thing a living room can measure honestly.

WHAT DIDN'T CHECK OUT — three limits, all worth stating plainly. THE CLAMP IS ON THE SHAFT, NOT THE FACE: out of the box the beam points wherever the clamp sits, and until the two are tied together the number is confident and wrong, which is worse than no number. Calibration is a book corner and three minutes, in real posture, because the beam is fixed in the SHAFT'S frame — calibrate standing up, measure bent over, and you have measured your posture. THE BEAM IS NOT THE START LINE: it reports face aim, and the ball's actual start line is face plus path plus strike, so an off-centre hit still bends a putt the laser called square (that is the tape test's job, and it is still unrun). AND A CLAMP SLIPS — so the calibration is re-checked at the END of a session, and a failed end-check voids the session's numbers rather than half of them.

THE TRAP, and it is the reason this section exists. The plans have carried a two-lane warning since Aug 10: LANE A keeps the barely-open feel and verifies it once; LANE B retrains the aim picture with a mirror or a laser until genuinely square looks square, and drops the barely-open language entirely. Doing both applies the correction twice and flips the miss RIGHT. The device that just arrived is a Lane B instrument by nature — stand over enough putts watching a green line and the eye recalibrates unasked. So the standing rule is that it MEASURES: set up without looking at the beam, let the camera read the floor, look at the number afterwards. If the audit says barely-open aims square, the laser has done its whole job and goes back in the box until the monthly re-check.

WHAT CHANGED. Four new At-Home Putting lessons in Coach — calibration, the ten-ball aim audit, the measure-don't-retrain rule, and the three filming angles with the scale that makes them measurable. The Routine plan's FACE section now names the laser as the instrument for the check it has been owing and for the monthly number, with the Lane A/B guard widened to name it. A new action item says run the audit BEFORE practising with the thing.

NOT MEASURED — all of it, and that is the point. Not one ball has been struck with this device. ‘Barely open’ remains an unquantified feel; the two-drop eye-dominance test is still owed; the overhead five on a real green is still owed; the tape test is still unrun. What changed on Aug 13 is that the instrument exists, not that anything has been established.

SOURCES. Retailer and review pages for the same green-line shaft-clamp trainer (360° adjustable head, green beam for contrast indoors); the geometry is plain trigonometry — 72 inches × tan(1°) = 1.26 in. The Jul 30 impact figures and the Aug 10 reclassification are this project's own record.

sections.t: Aug 13 2026 — The pop stroke, adapted for a zero-torque head
sections.k: The geometry survives and the wrist mechanism does not — which is the whole reason the version in your plan is not the version Casper played.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. You wanted a pop stroke on the short ones: short back, short through. Does it hold up on a Lie Angle Balanced blade, and what has to change?

WHAT THE STROKE ACTUALLY IS. A short backstroke, a firm accelerating rap, and an abbreviated follow-through. Gary Player rapped it with almost no finish. Billy Casper is the canonical version — compact, hands close to the body, the face hooded going back, ball-then-turf contact and a finish that stopped dead, standardly described as tapping a tack with a hammer. Arnold Palmer and Nicklaus are named in the same tradition.

WHAT CHECKED OUT, AND IS GENUINELY IN ITS FAVOUR. The stroke came out of SLOW GREENS — it was developed by players who needed extra pop to reach the hole on surfaces that did not run. Your pace is calibrated at an estimated 8-9 stimp, which is exactly that world, so the historical fit is real. It is also the warning that comes with it: on a fast downhill four-footer a stroke built to add force is the wrong instinct. And the speed target has research behind it rather than folklore — the ring roughly one to six feet around any hole takes all the foot traffic, so it is trodden flat and bumpy (Dave Pelz's 'lumpy donut'), and a ball arriving with no pace wobbles through the worst-conditioned part of the green. Pelz's number is 17 INCHES PAST.

WHAT DIDN'T, and it is the core of the whole thing. THE CLASSIC POP IS A WRIST STROKE. Casper cocked the wrists to hold the face square going back and released them into the ball, and the technique's own history says right-wrist action is what supplied the pop. That mechanism is unavailable to you twice over: your method is quiet hands with the shoulders running the stroke, and the head you play is built on the premise that the face squares ITSELF once the hands stop interfering. A wrist-released pop is the most hand-active stroke in putting, and bolting it onto a zero-torque putter asks the club to undo what you are doing to it. So the plan takes the GEOMETRY and not the MECHANISM — short backstroke, short through-stroke, both run from the shoulders.

THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT, kept rather than buried. A ball dying into the hole can fall in off the edges, so a softer putt has a genuinely bigger effective target and more room for a stroke error. That is real physics. Firm wins on a SHORT putt specifically because inside six feet there is no distance problem to solve — the ball has one job, which is to reach the hole on line before the green can do anything to it. The balance flips as the putt lengthens, which is why the stroke is quarantined inside six feet.

THE TRAP THAT EARNED THE MOST WORDS. Casper's pop hit ball-then-turf: a forward-leaning, descending delivery. Your face carries 2° of effective loft at 0° lean with nothing to spare, so a rap arriving with the shaft leaning forward delofts a face that has no loft to lose and drives the ball into the turf — skid, then roll, then short. The vertical-shaft rule does not relax because the stroke got shorter, and the no-camera check is the scuff in the sound.

WHAT IT FIXES AND WHAT IT DOESN'T. It is a real answer to deceleration and to the freeze, and it connects to the trigger work — a short committed stroke gives the conscious mind less time to intervene, and your failure lives on short putts under pressure. It does NOT touch AIM. The left miss was reclassified Aug 10 as an aim error, the Aug 10 pm mat set came back 0.8° right / 1.0° left / 0.6° right with no bias, and face angle decides about 80% of where a putt starts. Barely open still does the aiming.

TWO CORRECTIONS FROM YOU, same day, both of which changed the plan. The through-stroke is SHORT, not 'at least as long as the backstroke' — your version is the authentic one, so the anti-deceleration guard moved from LENGTH to ACCELERATION, which is the honest version anyway: a finish that accelerated and a finish that quit look identical afterwards, and the roll-out is what separates them. And the CLAW came out of play, held as the safety net. That one had structural consequences, because the claw was the PHYSICAL guard against the trail hand taking over a short hitting stroke; with it gone the guard is discipline, so the tell — the head passing your hands — matters more, and the trip-wire that brings the claw back was set as a number while nothing was going wrong.

WHAT CHANGED. A new plan, SHORT PUTTS — THE POP STROKE, which also took the claw section from the Routine plan. The Distance Grind was retitled LAG PUTTS so the pair reads as a split. A new At-Home Putting lesson in Coach trains the stroke and the 17-inch pace on carpet.

NOT MEASURED — all of it. No pop-stroke rep has been filmed or scored, the 20-ball five-footer has not been run on the LINK, and the face-on clip that would catch the shaft leaning forward is still owed. Until the scoreboard exists, that plan describes an experiment rather than a finding.

SOURCES. Australian Golf Digest on the shorter, firmer stroke; Kermit Zarley on Billy Casper's mechanics; The Recreational Golfer on the pop stroke's slow-green origins; Golf Digest and Golf.com on Pelz's lumpy donut and the 17-inch target, including the soft-putt counter-argument.

SINCE UPDATED, same day: the claw is not a safety net, it is a second short-putt SOLUTION on trial alongside the pop stroke — Jack's correction, and it stands. The plan was retitled Short Putts — Inside Six Feet so it is not named after one of two candidates. The finding above is unchanged; what changed is that grip and stroke shape are now treated as two independent dials with a test order, rather than one adopted stroke plus a contingency.

SINCE UPDATED: the 2° of effective loft quoted above is an ESTIMATE — no retailer and no L.A.B. page publishes a loft for this head. The finding stands (a forward-leaning rap delofts and drives the ball down) but the margin was stated more precisely than the evidence supports, and the language in the plans was softened on Aug 13.

sections.t: Aug 13 2026 — The trigger: what starts the stroke
sections.k: The trail thumb press is live by your decision; it survives because it changes pressure rather than position, and the full shelf of alternatives is here.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. With the forward press out, what starts the stroke? You brought a full taxonomy — kinetic triggers (a small movement starts the chain) and sensory ones (a cue that is not a movement at all) — and decided on the TRAIL THUMB PRESS.

WHY IT SURVIVES. It is a change in PRESSURE, not a change in POSITION. Everything in the Routine plan exists to hold the shaft vertical and the 2° of effective loft intact, and a thumb that presses without moving the handle leaves both alone. That is the promise a forward press cannot make.

WHAT CHECKED OUT. The forward-press objection is real and it is why that one stays out: a forward press delofts the face, and a delofted putt skids before it rolls and finishes short — on a head with 2° to give, with pace as the open fault, that is the last thing to buy. Nicklaus genuinely never grounded his putter, and his own stated reason was that a grounded club let his grip and arms go slack while hovering made the pressure uniform — he also described feeling the head's full weight, which is the same currency as the lag cue. And the physiology behind the exhale trigger is sound: breath-holding and tension arrive together, so a long exhale is the standard way of pulling that back.

THE ONE MECHANISM WORTH CARRYING. Trail-hand pressure directed ALONG the putter's plane leaves the face stable; pressure arriving at an angle tends to rotate it. That is the entire reason the instruction is 'down the shaft' rather than just 'press', and the reason the claw needs checking on its own — in a claw the trail thumb is not on top, so the same press can arrive across the handle instead of down it. The claw is on the short putts, which is exactly where a freeze shows up under pressure, so that is the half genuinely worth filming.

THE SHELF — KINETIC. MICRO-WAGGLE: a tiny back-and-forth of the head, or one small forward-and-back, run from the shoulders with the wrists silent. TOE TAP or HEEL LIFT: the trail foot taps, or a heel lifts and resets — releases a lower-body freeze without touching the arms, the safest kinetic option. HOVER-AND-SET: the head hovers then settles, or stays hovering (see Nicklaus above). GRIP SQUEEZE-AND-RELEASE: brief tighten, then relax to stroke pressure — the same family as your thumb press, one step cruder. TRAIL-KNEE KICK: the trigger your full-swing routine already runs, so the cheapest to learn. LEAD-SHOULDER SETTLE. FORWARD PRESS: ruled out here, and the only honest version builds the lean into address so the angle you set is the angle you deliver.

THE SHELF — SENSORY. No movement at all, so none of these can touch face angle or loft — the safer default if freezing is the real problem. LAST LOOK: eyes go to the hole, the stroke starts the instant they arrive back at the ball; nearly free for you, because your rehearsal order already ends on a look at the hole. EXHALE: the stroke starts on the out-breath — the one to reach for under pressure specifically. COUNT or BEAT: an internal 'one... two' before the putter moves; you already run a fixed beat count, so it is the smallest addition on the shelf.

ADDED TO YOUR LIST, all four about the freeze rather than the trigger: step off and restart if you freeze anyway, since no trigger rescues a freeze you are already inside; the dwell-time test, because the real variable is how long you stand still and a trigger that hasn't shortened it isn't working; one trigger never two; and same slot every putt, since where it sits matters as much as what it is.

WHAT CHANGED. The Routine plan carries the live trigger and its three guards. Its old 'NO PRESS' rule now reads NO FORWARD PRESS in both the Routine plan and the Distance Grind — you now have a press that is allowed, and the collision would have read as a contradiction on the practice green.

NOT MEASURED. Nothing about the thumb press has been filmed. That it leaves the shaft alone is reasoning from where your thumb sits, not a measurement.

SOURCES. MyGolfSpy on the forward press and deloft; Golf Digest (Jim Flick / Jack Nicklaus) on hovering the club; Golf Smart Academy on trail-hand pressure direction and face stability; MyGolfSpy on breathing under pressure.

SINCE UPDATED: the 2° of effective loft quoted above is an ESTIMATE — L.A.B. publishes no loft for this head. The conclusion is unchanged (the forward press stays out, the thumb press changes pressure rather than position); only the precision of the margin was overstated.

SINCE UPDATED (Aug 14 2026): the trail-thumb press this section landed on is no longer the live trigger. Jack ran the shelf and went back to the FORWARD PRESS, which this section had ruled out — see the Aug 14 section above for the distinction that let it back in (a press that RECOVERS versus one that is HELD) and for what it changed in the other plans. What this section concluded at the time stands as the record of what was reasoned on Aug 13; it just is not what he does now.

sections.t: Aug 13 2026 — The trail hand, and what L.A.B. actually claims
sections.k: Making the right hand the feel hand is a good cue on lags, but 'let the head release' contradicts the putter and was cut.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. Is 'right hand feels the speed, left hand just rides along' a sound cue on a zero-torque head?

WHAT HELD. L.A.B.'s premise is as advertised: the head is balanced to the shaft's lie, so it resists twisting and needs no hand manipulation. Light grip pressure and quiet hands are the manufacturer's own coaching here, not a teaching preference — Sam Hahn's line is that his job was just to LET IT STAY SQUARE, and the company's first drill is putting with your thumbs off the grip. Face angle is also the right thing to protect: over 1301 putts from 4 m by 71 elite players, face angle decided 80% of direction consistency, against 17% for path and 3% for strike (Karlsen, Smith & Nilsson, J Sports Sci 2008).

WHAT DIDN'T, and this is the one that would have changed what you do. 'LET THE HEAD RELEASE' was cut. A release means the face rotating through impact, and this head is built so it does not — the instruction is the opposite of a release. It also contradicted the paragraph it sat in. And your stroke is straight back and straight through, confirmed across four heads, so there is no rotation to time even if you wanted one.

THREE SMALLER CORRECTIONS. 'Square to your arc' is L.A.B.'s own wording and fine generically, but you do not have an arc — on your stroke it is square to the LINE, and arc language is what put a toe-hang blade in the bag in the first place. 'Passive lead hand' was scoped to the LAGS, because the claw inverts the pressure hierarchy: the claw exists to take the trail hand out, moving pressure into the lead hand and leaving the right as a guide, so on short putts there is no feel hand and there should not be. And 'most face-control trouble is anxiety and deceleration' was dropped — an unmeasured teaching claim, and not your diagnosis anyway now the left miss reads as an AIM error and the Aug 10 pm mat set (0.8° right / 1.0° left / 0.6° right) failed to reproduce a pull.

ONE GUARD ADDED. An active trail hand has a quiet way of shoving the handle forward, which breaks the vertical-shaft rule without ever feeling like it did.

WHAT CHANGED. The Routine plan gained the rule 'TRAIL HAND senses the weight on LAGS — it never pushes, and nothing releases' and a section beside the claw section carrying the cue, its scope and its guards.

STILL UNMEASURED. Whether an active trail hand was ever in your stroke to begin with. No film has been asked that question.

SOURCES. Outtabounds on lie angle balance; MyGolfSpy on Sam Hahn's instruction; Karlsen, Smith & Nilsson 2008 (PubMed 17917952); Golf Monthly on the claw grip.

SINCE UPDATED, same day: the claw came out of play by his call, so the scoping conclusion still stands but is currently dormant — conventional on every length, with the claw held as the short-putt reserve. What survives unchanged is the reasoning: whenever the claw IS on, there is no feel hand.

sections.t: Aug 13 2026 — Eye dominance: an explanation, not a second fix
sections.k: Same-side dominance predicts a left aim bias — your exact miss — but the standing measurement doesn't predict the putting one, so nothing changes until the overhead five reports.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. You are right-eye dominant and right-handed — SAME-SIDE dominant, the group taught to aim left. Does that explain the signature miss?

WHY IT FITS. The bias that setup is supposed to produce is LEFT, which is your miss exactly, and it is the only candidate cause that predates every putter you have owned. That makes it a real explanation for why 'barely open' had to become your square.

THE STUDY THAT SAYS SLOW DOWN. The dominance you measured standing up is almost certainly a primary-gaze result, and the only peer-reviewed work here (Dalton, Guillon & Naroo, Optom Vis Sci 2015;92(10):968–75, n=31) found primary-gaze and putting-gaze dominance are neither equal nor predictive of each other, with putting-gaze the weaker. So your PUTTING dominance is unmeasured. Everything else on this topic is teaching claim, not evidence.

THE ONE THING TO ACTUALLY DO — THE TWO-DROP TEST. Add one drop to the overhead five you already owe: drop a ball from the nose, then drop one from directly under the right eye, and measure the gap between the two marks. That gap is whether dominance is live for you at all, measured in the posture that counts rather than standing up.

THE GUARD THAT MATTERS MOST. DON'T STACK IT. The barely-open feel already cancels whatever aims you left. Adding an eye-dominance correction on top applies the fix twice and the miss flips RIGHT. This is an explanation, never a second correction. Getting low and standing close already shrinks it too — eyes over the ball leaves less parallax to have.

WHERE IT RANKS. Hypothesis two behind the LINK adaptation pattern, with head shape third and weakest.

WHAT CHANGED. Nothing about the stroke, the setup or the putter — that was the finding. The two-drop test rides along with the overhead five in the Routine plan's FACE section.

STILL UNMEASURED. Putting-gaze dominance, and the overhead five itself.

sections.t: Jul 30 – Aug 12 2026 — The putter saga, end to end
sections.k: Four head movements in a month, every one decided on an unmeasured round — and the LINK.2.1 is the one that stayed.
sections.b:
THE SEQUENCE. Jul 30: DF3i out, LINK.2.1 in, after a round of short lags and hot short putts. Aug 1: a Beekman scramble where pace felt dialled put the DF3i straight back in and sent the LINK to storage on redundancy. Aug 10: the LINK came back and the DF3i was returned for distance control. Aug 12: you closed the return window by decision and KEPT the LINK for good. Four movements in twelve days.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY DECIDED, AND ON WHAT. Every one of those calls was made on feel, on a single unmeasured round, and not one of them was tested against a calibrated lag session. The Aug 1 reprieve came off a SCRAMBLE — where a teammate has often already shown you the line and the pace — on greens running an estimated 8-9 stimp, the friendliest putting environment that exists. Slow greens flatter you twice: you swing bigger, which forgives an off-centre strike, and you hit firmer, and firm takes the break out. That pattern, not any putter, is the thing the Distance Grind exists to break.

THE LEGAL-MOVE POINT, which still holds. The LINK.2.1 is Lie Angle Balanced — the same zero-torque technology as the DF3i, in a narrow heel-shafted blade. The thing that made the Phantom 7.5 wrong for you, toe flow against a straight-back-straight-through stroke, stayed absent throughout. So the whole saga was a SHAPE argument, not a technology one, and it never reopened the mismatch it started with.

WHAT YOU TRADED. The DF3i was a wide, deep, high-MOI mallet; the LINK is a narrow blade with far less MOI, so an off-centre strike costs more speed and more face angle. You moved to a head that is less tolerant of PACE, which is your one open fault. The counter-argument is real and it is the reason to keep going: a forgiving head HIDES strike quality, a blade reports it. The blade is more punishing and more informative.

THE SETUP CUE THAT MOVES WITH THE HEAD — the one thing in any swap that can cost strokes. The DF3i's Press Pistol 2° leaned the shaft for you, so its cue was 'hands EVEN with the ball, the grip supplies the lean'. The LINK ships a Pistol 0 — zero built-in lean — and Jul 30 film measured exactly what that produces: shaft dead vertical, hands about 1.35" BEHIND the ball, repeatable to 0.3° across 59 frames. That is not a flaw, it is the geometry the putter is built around (69° lie, 2° effective loft, 0° lean). The 'hands even' cue died with the DF3i and must never be carried across — on a Pistol 0 it is lean YOU are adding, on a face with almost nothing to deloft.

WHAT THE NUMBERS SAY, read fairly. AMBIGUOUS, not favourable. The LINK's column holds the only two reds on the evolution grid — face at impact and the 1.5-1.7° left start line, both measured Jul 30, on this head — while the DF3i's first filmed column carries none. But Jul 30 was by far the most-filmed day of the project (three sessions, fourteen clips, the first face-on at 120 fps), so some of that is measurement effort rather than a putter effect, and the DF3i's clean column is partly clean because less was measured in it. In the LINK's favour: tempo 2.0:1 across seven of eight clips against the DF3i's 2.4:1, with 2:1 the target. The only real scoreboard in the entire project is the DF3i's 8/10 from four feet on Jul 20 — and it went back with the mallet.

WHAT THE SAGA PROVED. That the left miss travels. It reappeared while you were holding a zero-torque putter, which is the cleanest evidence available that the head was never the cause — and it is why the miss was eventually reclassified as an AIM error rather than a delivery one. Also that lags finishing short and short putts running hot are not two faults but one: an uncalibrated power curve, where you default to too-small on the big number and too-big on the small one.

WHAT CHANGED. The LINK is the putter, permanently — `returnWindow` is off, the Home return-window card is gone, and Decisions reads DECIDED. The Routine plan carries the Pistol 0 geometry as its hands instruction. The Distance Grind owns the calibration work the whole saga skipped.

STILL UNMEASURED. Strike location, on any of the four putters owned this month — which remains the single candidate that explains both open faults at once, since a heel strike closes the face and bleeds ball speed. The tape-test protocol now lives in the Lag Putts plan.

SINCE UPDATED (Aug 14 2026) — the grip named above is a LAMKIN DEEP ETCHED, not a Pistol 0. The app carried the wrong name from Jul 30 to Aug 14. Both are 0° built-in lean, so every word of the geometry in this section stands, including the 59-frame film measurement. Left unedited on purpose: a log records what was believed at the time. Full correction in the Aug 14 section at the top of this log.

sections.t: How this log works
sections.k: Anything worked through end to end lands here as one section, so the doing-plans stay short.
sections.b:
The rule going forward: when a question gets worked through properly — research, a claim checked, a decision reached — it lands here as ONE section rather than being spread through the plans that tell you what to do.

That keeps the split clean. The Routine plan, the Setup plan and the Distance Grind say what you do NOW, in as few words as they can. This log says how each of those instructions was arrived at, what was rejected on the way, and where the sources were. When an instruction changes, the reasoning does not have to be re-derived and it does not have to sit in the middle of a plan you read on the practice green.

Each section carries the same skeleton: the question, what checked out, what did not, what changed in the other plans, what remains unmeasured, and the sources. The unmeasured line is not optional — a workshop that cannot say what it still does not know is a sales pitch.

entries.setup: 10 clips · slo-mo · L.A.B. LINK.2.1 · SEVEN PUTTS on the PuttOut AirBreak at a PuttOut Pressure Putt Trainer, in TWO BATCHES with the mat untouched between them — (1) three clips, phone on the table 25 in beyond the near end and 31 in above the surface; (2) four clips, phone re-placed 37.7 in beyond and 36.7 in above. Plus three clips on the long strip mat, phone flat directly behind the ball at ball height. Every camera position is ON the target line.
entries.finding: SEVEN PUTTS ON ONE TILT, and the mat's break now has a number. Every putt in both batches bends the same way — to his LEFT — and the second batch measures it: deviation from each ball's own start line grows as the SQUARE of distance rolled, and the ranking is monotonic in pace across all four (95% of speed retained → 2.54 in of break · 87% → 2.87 · 84% → 3.53 · 80% → 3.95). Slower ball, more break, same direction, four for four. That is the surface, not the stroke, and it is now proven rather than argued. THE RESULT THAT MATTERS: the mat wants about 2.5° of RIGHT start line — roughly 3.3 in of break over 6.4 ft at this pace — and the only miss in that batch is THE ONE THAT STARTED AT THE TARGET. It launched +0.10°, finished 4 in left and ran into the near bumper; the three that started 1.6–2.9° right all went in. Across both batches four holed, three missed, and every miss LEFT. That is an under-read break on a left-falling mat, not the signature aim fault — but the START LINE ITSELF is measurable here to about ±0.3°, which corrects a rule written earlier the same day. Also new: the shaft's frontal-plane angle holds from address to impact to within 0.2° on every stroke, and head and body move under 0.4 in. Still nothing on strike location, face angle, path or shaft lean — no angle all day could see any of them.

metrics.n: 7 putts, one tilt · every miss LEFT

detail.story:
SEVEN PUTTS, ONE MAT, ONE TILT — the mat was not touched between the two batches, only the phone was moved. So all seven are one sample.

BATCH 1, three putts, phone 25 in beyond the mat and 31 in above it. Putt 1 starts barely right, is taken left, catches the trainer's LEFT shoulder and runs around the outside of the rim to rest 0.5 in left and about 6 in past. Putt 2 never moves right at all and misses 6.3 in LEFT, about 5 in past. Putt 3 runs right, turns back, and finishes IN the trainer.

BATCH 2, four putts, phone re-placed 37.7 in beyond and 36.7 in above. This batch is the one with the numbers.

Putt A (the first, on an empty mat) — started +0.10°, i.e. dead at the target. MISSED 4 in LEFT, ran at least 10.5 in past into the near bumper and rebounded. Break 3.53 in. Kept 84% of its speed from 12 to 60 in.
Putt B — started 1.64° right. HOLED. Break 2.87 in. Kept 87%.
Putt C — started 2.70° right. HOLED. Break 2.54 in. Kept 95%.
Putt D — started 2.93° right. HOLED. Break 3.95 in. Kept 80%.

THE BREAK IS QUADRATIC, WHICH IS THE PROOF. A ball started off-line travels a STRAIGHT line and its offset from that line grows LINEARLY. All four of these grow as the square of distance rolled — constant lateral acceleration — with near-identical curvature. And the ranking is monotonic in pace with no exceptions: the ball that kept the most speed broke the least, the ball that kept the least broke the most. Slower ball, more break, same direction, four for four. Nothing about a stroke does that.

THE MISS IS THE ONE THAT STARTED AT THE TARGET. That is the sentence to keep. The mat wants roughly 2.5° of right start line at this pace and putt A gave it 0.10°. The three that allowed 1.6–2.9° went in. Read across both batches: four holed, three missed, every miss LEFT — and on a surface that falls left, that is what under-reading the break looks like, not the aim fault this project has been chasing since July.

IT ALSO CHECKS ITSELF. Start line, break curve and outcome were derived separately, so they can be cross-tested: project each start line to the hole, subtract its measured break, and see where it says the ball finished. The three makes come out 0.86 in right, 0.81 in left and 0.26 in left of centre — all inside the cup. Putt A comes out 3.7 in left, against a reported 4.0. Three separate measurements agreeing to a tenth of an inch is not luck.

TWO NEW THINGS THIS CAMERA GAVE FOR FREE. The lens cannot see shaft LEAN, because it looks straight down that plane — but it looks ACROSS the lie plane, so it can see the shaft's frontal-plane angle. That angle changes from address to impact by −0.14° to +0.19°, every stroke: zero within two tenths of a degree. No handle rise, no lie-presentation drift. It is rotation only and says nothing about the head lifting straight up. And head and body are dead still — 0.06 to 0.37 in of lateral movement from address to impact, under 0.35 in vertically.

TEMPO, MEASURED BUT SOFT. 1.64 to 2.13, mean about 1.86 against a 2:1 target. Take that with care: the backswing start is a departure from a plateau with only a few pixels of amplitude, and moving the detection threshold swings individual putts by 0.4. The ranking is stable and the spread is real; the individual numbers are ±0.15. The trustworthy figure is the DOWN-STROKE duration, which is threshold-free because the top of the stroke and impact are both hard events — and it runs 47 to 62 frames, a 32% spread across four putts.
detail.limits:
START LINE IS MEASURABLE HERE. AIM ERROR IS NOT. This corrects the rule written earlier the same day, which said the AirBreak could not score the line at all. Break contributes about 0.02 in over the first 8 in of roll, so launch direction reads to roughly ±0.3° — that is a real measurement and it should not be thrown away. What the mat cannot supply is INTENT: a 2.9° right start could be a perfect allowance or a shove, and nothing in the picture separates them. So the mat scores the line the ball LEAVES on, never whether he meant to put it there.

PATH AND SOLE HEIGHT ARE OUT, and now quantified rather than assumed. The entire backstroke moves the shaft's image position by only four to seven pixels, because the lens is staring straight down the axis of travel. A real half-inch path deviation would be about one pixel against that, and a tenth-inch lift would move the shaft line by four tenths of a pixel and be confounded with the back-and-through motion. Not measured, and nothing from this angle should be allowed to claim otherwise.

SHAFT LEAN AT IMPACT — still never filmed. All ten clips today look along the target line, which is the plane lean lives in. FACE-ON REMAINS THE ONLY ANGLE NEVER SHOT ON THE LINK.2.1.

FACE ANGLE AND STRIKE LOCATION — no clip shows the face. The head spans about 50 pixels at this distance and 1.5° is sub-pixel.

ONE NUMBER STILL UNRESOLVED. The ball is placed 2.20 to 2.57 in off the mat's own centre line and the trainer sits essentially on that centre, which over a 76-inch putt is about 1.9° — but the analysis quotes the same offset as 0.75 to 1.0°. Those cannot both be right, and it matters: at 1.9° a player lining up to the MAT'S EDGES rather than to the target would be aimed about two degrees off, which is uncomfortably close to the 1.5–1.7° left measured on Jul 30. Unresolved, and worth resolving.

n=7, one mat, one tilt, two pace bands, one distance.
detail.compare:
VERSUS THE SAME DAY'S FIRST BATCH: same mat, same tilt, phone moved. Both batches break the same way and the second one puts a number on it. The one thing that does NOT carry across is pace — batch 1's misses finished five to six inches past and read as a dying ball, while batch 2 kept 80–95% of its speed over six feet and ran one putt into the bumper. Two pace bands on one surface rather than a contradiction, and it matters for the break figure, which is a FAST-pace number and will be larger when the ball is dying.

VERSUS AUG 10 PM (about 20 putts off above-ground cups, nine finishing dead, nothing long): that session read calibrated-but-conservative. Batch 2 does not. Neither is a baseline and the ladder is still unrun.

VERSUS AUG 10 MAT (3 putts, 0.8 right / 1.0 left / 0.6 right against a printed line): that batch could score AIM because the mat was flat and lined. Today can score the LINE but not the aim, for the opposite reason. Complements, not a series — today's three left misses are not a worsening of that number, because they are not measuring the same thing.

VERSUS JUL 30 (1.5° and 1.7° LEFT on two of three, measured overhead, and 2.0:1 tempo): no overhead clip today, so nothing here re-tests the aim number. Tempo was measured today at 1.64–2.13 with a soft method, which is consistent with 2.0 and not precise enough to move it.

metrics.name: Path
metrics.verdict: SETTLED — straight back, straight through. Measured on the LINK on Jul 30 from three overhead clips: a quarter to a half inch inside at the top, back on line by impact. Neither Aug 10 batch could see it (the afternoon clips were all oblique, the mat set had no overhead), and it does not need re-testing — this is the finding the whole zero-torque case rests on, and nothing since has argued with it. Aug 24 could not see it and now knows why with a number: from a camera on the target line the whole backstroke moves the shaft's image by four to seven pixels, so a half-inch path deviation is about one pixel. Nothing from that angle can speak to this row.

metrics.name: Tempo / load
