Jul 30 measured 1.5° LEFT, 1.7° LEFT and one straight — three putts pulling the same way, which is what an AIM error looks like, because aim does not change between reps. Tonight is 0.8 right, 1.0 left, 0.6 right — scattered either side of zero. The one-way pull did not reproduce on any of the three.

So the signature left miss, measured, is GONE from these putts, and what is sitting in its place is DISPERSION. That distinction is worth more than the improvement itself, because the two point at different causes. A bias points at aim, and the barely-open setup is the obvious candidate for having removed it. A two-way scatter points at something that varies stroke to stroke — and the leading candidate, unmeasured on all four putters Jack has owned this month, is STRIKE LOCATION. Heel and toe contact rotate the face in opposite directions, which is exactly a scatter with no bias. That is an inference, not a measurement, and the foot-powder test settles it in twelve minutes.

By the project's own gate — median inside 0.5° — this does NOT come off the card. 0.8° is better than 1.6° and it is not yet passed.
detail.compare:
Beekman (Aug 1) said pace felt dialled; it was a feeling, from a scramble, on slow greens, with no camera. This is ~20 measured finishes landing on the same side: the pace curve is real, and the LINK matched the DF3i from every distance it was given. What today adds that Beekman couldn't: the short range — the closing 6–8 ft set went dead three times out of five with a 5-incher besides, and the five-foot DF3i set clustered inside 2.5 ft.

Against the Jul 30 indoor sessions, the same trade as before: the mat measured DIRECTION but had no green; today measured DISTANCE but has no line. The two halves of the diagnosis still haven't been in the same shot.

On the head-to-head, the sets never played the same putt from the same spot, so nothing ranks the putters — but both heads posting dead finishes everywhere means neither head is the variable that mattered today. The stroke behind them did the work. The one variable that DID separate results was the ball.

AND THE HALVES MET — partly. The line above about the two halves of the diagnosis never being in the same shot is now half-answered: Jul 30 measured direction indoors, the Aug 10 afternoon measured distance outdoors, and the Aug 10 evening measured direction again, on the first putts filmed since the barely-open discovery. What is still true is that direction has only ever been measured INDOORS, on a mat with a printed line, and distance has only ever been measured OUTDOORS. Neither session has yet measured both at once, and the mat is the reason the direction half keeps looking better than the scorecard does.
detail.limits:
THE CAVEAT THAT DECIDES WHAT THIS IS WORTH: this was a mat with a printed target line, and a printed line does the AIMING for you. The oldest unexplained split in this whole project is 10/10 start lines on the mat against a left miss that only ever shows up on the course, and the barely-open discovery is an explanation for exactly that split — an AIM error, not a stroke error. So this session tests whether the stroke can send the ball down a line it has been handed. It cannot test whether Jack aims correctly when nothing is drawn on the ground, which is the open question. Three putts on a lined mat are consistent with the aim hypothesis and do not confirm it. Note the scatter makes this sharper rather than softer: if the remaining misses are strike-driven, they will show up on a green too, because a printed line cannot fix where the ball meets the face.

FACE ANGLE IS NOT MEASURABLE IN THIS FOOTAGE. The putter head spans about 70 pixels in the reverse clip; a 1.5° rotation of the face would move its ends by under two pixels, well below the noise. So these clips cannot say what 'barely open' actually is in degrees — that still needs a close-up, phone directly above the ball with the head filling the frame, against a drawn line.

STILL OWED, and now the ONLY unshot angle: FACE-ON, square to the target line. Both cameras this evening were ON the line — excellent for start line, useless for shaft lean, because lean lives in the plane those cameras are looking down. So lean at address versus impact, the hands-behind-the-ball position the Pistol 0 wants, and ball position rep-to-rep are all still unmeasured. White tape on the shaft: still not on.

ALSO UNTOUCHED: strike location (foot-powder, still unrun) and pace — a 6-to-10-foot indoor mat cannot hold a 30-ft lag ladder, and distance control is the live priority and the reason the last putter went back.

ON THE PRECISION: each putt carries roughly ±0.5° of uncertainty once lens distortion, motion blur and the extrapolated centre line are allowed for, so a 0.6° reading and a 1.0° reading are not reliably different from each other. What IS robust across all three is the sign pattern — two right, one left, no one-way pull — because a 1.5–1.7° bias of the Jul 30 kind would have been far larger than the error bars and would have shown on every putt. Absence of the bias is the finding; the size of the residual scatter is not yet resolvable with a phone on a mat.
detail.gist: The one-way left pull is gone — 0.8° right, 1.0° left, 0.6° right against a printed mat line.

metrics.n: trail toe up, weight fully left, chest and hips through, balanced
clubhead still well behind at hands-hip-high — no cast
back to target, head stayed behind the ball
right for driver; stance width fine
chin down on the chest; spine curved rather than hinged from the hips
pelvis gives up its forward tilt before transition starts
taller than at address — but a rear-quarter angle exaggerates this
angle can't read the shaft against the target line — Jul 26 reading still stands
no launch data. Unmeasured since Jul 27

detail.story:
Seven stills spanning address, early takeaway, top, transition, past impact and a held finish. The bones are the same ones Jul 26 found and they are good: a genuinely full coil with the head behind the ball, and a transition that starts from the ground — at hands-hip-high the clubhead is still well behind him, which is the opposite of a cast.

The new frame is the finish, and it is the best one in the set. Fully up on the trail toe, weight completely on the lead side, chest and hips turned past the target, hands high with the club wrapped behind the lead shoulder, and he holds it. Post-impact backs it up: head still down and behind the ball well past the strike.

That finish is what forces the refinement. The open fault said the hips stall and slide instead of clearing. A swing that truly stalls does not finish like this — it hangs back on the trail foot or the lead arm collapses. So the rotation is not what is missing. What IS missing is the posture it rotates around: the upper back is rounded and the chin is down at address, the trail leg straightens at the top so the pelvis loses its forward tilt before the downswing begins, and by the delivery frame the body is plainly taller than it was at address. Three frames, one story — he turns around a rising spine rather than the one he set. The useful consequence is that the cheapest entry point is now the earliest one: address posture and a little trail-knee flex, both checkable in a mirror before a ball is hit.
detail.compare: Third full-swing entry on record, after the Jul 19 sim baseline and the Jul 26 driver/wedge stills. Confirms Jul 26's three positives a second time and on the course rather than in a bay — coil, head behind the ball, ground-up transition, balanced finish. Revises Jul 26's 'hips slide level through impact' from a rotation fault to a posture fault. Does NOT re-grade Jul 26's across-the-line top, which needs an angle this film does not have.
detail.limits: Rear-quarter camera — behind and off the rear shoulder, elevated — so shaft plane at the top, club path, face-to-path and attack angle are all unreadable, and nothing here can confirm or refute the over-the-top slice. No true impact frame: the sequence jumps from hands-hip-high to well past the strike. The apparent standing-up in the delivery frame is partly perspective, since a rear-quarter lens exaggerates it as the body rotates toward the camera — the ADDRESS frames are the solid evidence, because a static position does not depend on rotation. DATE AND COURSE ARE AN INFERENCE, not Jack's report: he described the film only as recent, and it is dated to the Aug 20 Lakeside Country Club round on the strength of the terrain and the day it arrived. Correct it and this row gets removed and re-added.
detail.gist: First swing film that catches the finish — it's complete, which argues against the hip stall.

metrics.n: 2nd camera · scale-free test · straight back & through
6 strokes, 2 sessions · quick of 2:1 · method biases low
7 putts, one tilt · every miss LEFT
grows as distance² · 4/4 monotonic in pace
10 clips, no view of the face

detail.story:
SEVEN PUTTS, ONE MAT, ONE TILT — the mat was not touched between the two AirBreak batches, only the phone was moved.

THE AIRBREAK, BATCH 1 — putt 1 starts barely right, is taken left, catches the trainer's LEFT shoulder and runs around the outside of the rim to rest 0.5 in left and about 6 in past. Putt 2 misses 6.3 in LEFT, about 5 in past. Putt 3 runs right, turns back and finishes IN the trainer.

CORRECTION TO PUTT 2, and it strengthens the read rather than weakening it. This entry said the ball "never moves right at all, left from the first frame." That overstates it. Tracked over 366 points, its lateral offset is FLAT at +1.37 to +1.40 in for the first 42 inches of roll and only then accelerates left. That matters, because a start-line error produces LINEAR drift from the very first inch and there is none here. Measured start line −0.29° against the mat axis — a hair right, effectively no allowance — and the entire leftward movement is accumulated break. Its raw-pixel curvature coefficient is 2.59e-4, sitting inside the 1.3–2.5e-4 band measured across batch 2. Same mat, same break signature.

THE AIRBREAK, BATCH 2 — four putts. A started +0.10°, dead at the target: MISSED 4 in LEFT and ran at least 10.5 in past into the near bumper. B started 1.64° right: HOLED. C started 2.70° right: HOLED. D started 2.93° right: HOLED. The break is quadratic in distance rolled and monotonic in pace with no exceptions, and it cross-checks itself — project each start line to the hole, subtract its measured break, and the three makes land 0.86 in right, 0.81 in left and 0.26 in left of centre while the miss lands 3.7 in left against a reported 4.0.

THE STROKE CLIPS, AND AN EARLIER CLAIM WITHDRAWN. This entry previously said the three ball-height clips "measure nothing." That was wrong, and wrong twice over. The head fills 224 to 365 pixels in them — the highest-resolution look at the club anywhere in this project — and they carry the best path measurement on file.

PATH: SBST CONFIRMED FROM A SECOND CAMERA. The test is the good part. For a head at depth Z, the image gives lateral position as (x − principal point)/W and depth as 1/W, where W is the head's apparent width; a STRAIGHT line in three dimensions makes the first linear in the second, and that holds whatever the focal length and whatever the head's real size. Run on two clips it returns residuals under 1% of the head's own lateral excursion, back and through, with the two directions fitting slopes within 2% of each other — the head essentially retraces its own line. No loop, no arc, no over-the-top.

A caveat found by re-running it here: the test is free of focal length and head size but NOT of the PRINCIPAL POINT, which is unknown. Sweeping that assumption across a plausible range moves the residual from about 3% to about 9% and the back-versus-through slope agreement from 17% to 42%. And if this really was shot on the ultra-wide — which the frame geometry suggests — barrel distortion bends straight lines, which is precisely what a straightness test measures. So: SBST is CONFIRMED in shape, from a second and independent camera, and the sub-1% precision should be read as softer than quoted. Given SBST was already settled across 20+ clips and four putters, that is exactly the weight this deserves.

TEMPO, RE-MEASURED AND RUNNING QUICK. Two stroke clips give 1.71:1 and 1.56:1. Pooled with the four AirBreak strokes (1.64, 1.82, 1.86, 2.13) that is SIX STROKES, mean about 1.79, five of six under 2:1 — two sessions, two mats, two camera positions, same direction. The mechanism is a backswing short relative to the downswing rather than a fast downswing: the down-stroke durations cluster tightly (42 and 41 frames in the stroke clips) while the backswings do not. The caveat that keeps this off the fault card for now: backswing START is detected as a departure from a plateau, which is threshold-sensitive in both analyses and biases in ONE direction — it clips the slow first inches of the takeaway and therefore shortens the ratio. Six strokes is a finding; the absolute number needs one hand-checked stroke to calibrate the method against Jul 30's.

BALL START LINE ON THE STRIP MAT: the two putts started on lines 1.25 px apart, under 0.1° however the focal length resolves, with sub-pixel residuals over the whole visible roll — so that mat puts no measurable break on the ball. But the horizon row differs by 2.7 px between clips, so the phone moved, and the whole 1.25 px could be that. Read as indistinguishable within setup error, n=2.
detail.limits:
EARLY LIFT WAS CHALLENGED AND THE CHALLENGE DID NOT SURVIVE — this is the most important thing on the page, because a settled fault nearly came back on it.

The challenge, which is a good method: compare the head at MATCHED APPARENT WIDTH, so the two passes are at the same depth, the mat's convex profile cancels and no scale enters; any difference in the sole's image row is then real height. Done that way it reported the head coming through HIGHER than it went back by 3.6 px near the top rising to 19.5 and 29.6 px approaching the ball — 0.3 to 0.5 in — which is the exact shape early lift has, and two to six times the 0.05–0.08 in Jul 30 measured.

Two checks were run against it here and it does not hold up. FIRST, the bucketing was right: address sits at a head width of 224 px and the top of the backswing at 365, so the 220–226 px bucket where the effect is largest really is at ball depth, not somewhere in the follow-through. That part is sound. SECOND, and decisively, an independent replication using a background-difference mask instead of a darkness threshold returns the OPPOSITE SIGN at every matched depth — the head reads 2 to 19 px LOWER coming through, not higher.

Why the two disagree is measurable rather than speculative. At matched depth the downswing silhouette carries 5 to 18% fewer core-dark pixels than the backswing, and the deficit is LARGEST NEAR IMPACT, where the soft-edge fraction jumps from 0.26 to 0.42. The head is about 1.7 times faster through the same depths on the way down (72 frames back against 42 down), so it is more motion-blurred there. A threshold that EXCLUDES the blur halo eats the smeared bottom edge and raises the apparent sole; one that INCLUDES it extends the blob downward and lowers it. Two methods, opposite signs, and each in the direction its own bias predicts. That is the signature of a measurement dominated by artifact at the size of the effect.

So early lift stays CLOSED, and this is recorded rather than dropped so the next reader who finds the same apparent effect knows it was chased. What settles it is a reshoot, spec'd below.

STILL NEVER MEASURED after ten clips: FACE ANGLE at impact — one indirect attempt via start-line-minus-path gave 0.30° and 0.80° on the two clips, which do not agree well enough to publish. STRIKE LOCATION — no clip shows the face. SHAFT LEAN at impact — every camera today looks along the target line, which is the plane lean lives in.

ONE OBSERVATION THAT IS NOT A MEASUREMENT: at address the ball sits toward the TOE side of the head's silhouette centre, read at roughly 7% of head width by eye, ±4%, from a single frame — two automated attempts were contaminated by the bright wall behind. It is address position, not strike location. But it points straight at the fault that has never been measured on any of four putters, and this camera position is one change away from closing it: impact tape or dry shampoo on the face, one set.

TWO CALIBRATION GAPS worth fixing at source rather than arguing about. The lens is unknown and the geometry only reconciles at a focal length around 700–780 px, i.e. the 0.5x ultra-wide — which makes every quoted ANGLE scale with an unknown and adds barrel distortion on top. And there is no scale in frame. Both cost nothing to fix.

ONE FLAG ON POOLING, RAISED AND CLOSED. A shirt-colour difference was spotted between the two AirBreak batches and read off the film as two separate sessions, which would have meant the seven putts could not be pooled. Jack: he changed shirts, and all of it is one day. So the pooling stands — one day, one mat, one untouched tilt, seven putts. Worth keeping as a worked example of the standing rule rather than deleting: WHAT HE DID is his to state and film does not outrank it. Film wins on positions and sensations; it does not get to tell him which afternoon he was standing in.

n=7 putts on one mat, n=2 stroke clips, n=6 strokes for tempo. Nothing here is a baseline.
detail.compare:
VERSUS JUL 30, which is the session this batch actually argues with. Tempo was 2.0:1 there across 7 of 8 clips landing 1.9–2.1; six strokes now average 1.79 with five under 2.0. Different method on both sides, and the current method biases low, so treat the DIRECTION as the finding and the gap as unquantified. Path was straight there from three overhead clips and is straight here from a ball-height camera by a completely different test — that is the strongest thing in this comparison, because two unrelated methods agreeing is worth more than either. Early lift was closed there at 120 fps with the sole held within 0.05–0.08 in of address height across ten consecutive frames; the challenge raised here did not survive its own replication and does not overturn it.

VERSUS AUG 10 PM and AUG 10 MAT: unchanged by this batch. The mat set could score AIM because it was flat and lined; the AirBreak can score the LINE but not the aim, and the strip mat's two putts are too few and too confounded with camera movement to add anything.

WITHIN THE DAY: batch 1 of the AirBreak read as a dying ball at five to six inches past; batch 2 kept 80–95% of its speed over six feet and ran one putt into the bumper; and IMG_3665, tracked frame by frame, was still rolling past the hole when its clip ended. Two pace bands on one surface in one session — which is itself the finding, and the clearest argument yet that pace is not repeatable enough to carry a single number.
detail.gist: Seven putts on one tilt: the mat's break gets a number, SBST confirmed twice, early lift held.

notes: 23 clips and 4 stills, every angle — the first full day on the LINK.2.1
Outdoor practice green, ~20 putts scored for pace. Direction unscored: every clip was oblique
Indoor mat with a printed centre line, 3 putts. Direction only
10 clips — 7 putts at a PuttOut trainer on the BREAKING AirBreak mat, two batches on one tilt, plus 3 ball-height stroke clips
evolution.foot: A curving mat can score the line a putt LEAVES on, never whether you aimed it there — which is why Aug 24 moves Start line without closing it. Pre-LINK film was cleared on Aug 14; every number it produced is kept in the Workshop Log.

metrics.name: Path
metrics.verdict: SETTLED — straight back, straight through, and now confirmed twice by unrelated methods. Jul 30, three overhead clips: a quarter to a half inch inside at the top, back on line by impact. Aug 24, the ball-height stroke clips: the head travels a straight line back AND through and essentially retraces it, by a test that needs no scale — residuals under 1% of its own lateral excursion. Two caveats on that second one: it is not free of the principal point, and barrel distortion bends straight lines if it was shot on the ultra-wide. Neither Aug 10 batch could see this row. It is the finding the whole zero-torque case rests on, and nothing has argued with it.

metrics.name: Tempo / load
metrics.verdict: HOLDING, BUT RUNNING QUICK. Jul 30 measured 2.0:1, with 7 of 8 clips landing 1.9–2.1. Aug 24 measured six strokes across two mats and two cameras: 1.56 to 2.13, mean about 1.79, five of six under 2:1. The direction is consistent enough to be a finding. The number is not — both analyses detect the start of the backswing as a departure from a plateau, which clips the slow first inches of the takeaway and shortens the ratio in ONE direction. If it is real the mechanism is a short backswing rather than a fast downswing, because the down-stroke durations cluster tightly and the backswings do not. ONE HAND-COUNTED STROKE calibrates the method against Jul 30's and settles this.

metrics.name: Early lift
metrics.verdict: CLOSED Jul 30 — at 120 fps the sole held within 0.05–0.08 inches of its address height for the full 83 ms into impact, flat across ten consecutive frames. CHALLENGED Aug 24, AND THE CHALLENGE DID NOT SURVIVE, which is why that column is a question mark rather than a dash: the angle was tried and could not settle it. Comparing the head at matched depth reported it coming through up to half an inch higher — the exact shape lift has — but an independent replication using a different edge threshold returns the OPPOSITE sign, because the head is about 1.7× faster coming down and therefore more motion-blurred. Two methods, opposite signs, each in the direction its own bias predicts. Stays on the grid as maintenance; this is the fault that comes back quietly.

metrics.name: Start line / aim
metrics.verdict: THE BIAS IS GONE. THE SCATTER IS NOT. Jul 30: 1.5° and 1.7° LEFT plus one straight — three putts pulling the same way, which is what an AIM error looks like, because aim does not vary between reps. Aug 10 against a printed line: 0.8° right, 1.0° left, 0.6° right, mean bias about 0.1°, and the one-way pull did not reproduce once. Aug 24 splits the row in two, and the split is the finding: on a BREAKING mat the start line IS measurable, to about ±0.3°, but aim ERROR is not, because nothing in the picture supplies intent — a 2.9° right start is either a perfect allowance or a shove. Four putts spread 3.0°, roughly 4 in at the hole, and THE ONLY MISS IS THE ONE THAT STARTED AT THE TARGET. Moving this row to AIM takes a FLAT mat with a printed line.

metrics.name: Face at impact
metrics.verdict: NEVER DIRECTLY MEASURED — every reading here is inferred. Jul 30 was a red by deduction: neutral path, square stance, and the ball still starting left, so the face was pointing left at impact. Aug 10 could not resolve it — the head spans about 70 pixels in those clips and 1.5° is under two of them. Aug 24 could not either: all ten clips were shot along the target line, none overhead, none face-on. On a zero-torque head this is the same question as AIM, since the face you set is the face you deliver. An OVERHEAD set is the only realistic route, and it pays this row and Path at the same time.

metrics.name: Strike location
metrics.verdict: NEVER MEASURED, on any of the four putters owned this month, and still the leading candidate for what is left. Heel and toe contact rotate the face in opposite directions, which produces scatter with NO bias — the exact shape the Aug 10 mat set came back in. That is an inference, not a finding. Aug 24 added the first thing in the record that POINTS at it rather than inferring it: at address the ball sits toward the TOE side of the head, read by eye at roughly 7% of head width, ±4%. That is address position, not strike, and it proves nothing. The foot-powder or impact-tape test settles the whole row in twelve minutes and has been owed since Jul 30.

metrics.name: Pace / distance
metrics.verdict: THE OPEN FAULT, and still the least-measured thing on this page — it has decided the fate of two putters. Aug 10 afternoon: about 20 putts off above-ground cups, nine finishing dead, the worst about 4 ft, nothing long all day. Aug 24 on the AirBreak: seven putts, the first batch dying at five to six inches past and the second keeping 80–95% of its speed over six feet with one running into the bumper. TWO PACE BANDS IN ONE SESSION is itself the finding — pace is not repeatable enough yet to carry a single number. On that mat it also decides LINE, because the break is monotonic in speed. The 30-ft ladder is what turns this row into a number, and it has still never been run.

briefing.focus: Mostly general best practice, and it says so wherever it matters — the tailoring comes as you send lies, misses and results. One idea runs through all of it: pick the shot with the LEAST air time that still works, land it on a spot you chose, and let the ground do the rest. One section is now yours rather than the textbook's: the through-the-ball delivery you found on Aug 25.
rules: PUTT if you can · CHIP if you can't putt · PITCH only to carry something
Pick a LANDING SPOT, never the pin — and a flat, predictable one
Least loft that clears the trouble. The boring shot wins
From a bad lie or short-sided: GET IT ON THE GREEN. Two putts is fine
Hands LEVEL, not jammed forward — let the bounce slide, don't dig
THROUGH the ball, not DOWN into it — the club keeps travelling low past impact
Bunkers: same splash every time, distance is FOLLOW-THROUGH length
Never short-side yourself on the approach — that is where this gets hard

sections.t: THE LADDER — putt, then chip, then pitch
sections.k: Take the least air time that still works; a ball on the ground behaves, a ball in the air does not.
sections.b:
The default order around a green, and it settles most shots before you think about technique. PUTT IT if the ground between you and the hole is reasonable — fringe, firm collar, even light rough. A bad putt finishes ten feet away; a bad chip finishes anywhere. CHIP IT if you cannot putt it: minimum loft, ball runs most of the way. PITCH IT only when you must carry something — a bunker, rough, a tier.

The reason is error size, not elegance. Every foot of air time is a foot where strike quality decides the outcome. On the ground the ball is just rolling, and rolling is the thing you do best. The best short-game players are the most boring ones.

sections.t: THE LANDING SPOT — the only decision that matters
sections.k: Choose a spot on the green and hit that; the pin is a distraction and the roll-out does the rest.
sections.b:
Most amateurs aim at the hole, which is the single most common short-game error. You are not trying to hit the hole — you are trying to land the ball on a chosen spot and let a predictable roll take it there.

How to pick one. Get it ON THE GREEN, usually a couple of paces on, and choose FLAT ground: a landing spot on a slope or on the fringe gives you a bounce nobody can predict. Give yourself a big spot rather than a coin — you want room for error, and a big target reduces tension by itself.

Then commit to it and stop looking at the flag. Once you can land the ball in the same area reliably, the roll-out becomes arithmetic instead of a guess, and you get closer to the hole without changing anything about the swing.

sections.t: CLUB BY ROLL-OUT — the ratios you are choosing between
sections.k: Same landing spot, three clubs, three finishing distances — that is the whole short game in one sentence.
sections.b:
Rough working ratios off a standard chipping motion: the 50° runs about 2× its carry, the 56° about 1×, the 60° about half. So land all three on the same spot and you get three different finishing distances — which means the club is how you control distance, not the size of the swing.

Use it backwards on the course: measure the carry to your landing spot and the roll from there to the hole, take the ratio, and the club picks itself. Lots of green to work with is a 50°. Short-sided over a bunker is the 60°.

These are STARTING numbers, not yours. The Coach lesson 'Distance control is landing-spot control' trains them, and the real ratios come from you hitting the three clubs to one spot and pacing the roll — send those and this section gets replaced with your figures.

sections.t: THE SETUP THAT REPEATS
sections.k: Narrow stance, ball just back of centre, weight a touch forward, hands LEVEL — and let the bounce slide instead of digging.
sections.b:
Standard chipping setup, and it exists to make the low point repeatable rather than to look like anything. Feet about one clubhead apart. Ball slightly back of centre. Weight favouring the lead foot and staying there — hanging back is what produces the thin one. Hands slightly ahead of the ball, and no more than slightly.

That last one matters more for you than the rest, because it is the one that is easy to overdo. Your wedges run mid bounce (10° on the 56, 8° on the 50 and 60), which is built to SLIDE under the ball. Jam the hands forward and you present the leading edge to the turf, which digs — and digging is where both the chunk and the blade come from. Hands level, let the sole do its job.

Then it is a putting-stroke motion: rock the shoulders, quiet wrists, accelerate through. Deceleration is the fault that produces most bad chips, exactly as it does on short putts — which is the same instruction as the section below, arriving from the other side.

sections.t: THROUGH THE BALL, NOT DOWN INTO IT
sections.k: On a greenside wedge the strike is a shallow pass THROUGH the ball, not a chop down at it — you already have more loft on the face than the ball can grip.
sections.b:
Your Aug 25 finding, and it is the first thing on this page that came from you rather than from a textbook. You have always been told to hit DOWN into a chip to get backspin; hitting THROUGH it gave you more zip and more control off all three wedges. That reads as correct, and it is worth knowing WHY so it survives a bad day.

WHAT 'THROUGH' MEANS HERE. Same setup as the section above — narrow stance, ball just back of centre, weight forward, hands level. From there the clubhead travels low and long: it arrives shallow, the sole skims the turf, and it keeps going down the target line after the ball has gone. The follow-through is at least as long as the backswing. What you are not doing is driving the handle down and quitting on it.

WHY IT MAKES MORE SPIN, NOT LESS. Spin comes mostly from SPIN LOFT — how much loft is on the face relative to how steeply the club is travelling. More of it does make more spin, but only to a point: above roughly 45–50° the ball stops gripping and starts SLIDING up the face, friction is lost, and spin falls. A 56° or a 60° delivered at greenside speed is already at or past that line before you add any attack angle at all. So every extra degree of down is spin loft you cannot cash — and you pay for it twice, in clubhead speed and in the leading edge going into the turf ahead of the bounce. What is left that genuinely makes spin at this speed is a clean, centred strike and a club that is still accelerating. Both are exactly what 'through' buys you, which is why the 50° feels better too.

THE ONE WAY TO GET THIS WRONG. 'Through' is not 'up'. Hanging back, adding loft with the hands, or scooping at it is the opposite fault and it produces the thin one. The low point still lives at or just past the ball, the weight still stays on the lead side, the hands stay level rather than behind. Shallow THROUGH the ball, not early OUT of it.

WHERE YOU STILL GO DOWN. Two, and both are already on this page. A buried or grabby lie in thick rough needs a steeper arrival, or the club never reaches the ball — ball back, stance wider, weight into the lead leg. A plugged bunker lie is a deliberate chop. And this is a SHORT-GAME rule only: a full iron off the turf still wants a descending strike and a divot after the ball.

HONEST STATUS: this is your feel, from one session, indoors, and nothing has measured it. The Workshop Log says what a measurement would look like and there is a to-do on the board for it.

sections.t: THE MEDICINE RULE — bad lie, short side, or both
sections.k: From a genuinely bad spot the shot is 'on the green', not 'close' — the hero flop is where doubles come from.
sections.b:
Two situations where the goal changes: a buried or grabby lie, and being short-sided with almost no green between you and the flag. In both, the honest play is to get the ball ON THE GREEN, take two putts, and walk off with a bogey.

This is the same rule as the recovery rule in Golf Mind, applied thirty yards from the hole: pick the shot you would bet a hundred dollars you can execute nine times in ten. From a tight lie over a bunker, the flop is not that shot for anybody.

And the cheapest version of this rule is played earlier, on the approach: aim at the MIDDLE of the green. Short-siding yourself is what turns a routine up-and-down into the shot you cannot play.

sections.t: BUNKERS — one shot, and the finish sets the distance
sections.k: Never touch the ball: enter the sand two inches behind it, same swing every time, and let follow-through length decide the distance.
sections.b:
The standard splash shot does not contact the ball at all — the club enters the sand about two inches behind it and the sand throws the ball out. Setup does most of the work: face slightly open BEFORE you take your grip, ball forward of centre, weight favouring the lead foot, and swing along your body line with commitment. Your 56° with 10° of bounce is built for this — let the sole skid, do not dig the leading edge.

DISTANCE IS FOLLOW-THROUGH LENGTH. Keep the entry point and the effort identical and change only how far the club swings through: a short finish throws it a few paces, a full high finish sends it twenty yards or more. Deceleration is the one unforgivable sin in sand — always finish.

PLUGGED LIES reverse the rules: square or slightly closed face, ball back of centre, steep chop right behind the ball. It comes out low with no spin and runs, so plan for the roll and just get it on the green.

sections.t: THE AWKWARD ZONE — 30 to 70 yards
sections.k: The worst shot in golf for most amateurs, and the fix is calibrated swings rather than feel.
sections.b:
Too long for a chip, too short for a full wedge, and the reason it hurts is that a half swing has infinite speeds while a full swing has one. Guessing at it is how you end up between clubs on a shot you should own.

The fix is the clock system, trained in Coach: give each wedge three calibrated swings — hands to 9 o'clock, 10:30, and full — which turns three wedges into nine reliable numbers covering roughly 45 to 110 yards. Fill the matrix once at the range with five balls per swing, then trust it on the course.

This also feeds your par-5 job: lay up to one of those numbers deliberately rather than to wherever a comfortable swing finishes.

sections.t: WHAT GOOD ACTUALLY LOOKS LIKE
sections.k: Tour scrambling is 57–60%, low single figures save par about half the time, and a 10-handicap converts around a third.
sections.b:
Benchmarks, so a number on your card means something. PGA Tour scrambling runs about 57–60%. Scratch-to-3 handicaps save par close to half the time they miss a green. A 10-handicap sits roughly 25 points below tour, so around a third. And a typical 10-handicap loses about 1.5 to 2.0 strokes a round around the green against a scratch player.

That last figure is the one worth holding onto: around the green is one of the biggest single pools of strokes available to you, and it is skill rather than speed or distance, so it is available at any age and in any weather.

A fair first target is 25–30% up-and-down. That is not close to tour and it does not need to be — it is two or three saved shots a round against where the cards currently sit.

sections.t: WHAT YOUR OWN CARDS SAY — and how little that is
sections.k: One round: 0 up-and-downs from 12 chances, 7 of 12 misses short. A flag, not a rate.
sections.b:
The honest state of the evidence, because this plan is otherwise generic. ONE round is recorded with green data: Sterling Farms, Aug 12, 18 holes. Six greens in regulation, twelve missed, ZERO up-and-downs, and 7 of the 12 misses finished SHORT against 2 left, 1 right and 1 long.

What that supports: a flag worth chasing. Twelve chances cannot separate a bad short game from a bad day, so nothing here is a rate yet and the 0% should not be read as your ability.

What the short-miss pattern hints at, with the same caveat: it points upstream of the short game. Missing short means the approach club or the strike is leaving you the LONGEST recovery every time, which is the hardest place to get up and down from. Taking enough club and aiming at the middle is the cheapest fix on this page and it is not a short-game change at all.

WHAT WOULD MAKE THIS PLAN YOURS: log greens and where the misses finished on the next two live rounds — at 36 recorded holes the app stops hedging. Beyond that, tell me what shot you reach for by default, what lie frightens you, and where the bad ones actually finish (chunked short, bladed long, or fine but 25 feet away). Each of those replaces a paragraph of general advice with something built for you.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: Written as general best practice on purpose, with the sources and the one thing that came from your own cards.
sections.b:
Written Aug 13 2026 at Jack's request as GENERAL best practice, to be tailored as he sends information. Nothing in the first seven sections came from his game.

RESEARCHED: the putt-chip-pitch default and the landing-spot method are standard short-game teaching; the setup (narrow stance, ball back of centre, weight forward, hands only slightly ahead) and the bounce-versus-dig mechanism likewise. Benchmarks: PGA Tour scrambling 57–60%, low single-figure handicaps near 50%, a 10-handicap roughly 25 points below tour, and a 1.5–2.0 stroke-per-round around-the-green gap between a 10 and scratch.

FROM THE BAG: the 50/56/60 with mid bounce (F/8°, S/10°, M/8°) off a 44° PW, and the roll-out ratios as starting figures rather than measured ones.

FROM HIS CARDS, and it is one round: Sterling Farms Aug 12, 6 GIR, 0 up-and-downs from 12, 7 of 12 misses short.

DELIBERATELY NOT RESTATED HERE: the drills. The clock system, bounce, chip-versus-pitch and landing-spot control are Coach lessons on the Wedges & Short Game shelf, and the bunker work is on the Bunker Play shelf. Plans say what to do on the course; Coach trains it.

AUG 25 2026 — added THROUGH THE BALL, NOT DOWN INTO IT, plus a rule chip, and pointed the setup section at it so there is one source for the instruction rather than two. FROM JACK: the change and the result he felt — more zip and more control off the 50°, 56° and 60° — reported after practising at home. RESEARCHED: the spin-loft friction limit (spin climbs with spin loft only to roughly 45–50°, past which the ball slides up the face and spin drops), the shallow-versus-steep leading-edge argument, and the deep-rough exception. UNMEASURED: the result, entirely. Worked through end to end in Short Game — The Workshop Log, Aug 25.

briefing.focus: Every short-game question worked through end to end, one per section, newest first. This is the reference shelf — what you actually do lives in Short Game — Around the Green.
rules: One section per workshop, NEWEST FIRST — tap to open
Every section says WHAT CHANGED in the short-game plan as a result
Every section says what is STILL UNMEASURED. That line is not optional
This is a REFERENCE. What you actually do lives in Short Game — Around the Green

sections.t: Aug 25 2026 — Hit down for spin, or through the ball?
sections.k: 'Hit down for backspin' is a full-swing rule that travels badly: at chipping speed a lofted wedge is already past the friction limit, so extra steepness only costs speed and puts the leading edge into the turf.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. Jack has always been taught that you hit DOWN into a chip to get backspin. Practising at home on Aug 25 he found the opposite works better — hitting THROUGH the ball — and reported more zip and more control off the 50°, the 56° and the 60°. Is the received cue simply wrong, or is he describing something narrower?

WHAT HE REPORTED, and which half of it stands on his say-so. The change and the intent are his: he is now delivering the club through the ball rather than down at it on short wedge shots, and he likes it on the 50° chips as much as on the two higher-lofted wedges. Nobody else can report that, so it stands. The RESULT — 'more zip, more control' — is a feel, and nothing has measured it.

WHAT CHECKED OUT — the mechanism, and it is specific to this shot. Spin comes mostly from SPIN LOFT: dynamic loft minus attack angle, i.e. how much loft is on the face relative to how steeply the club is moving. More spin loft does make more spin, but only up to a limit. Above roughly 45–50° the ball stops gripping and starts SLIDING up the face, friction is lost, and the spin rate falls. A 56° or 60° delivered at greenside speed sits at or past that number before any attack angle is added at all — so extra 'down' adds spin loft that cannot be converted into spin. Meanwhile it subtracts the two things that DO make spin at this speed: clubhead speed, and a clean centred strike. Where you catch it on the face matters more here than how steeply you arrive. And a steeper arrival presents the leading edge rather than the sole, which is the digging mechanism the plan already warns about in its setup section. So on a greenside wedge from a decent lie, shallower-and-through is the HIGHER-spin, higher-control delivery. His feel and the physics agree, which is not always how these end.

WHAT DID NOT CHECK OUT — 'hit down' as a blanket error. The cue is not nonsense; it is a full-swing rule that travels badly. On a full iron off the turf the low point genuinely belongs after the ball and a descending strike is right. And there are two greenside cases where you deliberately steepen: a buried or grabby lie in thick rough, where a shallow club never reaches the ball, and a plugged bunker lie, which is a chop by design and already written up that way. Sieckmann teaches the rough version through setup — ball back, stance wider, weight into the lead leg — so the exception is real teaching rather than a hedge. Both are now stated in the plan, because an instruction this good is exactly the kind that gets over-applied.

ALSO NOT ESTABLISHED — that 'through' licenses hanging back. The opposite fault is the flip: weight staying back, loft added with the hands, thin. The plan says so explicitly, because that is the predictable way to hear this instruction wrong.

WHAT CHANGED IN THE PLANS. Short Game — Around the Green gained a section, THROUGH THE BALL, NOT DOWN INTO IT, and a rule chip with it. THE SETUP THAT REPEATS was already saying the compatible half — hands level, let the bounce slide, don't dig — and now points forward to the new section rather than standing as a second source for one instruction. Two Coach drills were added to train it: 'Through the ball, not down into it' for the practice green, and a no-ball version for the room. No fault was opened: nothing was filmed, and a fault with no film behind it is a feel wearing a badge.

WHAT IS STILL UNMEASURED, and it is very nearly everything. Nothing in this app has ever recorded a chip. There is no launch-monitor number, no film of the delivery, and no scorecard field that sees a greenside shot — the live logger records whether the green was missed and where it finished, not what the recovery did. Beyond that, the session was indoors: carpet or a mat punishes a digging strike far harder than grass does, so the room may be rewarding the change for reasons that will not survive turf. Three things would settle it, cheapest first. FILM ten chips face-on and look at where the low point actually sits and whether the club keeps travelling past it. RUN THE ROLL-OUT TEST already owed for the club-by-roll-out ratios, with the new delivery — a change in spin shows up as a change in ROLL long before it shows up anywhere else, and it fills in the ratios that are still textbook figures rather than yours. Then the up-and-down rate over the next handful of live rounds, which is the outcome number and much the slowest to move: one round is 12 chances, which decided nothing last time either.

SOURCES. Spin loft and the friction limit: TrackMan's spin-rate guidance and GolfWRX's spin-loft explainers, which give the same 45–50° figure past which the ball slides up the face and spin drops. The shallow-versus-steep leading-edge argument, and 'where you hit the face matters more than how steep you come in': TrackMan's chip-shot material and Performance Golf's pitching and chipping guide. Deceleration as the chipping fault that costs spin: Practical Golf and Golf Distillery. Steepening from deep rough: James Sieckmann via Titleist's 18 Shots series. All of it read through search snippets — the sites themselves were blocked from here — so the figures are consistent across independent sources but none was read in full. Flagging that rather than letting a snippet read like a paper.

sections.t: How this log works
sections.k: Anything worked through end to end lands here as one section, so the doing-plan stays short.
sections.b:
When a short-game question gets worked through properly — research, a claim checked, a decision reached — it lands here as ONE section rather than being spread through the plan that tells you what to do.

That keeps the split clean. Short Game — Around the Green says what you do NOW. This log says how those instructions were arrived at and what was rejected on the way.

Each section carries the same skeleton: the question, what checked out, what did not, what changed in the plan as a result, what remains unmeasured, and the sources. The unmeasured line is not optional — a workshop that cannot say what it still does not know is a sales pitch.

And a log is a record, so a section is not rewritten when a later decision overtakes it. It gets a SINCE UPDATED line appended instead.

lesson.title: Through the ball, not down into it
lesson.body: The cue you grew up with — hit DOWN to make it check — is a full-swing rule that does not survive the trip to a greenside wedge. Spin comes mostly from spin loft, which is loft on the face relative to how steeply the club is travelling, and it only buys you spin up to about 45–50 degrees. Past that the ball slides up the face instead of gripping it and the spin rate goes DOWN. A 56 or a 60 at chipping speed is already there before you add a single degree of attack angle — so steepening costs you clubhead speed and puts the leading edge into the turf ahead of the bounce, and buys you nothing back. What actually makes a chip check at this speed is a clean, centred strike with a club that is still accelerating, and both of those come from the club travelling low and long THROUGH the ball. Two guards. This is not permission to hang back and scoop — the low point still sits at or just past the ball and the weight stays forward; shallow through it, not early out of it. And you still steepen deliberately from a buried lie in thick rough or a plugged bunker lie, where the club has to dig to reach the ball at all.
lesson.drill: The tee gate ahead. Push a tee into the ground four inches AHEAD of the ball on the target line, standing just proud of the grass. Hit ten with the 56 and check two things after each: the sole reached and passed over the tee (the club kept going), and the mark left on the turf starts at or just past the ball and is a long shallow bruise rather than a short deep gouge. A gouge behind the tee is the old steep pattern showing itself. Score out of ten, then ten more with the 50 and ten with the 60, and log the total out of 30.

lesson.title: Train the through-strike in the room — no ball needed
lesson.body: The room is where you found this, and it is the right place to keep it, because the motion is the whole drill — there is no outcome to chase and nothing to judge afterwards. Two things it trains: the club arriving shallow rather than chopping down, and the club still TRAVELLING after the ball would have gone. One honest warning about carpet, and it is the same warning the workshop log gives. A hard floor under a rug punishes a digging strike far harder than grass does, so the room flatters a shallow delivery for reasons that have nothing to do with whether it works off turf. So train the motion here and grade it on the green — and film it, because a feel that has never been filmed is the one thing this app keeps learning not to trust.
lesson.drill: Two coins on the carpet: one where the ball would be, one four inches ahead on the target line. With the 56, brush the carpet — the low point at the near coin, and the sole must reach and pass OVER the far coin every single time. Twenty slow reps listening for one continuous brush rather than a thump that stops, then twenty at chipping speed, then ten with the 60. Once a week, prop the phone at hand height face-on and film five: you are looking for the shaft staying quiet and the head chasing low past the near coin, not the handle diving.

entries.text: SHORT GAME — MEASURE THE THROUGH-STRIKE. The Aug 25 change (through the ball, not down into it) is a feel, from one indoor session, and this app has never recorded a chip of any kind. Two jobs settle most of it. (1) FILM ten chips with the 56 FACE-ON at hand height — where the low point actually sits, and whether the club keeps travelling low past the ball or the handle dives. (2) RUN THE ROLL-OUT TEST that the short-game plan's club-by-roll-out ratios have been owed since Aug 13, with the new delivery: 5 balls each with the 50, 56 and 60 onto one towel three paces on, and pace the roll from there. A spin change shows up as a change in ROLL before it shows up anywhere else — and it replaces the textbook 2x / 1x / half ratios with yours in the same session.

briefing.focus: The routine as you run it now: read it from behind, rehearse beside the ball with the pace look last, aim the FACE barely open and build the stance to it, release and RE-GRIP, and go — same beat count every putt. No forward press: this trigger changes what is IN your hands rather than where the shaft is, so the shaft is vertical at address AND at impact. How you stand and what is in your hands is the GRIP & POSTURE plan; the short ones and the lags each have their own.
rules: READ IT FIRST — pace before break. The how lives in the Reading plan
Aim the FACE first, then build the stance to it
Set the face BARELY OPEN — that's your square
Rehearse BESIDE the ball — ball-look first, HOLE-look last, always
TRIGGER = a late RELEASE AND RE-GRIP before the takeaway — same LIGHT pressure every time
Same BEAT COUNT every putt — a routine that varies in length is a pace variable
POP on the short ones, full length on the lags — each has its own plan
Setup and grip live in GRIP & POSTURE — get low, ball inside the lead heel, shaft vertical at ADDRESS and at IMPACT
steps: Read it from BEHIND the ball — pick the line and a spot a few inches ahead of it
Step BESIDE the ball — BEND OVER, stand close, full putting posture
Rehearsal 1 — eyes on the BALL. Path and contact.
Rehearsal 2 — eyes on the HOLE. Pace. This one goes last, always.
Step in — set the FACE to the spot, BARELY OPEN, then build the stance around it (trail foot a touch BACK)
Spot → ball → RE-GRIP → go. The stroke starts as a motion — quiet hands.

sections.t: THE READ — its own plan now
sections.k: What the putt is going to do, before you aim anything at it, moved to the Reading the Green plan.
sections.b:
Step one of this routine is still read it from behind — but the HOW moved out on Aug 14, the same way grip and the short stroke did.

The short version, so you are not left with nothing: behind the ball for the line, the low side for the amount, feet first on a green that looks flat, and pick the PACE before you read the break, because a putt has a different line at every speed. Past six feet the pace target is the Lag Putts circle; inside six it is seventeen inches past.

Everything else — grain, the pro side, the fall line, and the three minutes on the practice green that buy you the day's speed — is in Reading the Green.

sections.t: THE FACE — barely open is your square
sections.k: Set what reads to you as barely open — that is square. Verify at a real target once; re-check monthly.
sections.b:
On this putter the face points where you set it — zero-torque means it doesn't twist through the stroke, so address IS impact. What reads to your eye as barely open is, on the actual line, square. Trust it and set it the same way every putt.

Two standing guards. DON'T STACK FIXES: keep this feel, or retrain the aim picture with a mirror or a laser — never both, or the correction gets applied twice and the miss flips right. That guard got sharper on Aug 13, because a laser is a Lane B instrument by nature: watch a green line on the carpet long enough and your eye recalibrates whether you asked it to or not. Use it to MEASURE and look at the number afterwards. PUT A NUMBER ON IT: the laser does this properly now — at six feet, 1.26 inches of offset is one degree, so ten balls filmed against a marked scale turns barely open into an average you can re-check monthly. An unquantified feel drifts toward the exaggeration.

One check still owed, and it's the last one: five putts at a coin on a real green, nothing drawn on the ground, filmed from behind the ball. If the misses still fall on both sides, this closes for good. The indoor half of it can now be done any evening — the PUTTLAZR (Aug 13) reads the aim directly once it is calibrated to the FACE rather than the shaft, and the whole protocol is in Coach → At-Home Putting. Aim by feel, never at the beam.

Run the TWO-DROP TEST in the same session, since you are already in posture: drop a ball from your nose, then drop one from directly under your right eye, and measure the gap between the two marks. You are same-side dominant — right hand, right eye — and that predicts a LEFT aim bias, which is your miss exactly. The gap says whether that is live for you at all, measured bent over rather than standing up, which is the only version that counts. It is a reading, NOT a second correction: barely-open already cancels whatever aims you left, and stacking a fix on top misses right. Full write-up is in the Workshop Log.

sections.t: GRIP & POSTURE — its own plan now
sections.k: How you stand, what is in your hands, ball position, the shaft and the low point all moved to one plan.
sections.b:
Everything that is true BEFORE the putter moves now lives in GRIP & POSTURE — THE SETUP: get low and why the bend matters, the conventional grip and light pressure, ball one to two widths inside the lead heel, hands over the head of the putter, the vertical shaft at both ends, the trail foot back, lead-side pressure and the low point, and the trail hand's job on lags.

What stayed here is the ROUTINE: the read, the rehearsals, the aim, the trigger and the beat count. Those are the things you do in an order, every putt, and they are what this plan is for.

sections.t: SHORT PUTTS — they have their own plan now
sections.k: Everything inside about six feet — the claw, the pop stroke, the speed target and the scoreboard — lives in the Short Putts plan.
sections.b:
This plan is the stroke and the routine you run on every putt. The short ones have enough of their own content — a different grip, a different stroke shape and a different speed target — that they now have their own plan: SHORT PUTTS — THE POP STROKE.

What moved there: the pop stroke (short back, short through), the claw as a reserve grip, the 17-inch speed target, the loft trap that comes with rapping a ball on this face, and the 20-ball five-footer that settles whether any of it is better.

What stayed here, because it is true on every putt regardless of length: get low, ball position, the vertical shaft, barely open, trail foot back, the trigger, and the rehearsals.

sections.t: THE TRIGGER — the release and re-grip
sections.k: Your live trigger is a late release and re-grip of the hands; it is safe on this putter because it moves PRESSURE rather than position, which is also the thing it can get wrong.
sections.b:
LIVE, your call, Aug 25: NO forward press. What you actually run is a late RELEASE AND RE-GRIP — the hands come off the handle late and re-set on it — and then you go. Which trigger you run is yours to decide.

WHY THIS IS THE SAFE KIND OF TRIGGER ON THIS PUTTER. A re-grip changes what is in your hands, not where the shaft is. Nothing leans, so nothing has to be given back, and the 2° of effective loft this head is built to deliver at zero lean stays untouched (CONFIRMED Aug 14 from L.A.B.'s own specifications). That is what lets the shaft rule go back to what it was: VERTICAL AT ADDRESS AND AT IMPACT, in this plan and in GRIP & POSTURE, SHORT PUTTS and LAG PUTTS. Address is a real check again, because nothing moves you off it.

THE GUARD THIS TRIGGER BRINGS WITH IT IS A DIFFERENT ONE. A press risked a POSITION; a re-grip risks a PRESSURE. Grip pressure is the main way a hand gets back into a stroke that does not want one, and re-gripping is by definition the moment you set it. So: RE-GRIP TO THE SAME LIGHT PRESSURE YOU RELEASED. If the regrab lands firmer than the grip you let go of, you have just put the trail hand back into a stroke this whole plan is built to keep it out of — and firmer hands is a quicker putt, which lands on the open fault. Nothing measures this but you, and a squeeze is one of the few things a feel reports honestly.

IS IT ACTUALLY A TRIGGER YET? Your words were 'I kinda just do' it, which describes a habit rather than a decision — and a habit is exactly what goes missing when you are hot or rushed, which is the moment a trigger exists for. So make it deliberate: same slot, last thing before the stroke, every putt. If you would rather leave it as a habit, that is a fine answer, but then this plan says you are running NO trigger and the dwell count below is the only thing watching for a freeze.

FOUR RULES for whichever trigger you run. ONE trigger, never two. SAME SLOT every putt — it is the last thing before the stroke. IT MUST SHORTEN THE DWELL — count the seconds you stand still over the ball; if a trigger hasn't shortened it, it isn't working, whatever it feels like. AND IF YOU FREEZE ANYWAY, STEP OFF — no trigger rescues a freeze you are already inside; walk back behind the ball and restart. Eight seconds, always cheaper than the putt.

AND THE LADDER IS STILL A DETECTOR, watching for something new. It used to watch for a press that leaked lean and finished putts SHORT; it now watches for a re-grip that arrives firm and sends them LONG. Either way the rule holds: if the 30-ft ladder starts showing a pattern it was not showing before, suspect the trigger before you suspect your pace.

IF THE CLAW EVER COMES BACK OFF THE SHELF, the re-grip is the thing to re-check there. The trail hand sits differently in a claw, so 're-set it the same way' is a different physical act and the pressure it lands on is not the one your hands are used to. The claw is in reserve, not in play, so this is a note for later rather than a live check.

The full shelf of alternatives — kinetic and sensory, and what each one costs — is in the Putting Workshop Log under Aug 13; Aug 14 carries the press reversal and the Aug 25 line on it carries this one.

sections.t: THE REHEARSALS — beside the ball, pace last
sections.k: Rehearse in real posture beside the ball; ball-look first, hole-look second; same beat count every putt.
sections.b:
Read from BEHIND the ball — line, and a spot a few inches ahead of it. Then rehearse BESIDE the ball in full putting posture: same bend, same arm hang. Magnitude transfers one-to-one from that posture; behind-the-ball rehearsals read break better but run upright, so the size they teach is an approximation — and size is the thing you're training.

Order is fixed. Rehearsal 1, eyes on the BALL: path and contact. Rehearsal 2, eyes on the HOLE: pace. The last thing you feel is what you carry in, so the pace stroke goes last, always.

Same BEAT COUNT every putt — a routine that varies in length is itself a pace variable, and the putts that get an extra look are the ones that come up short. Backstop worth testing: say the pace intention out loud before stepping in ('die it a foot past', 'back of the cup'). Feel decays; a word doesn't.

Past 25 feet, test eyes ON THE HOLE through the stroke — as a block test on the practice green, not mid-round.

sections.t: THE STANDING WORK — where it lives
sections.k: Ten balls from thirty feet twice a week, and the whole protocol is in the Lag Putts plan.
sections.b:
Twice a week on the LINK, gamer ball only: 10 balls from 30 feet, logging SHORTS, SPREAD and GREEN SPEED, plus the 20/30/40 backstroke map. That is the standing work, and it belongs to pace rather than to the routine.

The full protocol, the targets and the tape test all live in the LAG PUTTS plan. The short-putt scoreboard — the 20-ball five-footer — lives in SHORT PUTTS.

sections.t: Feel versus real — how this plan is written
sections.k: Your words set the intent; the film sets the positions. Where they disagree, the film wins.
sections.b: Standing rule, in your words: the film study is king. What you're DOING — grips, triggers, decisions — is yours and authoritative. Where a POSITION or a SENSATION is claimed, the measurement outranks the description, and where there's no measurement the plan says so instead of repeating the feel as if it were established.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: History, condensed. Nothing here changes what you do above.
sections.b:
Aug 25: the FORWARD PRESS is out, your call — you run a late release and re-grip instead, and no press at all. Because a re-grip moves PRESSURE rather than position, the vertical-shaft rule reverted from 'IMPACT, and the press recovers into it' back to VERTICAL AT ADDRESS AND AT IMPACT across this plan, GRIP & POSTURE, SHORT PUTTS and LAG PUTTS — changed in one pass so there is one live source. The owed press clip closed with it: there is no press left to film, and the face-on clip it was folded into got easier to grade rather than harder. The guard changed shape too — it is pressure now, not position. Adopted on FEEL and UNFILMED, exactly like the two triggers before it, which is the third time in fifteen days; the Workshop Log's Aug 14 section keeps its finding and carries a SINCE UPDATED line rather than being rewritten.

Aug 14, later: the loft was confirmed at 2° from L.A.B.'s specifications, so the trigger section no longer calls it an estimate. Nothing about the press changed — a confirmed-small loft budget makes the case for a press that RECOVERS slightly stronger, not weaker.

Aug 14: the FORWARD PRESS came back, your call — you tried the shelf and it felt best of them all. It replaces the trail-thumb press, which was only ever yours by decision too and was never filmed. The Aug 10 'NO FORWARD PRESS' rule and this plan's own 'forward press stays out permanently' line are both gone; the vertical-shaft rule was re-scoped from 'address AND impact' to 'IMPACT, and the press recovers into it' across the Routine, GRIP & POSTURE and SHORT PUTTS plans, so there is only one live source. Adopted on FEEL and UNMEASURED — this project's own worked example is 'pace felt dialled' (Aug 1), which un-benched a putter that went back nine days later.

Aug 10: the press came out (your call — the 2° loft budget has nothing to spare, and a varying press is a varying pace). The DF3i was returned for distance control; its Press Pistol 2° went with it, and every 'hands even / hands ahead' cue died with that grip. The claw reopened for shorts — the old 'claw shelved' verdict came from a different putter, a different grip and a live left miss, so it doesn't bind. 'Hands over the ball' was corrected to 'hands over the HEAD of the putter' — the corrected version matches the Jul 30 stills exactly (vertical shaft = hands ~1.35" behind the ball centre), the first time a feel and a measurement have landed on each other in this project.

Aug 10 pm film: three putts on a lined mat went 0.8° right / 1.0° left / 0.6° right — the one-way LEFT pull from Jul 30 (1.5°, 1.7°) did not reproduce. Start line downgraded; the residual dispersion points at strike, not aim; the old 0.5° gate is retired as too strict for the player and the method.

Jul 30 film, still standing: SBST path confirmed across four putters; tempo 2.0:1; early lift closed; stance line closed (toes never open); vertical shaft repeatable to 0.3°. Pace remains the open fault — it decided the fate of two putters without ever being measured, which is why the ladder is the standing work.

Aug 13 — two workshops, both written up in full in the PUTTING WORKSHOP LOG rather than here. THE TRAIL HAND: the L.A.B. framing checked out, 'let the head release' did not and was cut, and the lead-hand half was scoped to the lags because the claw inverts it. THE TRIGGER: the trail thumb press is yours by decision, and the old 'NO PRESS' rule was renamed NO FORWARD PRESS to kill the collision. Neither has been filmed — that the thumb press leaves the shaft alone is reasoning from where your thumb sits, not a measurement.

Aug 13, later: the setup and grip sections moved out to GRIP & POSTURE and the claw section moved to SHORT PUTTS, leaving this plan as the routine alone. Also Aug 13 — the claw came out of play by your call; conventional on every length now, with the claw held as the reserve.

briefing.focus: Everything that is true before the putter moves, in one place: how you stand, what is in your hands, where the ball is, and where the low point ends up. One mechanism runs through it — lead-side pressure pins the low point, the low point decides whether the ball rolls or hops, and ball position plus a vertical shaft decide where that low point meets the ball. Keep any feel that passes the four checks. The routine that sits on top of this is the Putting Routine plan.
rules: GET LOW — the deep bend is what presents the lie this putter needs
CONVENTIONAL grip, both lengths — the claw is in reserve, not in play
Ball 1–2 BALL-WIDTHS inside the lead heel — mark it
HANDS OVER THE HEAD OF THE PUTTER — that IS the straight shaft
NO FORWARD PRESS (Aug 25) — the trigger is a RE-GRIP, so the shaft is VERTICAL at ADDRESS and at IMPACT
QUIET HANDS — the shoulders run the stroke, the hands just hold on
Pressure ~55/45 LEAD — its one job is pinning the low point
TRAIL FOOT back — square will feel closed
TRAIL HAND senses the weight on LAGS — it never pushes, and nothing releases

sections.t: THE HEADLINE — get low
sections.k: Bend over and get low — the anchor feel everything else hangs off, and it is what switches the putter's technology on.
sections.b:
Your words, and they go at the top: bending over is the most massive thing, and getting low is where you feel most comfortable. That is the feel to remember when everything else has drifted. If you carry one thought to the practice green, carry this one. Deep bend, stand close, eyes down.

Two mechanisms under the feel. FIRST — the LINK is Lie Angle Balanced, and that balance is only true when the shaft is presented at its built lie (69° lie, ~2° effective loft — an estimate, see the Notes — 0° lean, 34"). Stand tall or reach and the toe drops, the shaft leaves its lie, and the self-squaring property you bought quietly degrades. Posture is what delivers the technology.

SECOND — more bend hangs the arms freer and tilts the shoulders onto a STEEPER plane, and a steeper shoulder plane is what produces a straight-back-straight-through stroke. Standing tall builds in an arc you don't want.

sections.t: THE GRIP — what is actually in your hands
sections.k: Conventional on every length right now, light pressure, and the claw held in reserve rather than in play.
sections.b:
CONVENTIONAL, BOTH LENGTHS. As of Aug 13 the claw is not in play — you are running the conventional grip on short putts and on lags alike. The claw has not been thrown away; it is the reserve, and the Short Putts plan holds the trip-wire that would bring it back.

LIGHT PRESSURE, and this is the manufacturer's instruction rather than a preference. A Lie Angle Balanced head is built so the face squares itself when the hands stop interfering — L.A.B.'s own coaching is that your job is only to let it stay square, and their first drill is putting with your thumbs off the grip. Grip pressure is the main way a hand gets back into a stroke that does not want one.

THE ZERO-LEAN GRIP GEOMETRY. This putter carries a LAMKIN DEEP ETCHED — zero built-in lean. The shaft stands vertical and your hands sit about 1.35" behind the ball's centre, and that is correct rather than something to fix. The DF3i's 'hands EVEN with the ball' cue belonged to its Press Pistol 2°, which leaned the shaft for you; that grip went back with that putter and the cue died with it. Never carry it across.

THE TRAIL HAND. On LAGS, conventional grip: let the RIGHT hand be the one that senses the weight of the head, and let the left just ride along. Keep that — it is a good cue and it is pointed at the right fault. Pace is the open one, distance on this putter is stroke LENGTH at a fixed tempo, and a hand that reports how heavy the head feels going back is reporting the exact thing the ladder exists to calibrate.

SENSE the weight, never PUSH the club. A trail hand that drives through the ball is a second pace input stacked on stroke length, and it has a quiet way of shoving the handle forward — which breaks the vertical-shaft rule without ever feeling like it did. On SHORT putts there is no distance to feel, so the trail hand is just holding on; the feel job belongs to the lags.

sections.t: THE SETUP — the four checks
sections.k: Ball inside the lead heel · low point just behind it · shaft back to vertical · 55/45. Pass all four and keep your feel.
sections.b:
BEND OVER, stand close, eyes down through the strike. BALL one to two ball-widths inside the lead heel — forward of centre so the head is a hair ASCENDING at contact, which is what produces true roll. Mark the spot and keep it; launch is sensitive to it, and a ball position that wanders reads as bad distance control even when the stroke was fine. Weight stacked ON the ball. TRAIL FOOT a touch back. Rock the shoulders, QUIET HANDS, loose grip. Face set BARELY OPEN — its own section below.

HANDS OVER THE HEAD OF THE PUTTER — shaft straight up and down. That is the entire hands instruction. Don't add lean to make it look like a normal putter: this face carries little loft and is delivered at 0° lean, so there is nothing to spare, and a driven ball skids before it rolls and finishes short.

(A vertical shaft photographs as hands ~1.35" behind the ball's centre — half a ball from face to centre plus the riser hosel's offset. Same position, the camera's description of it. Ball position is set by your FEET; the shaft is set by your HANDS.)

(1) BALL one to two ball-widths INSIDE THE LEAD HEEL. Use the heel, not a body reference — a deep-bend posture moves your chest line; the heel doesn't move. Mark it on the mat.

(2) LOW POINT at or just behind the ball, so the head is a HAIR ascending at contact. This is what ball position is for.

(3) SHAFT RETURNS TO VERTICAL at impact — the same place it started.

(4) PRESSURE about 55/45 lead — enough to anchor the low point, not so much you start steering.

If a feel you're comfortable in delivers all four, keep the feel. The checks are the rule; the feel is yours.

sections.t: WEIGHT AND THE LOW POINT — the mechanism under all of it
sections.k: Lead pressure pins where the stroke bottoms out, and hanging back adds loft you never asked for.
sections.b:
Lead-side pressure does one job: it PINS THE LOW POINT of the stroke. Where your weight sits decides where the arc bottoms out, and where the arc bottoms out decides how the putter meets the ball. Everything below follows from that, on any head.

Weight back moves the bottom of the arc BEHIND the ball, so the head arrives climbing hard with the shaft leaning away from the target. That adds loft you never asked for: the ball launches slightly, HOPS, SKIDS, and only then rolls. Every bit of hop is energy that was supposed to become roll, so the putt arrives soft — and skid distance changes with green speed and grain, so your pace stops being repeatable between surfaces.

The window on this head is narrow in both directions, because a putter's loft budget is small to start with. Lean away from the target and you add loft; lean toward it and you go below zero and drive the ball down. Both mistakes produce the same symptom: a skidding ball that finishes short of what the stroke intended.

sections.t: THE SHAFT — vertical at address and at impact
sections.k: Nothing moves you off vertical any more, so address is a real check again — and both ends have to read the same number.
sections.b:
The shaft is VERTICAL AT ADDRESS AND VERTICAL AT IMPACT. Impact is the end that matters, and address is a fair proxy for it again as of Aug 25: the forward press is out and the trigger is a RE-GRIP (it lives in the ROUTINE plan), which changes what is in your hands rather than where the shaft is. Nothing takes you off vertical on purpose any more, so nothing has to be given back — and the two ends reading the same number is the whole test. Forward at IMPACT delofts a face with little to give and drives the ball into the turf — it skids, then rolls, and finishes short. Hands falling BACK invite the wrist flick. Both directions off vertical at impact are misses.

Check with a camera: one face-on clip, shaft angle at address versus impact, same number both times — pass. Check without one: LISTEN. A purely rolling ball makes one clean click; a driven ball adds a faint scuff a beat later. If you hear the scuff, the shaft leaned forward, whatever your hands report.

Two different variables, two different controls. Ball position is set by your FEET (check 1). Shaft lean at impact is set by your HANDS (check 3), and the target is zero.

A vertical shaft photographs as the hands sitting about 1.35" behind the ball's centre — half a ball (0.84") from face to centre, plus roughly half an inch from shaft axis to face on this riser-hosel blade. That's not a position to set; it's what 'hands over the head of the putter' produces on its own. If you try to put the hands somewhere, you're adding lean. Nothing in the routine asks you to any more, which is the point of a trigger that lives in your grip pressure instead.

sections.t: THE TRAIL FOOT — set it back
sections.k: Trail foot back, square will feel closed — and always face first, then stance.
sections.b:
Set the trail foot a touch further back than feels natural, and expect square to feel CLOSED. You're recalibrating off an open baseline, so trust the line you set rather than the feel for the first few sessions.

Why it matters this much: in an SBST stroke the shoulder line IS the track. An open stance doesn't just aim you left — it points the whole stroke left, and then either the hands steer the takeaway to save it, or the ball starts left. A stance error shows up disguised as a takeaway problem.

Ten-second check: alignment stick down the line, toes PARALLEL, not converging. And keep the order religiously — aim the FACE to the spot first, then build the stance around it. Face-first means a creeping stance shows up as discomfort, and discomfort you can feel is information you can act on.

sections.t: The blade tells you
sections.k: This head reports a bad strike instead of muffling it — use that, then measure.
sections.b:
A narrow blade carries less MOI, so a strike off the middle bleeds real distance and you can FEEL it. That makes your hands a better instrument on this putter than on a big mallet — a mediocre low point won't hide.

Use it, but don't stop there. The sound check costs nothing: one clean click is a rolling ball; a faint scuff a beat later is a driven one. The measurement is the tape test — twelve minutes, its own plan — and it's the thing to run before drawing any conclusion about this putter's pace.

sections.t: Settle any change with data
sections.k: A/B it on the ladder and let the stopping points decide, not the feel.
sections.b:
A/B LAG LADDER — 30 feet, two blocks of 10. Block A: current feel. Block B: the change, everything else identical. Mark where each ball STOPS and measure the spread; tighter spread wins, and that's the answer, not anyone's opinion.

FACE-ON CLIP — the one measurement this plan keeps asking for: shaft angle at address versus impact (matching at address and impact is the pass, and as of Aug 25 that is the plain question again — nothing in the routine moves the shaft, and the grip has no built-in lean either, so whatever the tape shows IS your hands), where the head bottoms out relative to the ball, and ball position rep to rep. White tape on the shaft, 240 fps, camera at ball height square to the line.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: History, condensed. Nothing here changes the checks above.
sections.b:
Aug 25: the forward press is out by your decision — a late release and re-grip instead — so this plan's shaft rule reverts to VERTICAL AT ADDRESS AND AT IMPACT, which is where it stood before Aug 14. The reasoning that re-scoped it to impact alone is not wrong and is not retired; it simply has nothing to act on while nothing moves the hands off vertical. New guard, and it belongs to this plan because this is where grip pressure lives: re-grip to the SAME LIGHT PRESSURE you released, because a firmer regrab is a trail hand back in the stroke.

Aug 14: the forward press returned by your decision, so this plan's 'NO FORWARD PRESS' rule is retired and the shaft rule re-scoped to IMPACT. What did NOT change: the mechanism. A shaft still leaning at impact still delofts and still finishes short — the press is only safe because it recovers, and that recovery is UNFILMED. The face-on address-versus-impact clip is now the owed measurement rather than a nice-to-have.

The 'hands level or a touch ahead at impact' rule that used to be check 3 belonged to the DF3i's Press Pistol 2° — a grip with lean built in — and left with that putter on Aug 10; on a 0°-lean build, hands ahead delofts and drives it. The press was removed the same day, which also retired the old 'keep it tiny' arithmetic. The ball-forward, weight-on-the-ball question was settled on the mat back in July; what this plan adds is the number (1–2 widths inside the lead heel) and the ground reference. This plan's forgiveness section flipped twice with the bag — the mallet that muffled a wandering low point is gone, which raises the stakes and sharpens the feedback. And the reason the plan exists at all: pace decided the fate of two putters on feel alone, with zero calibrated lag sessions behind any verdict.

Aug 13: this plan was assembled from the old 'Putting Setup — Weight & Low Point' plus the posture, shaft, trail-foot and grip sections that used to live in the Routine plan — they were all one subject, and the Routine plan is now only the routine. The tape test moved to the LAG PUTTS plan. Also Aug 13: the claw came OUT of play by your call, so grip is conventional on every length until the Short Putts trip-wire says otherwise.
