SOURCES. Spin loft and the friction limit: TrackMan's spin-rate guidance and GolfWRX's spin-loft explainers, which give the same 45–50° figure past which the ball slides up the face and spin drops. The shallow-versus-steep leading-edge argument, and 'where you hit the face matters more than how steep you come in': TrackMan's chip-shot material and Performance Golf's pitching and chipping guide. Deceleration as the chipping fault that costs spin: Practical Golf and Golf Distillery. Steepening from deep rough: James Sieckmann via Titleist's 18 Shots series. All of it read through search snippets — the sites themselves were blocked from here — so the figures are consistent across independent sources but none was read in full. Flagging that rather than letting a snippet read like a paper.

ADDED LATER THE SAME DAY — the other half of the feel, and it answers a question he asked directly. For the record, since the plans were versioned in three passes: ALL of this is Aug 25, one day's practice and one conversation. Nothing here spans two sessions. Jack: "when I sit down into it, it's like through the ball. So I'm almost going through the back end of the ball into the ground after and then hitting the ground after the ball. I don't know if that's right." It is right, and it is worth writing down WHY, because it is the piece that makes the whole finding coherent rather than merely contrarian.

THE STRIKE HAS TWO INDEPENDENT VARIABLES AND THE OLD CUE CONFLATES THEM. One is how STEEPLY the club arrives — the attack angle, which is what the first half of this workshop is about. The other is WHERE THE ARC BOTTOMS OUT relative to the ball. They are not the same thing and they do not have to move together: a shallow arc can bottom out well past the ball, and that combination is the shot. 'Hit down into it' is an instruction that buys a correct low point by paying in steepness — it gets the right answer to the second question by getting the first one wrong. What Jack is now describing is both answers at once: shallow through the ball, low point past it. That is why the two halves of his feel do not contradict each other, and it is the cleanest statement of the finding this workshop has produced.

WHY THE LOW POINT MUST BE PAST THE BALL, stated so it survives a bad day. There are three places it can be and two are bad shots. Behind the ball: the club reaches the turf first, the chunk. Never arriving, because the body rose and the club is still descending when it meets the ball's equator: the thin. Past the ball: the only one that produces a struck golf shot. Nothing about this is specific to the through-the-ball delivery — it is true of every strike off the turf — which is precisely why 'hit down' persists as a cue. It is aiming at a real target by a poor route.

WHAT WAS ADDED AS A GUARD RATHER THAN AS INSTRUCTION. Two, both because this feel has an obvious way to drift. DEPTH: contact after the ball is right, but how much ground is the variable, and a deep gouge means the leading edge beat the bounce to the turf — i.e. he has steepened again without noticing. The target is a long shallow bruise starting at or just past the ball, and a clean skim that barely marks is equally fine. AND DO NOT AIM AT THE GROUND: the ball is the target and the turf contact is a consequence. A player who starts hitting AT the ground finds it early, which is the chunk — the exact fault the low-point rule exists to prevent.

WHAT THIS CHANGES ABOUT THE MEASUREMENT PICTURE, and it is the best news in the workshop. The first half of this finding needed film or a launch monitor to check. This half does not: THE TURF MARK IS THE MEASUREMENT. Where it starts relative to where the ball sat answers the low-point question outright, and how deep it runs answers the steepness question well enough to catch a drift. It is free, it is available on any patch of grass, and it needs no equipment at all — so it has been added to the drill and to the to-do. The one thing it needs is GRASS. On a mat or carpet the club cannot enter the ground, so the room can train the club TRAVELLING but can neither train nor check where the arc bottoms out. That limitation is now stated in the at-home lesson, which was written earlier the same day and implied more than the surface can deliver.

STILL UNMEASURED. Everything from the first half stands unchanged, minus the low-point question the moment he reads a mark on real grass. Note what has and has not been established here: that the low point belongs past the ball is settled teaching and needs no defending. That HIS low point is now there is his feel and nothing more — which is exactly the sort of claim this project has learned to distrust, and exactly the sort the turf mark can settle in one session.

sections.t: How this log works
sections.k: Anything worked through end to end lands here as one section, so the doing-plan stays short.
sections.b:
When a short-game question gets worked through properly — research, a claim checked, a decision reached — it lands here as ONE section rather than being spread through the plan that tells you what to do.

That keeps the split clean. Short Game — Around the Green says what you do NOW. This log says how those instructions were arrived at and what was rejected on the way.

Each section carries the same skeleton: the question, what checked out, what did not, what changed in the plan as a result, what remains unmeasured, and the sources. The unmeasured line is not optional — a workshop that cannot say what it still does not know is a sales pitch.

And a log is a record, so a section is not rewritten when a later decision overtakes it. It gets a SINCE UPDATED line appended instead.

briefing.focus: Mostly general best practice, and it says so wherever it matters — the tailoring comes as you send lies, misses and results. One idea runs through all of it: pick the shot with the LEAST air time that still works, land it on a spot you chose, and let the ground do the rest. One section is now yours rather than the textbook's: the through-the-ball delivery you found on Aug 25.
rules: PUTT if you can · CHIP if you can't putt · PITCH only to carry something
Pick a LANDING SPOT, never the pin — and a flat, predictable one
Least loft that clears the trouble. The boring shot wins
From a bad lie or short-sided: GET IT ON THE GREEN. Two putts is fine
Hands LEVEL, not jammed forward — let the bounce slide, don't dig
THROUGH the ball, not DOWN into it — the club keeps travelling low past impact
BALL first, GROUND after — the low point lives PAST the ball, and it is a bruise not a gouge
Bunkers: same splash every time, distance is FOLLOW-THROUGH length
Never short-side yourself on the approach — that is where this gets hard

sections.t: THE LADDER — putt, then chip, then pitch
sections.k: Take the least air time that still works; a ball on the ground behaves, a ball in the air does not.
sections.b:
The default order around a green, and it settles most shots before you think about technique. PUTT IT if the ground between you and the hole is reasonable — fringe, firm collar, even light rough. A bad putt finishes ten feet away; a bad chip finishes anywhere. CHIP IT if you cannot putt it: minimum loft, ball runs most of the way. PITCH IT only when you must carry something — a bunker, rough, a tier.

The reason is error size, not elegance. Every foot of air time is a foot where strike quality decides the outcome. On the ground the ball is just rolling, and rolling is the thing you do best. The best short-game players are the most boring ones.

sections.t: THE LANDING SPOT — the only decision that matters
sections.k: Choose a spot on the green and hit that; the pin is a distraction and the roll-out does the rest.
sections.b:
Most amateurs aim at the hole, which is the single most common short-game error. You are not trying to hit the hole — you are trying to land the ball on a chosen spot and let a predictable roll take it there.

How to pick one. Get it ON THE GREEN, usually a couple of paces on, and choose FLAT ground: a landing spot on a slope or on the fringe gives you a bounce nobody can predict. Give yourself a big spot rather than a coin — you want room for error, and a big target reduces tension by itself.

Then commit to it and stop looking at the flag. Once you can land the ball in the same area reliably, the roll-out becomes arithmetic instead of a guess, and you get closer to the hole without changing anything about the swing.

sections.t: CLUB BY ROLL-OUT — the ratios you are choosing between
sections.k: Same landing spot, three clubs, three finishing distances — that is the whole short game in one sentence.
sections.b:
Rough working ratios off a standard chipping motion: the 50° runs about 2× its carry, the 56° about 1×, the 60° about half. So land all three on the same spot and you get three different finishing distances — which means the club is how you control distance, not the size of the swing.

Use it backwards on the course: measure the carry to your landing spot and the roll from there to the hole, take the ratio, and the club picks itself. Lots of green to work with is a 50°. Short-sided over a bunker is the 60°.

These are STARTING numbers, not yours. The Coach lesson 'Distance control is landing-spot control' trains them, and the real ratios come from you hitting the three clubs to one spot and pacing the roll — send those and this section gets replaced with your figures.

sections.t: THE SETUP THAT REPEATS
sections.k: Narrow stance, ball just back of centre, weight a touch forward, hands LEVEL — and let the bounce slide instead of digging.
sections.b:
Standard chipping setup, and it exists to make the low point repeatable rather than to look like anything. Feet about one clubhead apart. Ball slightly back of centre. Weight favouring the lead foot and staying there — hanging back is what produces the thin one. Hands slightly ahead of the ball, and no more than slightly.

That last one matters more for you than the rest, because it is the one that is easy to overdo. Your wedges run mid bounce (10° on the 56, 8° on the 50 and 60), which is built to SLIDE under the ball. Jam the hands forward and you present the leading edge to the turf, which digs — and digging is where both the chunk and the blade come from. Hands level, let the sole do its job.

Then it is a putting-stroke motion: rock the shoulders, quiet wrists, accelerate through. Deceleration is the fault that produces most bad chips, exactly as it does on short putts — which is the same instruction as the section below, arriving from the other side.

sections.t: THROUGH THE BALL, NOT DOWN INTO IT
sections.k: On a greenside wedge the strike is a shallow pass THROUGH the ball with the low point PAST it — ball first, ground after — not a chop down at it.
sections.b:
Your Aug 25 finding, and it is the first thing on this page that came from you rather than from a textbook. You have always been told to hit DOWN into a chip to get backspin; hitting THROUGH it gave you more zip and more control off all three wedges. That reads as correct, and it is worth knowing WHY so it survives a bad day.

WHAT 'THROUGH' MEANS HERE. Same setup as the section above — narrow stance, ball just back of centre, weight forward, hands level. From there the clubhead travels low and long: it arrives shallow, the sole skims the turf, and it keeps going down the target line after the ball has gone. The follow-through is at least as long as the backswing. What you are not doing is driving the handle down and quitting on it.

WHY IT MAKES MORE SPIN, NOT LESS. Spin comes mostly from SPIN LOFT — how much loft is on the face relative to how steeply the club is travelling. More of it does make more spin, but only to a point: above roughly 45–50° the ball stops gripping and starts SLIDING up the face, friction is lost, and spin falls. A 56° or a 60° delivered at greenside speed is already at or past that line before you add any attack angle at all. So every extra degree of down is spin loft you cannot cash — and you pay for it twice, in clubhead speed and in the leading edge going into the turf ahead of the bounce. What is left that genuinely makes spin at this speed is a clean, centred strike and a club that is still accelerating. Both are exactly what 'through' buys you, which is why the 50° feels better too.

THE ONE WAY TO GET THIS WRONG. 'Through' is not 'up'. Hanging back, adding loft with the hands, or scooping at it is the opposite fault and it produces the thin one. The low point still lives at or just past the ball, the weight still stays on the lead side, the hands stay level rather than behind. Shallow THROUGH the ball, not early OUT of it.

WHERE YOU STILL GO DOWN. Two, and both are already on this page. A buried or grabby lie in thick rough needs a steeper arrival, or the club never reaches the ball — ball back, stance wider, weight into the lead leg. A plugged bunker lie is a deliberate chop. And this is a SHORT-GAME rule only: a full iron off the turf still wants a descending strike and a divot after the ball.

WHERE THE BOTTOM OF THE ARC GOES — your own words, and they are the other half of this. Sitting down into it, the club goes through the back of the ball and into the ground AFTER it. That is right, and it is right for a reason worth holding: there are only three places the low point can be, and two of them are bad shots. Behind the ball is the CHUNK. Never arriving — the body rising, the club still on the way down — is the THIN. Past the ball is the only one of the three that hits a golf shot. So ball first, ground after, every time.

AND THESE ARE TWO SEPARATE DIALS, which is exactly why the old cue misfires. How STEEP the club arrives and WHERE the arc bottoms out are independent of each other — you can have a shallow arc whose low point is well past the ball, and that is the shot. 'Hit down' collapses the two into one instruction and buys the low point by paying in steepness, when your setup was already buying it for free: ball just back of centre, weight forward, staying down. Sitting down into it and STAYING down is what holds the low point where the setup put it; standing up through the shot is what drags it back behind the ball.

HOW MUCH GROUND. Contact after the ball is right; the DEPTH is the variable, and it is the one place this feel can drift back into a chop. You are looking for a long shallow bruise starting at or just past where the ball was — a skim that barely marks is fine too. A short deep gouge means the leading edge beat the bounce to the turf and you have steepened again without noticing. And do not aim AT the ground: the ball is the target and the turf contact is a consequence. Aim at the ground and you will find it early, which is the chunk.

AND THE TARGET IS REPEATABLE, NOT MAXIMUM. Control and spin are two different goals, and the one worth chasing is control: same launch, same spin, same first bounce. That comes from a repeatable low point, not from the most spin you can generate. A chip that checks three feet every time beats one that sometimes zips back eight and sometimes runs fifteen — the second is a better story and a worse short game.

HONEST STATUS: this is your feel, from one session, and nothing has measured it. The Aug 25 room film did not change that — there was no struck shot in it. But this half is cheap to check and needs no camera — read the mark you leave on the grass. The Workshop Log has the rest of what a measurement would look like and there is a to-do on the board for it.

sections.t: THE MEDICINE RULE — bad lie, short side, or both
sections.k: From a genuinely bad spot the shot is 'on the green', not 'close' — the hero flop is where doubles come from.
sections.b:
Two situations where the goal changes: a buried or grabby lie, and being short-sided with almost no green between you and the flag. In both, the honest play is to get the ball ON THE GREEN, take two putts, and walk off with a bogey.

This is the same rule as the recovery rule in Golf Mind, applied thirty yards from the hole: pick the shot you would bet a hundred dollars you can execute nine times in ten. From a tight lie over a bunker, the flop is not that shot for anybody.

And the cheapest version of this rule is played earlier, on the approach: aim at the MIDDLE of the green. Short-siding yourself is what turns a routine up-and-down into the shot you cannot play.

sections.t: BUNKERS — one shot, and the finish sets the distance
sections.k: Never touch the ball: enter the sand two inches behind it, same swing every time, and let follow-through length decide the distance.
sections.b:
The standard splash shot does not contact the ball at all — the club enters the sand about two inches behind it and the sand throws the ball out. Setup does most of the work: face slightly open BEFORE you take your grip, ball forward of centre, weight favouring the lead foot, and swing along your body line with commitment. Your 56° with 10° of bounce is built for this — let the sole skid, do not dig the leading edge.

DISTANCE IS FOLLOW-THROUGH LENGTH. Keep the entry point and the effort identical and change only how far the club swings through: a short finish throws it a few paces, a full high finish sends it twenty yards or more. Deceleration is the one unforgivable sin in sand — always finish.

PLUGGED LIES reverse the rules: square or slightly closed face, ball back of centre, steep chop right behind the ball. It comes out low with no spin and runs, so plan for the roll and just get it on the green.

sections.t: THE AWKWARD ZONE — 30 to 70 yards
sections.k: The worst shot in golf for most amateurs, and the fix is calibrated swings rather than feel.
sections.b:
Too long for a chip, too short for a full wedge, and the reason it hurts is that a half swing has infinite speeds while a full swing has one. Guessing at it is how you end up between clubs on a shot you should own.

The fix is the clock system, trained in Coach: give each wedge three calibrated swings — hands to 9 o'clock, 10:30, and full — which turns three wedges into nine reliable numbers covering roughly 45 to 110 yards. Fill the matrix once at the range with five balls per swing, then trust it on the course.

This also feeds your par-5 job: lay up to one of those numbers deliberately rather than to wherever a comfortable swing finishes.

sections.t: WHAT GOOD ACTUALLY LOOKS LIKE
sections.k: Tour scrambling is 57–60%, low single figures save par about half the time, and a 10-handicap converts around a third.
sections.b:
Benchmarks, so a number on your card means something. PGA Tour scrambling runs about 57–60%. Scratch-to-3 handicaps save par close to half the time they miss a green. A 10-handicap sits roughly 25 points below tour, so around a third. And a typical 10-handicap loses about 1.5 to 2.0 strokes a round around the green against a scratch player.

That last figure is the one worth holding onto: around the green is one of the biggest single pools of strokes available to you, and it is skill rather than speed or distance, so it is available at any age and in any weather.

A fair first target is 25–30% up-and-down. That is not close to tour and it does not need to be — it is two or three saved shots a round against where the cards currently sit.

sections.t: WHAT YOUR OWN CARDS SAY — and how little that is
sections.k: One round: 0 up-and-downs from 12 chances, 7 of 12 misses short. A flag, not a rate.
sections.b:
The honest state of the evidence, because this plan is otherwise generic. ONE round is recorded with green data: Sterling Farms, Aug 12, 18 holes. Six greens in regulation, twelve missed, ZERO up-and-downs, and 7 of the 12 misses finished SHORT against 2 left, 1 right and 1 long.

What that supports: a flag worth chasing. Twelve chances cannot separate a bad short game from a bad day, so nothing here is a rate yet and the 0% should not be read as your ability.

What the short-miss pattern hints at, with the same caveat: it points upstream of the short game. Missing short means the approach club or the strike is leaving you the LONGEST recovery every time, which is the hardest place to get up and down from. Taking enough club and aiming at the middle is the cheapest fix on this page and it is not a short-game change at all.

WHAT WOULD MAKE THIS PLAN YOURS: log greens and where the misses finished on the next two live rounds — at 36 recorded holes the app stops hedging. Beyond that, tell me what shot you reach for by default, what lie frightens you, and where the bad ones actually finish (chunked short, bladed long, or fine but 25 feet away). Each of those replaces a paragraph of general advice with something built for you.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: Written as general best practice on purpose, with the sources and the one thing that came from your own cards.
sections.b:
Written Aug 13 2026 at Jack's request as GENERAL best practice, to be tailored as he sends information. Nothing in the first seven sections came from his game.

RESEARCHED: the putt-chip-pitch default and the landing-spot method are standard short-game teaching; the setup (narrow stance, ball back of centre, weight forward, hands only slightly ahead) and the bounce-versus-dig mechanism likewise. Benchmarks: PGA Tour scrambling 57–60%, low single-figure handicaps near 50%, a 10-handicap roughly 25 points below tour, and a 1.5–2.0 stroke-per-round around-the-green gap between a 10 and scratch.

FROM THE BAG: the 50/56/60 with mid bounce (F/8°, S/10°, M/8°) off a 44° PW, and the roll-out ratios as starting figures rather than measured ones.

FROM HIS CARDS, and it is one round: Sterling Farms Aug 12, 6 GIR, 0 up-and-downs from 12, 7 of 12 misses short.

DELIBERATELY NOT RESTATED HERE: the drills. The clock system, bounce, chip-versus-pitch and landing-spot control are Coach lessons on the Wedges & Short Game shelf, and the bunker work is on the Bunker Play shelf. Plans say what to do on the course; Coach trains it.

AUG 25 2026 — added THROUGH THE BALL, NOT DOWN INTO IT, plus a rule chip, and pointed the setup section at it so there is one source for the instruction rather than two. FROM JACK: the change and the result he felt — more zip and more control off the 50°, 56° and 60° — reported after practising at home. RESEARCHED: the spin-loft friction limit (spin climbs with spin loft only to roughly 45–50°, past which the ball slides up the face and spin drops), the shallow-versus-steep leading-edge argument, and the deep-rough exception. UNMEASURED: the result, entirely. Worked through end to end in Short Game — The Workshop Log, Aug 25.

AUG 25 2026, later the same day — Jack described where the bottom of the arc goes: sitting down into it, through the back of the ball and into the ground AFTER it, asked whether that was right. It is, and the section gained it plus a rule chip. FROM JACK: the feel, again his. REASONED FROM IT, and the section says so: that steepness and low-point location are two independent variables, which is why 'hit down' misfires — it buys a low point past the ball by paying in steepness, when ball-back and weight-forward were already buying it for nothing. The depth calibration (a bruise, not a gouge) and 'do not aim at the ground' are guards on the same feel, not new instructions.

AUG 25 2026, the film — nothing measured, and the section is unchanged because of it. The first chipping clip in the project showed the club pushing the ball 3.8 inches at 1.9 mph on carpet, from an angle that cannot produce shaft lean. Added from the second reading Jack brought back, and the only thing in it that changes what he does: control is repeatability, not maximum spin. Full write-up, the numbers, what was NOT adopted from that reading and the filming spec are in Short Game — The Workshop Log.

lesson.body: The room is where you found this, and it is the right place to keep it, because the motion is the whole drill — there is no outcome to chase and nothing to judge afterwards. Two things it trains: the club arriving shallow rather than chopping down, and the club still TRAVELLING after the ball would have gone. TWO HONEST LIMITS ON CARPET, and the second one is the important one. A hard floor under a rug punishes a digging strike far harder than grass does, so the room flatters a shallow delivery for reasons that have nothing to do with whether it works off turf. And the club cannot ENTER a floor — so the half of this you found by feel, the low point sitting past the ball with the club going into the ground after it, can be neither trained nor checked in here. The room trains the club TRAVELLING. TWO RULES THAT CAME OUT OF FILMING IT (Aug 25). NO BALL for the motion reps — a real ball on carpet at rehearsal speed gets PUSHED rather than struck, which is exactly what the first chipping clip caught: 3.8 inches of travel at 1.9 mph with the face never leaving the ball. It teaches nothing and it films like a shot that never happened. And IF YOU FILM IT, FILM IT AT FULL SPEED — a slow demonstration pass is not the delivery you are trying to change, so no camera and no angle can rescue it. Where the arc bottoms out is a grass question, and the mark you leave on it is the answer. So train the motion here and grade it on the green — and film it, because a feel that has never been filmed is the one thing this app keeps learning not to trust.

entries.text: SHORT GAME — MEASURE THE THROUGH-STRIKE. The Aug 25 change (through the ball, not down into it) is a feel, from one indoor session, and this app has never recorded a chip of any kind. Three jobs settle most of it, and the first one is free. (1) READ THE TURF MARK, on GRASS — where it starts relative to where the ball sat answers the low-point question outright (at or just past the ball is the pass), and how deep it runs catches a drift back into steepness (a long shallow bruise or a clean skim, never a short deep gouge). No camera, no kit, any patch of grass. A mat cannot do this: the club never enters the ground. (2) FILM ten chips with the 56 FACE-ON — and here is the spec, because the Aug 25 room clip failed on every line of it. PERPENDICULAR to the target line, lens at about KNEE height, LEVEL rather than tilted down, six to eight feet away, ball centred: that is the only angle shaft lean lives in. 120 or 240 fps and LIGHTS ON — that clip ran 60 fps dropping to 30 because the room was dark, which is the phone quietly halving the one thing that makes impact visible. A SCALE in frame, though the ball is already one at 1.68 inches. REAL SHOTS AT REAL LENGTH off turf or a mat — a rehearsal-speed pass measures nothing however well it is shot, and the last one had the club pushing the ball 3.8 inches at 1.9 mph with the face never leaving it. And FOOT SPRAY OR IMPACT TAPE on the face for a couple, because strike location is the highest-value thing you are not measuring — the same gap that is open on the putter across five heads — where the low point actually sits, and whether the club keeps travelling low past the ball or the handle dives. (3) RUN THE ROLL-OUT TEST that the short-game plan's club-by-roll-out ratios have been owed since Aug 13, with the new delivery: 5 balls each with the 50, 56 and 60 onto one towel three paces on, and pace the roll from there. A spin change shows up as a change in ROLL before it shows up anywhere else — and it replaces the textbook 2x / 1x / half ratios with yours in the same session.

entries.setup: 1 clip · CHIPPING, first ever filmed · 56° wedge on carpet, indoors and dim · SLOW MOTION, and the file's own metadata does not say so · one struck chip, ball exits the bottom of frame · iPhone ELEVATED and IN FRONT of him, off the target line, looking down · framing drifts
entries.finding:
CORRECTED Aug 25 — the first read of this clip said the ball was never struck. It was, and Jack said so: it is a slow-motion clip and the ball went out of frame. Both halves are confirmed on the film. The ball sits still at frames 245–249, is moving by f252, doubles in apparent size on its way to the lens (radius 17.4 px at rest to 34.6 px at f290) and leaves the bottom of the frame at f291. The first read cropped too tightly, lost the ball as it exited, and mistook the clubhead following through for the head still carrying the ball. The error and its cause are written up in the Short Game Workshop Log rather than quietly fixed.

WHAT THE FILM DOES ESTABLISH. A struck chip, flying at the camera and out of shot: about 27 inches of three-dimensional travel between the ball leaving its resting spot and leaving the frame, reconstructed from the ball's own diameter (1.68 in) as the ruler and its apparent size as the range. Impact falls between f249 and f252.

AND IT IS SLOWED, WHICH THE FILE HIDES. The container presents 368 samples at a nominal 60 fps with drops to 30 — no slow-motion ramp anywhere in it. Physics says otherwise: 27 inches over 40 frames at 60 fps would be two thirds of a second, and a ball in free flight falls SEVEN FEET in that time. This one flew nearly straight. So the presented time base is not real time, and every speed computed from it is wrong by the slow-motion factor. At a 240 fps capture the numbers land at roughly 9 mph of ball speed with about five inches of gravity drop, which is a real if small indoor chip and is self-consistent; at 120 fps it is about 4.6 mph and the drop stops fitting. So 240 is the best reading, and it is an INFERENCE from the flight rather than anything the file admits.

STILL NOT MEASURABLE, and this part did not change: shaft lean at impact, angle of attack, low point and strike location. They live in the vertical plane containing the target line, and the lens is elevated, in front and off that line. The through-the-ball finding from earlier today remains unmeasured.

detail.gist: CORRECTED — a struck chip that exits frame, slowed by an unknown factor the file does not record.

metrics.n: still f245–249 · moving f252 · gone f291
INFERRED — the file hides the time base
camera elevated and off the target line
and a carpet cannot be entered
the face is never in shot

detail.story:
HOW THE CLIP RUNS. 340 decoded frames. He holds address to about frame 125, takes it back slowly through frame 200, returns, and the ball is struck between f249 and f252. From there it tracks smoothly down and right across the frame at a steady 22–28 px a frame, growing from 17.4 px of radius to nearly 35 — that growth is the ball closing on the camera, and it is the measurement that makes a three-dimensional reconstruction possible at all. It leaves the bottom of the frame at f291.

THE RULER IS THE BALL. A golf ball is 1.68 inches across, so its apparent radius gives both the scale and the range in every frame it appears in, with no calibration and no scale object needed. That is the trick worth keeping from this session: whatever else is wrong with a clip, if the ball is in it, it can be measured.

ONE OBSERVATION THAT IS NOT A MEASUREMENT: he does not stand up before contact. Through the downswing the posture looks held and the rise comes after the ball, which is the right order. Not scored — the framing drifts and there is no scale on his body.
detail.limits:
THE TIME BASE IS THE PROBLEM, and it is new. The clip is slowed and the file does not record by how much, so no speed, tempo or duration in it can be trusted without knowing the capture setting. That is now a line in the filming spec: write down what you shot at, because the file will not.

SHAFT LEAN, ANGLE OF ATTACK AND LOW POINT: unmeasurable, the lens is not in the plane those angles live in. STRIKE LOCATION: the face is never visible. SPIN: not measurable here, and not creatable on carpet at any speed — chip spin comes from friction between grooves and cover with nothing in between. The surface argues the other way too: the ball sits up on the pile so the leading edge can slide under it, and a hard floor sits under 3/8 in of pile, so a descending strike has nowhere to go. The room rewards a shallow sweep and punishes the delivery being trained.
detail.compare: VERSUS THE PUTTING FILM. Every putting session since Jul 30 has been blind to shaft lean because every camera sat ON the target line; this one is blind to it because the camera sat off the line and above it. Different error, same missing measurement — FACE-ON AT BALL HEIGHT is still the angle this project has never once shot, now across two disciplines. VERSUS AUG 24 (ten AirBreak clips, none able to touch aim): that set measured a roll. This one measures a flight, which is more than the first read of it credited, and still not the thing that was asked of it.

Every section says what is STILL UNMEASURED. That line is not optional

sections.t: Aug 25 2026 — The first chipping film, the read that was wrong, and what a room can still measure
sections.k: A struck chip that exits frame, slowed by a factor the file does not record — so the delivery is still unmeasured, and the first read of this clip was wrong about the most basic fact in it.
sections.b:
CORRECTED, and the correction came from Jack: "It's a slow mo video and the ball went out of frame." Both halves check out on the film, and the first version of this section got the most basic fact in the clip wrong. What it said is preserved at the bottom, because a log that quietly edits its own errors is worth less than one that keeps them.

WHAT THE FILM ACTUALLY SHOWS. The ball sits still at frames 245–249. By f252 it is moving. It then tracks smoothly across the frame at 22–28 px a frame while its apparent radius grows from 17.4 px to 34.6 — doubling in size, which means it halved its distance to the lens — and it leaves the bottom of the frame at f291. That is a struck chip flying at the camera and out of shot. Reconstructed in three dimensions using the ball's own 1.68-inch diameter as both scale and rangefinder: about 27 inches of travel from rest to the edge of frame, impact between f249 and f252.

WHY THE FIRST READ WAS WRONG, because the mechanism matters more than the mistake. The impact crop was 600 px wide and the ball left it almost immediately, so the frames that were examined showed the ball and the clubhead close together and both moving down-right — which reads as the head carrying the ball. Widening the crop to the full frame shows the gap opening every frame and the ball exiting below. TWO LESSONS. Never crop before you know where the ball goes; find the exit first, then crop. And a claim as categorical as 'nothing was struck' needed the ball tracked to the edge of the frame before it was written, not six frames of it.

AND THE CLIP IS SLOWED, WHICH THE FILE DOES NOT ADMIT. The container presents 368 samples at a nominal 60 fps with drops to 30, and carries no slow-motion ramp anywhere — read literally it claims to be real time. It is not, and physics is what proves it: 27 inches of flight over 40 frames at 60 fps would take two thirds of a second, and a ball in free flight falls SEVEN FEET in that time. This one flew nearly straight. So the presented time base is fiction and every speed derived from it is wrong by the slow-motion factor — which is exactly how the first read produced 1.9 mph for a shot that was struck. Fitting the drop, a 240 fps capture lands at roughly 9 mph of ball speed with about five inches of gravity drop and is self-consistent; 120 fps gives 4.6 mph and the drop no longer fits. So 240 is the best reading, and it is an INFERENCE from the trajectory rather than anything the file records. Credit where it is due: the second reading Jack brought back estimated about 8 mph and landed in the right place.

THE NEW RULE THAT COMES OUT OF IT, and it applies to every clip from here in every discipline: SAY WHAT YOU SHOT AT. The frame rate did not survive the trip out of the phone, and without it nothing timed in a clip — speed, tempo, duration, dwell — can be trusted. One line typed with the clip fixes it permanently. It is now in the filming spec on the to-do.

AND THE ONE GOOD TECHNIQUE FROM THE WHOLE EXERCISE: THE BALL IS THE RULER. It is 1.68 inches across, so its apparent radius gives the scale AND the range in any frame it appears in — no calibration, no scale object, no known camera. That is what made a three-dimensional reconstruction possible from an unusable angle, and it is worth remembering the next time a clip looks ungradeable.

WHAT IS STILL NOT MEASURABLE, and this part never changed. Shaft lean at impact, angle of attack, low point and strike location: all in the vertical plane containing the target line, and the lens is elevated, in front and off that line. So the through-the-ball finding from earlier today is exactly as unmeasured as it was before this clip existed. Carpet is still the wrong surface for the question as well — the ball sits up on the pile, a hard floor sits under 3/8 in of it, and chip spin needs groove-to-cover friction that does not exist here.

ONE LINE ADOPTED from the second reading, and it survives all of the above: control and spin are not the same goal. Control is repeatability — same launch, same spin, same first bounce — and it comes from a repeatable low point rather than from maximum spin. A chip that checks three feet every time beats one that sometimes zips back eight and sometimes runs fifteen. That is in the plan.

ONE LINE NOT ADOPTED, deliberately. That reading recommends 'the handle continuing toward the target through impact, so the head never passes the hands'. As an anti-flip cue it is fine and it agrees with the plan's quiet wrists. Held to the end of the follow-through it becomes a blocked chip that takes the bounce out of play and steepens the strike, which is the exact thing this workshop spent the day moving away from. The plan already says it better, so nothing changed and there is no second live source.

HOW TO FILM A CHIP SO IT CAN BE MEASURED. Face-on and PERPENDICULAR to the target line, lens at about knee height, level rather than tilted down, six to eight feet away, ball centred — the only angle shaft lean lives in. 120 or 240 fps, LIGHTS ON, and SAY WHICH. Real shots at real length off turf. Foot spray or impact tape on the face for a couple, because strike location is the highest-value thing not being measured — the same gap that has been open on the putter across five heads and is now open on the wedges too.

STILL UNMEASURED. The delivery, entirely. n = 1, on carpet, from an angle that cannot see the thing in question. Nothing in the plan moved on this evidence. The free measurement written up earlier today — read the turf mark on grass — remains the fastest route to an answer and needs no camera at all.

WHAT THIS SECTION SAID BEFORE IT WAS CORRECTED, kept on purpose. It said the ball was never struck: that over frames 279–286 the ball moved 3.8 inches in 0.117 s at about 1.9 mph with the clubhead in contact throughout, that the face and ball never separated, and that there was therefore no strike in the clip to grade. Every number in that sentence came from a six-frame crop that had already lost the ball, on a time base the file had misreported. The conclusion drawn from it — that nothing could be graded — happened to survive, for entirely different reasons. That is the least reassuring way for a wrong reading to end up looking right, and it is why this paragraph stays here.

SOURCES. The clip itself, decoded frame by frame with the ball as the scale, and its container atoms read directly for the time base. Jack's correction, which is what prompted the re-read. The second reading he brought back, credited where it was right.

sections.t: Aug 25 2026 — Hit down for spin, or through the ball?
sections.k: 'Hit down for backspin' is a full-swing rule that travels badly: at chipping speed a lofted wedge is already past the friction limit, so extra steepness only costs speed and puts the leading edge into the turf.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. Jack has always been taught that you hit DOWN into a chip to get backspin. Practising at home on Aug 25 he found the opposite works better — hitting THROUGH the ball — and reported more zip and more control off the 50°, the 56° and the 60°. Is the received cue simply wrong, or is he describing something narrower?

WHAT HE REPORTED, and which half of it stands on his say-so. The change and the intent are his: he is now delivering the club through the ball rather than down at it on short wedge shots, and he likes it on the 50° chips as much as on the two higher-lofted wedges. Nobody else can report that, so it stands. The RESULT — 'more zip, more control' — is a feel, and nothing has measured it.

WHAT CHECKED OUT — the mechanism, and it is specific to this shot. Spin comes mostly from SPIN LOFT: dynamic loft minus attack angle, i.e. how much loft is on the face relative to how steeply the club is moving. More spin loft does make more spin, but only up to a limit. Above roughly 45–50° the ball stops gripping and starts SLIDING up the face, friction is lost, and the spin rate falls. A 56° or 60° delivered at greenside speed sits at or past that number before any attack angle is added at all — so extra 'down' adds spin loft that cannot be converted into spin. Meanwhile it subtracts the two things that DO make spin at this speed: clubhead speed, and a clean centred strike. Where you catch it on the face matters more here than how steeply you arrive. And a steeper arrival presents the leading edge rather than the sole, which is the digging mechanism the plan already warns about in its setup section. So on a greenside wedge from a decent lie, shallower-and-through is the HIGHER-spin, higher-control delivery. His feel and the physics agree, which is not always how these end.

WHAT DID NOT CHECK OUT — 'hit down' as a blanket error. The cue is not nonsense; it is a full-swing rule that travels badly. On a full iron off the turf the low point genuinely belongs after the ball and a descending strike is right. And there are two greenside cases where you deliberately steepen: a buried or grabby lie in thick rough, where a shallow club never reaches the ball, and a plugged bunker lie, which is a chop by design and already written up that way. Sieckmann teaches the rough version through setup — ball back, stance wider, weight into the lead leg — so the exception is real teaching rather than a hedge. Both are now stated in the plan, because an instruction this good is exactly the kind that gets over-applied.

ALSO NOT ESTABLISHED — that 'through' licenses hanging back. The opposite fault is the flip: weight staying back, loft added with the hands, thin. The plan says so explicitly, because that is the predictable way to hear this instruction wrong.

WHAT CHANGED IN THE PLANS. Short Game — Around the Green gained a section, THROUGH THE BALL, NOT DOWN INTO IT, and a rule chip with it. THE SETUP THAT REPEATS was already saying the compatible half — hands level, let the bounce slide, don't dig — and now points forward to the new section rather than standing as a second source for one instruction. Two Coach drills were added to train it: 'Through the ball, not down into it' for the practice green, and a no-ball version for the room. No fault was opened: nothing was filmed, and a fault with no film behind it is a feel wearing a badge.

WHAT IS STILL UNMEASURED, and it is very nearly everything. Nothing in this app has ever recorded a chip. There is no launch-monitor number, no film of the delivery, and no scorecard field that sees a greenside shot — the live logger records whether the green was missed and where it finished, not what the recovery did. Beyond that, the session was indoors: carpet or a mat punishes a digging strike far harder than grass does, so the room may be rewarding the change for reasons that will not survive turf. Three things would settle it, cheapest first. FILM ten chips face-on and look at where the low point actually sits and whether the club keeps travelling past it. RUN THE ROLL-OUT TEST already owed for the club-by-roll-out ratios, with the new delivery — a change in spin shows up as a change in ROLL long before it shows up anywhere else, and it fills in the ratios that are still textbook figures rather than yours. Then the up-and-down rate over the next handful of live rounds, which is the outcome number and much the slowest to move: one round is 12 chances, which decided nothing last time either.

SOURCES. Spin loft and the friction limit: TrackMan's spin-rate guidance and GolfWRX's spin-loft explainers, which give the same 45–50° figure past which the ball slides up the face and spin drops. The shallow-versus-steep leading-edge argument, and 'where you hit the face matters more than how steep you come in': TrackMan's chip-shot material and Performance Golf's pitching and chipping guide. Deceleration as the chipping fault that costs spin: Practical Golf and Golf Distillery. Steepening from deep rough: James Sieckmann via Titleist's 18 Shots series. All of it read through search snippets — the sites themselves were blocked from here — so the figures are consistent across independent sources but none was read in full. Flagging that rather than letting a snippet read like a paper.

ADDED LATER THE SAME DAY — the other half of the feel, and it answers a question he asked directly. For the record, since the plans were versioned in three passes: ALL of this is Aug 25, one day's practice and one conversation. Nothing here spans two sessions. Jack: "when I sit down into it, it's like through the ball. So I'm almost going through the back end of the ball into the ground after and then hitting the ground after the ball. I don't know if that's right." It is right, and it is worth writing down WHY, because it is the piece that makes the whole finding coherent rather than merely contrarian.

THE STRIKE HAS TWO INDEPENDENT VARIABLES AND THE OLD CUE CONFLATES THEM. One is how STEEPLY the club arrives — the attack angle, which is what the first half of this workshop is about. The other is WHERE THE ARC BOTTOMS OUT relative to the ball. They are not the same thing and they do not have to move together: a shallow arc can bottom out well past the ball, and that combination is the shot. 'Hit down into it' is an instruction that buys a correct low point by paying in steepness — it gets the right answer to the second question by getting the first one wrong. What Jack is now describing is both answers at once: shallow through the ball, low point past it. That is why the two halves of his feel do not contradict each other, and it is the cleanest statement of the finding this workshop has produced.

WHY THE LOW POINT MUST BE PAST THE BALL, stated so it survives a bad day. There are three places it can be and two are bad shots. Behind the ball: the club reaches the turf first, the chunk. Never arriving, because the body rose and the club is still descending when it meets the ball's equator: the thin. Past the ball: the only one that produces a struck golf shot. Nothing about this is specific to the through-the-ball delivery — it is true of every strike off the turf — which is precisely why 'hit down' persists as a cue. It is aiming at a real target by a poor route.

WHAT WAS ADDED AS A GUARD RATHER THAN AS INSTRUCTION. Two, both because this feel has an obvious way to drift. DEPTH: contact after the ball is right, but how much ground is the variable, and a deep gouge means the leading edge beat the bounce to the turf — i.e. he has steepened again without noticing. The target is a long shallow bruise starting at or just past the ball, and a clean skim that barely marks is equally fine. AND DO NOT AIM AT THE GROUND: the ball is the target and the turf contact is a consequence. A player who starts hitting AT the ground finds it early, which is the chunk — the exact fault the low-point rule exists to prevent.

WHAT THIS CHANGES ABOUT THE MEASUREMENT PICTURE, and it is the best news in the workshop. The first half of this finding needed film or a launch monitor to check. This half does not: THE TURF MARK IS THE MEASUREMENT. Where it starts relative to where the ball sat answers the low-point question outright, and how deep it runs answers the steepness question well enough to catch a drift. It is free, it is available on any patch of grass, and it needs no equipment at all — so it has been added to the drill and to the to-do. The one thing it needs is GRASS. On a mat or carpet the club cannot enter the ground, so the room can train the club TRAVELLING but can neither train nor check where the arc bottoms out. That limitation is now stated in the at-home lesson, which was written earlier the same day and implied more than the surface can deliver.

STILL UNMEASURED. Everything from the first half stands unchanged, minus the low-point question the moment he reads a mark on real grass. Note what has and has not been established here: that the low point belongs past the ball is settled teaching and needs no defending. That HIS low point is now there is his feel and nothing more — which is exactly the sort of claim this project has learned to distrust, and exactly the sort the turf mark can settle in one session.

sections.t: How this log works
sections.k: Anything worked through end to end lands here as one section, so the doing-plan stays short.
sections.b:
When a short-game question gets worked through properly — research, a claim checked, a decision reached — it lands here as ONE section rather than being spread through the plan that tells you what to do.

That keeps the split clean. Short Game — Around the Green says what you do NOW. This log says how those instructions were arrived at and what was rejected on the way.

Each section carries the same skeleton: the question, what checked out, what did not, what changed in the plan as a result, what remains unmeasured, and the sources. The unmeasured line is not optional — a workshop that cannot say what it still does not know is a sales pitch.

And a log is a record, so a section is not rewritten when a later decision overtakes it. It gets a SINCE UPDATED line appended instead.

briefing.focus: Mostly general best practice, and it says so wherever it matters — the tailoring comes as you send lies, misses and results. One idea runs through all of it: pick the shot with the LEAST air time that still works, land it on a spot you chose, and let the ground do the rest. One section is now yours rather than the textbook's: the through-the-ball delivery you found on Aug 25.
rules: PUTT if you can · CHIP if you can't putt · PITCH only to carry something
Pick a LANDING SPOT, never the pin — and a flat, predictable one
Least loft that clears the trouble. The boring shot wins
From a bad lie or short-sided: GET IT ON THE GREEN. Two putts is fine
Hands LEVEL, not jammed forward — let the bounce slide, don't dig
THROUGH the ball, not DOWN into it — the club keeps travelling low past impact
BALL first, GROUND after — the low point lives PAST the ball, and it is a bruise not a gouge
Bunkers: same splash every time, distance is FOLLOW-THROUGH length
Never short-side yourself on the approach — that is where this gets hard

sections.t: THE LADDER — putt, then chip, then pitch
sections.k: Take the least air time that still works; a ball on the ground behaves, a ball in the air does not.
sections.b:
The default order around a green, and it settles most shots before you think about technique. PUTT IT if the ground between you and the hole is reasonable — fringe, firm collar, even light rough. A bad putt finishes ten feet away; a bad chip finishes anywhere. CHIP IT if you cannot putt it: minimum loft, ball runs most of the way. PITCH IT only when you must carry something — a bunker, rough, a tier.

The reason is error size, not elegance. Every foot of air time is a foot where strike quality decides the outcome. On the ground the ball is just rolling, and rolling is the thing you do best. The best short-game players are the most boring ones.

sections.t: THE LANDING SPOT — the only decision that matters
sections.k: Choose a spot on the green and hit that; the pin is a distraction and the roll-out does the rest.
sections.b:
Most amateurs aim at the hole, which is the single most common short-game error. You are not trying to hit the hole — you are trying to land the ball on a chosen spot and let a predictable roll take it there.

How to pick one. Get it ON THE GREEN, usually a couple of paces on, and choose FLAT ground: a landing spot on a slope or on the fringe gives you a bounce nobody can predict. Give yourself a big spot rather than a coin — you want room for error, and a big target reduces tension by itself.

Then commit to it and stop looking at the flag. Once you can land the ball in the same area reliably, the roll-out becomes arithmetic instead of a guess, and you get closer to the hole without changing anything about the swing.

sections.t: CLUB BY ROLL-OUT — the ratios you are choosing between
sections.k: Same landing spot, three clubs, three finishing distances — that is the whole short game in one sentence.
sections.b:
Rough working ratios off a standard chipping motion: the 50° runs about 2× its carry, the 56° about 1×, the 60° about half. So land all three on the same spot and you get three different finishing distances — which means the club is how you control distance, not the size of the swing.

Use it backwards on the course: measure the carry to your landing spot and the roll from there to the hole, take the ratio, and the club picks itself. Lots of green to work with is a 50°. Short-sided over a bunker is the 60°.

These are STARTING numbers, not yours. The Coach lesson 'Distance control is landing-spot control' trains them, and the real ratios come from you hitting the three clubs to one spot and pacing the roll — send those and this section gets replaced with your figures.

sections.t: THE SETUP THAT REPEATS
sections.k: Narrow stance, ball just back of centre, weight a touch forward, hands LEVEL — and let the bounce slide instead of digging.
sections.b:
Standard chipping setup, and it exists to make the low point repeatable rather than to look like anything. Feet about one clubhead apart. Ball slightly back of centre. Weight favouring the lead foot and staying there — hanging back is what produces the thin one. Hands slightly ahead of the ball, and no more than slightly.

That last one matters more for you than the rest, because it is the one that is easy to overdo. Your wedges run mid bounce (10° on the 56, 8° on the 50 and 60), which is built to SLIDE under the ball. Jam the hands forward and you present the leading edge to the turf, which digs — and digging is where both the chunk and the blade come from. Hands level, let the sole do its job.

Then it is a putting-stroke motion: rock the shoulders, quiet wrists, accelerate through. Deceleration is the fault that produces most bad chips, exactly as it does on short putts — which is the same instruction as the section below, arriving from the other side.

sections.t: THROUGH THE BALL, NOT DOWN INTO IT
sections.k: On a greenside wedge the strike is a shallow pass THROUGH the ball with the low point PAST it — ball first, ground after — not a chop down at it.
sections.b:
Your Aug 25 finding, and it is the first thing on this page that came from you rather than from a textbook. You have always been told to hit DOWN into a chip to get backspin; hitting THROUGH it gave you more zip and more control off all three wedges. That reads as correct, and it is worth knowing WHY so it survives a bad day.

WHAT 'THROUGH' MEANS HERE. Same setup as the section above — narrow stance, ball just back of centre, weight forward, hands level. From there the clubhead travels low and long: it arrives shallow, the sole skims the turf, and it keeps going down the target line after the ball has gone. The follow-through is at least as long as the backswing. What you are not doing is driving the handle down and quitting on it.

WHY IT MAKES MORE SPIN, NOT LESS. Spin comes mostly from SPIN LOFT — how much loft is on the face relative to how steeply the club is travelling. More of it does make more spin, but only to a point: above roughly 45–50° the ball stops gripping and starts SLIDING up the face, friction is lost, and spin falls. A 56° or a 60° delivered at greenside speed is already at or past that line before you add any attack angle at all. So every extra degree of down is spin loft you cannot cash — and you pay for it twice, in clubhead speed and in the leading edge going into the turf ahead of the bounce. What is left that genuinely makes spin at this speed is a clean, centred strike and a club that is still accelerating. Both are exactly what 'through' buys you, which is why the 50° feels better too.

THE ONE WAY TO GET THIS WRONG. 'Through' is not 'up'. Hanging back, adding loft with the hands, or scooping at it is the opposite fault and it produces the thin one. The low point still lives at or just past the ball, the weight still stays on the lead side, the hands stay level rather than behind. Shallow THROUGH the ball, not early OUT of it.

WHERE YOU STILL GO DOWN. Two, and both are already on this page. A buried or grabby lie in thick rough needs a steeper arrival, or the club never reaches the ball — ball back, stance wider, weight into the lead leg. A plugged bunker lie is a deliberate chop. And this is a SHORT-GAME rule only: a full iron off the turf still wants a descending strike and a divot after the ball.

WHERE THE BOTTOM OF THE ARC GOES — your own words, and they are the other half of this. Sitting down into it, the club goes through the back of the ball and into the ground AFTER it. That is right, and it is right for a reason worth holding: there are only three places the low point can be, and two of them are bad shots. Behind the ball is the CHUNK. Never arriving — the body rising, the club still on the way down — is the THIN. Past the ball is the only one of the three that hits a golf shot. So ball first, ground after, every time.

AND THESE ARE TWO SEPARATE DIALS, which is exactly why the old cue misfires. How STEEP the club arrives and WHERE the arc bottoms out are independent of each other — you can have a shallow arc whose low point is well past the ball, and that is the shot. 'Hit down' collapses the two into one instruction and buys the low point by paying in steepness, when your setup was already buying it for free: ball just back of centre, weight forward, staying down. Sitting down into it and STAYING down is what holds the low point where the setup put it; standing up through the shot is what drags it back behind the ball.

HOW MUCH GROUND. Contact after the ball is right; the DEPTH is the variable, and it is the one place this feel can drift back into a chop. You are looking for a long shallow bruise starting at or just past where the ball was — a skim that barely marks is fine too. A short deep gouge means the leading edge beat the bounce to the turf and you have steepened again without noticing. And do not aim AT the ground: the ball is the target and the turf contact is a consequence. Aim at the ground and you will find it early, which is the chunk.

AND THE TARGET IS REPEATABLE, NOT MAXIMUM. Control and spin are two different goals, and the one worth chasing is control: same launch, same spin, same first bounce. That comes from a repeatable low point, not from the most spin you can generate. A chip that checks three feet every time beats one that sometimes zips back eight and sometimes runs fifteen — the second is a better story and a worse short game.

HONEST STATUS: this is your feel, from one session, and nothing has measured it. The Aug 25 room film did not change it either: it caught a real chip, but from an angle that cannot see shaft lean or low point, on a surface a wedge cannot enter. But this half is cheap to check and needs no camera — read the mark you leave on the grass. The Workshop Log has the rest of what a measurement would look like and there is a to-do on the board for it.

sections.t: THE MEDICINE RULE — bad lie, short side, or both
sections.k: From a genuinely bad spot the shot is 'on the green', not 'close' — the hero flop is where doubles come from.
sections.b:
Two situations where the goal changes: a buried or grabby lie, and being short-sided with almost no green between you and the flag. In both, the honest play is to get the ball ON THE GREEN, take two putts, and walk off with a bogey.

This is the same rule as the recovery rule in Golf Mind, applied thirty yards from the hole: pick the shot you would bet a hundred dollars you can execute nine times in ten. From a tight lie over a bunker, the flop is not that shot for anybody.

And the cheapest version of this rule is played earlier, on the approach: aim at the MIDDLE of the green. Short-siding yourself is what turns a routine up-and-down into the shot you cannot play.

sections.t: BUNKERS — one shot, and the finish sets the distance
sections.k: Never touch the ball: enter the sand two inches behind it, same swing every time, and let follow-through length decide the distance.
sections.b:
The standard splash shot does not contact the ball at all — the club enters the sand about two inches behind it and the sand throws the ball out. Setup does most of the work: face slightly open BEFORE you take your grip, ball forward of centre, weight favouring the lead foot, and swing along your body line with commitment. Your 56° with 10° of bounce is built for this — let the sole skid, do not dig the leading edge.

DISTANCE IS FOLLOW-THROUGH LENGTH. Keep the entry point and the effort identical and change only how far the club swings through: a short finish throws it a few paces, a full high finish sends it twenty yards or more. Deceleration is the one unforgivable sin in sand — always finish.

PLUGGED LIES reverse the rules: square or slightly closed face, ball back of centre, steep chop right behind the ball. It comes out low with no spin and runs, so plan for the roll and just get it on the green.

sections.t: THE AWKWARD ZONE — 30 to 70 yards
sections.k: The worst shot in golf for most amateurs, and the fix is calibrated swings rather than feel.
sections.b:
Too long for a chip, too short for a full wedge, and the reason it hurts is that a half swing has infinite speeds while a full swing has one. Guessing at it is how you end up between clubs on a shot you should own.

The fix is the clock system, trained in Coach: give each wedge three calibrated swings — hands to 9 o'clock, 10:30, and full — which turns three wedges into nine reliable numbers covering roughly 45 to 110 yards. Fill the matrix once at the range with five balls per swing, then trust it on the course.

This also feeds your par-5 job: lay up to one of those numbers deliberately rather than to wherever a comfortable swing finishes.

sections.t: WHAT GOOD ACTUALLY LOOKS LIKE
sections.k: Tour scrambling is 57–60%, low single figures save par about half the time, and a 10-handicap converts around a third.
sections.b:
Benchmarks, so a number on your card means something. PGA Tour scrambling runs about 57–60%. Scratch-to-3 handicaps save par close to half the time they miss a green. A 10-handicap sits roughly 25 points below tour, so around a third. And a typical 10-handicap loses about 1.5 to 2.0 strokes a round around the green against a scratch player.

That last figure is the one worth holding onto: around the green is one of the biggest single pools of strokes available to you, and it is skill rather than speed or distance, so it is available at any age and in any weather.

A fair first target is 25–30% up-and-down. That is not close to tour and it does not need to be — it is two or three saved shots a round against where the cards currently sit.

sections.t: WHAT YOUR OWN CARDS SAY — and how little that is
sections.k: One round: 0 up-and-downs from 12 chances, 7 of 12 misses short. A flag, not a rate.
sections.b:
The honest state of the evidence, because this plan is otherwise generic. ONE round is recorded with green data: Sterling Farms, Aug 12, 18 holes. Six greens in regulation, twelve missed, ZERO up-and-downs, and 7 of the 12 misses finished SHORT against 2 left, 1 right and 1 long.

What that supports: a flag worth chasing. Twelve chances cannot separate a bad short game from a bad day, so nothing here is a rate yet and the 0% should not be read as your ability.

What the short-miss pattern hints at, with the same caveat: it points upstream of the short game. Missing short means the approach club or the strike is leaving you the LONGEST recovery every time, which is the hardest place to get up and down from. Taking enough club and aiming at the middle is the cheapest fix on this page and it is not a short-game change at all.

WHAT WOULD MAKE THIS PLAN YOURS: log greens and where the misses finished on the next two live rounds — at 36 recorded holes the app stops hedging. Beyond that, tell me what shot you reach for by default, what lie frightens you, and where the bad ones actually finish (chunked short, bladed long, or fine but 25 feet away). Each of those replaces a paragraph of general advice with something built for you.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: Written as general best practice on purpose, with the sources and the one thing that came from your own cards.
sections.b:
Written Aug 13 2026 at Jack's request as GENERAL best practice, to be tailored as he sends information. Nothing in the first seven sections came from his game.

RESEARCHED: the putt-chip-pitch default and the landing-spot method are standard short-game teaching; the setup (narrow stance, ball back of centre, weight forward, hands only slightly ahead) and the bounce-versus-dig mechanism likewise. Benchmarks: PGA Tour scrambling 57–60%, low single-figure handicaps near 50%, a 10-handicap roughly 25 points below tour, and a 1.5–2.0 stroke-per-round around-the-green gap between a 10 and scratch.

FROM THE BAG: the 50/56/60 with mid bounce (F/8°, S/10°, M/8°) off a 44° PW, and the roll-out ratios as starting figures rather than measured ones.

FROM HIS CARDS, and it is one round: Sterling Farms Aug 12, 6 GIR, 0 up-and-downs from 12, 7 of 12 misses short.

DELIBERATELY NOT RESTATED HERE: the drills. The clock system, bounce, chip-versus-pitch and landing-spot control are Coach lessons on the Wedges & Short Game shelf, and the bunker work is on the Bunker Play shelf. Plans say what to do on the course; Coach trains it.

AUG 25 2026 — added THROUGH THE BALL, NOT DOWN INTO IT, plus a rule chip, and pointed the setup section at it so there is one source for the instruction rather than two. FROM JACK: the change and the result he felt — more zip and more control off the 50°, 56° and 60° — reported after practising at home. RESEARCHED: the spin-loft friction limit (spin climbs with spin loft only to roughly 45–50°, past which the ball slides up the face and spin drops), the shallow-versus-steep leading-edge argument, and the deep-rough exception. UNMEASURED: the result, entirely. Worked through end to end in Short Game — The Workshop Log, Aug 25.

AUG 25 2026, later the same day — Jack described where the bottom of the arc goes: sitting down into it, through the back of the ball and into the ground AFTER it, asked whether that was right. It is, and the section gained it plus a rule chip. FROM JACK: the feel, again his. REASONED FROM IT, and the section says so: that steepness and low-point location are two independent variables, which is why 'hit down' misfires — it buys a low point past the ball by paying in steepness, when ball-back and weight-forward were already buying it for nothing. The depth calibration (a bruise, not a gouge) and 'do not aim at the ground' are guards on the same feel, not new instructions.

AUG 25 2026, the film — nothing measured, and the section is unchanged because of it. The first chipping clip in the project caught a real struck chip — ball still at f245, gone from frame at f291 — but from an angle that cannot produce shaft lean or low point, and slowed by a factor the file does not record. (The first read of it claimed nothing was struck; that was wrong and is corrected in the log.) Added from the second reading Jack brought back, and the only thing in it that changes what he does: control is repeatability, not maximum spin. Full write-up, the numbers, what was NOT adopted from that reading and the filming spec are in Short Game — The Workshop Log.

lesson.body: The room is where you found this, and it is the right place to keep it, because the motion is the whole drill — there is no outcome to chase and nothing to judge afterwards. Two things it trains: the club arriving shallow rather than chopping down, and the club still TRAVELLING after the ball would have gone. TWO HONEST LIMITS ON CARPET, and the second one is the important one. A hard floor under a rug punishes a digging strike far harder than grass does, so the room flatters a shallow delivery for reasons that have nothing to do with whether it works off turf. And the club cannot ENTER a floor — so the half of this you found by feel, the low point sitting past the ball with the club going into the ground after it, can be neither trained nor checked in here. The room trains the club TRAVELLING. TWO RULES THAT CAME OUT OF FILMING IT (Aug 25). NO BALL for the motion reps. The point of a rep in here is the motion, and a ball turns it into an outcome to chase and a thing to judge — which is the one advantage the room has over the green, thrown away. And IF YOU FILM IT, WRITE DOWN THE FRAME RATE. The first chipping clip was shot in slow motion and the file did not record by how much, which made every speed and duration in it untrustworthy and produced a confidently wrong reading. One typed line with the clip fixes it permanently. Where the arc bottoms out is a grass question, and the mark you leave on it is the answer. So train the motion here and grade it on the green — and film it, because a feel that has never been filmed is the one thing this app keeps learning not to trust.

entries.text: SHORT GAME — MEASURE THE THROUGH-STRIKE. The Aug 25 change (through the ball, not down into it) is a feel, from one indoor session, and this app has never recorded a chip of any kind. Three jobs settle most of it, and the first one is free. (1) READ THE TURF MARK, on GRASS — where it starts relative to where the ball sat answers the low-point question outright (at or just past the ball is the pass), and how deep it runs catches a drift back into steepness (a long shallow bruise or a clean skim, never a short deep gouge). No camera, no kit, any patch of grass. A mat cannot do this: the club never enters the ground. (2) FILM ten chips with the 56 FACE-ON — and here is the spec, because the Aug 25 room clip failed on every line of it. PERPENDICULAR to the target line, lens at about KNEE height, LEVEL rather than tilted down, six to eight feet away, ball centred: that is the only angle shaft lean lives in. 120 or 240 fps and LIGHTS ON — that clip ran 60 fps dropping to 30 because the room was dark, which is the phone quietly halving the one thing that makes impact visible. A SCALE in frame, though the ball is already one at 1.68 inches. REAL SHOTS AT REAL LENGTH off turf or a mat. AND SAY WHAT YOU SHOT AT — this is the one that bit: the Aug 25 clip was slow motion and the file recorded a flat 60 fps with no ramp anywhere in it, so the slow-motion factor was simply lost and every speed read off it was wrong. One line typed with the clip ('240 fps slo-mo') fixes it for good. And FOOT SPRAY OR IMPACT TAPE on the face for a couple, because strike location is the highest-value thing you are not measuring — the same gap that is open on the putter across five heads — where the low point actually sits, and whether the club keeps travelling low past the ball or the handle dives. (3) RUN THE ROLL-OUT TEST that the short-game plan's club-by-roll-out ratios have been owed since Aug 13, with the new delivery: 5 balls each with the 50, 56 and 60 onto one towel three paces on, and pace the roll from there. A spin change shows up as a change in ROLL before it shows up anywhere else — and it replaces the textbook 2x / 1x / half ratios with yours in the same session.

entries.setup: 1 clip · CHIPPING, first ever filmed · 56° wedge on carpet, indoors and dim · SLOW MOTION, and the file's own metadata does not say so · one struck chip — a 10-yard one he liked, ball exits the bottom of frame · iPhone ELEVATED and IN FRONT of him, off the target line, looking down · framing drifts
entries.finding:
A 10-YARD CHIP, AND A GOOD ONE — Jack's report, and the first chip in this project with any outcome attached. He also saw backspin zip on it. What the shot was is his to say; what it proves is a separate question, and on carpet the answer is not much, because carpet stops a ball whether it is spinning or not.

THE USEFUL THING THE REPORT DOES IS DATE THE FILM. A 10-yard chip needs roughly 19–22 mph of ball speed, and reconciling that with 40 presented frames of flight puts this clip at about EIGHT times slow — a 240 fps capture shown the standard way. The file itself says none of this: it presents a flat nominal 60 fps with no slow-motion ramp anywhere in it, which is what produced first a wrong reading of 1.9 mph and then a low one of 9 mph. So the shot dated the film rather than the film measuring the shot. That is backwards, and the fix is the standing rule already added: SAY WHAT YOU SHOT AT.

WHAT THE FILM ITSELF STILL ESTABLISHES: the ball is at rest through f245–249, moving by f252, grows from 17.4 px of apparent radius to 34.6 as it closes on the lens, and leaves the bottom of the frame at f291. A struck chip flying at the camera and out of shot.

WHAT IT STILL CANNOT SEE, and a good shot does not change it: shaft lean at impact, angle of attack, low point and strike location. They live in the vertical plane containing the target line and the lens is elevated, in front, and off it. The through-the-ball finding remains unmeasured — an outcome he liked is not evidence about a mechanism.

detail.story:
JACK'S REPORT, and it is the best evidence about this clip: a 10-YARD CHIP, a good one, with some backspin zip. What the shot was and how it came off are his to report, and this is the first chip in the whole project with an outcome attached to it at all.

AND IT DATES THE FILM, which is the wrong way round and worth saying plainly. A 10-yard chip needs roughly 19 to 22 mph of ball speed — that is projectile arithmetic on an 8-to-9-yard carry at a chip's launch angle, and it barely moves whether you assume 30° or 40°. Reconciling that with 40 presented frames of flight puts the clip at about EIGHT times slow, i.e. a 240 fps capture shown the standard way. The earlier figure here — about 9 mph, from assuming 4× — was low by half, and the reason it was low is that the file records no slow-motion factor at all. So the only reliable timing information about this clip came from Jack saying what the shot was. That is a failure of the file, not of the eye, and the fix is already the standing rule: say what you shot at.

ONE PLACE THE ARITHMETIC DOES NOT FULLY CLOSE, stated rather than smoothed. The three-dimensional travel reconstructed here — about 27 inches from rest to the frame edge — needs a focal length that was estimated rather than known, and at 8× slow it yields 11 to 15 mph rather than the 19 to 22 the shot requires. The most likely explanation is that the depth reconstruction UNDER-measures, since the sideways component needs no focal length and the depth component is the guessed one. Recorded as an open gap. It does not touch the conclusion, which was never a speed.

HOW THE CLIP RUNS. 340 decoded frames. Address held to about frame 125, a slow takeaway through frame 200, impact between f249 and f252, and the ball tracking smoothly down and right — its apparent radius growing 17.4 px to 34.6 px as it closes on the lens — before leaving the bottom of the frame at f291.

THE RULER IS THE BALL. A golf ball is 1.68 inches across, so its apparent radius gives both the scale and the range in every frame it appears in, with no calibration and no scale object. That is the technique worth keeping: if the ball is in shot, something can be measured.

ONE OBSERVATION THAT IS NOT A MEASUREMENT: he does not stand up before contact. The posture looks held through the downswing with the rise coming after the ball, which is the right order. Not scored — the framing drifts and there is no scale on his body.
detail.limits:
THE ZIP IS REAL AS AN OBSERVATION AND USELESS AS EVIDENCE, and the reason is the surface rather than the swing. Carpet stops a golf ball whether it is spinning or not — it is far more retentive than any green — so a ball that checks in here would check with backspin, without it, and with topspin. Nothing about a ball behaving on carpet supports a claim that the delivery is producing spin. This is the same shape as 'pace felt dialled' on Aug 1, which un-benched a putter that went back nine days later. It goes on file as what he saw, not as a result.

THE TIME BASE. The clip is slowed and the file does not record by how much, so no speed, tempo or duration in it can be trusted on the file's own terms.

SHAFT LEAN, ANGLE OF ATTACK AND LOW POINT: unmeasurable — the lens is not in the plane those angles live in. STRIKE LOCATION: the face is never visible. So the through-the-ball finding is exactly as unmeasured as it was before this clip existed, and a good shot does not change that: one struck chip he liked is an outcome, and the open question is a mechanism.
detail.compare: VERSUS THE PUTTING FILM. Every putting session since Jul 30 has been blind to shaft lean because every camera sat ON the target line; this one is blind to it because the camera sat off the line and above it. Different error, same missing measurement — FACE-ON AT BALL HEIGHT is still the angle this project has never once shot, now across two disciplines. VERSUS AUG 24 (ten AirBreak clips, none able to touch aim): that set measured a roll. This one measures a flight, which is more than the first read of it credited, and still not the thing that was asked of it.
