Jack ran the shelf and went back to the FORWARD PRESS, which this section had ruled out — see the Aug 14 section above for the distinction that let it back in (a press that RECOVERS versus one that is HELD) and for what it changed in the other plans. What this section concluded at the time stands as the record of what was reasoned on Aug 13; it just is not what he does now.

sections.t: Aug 13 2026 — The trail hand, and what L.A.B. actually claims
sections.k: Making the right hand the feel hand is a good cue on lags, but 'let the head release' contradicts the putter and was cut.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. Is 'right hand feels the speed, left hand just rides along' a sound cue on a zero-torque head?

WHAT HELD. L.A.B.'s premise is as advertised: the head is balanced to the shaft's lie, so it resists twisting and needs no hand manipulation. Light grip pressure and quiet hands are the manufacturer's own coaching here, not a teaching preference — Sam Hahn's line is that his job was just to LET IT STAY SQUARE, and the company's first drill is putting with your thumbs off the grip. Face angle is also the right thing to protect: over 1301 putts from 4 m by 71 elite players, face angle decided 80% of direction consistency, against 17% for path and 3% for strike (Karlsen, Smith & Nilsson, J Sports Sci 2008).

WHAT DIDN'T, and this is the one that would have changed what you do. 'LET THE HEAD RELEASE' was cut. A release means the face rotating through impact, and this head is built so it does not — the instruction is the opposite of a release. It also contradicted the paragraph it sat in. And your stroke is straight back and straight through, confirmed across four heads, so there is no rotation to time even if you wanted one.

THREE SMALLER CORRECTIONS. 'Square to your arc' is L.A.B.'s own wording and fine generically, but you do not have an arc — on your stroke it is square to the LINE, and arc language is what put a toe-hang blade in the bag in the first place. 'Passive lead hand' was scoped to the LAGS, because the claw inverts the pressure hierarchy: the claw exists to take the trail hand out, moving pressure into the lead hand and leaving the right as a guide, so on short putts there is no feel hand and there should not be. And 'most face-control trouble is anxiety and deceleration' was dropped — an unmeasured teaching claim, and not your diagnosis anyway now the left miss reads as an AIM error and the Aug 10 pm mat set (0.8° right / 1.0° left / 0.6° right) failed to reproduce a pull.

ONE GUARD ADDED. An active trail hand has a quiet way of shoving the handle forward, which breaks the vertical-shaft rule without ever feeling like it did.

WHAT CHANGED. The Routine plan gained the rule 'TRAIL HAND senses the weight on LAGS — it never pushes, and nothing releases' and a section beside the claw section carrying the cue, its scope and its guards.

STILL UNMEASURED. Whether an active trail hand was ever in your stroke to begin with. No film has been asked that question.

SOURCES. Outtabounds on lie angle balance; MyGolfSpy on Sam Hahn's instruction; Karlsen, Smith & Nilsson 2008 (PubMed 17917952); Golf Monthly on the claw grip.

SINCE UPDATED, same day: the claw came out of play by his call, so the scoping conclusion still stands but is currently dormant — conventional on every length, with the claw held as the short-putt reserve. What survives unchanged is the reasoning: whenever the claw IS on, there is no feel hand.

sections.t: Aug 13 2026 — Eye dominance: an explanation, not a second fix
sections.k: Same-side dominance predicts a left aim bias — your exact miss — but the standing measurement doesn't predict the putting one, so nothing changes until the overhead five reports.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. You are right-eye dominant and right-handed — SAME-SIDE dominant, the group taught to aim left. Does that explain the signature miss?

WHY IT FITS. The bias that setup is supposed to produce is LEFT, which is your miss exactly, and it is the only candidate cause that predates every putter you have owned. That makes it a real explanation for why 'barely open' had to become your square.

THE STUDY THAT SAYS SLOW DOWN. The dominance you measured standing up is almost certainly a primary-gaze result, and the only peer-reviewed work here (Dalton, Guillon & Naroo, Optom Vis Sci 2015;92(10):968–75, n=31) found primary-gaze and putting-gaze dominance are neither equal nor predictive of each other, with putting-gaze the weaker. So your PUTTING dominance is unmeasured. Everything else on this topic is teaching claim, not evidence.

THE ONE THING TO ACTUALLY DO — THE TWO-DROP TEST. Add one drop to the overhead five you already owe: drop a ball from the nose, then drop one from directly under the right eye, and measure the gap between the two marks. That gap is whether dominance is live for you at all, measured in the posture that counts rather than standing up.

THE GUARD THAT MATTERS MOST. DON'T STACK IT. The barely-open feel already cancels whatever aims you left. Adding an eye-dominance correction on top applies the fix twice and the miss flips RIGHT. This is an explanation, never a second correction. Getting low and standing close already shrinks it too — eyes over the ball leaves less parallax to have.

WHERE IT RANKS. Hypothesis two behind the LINK adaptation pattern, with head shape third and weakest.

WHAT CHANGED. Nothing about the stroke, the setup or the putter — that was the finding. The two-drop test rides along with the overhead five in the Routine plan's FACE section.

STILL UNMEASURED. Putting-gaze dominance, and the overhead five itself.

sections.t: Jul 30 – Aug 12 2026 — The putter saga, end to end
sections.k: Four head movements in a month, every one decided on an unmeasured round — and the LINK.2.1 is the one that stayed.
sections.b:
THE SEQUENCE. Jul 30: DF3i out, LINK.2.1 in, after a round of short lags and hot short putts. Aug 1: a Beekman scramble where pace felt dialled put the DF3i straight back in and sent the LINK to storage on redundancy. Aug 10: the LINK came back and the DF3i was returned for distance control. Aug 12: you closed the return window by decision and KEPT the LINK for good. Four movements in twelve days.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY DECIDED, AND ON WHAT. Every one of those calls was made on feel, on a single unmeasured round, and not one of them was tested against a calibrated lag session. The Aug 1 reprieve came off a SCRAMBLE — where a teammate has often already shown you the line and the pace — on greens running an estimated 8-9 stimp, the friendliest putting environment that exists. Slow greens flatter you twice: you swing bigger, which forgives an off-centre strike, and you hit firmer, and firm takes the break out. That pattern, not any putter, is the thing the Distance Grind exists to break.

THE LEGAL-MOVE POINT, which still holds. The LINK.2.1 is Lie Angle Balanced — the same zero-torque technology as the DF3i, in a narrow heel-shafted blade. The thing that made the Phantom 7.5 wrong for you, toe flow against a straight-back-straight-through stroke, stayed absent throughout. So the whole saga was a SHAPE argument, not a technology one, and it never reopened the mismatch it started with.

WHAT YOU TRADED. The DF3i was a wide, deep, high-MOI mallet; the LINK is a narrow blade with far less MOI, so an off-centre strike costs more speed and more face angle. You moved to a head that is less tolerant of PACE, which is your one open fault. The counter-argument is real and it is the reason to keep going: a forgiving head HIDES strike quality, a blade reports it. The blade is more punishing and more informative.

THE SETUP CUE THAT MOVES WITH THE HEAD — the one thing in any swap that can cost strokes. The DF3i's Press Pistol 2° leaned the shaft for you, so its cue was 'hands EVEN with the ball, the grip supplies the lean'. The LINK ships a Pistol 0 — zero built-in lean — and Jul 30 film measured exactly what that produces: shaft dead vertical, hands about 1.35" BEHIND the ball, repeatable to 0.3° across 59 frames. That is not a flaw, it is the geometry the putter is built around (69° lie, 2° effective loft, 0° lean). The 'hands even' cue died with the DF3i and must never be carried across — on a Pistol 0 it is lean YOU are adding, on a face with almost nothing to deloft.

WHAT THE NUMBERS SAY, read fairly. AMBIGUOUS, not favourable. The LINK's column holds the only two reds on the evolution grid — face at impact and the 1.5-1.7° left start line, both measured Jul 30, on this head — while the DF3i's first filmed column carries none. But Jul 30 was by far the most-filmed day of the project (three sessions, fourteen clips, the first face-on at 120 fps), so some of that is measurement effort rather than a putter effect, and the DF3i's clean column is partly clean because less was measured in it. In the LINK's favour: tempo 2.0:1 across seven of eight clips against the DF3i's 2.4:1, with 2:1 the target. The only real scoreboard in the entire project is the DF3i's 8/10 from four feet on Jul 20 — and it went back with the mallet.

WHAT THE SAGA PROVED. That the left miss travels. It reappeared while you were holding a zero-torque putter, which is the cleanest evidence available that the head was never the cause — and it is why the miss was eventually reclassified as an AIM error rather than a delivery one. Also that lags finishing short and short putts running hot are not two faults but one: an uncalibrated power curve, where you default to too-small on the big number and too-big on the small one.

WHAT CHANGED. The LINK is the putter, permanently — `returnWindow` is off, the Home return-window card is gone, and Decisions reads DECIDED. The Routine plan carries the Pistol 0 geometry as its hands instruction. The Distance Grind owns the calibration work the whole saga skipped.

STILL UNMEASURED. Strike location, on any of the four putters owned this month — which remains the single candidate that explains both open faults at once, since a heel strike closes the face and bleeds ball speed. The tape-test protocol now lives in the Lag Putts plan.

SINCE UPDATED (Aug 14 2026) — the grip named above is a LAMKIN DEEP ETCHED, not a Pistol 0. The app carried the wrong name from Jul 30 to Aug 14. Both are 0° built-in lean, so every word of the geometry in this section stands, including the 59-frame film measurement. Left unedited on purpose: a log records what was believed at the time. Full correction in the Aug 14 section at the top of this log.

sections.t: How this log works
sections.k: Anything worked through end to end lands here as one section, so the doing-plans stay short.
sections.b:
The rule going forward: when a question gets worked through properly — research, a claim checked, a decision reached — it lands here as ONE section rather than being spread through the plans that tell you what to do.

That keeps the split clean. The Routine plan, the Setup plan and the Distance Grind say what you do NOW, in as few words as they can. This log says how each of those instructions was arrived at, what was rejected on the way, and where the sources were. When an instruction changes, the reasoning does not have to be re-derived and it does not have to sit in the middle of a plan you read on the practice green.

Each section carries the same skeleton: the question, what checked out, what did not, what changed in the other plans, what remains unmeasured, and the sources. The unmeasured line is not optional — a workshop that cannot say what it still does not know is a sales pitch.

briefing.focus: Mostly general best practice, and every section now says which it is — SOURCE · STANDARD PRACTICE means textbook teaching, SOURCE · YOURS means it came from you, so you can see at a glance where you are off the beaten track and where you are simply following it. One idea runs through all of it: pick the shot with the LEAST air time that still works, land it on a spot you chose, and let the ground do the rest. Two sections are yours rather than the textbook's now — the through-the-ball delivery you found on Aug 25, and the ball-position loft dial you worked out on Aug 30.
rules: PUTT if you can · CHIP if you can't putt · PITCH only to carry something
Pick a LANDING SPOT, never the pin — and a flat, predictable one
Least loft that clears the trouble. The boring shot wins
From a bad lie or short-sided: GET IT ON THE GREEN. Two putts is fine
On the standard chip: hands LEVEL, not jammed forward — let the bounce slide, don't dig
Ball position is the LOFT DIAL — the hands stay in the MIDDLE of your stance
The high one: hands behind is a SETUP, not a flip — weight still forward, and it needs grass UNDER the ball
THROUGH the ball, not DOWN into it — the club keeps travelling low past impact
BALL first, GROUND after — the low point lives PAST the ball, and it is a bruise not a gouge
Bunkers: same splash every time, distance is FOLLOW-THROUGH length
Never short-side yourself on the approach — that is where this gets hard

sections.t: THE LADDER — putt, then chip, then pitch
sections.k: Take the least air time that still works; a ball on the ground behaves, a ball in the air does not.
sections.b:
SOURCE · STANDARD PRACTICE — textbook teaching, and nothing of yours has moved it yet.

The default order around a green, and it settles most shots before you think about technique. PUTT IT if the ground between you and the hole is reasonable — fringe, firm collar, even light rough. A bad putt finishes ten feet away; a bad chip finishes anywhere. CHIP IT if you cannot putt it: minimum loft, ball runs most of the way. PITCH IT only when you must carry something — a bunker, rough, a tier.

The reason is error size, not elegance. Every foot of air time is a foot where strike quality decides the outcome. On the ground the ball is just rolling, and rolling is the thing you do best. The best short-game players are the most boring ones.

sections.t: THE LANDING SPOT — the only decision that matters
sections.k: Choose a spot on the green and hit that; the pin is a distraction and the roll-out does the rest.
sections.b:
SOURCE · STANDARD PRACTICE — textbook teaching, and nothing of yours has moved it yet.

Most amateurs aim at the hole, which is the single most common short-game error. You are not trying to hit the hole — you are trying to land the ball on a chosen spot and let a predictable roll take it there.

How to pick one. Get it ON THE GREEN, usually a couple of paces on, and choose FLAT ground: a landing spot on a slope or on the fringe gives you a bounce nobody can predict. Give yourself a big spot rather than a coin — you want room for error, and a big target reduces tension by itself.

Then commit to it and stop looking at the flag. Once you can land the ball in the same area reliably, the roll-out becomes arithmetic instead of a guess, and you get closer to the hole without changing anything about the swing.

sections.t: CLUB BY ROLL-OUT — the ratios you are choosing between
sections.k: Same landing spot, three clubs, three finishing distances — that is the whole short game in one sentence.
sections.b:
SOURCE · STANDARD PRACTICE — and the numbers in it are the textbook's, not yours. The section says so where it matters.

Rough working ratios off a standard chipping motion: the 50° runs about 2× its carry, the 56° about 1×, the 60° about half. So land all three on the same spot and you get three different finishing distances — which means the club is how you control distance, not the size of the swing.

Use it backwards on the course: measure the carry to your landing spot and the roll from there to the hole, take the ratio, and the club picks itself. Lots of green to work with is a 50°. Short-sided over a bunker is the 60°.

These are STARTING numbers, not yours. The Coach lesson 'Distance control is landing-spot control' trains them, and the real ratios come from you hitting the three clubs to one spot and pacing the roll — send those and this section gets replaced with your figures.

sections.t: THE SETUP THAT REPEATS
sections.k: Narrow stance, ball just back of centre, weight a touch forward, hands LEVEL — and let the bounce slide instead of digging.
sections.b:
SOURCE · STANDARD PRACTICE, tuned to your bag — the setup is the textbook one; the bounce paragraph is about your actual wedges.

Standard chipping setup, and it exists to make the low point repeatable rather than to look like anything. Feet about one clubhead apart. Ball slightly back of centre. Weight favouring the lead foot and staying there — hanging back is what produces the thin one. Hands slightly ahead of the ball, and no more than slightly.

That last one matters more for you than the rest, because it is the one that is easy to overdo. Your wedges run mid bounce (10° on the 56, 8° on the 50 and 60), which is built to SLIDE under the ball. Jam the hands forward and you present the leading edge to the turf, which digs — and digging is where both the chunk and the blade come from. Hands level, let the sole do its job.

Then it is a putting-stroke motion: rock the shoulders, quiet wrists, accelerate through. Deceleration is the fault that produces most bad chips, exactly as it does on short putts — which is the same instruction as the section below, arriving from the other side.

AND THIS IS THE MIDDLE ONE OF THREE. Everything above describes your DEFAULT chip. The next section is the same setup with the ball moved, which is how you change the height without changing the swing — so read the two together and treat this one as the position you come back to.

sections.t: THE LOFT DIAL — three ball positions, one hand position
sections.k: Ball position sets the loft while your hands stay parked in the middle of your stance — back runs it, middle is the standard chip, forward flies it high and lands it soft.
sections.b:
SOURCE · YOURS, AND THE TEXTBOOK AGREES WITH YOU — you worked this out yourself on Aug 30; standard practice is set out beside it below so you can see exactly where the two part company.

WHAT YOU SAID. The shaft goes in the MIDDLE of your stance and stays there, and you move the BALL. Ball back, and your hands end up ahead of it. Ball forward, and your hands end up — your words — really behind the ball, which feels uncomfortable, and which you have watched tour players use to get the ball up and land it soft. That last one is the one you are emphasising.

WHAT STANDARD PRACTICE SAYS. The same thing, and this is one of the few genuinely tour-standard short-game models rather than a piece of folklore. It is usually taught as ONE SETUP, THREE BALL POSITIONS: you own one motion and change the club's effective loft by where the ball sits relative to a fixed handle. Effective loft at impact is the stamped loft plus or minus the shaft lean — handle ahead of the head takes loft off, handle behind it puts loft on — so moving the ball is moving a dial. What makes it better than the alternatives is what does NOT move: your hands, your arc and the bottom of your swing all stay where they were, so the strike stays the same while the flight changes. You are not learning three swings. You are learning three addresses.

So: nothing to correct. What follows is the part the model does not say out loud, which is where it can go wrong.

THE THREE POSITIONS.

BACK — THE RUNNER. Ball back of centre, handle ahead of the head, loft comes off, ball comes out low and releases. Your 50° lives here. Lowest air time and the biggest margin of the three, which is why the LADDER section says take it whenever it will do.

MIDDLE — THE STANDARD CHIP. Ball just back of centre, hands level. That is THE SETUP THAT REPEATS above, and it is your default.

FORWARD — THE HIGH ONE. Ball forward of centre with the handle still in the middle, so the shaft leans BACK and loft goes on. Higher, softer, less roll. Your 60.08M is the right club for it and not by accident: the M grind has relief ground off the heel, toe and trailing edge specifically so the face can be opened and the loft manipulated without the head sitting up off the turf.

WHY IT FEELS UNCOMFORTABLE, AND WHY THAT IS FINE. Every other instruction in golf tells you to get the handle ahead of the ball, so hands-behind reads as the scoop you have spent years being told not to make. The difference is WHEN, not WHERE. You are setting the loft at ADDRESS and then holding that relationship through the shot — your hands are behind the ball because the ball moved forward, not because your hands flipped past. Loft set at address is a shot. Loft added by the hands during the strike is the thin one. That single distinction is the whole difference between this section and the fault named in the one below it, and it is worth being able to say out loud.

WHAT ELSE MOVES — AND WHAT MUST NOT.

YOUR WEIGHT DOES NOT GO BACKWARDS. Leaning away to help the ball into the air is the single most common way this shot gets ruined, and it is the mistake that looks most like the shot. It drags the low point behind the ball, which is the chunk; or the body rescues it late, which is the blade. Weight keeps favouring the lead side. The ball goes up because the LOFT is up, not because you are.

THE STRIKE CHANGES, AND THIS IS THE HONEST DEPARTURE FROM THE SECTION BELOW. On the back and middle positions you catch the ball on the way down — ball first, ground after. Ball forward, you are catching it AT or just past the bottom of the arc, sliding the sole under it rather than pinching it. Leaning the shaft back also adds effective bounce, which is exactly what lets the sole skid instead of dig and is why this works at all with only 8° under the 60. But the margin gets thinner in BOTH directions: arrive early and the bounce skids in behind the ball, arrive late and the leading edge meets it on the rise and you skull it across the green. That is not a reason to avoid the shot. It is the reason it gets practised before it gets played.

WHICH MAKES THE LIE THE GATE. This shot needs grass UNDER the ball so the sole has something to slide through. Ball sitting up on a decent lie: yes. Tight, bare or baked: no — there is nowhere for the leading edge to go and the skull is live. Take the middle position and a lower shot instead. That is not caution, it is the difference between the shot working and it costing you two.

TWO DIALS, NOT ONE — AND ONLY LEARN ONE AT A TIME. Moving the ball forward is the FIRST way to add loft. OPENING THE FACE is the second, and the tour flop you have been watching is almost always both at once. They are not interchangeable: an open face adds loft AND aims the face right of your target, so it has to be paid for by aiming your body and swing left by roughly as much. Move the ball forward with a square face and the ball still starts where you aimed. So learn the ball-position dial on its own and get a number on it before you add the open face on top — two variables changed at once is how you end up with a shot that works some days and nobody can say why. The same split is already protecting the claw trial on the putting side.

HONEST STATUS. Your feel plus standard teaching, and none of your version has been measured — this app has still never recorded a chip of any kind. Two things would settle it and both are already on the board: one face-on clip per ball position, which is the only angle that shows what the shaft is actually doing at address versus at impact, and the roll-out test, which puts three numbers on the three positions in twenty minutes on a practice green.

sections.t: THROUGH THE BALL, NOT DOWN INTO IT
sections.k: On a greenside wedge the strike is a shallow pass THROUGH the ball with the low point PAST it — ball first, ground after — not a chop down at it.
sections.b:
SOURCE · YOURS, CHECKED AGAINST STANDARD PRACTICE — you found it; the physics underneath it was researched afterwards and backs you up.

Your Aug 25 finding, and it is the first thing on this page that came from you rather than from a textbook. You have always been told to hit DOWN into a chip to get backspin; hitting THROUGH it gave you more zip and more control off all three wedges. That reads as correct, and it is worth knowing WHY so it survives a bad day.

WHAT 'THROUGH' MEANS HERE. Same setup as the section above — narrow stance, ball just back of centre, weight forward, hands level. From there the clubhead travels low and long: it arrives shallow, the sole skims the turf, and it keeps going down the target line after the ball has gone. The follow-through is at least as long as the backswing. What you are not doing is driving the handle down and quitting on it.

WHY IT MAKES MORE SPIN, NOT LESS. Spin comes mostly from SPIN LOFT — how much loft is on the face relative to how steeply the club is travelling. More of it does make more spin, but only to a point: above roughly 45–50° the ball stops gripping and starts SLIDING up the face, friction is lost, and spin falls. A 56° or a 60° delivered at greenside speed is already at or past that line before you add any attack angle at all. So every extra degree of down is spin loft you cannot cash — and you pay for it twice, in clubhead speed and in the leading edge going into the turf ahead of the bounce. What is left that genuinely makes spin at this speed is a clean, centred strike and a club that is still accelerating. Both are exactly what 'through' buys you, which is why the 50° feels better too.

THE ONE WAY TO GET THIS WRONG. 'Through' is not 'up'. Hanging back, adding loft with the hands, or scooping at it is the opposite fault and it produces the thin one. The low point still lives at or just past the ball, the weight still stays on the lead side, and the hands stay level rather than behind — ON THE STANDARD CHIP. Setting the hands behind the ball deliberately, by moving the BALL forward at address, is a different shot and it is the section above this one. What is never right on any of them is the hands ARRIVING behind where they started. Loft set at address is a shot; loft added by the hands during the strike is the thin one. Shallow THROUGH the ball, not early OUT of it.

WHERE YOU STILL GO DOWN. Two, and both are already on this page. A buried or grabby lie in thick rough needs a steeper arrival, or the club never reaches the ball — ball back, stance wider, weight into the lead leg. A plugged bunker lie is a deliberate chop. And this is a SHORT-GAME rule only: a full iron off the turf still wants a descending strike and a divot after the ball.

WHERE THE BOTTOM OF THE ARC GOES — your own words, and they are the other half of this. Sitting down into it, the club goes through the back of the ball and into the ground AFTER it. That is right, and it is right for a reason worth holding: there are only three places the low point can be, and two of them are bad shots. Behind the ball is the CHUNK. Never arriving — the body rising, the club still on the way down — is the THIN. Past the ball is the only one of the three that hits a golf shot. So ball first, ground after, every time.

AND THESE ARE TWO SEPARATE DIALS, which is exactly why the old cue misfires. How STEEP the club arrives and WHERE the arc bottoms out are independent of each other — you can have a shallow arc whose low point is well past the ball, and that is the shot. 'Hit down' collapses the two into one instruction and buys the low point by paying in steepness, when your setup was already buying it for free: ball just back of centre, weight forward, staying down. Sitting down into it and STAYING down is what holds the low point where the setup put it; standing up through the shot is what drags it back behind the ball.

HOW MUCH GROUND. Contact after the ball is right; the DEPTH is the variable, and it is the one place this feel can drift back into a chop. You are looking for a long shallow bruise starting at or just past where the ball was — a skim that barely marks is fine too. A short deep gouge means the leading edge beat the bounce to the turf and you have steepened again without noticing. And do not aim AT the ground: the ball is the target and the turf contact is a consequence. Aim at the ground and you will find it early, which is the chunk.

AND THE TARGET IS REPEATABLE, NOT MAXIMUM. Control and spin are two different goals, and the one worth chasing is control: same launch, same spin, same first bounce. That comes from a repeatable low point, not from the most spin you can generate. A chip that checks three feet every time beats one that sometimes zips back eight and sometimes runs fifteen — the second is a better story and a worse short game.

HONEST STATUS: this is your feel, from one session, and nothing has measured it. The Aug 25 room film did not change it either: it caught a real chip, but from an angle that cannot see shaft lean or low point, on a surface a wedge cannot enter. But this half is cheap to check and needs no camera — read the mark you leave on the grass. The Workshop Log has the rest of what a measurement would look like and there is a to-do on the board for it.

sections.t: THE MEDICINE RULE — bad lie, short side, or both
sections.k: From a genuinely bad spot the shot is 'on the green', not 'close' — the hero flop is where doubles come from.
sections.b:
SOURCE · STANDARD PRACTICE — textbook course management, and it agrees with the recovery rule in your swing plan.

Two situations where the goal changes: a buried or grabby lie, and being short-sided with almost no green between you and the flag. In both, the honest play is to get the ball ON THE GREEN, take two putts, and walk off with a bogey.

This is the same rule as the recovery rule in Golf Mind, applied thirty yards from the hole: pick the shot you would bet a hundred dollars you can execute nine times in ten. From a tight lie over a bunker, the flop is not that shot for anybody.

And the cheapest version of this rule is played earlier, on the approach: aim at the MIDDLE of the green. Short-siding yourself is what turns a routine up-and-down into the shot you cannot play.

THIS DOES NOT ARGUE WITH THE LOFT DIAL, ADDED AUG 30. That section is HOW to hit the high one and it is worth owning; this one is WHEN, and it has not moved. The two only look like a contradiction if you read the flop as a shot you either have or do not have. Own it on the practice green, off a lie that supports it, and it becomes a CHOICE you make from a good lie rather than a hope you reach for from a bad one — which is exactly the difference this rule is drawing.

sections.t: BUNKERS — one shot, and the finish sets the distance
sections.k: Never touch the ball: enter the sand two inches behind it, same swing every time, and let follow-through length decide the distance.
sections.b:
SOURCE · STANDARD PRACTICE — textbook technique; you have sent nothing from a bunker yet.

The standard splash shot does not contact the ball at all — the club enters the sand about two inches behind it and the sand throws the ball out. Setup does most of the work: face slightly open BEFORE you take your grip, ball forward of centre, weight favouring the lead foot, and swing along your body line with commitment. Your 56° with 10° of bounce is built for this — let the sole skid, do not dig the leading edge.

DISTANCE IS FOLLOW-THROUGH LENGTH. Keep the entry point and the effort identical and change only how far the club swings through: a short finish throws it a few paces, a full high finish sends it twenty yards or more. Deceleration is the one unforgivable sin in sand — always finish.

PLUGGED LIES reverse the rules: square or slightly closed face, ball back of centre, steep chop right behind the ball. It comes out low with no spin and runs, so plan for the roll and just get it on the green.

sections.t: THE AWKWARD ZONE — 30 to 70 yards
sections.k: The worst shot in golf for most amateurs, and the fix is calibrated swings rather than feel.
sections.b:
SOURCE · STANDARD PRACTICE — textbook, and the drill that trains it is in Coach.

Too long for a chip, too short for a full wedge, and the reason it hurts is that a half swing has infinite speeds while a full swing has one. Guessing at it is how you end up between clubs on a shot you should own.

The fix is the clock system, trained in Coach: give each wedge three calibrated swings — hands to 9 o'clock, 10:30, and full — which turns three wedges into nine reliable numbers covering roughly 45 to 110 yards. Fill the matrix once at the range with five balls per swing, then trust it on the course.

This also feeds your par-5 job: lay up to one of those numbers deliberately rather than to wherever a comfortable swing finishes.

sections.t: WHAT GOOD ACTUALLY LOOKS LIKE
sections.k: Tour scrambling is 57–60%, low single figures save par about half the time, and a 10-handicap converts around a third.
sections.b:
SOURCE · STANDARD PRACTICE — published benchmarks, so they are somebody else's numbers by definition.

Benchmarks, so a number on your card means something. PGA Tour scrambling runs about 57–60%. Scratch-to-3 handicaps save par close to half the time they miss a green. A 10-handicap sits roughly 25 points below tour, so around a third. And a typical 10-handicap loses about 1.5 to 2.0 strokes a round around the green against a scratch player.

That last figure is the one worth holding onto: around the green is one of the biggest single pools of strokes available to you, and it is skill rather than speed or distance, so it is available at any age and in any weather.

A fair first target is 25–30% up-and-down. That is not close to tour and it does not need to be — it is two or three saved shots a round against where the cards currently sit.

sections.t: WHAT YOUR OWN CARDS SAY — and how little that is
sections.k: One round: 0 up-and-downs from 12 chances, 7 of 12 misses short. A flag, not a rate.
sections.b:
SOURCE · YOURS — one round of your own data, and the section is mostly about how little that is.

The honest state of the evidence, because this plan is otherwise generic. ONE round is recorded with green data: Sterling Farms, Aug 12, 18 holes. Six greens in regulation, twelve missed, ZERO up-and-downs, and 7 of the 12 misses finished SHORT against 2 left, 1 right and 1 long.

What that supports: a flag worth chasing. Twelve chances cannot separate a bad short game from a bad day, so nothing here is a rate yet and the 0% should not be read as your ability.

What the short-miss pattern hints at, with the same caveat: it points upstream of the short game. Missing short means the approach club or the strike is leaving you the LONGEST recovery every time, which is the hardest place to get up and down from. Taking enough club and aiming at the middle is the cheapest fix on this page and it is not a short-game change at all.

WHAT WOULD MAKE THIS PLAN YOURS: log greens and where the misses finished on the next two live rounds — at 36 recorded holes the app stops hedging. Beyond that, tell me what shot you reach for by default, what lie frightens you, and where the bad ones actually finish (chunked short, bladed long, or fine but 25 feet away). Each of those replaces a paragraph of general advice with something built for you.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: Written as general best practice on purpose, with the sources and the one thing that came from your own cards.
sections.b:
Written Aug 13 2026 at Jack's request as GENERAL best practice, to be tailored as he sends information. Nothing in the first seven sections came from his game.

RESEARCHED: the putt-chip-pitch default and the landing-spot method are standard short-game teaching; the setup (narrow stance, ball back of centre, weight forward, hands only slightly ahead) and the bounce-versus-dig mechanism likewise. Benchmarks: PGA Tour scrambling 57–60%, low single-figure handicaps near 50%, a 10-handicap roughly 25 points below tour, and a 1.5–2.0 stroke-per-round around-the-green gap between a 10 and scratch.

FROM THE BAG: the 50/56/60 with mid bounce (F/8°, S/10°, M/8°) off a 44° PW, and the roll-out ratios as starting figures rather than measured ones.

FROM HIS CARDS, and it is one round: Sterling Farms Aug 12, 6 GIR, 0 up-and-downs from 12, 7 of 12 misses short.

DELIBERATELY NOT RESTATED HERE: the drills. The clock system, bounce, chip-versus-pitch and landing-spot control are Coach lessons on the Wedges & Short Game shelf, and the bunker work is on the Bunker Play shelf. Plans say what to do on the course; Coach trains it.

AUG 25 2026 — added THROUGH THE BALL, NOT DOWN INTO IT, plus a rule chip, and pointed the setup section at it so there is one source for the instruction rather than two. FROM JACK: the change and the result he felt — more zip and more control off the 50°, 56° and 60° — reported after practising at home. RESEARCHED: the spin-loft friction limit (spin climbs with spin loft only to roughly 45–50°, past which the ball slides up the face and spin drops), the shallow-versus-steep leading-edge argument, and the deep-rough exception. UNMEASURED: the result, entirely. Worked through end to end in Short Game — The Workshop Log, Aug 25.

AUG 25 2026, later the same day — Jack described where the bottom of the arc goes: sitting down into it, through the back of the ball and into the ground AFTER it, asked whether that was right. It is, and the section gained it plus a rule chip. FROM JACK: the feel, again his. REASONED FROM IT, and the section says so: that steepness and low-point location are two independent variables, which is why 'hit down' misfires — it buys a low point past the ball by paying in steepness, when ball-back and weight-forward were already buying it for nothing. The depth calibration (a bruise, not a gouge) and 'do not aim at the ground' are guards on the same feel, not new instructions.

AUG 25 2026, the film — nothing measured, and the section is unchanged because of it. The first chipping clip in the project caught a real struck chip — ball still at f245, gone from frame at f291 — but from an angle that cannot produce shaft lean or low point, and slowed by a factor the file does not record. (The first read of it claimed nothing was struck; that was wrong and is corrected in the log.) Added from the second reading Jack brought back, and the only thing in it that changes what he does: control is repeatability, not maximum spin. Full write-up, the numbers, what was NOT adopted from that reading and the filming spec are in Short Game — The Workshop Log.

AUG 30 2026 — added THE LOFT DIAL, two rule chips, and a SOURCE line at the top of every section. FROM JACK, and it is the substance of the section: the shaft stays in the middle of the stance and the BALL moves — back for hands-ahead, forward for hands-behind — plus the report that hands-behind feels uncomfortable, and that this is the shot he is emphasising. RESEARCHED: that this is standard one-setup-three-ball-positions teaching rather than a quirk; that effective loft at impact is stamped loft plus or minus shaft lean; that leaning the shaft back INCREASES effective bounce, which is the mechanism that lets the sole slide rather than dig; that the Vokey M grind carries heel, toe and trailing-edge relief ground for opening the face and manipulating loft; and that an open face adds loft while also aiming the face right, so it is a second dial that has to be paid for with alignment. REASONED, AND SAYING SO: that the forward position catches the ball at or just past the low point and therefore has a thinner margin on both sides — that follows from where the ball sits in an unchanged arc, it has not been filmed. FROM THE BAG: the 60.08M as the club for it. ALSO CHANGED: the hands-level rule chip now says ON THE STANDARD CHIP, the THROUGH THE BALL section now separates loft set at ADDRESS from loft added by the HANDS, and THE MEDICINE RULE now says explicitly that it governs WHEN rather than whether — three places that would otherwise have read as contradicting the new section. SOURCE LINES: added at Jack's request on Aug 30 — he asked to always be able to see what is his own thinking and what is standard practice, separately, so he can tell when he is off track.
