sections.t: Aug 30 2026 — Ball position as the loft dial, and the flop that comes with it
sections.k: Jack's own model — park the hands in the middle of the stance and move the ball — is standard tour teaching; the work was in the three places it contradicted the plan and the two guards it needed.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. Jack described, unprompted, a chipping model he had arrived at by working through it: the shaft sits in the MIDDLE of his stance and stays there, and the BALL moves. Ball back, hands finish ahead of it. Ball forward, hands finish — his words — really behind the ball, which feels uncomfortable, and which he has seen tour players use to hit the high soft one. He is emphasising that third position. Two things to establish: is he right, and what does it break.

WHAT HE SAID, KEPT SEPARATE. His model, his words, his stated intent to work on the forward position. Under the film-is-king rule his INTENT is authoritative and nobody overrides it. His claimed POSITIONS — where the hands actually end up, how far the ball actually moves — are feel, and no chip of his has ever been filmed or measured. Nothing here promotes the feel to a measurement.

WHAT STANDARD PRACTICE SAYS, KEPT SEPARATE. He is right, and it is not a marginal read. This is taught almost universally as one setup, three ball positions: a single motion whose effective loft is dialled by ball position against a fixed handle. The mechanism is arithmetic — effective loft at impact is stamped loft plus or minus shaft lean, so handle-ahead delofts and handle-behind adds loft. The reason it is preferred to changing the swing is that the hands, the arc and the low point all stay put, so the strike is unchanged while the flight changes. His bag already supports the forward position specifically: the 60.08M is an M grind, which carries heel, toe and trailing-edge relief ground for exactly this — opening the face and manipulating loft without the head sitting up off the turf. So the verdict on the model itself is: no correction, and it is a better model than the one it replaces.

WHERE THE WORK ACTUALLY WAS. Not in the model — in what it contradicted, and in what it does not say out loud.

THE CONTRADICTIONS, ALL THREE FIXED IN THE DOING-PLAN. (1) The rule chip read 'Hands LEVEL, not jammed forward', flat, with no scope. It now reads ON THE STANDARD CHIP. (2) THROUGH THE BALL, NOT DOWN INTO IT contained the sentence 'the hands stay level rather than behind' as a blanket instruction, which is a direct contradiction of the forward position. The fix is the distinction that makes both true: loft set at ADDRESS is a shot, loft added by the HANDS during the strike is the thin one — hands behind because the ball moved is fine, hands ARRIVING behind where they started never is. (3) THE MEDICINE RULE calls the hero flop where doubles come from. That one is not a contradiction once stated properly: the medicine rule governs WHEN, the loft dial governs HOW, and owning the shot is what turns it from a hope into a choice. Said so explicitly in both sections rather than leaving a reader to reconcile them.

THE TWO GUARDS, AND THEY ARE THE VALUE THIS SECTION ADDS. First, THE WEIGHT DOES NOT GO BACKWARDS. Leaning away to help the ball up is the most common way this shot is ruined and it looks more like the shot than the shot does — it drags the low point behind the ball (chunk) or the body rescues it late (blade). Second, THE LIE IS THE GATE. The forward position catches the ball at or just past the low point and slides the sole under it, so it needs grass under the ball; off a tight or bare lie the leading edge has nowhere to go and the skull is live. Leaning the shaft back does raise effective bounce, which is what lets the sole skid rather than dig and is why 8° under the 60 is enough — but it does not manufacture grass.

AND ONE SPLIT WORTH PROTECTING. Adding loft with BALL POSITION and adding it by OPENING THE FACE are two dials, and the tour flop he has watched is both at once. An open face aims the face right as well as adding loft, so it has to be paid for in alignment; the ball-position dial alone leaves the face aimed where he aimed it. Learn one, get a number on it, then add the other — the same discipline the claw trial is running under on the putting side, and for the same reason.

WHAT CHANGED IN THE SHORT-GAME PLAN. New section THE LOFT DIAL — three ball positions, one hand position, placed straight after THE SETUP THAT REPEATS (which is now labelled as the middle one of three). Two new rule chips. The three contradictions above, resolved in place. And, at Jack's request, a SOURCE line at the top of every section saying whether it is his or the textbook's — see below.

WHAT CHANGED IN COACH. Two lessons on the Wedges & Short Game shelf: 'The loft dial: three ball positions, one hand position', whose drill puts three roll-out numbers on the three positions with one club and one landing spot, and 'Earn the flop before you play it', which is the lie gate and a pass mark rather than a technique lesson. Both tagged so they reach the open up-and-down fault, which had drills attached but none that trained this.

THE NEW STANDING CONVENTION, ALSO AUG 30. Jack asked that these write-ups always separate what HE is thinking and feeling from what standard practice typically is, clearly, so he can see when he is off track. That is now how the short-game plan is labelled and how this log is written, and it is recorded in the project's own instructions so it holds for every plan from here. It is the same ladder as film-is-king seen from a different side: that rule ranks his FEEL against MEASUREMENT, this one ranks his READ against the TEXTBOOK. On this particular question the answer was that he is on track, which is only worth knowing because the labelling makes it sayable.

STILL UNMEASURED, AND IT IS MOST OF IT. Every number in this section is the textbook's. Nothing of Jack's has been measured: not the ball positions, not the shaft lean at address or at impact in any of the three, not the low point, not the launch or the roll-out of any of them. This app has still never recorded a single chip. The standing capture action now carries a fourth job for it — one face-on clip per ball position, which is the only angle shaft lean lives in — and the roll-out test that has been owed since Aug 13 answers the three positions and the three clubs in the same twenty minutes.

SOURCES. FROM JACK: the model, the discomfort, and the intent to work on the forward position. RESEARCHED: one-setup-three-ball-positions as standard teaching; effective loft as stamped loft plus or minus shaft lean; shaft lean back increasing effective bounce; the Vokey M grind's heel, toe and trailing-edge relief and its stated purpose; the open face as a separate dial requiring an alignment offset. REASONED AND FLAGGED AS SUCH: the thinner two-sided margin on the forward position, which follows from where the ball sits in an unchanged arc rather than from any film. FROM THE BAG: the 50/56/60 at F/8°, S/10°, M/8°.

sections.t: Aug 25 2026 — Two more batches of chipping film: one real number, a frame-rate regression, and a mirror that lies
sections.k: The first real chipping speed on file — 0.28 s, which is normal — and the day's other batch measured nothing at all, for reasons that are all free to fix.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. Two more batches of chipping film arrived on Aug 25 after the morning clip: a 50°/56° pair at ~59 fps, and two 50-ball hallway sets at 30 fps. Can either of them see the delivery — shaft lean, low point, attack angle — that the morning clip could not?

WHAT CHECKED OUT. One thing, and it is the thing that had failed every time before: the motion on the film is finally a real chip. Downswing duration comes out at 0.28 s on the 50° (n=9) and 0.34 s on the 56° (n=5), everything falling between 0.17 and 0.47 s. Published real-chip downswings run about 0.25–0.30 s, so the 50 lands on it — your chipping speed is normal, and that is the first statement of any kind this project has been able to make about a chip. The camera also held still between the two clips (0.30 px), which would have made a 50-versus-56 comparison valid if anything comparable had been measurable.

WHAT DID NOT. Nearly everything else, and none of it for want of processing. The tempo RATIO is blocked for the third session running — a polished steel wedge head merges with the shaft and defeats a dark-blob tracker, and a motion-centroid method returned ratios between 0.01 and 9.5, a spread that cannot be defended. The hallway sets are a straight regression: 30 fps instead of 59, and one of them dropping 11.6% of its frames as duplicates for an effective 26.5. The one duration they produced (0.252 s) was reported as REJECTED and is recorded that way here, because the detector was firing on a continuous hover-and-waggle rather than on strikes — 198 events in 337 seconds, median gap 0.57 s, and a hand-validated tracker watching the clubhead move 69 px in four seconds while the detector claimed seven strikes in the same window.

AND A NEW FAILURE MODE WORTH MORE THAN THE NUMBER. There is a full-length mirror behind you in the hallway. A tracker locks onto the reflected club mid-stroke and returns a smooth, plausible, completely wrong path. Dark frames and dropped frames announce themselves; this one does not, and that makes it the most expensive thing in the two clips.

ONE READ THIS SIDE DID NOT ACCEPT. The analysis compares the new batch against the morning clip and calls that one a rehearsal — 0.68 s, 8 mph, one rep. This log had already corrected that clip twice, on your own report: a struck 10-yard chip you liked, filmed in slow motion the file never declares. The 0.68 s therefore sits on a presented time base rather than a real one, and the rehearsal framing does not carry. Ingested as written it would have walked a settled correction backwards — which is the whole reason a report gets read against the app before anything is pushed, and not the other way round. The analysis side has no view of this repo and cannot know what has landed; checking is this side's job.

THE SAME CHECK, RUN FORWARDS. Every duration in the good batch is read off the file's own time base, and this project learned that morning that a file can claim 60 fps while running eight times slow. So the cadence was checked here: nine detected chips across 43.5 s of presented time is one chip every five seconds, which is a normal rhythm with a ball to place between each. Eight times slow would make it nine chips in five seconds, and a 0.17 s downswing would become 0.02 s. The time base reads as real — by inference from cadence, not because the file says so.

WHAT CHANGED IN THE SHORT-GAME PLAN. Nothing about what you do around a green, and that is the honest answer: a downswing duration inside the normal range opens no fault and prescribes no change. What changed is the capture action, which now carries the full spec — 240 fps, knee height, square to the target line with the stick laid ALONG it, discrete reps with a pause between them, the mirror out of frame, a high-contrast sticker on the clubhead, two balls 12 inches apart for scale once a session — and, above all of it, that strike questions go OUTSIDE. The at-home lesson's drill also stopped recommending a weekly indoor film: three batches in one day timed the motion and never once saw the low point, and the coins already answer that for free.

WHAT THE REPORTS RANKED FIRST WAS ALREADY SHIPPED. Both name a coin or tee three inches ahead of the ball as the highest-value next step — no camera, no calibration, answers low point today. That has been in Coach since the morning in two forms: the near/far coin pair for the room, and the tee gate for grass, scored out of thirty across the 50, 56 and 60. The app's version is the stronger one. Nothing was pushed for it.

STILL UNMEASURED, and the list has not moved: shaft lean at impact, angle of attack, low point, strike location, club path, launch direction, spin, and the back-to-through tempo ratio. The first four are gated by the SURFACE before the camera matters at all — a wedge cannot enter carpet, the ball sits up on the pile so the leading edge slides under it, and the hard floor beneath punishes exactly the descending strike a real lie would reward. Also unmeasured: how many balls were actually struck in the hallway sets, which the footage could not settle.

SOURCES. Two analysis reports off Drive, both dated 2026-08-25 and both filed under Short Game: “Chipping film, 50° vs 56° (both gates failed)” and “Chipping film, 50-ball indoor sets (IMG_3722/3723) — both gates failed”. Evidence tags as given: 0.28/0.34 s and the frame-rate and camera-geometry figures are [DERIVED], the static-camera checks [VERIFIED], the tempo ratio and the lens [UNKNOWN]. The cadence check on the time base, and the refusal of the rehearsal framing, were done here against the existing record.

SINCE UPDATED (Aug 25, later). The frame-rate regression got a cause and three switches. The 60-to-30 drop INSIDE a clip is Auto FPS — a deliberate iPhone feature that lengthens exposure in dim light by halving the frame rate, costing you half your frames and adding blur to the rest. Now turned off. The 59-to-30 BETWEEN clips was almost certainly not a regression at all but the camera reverting to a default format, which Preserve Settings → Camera Mode holds. And the duplicate frames on the shorter, later clip fit heat accumulating across a session rather than load within one, which is an argument for short clips — the same change that fixes the hover-and-waggle problem.

One thing clarified rather than changed: SLO-MO WAS NEVER THE PROBLEM. It is the only way this phone reaches 240 fps, so it is what to shoot. The morning clip failed on its LABEL — the file presented a flat nominal 60 while actually running about eight times slow, so every speed read off it was wrong by an unknown factor until you said what the shot was. Likeliest mechanism: an exported copy rather than the original, since iOS keeps the slowdown as an edit over full-rate footage and some share paths flatten it. Both the chipping capture action and the putting face-on ask now carry all of this.

sections.t: Aug 25 2026 — The first chipping film, the read that was wrong, and what a room can still measure
sections.k: A 10-yard chip he liked, filmed from an angle that cannot see the delivery — and the shot had to date the film, because the file records no slow-motion factor at all.
sections.b:
CORRECTED, and the correction came from Jack: "It's a slow mo video and the ball went out of frame." Both halves check out on the film, and the first version of this section got the most basic fact in the clip wrong. What it said is preserved at the bottom, because a log that quietly edits its own errors is worth less than one that keeps them.

WHAT THE FILM ACTUALLY SHOWS. The ball sits still at frames 245–249. By f252 it is moving. It then tracks smoothly across the frame at 22–28 px a frame while its apparent radius grows from 17.4 px to 34.6 — doubling in size, which means it halved its distance to the lens — and it leaves the bottom of the frame at f291. That is a struck chip flying at the camera and out of shot. Reconstructed in three dimensions using the ball's own 1.68-inch diameter as both scale and rangefinder: about 27 inches of travel from rest to the edge of frame, impact between f249 and f252.

WHY THE FIRST READ WAS WRONG, because the mechanism matters more than the mistake. The impact crop was 600 px wide and the ball left it almost immediately, so the frames that were examined showed the ball and the clubhead close together and both moving down-right — which reads as the head carrying the ball. Widening the crop to the full frame shows the gap opening every frame and the ball exiting below. TWO LESSONS. Never crop before you know where the ball goes; find the exit first, then crop. And a claim as categorical as 'nothing was struck' needed the ball tracked to the edge of the frame before it was written, not six frames of it.

AND THE CLIP IS SLOWED, WHICH THE FILE DOES NOT ADMIT. The container presents 368 samples at a nominal 60 fps with drops to 30, and carries no slow-motion ramp anywhere — read literally it claims to be real time. It is not, and physics is what proves it: 27 inches of flight over 40 frames at 60 fps would take two thirds of a second, and a ball in free flight falls SEVEN FEET in that time. This one flew nearly straight. So the presented time base is fiction and every speed derived from it is wrong by the slow-motion factor — which is exactly how the first read produced 1.9 mph for a shot that was struck. Fitting the drop, a 240 fps capture lands at roughly 9 mph of ball speed with about five inches of gravity drop and is self-consistent; 120 fps gives 4.6 mph and the drop no longer fits. So 240 is the best reading, and it is an INFERENCE from the trajectory rather than anything the file records. Credit where it is due: the second reading Jack brought back estimated about 8 mph and landed in the right place.

THE NEW RULE THAT COMES OUT OF IT, and it applies to every clip from here in every discipline: SAY WHAT YOU SHOT AT. The frame rate did not survive the trip out of the phone, and without it nothing timed in a clip — speed, tempo, duration, dwell — can be trusted. One line typed with the clip fixes it permanently. It is now in the filming spec on the to-do.

AND THE ONE GOOD TECHNIQUE FROM THE WHOLE EXERCISE: THE BALL IS THE RULER. It is 1.68 inches across, so its apparent radius gives the scale AND the range in any frame it appears in — no calibration, no scale object, no known camera. That is what made a three-dimensional reconstruction possible from an unusable angle, and it is worth remembering the next time a clip looks ungradeable.

WHAT IS STILL NOT MEASURABLE, and this part never changed. Shaft lean at impact, angle of attack, low point and strike location: all in the vertical plane containing the target line, and the lens is elevated, in front and off that line. So the through-the-ball finding from earlier today is exactly as unmeasured as it was before this clip existed. Carpet is still the wrong surface for the question as well — the ball sits up on the pile, a hard floor sits under 3/8 in of it, and chip spin needs groove-to-cover friction that does not exist here.

ONE LINE ADOPTED from the second reading, and it survives all of the above: control and spin are not the same goal. Control is repeatability — same launch, same spin, same first bounce — and it comes from a repeatable low point rather than from maximum spin. A chip that checks three feet every time beats one that sometimes zips back eight and sometimes runs fifteen. That is in the plan.

ONE LINE NOT ADOPTED, deliberately. That reading recommends 'the handle continuing toward the target through impact, so the head never passes the hands'. As an anti-flip cue it is fine and it agrees with the plan's quiet wrists. Held to the end of the follow-through it becomes a blocked chip that takes the bounce out of play and steepens the strike, which is the exact thing this workshop spent the day moving away from. The plan already says it better, so nothing changed and there is no second live source.

HOW TO FILM A CHIP SO IT CAN BE MEASURED. Face-on and PERPENDICULAR to the target line, lens at about knee height, level rather than tilted down, six to eight feet away, ball centred — the only angle shaft lean lives in. 120 or 240 fps, LIGHTS ON, and SAY WHICH. Real shots at real length off turf. Foot spray or impact tape on the face for a couple, because strike location is the highest-value thing not being measured — the same gap that has been open on the putter across five heads and is now open on the wedges too.

STILL UNMEASURED. The delivery, entirely. n = 1, on carpet, from an angle that cannot see the thing in question. Nothing in the plan moved on this evidence. The free measurement written up earlier today — read the turf mark on grass — remains the fastest route to an answer and needs no camera at all.

AND THEN JACK SAID WHAT THE SHOT WAS: a 10-yard chip, a good one, with some backspin zip. That is the first chip in this project with an outcome attached to it, and it inverts the whole exercise. A 10-yard chip needs roughly 19 to 22 mph of ball speed — projectile arithmetic on an 8-to-9-yard carry, insensitive to whether you assume a 30° or a 40° launch. Reconciling that with 40 presented frames of flight puts the clip at about EIGHT times slow, i.e. a 240 fps capture shown the standard way, which makes the 9 mph figure above low by half. THE SHOT DATED THE FILM. That is precisely backwards from what a camera is for, and it is the strongest possible argument for the rule this session produced: say what you shot at, because the file will not.

ONE PLACE THE ARITHMETIC DOES NOT CLOSE, recorded rather than smoothed over. The reconstructed 3D travel — about 27 inches — yields 11 to 15 mph at 8× slow, not the 19 to 22 the shot requires. The sideways component of that reconstruction needs no focal length; the depth component uses one that was estimated. So the depth is the suspect and the reconstruction most likely under-measures. Left open, because it changes nothing that matters here.

AND THE ZIP, WHICH IS THE PART TO BE CAREFUL WITH. He saw the ball check. On carpet that is not evidence of anything, because carpet stops a golf ball whether it is spinning or not — it is far more retentive than a green, so a ball checks in there with backspin, without it, or with topspin. The observation goes on file as what he saw. It is the same shape as 'pace felt dialled' on Aug 1, which un-benched a putter that went back nine days later, and the reason that example is kept visible is exactly this moment. A good shot is an outcome; the open question is a mechanism, and this surface cannot connect them.

WHAT THIS SECTION SAID BEFORE IT WAS CORRECTED, kept on purpose. It said the ball was never struck: that over frames 279–286 the ball moved 3.8 inches in 0.117 s at about 1.9 mph with the clubhead in contact throughout, that the face and ball never separated, and that there was therefore no strike in the clip to grade. Every number in that sentence came from a six-frame crop that had already lost the ball, on a time base the file had misreported. The conclusion drawn from it — that nothing could be graded — happened to survive, for entirely different reasons. That is the least reassuring way for a wrong reading to end up looking right, and it is why this paragraph stays here.

SOURCES. The clip itself, decoded frame by frame with the ball as the scale, and its container atoms read directly for the time base. Jack's correction, which is what prompted the re-read. The second reading he brought back, credited where it was right.

sections.t: Aug 25 2026 — Hit down for spin, or through the ball?
sections.k: 'Hit down for backspin' is a full-swing rule that travels badly: at chipping speed a lofted wedge is already past the friction limit, so extra steepness only costs speed and puts the leading edge into the turf.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. Jack has always been taught that you hit DOWN into a chip to get backspin. Practising at home on Aug 25 he found the opposite works better — hitting THROUGH the ball — and reported more zip and more control off the 50°, the 56° and the 60°. Is the received cue simply wrong, or is he describing something narrower?

WHAT HE REPORTED, and which half of it stands on his say-so. The change and the intent are his: he is now delivering the club through the ball rather than down at it on short wedge shots, and he likes it on the 50° chips as much as on the two higher-lofted wedges. Nobody else can report that, so it stands. The RESULT — 'more zip, more control' — is a feel, and nothing has measured it.

WHAT CHECKED OUT — the mechanism, and it is specific to this shot. Spin comes mostly from SPIN LOFT: dynamic loft minus attack angle, i.e. how much loft is on the face relative to how steeply the club is moving. More spin loft does make more spin, but only up to a limit. Above roughly 45–50° the ball stops gripping and starts SLIDING up the face, friction is lost, and the spin rate falls. A 56° or 60° delivered at greenside speed sits at or past that number before any attack angle is added at all — so extra 'down' adds spin loft that cannot be converted into spin. Meanwhile it subtracts the two things that DO make spin at this speed: clubhead speed, and a clean centred strike. Where you catch it on the face matters more here than how steeply you arrive. And a steeper arrival presents the leading edge rather than the sole, which is the digging mechanism the plan already warns about in its setup section. So on a greenside wedge from a decent lie, shallower-and-through is the HIGHER-spin, higher-control delivery. His feel and the physics agree, which is not always how these end.

WHAT DID NOT CHECK OUT — 'hit down' as a blanket error. The cue is not nonsense; it is a full-swing rule that travels badly. On a full iron off the turf the low point genuinely belongs after the ball and a descending strike is right. And there are two greenside cases where you deliberately steepen: a buried or grabby lie in thick rough, where a shallow club never reaches the ball, and a plugged bunker lie, which is a chop by design and already written up that way. Sieckmann teaches the rough version through setup — ball back, stance wider, weight into the lead leg — so the exception is real teaching rather than a hedge. Both are now stated in the plan, because an instruction this good is exactly the kind that gets over-applied.

ALSO NOT ESTABLISHED — that 'through' licenses hanging back. The opposite fault is the flip: weight staying back, loft added with the hands, thin. The plan says so explicitly, because that is the predictable way to hear this instruction wrong.

WHAT CHANGED IN THE PLANS. Short Game — Around the Green gained a section, THROUGH THE BALL, NOT DOWN INTO IT, and a rule chip with it. THE SETUP THAT REPEATS was already saying the compatible half — hands level, let the bounce slide, don't dig — and now points forward to the new section rather than standing as a second source for one instruction. Two Coach drills were added to train it: 'Through the ball, not down into it' for the practice green, and a no-ball version for the room. No fault was opened: nothing was filmed, and a fault with no film behind it is a feel wearing a badge.

WHAT IS STILL UNMEASURED, and it is very nearly everything. Nothing in this app has ever recorded a chip. There is no launch-monitor number, no film of the delivery, and no scorecard field that sees a greenside shot — the live logger records whether the green was missed and where it finished, not what the recovery did. Beyond that, the session was indoors: carpet or a mat punishes a digging strike far harder than grass does, so the room may be rewarding the change for reasons that will not survive turf. Three things would settle it, cheapest first. FILM ten chips face-on and look at where the low point actually sits and whether the club keeps travelling past it. RUN THE ROLL-OUT TEST already owed for the club-by-roll-out ratios, with the new delivery — a change in spin shows up as a change in ROLL long before it shows up anywhere else, and it fills in the ratios that are still textbook figures rather than yours. Then the up-and-down rate over the next handful of live rounds, which is the outcome number and much the slowest to move: one round is 12 chances, which decided nothing last time either.

SOURCES. Spin loft and the friction limit: TrackMan's spin-rate guidance and GolfWRX's spin-loft explainers, which give the same 45–50° figure past which the ball slides up the face and spin drops. The shallow-versus-steep leading-edge argument, and 'where you hit the face matters more than how steep you come in': TrackMan's chip-shot material and Performance Golf's pitching and chipping guide. Deceleration as the chipping fault that costs spin: Practical Golf and Golf Distillery. Steepening from deep rough: James Sieckmann via Titleist's 18 Shots series. All of it read through search snippets — the sites themselves were blocked from here — so the figures are consistent across independent sources but none was read in full. Flagging that rather than letting a snippet read like a paper.

ADDED LATER THE SAME DAY — the other half of the feel, and it answers a question he asked directly. For the record, since the plans were versioned in three passes: ALL of this is Aug 25, one day's practice and one conversation. Nothing here spans two sessions. Jack: "when I sit down into it, it's like through the ball. So I'm almost going through the back end of the ball into the ground after and then hitting the ground after the ball. I don't know if that's right." It is right, and it is worth writing down WHY, because it is the piece that makes the whole finding coherent rather than merely contrarian.

THE STRIKE HAS TWO INDEPENDENT VARIABLES AND THE OLD CUE CONFLATES THEM. One is how STEEPLY the club arrives — the attack angle, which is what the first half of this workshop is about. The other is WHERE THE ARC BOTTOMS OUT relative to the ball. They are not the same thing and they do not have to move together: a shallow arc can bottom out well past the ball, and that combination is the shot. 'Hit down into it' is an instruction that buys a correct low point by paying in steepness — it gets the right answer to the second question by getting the first one wrong. What Jack is now describing is both answers at once: shallow through the ball, low point past it. That is why the two halves of his feel do not contradict each other, and it is the cleanest statement of the finding this workshop has produced.

WHY THE LOW POINT MUST BE PAST THE BALL, stated so it survives a bad day. There are three places it can be and two are bad shots. Behind the ball: the club reaches the turf first, the chunk. Never arriving, because the body rose and the club is still descending when it meets the ball's equator: the thin. Past the ball: the only one that produces a struck golf shot. Nothing about this is specific to the through-the-ball delivery — it is true of every strike off the turf — which is precisely why 'hit down' persists as a cue. It is aiming at a real target by a poor route.

WHAT WAS ADDED AS A GUARD RATHER THAN AS INSTRUCTION. Two, both because this feel has an obvious way to drift. DEPTH: contact after the ball is right, but how much ground is the variable, and a deep gouge means the leading edge beat the bounce to the turf — i.e. he has steepened again without noticing. The target is a long shallow bruise starting at or just past the ball, and a clean skim that barely marks is equally fine. AND DO NOT AIM AT THE GROUND: the ball is the target and the turf contact is a consequence. A player who starts hitting AT the ground finds it early, which is the chunk — the exact fault the low-point rule exists to prevent.

WHAT THIS CHANGES ABOUT THE MEASUREMENT PICTURE, and it is the best news in the workshop. The first half of this finding needed film or a launch monitor to check. This half does not: THE TURF MARK IS THE MEASUREMENT. Where it starts relative to where the ball sat answers the low-point question outright, and how deep it runs answers the steepness question well enough to catch a drift. It is free, it is available on any patch of grass, and it needs no equipment at all — so it has been added to the drill and to the to-do. The one thing it needs is GRASS. On a mat or carpet the club cannot enter the ground, so the room can train the club TRAVELLING but can neither train nor check where the arc bottoms out. That limitation is now stated in the at-home lesson, which was written earlier the same day and implied more than the surface can deliver.

STILL UNMEASURED. Everything from the first half stands unchanged, minus the low-point question the moment he reads a mark on real grass. Note what has and has not been established here: that the low point belongs past the ball is settled teaching and needs no defending. That HIS low point is now there is his feel and nothing more — which is exactly the sort of claim this project has learned to distrust, and exactly the sort the turf mark can settle in one session.

sections.t: How this log works
sections.k: Anything worked through end to end lands here as one section, so the doing-plan stays short.
sections.b:
When a short-game question gets worked through properly — research, a claim checked, a decision reached — it lands here as ONE section rather than being spread through the plan that tells you what to do.

That keeps the split clean. Short Game — Around the Green says what you do NOW. This log says how those instructions were arrived at and what was rejected on the way.

Each section carries the same skeleton: the question, what checked out, what did not, what changed in the plan as a result, what remains unmeasured, and the sources. The unmeasured line is not optional — a workshop that cannot say what it still does not know is a sales pitch.

And a log is a record, so a section is not rewritten when a later decision overtakes it. It gets a SINCE UPDATED line appended instead.

lesson.title: The loft dial: three ball positions, one hand position
lesson.body: YOURS: park the shaft in the middle of your stance and move the BALL — back puts your hands ahead of it, forward puts them behind it. STANDARD PRACTICE: the same model, taught as one setup and three ball positions, and it is one of the few short-game ideas that is genuinely tour-standard. Effective loft at impact is the stamped loft plus or minus the shaft lean, so moving the ball moves a dial — and because your hands, your arc and the bottom of your swing all stay where they were, the strike does not change while the flight does. Three addresses, not three swings. The one thing the model does not say out loud: your weight still favours the lead side in all three. Hanging back to help the ball up is what turns the forward position into a chunk or a blade. And the forward one needs grass UNDER the ball — off a bare lie there is nowhere for the leading edge to go. Keep the face SQUARE for now: opening it is a second dial and a second lesson.
lesson.drill: The dial ladder. ONE club (start with the 56), ONE landing spot — a towel three paces onto the green. Five balls with the ball BACK of centre, five from the MIDDLE, five from FORWARD, hands staying in the middle of your stance all fifteen. Pace the roll from the towel for each group and average it. You now own three finishing distances off one club and one swing, which is the whole point of the dial. Log the three numbers as your score (e.g. '9/5/3 paces'). Repeat with the 60 when the 56 numbers stop moving.

lesson.title: Earn the flop before you play it
lesson.body: This is not a technique lesson — the technique is in 'The loft dial'. This is the gate you put in front of it, because the high soft one is the highest-variance shot you own and the plan's medicine rule is right that it is where doubles come from. The two are not in conflict: the medicine rule governs WHEN, and owning the shot is what turns it from a hope into a choice. THE LIE DECIDES, ALWAYS. Ball sitting up on grass, the sole has something to slide through and the shot is on. Tight, bare or baked, the leading edge has nowhere to go and the miss is a skull across the green — that is a two-shot mistake, from a spot where the boring shot costs you one. STANDARD PRACTICE agrees on the number, and it is a useful one: play the shot you would bet a hundred dollars you can execute nine times in ten. A flop off a tight lie is not that shot for anybody, tour players included — they are hitting it off lies you have not looked at closely.
lesson.drill: The nine-in-ten test, and it is a scoreboard rather than a rehearsal. Ten balls, forward ball position, from a GOOD lie with the ball sitting up, to a pin with room behind it. Count how many finish ON the green — not close, on. Nine or ten and the shot is yours from that lie; anything less and it is a practice shot, not a course shot, and you take the middle position instead. Then drop five on a TIGHT lie and do not hit them — just look, so you learn to recognise the lie that says no. Log the make-count out of ten.

entries.text: SHORT GAME — MEASURE THE THROUGH-STRIKE. The Aug 25 change (through the ball, not down into it) is a feel, from one indoor session, and this app has never recorded a chip of any kind. Three jobs settle most of it, and the first one is free. (1) READ THE TURF MARK, on GRASS — where it starts relative to where the ball sat answers the low-point question outright (at or just past the ball is the pass), and how deep it runs catches a drift back into steepness (a long shallow bruise or a clean skim, never a short deep gouge). No camera, no kit, any patch of grass. A mat cannot do this: the club never enters the ground. (2) FILM ten chips with the 56 FACE-ON — and the spec below is now written off four failed attempts rather than one. PERPENDICULAR to the target line, lens at about KNEE height, LEVEL rather than tilted down, six to eight feet away, ball centred: that is the only angle shaft lean, attack angle and low point live in, and every clip so far has been elevated and in front, which sees none of them. Lay the alignment stick ALONG the target line and set the phone square to it — across the line, as on Aug 25, it measures nothing. SET THE PHONE UP ONCE AND IT STOPS COSTING YOU SESSIONS — three switches, and two of them are why Aug 25 went the way it did. AUTO FPS OFF (Settings → Camera → Record Video). This is the one that halved the morning clip mid-recording: in a dim room the phone drops 60 fps to 30 so it can expose each frame for twice as long, and it does it silently. You lose half your frames AND gain motion blur on the ones you keep, which is the pair of things that defeats a tracker. Turned off Aug 25 — done. PRESERVE SETTINGS → CAMERA MODE ON, so the app stops reverting to its default format when you reopen it. That is the likeliest reason the rate went from ~59 fps at 12:0x to 30 at 12:18: nothing degraded, the camera was just in a different mode. AND SEND THE ORIGINAL, not an export — iOS stores a slo-mo clip at full rate with the slowdown applied as an edit, and some share paths bake the slowed version into a new file at a normal frame rate, which is exactly what the morning clip looked like when it arrived. SLO-MO IS RIGHT, TO BE CLEAR: it is how this phone reaches 240 and Video mode cannot, so shoot Slo-Mo. What failed on Aug 25 was the LABEL, not the slow motion — the pixels were good and the timestamp was a lie. One more thing slo-mo costs you: at 240 fps the longest exposure possible is 1/240 s, about three stops darker than 30 fps, so it is hungrier for light than anything else you shoot. That is a second reason the strike work goes outside — daylight is close to the only source that comfortably feeds 240. 240 fps AND LIGHTS ON. This is the line that regressed: the midday clips ran ~59 fps and produced the one real number of the day, the 12:18 clips ran 30 and produced none, and one of those quietly dropped 11.6% of its frames as duplicates on top — an effective 26.5 fps — which is what a phone does in a dim hallway. At 30 fps the head covers 17.6 inches between frames; at 240 it covers 2.2. SHOOT DISCRETE REPS: pause between shots, or one short clip per shot. Fifty balls hit continuously with a hover and a waggle between them is what made 337 seconds of film unreadable — the detector could not find where one chip ended and the next began. GET THE MIRROR OUT OF FRAME: the hallway mirror hands a tracker a second, complete, moving club, and it switches to the reflection mid-stroke and returns a smooth trajectory that is entirely wrong. STICK A HIGH-CONTRAST MARKER ON THE CLUBHEAD — a polished steel wedge head merges with the shaft and defeats every tracker tried; the back-to-through tempo ratio is blocked for the third session running and a sticker is the whole fix. TWO BALLS EXACTLY 12 INCHES APART in frame, once per session, five seconds, and the focal-length unknown is gone for good. A SCALE in frame, though the ball is already one at 1.68 inches. REAL SHOTS AT REAL LENGTH off turf. AND SAY WHAT YOU SHOT AT — this is the one that bit: the Aug 25 morning clip was slow motion and the file recorded a flat 60 fps with no ramp anywhere in it, so the factor was lost and every speed read off it was wrong. One line typed with the clip ('240 fps slo-mo') fixes it for good. And FOOT SPRAY OR IMPACT TAPE on the face for a couple — at chipping speed that beats any phone angle, and it takes strike location off the blocked list permanently rather than waiting on a reshoot. LAST, AND IT OUTRANKS ALL OF IT: take the strike questions OUTSIDE. Low point, attack angle, contact quality and spin are gated by the surface before the camera is even considered — no indoor capture answers them at any frame rate, because a wedge cannot enter carpet. Indoors, film the MOTION and let the coins measure the low point. (3) SHOOT THE THREE BALL POSITIONS, ONE CLIP EACH — added Aug 30 with the loft dial, and it is the same face-on setup as (2) so it costs three extra clips rather than a second session. Ball BACK, ball MIDDLE, ball FORWARD, five chips each with the 56, hands staying in the middle of your stance. Face-on is the only angle shaft lean lives in, and shaft lean is the entire claim: the dial says the handle is ahead of the head in the first and behind it in the third, and nothing has ever checked that it is. What comes off it is the address angle against the impact angle for each position — which also settles the guard that matters, whether the hands are behind at address (the shot) or ARRIVING behind (the flip). Say which club and which position with each clip. (4) RUN THE ROLL-OUT TEST that the short-game plan's club-by-roll-out ratios have been owed since Aug 13, with the new delivery: 5 balls each with the 50, 56 and 60 onto one towel three paces on, and pace the roll from there. A spin change shows up as a change in ROLL before it shows up anywhere else — and it replaces the textbook 2x / 1x / half ratios with yours in the same session.

briefing.focus: The routine as you run it now: read it from behind, rehearse beside the ball with the pace look last, aim the FACE barely open and build the stance to it, release and RE-GRIP, and go — same beat count every putt. No forward press: this trigger changes what is IN your hands rather than where the shaft is, so the shaft is vertical at address AND at impact. How you stand and what is in your hands is the GRIP & POSTURE plan; the short ones and the lags each have their own.
rules: READ IT FIRST — pace before break. The how lives in the Reading plan
Aim the FACE first, then build the stance to it
Set the face BARELY OPEN — that's your square
Rehearse BESIDE the ball — ball-look first, HOLE-look last, always
TRIGGER = a late RELEASE AND RE-GRIP, LAST thing before the takeaway — same slot, same LIGHT pressure
Same BEAT COUNT every putt — a routine that varies in length is a pace variable
POP on the short ones, full length on the lags — each has its own plan
Setup and grip live in GRIP & POSTURE — get low, ball inside the lead heel, shaft vertical at ADDRESS and at IMPACT
steps: Read it from BEHIND the ball — pick the line and a spot a few inches ahead of it
Step BESIDE the ball — BEND OVER, stand close, full putting posture
Rehearsal 1 — eyes on the BALL. Path and contact.
Rehearsal 2 — eyes on the HOLE. Pace. This one goes last, always.
Step in — set the FACE to the spot, BARELY OPEN, then build the stance around it (trail foot a touch BACK)
Spot → ball → RE-GRIP → go. The stroke starts as a motion — quiet hands.

sections.t: THE READ — its own plan now
sections.k: What the putt is going to do, before you aim anything at it, moved to the Reading the Green plan.
sections.b:
Step one of this routine is still read it from behind — but the HOW moved out on Aug 14, the same way grip and the short stroke did.

The short version, so you are not left with nothing: behind the ball for the line, the low side for the amount, feet first on a green that looks flat, and pick the PACE before you read the break, because a putt has a different line at every speed. Past six feet the pace target is the Lag Putts circle; inside six it is seventeen inches past.

Everything else — grain, the pro side, the fall line, and the three minutes on the practice green that buy you the day's speed — is in Reading the Green.

sections.t: THE FACE — barely open is your square (your read, still unconfirmed)
sections.k: YOUR find, not the textbook's: set what reads to you as barely open — on this putter that should play as square. One check on a real green still owed; put a number on it and re-check monthly.
sections.b:
SOURCE · YOURS, AND NOT A TEXTBOOK INSTRUCTION — no putting method tells anyone to aim open. You arrived at this yourself, it is the load-bearing correction for your oldest miss, and it has not been measured on a real green. Treat it as your working setting rather than a fact.

WHAT STANDARD PRACTICE SAYS: aim the face square to the start line. That is universal, and it is not in dispute.

WHAT YOU FOUND: that setting the face to what reads to your eye as barely OPEN is what actually gets the ball started on line. Those are only in conflict if your eye and the face agree, and the whole point is that yours may not — the likely explanation is an aim error that predates every putter you have owned, so 'barely open' is the correction that cancels it and 'square' is what it produces.

SO: on this putter the face points where you set it — zero-torque means it doesn't twist through the stroke, so address IS impact, and whatever you set is what the ball gets. Set it the same way every putt and trust it until something measures it. What is NOT established is the amount: 'barely' has no number on it yet, which is the next paragraph.

Two standing guards. DON'T STACK FIXES: keep this feel, or retrain the aim picture with a mirror or a laser — never both, or the correction gets applied twice and the miss flips right. That guard got sharper on Aug 13, because a laser is a Lane B instrument by nature: watch a green line on the carpet long enough and your eye recalibrates whether you asked it to or not. Use it to MEASURE and look at the number afterwards. PUT A NUMBER ON IT: the laser does this properly now — at six feet, 1.26 inches of offset is one degree, so ten balls filmed against a marked scale turns barely open into an average you can re-check monthly. An unquantified feel drifts toward the exaggeration.

One check still owed, and it's the last one: five putts at a coin on a real green, nothing drawn on the ground, filmed from behind the ball. If the misses still fall on both sides, this closes for good. The indoor half of it can now be done any evening — the PUTTLAZR (Aug 13) reads the aim directly once it is calibrated to the FACE rather than the shaft, and the whole protocol is in Coach → At-Home Putting. Aim by feel, never at the beam.

Run the TWO-DROP TEST in the same session, since you are already in posture: drop a ball from your nose, then drop one from directly under your right eye, and measure the gap between the two marks. You are same-side dominant — right hand, right eye — and that predicts a LEFT aim bias, which is your miss exactly. The gap says whether that is live for you at all, measured bent over rather than standing up, which is the only version that counts. It is a reading, NOT a second correction: barely-open already cancels whatever aims you left, and stacking a fix on top misses right. Full write-up is in the Workshop Log.

sections.t: GRIP & POSTURE — its own plan now
sections.k: How you stand, what is in your hands, ball position, the shaft and the low point all moved to one plan.
sections.b:
Everything that is true BEFORE the putter moves now lives in GRIP & POSTURE — THE SETUP: get low and why the bend matters, the conventional grip and light pressure, ball one to two widths inside the lead heel, hands over the head of the putter, the vertical shaft at both ends, the trail foot back, lead-side pressure and the low point, and the trail hand's job on lags.

What stayed here is the ROUTINE: the read, the rehearsals, the aim, the trigger and the beat count. Those are the things you do in an order, every putt, and they are what this plan is for.

sections.t: SHORT PUTTS — they have their own plan now
sections.k: Everything inside about six feet — the claw, the pop stroke, the speed target and the scoreboard — lives in the Short Putts plan.
sections.b:
This plan is the stroke and the routine you run on every putt. The short ones have enough of their own content — a different grip, a different stroke shape and a different speed target — that they now have their own plan: SHORT PUTTS — THE POP STROKE.

What moved there: the pop stroke (short back, short through), the claw as a reserve grip, the 17-inch speed target, the loft trap that comes with rapping a ball on this face, and the 20-ball five-footer that settles whether any of it is better.

What stayed here, because it is true on every putt regardless of length: get low, ball position, the vertical shaft, barely open, trail foot back, the trigger, and the rehearsals.

sections.t: THE TRIGGER — the release and re-grip
sections.k: Your trigger is a late release and re-grip, deliberate and in the slot as of Aug 25; it is safe on this putter because it moves PRESSURE rather than position, which is also the thing it can get wrong.
sections.b:
LIVE, your call, Aug 25: NO forward press. What you actually run is a late RELEASE AND RE-GRIP — the hands come off the handle late and re-set on it — and then you go. Which trigger you run is yours to decide.

WHY THIS IS THE SAFE KIND OF TRIGGER ON THIS PUTTER. A re-grip changes what is in your hands, not where the shaft is. Nothing leans, so nothing has to be given back, and the 2° of effective loft this head is built to deliver at zero lean stays untouched (CONFIRMED Aug 14 from L.A.B.'s own specifications). That is what lets the shaft rule go back to what it was: VERTICAL AT ADDRESS AND AT IMPACT, in this plan and in GRIP & POSTURE, SHORT PUTTS and LAG PUTTS. Address is a real check again, because nothing moves you off it.

THE GUARD THIS TRIGGER BRINGS WITH IT IS A DIFFERENT ONE. A press risked a POSITION; a re-grip risks a PRESSURE. Grip pressure is the main way a hand gets back into a stroke that does not want one, and re-gripping is by definition the moment you set it. So: RE-GRIP TO THE SAME LIGHT PRESSURE YOU RELEASED. If the regrab lands firmer than the grip you let go of, you have just put the trail hand back into a stroke this whole plan is built to keep it out of — and firmer hands is a quicker putt, which lands on the open fault. Nothing measures this but you, and a squeeze is one of the few things a feel reports honestly.

IT IS A DECISION NOW — your call, Aug 25, and FOR NOW is your framing and the honest one. You started from 'I kinda just do' it, which describes a habit, and a habit is the thing that goes missing exactly when you are hot or rushed, which is the moment a trigger exists for. So it is deliberate from here: the release and re-grip IS the trigger, it happens in the SAME SLOT every putt, and it is the LAST thing before the stroke starts. Provisional, held until something either measures it or you change your mind — nothing has filmed it, and none of the three triggers you have run since Aug 10 has ever been measured.

FOUR RULES for whichever trigger you run. ONE trigger, never two. SAME SLOT every putt — it is the last thing before the stroke. IT MUST SHORTEN THE DWELL — count the seconds you stand still over the ball; if a trigger hasn't shortened it, it isn't working, whatever it feels like. AND IF YOU FREEZE ANYWAY, STEP OFF — no trigger rescues a freeze you are already inside; walk back behind the ball and restart. Eight seconds, always cheaper than the putt.

AND NOW THAT IT IS A DECISION, IT CAN BE GRADED — cheaply, and this is the only trigger you have run that has ever had a number attached. A trigger has exactly one job: it gets you out of standing still. So COUNT THE DWELL. Ten putts, stopwatch or just a beat count, from your last look at the hole to the takeaway; write the average down. Do it once in the next session while the trigger is new, and again in a fortnight. If the number has not come down, the re-grip is decoration and you are running no trigger whatever it feels like. No camera, no kit, and it is the cheapest scoreboard on this plan.

AND THE LADDER IS STILL A DETECTOR, watching for something new. It used to watch for a press that leaked lean and finished putts SHORT; it now watches for a re-grip that arrives firm and sends them LONG. Either way the rule holds: if the 30-ft ladder starts showing a pattern it was not showing before, suspect the trigger before you suspect your pace.

IF THE CLAW EVER COMES BACK OFF THE SHELF, the re-grip is the thing to re-check there. The trail hand sits differently in a claw, so 're-set it the same way' is a different physical act and the pressure it lands on is not the one your hands are used to. The claw is in reserve, not in play, so this is a note for later rather than a live check.

The full shelf of alternatives — kinetic and sensory, and what each one costs — is in the Putting Workshop Log under Aug 13; Aug 14 carries the press reversal and the Aug 25 line on it carries this one.

sections.t: THE REHEARSALS — beside the ball, pace last
sections.k: Rehearse in real posture beside the ball; ball-look first, hole-look second; same beat count every putt.
sections.b:
Read from BEHIND the ball — line, and a spot a few inches ahead of it. Then rehearse BESIDE the ball in full putting posture: same bend, same arm hang. Magnitude transfers one-to-one from that posture; behind-the-ball rehearsals read break better but run upright, so the size they teach is an approximation — and size is the thing you're training. REASONED, NOT SOURCED: that last step follows from where the arms hang in each posture. It is not a published finding and nobody has measured it on you — the ORDER below is the part that is standard teaching.

Order is fixed. Rehearsal 1, eyes on the BALL: path and contact. Rehearsal 2, eyes on the HOLE: pace. The last thing you feel is what you carry in, so the pace stroke goes last, always.

Same BEAT COUNT every putt — a routine that varies in length is itself a pace variable, and the putts that get an extra look are the ones that come up short. Backstop worth testing: say the pace intention out loud before stepping in ('die it a foot past', 'back of the cup'). Feel decays; a word doesn't.

Past 25 feet, test eyes ON THE HOLE through the stroke — as a block test on the practice green, not mid-round.

sections.t: THE STANDING WORK — where it lives
sections.k: Ten balls from thirty feet twice a week, and the whole protocol is in the Lag Putts plan.
sections.b:
Twice a week on the LINK, gamer ball only: 10 balls from 30 feet, logging SHORTS, SPREAD and GREEN SPEED, plus the 20/30/40 backstroke map. That is the standing work, and it belongs to pace rather than to the routine.

The full protocol, the targets and the tape test all live in the LAG PUTTS plan. The short-putt scoreboard — the 20-ball five-footer — lives in SHORT PUTTS.

sections.t: Feel versus real — how this plan is written
sections.k: Your words set the intent; the film sets the positions. Where they disagree, the film wins.
sections.b: Standing rule, in your words: the film study is king. What you're DOING — grips, triggers, decisions — is yours and authoritative. Where a POSITION or a SENSATION is claimed, the measurement outranks the description, and where there's no measurement the plan says so instead of repeating the feel as if it were established.

sections.k: History, condensed. Nothing here changes what you do above.

briefing.focus: Everything that is true before the putter moves, in one place: how you stand, what is in your hands, where the ball is, and where the low point ends up. One mechanism runs through it — lead-side pressure pins the low point, the low point decides whether the ball rolls or hops, and ball position plus a vertical shaft decide where that low point meets the ball. Keep any feel that passes the four checks. The routine that sits on top of this is the Putting Routine plan.
rules: GET LOW — the deep bend is what presents the lie this putter needs
CONVENTIONAL grip, both lengths — the claw is in reserve, not in play
Ball 1–2 BALL-WIDTHS inside the lead heel — mark it
HANDS OVER THE HEAD OF THE PUTTER — that IS the straight shaft
NO FORWARD PRESS (Aug 25) — the trigger is a RE-GRIP, so the shaft is VERTICAL at ADDRESS and at IMPACT
QUIET HANDS — the shoulders run the stroke, the hands just hold on
Pressure ~55/45 LEAD — its one job is pinning the low point
TRAIL FOOT back — square will feel closed
TRAIL HAND senses the weight on LAGS — it never pushes, and nothing releases

sections.t: THE HEADLINE — get low
sections.k: Bend over and get low — the anchor feel everything else hangs off, and it is what switches the putter's technology on.
sections.b:
Your words, and they go at the top: bending over is the most massive thing, and getting low is where you feel most comfortable. That is the feel to remember when everything else has drifted. If you carry one thought to the practice green, carry this one. Deep bend, stand close, eyes down.

Two mechanisms under the feel. FIRST — the LINK is Lie Angle Balanced, and that balance is only true when the shaft is presented at its built lie (69° lie, ~2° effective loft — an estimate, see the Notes — 0° lean, 34"). Stand tall or reach and the toe drops, the shaft leaves its lie, and the self-squaring property you bought quietly degrades. Posture is what delivers the technology.

SECOND — more bend hangs the arms freer and tilts the shoulders onto a STEEPER plane, and a steeper shoulder plane is what produces a straight-back-straight-through stroke. Standing tall builds in an arc you don't want.

sections.t: THE GRIP — what is actually in your hands
sections.k: Conventional on every length right now, light pressure, and the claw held in reserve rather than in play.
sections.b:
CONVENTIONAL, BOTH LENGTHS. As of Aug 13 the claw is not in play — you are running the conventional grip on short putts and on lags alike. The claw has not been thrown away; it is the reserve, and the Short Putts plan holds the trip-wire that would bring it back.

LIGHT PRESSURE, and this is the manufacturer's instruction rather than a preference. A Lie Angle Balanced head is built so the face squares itself when the hands stop interfering — L.A.B.'s own coaching is that your job is only to let it stay square, and their first drill is putting with your thumbs off the grip. Grip pressure is the main way a hand gets back into a stroke that does not want one.

THE ZERO-LEAN GRIP GEOMETRY. This putter carries a LAMKIN DEEP ETCHED — zero built-in lean. The shaft stands vertical and your hands sit about 1.35" behind the ball's centre, and that is correct rather than something to fix. The DF3i's 'hands EVEN with the ball' cue belonged to its Press Pistol 2°, which leaned the shaft for you; that grip went back with that putter and the cue died with it. Never carry it across.

THE TRAIL HAND — YOURS, CHECKED. You proposed this one: on LAGS, conventional grip, with the RIGHT hand sensing the weight of the head and the left just riding along. Keep it — it is a good cue and it is pointed at the right fault. It is not standard putting instruction, but it survived a check against L.A.B.'s own quiet-hands design, and the instruction you paired it with — 'let the head release' — was cut precisely because that half contradicts a zero-torque head. Pace is the open one, distance on this putter is stroke LENGTH at a fixed tempo, and a hand that reports how heavy the head feels going back is reporting the exact thing the ladder exists to calibrate.

SENSE the weight, never PUSH the club. A trail hand that drives through the ball is a second pace input stacked on stroke length, and it has a quiet way of shoving the handle forward — which breaks the vertical-shaft rule without ever feeling like it did. On SHORT putts there is no distance to feel, so the trail hand is just holding on; the feel job belongs to the lags.

sections.t: THE SETUP — the four checks
sections.k: Ball inside the lead heel · low point just behind it · shaft back to vertical · 55/45. Pass all four and keep your feel.
sections.b:
BEND OVER, stand close, eyes down through the strike. BALL one to two ball-widths inside the lead heel — forward of centre so the head is a hair ASCENDING at contact, which is what produces true roll. Mark the spot and keep it; launch is sensitive to it, and a ball position that wanders reads as bad distance control even when the stroke was fine. Weight stacked ON the ball. TRAIL FOOT a touch back. Rock the shoulders, QUIET HANDS, loose grip. Face set BARELY OPEN — its own section below.

HANDS OVER THE HEAD OF THE PUTTER — shaft straight up and down. That is the entire hands instruction. Don't add lean to make it look like a normal putter: this face carries little loft and is delivered at 0° lean, so there is nothing to spare, and a driven ball skids before it rolls and finishes short.

(A vertical shaft photographs as hands ~1.35" behind the ball's centre — half a ball from face to centre plus the riser hosel's offset. Same position, the camera's description of it. Ball position is set by your FEET; the shaft is set by your HANDS.)

(1) BALL one to two ball-widths INSIDE THE LEAD HEEL. Use the heel, not a body reference — a deep-bend posture moves your chest line; the heel doesn't move. Mark it on the mat.

(2) LOW POINT at or just behind the ball, so the head is a HAIR ascending at contact. This is what ball position is for.

(3) SHAFT RETURNS TO VERTICAL at impact — the same place it started.

(4) PRESSURE about 55/45 lead — enough to anchor the low point, not so much you start steering.

If a feel you're comfortable in delivers all four, keep the feel. The checks are the rule; the feel is yours.

sections.t: WEIGHT AND THE LOW POINT — the mechanism under all of it
sections.k: Lead pressure pins where the stroke bottoms out, and hanging back adds loft you never asked for.
sections.b:
Lead-side pressure does one job: it PINS THE LOW POINT of the stroke. Where your weight sits decides where the arc bottoms out, and where the arc bottoms out decides how the putter meets the ball. Everything below follows from that, on any head.

Weight back moves the bottom of the arc BEHIND the ball, so the head arrives climbing hard with the shaft leaning away from the target. That adds loft you never asked for: the ball launches slightly, HOPS, SKIDS, and only then rolls. Every bit of hop is energy that was supposed to become roll, so the putt arrives soft — and skid distance changes with green speed and grain, so your pace stops being repeatable between surfaces.

The window on this head is narrow in both directions, because a putter's loft budget is small to start with. Lean away from the target and you add loft; lean toward it and you go below zero and drive the ball down. Both mistakes produce the same symptom: a skidding ball that finishes short of what the stroke intended.

sections.t: THE SHAFT — vertical at address and at impact
sections.k: Nothing moves you off vertical any more, so address is a real check again — and both ends have to read the same number.
sections.b:
The shaft is VERTICAL AT ADDRESS AND VERTICAL AT IMPACT. Impact is the end that matters, and address is a fair proxy for it again as of Aug 25: the forward press is out and the trigger is a RE-GRIP (it lives in the ROUTINE plan), which changes what is in your hands rather than where the shaft is. Nothing takes you off vertical on purpose any more, so nothing has to be given back — and the two ends reading the same number is the whole test. Forward at IMPACT delofts a face with little to give and drives the ball into the turf — it skids, then rolls, and finishes short. Hands falling BACK invite the wrist flick. Both directions off vertical at impact are misses.

Check with a camera: one face-on clip, shaft angle at address versus impact, same number both times — pass. Check without one: LISTEN. A purely rolling ball makes one clean click; a driven ball adds a faint scuff a beat later. If you hear the scuff, the shaft leaned forward, whatever your hands report.

Two different variables, two different controls. Ball position is set by your FEET (check 1). Shaft lean at impact is set by your HANDS (check 3), and the target is zero.

A vertical shaft photographs as the hands sitting about 1.35" behind the ball's centre — half a ball (0.84") from face to centre, plus roughly half an inch from shaft axis to face on this riser-hosel blade. That's not a position to set; it's what 'hands over the head of the putter' produces on its own. If you try to put the hands somewhere, you're adding lean. Nothing in the routine asks you to any more, which is the point of a trigger that lives in your grip pressure instead.

sections.t: THE TRAIL FOOT — set it back
sections.k: Trail foot back, square will feel closed — and always face first, then stance.
sections.b:
Set the trail foot a touch further back than feels natural, and expect square to feel CLOSED. You're recalibrating off an open baseline, so trust the line you set rather than the feel for the first few sessions.

Why it matters this much: in an SBST stroke the shoulder line IS the track. An open stance doesn't just aim you left — it points the whole stroke left, and then either the hands steer the takeaway to save it, or the ball starts left. A stance error shows up disguised as a takeaway problem.

Ten-second check: alignment stick down the line, toes PARALLEL, not converging. And keep the order religiously — aim the FACE to the spot first, then build the stance around it. Face-first means a creeping stance shows up as discomfort, and discomfort you can feel is information you can act on.

sections.t: The blade tells you
sections.k: This head reports a bad strike instead of muffling it — use that, then measure.
sections.b:
A narrow blade carries less MOI, so a strike off the middle bleeds real distance and you can FEEL it. That makes your hands a better instrument on this putter than on a big mallet — a mediocre low point won't hide.

Use it, but don't stop there. The sound check costs nothing: one clean click is a rolling ball; a faint scuff a beat later is a driven one. The measurement is the tape test — twelve minutes, its own plan — and it's the thing to run before drawing any conclusion about this putter's pace.

sections.t: Settle any change with data
sections.k: A/B it on the ladder and let the stopping points decide, not the feel.
sections.b:
A/B LAG LADDER — 30 feet, two blocks of 10. Block A: current feel. Block B: the change, everything else identical. Mark where each ball STOPS and measure the spread; tighter spread wins, and that's the answer, not anyone's opinion.

FACE-ON CLIP — the one measurement this plan keeps asking for: shaft angle at address versus impact (matching at address and impact is the pass, and as of Aug 25 that is the plain question again — nothing in the routine moves the shaft, and the grip has no built-in lean either, so whatever the tape shows IS your hands), where the head bottoms out relative to the ball, and ball position rep to rep. White tape on the shaft, 240 fps, camera at ball height square to the line.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: History, condensed. Nothing here changes the checks above.
sections.b:
Aug 25: the forward press is out by your decision — a late release and re-grip instead — so this plan's shaft rule reverts to VERTICAL AT ADDRESS AND AT IMPACT, which is where it stood before Aug 14. The reasoning that re-scoped it to impact alone is not wrong and is not retired; it simply has nothing to act on while nothing moves the hands off vertical. New guard, and it belongs to this plan because this is where grip pressure lives: re-grip to the SAME LIGHT PRESSURE you released, because a firmer regrab is a trail hand back in the stroke.

Aug 14: the forward press returned by your decision, so this plan's 'NO FORWARD PRESS' rule is retired and the shaft rule re-scoped to IMPACT. What did NOT change: the mechanism. A shaft still leaning at impact still delofts and still finishes short — the press is only safe because it recovers, and that recovery is UNFILMED. The face-on address-versus-impact clip is now the owed measurement rather than a nice-to-have.

The 'hands level or a touch ahead at impact' rule that used to be check 3 belonged to the DF3i's Press Pistol 2° — a grip with lean built in — and left with that putter on Aug 10; on a 0°-lean build, hands ahead delofts and drives it. The press was removed the same day, which also retired the old 'keep it tiny' arithmetic. The ball-forward, weight-on-the-ball question was settled on the mat back in July; what this plan adds is the number (1–2 widths inside the lead heel) and the ground reference. This plan's forgiveness section flipped twice with the bag — the mallet that muffled a wandering low point is gone, which raises the stakes and sharpens the feedback. And the reason the plan exists at all: pace decided the fate of two putters on feel alone, with zero calibrated lag sessions behind any verdict.

Aug 13: this plan was assembled from the old 'Putting Setup — Weight & Low Point' plus the posture, shaft, trail-foot and grip sections that used to live in the Routine plan — they were all one subject, and the Routine plan is now only the routine. The tape test moved to the LAG PUTTS plan. Also Aug 13: the claw came OUT of play by your call, so grip is conventional on every length until the Short Putts trip-wire says otherwise.

Aug 13 — a correction to this plan's own arithmetic. The 2° of effective loft quoted throughout is an ESTIMATE. No retailer and no L.A.B. page publishes a loft for the LINK.2.1, so it was inferred rather than looked up, and every de-lofting calculation downstream of it is softer than it read. The mechanism is unaffected — a forward-leaning shaft delofts a face that has little to spare, and a delofted putt skids — but the margin is not a measured quantity. Language across the plans was softened accordingly.

AUG 30 2026 — labelled the TRAIL HAND cue as Jack's own, checked against the manufacturer's design, under the new yours-versus-textbook rule. It read as handed-down instruction; it is his, and the half of it that was cut is why that distinction matters.

briefing.focus:
Your own swing thoughts and setup keys, club by club, in your words — the go-to reference before a round or a range session. Where a line is standard technique rather than something you said, it is marked [STANDARD] inline, so the page can stay short and you can still tell which is which at a glance. Grip settled: conventional. Everything about putting lives in the Putting lab, so there is one source for it rather than two.

Renamed from ‘Golf Mind’ on Aug 14 2026: the page has always been driver / 5-wood / irons / wedges, and the old title read as the mental game, which now has a lab of its own.

sections.t: Driver — the big stick
sections.b: Aim the CENTER of the fairway — the start line tends to pull left, so center-aim leaves room. [STANDARD] The pull-left read is yours; aiming away from a known miss is textbook, not something you worked out. The straight ball comes from a LONGER, fuller swing — commit to that one. A tighter, shorter swing turns it into a cut, and when that goes wrong the miss is a PUSH-SLICE. So: full swing for straight; if you shorten it, expect the cut and know the push-slice is the bad one.
sections.k: Aim centre — your start line pulls left, and the straight ball needs a LONGER swing, not a tighter one.

sections.t: The fairway finder — 5-wood
sections.b:
The mini driver came OUT of the bag on Aug 12 and the Cobra Darkspeed X 5-wood (16.5°, bumped down from stock) took its slot as the fairway finder. Same job as before: a club you can put in play when the driver is the wrong risk.

One honest gap — its CARRY is unmeasured. It has been out of the bag a year, and there is no number for it on the ladder. Leave that blank until you hit some; a guessed number on a calibrated ladder reads exactly like a measured one, and that is how you end up short of a green with the right club in your hands.

And an open question worth knowing you have: at 16.5° it sits about half a degree off the 2-iron utility, so whether both belong in the bag is genuinely unsettled.

(The mini driver was kept, not sold — teed LOW with the weights back for the piercing ball, if it ever comes back.)
sections.k: The Cobra Darkspeed X 16.5° took this slot on Aug 12; its carry is unmeasured, so don't guess a number.

sections.t: Irons
sections.b:
Ball position right of center, toward the trail (right) thigh. [STANDARD] — stock iron ball position, not your own feel; nothing has measured yours. The new KING TECs fly HIGHER and longer than the old set — trust the extra height. When you need to flight it down or take something off, CHOKE DOWN and hit the control shot rather than just swinging soft.

WHICH iron is a different question from how to hit one, and it moved to its own plan on Aug 14: APPROACH PLAY — CLUB UP. Short version — club for the MIDDLE of the green, and lean to the longer club, because 7 of your 12 recorded green misses finished short.
sections.k: Ball back toward the trail thigh; the KING TECs fly higher than the old set, so trust the height.

sections.t: Wedges
sections.b: (Open — fill in as you dial the Vokeys: your go-to feels for full vs. partial, and any open-face/flop keys. Ladder to stay honest: 60°→80 · 56°→95 · 50°→108 · PW→122.)
sections.k: Open — fill in your Vokey feels as you dial them. Ladder: 60°→80 · 56°→95 · 50°→108 · PW→122.

sections.t: Putting — it lives in the Putting lab
sections.b:
This section used to carry a putting key, and it went stale the moment the putter changed — it still said 'hands EVEN with the ball, press stays tiny', which was the DF3i's Press Pistol 2° geometry. The DF3i went back on Aug 10, and on the LINK's zero-lean grip that same cue is lean YOU are adding to a face with 2° to give.

That is the argument for not keeping it here at all. Two plans describing one stroke is exactly how a retired cue survives a putter change, and this one did for three days.

So: putting lives in the PUTTING LAB. The Routine plan is the whole stroke, the Setup plan is the low point and the weight, and the Distance Grind is the pace work. Nothing about putting gets written here again.
